His apprentices share the same spirit as they create their dishes together.

name: HOMMAGE
review: Noboru Arai was born and raised in Asakusa and went to France to study gastronomy. He incorporates elements from various countries and not just France and Japan to make his cuisine more memorable. He also continually adds touches of novelty and refinement that express the joy of food; his dishes really do surprise with their creativity and looks. He and his kimono-clad wife convey everything that is wonderful about Japan.

name: Nabeno-Ism
review: Chef Yuichiro Watanabe styles his approach ‘Watanabe-ism’ – a fusion of local food culture with French cuisine. For example, the kaminari-okoshi sweet rice puff snack produced in Komagata Asakusa and sobagaki are made French style. The meal flows like a story, from Edo-era elegance to authentic French traditions. The scenery, which includes pleasure boats on the Sumida River and the Tokyo SkyTree, is reminiscent of the Seine River and the Eiffel Tower.

name: Kutan
review: Kotaro Nakashima develops new ideas based on study of the past and on time spent overseas. Here you’ll find a fusion of traditional and modern elements, including a hinoki counter and Western paintings on white walls. Care is taken with the fragrance and temperature of the food. White asparagus wrapped in pork, and bigfin reef squid is dressed with egg yolk and soy sauce and garnished with caviar. Nakashima strives to create Japanese cuisine that’s ahead of the times.

name: Kaiseki Komuro
review: The extravagant cuisine of Mitsuhiro Komuro makes the heart sing with joy. In spring, Tsukahara bamboo shoots are a long-awaited treat. Pepper flowers spice up beef nabe. Takikomi-gohan of icefish and young pepper leaves is another pleasure. With the end of the rainy season, summer brings Akashi hamo pike conger eel, with the sound of the small bones being cut creating a cooling sensation. The extensive hamo menu includes seared hamo tsukuri, peony-shaped hamo in soup and hamo sushi.

name: ESqUISSE
review: The ingredients and dishes on the menu have themes such as time spent with family on Corsica or experiences travelling in Japan. In other words, they are woven from Lionel Beccat’s memories. He makes skilful use of herbs and spices to breathe new life into seasonal ingredients. Bringing together Japan and France, the dishes are somehow poetic and the intuition and refined sensibilities of Beccat shine through in the set menus.

name: Seisoka
review: The name of the restaurant means ‘space surrounded by green plants’, and indeed Seisoka exudes a serene atmosphere, surrounded by the trees and shrubs of the Tengenji temple precincts. The name was inspired by a calligraphed tablet by Rosanjin Kitaoji (1883–1959) that adorns the wall. The cuisine is redolent with the spirit of chakaiseki (tea ceremony cuisine), while always evolving; for example, in summer tomato surinagashi appears in cocktails.

name: Kioicho Fukudaya
review: This ryotei is associated with Kitaoji Rosanjin. Seal engravings, calligraphy and pots decorate it, hinting at the deep friendship between the founder and Rosanjin; many of the serving dishes were also made by Rosanjin. Chef Shunichi Matsushita prepares the choice ingredients and plates the food as if clothing the dishes. It’s an embodiment of Rosanjin’s statement that “Cooking is not something to taste with just your tongue, but to enjoy the harmony between beauty and flavour”.

name: Den
review: With soy sauce, mirin and katsuo-bushi (dried bonito flakes) in hand, Zaiyu Hasegawa is spreading Japanese cuisine to the world. Generally eschewing the use of kombu, he is skilled in generating flavours through combinations of ingredients and the umami of the meat. The “Dentucky” chicken wings stuffed with steamed mochi rice are like a snack between mains. The Den team and customers come together as one to create a fun atmosphere.

name: Usukifugu Yamadaya
review: The restaurant serves Bungosuido tora fugu because it is a branch of a restaurant in Usuki, Oita Prefecture, a place celebrated as ‘the home of fugu’. Fugu sashimi is served with ponzu made with soy sauce and kabosu, both from Oita. From winter through spring, grilled shirako is served as sushi. ‘Ohan’, rice coloured yellow with essence of gardenia fruit, is used in place of vinegared rice, as this regional cuisine was a favourite of the lords of the Usuki feudal domain.

name: Ryuzu
review: Influenced by the refined taste of Japanese cuisine, Ryuta Iizuka respects the flavour of the ingredients above all else. He applies the techniques he cultivated in French cuisine to prepare dishes that overflow with creativity. The ‘Uonuma Yairo Shiitake Tart’ is a speciality that embodies both his love for his hometown and his credo. Incorporating numerous seasonal ingredients, the menu is also an expression of gratitude toward producers.

name: Ginza Shinohara
review: Takemasa Shinohara’s hassun recollects the Shiga countryside where he played as a child. The nabe dishes he serves are those his father would make for the family. There’s a warmheartedness to the cuisine, sensed in every dish. The Koka rice cooked in an earthenware pot is also an expression of love for his roots. Incorporating traditional events and the five annual Imperial Court ceremonies into the menu, he conveys the culture and customs of Japan.

name: Kobikicho Tomoki
review: While respecting Edomae traditions, Tomoki Kobayashi adds his own touches. Between elaborate snacks, he serves three of the recommended nigiri of the day. The idea of serving sushi when the customer is hungry displays an understanding of kaiseki cuisine, where sushi is served to tide customers over between courses. The red uni with vegetables pickled in sake lees is a speciality. We recommend the ‘Tomoki-style’ omakase which is tailored to the customer’s preferences.

name: ASAHINA Gastronome
review: Satoru Asahina focuses on creating light dishes, prizing the classic approach. He puts a modern touch on the chaudfroid, featuring grilled seafood and meat, served cold. He serves consommé with the main dish based on the Japanese sensibility of serving a hot soup at the end. The dishes are both creative and visually pleasing, with a logical combination of main ingredients, sauce and garnishes.

name: LA TABLE de Joël Robuchon
review: The restaurant’s name simply means “Joël Robuchon’s dining table”. The informal service melts into the elegant lavender-schemed dining room. True to Robuchon’s conviction that “cooking is an art form that begins with love”, the spirit of gourmet food is everywhere on display. The menu consists of simple, modern dishes and a series of specialities. A place to let time slip through your fingers.

name: Ginza Kojyu
review: Toru Okuda fills serving dishes made by modern artists with ingredients that sprout to life season by season. Polished culinary techniques and ingredients from all over Japan resonate together; the chargrilled dishes are highlights. Young ayu in early summer are grilled slowly to seal in the flavour. The menu bursts with the vitality of the ingredients and dishes appeal with their dynamism and delicacy. This is Japanese cuisine prepared with passion.

name: Tempura Kondo
review: Fumio Kondo sets a modern example for Edomae tempura. He was one of the first to put the focus on vegetables, elevating their status from that of a side dish. Two examples are the shredded carrots fried in a pot and arranged like fireworks, and the cylindrical sweet potatoes made to resemble those baked on hot pebbles. He has had great success going where none has gone before.

name: BEIGE Alain Ducasse
review: The elegance of Chanel and Ducasse come together in the beige dining room. In charge of the kitchen is Kei Kojima, who visits the fields in Kamakura to get a feel for the seasons. He also incorporates a Japanese approach while following the path of ‘Ducasseism’, such as making use of the fragrance of charcoal.

name: Harutaka
review: Harutaka Takahashi honed his skills at Sukiyabashi Jiro where he learned to make authentic sushi. The quality of the toppings is excellent, and it’s more than evident why he enjoys the trust of connoisseurs and those in the business. The rice is cooked firm in a broad-brimmed pot several times to give it just the right chewiness. Enjoy sushi of varying levels of sweetness and sourness and different temperatures, in keeping with the traditions.

name: Sushi Kanesaka
review: Owner-chef Shinji Kanesaka is devoted to sushi. He charms his customers as he trains his small army of apprentices. Through the sushi he shapes, Kanesaka conveys his thoughts and understanding of the sea, the fish market, and the work of the artisan. The key to great sushi, he says, is the three-way interplay between topping, vinegared rice, and wasabi. Fixing a keen eye on the condition of the seafood, Kanesaka deftly executes his techniques, harmonising the vinegared rice with each topping.

name: Akasaka Kikunoi
review: Experience the tradition and innovation of Kyoto’s venerable Kikunoi ryotei, but in Tokyo. A watered cobblestone path along with sukiya-style furnishings make for a Kyoto-esque atmosphere. The restaurant serves beautiful, refined Kyoto-style kaiseki. Yoshihiro Murata values the beloved old ceremonial events that make up the Japanese year, as well as the changes brought by the seasons, and incorporates them into the menu.

name: Ginza Fukuju
review: Katsuhiro Onodera is very well versed in traditional Japanese culture, including the Shijo school of knife ceremony and the Omotesenke Fuhaku school of tea ceremony. He may have his feet in tradition, but he’s unfettered by form. The menu is one you’ll remember, harbouring a sense of classic Japanese cuisine while cleverly incorporating Western flavours like truffle and caviar. The Mineoka tofu speciality made from kudzu and milk is based on Edo period literature.

name: Florilège
review: Hiroyasu Kawate uses ingredients from producers he has a relationship with. Investing these ingredients with his sensibilities, he produces one-of-a-kind dishes. He brings out each dish to the table himself and explains it enthusiastically. Talking about past experiences involving the dishes is part of the recipe, and he weaves a story into the dishes as they’re created in the theatre-like open kitchen. The speciality is beef from cows that have calved.

name: Sukiyabashi Jiro Roppongiten
review: A typical meal might begin with the subtle flavour of white fish, followed by red fish, then chu-toro. After gizzard shad for the sourness come richer flavours such as horse mackerel or shrimp, then mackerel marinated in vinegar to cleanse the palate; uni and anago follow. The changes in flavour are carefully calibrated for the aftertaste that lingers in between. Underneath chef Takashi Ono’s strict demeanour toward his apprentices lies a gentle affection.

name: Glam Enrico Bartolini
review: The discreet, partially hidden entrance to Palazzo Venart opens into what is a rarity in Venice – a small but charming garden with beautiful furniture. A second garden overlooks the Grand Canal and offers tables where guests can enjoy a coffee or liqueur after their meal. Nestled between these two gardens, a magnificent hotel is home to the restaurant itself, where Michelin-starred chef Enrico Bartolini and the highly talented Donato Ascani, who is at the helm in the kitchen here, offer guests a fine dining experience. The tasting menus feature memorable dishes of extraordinary quality, such as the amazing selection of finger food presented at the beginning of the meal, inspired by traditional Venetian “cicchetti” (a type of tapas) and made from the best seasonal ingredients. Every course is prepared with care and passion and full of intense and harmonious flavours, resulting in cuisine which has made this restaurant a must not only for Venetians but also for visitors from far and wide.

name: San Domenico
review: When we use the word “classic” to describe this recently renovated restaurant, we are referring to its timeless charm from the almost English-style ambience of its dining rooms to the outdoor tables overlooking an attractive square with public gardens. This setting provides the perfect backdrop for a selection of local and Italian dishes, all prepared simply and without excessive frills and with a focus on flavour and guest satisfaction that avoids modern trends. The extensive wine list offers an array of excellent labels. San Domenico is quite simply a landmark in the history of Italian cuisine!

name: Seta by Antonio Guida
review: A complete dining experience offering sophisticated elegance, glamour and beautifully presented cuisine prepared by chef Antonio Guida, who hails originally from Salento but now considers himself Milanese by adoption! Classic and modern, light and yet luxurious, Guida’s cuisine includes meat and fish dishes, combining the flavours of northern Italy with the scents of the south, and exotic influences with traditional Italian ingredients, plus a strong Nordic touch in his use of sauces in many dishes. The wine pairing options are extensive, thanks to a cellar that is home to more than 1 000 labels, and there’s also a good choice of cocktails. In summer, a small number of tables in the inner courtyard provide the perfect setting for the lucky few.

name: Il Piccolo Principe
review: As in a well-orchestrated symphony, chef Giuseppe Mancino, originally from Salerno but with a real admiration for French cuisine, brings together a host of different elements in his dishes, including creativity, elegance, excellent techniques and superb presentation. As well as its à la carte, the restaurant offers tasting menus with a focus on meat, fish and (as a result of recent interest in vegetarian cuisine) vegetables. The impressive wine list boasts a selection of over 800 labels mainly from Tuscany, although wines from other regions and outside Italy also feature, alongside a good choice of champagnes. Last but not least, the restaurant is situated in one of the smartest hotels in town, Il Grand Hotel Principe di Piemonte, which celebrated its centenary in 2022.

name: Il Pagliaccio
review: The fusion cuisine served at this restaurant tells the story of the chef’s life, blending influences from his experiences and travels around the world to create cuisine that combines Mediterranean flavours with hints of the Orient, something that is quite rare in Italy. Special mention should also be made of the attentive and courteous service overseen by Matteo Zappile, as well as the interesting wine list which boasts a good selection of champagnes.

name: Quattro Passi
review: The story of Quattro Passi is linked to that of Antonio Mellino, one of the most charismatic and exuberant figures in Italian hospitality who, over the years, has established this extraordinarily elegant restaurant following years of dedication and sacrifice and time spent working in France. The beauty of the setting will take your breath away, as will the views of Nerano bay from the terrace and the delicious cuisine showcasing the flavours and colours of Campania. Highly committed to his work front of house, much to the joy and delight of his guests, Antonio has handed over the reins in the kitchen to his son Fabrizio, who has succeeded in the difficult task of continuing to improve what already seemed perfect. The quintessentially Mediterranean cuisine showcases the purity of the extraordinary ingredients used, all of which are skilfully combined in dishes that appear simple but are in fact the result of highly sophisticated techniques, featuring superb natural flavours and harmonious combinations. The wine list is also excellent, with fine recommendations offered by the talented sommelier.

name: Locanda Sant'Uffizio Enrico Bartolini
review: Nestled amid the picturesque hills of the Monferrato region, this restaurant overseen by multi-Michelin-starred Enrico Bartolini sees Gabriele Boffa at the helm in the kitchen, a chef who is young in years but already a real connoisseur of Piedmontese cuisine. With experience in some of the world’s best restaurants behind him, Boffa has accumulated expert knowledge and remarkable technical skills. His cuisine ranges from classic regional dishes interpreted in their purest form – such as his extraordinary agnolotti del plin – to more creative options, which demonstrate a connection with the region, whether in their ingredients or recipes. The setting here is that of an old monastery converted into a smart hotel, with meals served either in an elegant dining room or in the old limonaia (where lemon trees were once stored). The dishes on offer will linger long in the memory, from the generous amuses-bouches to the delicious bread and incredible focaccia, the top-quality meat and much more besides!

name: Enoteca La Torre
review: Situated just outside the Aurelian Walls, the aristocratic Hotel Villa Laetitia boasts an elegant Art Nouveau ambience thanks to its antique furniture, flowers, columns and stucco that would not look out of place in Paris. Here, talented young chef Domenico Stile celebrates his native region of Campania with passion, exuberance and creativity, skilfully using typical Mediterranean ingredients from this abundant region on a menu which also features a few typical Roman specialities. The service is on a par with the excellent cuisine, with many dishes (such as the enormous “babà”) finished directly in front of guests in the dining room. A superb all-round dining experience for food-lovers, complemented by a well-stocked wine cellar offering an excellent selection of pairing options to enhance their meal.

name: Piccolo Lago
review: Marco Sacco is the owner-chef of this charming restaurant with a timeless feel. Leaving busy Lake Maggiore behind, you come to tranquil Lake Mergozzo where this restaurant offers picture-postcard views of the water from its terrace. The chef’s technical and creative cuisine is showcased on two 7-course tasting menus, one featuring new dishes created by the chef, the other his classic favourites. There’s also a chef’s table, where you are served a limitless number of courses in the kitchen: the only certainty here is the time you start!

name: Gourmetstube Einhorn
review: Occupying a 13C post house, this charming, elegant hotel is now home to a gourmet restaurant with just five tables set out in a romantic Stube decorated with inlaid wood of medieval origin. Guests can either choose the full tasting menu offered by Peter Girtler, the chef at the “Unicorn” (Einhorn in German), or a selection of 4-6 courses. The creative cuisine here is among the most interesting in the region, featuring evocative and often highly original dishes with light and balanced recipes that showcase the best local ingredients to the full. Meat and fish feature on the menu, alongside often forgotten vegetables such as sorrel, black salsify and watercress.

name: La Madia
review: As well as shining a spotlight on Sicily’s top-quality ingredients, Pino Cuttaia does his best to create dishes that are easily accessible to all. His cuisine aims to awaken our culinary memories, focusing on homely flavours and traditional recipes. “Memory is the secret ingredient in dishes, which all tell a story”, says Cuttaia, and he is also found in the dining room explaining this to his guests. The emotional nostalgia of his cuisine is striking, as his carefully researched and innovative approach. His extraordinary work focuses on his ingredients, which he transforms by highlighting their essential character. The results are often highly original, as in the “Scala dei Turchi” menu which showcases Sicilian meat and fish dishes enabling guests to deepen their knowledge of the island.

name: Miramonti l'Altro
review: A French-Italian couple is at the helm in this attractive classic-style villa on the outskirts of Brescia, where a few tables have been laid out in the bay windows overlooking the garden. The friendly, experienced wife oversees the front of house, while her Breton husband is in the kitchen, where he recreates memories of his childhood in France through his use of French ingredients and culinary techniques. The menu also features more obviously Italian and Mediterranean dishes, all of which showcase the delicious, generous flavours that are the hallmark of the cuisine here. There is also an unforgettable cheese trolley with an excellent selection of cheeses in which Italy has the upper hand!

name: Arnolfo
review: Moved to Viale della Rimembranza 24, Colle di Val d’Elsa Situated in Italy’s capital of crystal, this restaurant takes its name from the 14C architect Arnolfo di Cambio, whose birthplace is just a few hundred metres from here. Arnolfo is first and foremost a family business, which gives it a friendly, welcoming ambience. Guests are served delicious seasonal specialities that are typical of the region, on a menu that showcases a wide variety of ingredients with a range of flavours (sweet, bitter, sharp and crunchy). Chef Gaetano Trovato travels all over the region in search of the best producers to ensure that his ingredients are of the highest quality. From these carefully selected ingredients, he creates cuisine that is respectful of Tuscan traditions while also adding his own touch of creativity and personality. Although some dishes are influenced by Sicilian culinary traditions, the chef’s favourite dish is pigeon, for which he will always find space on the menu!

name: D'O
review: The focus at this restaurant is on local ingredients and simple preparation, showcased on four tasting menus (Esattezza, Armonia, Molteplicità, andLeggerezza , the restaurant’s “green” menu) which reflect the past and present of chef Davide Oldani’s professional culinary career. Situated on the outskirts of Milan, in a simple, modern dining room which seems to jut out into the piazza thanks to its large windows, the restaurant serves as a backdrop for “pop” cuisine which is accessible and always manages to retain a sustainable focus – ingredients are used to the full and there’s no food waste. An extensive wine list completes the picture.

name: L'Olivo
review:
A huge, elegant dining room where candlelight and lamps highlight every decorative detail and where guests dine in comfort on light cashmere sofas and armchairs in a relaxing and stylish atmosphere. In the kitchen, chef Andrea Migliaccio from Ischia is a standard-bearer for creative, elegant and sophisticated Mediterranean cuisine.
The principles that guide this chef’s work are simple: innovation and tradition, new dishes and reinterpreted regional classics, plus a careful selection of the best ingredients that the Mediterranean has to offer. L’Olivo’s outdoor terrace has been completely renovated so that it forms a harmonious extension of the dining room, creating the impression of a vast space extending into the horizon. p>
The wine list focuses on the region while also including renowned labels from elsewhere in Italy and further afield.

name: La Peca
review: A restaurant with a warm, contemporary-style design, enhanced by carefully chosen decor such as charming centrepieces on the tables (the work of the female owner), modern paintings on the walls and comfortable chairs designed by Philippe Starck. This restaurant’s many attractions include an elegant, dedicated smoking room on the ground floor, where guests can enjoy top-quality spirits accompanied by a selection of the best cigars from around the world. Nicola Portinari creates highly personalised cuisine, with influences from the Veneto and further afield, especially in the cooking methods that he uses. The dessert menu deserves a special mention, thanks to its extensive choice (unusual in a restaurant of this standard), which is complemented by an array of home-made ice creams and sorbets. A superb all-round dining experience, which is further enhanced by the restaurant’s excellent wine list.

name: Acquolina
review: Located on the ground floor of the centrally located luxury The First Roma hotel, with its elegant atmosphere and decor of original artwork, paintings and sculptures, Acquolina serves fish-based dishes with a Mediterranean flavour and an added twist of creativity. The perfectly balanced recipes include delicious options such as “mullet, duck heart, juniper and cherry” and “mushroom, snail and parsley”. The service is of the same high standard as the food, with staff offering efficient and discreet assistance throughout the meal. An excellent wine selection completes the picture.

name: Antica Osteria Cera
review: One of Italy’s most famous addresses for fish and seafood, this restaurant offers an extensive menu featuring classic house favourites alongside a growing list of more modern options. In this elegant, modern and minimalist-style setting (despite the name, don’t expect a trattoria-style ambience here!) enjoy raw fish dishes and grilled options alongside more traditional, often Venetian, specialities such as the Venetian-style spider crab, and classic Italian dishes such as the warm steamed fish salad and the fritto misto (mixed fried fish). In all dishes, the excellent quality of the ingredients shines through. There’s also an excellent wine list, with a particular focus on white wines.

name: Antica Corona Reale
review: Situated between the Langhe and Monviso, this long-established restaurant celebrated its 200th anniversary a few years ago. Run by the Vivalda family for five generations, the restaurant was first established as a dairy farm before gaining a well-earned reputation for its cuisine. Owner-chef Gian Piero creates top-quality menus featuring expertly prepared, colourful and aromatic dishes. Popular with food-lovers from Italy and abroad, Cervere is also a point of reference for many local businesses who supply the restaurant with capon, guinea fowl, veal, Carmagnola peppers, porcini mushrooms and much more besides. In summer, dine alfresco in the shade of a beautiful pergola among colourful flowers and a small fountain. Two small private rooms are available for intimate dinners, one of which is in the wine cellar surrounded by legendary bottles of wine.

name: Santa Elisabetta
review: Thought to date back to Byzantine times, the Torre della Pagliazza has had many uses over the centuries, including housing a women’s prison in the 12C. Today it is home to one of the most interesting gourmet restaurants in Florence, where chef Rocco De Santis creates imaginative Mediterranean cuisine which is precise and full of flavour, with influences from his native Campania and an emphasis on fish and seafood. At lunchtime, a tasting menu of just three courses (“Carte Blanche”) is also available. As there are just a few tables here, guests are advised to book well in advance.

name: Taverna Estia
review: Relaxing niches separated by “walls” of jasmine and a delightful herb garden at the entrance greet guests when they arrive at this restaurant, where the dining room has a welcoming and personalised feel with a mix of modern and rustic decorative features. Taverna Estia always meets expectations with its typical regional cuisine, which is refined, elegant and complex thanks to the skill and creativity of the chef here. There are three tasting menus: one focused on meat dishes, a second on fish and seafood, and a third (the most creative and exciting) where the chef gives free rein to his imagination in creations such as the delicious rice and seaweed chips. The wine list is as impressive as the cuisine, featuring well-known labels from Campania and elsewhere in Italy alongside bottles from small wineries discovered over the years. There’s also an extensive selection of European mineral waters, plus typical Neapolitan Moka-pot coffee for those who like their coffee strong.

name: Magnolia
review: The memorable dishes served at this restaurant have earned it two Michelin stars, thanks to its consistent focus on careful preparation, its imaginative dishes, original combinations and beautiful, colourful presentation. The service is precise and professional, while the extensive and well-structured wine list demonstrates an enthusiasm for French wines, which is much appreciated by wine buffs. Careful attention is also paid to the bread served here, which is made in its own dedicated space. In new premises since spring 2022, the restaurant is now even more elegant than before!

name: Terra
review: Terra is reached via a road that runs uphill through the woods, a magical landscape that is reflected in its cuisine – a real love letter to the mountains! In this elegant and unusual restaurant, which combines modern features with a profusion of wood and wines exhibited in a glass-walled room suspended over the dining room, the cuisine is served on a long tasting menu made up of small, delicious courses that are perfectly prepared and show remarkably impressive techniques, one delightful surprise following another. Almost all the ingredients come from the region (many from the Sarentino valley itself), and there’s a particular focus on aromatic herbs – the chef is a real expert. As the restaurant is in a somewhat isolated location, you make like to take advantage of the beautiful guestrooms to round off your experience and avoid driving after dinner.

name: Krèsios
review: Krèsios – one of the names given to Bacchus or Dionysus – is run by chef Giuseppe Iannotti. This welcoming country house boasts an attractive mix of traditional and modern decor, with its stone walls, rustic atmosphere and wine cellar carved out of the tufa rock. In the latter, a selection of 2 000 labels is overseen by talented sommelier Alfredo who is always on hand to recommend the best wine to accompany your meal. The open-view kitchen offers views of the chef and his excellent team at work, busy preparing creative, personalised dishes which are often stylish and always out of the ordinary, all presented on just one tasting menu (its name “Mr Brown” is a reference to Quentin Tarantino’s film “Reservoir Dogs”). Iannotti’s cuisine is based on his philosophy of research and imagination, with touches of improvisation and ingredients of the highest quality from around the world. Three welcoming guestrooms are also available.

name: Castel finedining
review: Situated within the exclusive Castel hotel, this restaurant occupies a curve-shaped dining room with just a few tables arranged in front of floor-to-ceiling windows offering stunning views of Merano, the valley and the Alpine peaks in the distance. Gerhard Wieser’s precise, technical and carefully prepared cuisine is equal to the fine setting, featuring a selection of classic dishes with an international influence alongside specialities from the Alto Adige. An excellent selection of wine and highly professional service complete the picture, making this an all-round dining experience to remember.

name: Agli Amici
review: Serving signature cuisine, Agli Amici is one of the leading restaurants in Friuli-Venezia Giulia, a border region of diverse cultural influences that is bursting with top-quality ingredients. Many of these ingredients are showcased on the three tasting menus (one vegetarian) served here, from which guests can also choose individual dishes à la carte. Chef Emanuele Scarello makes full use of the region’s abundant produce, an inexhaustible array of ingredients from pastureland, mountains and vegetable gardens, which he transforms into culinary works of art. His vegetables are grown by local gardeners, while his fresh fish is nearly always sourced from Grado market. Front of house, Michela is responsible for a young and harmonious professional team of staff. Following recent refurbishment, the restaurant is now even more attractive than before.

name: Harry's Piccolo
review: With a hushed ambience made even more glamorous by recent refurbishment, Harry’s Piccolo is an ideal choice for a romantic dinner or a business meal, thanks to the fine cuisine prepared by chefs Matteo Metullio and Davide De Pra. Despite their youth, these two chefs demonstrate plenty of ability and creativity, serving dishes that showcase local meat, fish and seafood, and seasonal vegetables, as well as hints of the Orient, in this elegant setting. Matteo describes their cuisine as “vero-km” (a pun on “zero-km”), by which he means that it focuses on quality irrespective of geographical origin. Friendly service, plus an outdoor space for an aperitif or after-dinner drink with views of one of Italy’s most beautiful squares.

name: Torre del Saracino
review: The name of this restaurant refers to its location in a 13C fortified tower, one of many dotted along this coastline. Here, guests can savour a pre-dinner drink or a coffee, before moving into the more classic, elegant dining rooms. Looking across at Vesuvius, the word volcano comes to mind when describing chef Gennaro Esposito – he positively explodes with ideas, creating dishes and anticipating culinary trends as only a few chefs can, trends which are then picked up and copied by other restaurants. His Mediterranean cuisine makes much use of ingredients from Campania, some with combinations that sound strange on the menu but in the hands of Esposito reveal themselves to be full of harmonious contrasts. He uses the simplest fish and seafood (such as horse mackerel, grouper and albacore tuna) in his carefully prepared recipes which feature on tasting menus that showcase his culinary philosophy to the full. His raw fish dishes provide a feast for the eyes and the palate – the fish is sourced directly from local fishermen who bring the best of their catch here. The wine list includes renowned labels and fine vintages; a visit to the historic wine cellar in the tower basement is highly recommended.

name: Madonnina del Pescatore
review: It’s almost forty years since the Madonnina opened in 1984, yet chef Moreno Cedroni has not lost the creative touch that has resulted in him becoming one of the most influential chefs of his generation. Year after year, eating at La Madonnina remains a novelty: the menu succeeds like no other in reflecting past traditions and future culinary trends, especially in its fish and seafood dishes. The chef’s wife Mariella oversees the excellent service front of house, while this wonderful couple’s commitment to their cuisine is also demonstrated by their vegetable garden situated almost right on the beach, which provides vegetables infused with the salty sea air – a brilliant idea that represents their strong connection to the land. The wine list features a popular selection of French sparkling wines.

name: Casa Perbellini
review: Almost hidden in a charming small house overlooking Piazza San Zeno, also home to the famous basilica of the same name, Casa Perbellini boasts an elegant yet relaxing ambience, where guests can watch the chefs at work in the open-view kitchen. There are three tasting menus available, including a vegetarian option, with some flexibility for guests who prefer à la carte dining. Whether you choose fish, meat or vegetables, all the dishes are cooked to perfection, balanced in flavour and beautifully presented. Special mention must be made of the excellent service charmingly overseen by Barbara, as well as of the superb wine list which includes an extensive selection of French wines, of which both the sommelier and owner-chef Giancarlo are huge fans.

name: St. George by Heinz Beck
review: This restaurant boasts an elegant dining room with a vaguely British feel, as well as a terrace for summer dining overlooking a lush garden with an infinity pool and views of the Strait of Messina and the Sicilian and Calabrian coasts in the distance. Since the summer of 2022, Salvatore Iuliano has been at the helm in the kitchen here, creating dishes which are modern and creative in style. This young yet serious chef is both talented and professional, having previously demonstrated his ability to manage a team with excellent results during his time as sous-chef here.

name: Villa Feltrinelli
review: Villa Feltrinelli, a magnificent Art Nouveau villa full of individual charm and beautifully maintained over the years, provides the perfect setting for chef Stefano Baiocco’s creative cuisine. A romantic aperitif on the lakeside is highly recommended, after which guests can enjoy the “blind” tasting menu which has been served here since 2021. This technically expert and imaginative chef, equally at ease with meat and fish, demonstrates his true culinary ability in his use of vegetarian ingredients. His skill in the use of herbs and edible flowers is unequalled, as demonstrated in his highly original salad with over a hundred different herbs and more than 20 flowers, all of which come from the property’s own bucolic kitchen garden. In short, this restaurant has it all – delicious cuisine, striking architecture, breathtaking beauty and a nostalgic, timeless and relaxing ambience.

name: Bracali
review: The small, fairly ordinary village of Ghirlanda in the heart of the Colline Metallifere is home to an unexpectedly elegant restaurant, where chef Francesco creates highly original and personalised cuisine. His focus is mainly on meat dishes, which are full of contrasting yet harmoniously balanced flavours (vegetable-meat, fatty-acidic, sweet-sour, soft-crunchy etc). Francesco’s brother Luca takes care of the wine and front of house with skill and dedication; the wine list is extensive and well structured, subdivided into two separate sections (Italy and the rest of the world). Bracali has established a partnership with the local diocese, including helping with the social integration of refugees and managing food waste. In the dining room, works of art are exhibited on a rotation basis and listed in a catalogue.

name: daní maison
review: “Home, family, tradition” is the motto of Danì Maison, a restaurant opened in 2016 by chef Nino Di Costanzo in his old family house surrounded by the fertile vegetable gardens of Ischia. A small, romantic dining room surrounded by beautiful herb-scented Mediterranean maquis acts as the backdrop for the delicious cuisine which has made this chef famous, thanks to his creativity and technical expertise. For many years, Nino has experimented with combinations that showcase every single ingredient in a dish, which are intended to be instantly recognisable however complex the recipe. Although there are no sea views here, it is fish (from around the island and neighbouring Procida) that takes pride of place on the menu in dishes that are memorable for their stunning presentation. If available, book the chef’s table where you’ll have the best view of the chef at work, although you can also catch glimpses of the activity in the kitchen from elsewhere in the dining room. Last but not least, the recently opened Salumeria bistro at the garden entrance serves traditional dishes from Campania in a small dining room, as well as outdoors on its shady terrace.

name: Caino
review: Inextricably connected to the land around it, this restaurant has the distinction of having introduced the world to the cuisine of the Maremma, reinterpreted in elegant, contemporary and often creative fashion by skilful chef Valeria Piccini, now ably assisted by her son Andrea. The philosophy of this great cook is based on a belief that guests should know exactly what they are eating, which means that she avoids techniques that are excessive or too elaborate and always prepares her food using the best possible ingredients. Situated in a small, picturesque village in the hills, Caino stands not far from the romantic Piazza del Castello, which is well worth a visit.

name: Duomo
review: The mysterious and allusive menu at the Duomo is interwoven with references to the Sicilian world and makes fascinating reading. It explains the dishes but does so in a highly evocative and subtle manner. The chef takes inspiration from the Baroque style of San Giorgio church, which stands at the end of flight of steps just a few metres away from the restaurant. This Baroque is echoed in the chef’s extraordinarily imaginative dishes which seem to compete with the exuberant decor of the surrounding aristocratic palazzi. Housed in Palazzo La Rocca, the restaurant is discreetly elegant in style, as is the impeccable service. But it is the spectacular cuisine that takes centre stage here, along with an excellent wine list.

name: Tre Olivi
review: Housed in the Savoy Beach Hotel, yet with its own entrance, Tre Olivi burst on to the culinary scene after being awarded two Michelin stars when previously it held none, so impressed were our inspectors by the skilful chef here. Today Giovanni Solofra works hard to consolidate his success, continuing to improve and always with a focus on the Cilento region. Originally from Torre Annunziata, not too far from here, this chef has fallen in love with the Cilento and its extraordinary ingredients, such as buffalo milk, Menaica anchovies and heritage flour varieties. Particular mention should be made of the various types of bread, including an outstanding brioche. Meals are served in an elegant, contemporary-style dining room adorned with decorations that pay tribute to olives.

name: Il Luogo di Aimo e Nadia
review: This long-established restaurant, which opened nearly 60 years ago, now offers two generous tasting menus, one with a seasonal focus, the other showcasing top-quality ingredients from all over Italy. The atmosphere here is decidedly contemporary and yet also simple, providing the perfect backdrop for dishes prepared with a professional approach which is accessible to all. The cuisine is inspired by Italian traditions which are reinterpreted in dishes that allow the quality of the ingredients to shine through.

name: Stand
review: A central glass-walled kitchen is the focal point of this eye-catching modern restaurant; a dining room sits either side, and there’s a chatty buzz to the room – helped along by the personable service team. The two experienced chef-owners are proud of their Hungarian roots and skilfully reinvent and modernise classic Hungarian dishes using a wide range of techniques. Wonderful flavours and textures abound, and build steadily throughout the meal. When it comes to wine, look to the Hungarian options – there are some great sweet Tokajis on the list.

name: Platán Gourmet
review: Your evening starts with an aperitif and snacks on the terrace beneath the castle, before you are shown through to a barrel-vaulted cellar where four tables sit in front of the open kitchen. Here, the team work with calm efficiency and meticulous precision to create highly sophisticated dishes which are packed with deep, well-balanced flavours and bags of personality; choose 4, 6 or 8 courses, with wines to match. For the full experience, stay the night in one of the nearby bedrooms and make the most of their spa.

name: Yu Zhi Lan
review: This low-key dining concept doesn’t need a sign. The owner-chef Lan Guijun is a local legend who took Sichuanese to the level of haute cuisine so gourmands will always find their way here. The rooms exude rustic charm, dotted by ceramic art and pottery made by the chef himself. Before you can taste his elegant, elaborate multi-course meal that brings out the ingredients’ natural flavours, you need to book a table with a deposit.

name: Maison Wenger
review: The drive through picture postcard landscapes is not only delightful, at the end you will be rewarded by the excellent menu of this elegant restaurant in a pretty country village. The owner-chef Jérémy Desbraux, who worked with Franck Giovannini at Crissier for a spell, has a knack for imparting incredible depth and flavour to classical dishes. Every dish is perfectly balanced, with neither too little nor too many enticing aromas. The ingredients are naturally first class, and some are sourced locally. The lunchtime menu is also very enticing. The service is unstuffy yet professional and the wines of the moment are particularly excellent. A handful of luxuriously appointed guestrooms for overnight stays.

name: Da Vittorio
review: If you happen to be in St Moritz in the winter season, then take advantage of the opportunity to dine at the stylish yet cosy restaurant of the Carlton Hotel, in its serene location overlooking the lake. During the winter months, a fantastic kitchen team serves up precise and light Italian cuisine that steers clear of fuss and frills. The focus lies squarely on the produce that goes into the dishes. Some of the brilliantly prepared specialties from the parent restaurant in Brusaporto, Lombardy, make an appearance, including, of course, the signature pasta dish, paccheri alla Vittorio, but also many fish dishes, such as crudo d'Amare, raw fish and shellfish. Plus, an excellent front-of-house team: confident, charming and classy!

name: 7132 Silver
review: The 7132 Hotel is a real heritage building and akin to a place of pilgrimage for design and architecture fans. Silver, with its stylishly elegant interior and, above all, Mitja Birlo's cuisine, will also turn your head. Excellent ingredients and sophisticated techniques go into each course of his set menu, which is stamped with his own distinctive style. The professional front-of-house staff have plenty of good wine recommendations. The chefs also bring the food to your table, sometimes finishing off the dishes there – they talk you through it all, also providing information on the high-quality ingredients. The team is bubbling over with enthusiasm and expertise – sophisticated but by no means stuffy. If you sit at the large window front, you get a view of the Hörnli and Tomül mountains. Or perhaps you would rather book the chef's table in the kitchen?

name: Einstein Gourmet
review: Without a doubt one of the top restaurants in Switzerland, thanks to Sebastian Zier's and Richard Schmidtkonz's dedicated kitchen team. Here, they put on a veritable culinary fireworks show, throughout which they succeed in skilfully putting their own stamp on the cuisine. With its full-bodied and expressive dishes, the set menu gives a creative spin to classic foundations. In addition, you can look forward to excellent service courtesy of a team that includes a sommelier who has a great repertoire of first-class wines at his fingertips, in a selection that shows a penchant for Bordeaux and Switzerland.

name: La Brezza
review: This is the elegant gourmet restaurant in the impressive Tschuggen Grand Hotel, perched at 1 800m above sea level. It serves modern cuisine that is sophisticated but never ostentatious; rather, made with top-notch ingredients, it is crisp, light and accessible. Of its two set menus - "Inspiration" and "Moving Mountains" - the latter is completely vegan. The service is always friendly and professional.

name: Widder Restaurant
review: In the chic fine dining restaurant of the luxurious boutique hotel of the same name, head chef Stefan Heilemann and his team skilfully bridge the gap between classic and modern cuisine, with a few international influences thrown in for good measure. The dishes come in the form of refined, flavoursome and technically very precise compositions with a clear liking for layering in different textures. A set menu of four to six courses is served; a vegetarian version is also available. In addition, you can choose classics by Stefan Heilemann from the "Supplements" menu. Stefano Petta's highly competent front-of-house team takes a pleasingly relaxed approach when it comes to serving guests. For a view of the kitchen while you dine, reserve the chef's table! And after the meal, perhaps you'd like to head to the Widder Bar one floor below for a drink?

name: IGNIV Zürich by Andreas Caminada
review: Andreas Caminada is the man behind this fabulous new venture in the Marktgasse Hotel, situated in the heart of the historical district on the right bank of the Limmat. You access the tastefully designed restaurant via the beautiful, classically styled bar (where they will be happy to serve you an aperitif). A set menu proposes courses for sharing; supplementary dishes can be ordered à la carte. Talented young chef Daniel Zeindlhofer sticks to the IGNIV philosophy and combines it with his own ideas. His cuisine is complex but accessible – this is food that puts a smile on your face! From the excellent wine list, opt for the wines from the Zurich region, available by the glass. First-class service is provided by the charming and accomplished front-of-house team led by Ines Triebenbacher. To round off the experience, the "Candy Store" is typical of the IGNIV experience!

name: The Restaurant
review: The Dolder Grand luxury hotel (a former "Kurhaus" or health resort, built in 1899) boasts a truly fantastic location above Zurich – even the driveway to the garage is impressive! If possible, book a window seat in the hotel's chic fine dining restaurant so you can savour the magnificent view of the city while you eat. The huge glass wine cabinet also draws the eye. Chef Heiko Nieder's elaborate and detail-oriented cooking is modern and creative but equally classical. This Schleswig-Holstein native always puts the (top-notch) produce centre stage and cooks up fantastically harmonious compositions. His vegetarian alternatives are no less impressive. Tip: the five-course "amuse-bouche menu", served at lunchtime, allows you to sample a good cross-section of the food.

name: roots
review: You might not expect to find such an outstanding fine dining restaurant in a congress and event venue such as the Rhypark. The location next to the Dreirosenbrücke, directly on the Rhine, is superb, the interior is chic and modern, and the terrace is wonderful. Then there is the creative cuisine of Pascal Steffen and his team. The five- to nine-course set menu may have a predominantly vegetarian slant (try, for example, the "roots garten" – a signature dish), but fish and meat are also on offer. The chefs take an appealingly pared-down approach, which does not at all detract from the depth and sophistication of their dishes showcasing excellent produce from the region. Restaurant manager Jonas Brucker oversees the highly accomplished yet delightfully relaxed and informal front-of-house team.

name: Anne-Sophie Pic
review: The famous French chef presides over the fate of this cutting-edge gourmet venue in the Beau-Rivage Palace Hotel, facing the tranquil waters of Lake Geneva. Ms Pic has entrusted the culinary score to the competent hands of the restaurant’s former sous-chef, youthful Kevin Vaubourg. A change of cast but the house signature dishes remain firm fixtures on the menu. Diners can be reassured that the demanding inventive streak that has ever linked the Pic name to high-flying Gallic gastronomy continues to thrive here. A culinary masterclass throbbing with flavour.

name: Ecco St. Moritz
review: Ascona in summer, St Moritz in winter? This is how top chef Rolf Fliegauf and his team do it, changing locations according to the seasons. In the warm season they cook at Ecco on Lake Maggiore and as the snow settles on the ground they migrate to the Engadine valley, to the fine dining restaurant of the Giardino Mountain hotel. You can sense the energy and expertise of this Swabian-born chef – this is cuisine you can rely on! He wins over diners with the light and playful touch he brings to his modern dishes. Throughout the four to seven courses of the set menu, the focus is on the top-notch ingredients. Your highly committed and charming host, Jenifer Fliegauf, is the driving force behind the extremely friendly front-of-house team, ensuring her guests receive attentive and unflappable service.

name: Magdalena
review: The adage here is "raw, rugged, regional". Head chef Dominik Hartmann (whose CV includes a stint with Andreas Caminada) and his kitchen team delight with an extremely expressive and technically excellent aromatic cuisine that is rich in contrasts. He homes in on regional produce, and small-scale producers are his go-to suppliers. The modern and seasonal surprise menu comprises five to seven courses, with five courses for Sunday lunch. Having a penchant for vegetables, the chef has switched to 100% vegetarian cooking here. Inside the refined, upscale restaurant (at its best at sunset!), you only have to glance out of the floor-to-ceiling windows at the village, mountains and lake to understand why this young trio chose to fulfil their dream of running their own restaurant in this spot!

name: IGNIV by Andreas Caminada
review: The name, a Romansh word meaning "nest", is spot on – it sums up just how comfortable you feel here in the culinary nucleus of the traditional "Badrutt's Palace", which you might say is the beating heart of the Engadine luxury hotel industry! The elegant restaurant giving onto the open kitchen, coupled with the romantic, old-fashioned little dining room make for a plush setting in which to savour Andreas Caminada's renowned fine dining sharing concept. "IGNIV" classics rub shoulders with other dishes, the wine cellar counts over 30 000 bottles, and the excellent service is accomplished, charming and skilful!

name: Pavillon
review: As you would expect in this luxurious grand hotel dating from 1844, everything at Restaurant Pavillon is also the height of style and premium quality. The restaurant is located in an almost 360° glazed building designed by architect Pierre-Yves Rochon, complete with a light-filled rotunda. With Laurent Eperon running the show, the food, rooted in French cuisine, is pleasantly refined and modern. The Vaudois-born chef has been with the restaurant since 1999 and you might say he is part of the furniture. Fabulous ingredients are properly celebrated; you won't find any ostentation or fuss, but rather intense flavours, from the bouillabaisse to the venison from Austria. There are wines from their own vineyard to go with your food. Very professional service from a classical front-of-house team that includes an excellent sommelier.

name: Gasthaus Zur Fernsicht - Incantare
review: Incantare is the Italian verb for "delight", which precisely describes the effect of the modern cuisine served at this chic restaurant. Tobias Funke and Martin Weber preside in the kitchen, creatively and harmoniously combining flavours, textures, fruit and acidity. They place great value on sourcing seasonal ingredients from the region and using environmentally friendly and resource-conserving producers. Some of the vegetables are grown especially for this establishment. The patisserie is rather special: they do their own thing, entirely dispensing with white sugar, for example. The exclusive wine pairings are also worth mentioning, with around 1 000 labels to choose from; the alcohol-free alternatives may also pique your interest. Extremely charming, competent and ever-attentive service. And then there's the great view!

name: IGNIV by Andreas Caminada
review: This stylish restaurant in a historical vaulted room inside the Grand Resort Bad Ragaz showcases a concept that was devised by none other than celebrated chef Andreas Caminada: an elaborate, creative "fine dining sharing experience". In keeping with the name (igniv is a Romansh word meaning "nest"), the focus is on the well-being of guests and the pleasure of communal dining. First-rate ingredients are used to create a very special set menu, each course of which is made up of several small dishes – all designed for sharing. Shored up by a competent sommelier, the charming service team is second to none. The outstanding wine list features top-notch wines, often regional, that are available by the glass. Last but not least, the impressive Candy Store awaits you.

name: RICO'S
review: Rico Zandonella's restaurant stands out from the crowd. Charming, cosy, colourful and packed with art – a tastefully eclectic mix of styles and highly individual decorative details. In addition, the service is pleasingly laid-back and professional. Then there is the food, which, with its colourful presentation, mirrors the offbeat flair of your surroundings. This is modern and creative fare, with classic and Mediterranean influences; needless to say, only the best ingredients make it onto your plate. To accompany these great dishes, choose from the nicely curated wine list with a particularly appealing selection of labels from Switzerland and France. A lunch menu is available Tue-Fri. A tip for those looking for a venue for private events: you can book Rico's Privé.

name: Domaine de Châteauvieux
review: The owner-chef, Philippe Chevrier, has treated this stylish, local institution, off the beaten tourist track, oozing in charm and idyllically surrounded by vineyards, to a youthful makeover. All the more reason to discover this culinary landmark in the vicinity of Geneva. Assisted by a seasoned, white-jacketed brigade, Philippe crafts quintessential French cuisine, ranging from modern to classical, based on outstanding seasonal produce and immediately identifiable flavours. Seamless, attentive service and a mouth-watering wine list. Book yourself into one of the exquisitely decorated guestrooms to recover from this culinary experience in style.

name: Taverne zum Schäfli
review: Even the gorgeous exterior of the 300-year-old Riegelhaus does not prepare you for the level of sophistication of the cuisine that awaits you here. Chef-patron Christian Kuchler is a master of the classics, as is borne out by his dishes, which are prepared from excellent ingredients that focus on taste rather than gimmickry – and that includes the excellent sauces! In addition, there is a wine list that leaves hardly anything to be desired: wonderful German Rieslings, great regional wines, red wines from France and Italy with an impressive range of vintages... It is delightful to sit in the tasteful and cosy dining rooms or out on the charming terrace. First-class service rounds off the experience perfectly. And should you wish to stay overnight, they have some lovely guestrooms.

name: Stucki - Tanja Grandits
review: The name "Stucki" is a tribute to Tanja Grandits's legendary predecessor, Hans Stucki. A chic ambience prevails in this historical villa; the stylish, relaxed and professional service comes courtesy of an experienced and ever-present front-of-house team that is headed up by Grégory Rohmer. As for the food, you will be able to experience Tanja Grandits's inimitable culinary style, characterised by her penchant for subtly incorporating flowers, leaves and colours. She conjures up fresh and elegant dishes that are bursting with skilfully combined flavours. Diners never feel overwhelmed – her creations never tip into overkill. Nine-course evening set menu (vegetarian possible); at lunchtime a shorter menu is also available. In summer, the garden terrace is a true oasis! Tip: the small shop sells tea, spices, condiments etc.

name: Ecco
review: Situated in the Giardino hotel, the first dining room at this restaurant boasts an open-view kitchen and a wall adorned with more than eleven thousand rose petals, so beautiful that they seem real. From here, you pass into a second dining area comprising a veranda overlooking a splendid garden with a small lake, which transforms into a single outdoor space in summer. Wherever you choose to eat, the setting is idyllic. Chef Rolf Fliegauf’s cuisine focuses on modern dishes with classic roots, including iconic and highly recommended recipes such as the delicious “braised shoulder of lamb (from Sisteron) with green asparagus, spring herbs and salted lemon”. The tasting menu offers a choice of four or seven courses, while the wine list features a number of refined labels to satisfy the most discerning of wine-lovers. Excellent service.

name: Skin's - the restaurant
review: The restaurant is on the first floor of a former factory in a somewhat unremarkable location not far from the train station. Modern dishes inspired by cuisines from around the globe, but also by produce from Switzerland, are cooked up in the open kitchen and served in the upscale interior. The patisserie is a real highlight! Charming, professional service. Sophisticated non-alcoholic drinks.

name: Sens
review: Not far from the beautiful Hotel Vitznauerhof, this modern restaurant is housed in what was once the boathouse. The location right by the water is fantastic and the terrace with its small "island" is simply magical. This all makes for a maritime atmosphere, complete with wonderful sunsets! The cuisine is also rather special: not only do they use exceptionally good ingredients, they also prepare them intelligently and bring their own ideas into play. Dutchman Jeroen Achtien, who cooked for many years in Jonnie Boer's three-star restaurant, presents a surprise menu that is technically very sophisticated, but unpretentious for all that. Intense flavours are creatively combined in exciting ways and with a truly delicate touch. Guests are treated to a warm reception, and the wine recommendations also hit the mark.

name: focus ATELIER
review: The prestigious nature of the Park Hotel Vitznau extends to its restaurant. Led by head chef Patrick Mahler, the kitchen crew cooks up a thrillingly creative set menu that showcases the well-thought-out, detailed preparation and strong sense of finesse. There is no room for cheap showmanship, each dish concentrating instead on excellent ingredients. The wine list verges on overwhelming with its choice of around 35 000 bottles, including first-rate labels in numerous vintages. The service is also excellent: courteous and professional from start to finish, but by no means stiff. The restaurant itself has a chic, upscale design and transparent, light-filled architecture; for the entirely glass-paned pavilion, the name "Atelier" (or workshop) is spot on. On account of its picture-postcard location on Lake Lucerne, complete with panoramic view, the terrace is naturally tempting! Tip: Verlinde Bar.

name: La Brezza
review: Although La Brezza is not a new name amid the different gastronomic options at this exclusive hotel, it is one that is improving year after year, and such “dynamism” undoubtedly brings results. Surrounded by the lush gardens of the Eden Roc hotel, skilled chef Marco Campanella (German by birth but with Italian roots) creates expressive, intense yet delicate cuisine that appeals to the eye and the palate. Carefully selected ingredients (many sourced locally), well-balanced and well-structured menus, plus a wine list that will more than satisfy connoisseurs, who are encouraged to ask for recommendations from the excellent sommelier. Professional service from the young front of house team.

name: Jungsik
review: Touted as a pioneer of modern Korean fine dining, Chef Yim Jung-sik — with his Seoul and New York restaurants - is credited for introducing Korean cuisine to the world with an innovative flair that is entirely his own. What Yim does best is drawing inspiration from the familiar — gimbap, bibimbap, platter of nine delicacies and napa wraps with pork — and creating something unexpected yet surprisingly evocative and authentic. Whimsical desserts, a good wine list and attentive service — Jungsik has it all.

name: Kwonsooksoo
review: Chef Kwon Woo-joong’s homage to tradition is evident in every facet of Kwonsooksoo, even in the name itself (sooksoo is an archaic term for professional cook). Inspired by time-honored methods of cooking, Kwon digs deep into his own roots. He tirelessly scours the country for rare finds that best represent each of the seasons and transforms even the most mundane ingredients into something special. What the diners get to experience is passion on a plate, coupled with a good dose of ingenuity.

name: Mingles
review: Chef Kang Min-goo's keen eye for detail shines in Mingles, from the ceramic ware that highlights the beauty of Korean cuisine to the warm luxury of empty space apparent in the interior design. From the beginning, Kang has marched to the beat of his own drum, breaking down barriers by marrying the old with the new, but always with a deep respect for tradition. His journey and evolution continues, with dishes like Abalone and Cabbage Seon and Fish Mandu showcasing the creativity of the chef and his talented team.

name: La Yeon
review: Time-honored traditions of Korean cuisine are given a contemporary touch at La Yeon. Located on the 23rd floor of The Shilla Hotel, this refined dining space offers stunning vistas over Namsan Park. It's the detail here that are noteworthy, from the fine tableware to the attentive service. Hansik and wine pairings elevate the dining experience to another level.

name: Joo Ok
review: The name of the restaurant Joo Ok embodies the simple philosophy of Chef Shin Chang-ho, which is to serve dishes that are as exquisite as precious gems. Shin's culinary creations are a testament to how a city's food culture deeply rooted in tradition withstands the test of time. The restaurant's most prized ingredients consist of some 30 different varieties of fermented condiments; shots of house-made vinegar are offered as an aperitif before the meal. The restaurant's celebrated perilla oil is pressed from perilla seed harvested from his family farm in Jinju. Enjoy the great view of one of the most dynamic areas of the city.

name: alla Prima
review: Chef Kim Jin-hyuk continues to attract discerning gourmets with his whimsically creative and modern offerings. His reverence for seasonal ingredients, his attention to balance, and his delicate yet assertive sauces come together like a symphony that pairs well with both wine and sake. The L-shaped counter with ample seating, the gleaming open kitchen, the spacious dining hall, and the private dining room each do their part to make the diners feel comfortable. Be sure to reserve ahead.

name: Kojima
review: The serene and reposeful space in Kojima allows patrons to concentrate solely on their sushi. A perfect match between shari (rice) and neta (fish topping), replete with the integral taste of the ingredients, the diner’s plump sushi somehow resembles its creator, Chef Park Kyung-jae. Prepared from ingredients that change daily, the sushi has an unadorned and fine taste, that is, seemingly plain yet flavorful and brims with umami. Be sure to make a reservation if you wish to relish the art of Kojima’s elegant items.

name: Soigné
review: Meaning “well-groomed” in French, Soigné lives up to its name with its elegant menu, inspired by global cuisine with distinct undertones of Korea’s culinary philosophy. Chef Lee Jun’s creations are both creative and modern, but the local ingredients he uses always take on the starring roles in his meticulously curated “episodes,” each with its own unique color and lyrical flow. Try the suggested wine pairings for the full gustatory experience.

name: Turk Fatih Tutak
review: Fatih Tutak expresses his love for his Turkish terroir. Every day he puts ingredients from his region and produce from local traders on a pedestal. This is a chef who cooks with respect for tradition and what nature has to offer. His predilection for sustainability is reflected, among other ways, in his no-waste approach and use of preservation techniques such as fermentation and dry-ageing. Traditional flavours take on an extra dimension. Part of his originality lies in his nuanced use of delicate acidic and smoky flavours, with which he puts his own stamp on dishes. Take his preparation of manti, a delicate stuffed pasta; he fills them with rich lamb and serves them alongside a sublime smoked yoghurt cream, tomato tapenade and chilli butter. For dessert, he invites you into the open kitchen of this chic, contemporary establishment. Here you will find yourself in the thick of the action.

name: Blue Hill at Stone Barns
review:
The tasting menu offered here echoes the farm’s seasonal best and might very well change the way you think about food. Culinary wunderkind Dan Barber has become a global icon for his zero-waste philosophy, which is expressed all the way down to the bone ash china gracing the tables and kitchen scraps transformed into charcoal. 
Meals begin with an onslaught of clever bites, mostly vegetables plucked from the property's greenhouses and working farm. The kitchen infuses even the most unlikely ingredients with magic, like zesty green gazpacho paired with surf clam and radicchio; or dry-aged golden beet "steak" adorned with beef-studded jus. A block of Stone Barns honey semifreddo with strawberry compote brings the kitchen's farm-to-fork mantra full circle.

name: Jean-Georges
review:
The longevity of Chef Jean-Georges Vongerichten’s flagship is  be due to many factors—a sumptuous setting, a discreet aura and superior French cuisine. Like walking through Business on your way to First Class, you have to pass through buzzy Nougatine to get here. Low-slung chairs and large tables mean you need a certain confidence in your conversational delivery if you wish to entertain the whole table.
Dishes showcase everything from attention to detail and impeccable products to thoughtful garnishes and nuanced flavors. The omnivore menu is also appealingly versatile thanks to contemporary accents and classic techniques. Picture charred beets with tamarind and saffron or buttery Wagyu with crispy potato and black truffle to get those taste buds going.

name: Jungsik
review:
Jungsik's "New Korean" cuisine leans westwards. Indeed, some of this kitchen's wonderful sauces wouldn’t be out of place at a grand French table, but what is most impressive here is that the Korean elements of the dishes seem to raise them to another level. Bibimbap composed with gochujang, crispy quinoa and tender Wagyu beef tartare will live long in the memory; while the branzino served simply with white kimchi shows that this is also a kitchen with the utmost confidence in the quality of its ingredients.
This is cooking that is original, impeccably executed and enormously satisfying. It’s the sort of food that makes you involuntarily nod to yourself while you’re eating. The space is cool, crisp and elegant; the service team sharp, keen and organized.

name: The Modern
review:
The Modern is designed to capture the iconic feel of the MoMA in which it is housed. Art enthusiasts can't help ogling at its glorious surrounds; while excellent acoustics facilitating quiet conversations ensure a steady stream of couples and globe-trotters. The kitchen is state of the art, so for a truly special experience book the chef's table inside. The staff perform a veritable ballet as they present diners with such appealingly nuanced dishes as a seed cracker with aged cheddar and butternut squash butter; or eggs on eggs, starring none other than soft-boiled eggs with sturgeon caviar. Turbot roasted on the bone may then arrive alongside rich parmesan cream.
Nurse a digestif—and marvel at the timeless sculpture garden view —for serenity embodied.

name: Ko
review:
Ko has been the pride and joy of David Chang's culinary empire. Open since 2014 and tucked into an East Village alley, it begins a new chapter under the stewardship of Chef Esther Ha. Some things remain unchanged, like the upbeat soundtrack, sleek counter staged around a kitchen with nowhere to hide and a vibe so relaxed that diners might even sing along.
Favored dishes, like the chickpea hozon with sea urchin, are still here and still excellent. Chef Ha  carries the torch forward though, bringing new ideas to the fore—aged strip loin with onion béarnaise and aged cheddar is a cheeky twist on the cheeseburger. Smoked onion soufflé is exemplary, while bonito ice cream with sweet potato skins reflects a bold brand of cooking—a cornerstone of this kitchen.

name: Gabriel Kreuther
review:
Distinctively housed at the base of the Grace building, this modern dining room happens to be perfect for celebrating special occasions. 
Dishes reflect global sensibilities with a strong creative edge, as in the langoustine tartare topped with a crispy tuile and enriched with cauliflower cream. Foie gras arrives in myriad guises, perhaps as a seared lobe as rich as custard, surrounded by roasted quince, chestnuts and vanilla gastrique. Old-school luxuries extend right through to the cheese trolley. The cocktail list is dedicated to the history of Bryant Park across the street, while as an homage to the eponymous chef’s Alsatian heritage, the wine selection prominently features rieslings, pinot blancs and gewürztraminers.

name: Aquavit
review: No detail goes unnoticed at this contemporary Swedish beauty, sporting a sleek bar and open kitchen with Chef Emma Bengtsson at the helm. Enjoy the eponymous infused spirit along with bites from one of two tasting menus. Expect glazed earthenware, slate platters and wooden boxes cradling the likes of a medallion of North Sea cod, torched ever so slightly, and accompanied by a light-textured mussel foam and petite wedges of roasted red endive. Lean and tender duck breast sided by a petite block of compressed leg meat is dressed tableside with a beet sauce enriched with duck jus. The meal may end with a composition of green apple and fennel featuring rye cake, apple ice, bitter caramel and whipped, smoked crème fraîche.

name: Aska
review:
Eating here is serious business, but happily the place isn’t blighted by a monastic atmosphere—a contented buzz fills the room, helped along by the chefs who deliver the dishes themselves.
Chef Fredrik Berselius and his ace team delight diners with their highly accomplished Nordic cuisine. Local products are woven in to the seasonal tasting, and items like prawn shells and venison bones are transformed into luscious sauces that enhance each plating. Dinner is sure to start on a high note, when Danish kingfish crudo crowned by a dollop of Osetra caviar and dressed with a gooseberry and juniper oil vinaigrette is set on the table. New York state trout may be composed with salted white currant and paired with an aebleskiver enriched with trout belly.

name: Atera
review:
Counter dining can sometimes mean lots of elbows; fortunately, this one is large enough to ensure you’re sufficiently secluded, while still letting you enjoy the immersive experience. Danish chef Ronny Emborg and team serve up a menu of courses that progress from light and subtle to rich and robust. Things are certainly grown-up here, with such fully realized dishes as a rye cracker piped with ham and topped with crisped chicken skin; or a potato dumpling smartly dressed with parmesan foam. Paper-thin Wagyu shavings may then be enhanced with a pour of hot dried shrimp bouillon and confit quail egg yolk.
There may be some tweezer action as the chefs assemble their beguiling plates, but that also means there’s nowhere to hide when food is this precise.

name: Atomix
review:
Junghyun Park and his wife Ellia serve the most memorable meal in this truly beautiful space inside a Gramercy brownstone. From start to finish, the experience is so exquisite that diners will leave awestruck. 
This team continues to push the boundaries of modern Korean cooking and even the most seasoned diners are in for a surprise.  Dishes are delicate, yet satisfying and display extraordinary finesse. Mastery of technique and depth of flavor are plain as day in the likes of striped beakfish fragrant with black truffle and Yangha ginger; or shrimp with eggplant, tomato gel and salmon roe. In a simple stroke of genius, hibiscus tea-panna cotta arrives with a crown of huckleberry ice.
A shortened tasting menu at the upstairs bar highlights dishes in development.

name: Daniel
review:
Everyone needs a little pomp and circumstance now and then and, for these grand occasions, there will always be Daniel. This iconic Manhattan dining room now sports a refreshed look featuring custom-made carpeting and bold artwork that beautifully complements the coffered ceilings and signature Bernardaud porcelain chandeliers.
Executive Chef Eddy Leroux skillfully executes the four-course seasonal prix-fixe or seven-course tasting menus. East coast crab duo, pairing a tempura soft-shell crab with peekytoe crab meat, and tender lamb chop with minted breadcrumbs, are just two standout dishes. 
Desserts are works of art, as in the Champagne mango baba, with a mango brandy-moistened sponge cake, green peppercorn custard and peaks of vanilla chantilly.

name: Saga
review:
Saga is the crown of 70 Pine Street, a landmark tower that rises over 60 stories. The space is unique and features an open-air balcony where an aperitif can be enjoyed alongside the stunning views. The elegant dining rooms are set with furnishings upholstered in peach and emerald velvet, green marble tables and carved stone accents.
Chef James Kent never allows his cuisine to be overshadowed by the setting, however. Along with his talented team, he presents diners with compositions that embrace luxury and urbane inspiration. Caviar and foie gras are on tap, as is seafood with laksa sauce or a dry-aged duck influenced by the chef's Moroccan background that comes complete with griddled flatbread, whipped yogurt flavored with preserved lemon, carrot hummus and harissa.

name: Al Coro
review:
Chef Melissa Rodriguez and Jeff Katz are behind this long-awaited spot, and the adage is true: good things do come to those who wait. Al Coro pours on the drama with old world glamour and live music. The buzzy dining room sets the stage for a kitchen that dances behind the curtain, reveling in the unexpected and sidestepping tradition for the fixed modern Italian menu. A meal here begins with an assortment of antipasti, including smoked ricotta and carrot sformato, and it's clear from those first few bites that this will be an experience to treasure. Pastas are a highlight, with diners choosing from such delights as culurgiones, or Sardinian dumplings. It concludes as it began, with a smattering of bites, from lemon verbena meringue to a rich crostata Barozzi.
-

name: Ryō-shō
review: ‘Ryō-shō’ means ‘to surpass the sky’. It could be a statement about chef Makoto Fujiwara’s ambitions. The sukiya-style building, constructed by master artisans, and the paintings, by luminaries of the artistic world, proclaim Fujiwara’s intentions. The fare preserves traditional Japanese cuisine while incorporating Western ingredients through a dialogue with French gastronomy. The very refinement of the cuisine attests to the chef’s humility.

name: Gion Owatari
review: Owner-chef Mahito Owatari’s approach is about bringing original touches to classic cuisine. The wonders he weaves with his ingenious combinations of ingredients make for memorable dining. In spring, white asparagus dressed with kinome miso is used in place of bamboo shoots. The meal ends with an enjoyable zosui made by adding leftover broth and other ingredients to rice. Owatari’s service is cheery and light-hearted, and it shows in the customers' relaxed smiles.

name: VELROSIER
review: In hanakotoba or ‘flower language’, the bellerose (a type of primrose) signifies ‘telling your true feelings to your sweetheart’. Owner-chef Yuji Iwasaki chose it to convey his feelings about gastronomy, and because it’s his birth flower. Foie gras-filled monaka wafer cakes are served with roses for colour and cloves for aroma. The imaginative pan-fried gyoza dish takes apart and reassembles the recipe bit by bit. Iwasaki’s fusion of Chinese and French is an original take.

name: Sushi Harasho
review: Featuring kappo technique, the omakase is something of a story about the path that Ko Ishikawa has taken. Nimono, grilled items, steamed items and other shuko are arranged on antique Kyo ware and on serving dishes by modern artists.
