The sensibilities he cultivated in general Japanese cuisine can also be seen in the nigiri. The first piece is squid, and the fine scoring brings out the sweetness. He does not use sugar in the vinegared rice, so as to keep the flavours light.

name: Kikunoi Roan
review: In winter, the masterpiece of the house is quail-and-lily-bulb dumpling with black truffle paste; in early summer, there is sorbet of passion fruit and wasabi. Accentuating Japanese cuisine with Western culinary elements is the epitome of ‘tradition and innovation’, as advocated by Kikunoi. At the counter, owner-chef Yoshiharu Murata and the other chefs are a whirlwind of activity. Taking in this bustle while enjoying the fare is the true pleasure of Kikunoi Roan.

name: KAHALA
review: More than half a century since he founded his restaurant, owner-chef Yoshifumi Mori’s inquisitive spirit is as unquenchable as ever. As he seeks out unknown ingredients and new cooking methods, he constantly generates original cuisines. The karasumi somen is piled on lacquer plates he painted himself. The beef millefeuille, served with three flavours, is a masterpiece. ‘I just want to create a little culinary movement of my own’ he says, as he earnestly faces his counter that seats eight.

name: Kenninji Gion Maruyama
review: The culinary journey of owner-chef Yoshio Maruyama is guided by his deep knowledge of the tea ceremony and flower arrangement. His room puts diners at ease; his menu matches the seasons. This is cuisine that reverberates in all five senses. He cooks ingredients from land and sea on a hot stone grill, patiently listening to the sizzle and waiting for the moment they yield up their aroma. Such moments convey the culture and spirt of Japan in ways the eye cannot see and the ear cannot hear.

name: Miyamaso
review: A devotee of the natural beauty of Hanase, Kyoto Prefecture, owner-chef Hisato Nakahigashi uses tsumikusa cuisine (cuisine using wild herbs and vegetables) to convey the food culture of the satoyama (rural villages hugging the hills). He travels into the mountains himself, gathering young herbs in spring and mushrooms in autumn. The edible wild plants in his tsumikusa basket are a signifier of spring. Each season brings its own special joy, like ayu in summer and boar and bear in winter.

name: Numata
review: Owner-chef Kazuya Numata skilfully manipulates the thickness and volume of the batter with a careful eye. He fries his tempura using techniques he developed himself. The menu, which interweaves seasonal ingredients that are just in with those on their way out, sees seafood and vegetables in alternating fashion. Start with the tiger prawn from Numata’s hometown, Amakusa. Possible conclusions to the meal include tendon, tencha, onigiri with shrimp tempura filling and tamagokake-gohan.

name: Koryu
review: The fare of owner-chef Shintaro Matsuo expresses the essence of Naniwa, another name for Osaka. He revels in talking about the culture of enjoying raw fish in Osaka, explaining that for him Naniwa means ‘garden of fish’”, from Osaka Bay being so rich in seafood. Koryu embodies that idea, stocked with seafood from nearby seas. He also explains Naniwa can mean a ‘garden of vegetables’, as the Kawachi Plain on which it sits is renowned as a vegetable-producing region.

name: Tenjimbashi Aoki
review: “Japanese cuisine is an art comprising multiple arts”, observes owner-chef Ryota Aoki. The décor reflects this creed with its harmonious blend of cultural elements. The interior is in the style of sukiya, and the food, served on a mix of antique and modern plates, is arranged to reflect traditional events and seasonal festivals. The star items on the menu are nimono soup, richly flavourful and nutritious, and hassun that pay homage to the classics.

name: Oryori Mitsuyasu
review: The owner-chef visits farmers and gathers vegetables to fire his culinary imagination. Consider the hassun: defying the standard practice of combining ingredients from both ocean and mountain, he serves only vegetables. In spring, sprouting buds are garnished with edible wild plants; in summer, chilled vegetables are cool to both eye and palate; in autumn, chestnuts and mushrooms are the stars of the crop; and in winter, root vegetables are cooked to express the warmth of the good earth.

name: Fujiya 1935
review: Owner-chef Tetsuya Fujiwara aspires to “a dining table of seasons and memories”. Passing through the entrance and moving through to the dining room, the guest is drawn into a unique space that titillates all senses. The fresh, seasonal ingredients are painstakingly selected, and the creative cuisine uses techniques the owner-chef made his own when in Europe. He delivers the food to guests himself and speaks sincerely about the appeal of the ingredients and their background.

name: Yusokuryori Mankamero
review: This long-standing establishment boasts three centuries of history. Renowned as the home of the Ikama school of culinary arts, its traditions have been passed from father to only one child for 10 generations to the current owner-chef, Masakiyo Konishi. The menu consists of yusoku ryori, associated with the seasonal banquets and other annual functions of the Imperial court, and kaiseki based on chakaiseki. Both types of meal conclude with a tai chazuke.

name: Otagi
review: The name of the restaurant derives from the location of owner-chef Kazuaki Baba’s restaurant in Takagamine, an area formerly known as Otagi County. “Since you took the trouble to come all this way…” is a favoured phrase with which he welcomes patrons. The exuberant uniqueness of the menu delights diners, with offerings such as duck charcoal-grilled on low heat, cream croquettes of fugu shirako, and dandan noodles à la mode japonais of hand-made udon.

name: Shunsaiten Tsuchiya
review: Osaka is a textile production centre, and Yukihiko Tsuchisaka says he uses cottonseed oil to contribute to the wellbeing of his hometown. Watching him put his all into the deep-frying, mindful of all the effort that went into producing the ingredients, is a wonderful sight. He is thorough in his preparations, adjusting the batter and the way he deep-fries, and even changing the sourness of the dipping sauce, according to the weather and ingredients. He puts to work the sensibilities he cultivated in the field of general Japanese cuisine in making the tempura and beautifully arranged hassun.

name: Ogata
review: Having your fill of Japanese cuisine stripped to its essentials, and lovingly served on antique and contemporary dishware, is the real pleasure of Ogata. Owner-chef Toshiro Ogata fills each plate with nature’s bounty. “Holding back on seasonings richly draws out the innate flavours of the ingredients”, he explains. He pairs bamboo shoots with shirako in spring and, in winter serves ebi-imo boiled in water only. His daring yet delicate cuisine is richly imbued with seasonal aromas.

name: Sushiyoshi
review: Hiroki Nakanoue had no mentor, instead blazing his own culinary trail. His nigiri, inspired by edomae techniques, are unique. To maximize appreciation, he coats the topping in sweet vinegar and drizzles soy sauce over it, repeatedly adding acidity for a multi-layered taste sensation. Expanding his enterprise beyond Japan, Nakanoue never slacks in honing his sensitivity. The menu breaks new ground, incorporating shuko and desserts made with Western culinary techniques.

name: Shimmonzen Yonemura
review: Masayasu Yonemura is rich in creativity and continues to hone his aesthetic faculties. Putting his experience to work in preparing the ingredients and serving dishes, he comes up with cuisine that defies genre. He brings Japanese and Western elements together, such as serving tapenade with hamo and serving fugu sashimi with citrus and salad. He also uses a variety of gorgeous serving dishes, some crafted by modern artists, some that are antiques, and some made in Europe. The Yonemura touch can be sensed in everything from the space to the dishes.

name: Kyokaiseki Kichisen
review: This ryotei stands close to Shimogamo Shrine, a World Heritage site. Yoshimi Tanigawa, the owner-chef, describes his art as “a quest for good flavour”, while the cup of sake that starts the meal conveys his spirit of hospitality. The choice of Ma-kombu for the dashi is because of the well-rounded umami it imparts. The arrangements reflect current festivals and the season, from an aesthetic sensibility tutored in the arts of tea ceremony and flower arranging.

name: Gion Nishikawa
review: The interior is painstakingly crafted in the style of a sukiya, for a sense of stylish elegance. Masayoshi Nishikawa is an owner-chef who treasures his establishment’s deep connection to the region. Viewing the dinner experience as a narrative arc, he interlaces Western ingredients and gastronomic methods to bring an original touch. His motto is a Chinese proverb: “True flavour is subtle flavour”: Understated flavours, he says, are truest to their ingredients.

name: Gion Maruyama
review: Owner-chef Yoshio Maruyama’s take on Kyo-ryori is that it is heir to the ancient capital’s history and culture. His dishes sparkle with originality, inventively resonating with all five senses, including colour, sound, and aroma. The dining room is designed in the restrained, elegant sukiya style with appropriate seasonal decorations to convey the beauty of Japanese cuisine. Guests can be seated at the counter to observe the chefs at work or at a table to dine in a graceful atmosphere.

name: Sojiki Nakahigashi
review: Sojiki-ryori, literally ‘herbivorous cuisine’, is all about appreciating nature’s bounty. Owner-chef Hisao Nakahigashi plans his dishes so that nothing goes to waste. The hassun expresses the rustic beauty of the country through all five senses. To match the mood of each season, the carp tsukuri is garnished with buds in spring and mushrooms in autumn, in a presentation the house calls ‘Koi no Karasawagi’, conveying Nakahigashi’s love of hill and dale.

name: Wagokoro Izumi
review: Owner-chef Masaki Izumi regards Japanese cuisine as the heart of Japanese culture, so approaches his work from the standpoint of wagokoro, the Japanese spirit. Naturally, he places great emphasis on dashi. The meal begins with a sour appetiser to accent the delicate flavours of the stewed dishes that follow. Ayu dried high above a fire is an early-summer speciality. Festive ingredients are arranged on the hassun to highlight the season and convey the traditions of the former capital.

name: Gion Matayoshi
review: Owner-chef Kazutomo Matayoshi scours Japan, from Hokkaido to his native Okinawa, seeking ingredients with the right flavour and builds a relationship of trust with each producer. His cooking is distinguished by techniques that bring out inherent flavours. Originality is everywhere: lily bulbs made into a dumpling with no filler; oil-baked vegetables cooked with an evenness and thoroughness usually seen only with deep-frying; and tsukuri garnished with rock tripe.

name: La Cime
review: Yusuke Takada has dedicated his life to pursuing French cuisine à la Japonaise. Focusing on Japanese ingredients, he sources items like pork and citrus fruits from his birthplace of Amamioshima Island. The set menu sets a modern, light-hearted tone, and weaves in elements of traditional cuisine that he has brought to refinement. He sets great store by classic techniques while fusing them with innovative ideas, to foster a gastronomical world view that is all his own.

name: Miyamoto
review: Owner-chef Daisuke Miyamoto’s open-minded approach to gastronomy is reflected in the unique menu. For example, when the vegetables, grown by the proprietress’s family, are delivered to the kitchen, you may be startled to find that the first dish is deep-fried. He ends the meal with rice cooked in an earthenware pot, pork miso soup and dashimaki tamago, which he calls the Miyamoto family breakfast. Some of the bowls and plates are antiques and some created by modern artists.

name: Sumibi Kappo Ifuki
review: Owner-chef Norio Yamamoto calls his style of restaurant sumibi-kappo, ‘charcoal-fired cuisine’, and tends his charcoal fire with practiced ease. In summer a sumashijiru soup of ayu is served. Ayu bones are added to the dashi for extra flavour. Another unique approach that charms customers is how the ayu flesh in the soup is fragrantly char-grilled. The duck is smoked using grapevines, in a touch that reflects the cuisine of the Basque Country straddling Spain and France.

name: Kodaiji Wakuden
review: The interior is skilfully crafted in the style of a sukiya and home to a lovingly tended design with beauty of form. The minimalist cuisine is prepared with great care, with unnecessary elements pruned for a memorable arrangement of rustic beauty. Seasonal flavours include Taiza crab and a grilled pairing of hamo and matsutake. These delicacies are charcoal-grilled in front of the customer, creating a feast for the senses. Simple yet subtle technique is on display here.

name: Delta
review: Located inside the spectacular Stavros Niarchos Foundation Cultural Centre (SNFCC), an avant-garde complex that is also home to the National Library of Greece and the Greek National Opera. The space and triangular shape of this restaurant on the fifth floor of the building come as a pleasant surprise, as does the exclusively designed bronze bar, the mass of greenery (including trees suspended from the ceiling!) and stunning sea views. The two chefs at the helm (George Papazacharias and Thanos Feskos), both of whom were trained in some of Northern Europe’s finest restaurants, have returned to their homeland to apply Scandinavian techniques and concepts to Greek ingredients. Their cuisine, which adopts a flawless approach to sustainability, is based around a creative Omnivore tasting menu (10 or 14 courses) that includes vegan and vegetarian options.

name: Sushi Masaki Saito
review: Even if you lived next door, omakase with Chef Masaki Saito would still feel like a faraway adventure. The foyer's marble staircase, a 200-year-old hinoki counter and traditional Japanese paneling and woodwork set the stage as he slices, scores and sauces the greatest treasures of the sea. Only here will you find shirako boldly skewered and grilled over binchotan, and only here will you eat melting slabs of chutoro buried under a blizzard of white truffles. Fish comes exclusively from Japan, and for the nigiri, assistants are quick to bring him his prized rice from Niigata prefecture, warm and tinged with his special blend of vinegars, after every round. Laughter fills the air, thanks to Saito and his jovial team, and for a few blissful hours, the world outside melts away.

name: Hiša Franko
review: Prepare yourselves for an exciting culinary adventure at this restaurant, which offers a single menu of several small courses, all of which are different in taste and concept. Acidity and bitterness are the chef's hallmarks, while the creation of sublime dishes using the highest quality produce from the surrounding area is the latest focus of this intense cuisine

name: Logy
review: Opened in 2018, this 13-seater restaurant is a spin-off from the celebrated Florilège in Tokyo. The dimly-lit concrete interior adds to the intriguing ambiance. On the menu, local ingredients are finessed by modern techniques and strong Asian influences. Egg custard in beef consommé with celery sorbet; and aiyu jelly, cocoa juice and nata de coco particularly stand out. The prix-fixe menu changes every two months. Online booking only.

name: L'Atelier de Joël Robuchon
review: The moody interior uses the iconic black and red colour scheme as the other members of the group – sit at the counter to appreciate the atmosphere to the fullest. French classics are re-invented with skill, care and a great deal of aplomb; service is engaging, confident and thoughtful. Since 2019, the kitchen has been helmed by the first female head chef in the group’s Asian bases; she adds an ethereal touch to the distinctive cooking.

name: Taïrroir
review: The 1,876 copper tiles hanging from the ceiling are quite a spectacle, but they don’t outshine the Taiwanese cuisine on the table – reinvented with local produce, French techniques and artful plating. Well versed in Western and Chinese cooking, Chef Kai relives his food memories with acumen and witty word play, as manifested by the 9-course menu. A portmanteau of Taiwan and terroir, Taïrroir pays tribute to his Taiwanese roots.

name: Shoun Ryugin
review: Sister to RyuGin in Tokyo, Shoun RyuGin delivers similarly creative cuisine using local produce. The head chef visits local farms regularly and prepares the food using traditional Japanese techniques. The 7- and 10-course menus are expertly rendered, with a map showing the ingredients’ origin. Squab from Pingtung is grilled over Bincho charcoal and straw to accentuate its delicate texture, while eel is cooked in various ways according to the season.

name: Raw
review: The owner-chef of the world-famous Restaurant André in Singapore opened Raw in his home town in 2014. The strikingly futuristic Weijenberg-designed interior features two gigantic pine wood organic forms that lend the faux industrial space a back-to-nature feel. The 9-course prix-fixe menu showcases chef's creative take on Taiwanese cuisine with the occasional street food influence – expect modern presentation and a stimulating blend of flavours, textures and temperatures.

name: The Guest House
review: Formerly a members-only dining club, it excites not with its décor, but with its food. Impressive skills transform seemingly simple dishes into tasteful presentations revealing great textures and taste. The menu is largely Huai Yang and Sichuan in origin, but with a Taiwanese twist. Signature dishes include double-boiled soups, chicken rice with sesame oil, pork tail braised in red yeast rice, and millefeuille tofu skin.

name: JL Studio
review: ‘JL’ is Chef Jimmy Lim who was brought up in Singapore and honed his skills by spending over 10 years working in a number of world-famous restaurants. He excels in re-inventing Singaporean and South East Asian cuisine underpinned with solid French techniques. The tasting menu deconstructs familiar items such as Hainan chicken rice, satay and chilli crab, and re-imagines them in ingenious forms and textures to playfully subvert diners’ expectations.

name: Jiang by Chef Fei
review: This elegant and relaxing décor shows a harmonious confluence of the East and West. Its classic Cantonese fare also strikes a fine balance between traditions and creativity, with an element of surprise and a touch of Japanese and Western influences. Specialities include roasted Wenchang Chicken with flaxseeds, and steamed Hele crab with minced pork. Dim sum, roast goose and char siu are also recommended.

name: Imperial Treasure Fine Chinese Cuisine
review: As in other branches of this Singapore-based chain, the kitchen team here never fails to deliver quality dishes thanks to shrewd judgment and honed skills. The must-try black pepper mud crab exudes an intoxicating aroma and seafood flavour, while double-boiled fish maw soup with shark bones warms the heart and soul. Save some room for the creamed walnut sweet soup that pleases the palate with robust nuttiness and silky texture.

name: Taian Table
review: If creative, refined dining with a modern twist is your thing, you should feel right at home in Taian Table. This kitchen team turns the best ingredients from around the world into sophisticated works of art in the display kitchen with their well-honed European techniques. There is only one 8-course degustation menu that changes bimonthly, but diners also have the option of ordering other seasonal and signature offerings.

name: Cloudstreet
review: The enchanting Cloudstreet is named after the Tim Winton book, which is fitting as Australia is where Sri Lankan chef Rishi Naleendra learnt his trade and developed his considerable skills. Diners at his restaurant are taken on a thrilling culinary journey, courtesy of his impressive creativity and artistry. He has also gathered together a service team who clearly share his pride and passion. When it comes to dessert, diners move to a room upstairs.

name: Jaan by Kirk Westaway
review: Embodying the quintessence of fine dining, this romantic restaurant has it all – food, service, ambiance and spectacular views. Chef Westaway makes good use of top-notch British produce and inspirations, such as scallops from Scotland and turbot from Cornwall, to turn out modern culinary creations that never fail to impress. Some British classics also got a makeover – “hen’s egg” is a refined take on the breakfast favourite dippy eggs with soldiers.

name: Shisen Hanten
review: Gather friends and family and prepare to feast at this outpost of the Szechwan restaurant group, which was founded in Japan by the late Chen Kenmin; his grandson is now the Executive Chef. The high-ceilinged dining room hosts large round tables and boasts great city views. The restaurant uses supreme ingredients – in specialities such as braised Australian 4-head whole abalone, steamed chicken with sesame sauce, and ‘Chen’s Mapo Doufu’.

name: Waku Ghin
review: After the move and decoration that took almost two years, this upmarket restaurant reopened its doors in March 2021. The room furnished in a contemporary style is now divided into three sections: a counter with seats, chef’s table and private rooms. Dinner featured one session only with a choice between classic and seasonal menus. Rest assured that the ingredients are top-notch and dishes are impeccably executed.

name: Saint Pierre
review: The unobstructed views of the Marina Bay, smart décor and discreet service don’t outshine Chef Emmanuel’s modern French cuisine, underpinned by solid skills and characterised by Asian overtones. His unique ability to accentuate the natural flavours of premium produce is what keeps diners returning. The seafood heavy tasting menu showcases the breadth and depth of his repertoire. It’s closed on some public holidays, so call ahead to check.

name: Thevar
review: Chef Mano Thevar serves a creative multi-course menu rooted in Indian traditions and crafted with European techniques. Signatures such as Chettinad chicken roti or Brittany lobster in curry beurre blanc pack a ton of oomph, all the while maintaining a fine balance with mindful touches. Amuse-bouches and snacks between courses are especially fun and a vegetarian version of the menu is also available. The bustling and lively vibe makes for a great experience.

name: Shoukouwa
review: Hailing from Nagoya, but having done time in China and Thailand, this Japanese head chef champions a refined and elegant take on sushi. Two omakase menus emphasise freshness, featuring white fish alongside other luxury dishes. Ingredients are shipped from Japan four times a week; and sushi rice from Yamagata and Ishikawa prefectures are mixed in a specific ratio to the best effect. Sushi is served with two sauces to accentuate the umami of the fish.

name: Kadeau Copenhagen
review: This beautiful restaurant offers a memorable, multi-course dining experience; the chefs are on display in the open kitchen and service is serene and well-paced. The owner hails from Bornholm and he and his team are passionate about the island’s ingredients, which are dried, cured, preserved, smoked and pickled to maximum effect in complex, skilfully crafted dishes.

name: Kong Hans Kælder
review: This elegant restaurant is set in an intimate, historic and wonderfully atmospheric cellar, where a charming team attend to your every need. Cooking is rooted in French gastronomy, with its luxury ingredients and rich flavours, but the chef also stamps his own mark on the accomplished, imaginative dishes, with some subtle modernisation and lighter touches.

name: Frederikshøj
review: A luxurious, contemporary restaurant set in the former staff lodge to the Royal Palace; ask for a table by the floor to ceiling windows for a view over the gardens and out to sea. The chef has a bold, daring style, and his elaborate, creative, modern dishes have French influences and a playful edge.

name: Oaxen Krog
review: A secret door in Oaxen Slip leads into this oak-furnished room overlooking the water. Produce from their nearby farm features on the set menu, which begins with elaborately presented canapés. Delicate and creative dishes then follow, some of which are finished off table-side. The owners also consider the restaurant’s impact on the environment. The boat opposite offers accommodation.

name: Alchemist
review: An immersive and perfectly choreographed dining experience. The 50-course dinner is divided into 5 acts, served at various locations, including a spectacular planetarium-like dome. Dishes are technically complex and highly creative with dramatic contrasts; some make a statement about issues such as plastic pollution in the oceans or overcrowding in chicken farms.

name: KOKS
review:
THIS RESTAURANT HAS RELOCATED TO GREENLAND FOR TWO SEASONS AND PLANS TO RETURN TO THE FAROE ISLANDS IN 2024.

Meet at the lakeside fermenting hut for an aperitif with a view; you’ll then be delivered to the picturesque and energy-efficient former farmhouse and forge for an intimate dining experience. The creative menu uses sustainably farmed seaweed, organic vegetables, locally caught seafood and free-range Faroese meat, with an emphasis on traditional techniques.

name: Il Ristorante-Niko Romito
review:
This uber-cool, stylish and understated restaurant is located within the Bulgari Resort Hotel, and diners are cossetted from the moment they step through the door by the charming Italian team. The sleek, design-led interior boasts an impressive cocktail bar, the atmosphere is intimate and romantic, and the walls are punctuated with black and white photos of Italian movie stars. When the weather allows, the terrace overlooking the marina is the place to hang out. 
Experienced Italian chef Giacomo Amicucci cooks assured, sophisticated modern Italian dishes, which are far more complex than they at first appear and come with balance, purity and clarity. Many of the top-quality ingredients are flown in from Italy; fish dishes are a highlight, as is the pasta. For the full experience, plump for the ‘Degustazione’ menu.

name: STAY by Yannick Alléno
review:
This elegant, high-ceilinged restaurant is exclusively set at the end of the Palm in a Colonial-style property, which is breathtakingly opulent in design, with magical tropical gardens and a private dock. Inside, it’s luxurious without being stuffy, and service follows suit, with staff that are attentive and professional yet relaxed and personable.
The wide range of menus could include surprise, tasting, seasonal caviar and truffle options; cooking has a French base and takes a ‘less is more’ approach to some outstanding ingredients. Precise, sophisticated dishes are perfectly judged and packed with flavour; beautifully conceived and skilfully crafted with an intelligent and intriguing array of textures, flavours and temperatures. The langoustine tart is a highlight.

name: L'Atelier de Joël Robuchon Miami
review:
Miami has joined the ranks of Paris, New York and Tokyo with its own on-brand and elegant L'Atelier de Joël Robuchon. The Design District setting bears all the beloved hallmarks with a counter and open kitchen plus rosewood walls and leather chairs.
The menu offers both tasting portions and large plates; but go with the seasonal prix fixe. The bread basket is a lovely opener, arriving in advance of such thrilling bites as a seared sea scallop with toasted spices. Tuna sashimi in a warm vinaigrette of brown butter, mustard and makrut lime dazzles, while artichokes, housed underneath a glass dome and floating in a chickpea and turmeric "cappuccino," delight. Finally, the aptly named le chocolat sensation is a thrill with its balance of textures and tastes.

name: Pure C
review:
The splendour of the North Sea and the Cadzand dunes strikes you as you walk into Pure C. The floor-to-ceiling windows, which afford unforgettable views of the water and surrounding natural beauty as far as the eye can see, give you the impression that you could just step out onto the beach. Characterised by modern style and a touch of Scandinavian minimalism, the dining area was designed in line with the wishes of chef Syrco Bakker, who comes in to serve the odd dish himself.
Exquisite produce from the sea and polders of Zeeland take centre stage here – there's hardly any meat on the menu, which instead is full of subtly salty and delicately acidic flavours. Chef Bakker's cuisine has its own unique identity, largely inspired by his surroundings and occasionally drawing on his Indonesian roots (nasi goreng is a house speciality). For instance, he tops chawanmushi seasoned with chamomile with North Sea crab, wraps it in cabbage leaves and smokes it on the barbecue. The dish is rounded off with arugula oil, a creamy crab jus and caviar. Such creativity can leave you quite lost for words. Perfectly balanced and nuanced, every bite is a new taste sensation that makes you crave more. Pure C is a real ode to Zeeland.

name: De Bokkedoorns
review: A joy from start to finish. The view over the wooded dunes is delightful, while the ample comforts of the dining room will ensure a pleasurable experience. The emphasis in the traditional kitchen, with its modern and original inspiration, is on the purest ingredients. All accompanied by an extensive wine list to complete your enjoyment.

name: Aan de Poel
review: A successful marriage of technical skill and brilliant produce ensures that every dish is a feast for the senses. Here, contemporary cuisine can be savoured in one of its most beautiful and tasteful forms. What’s more, this restaurant benefits from a superb lakeside setting, a chic and sophisticated designer interior and a skilled sommelier.

name: De Kromme Watergang
review:
Edwin Vinke is an ambassador for Zeelandic Flanders. The Eastern Scheldt and the North Sea are key sources of produce for this upscale restaurant. Fish and seafood are supplied by his father-in-law. Vegetables and fruits he grows himself. Chef Vinke works as much as possible from fin and head to tail. He now works side by side with his son Tom, who is increasingly making his mark.
This is ingredient-led cuisine, enhanced by exotic spices and modern culinary techniques. The chefs want to surprise you and take inspiration from the surrounding artworks, among other things. Dining at De Kromme Watergang is something of a show. Dishes such as exceptionally fine smoked eel served with different textures of polder potatoes demonstrate an appealing sense of invention. Smoky, briny, crisp, exotic, unctuous… A tribute to the ingredients!
Fabulous suites are available for overnight stays – you are bound to fall in love with the beautiful surroundings, just as both of the chefs here did.

name: Ciel Bleu
review:
Ciel Bleu immediately lives up to its name. Here, you dine on the top floor of the luxurious Okura Hotel with a spectacular view of the blue sky and the Amsterdam skyline as a backdrop. The modern elegance of the restaurant and the superlative presentation of the dishes are equally pleasing to the eye.
Arjan Speelman's cuisine is technically accomplished, creative and laced with international influences and seasonings. This chef effortlessly combines a classic beurre blanc with exotic spices and ingredients from around the globe. Every detail is precise, every bite a surprise. A nice touch: with each course, a herb in its original form is brought to the table – this herb will be featured in the next dish.
Dining at Ciel Bleu is intriguing. You will be served by one of the best front-of-house teams in the country, starring sommelier Noël Vanwittenbergh and maître d' Francesco Simonelli. The sky really is the limit here!

name: FG - François Geurds
review: François Geurds has a clear vision and he brings it to life in this restaurant, which is urban, trendy and original. The chef adopts a style that is very detailed, sometimes even playful, but always keeps his focus on the flavours of his high quality ingredients and sauces. FG could easily stand for Fantastically Good!

name: Fred
review: Fred Mustert takes his guests on a culinary adventure in this stylish restaurant, which boasts decorative highlights such as a leather and 24-carat gold work of art and an impressive lighting installation. Less really is more according to chef Mustert, who creates well-balanced culinary masterpieces which are exciting, modern and with no unnecessary frills.

name: Spectrum
review:
Sidney Schutte's spectrum of flavours is astonishing. At De Librije, he developed his own inventive culinary style, and at Amber (Hong Kong) he mastered the sophisticated techniques particular to Asian cuisine. His food looks as spectacular as it tastes – exciting and colourful with a unique interplay of textures.
First-class Dutch produce and international seasonings come together here in complex dishes. The technically gifted chef does not shy away from contrasts, and he is certainly an innovator rather than an imitator! This applies to his vegetarian set menu as well as to his fish and meat creations. His combination of crispy duck tongue, blue lobster and foie gras with liquorice and green apple is simply amazing. At Spectrum, every bite creates a new impression that increases the desire for more.
This typical canal house enchants visitors with its understated class and beautiful elegance. The extremely attentive service comes courtesy of the highly accomplished front-of-house team. A real fine dining experience!

name: Tribeca
review: The talented Jan Sobecki puts his ambition into practice in chic, elegant Tribeca. The refinement of his cooking, the balance of his dishes and the many wonderful flavours in every mouthful, are impressive. The chef knows how to translate his ideas to the plate, and this makes Tribeca a top restaurant. Chapeau!

name: Restaurant 212
review: The open-plan kitchen has a central place in this modern restaurant where guests enjoy interacting with the chefs from the seats at the counter. Here you can watch Richard van Oostenbrugge and Thomas Groot working with delicate precision, preparing inventive and creative dishes which surprise diners with their unexpectedly striking flavours.

name: Sabero
review: Nico and Sonja Boreas have made their name a quality assurance. At Sabero they operate on a smaller scale, in a cosy yet luxurious setting where they really pamper their guests. Here, less is more and top - quality produce is refined into sophisticated dishes that are technically flawless and extremely delicate. A real feast with Boreas’ signature.

name: De Groene Lantaarn
review: The magnificent De Groene Lantaarn occupies a stately property with lots of personality – you’ll even find the chef’s own skateboards as part of the decor here! The terrace overlooking the vegetable garden and the windmill is exquisite, and local ingredients are given exotic depth thanks to influences from further afield. The end result is surprising and challenging but always harmonious. An exhilarating culinary adventure!

name: Brut172
review: Hans van Wolde has opened up shop in the heart of the Limberg countryside, transforming a farmstead into an architectural gem oozing with contemporary appeal. The enticing menu focuses on outstanding ingredients and explosive sauces. Chef van Wolde is an adventurer at heart, always keen to try out new ideas – a unique experience awaits you!

name: Flore
review: Bas van Kranen showcases his culinary ideas at Flore (formerly Bord’Eau), where nature adds plenty of character to the interior and the view of the canal remains as unique as ever. This talented chef has a resolute focus on organic and local ingredients, resulting in a “conscious fine dining” concept that is clearly evident in creative and highly personal dishes. Here, original techniques, pure flavours and lots of passion combine to create a captivating spectacle!

name: Hertog Jan at Botanic
review: A meal at Hertog Jan, in the capable hands of chef Gert de Mangeleer and sommelier Joachim Bouden, is quite unique. The chef crafts subtle, intense and surprising cuisine, of Asian inspiration. A treat for all five senses and a total culinary experience that both overwhelms and is entirely unforgettable.

name: Colette - De Vijvers
review: Drive into this imposing private domain and admire the lake and sandy beach as you stroll across to the glitzy pavilion and enter the new home base of Thijs Vervloet – you’re sure to be impressed! This artisan has lost none of his classical soul. His finesse, love of top-quality products and meticulous approach are what make Colette tick, with captivating results.

name: Slagmolen
review: This characterful restaurant is located in a watermill, whose old machinery is visible inside. It boasts a frondy green terrace with lavish guestrooms in the neighbouring villa. Chef Meewis can be relied upon to serve sophisticated generous dishes that are both authentic and varied. Each dish is heavenly, each morsel blissful!

name: Ma Langue Sourit
review: Cyril Molard, enthusiastic and dedicated, devotes all his passion and talent to his culinary creations. Each ingredient is carefully chosen to add to the dish without unnecessary frills. Treating his diners’ taste buds to a festival of balanced flavours is the overriding objective. The intimate and welcoming interior further adds to the gastronomic experience.

name: Castor
review: Purity is the name of the game at the Castor. The contemporary choice of concrete, glass and wood endows this tasteful cube with a warm vibe. Stefanie embodies the restaurant’s classy style, while Maarten Bouckaert adds a contemporary delicate spin to his classical background. The sauces are to die for! The food of a seasoned chef who has lost none of his youthful enthusiasm.

name: d'Eugénie à Emilie
review: This elegant restaurant is the stage of a moving encounter between chef Fernez and his carefully selected ingredients. A genuine food lover, the chef treats his produce with respect and precision, revealing the full extent of his skill and know - how and showcasing his consummate talents in the field of classical culinary techniques.

name: Le Chalet de la Forêt
review: Pascal Devalkeneer’s chalet is magnificently set on the edge of the Sonian Forest and the chalet’s terrace makes the most of this splendid natural environment. The restaurant overlooking the cottage garden is the pinnacle of luxurious elegance. Chef Devalkeneer leaves his personal hallmark on each dish, blending classicism and creativity with consummate flair and talent. He scours the countryside of Belgium and France for the best ingredients from Aveyron lamb to abalone from the Brittany coast, further enhancing these exceptional ingredients with fascinating side dishes. For example, the exquisite flavour of Brittany crab is subtly underscored by a mint and coriander pesto, almonds and different textures of courgettes. His deep-seated understanding of the role and impact of each ingredient enables him to create combinations that intelligently enrich and exalt the original flavour. This chalet in the forest is a temple of high-flying culinary art that will surprise you over and over again.

name: L'Eau Vive
review: Imagine a romantic dinner on a riverside terrace surrounded by greenery… The table d’hôte right in the kitchen is also very popular! Veteran chef Pierre Résimont continues to surprise with his apparently simple dishes, yet his classicism is both inventive and subtle. Book one of the guestrooms to conclude a fine dining experience in style.

name: Château du Mylord
review: This elegant Anglo - Norman inspired manor (1861) has lost none of its charm, nor its superb terrace. Be prepared to be pampered by the Thomas brothers. They are masters at rustling up classic cuisine that is both creative and sophisticated. The fine cheese platter is further proof of their knowledge of good produce.

name: La Paix
review: La Paix, a culinary landmark of Brussels since 1892, was originally where the local butchers came for a bite to eat after their working day. Times have changed and chef David Martin has swapped the traditional brasserie score for a brand-new menu that is as impressive as the décor. La Paix now blends Brussels’ heritage with Japanese minimalism, depicted by a shimmering flock of origami birds hanging from the ceiling and soft lighting, setting an almost reverential vibe, while Martin and his team add the final touch to their creations on the “altar”. You can choose between two formulas, named after the respective fathers of the chef and the lady of the house, which pair polished pedigree Gallicism with Japanese purity, creating a distinctive gastronomic signature. Chef Martin is on a permanent quest for perfection and the flavours are often bold, sometimes even disruptive. He enjoys surprising diners right from the appetisers, with, for example, pig’s ears cooked in a hint of soy sauce with moist steamed mussels in a vinaigrette based on mussel stock. He masterfully works with dashi, miso and koji, adding a surprising new kick to noble ingredients such as monkfish or turbot. Martin’s inimitable character and steadfast commitment can be tasted in every bite of his subtle recipes that seek to encapsulate the microcosm of Belgium!

name: Bartholomeus
review: Bart Desmidt, with his right-hand man Philip and the gracious Sandra, take you on a whirlwind tour of flavours in Bartholomeus, a swanky restaurant with Japanese overtones. Admire the cheerful chefs seamlessly working together in the theatrically visible kitchen. The seats (only 18) around the counter are reserved for amateurs of high-flying cuisine. There is a single set 6-course menu and Sandra can be relied upon for judicious wine-food pairings, delving into a splendid cellar which boasts a knock-out selection of wines by the glass. The cast of exceptional ingredients features stars such as wagyu beef, turbot, langoustine, all of which are crafted with awe-inspiring know-how. Creative, bang-on recipes designed to showcase the produce: oysters, wagyu and lemon explode in a festival of flavour or textbook-perfect fluffy soufflé of langoustines, subtly flanked by caviar. The chefs’ consummate technique and boundless creativity left us reeling – you won’t be disappointed by their carte blanche menu…

name: Ralf Berendsen
review: Ralf Berendsen aims to provide a global experience, starting with the tree-lined drive to this classy modern building flanked by an opulent terrace, in which every detail has been puzzled and preened over! Even before the first bite, you are engulfed by the feeling of luxury as a birthright… Ralf, a true perfectionist, now makes his entrance. He spices up familiar flavours with delicate nuances and subtle international produce. Fabulous, rare ingredients such as hamachi and Polder’s hare are flawlessly prepared, but the chef also enjoys surprising us with bold associations. For example, his melt-in-the-mouth fillet of venison is set off by a concoction of taggiasca olives and the tangy sweetness of pineapple. The fascinating balance of these powerful flavours demonstrates the full gamut of this high-flying chef’s talent, particularly visible in his sauces. Discerning foodies will be further delighted to learn that Ralf was a baker-pastry chef in a former life, hence the irresistible bread and biscuit trolley.

name: La Villa Lorraine by Yves Mattagne
review: The Villa Lorraine has been luxuriously revamped to celebrate a match made in heaven with Yves Mattagne and now boasts a swish lounge and a trendy cocktail bar for city slickers. The restaurant shines the spotlight on outstanding produce, such as lobster and Anjou pigeon, that is assembled into subtle creations. Delicate yet never bland, subtlety of texture and inventiveness – the Villa is back!

name: Tsukumo
review: Masato Nishihara honed his skills in Kyoto, New York and London. He opened his restaurant in Nara after being drawn to the city’s history and its local charms. While following tradition, the menu is an outside-the-box creation. He sets out to create new tastes by combining local ingredients with elements of Shojin ryori, truffles and other such items. Smack your lips over refined, contemporary dishes that defy genre and national boundaries.

name: Oryori Hanagaki
review: The restaurant is named after Unohanagaki, an antique teacup designated a national treasure. Toshihiko Furuta’s father was a chef and he naturally acquired the sensibilities and set out on the path of Japanese cuisine. The restaurant is hidden in a residential area in a detached house he built himself. He takes only one party for lunch and dinner as he wants to focus on them exclusively. He is also an antique art dealer, so the serving dishes are another highlight of the meal.

name: NARA NIKON
review: Be charmed by kappo technique in an elegant atmosphere of sukiya-style architecture. Shojiro Shimizu showcases his one-of-a-kind dishes inspired by his experience in Kyoto. For the Star Festival, asparagus is coated in Miwa somen and deep-fried to look like a spool of thread . The elegant seasonal hassun is a sight to behold. The name of the restaurant means to ‘do what needs to be done in the moment’. He prepares his dishes with passion.

name: akordu
review: Akordu means ‘memories’ in the Basque language. Chef Hiroshi Kawashima looks over his life and weaves heartfelt memories into the dishes. The names on the menu such as ‘Spring and Things that Live in the Mountains’ and ‘Roots, Soil and Snow’ stir the imagination. Making local ingredients known and conveying their appeal was something he learnt in Spain. The vegetable dish ‘Verduras’ is a masterpiece that paints a picture of coexistence between humans and nature.

name: minibar
review:
A single door manned by a suited host marks the entrance to this culinary haven that extends well beyond its diminutive name. The lounge is ideal for a bit of bubbly, after which guests may settle in to a perch at the counter, set around the chefs' stainless steel workspace that literally makes their world a stage.
The team is unabashedly passionate, turning out a menu that's complete with whimsy. "Ramen en papillote" showcases how much fun they are having, but one may also look to the chalkboard for such specials as soy chicharrón with wakasabi (think guacamole sparked by wasabi); or Wagyu topped with pearls of caviar and petals of sunflower. Desserts, like a fried hojicha donut and cherry pâte de fruit atop miso "sable," make for an unorthodox finale.

name: Pineapple and Pearls
review:
This gem is a memorable dining destination with cooking that is ambitious yet whimsical. 
The small space is sure to fill up with an animated crowd, but the ambience is always pleasant. The prix-fixe menu includes beverage pairings, but guests at the bar may order drinks à la carte. The dishes spark interest. It may start with a pristine sea scallop with diced kohlrabi, dressed tableside with a brown butter sabayon, then perhaps a monkfish en papillote atop creamy Carolina Gold rice.
Invention is also a point of pride here, best seen in the baton of "French toast" that combines foie gras, blue cheese and black truffles. The butternut squash-ice cream cake with crème fraîche and pumpkin seeds is divine.

name: Jônt
review:
Dining at Ryan Ratino's daring offshoot of sister restaurant Bresca, which sits just above, is an intimate experience replete with surprises. Akin to stumbling into a gem off the beaten path, this space is abuzz, and the highly technical cooking is exemplary.
The staff glide about seamlessly delivering dishes that are bold and beautiful. The meal is awe inspiring from start to finish, as in a rye tart with crème fraîche and zucchini, or bluefin tuna mingled with maitake mushrooms and black truffles. However, the heart of this menu is its top-shelf ingredients, perhaps a sliver of melting Spanish turbot in caviar-almond sauce or dry-aged pork on a bed of soft leeks. Rohan duck may be familiar, but soars to new heights with a decadent sauce Royale.

name: Ever
review:
This stylish, gray-hued room, set off the beaten path in Fulton Market, has a peaceful and meditative mood. Fitted out with velvet-smooth leather seats and plush carpeting, there is an inviting sense of intimacy and diners are all the more ecstatic for it. The meal is first and foremost a visual thrill: inventive presentations that entice at every turn.
A penchant for sweet and herbaceous notes winds through each elegant composition, like green apple and nasturtium with a frozen celery root cream that balances briny flavors with earthiness. You'll also find notes of whimsy, evidenced by sweet bay scallops, presented under a sugar shell. Speaking of, desserts show substance and subtlety, like a combination of stout, sweet potato, and chocolate.

name: Oriole
review:
Thanks to a dramatic renovation, Oriole has resurfaced in fine fettle—even more graceful and luxurious than before. While its industrial bones remain, the space now has a bespoke elegance evidenced by imposing ceilings and an impressive bar. The beautifully appointed kitchen is in full view.
Chef Noah Sandoval and team are deeply committed to and passionate about their unbridled creations. Your meal may start with an aperitif and bites, like raw hiramasa in apple broth. New Zealand langoustine is elevated to luscious heights thanks to tapioca, melon, and a warm coconut broth; while sablefish nestled into koshihikari rice is enhanced tableside with amazake. Lemon soufflé with Délice de Bourgogne reflects an inspired take on the faithful cheese course.

name: Smyth
review:
Smyth is so very chic, styled with a small lounge area resembling a living room, while a large portion of the floor plan is devoted to the impressive open kitchen. 
This talented brigade, led by Chefs John Shields and Karen Urie Shields, has evolved since opening. Theirs is cooking that is desirable, impactful, and doesn't need an onslaught of luxury ingredients to impress. Instead, sheer creativity is applied to seasonal produce. Wild Maine mussels are in a savory licorice cream; chilled avocado delights with Bangkok guava paste and hoja santa. Then uni arrives glazed in egg yolk, while venison is spruced up with truffle liver ragout and sauce civet. For dessert, saffron ice cream drizzled with beeswax-thickened honey sits atop roasted quince.

name: Moody Tongue
review:
Chef Jared Wentworth and Brewmaster, Jared Rouben, have envisioned a unique showcase, whereby a hyper-seasonal and creative menu is brilliantly matched with a virtuosic array of house-crafted brews. Discreetly perched atop the working brewery, this is a contemporary if at times austere dining room. Unsurprisingly, the word "moody" befits the intimate yet masculine vibe.
Beverages are an equal partner to the food and even woven into the fabric of the elevated cuisine. Indulge in such innovative creations as gently poached Maine lobster in spiced tomato water, followed by seared Hudson Valley foie gras with burnt peach dashi. A dark chocolate cake with toasted rye ice cream will lift your spirits and have you returning for more—perhaps as soon as tomorrow.

name: La Table de Pavie
review: Yannick Alléno (appointed by Gérard Perse, emblematic owner of Château Pavie), now supervises this local institution that used to be a convent, whose nuns offered protection to pilgrims and travellers. The owners may have changed the name of the establishment (now Hôtel et Table de Pavie), but high standards and authenticity remain the order of the day. The chef from the Île-de-France region has installed a team of trusted cooks and is gradually reorienting the menu towards the South-West, albeit still with the sauces and reductions that are his trademark and his signature. Don't miss the iconic roast pigeon dish ("pigeon soufflé et rôti au feu de l'enfer"). Needless to say, the dishes are accompanied by the superb wines of St Émilion – a memorable experience.

name: William Frachot
review: Local boy William Frachot is something of a globetrotter (England, Quebec). Awarded his first star at the Hostellerie du Chapeau Rouge in 2003, he concocts dishes in his own image: serious and applied, juggling international flavours and regional produce, and just the right amount of inventiveness and energy. Meals are served in a distinctive interior featuring light wood panels, vine motifs and mustard yellow "shark" swivel chairs, each design choice a nod to Burgundy's heritage. Inspired and accomplished cuisine with influences from far and wide, such as calf's head and langoustines or roast leg of Aveyron lamb – their emblematic dishes.

name: Duende
review: Duende! Come and see how the arts of bullfighting and flamenco dancing have ignited the imagination of Pierre Gagnaire. The fine dining restaurant of the Hotel Imperator has its own separate entrance, which is indicative of the chef's independent spirit. Quality ingredients, proven technical expertise, spontaneity and originality in the execution by Nicolas Fontaine and Julien Caligo, who seem to know their mentor and his rebellious spirit inside out. The tasting menu pays a subtle tribute to the finest ingredients from the Gard and the Mediterranean region (Baron des Cévennes pork, vegetables from small market gardeners, fish from the Mediterranean) in subtle and delicate dishes. The superb list of over 1 000 wines has a clear penchant for regional productions. Charming welcome, highly professional and elegant service.

name: La Scène
review: Stéphanie Le Quellec, who has made a resounding comeback in Avenue Matignon (8th arrondissement) has professed her aim to "deconsecrate great cuisine". Finally with a place to call her own, she is committed heart and soul to this project. She cooks up a storm in three set menus composed of three, four or seven "acts". The dishes may appear simple but every last detail has been carefully considered (caviar, French toast, Pompadour apples) and the flavours come through loud and clear. She reprises some of her signature dishes, and we revel in pastry chef Pierre Chirac's top-notch desserts that are bursting with flavour, as in his Tahitian vanilla crème brûlée and Madagascan vanilla ice cream. There is a fine choice of wines by the glass served in magnum and even jeroboam... And it all comes together thanks to a team that runs like a well-oiled machine, from the kitchen to the front-of-house staff, to the attentive and friendly service. At lunchtime, you can eat in the bistro, where a tempting gourmet menu based on seasonal ingredients is served.

name: Palais Royal Restaurant
review: This elegant restaurant boasts an idyllic setting in the gardens of the Palais Royal, a stone's throw from the Ministry for Culture. Greek chef Philip Chronopoulos officiates, after working at Joël Robuchon's Atelier (its Étoile location) and with Alain Passard. Using superb ingredients, he cooks up creative and striking cuisine, designing invigorating and remarkably mature recipes: fine mezze as an amuse-bouche, green bean salad with caviar and Isigny cream; or the fig, vanilla and elderflower millefeuille – a simply remarkable dessert. In summer, the terrace under the arcades offers you a setting of a standard to match your meal. "Royal" is indeed the word.

name: Le Clarence
review: Christophe Pelé has taken over this sumptuous 1884 private mansion with characteristic enthusiasm and ability. It is located near the Champs-Élysées, a district the chef knows well, having worked at Ledoyen, Lasserre, Pierre Gagnaire, and Le Bristol. He has certainly found his feet in the kitchen. A true artist when it comes to combining produce from land and sea, he serves up highly personal cuisine with bold and distinct flavours – it never fails to deliver on what it promises. The "surprise" tasting menu, with its concept of "satellite" additions to the main dish, works well. The wine list is enough to make your head spin (ask to visit the beautiful vaulted cellar that houses the grands crus). A memorable experience.

name: Restaurant Le Meurice Alain Ducasse
review: Take an iconic luxury hotel opposite the Jardin des Tuileries and an incredibly gifted chef, Alain Ducasse, then add a sprinkling of luxury à la Versailles (white ceiling adorned with gilding, crystal chandeliers) and – voilà! – you get Le Meurice. This place has not failed to catch the imagination of wealthy foreign patrons, who come to soak up that certain Parisian je ne sais quoi. The Ducasse brand is cultivated by Amaury Bouhours, a loyal follower, with tasting menus comprised of small portions that pay homage to French tradition and the chef's creativity. The talented and media-savvy Cédric Grolet composes trompe-l'oeil desserts, images of which do the rounds on social networks.

name: Le Gabriel - La Réserve Paris
review: Just off the Champs-Élysées, this restaurant is ensconced in the elegant, luxurious setting of La Réserve, a stunning 19C Haussmann edifice. No stranger to top Parisian establishments (Bernard Pacaud, Alain Senderens), Jérôme Banctel has taken advantage of recent events to change course entirely. This Breton now invites his guests to partake in set menus (no choice) on a journey that revisits the flavours of Brittany and beyond, as inspired by his extensive travels, notably to Turkey. This reclaimed freedom unveils the chef’s genuine culinary identity, as he balances acidity, spices and seafood with the talent of a cosmopolitan alchemist. He prepares his dishes with superb ingredients (some of which you may never even have heard of, let alone tasted), never straying from his solid classical foundations. His lobster on a binchotan BBQ, almond pralines, peaches in verbena or his hake with morels in razor clam jus and green peas are truly out of this world.

name: Le Taillevent
review: A legendary Parisian establishment if ever there was one, Le Taillevent is the epitome of French classicism (a property of the Gardinier family, which also owns Les Crayères in Reims). This venerable setting, once the private mansion of the Duke of Morny (19C), is a hushed and intimate space, suitable for business meals. Dishes include saddle of lamb with green olives and chanterelles in pastry, or "Taillevent tradition" scampi black pudding. The desserts do not disappoint, especially the crêpes Suzette, flambéed first with Grand Marnier and then with Cognac – a classic. Finally, we must extol the superb list of 2 800 wines with a range of prices to suit all pockets – from under 40€ to 16 000€ per bottle. A reference point in the world of gastronomy.

name: David Toutain
review: David Toutain, who made a name for himself at a series of renowned establishments (Arpège, Agapé Substance), has brought a melting pot of culinary trends to this quiet street in a neighbourhood of government buildings. In a modern, loft-style space, he serves contemporary flavours in the form of an ambitious cuisine d'auteur: a light touch, a penchant for vegetables, and a refined aesthetic sensibility. You can sense the fire in the chef's belly and the wisdom that comes with that age when an inner balance allows one to get to grips with (and channel!) one's creativity.

name: L'Abysse au Pavillon Ledoyen
review: A Japanese sushi master, outstanding quality ingredients (ikejime fish from the Atlantic) and the creative touch of Yannick Alléno… an enticing prospect. The pared-back restaurant room features work by contemporary artists – the installation made up of thousands of wooden chopsticks is by Japanese artist Tadashi Kawamata and the ceramic walls were designed by the American William Coggin. Add to this the tip-top service typical of a high-calibre establishment, a sumptuous wine list full of sought-after sakes and 12 seats at the pale wood counter, where you are right in the middle of the action. Sensational!

name: La Fourchette des Ducs
review: Chef Nicolas Stamm-Corby strikes the perfect balance between celebrating the classics and a touch of inventiveness that hits the spot every time. Whatever the season, he regales us with artfully presented dishes, in which premium produce takes the limelight. In winter, Théo Kieffer's ballotine of squab and Alsace foie gras, cabbage stuffed with "fil d'or" sauerkraut and pigeon jus with truffles sing a heartfelt ode to Alsace! Gifted pastry chef Benjamin Mornay demonstrates his skill with an exquisite chocolate tart featuring a tempting array of cocoa flavours, on the menu all year round, while the memory of his bloody orange encased in a white chocolate shell with a bourbon vanilla ganache and a bloody orange sorbet lingers with us still, not to mention the almost indecent trolley of miniature delights: fruit tarts, kougelhopf, financiers and madeleines…

name: Maison Rostang
review: Chef Nicolas Beaumann enthusiastically perpetuates the tradition of delicious food that has always been synonymous with this emblematic establishment. His menu features a combination of "Rostang classics" and more personal dishes. Diners can still enjoy the oven-baked pike-perch quenelle, but also lobster glazed on the barbecue, or pressed duckling prepared in time-honoured tradition in the restaurant room with a silver press. The decor, at once luxurious and unusual, works its magic on newcomers and regulars alike: Art Nouveau Room, Lalique Room, Chef's Room with a window into the kitchen, artwork collection.

name: Yoann Conte
review: Breton chef Yoann Conte discovered the meaning of fraternity and the importance of food on the high seas. He champions the art of mixing unpolished, straightforward dishes with the exclusive world of fine dining. An extreme hiker in his spare time, he deploys his herbalist know-how in his lakeside garden. His cooking is in his likeness: physical, down-to-earth, adventurous and with a wry smile. Supported by a highly motivated team and often to be found doing the rounds in the dining room, he creates set menus such as "Ty bihan", "Lenn-Braz" and "Ultime Synthèse", in which mountain produce meets fish and seafood. The food and wine pairings, intelligently chosen by the chef and his sommelier, are emblematic of the establishment’s sustainable ethos. There are also eleven lovely guestrooms overlooking the lake.

name: Casadelmar
review: Here in Porto Vecchio, everything revolves around the sea. This ancient Genoese city resisted every barbarian invasion. Destroyed and rebuilt, its citadel is a symbol of pride for Corsicans. Another source of pride is the Casadelmar restaurant: a mecca for lovers of seafood. Don't be distracted by the enchanting view of the bay, or the location of this superb hotel – it is on the plate that the most amazing things happen! Chef Fabio Bragagnolo is inspired by both Corsica and Italy. Among his favourite dishes are the cannelloni dentex with crab, caviar, fresh vegetables and citrons from San Giuliano. The raw fish, cut into thin strips, is filled with crumbled crabmeat and topped with a small scoop of caviar for a dash of iodine flavour. The fresh sensation on the taste buds is insane. Meticulous work from start to finish, culminating in desserts that are light in sugar and rich in finesse.

name: Table - Bruno Verjus
review: Bruno Verjus has a credo: select the finest ingredients and cook them with humility and the utmost respect. The "self-taught chef", as he calls himself, is a remarkable character: an entrepreneur, blogger, food critic and now even an author. In his open kitchen facing the customers, he is a charismatic orator, talking about his suppliers and his desire to take a back seat to the artisans who produce what he cooks – on that note, when it comes to either the recipes or the ingredients, the chef considers himself above all a "middle man". Everything is made to order, with garnishes and sauces designed with just one thing in mind: to elevate the ingredient without distorting it. The deliberately short menu presents atypical compositions (some with equally unusual names): homard à croquer presque vivant sur son rocher ("lobster so fresh it's practically alive on its rock"); red mullet Rossini (and its succulent sauce); pink praline tart made according to Henry Cornil's recipe for Alain Chapel.

name: Le Pré - Xavier Beaudiment
review: "The Auvergne that I want to present to you is the one that we harvest every morning on our mountains, in our meadows and our forests". What is pleasing about Xavier Beaudiment, a native of the region, is that his proclamations are not empty words. Le Pré, in Clermont-Ferrand, is the epitome of simplicity – he draws on pork, eggs or peas, which are not necessarily ingredients that make your mouth water! But they are crafted with breathtaking technical skill: forget the menu and the seasons, and let yourself be swept along by instinctive cuisine that is moulded into poetic-sounding set menus – "Parfums des Prés", "Printemps dans nos Montagnes". And let's not forget the involvement of the 200 plants or wild herbs that grow around the volcanoes, nor the local snails served in a jus made with freshly picked linden. Chef Xavier Beaudiment is reason enough to visit Clermont-Ferrand.

name: La Chèvre d'Or
review: What is striking as you arrive at the Château de la Chèvre d'Or is its exceptional location. Perched high up on the flank of a rocky hillside in this medieval village, the place commands stunning views of the Côte d'Azur hinterland and the Mediterranean. Once you have taken in the jaw-dropping view, it is time to sit down to dinner – here again, there is plenty to get enthusiastic about. Drawing on delicious produce sourced in the area (fish, meat, vegetables, olive oil and herbs) and all the talent we associate with him, Arnaud Faye creates harmonious and precise dishes bordering on the irresistible. Meanwhile, pastry chef Julien Dugourd works wonders: his "vision of a local lemon" has become his signature dessert.

name: Le Grand Restaurant - Jean-François Piège
review: Welcome to Jean-François Piège's "laboratory of great cuisine", a tiny dining area beneath a sculptural ceiling made up of panes of glass that catch and reflect the light. The chef gives full expression to the scope and breadth of his experience and know-how, executing timeless signature cuisine that finds its source in historical cookbooks of French gastronomy (the chef is said to own one of the finest cookery libraries of Paris). There is no carte but a tasting menu that tours the regions of France and revolves around Piège’s "mijotés modernes". This consummate chef demonstrates his creative talent and ability to provoke culinary emotion and taste without falling foul of the temptation to needlessly showcase his skills … He thus surprises us with a dish that is the epitome of simplicity, such as his succulent langoustine, seared on a Parisian paving stone and flanked by delicate seaweed and a buckwheat sabayon.

name: La Côte d'Or
review: It has been 40 years since Patrick Bertron arrived at the Relais Bernard Loiseau. And in 2003, when Bernaud Loiseau suddenly passed away, it was he who took the reins in the kitchen. He has remained faithful to the philosophy of this institution, while enriching the menu with dishes of his own. He draws inspiration from his native Brittany, courtesy of its marvellous fish and seafood (lobster, langoustine, turbot), but also Burgundy, whose treasures he has learned to unlock. Nostalgic guests can hark back to Bernard Loiseau's time with some of his great "classics".

name: Le Skiff Club
review: In this 1930s Basque hotel nestled in a pine forest and redesigned by designer Philippe Starck, Le Skiff Club restaurant is a veritable haven with its cosy little dining area decorated in the style of a yacht club. Stéphane Carrade is a talented and skilled captain, cooking up delightful "progressive terroir" cuisine, in a superb celebration of the Aquitaine region of southwest France. This is a chef who combines generosity and finesse in dishes such as roasted lobster with grilled avocado and Cumeo pepper, or Pyrenean lamb noisettes with date juice, accompanied by fine slices of truffles and ceps. Finally, Alexandre Blay's desserts keep all the promises this restaurant makes: his raspberry with a creamy basil sablé biscuit, sorbet vinegar marmalade and beetroot foam is poetic, light and precise.

name: L'Oiseau Blanc
review: This is the "contemporary French fine dining" restaurant at The Peninsula, a luxury hotel located near the Arc de Triomphe. It is named after the plane in which Nungesser and Coli attempted the first North Atlantic crossing in 1927, and a life-size replica of the plane is affixed to the top of the hotel, as if poised to take to the skies before your very eyes. A fine tribute to the two aviation pioneers, as well as to the sky over Paris! Perched above the rooftops and encased in glass, the restaurant feels like it is in flight over the capital, while the terrace offers a fantastic view of the Eiffel Tower and the Sacré Cœur. A perfect setting in which to sample the fine cuisine of chef David Bizet, which hits the nail on the head in all respects: cooking, jus and sauces, visuals. As for the desserts, pastry chef Anne Coruble treats our taste buds to the fruits of her talents. A great success.

name: Anne de Bretagne
review: On the south bank of the Loire estuary, this large contemporary building stands facing the small port of Gravette. Mathieu Guibert is the talented chef here. Originally from the Pays de Retz and the son of a farmer, he has forged solid links with producers from the region who are just as passionate about what they do as he is. It is no surprise that seafood plays a leading role here. Depending on the catch of the day, the menu might feature whiting from small-scale fishing accompanied by iodine-rich cockles; pollack delicately preserved in a watercress sauce; "vialone nano" risotto cooked with smoked eel, thick carpaccio of Breton langoustines and parmesan emulsion (his signature dish!). Impeccable and smiling service orchestrated by Claire Bâcle. A moment well spent!

name: Villa René Lalique
review: Little known to the general public, René Lalique was the most prominent jeweller of the turn of the century and the Art Nouveau movement. His legacy lives on in Wingen-sur-Moder with a museum, a luxury hotel... and Villa René Lalique, which celebrated its 100th anniversary in 2020. At the helm of the restaurant is Paul Stradner, a chef influenced by his time in Austria and Germany; potato emulsion and truffle strips (a major classic of the house); goose liver terrine, grape jelly and pumpkin chutney; sea bass, cabernet sauce, shellfish and celery. Finesse, intelligence, creativity... right down to the desserts by Nicolas Multon: this pastry chef, who wanted to become a fine artist, now makes ephemeral masterpieces (mango, vanilla rice pudding and passion fruit). Don't miss the sumptuous glass-paned wine cellar.

name: La Table de l'Alpaga
review: How delightful it is to settle in at your table in this stylish, snug venue, in which untreated and premium materials (such as marble and oak) have been used to create a timeless decor. The gourmet table, which enjoys a matchless view of Mont Blanc, is devoted to enhancing Savoie produce with a weakness for vegetables. The bistro is open 7/7, for lunch and dinner. Take your time and relax in style in the cosy guestrooms fitted out in pretty chalets.

name: Le Neuvième Art
review: It was in the kitchens of Paul Bocuse and Régis Marcon, among others, that Christophe Roure learnt the ropes. He holds three professional qualifications (in cooking, charcuterie and pastry-making, no less!) and was named Meilleur Ouvrier de France in 2007. Based in Lyon since 2014, he showcases his qualities as a chef day in, day out: subtle inventiveness, precision in his marriages of flavours, and of course an irreproachable choice of ingredients. For example, his "oyster and razor clam in a peaty jelly, winter tartine and coffee cloud" is a marvel that succeeds in combining the aromas of seafood, undergrowth and roasting. A coherent and demanding dish in which everything is placed deliberately: to be savoured with all one's senses alert, as if listening to Mahler's Ninth Symphony.

name: Racine
review: Here in the heart of Reims, there is definitely something interesting afoot. This small restaurant has a delightfully pared-back and contemporary interior with bay windows looking out onto a charming Japanese garden. The setting is in perfect harmony with the cuisine of Kazuyuki Tanaka, a Japanese chef and former second-in-command to Régis Marcon. He crafts elegant and creative dishes that are rife with different flavours and influences. Each one surprises in terms of the quality of the ingredients, technical mastery and aesthetics. Aromatic herbs, vegetables, plants and condiments are savvily incorporated. Fine wine list, including 250 champagnes.

name: Les Morainières
review: Michaël Arnoult, who was sous-chef to Emmanuel Renaut, has transformed this place overlooking the hilly vineyards and the Rhone Valley into a veritable corner of paradise. His modus operandi: using fresh ingredients and respecting those who cultivated them. Choosing local producers, getting to know them and collaborating with them is a matter of priority. Game, green asparagus, suckling lamb, trout or Arctic char... you get a sense of his exacting standards in the dishes. If we had to pick a representative dish, it might be the superbly fresh crayfish tartar, enhanced by its subtle carcass jus, coriander flowers and sweet marigold: pure excellence! The refined interior reflects the chef's cuisine and looks out onto the valley. There are six comfortable guestrooms a few kilometres from the restaurant. More than ever, Les Morainières is worth the detour.

name: La Merise
review: This traditional Alsace house near Haguenau is a remarkable new construction built out of old materials so as to seamlessly blend in with its rural setting overlooking the hills and orchards. It is the haunt of Christelle and Cédric Deckert. Using high-quality ingredients, the chef concocts his own intriguing take on classical, yet never boring recipes, enhanced by subtle and skilfully prepared jus and sauces. The brilliant sommelier Joël Brendel is a treasure trove of insightful tips.

name: La Villa Archange
review: A cosy little venue with old wooden floorboards and big comfy armchairs – the ideal setting to sample chef Bruno Oger's cuisine. Breton by birth, he has adopted the Mediterranean as his home, and now concocts inspired seafood dishes drawn from Brittany and the French Riviera… Abalone from the island of Groix seared with artichokes rubs shoulders with Brittany lobster, followed by a lemon dessert of citrus fruits, bloody orange sorbet and olive oil. A table d'hôte in the kitchen provides the opportunity to glean insights into the culinary process. Also the official chef of the Cannes Film Festival, Bruno Oger has cooked for many an A-lister: Uma Thurman, Robert De Niro and Audrey Tautou... Confirmation, if any were needed, of his credentials.

name: Maison Aribert
review: Christophe Aribert is thriving in his restaurant in a fine 19C house built against the hillside in Uriage Park. A nature lover, he has made eco-responsibility the foundation of his establishment: waste management, pellet heating system, organic cotton fabrics... Every aspect has been considered in terms of its impact on the environment. The chef's passion for herbs and roots from the surrounding mountains is more pronounced than ever; these sit alongside the fruit, vegetables and flowers from the kitchen garden in the dishes. His cuisine is also an ode to freshwater fish. Finally, let's not forget the comfortable guestrooms on offer – ideal should you wish to stay a little longer.

name: Hostellerie Jérôme
review: Perhaps the first thing to mention is that Bruno Cirino's restaurant, housed in the converted refectory of an annexe of Lérins Abbey, has bags of style: high ceilings, painted vaults, Pompei-like frescoes of fruit and vegetables, beautiful tiles and a 17C fireplace, plus, a small flower-decked terrace with a sea view. As for the food, the dishes are a reflection of the chef himself: generous, full of character, the embodiment of the South of France… He uses ingredients from the Mediterranean region – sourced from both sides of the border with Italy – to great effect (fish from nearby ports, vegetables from neighbouring folk).

name: La Marine
review: Alexandre Couillon rises at dawn to go to Noirmoutier fish auction, which sells the best Atlantic fish, before stopping by his own vegetable garden, just a few minutes from the restaurant. The tasting menu, which religiously keeps pace with the seasons and availability, exalts and celebrates fine ingredients, allowing them to shout their name with a simplicity that only the world’s top chefs can attain. Knowing what and where to strip back and pare down to release the flavours and tantalise the eater’s imagination is a fine art. The quality of the fish, seafood and vegetables is exceptional. Alexandre’s other talents include cooking over a fire, harvesting coastal plants, fruit coulis and vegetable pickles, broth and gutsy jus, without forgetting cooking fish to absolute perfection! Memories shine bright of both the mackerel cooked over hot embers and accompanied by confit beetroot or an incredible lettuce grilled over a flame, blueberries in elderflower vinegar and the dessert of buckwheat, caramel mousse, confit citrus fruits and sea lettuce (seaweed) sorbet. The interior has been revamped in natural materials and soft colours, while the grocery shop, Le Petit Couillon, sells produce from the artisans and farmer partners.

name: Jean-Luc Tartarin
review: Le Havre – its port, its architects (especially Auguste Perret and Oscar Niemeyer, icons of 20C urbanism), its renewed joie de vivre... Jean-Luc Tartarin, a Caen native, who trained most notably at Les Crayères in Reims and at the restaurant Gill in Rouen, creates cuisine that expresses his passion for food. Some of the chef's inspiration comes from the catch brought into the port (line-caught or small-scale fishing) and the rest on ingredients from Normandy. Guaranteed freshness! It is a winning combination, to be enjoyed in a cosily refurbished interior done out in soothing beige tones. Plus, you are in a UNESCO World Heritage area. Nice wine list and good selection of calvados.

name: La Pyramide - Patrick Henriroux
review: Originally a modest inn opened in 1822, this Vienne institution went on to be made famous by the legendary Mado and Fernand Point in the early 20C, before being taken over by Patrick Henriroux in 1989. Since then, it has continued to evolve: a designer decor for the dining space, the addition of a second restaurant (PH3) and a charming hotel etc. As for the food here, classic recipes are given a contemporary twist, with everything being prepared precisely and with a sense of moderation. Lobster with tarragon orange vinaigrette; Arctic char cooked over an open flame, pulp of Cévennes sweet onions; chocolate piano, grilled coffee sauce. Note the great deal to be had with the lunch menu (a real bargain) and the service that is attentive down to the smallest detail, continuing in the tradition of the great French establishments.

name: Michel Kayser - Restaurant Alexandre
review:
