The website sets the tone with its disclaimer that "dishes can vary according to the availability of fresh ingredients and the inspirations of the chef". You get the picture! Between Nîmes and Arles, in grounds planted with hundred-year-old cedars, Michel Kayser does what he does best: cooking from the heart, elevating ingredients, putting his technical skills to good use in a bid to stir the emotions of visitors to his restaurant.
Simply put, there is no other chef in the area who celebrates the South of France with such precision and aplomb. Tarbouriech oysters and shellfish in a cardamom jelly, or tielle de Sète (octopus pie) with lobster and crab knuckles, Mediterranean squid and gambero rosso – a veritable procession of Mediterranean ingredients, from both land and sea combined, and a real treat for adventurous taste buds. This chef has a sure touch.

name: Jean Sulpice
review: The Auberge du Père Bise is more full of life than ever in the capable hands of Jean Sulpice and Magali, his wife! An avid sportsman, the chef serves fine cuisine that is also healthy and light. Herbs, flowers and wild plants bring contrasts and colours to his creative and incisive dishes, which are a delicious roll call of fish from the lake. For example, the "Omble chevalier beurre maître d'hôtel à l'épicéa" (Arctic char with a remarkable spruce butter) or the precisely prepared and extremely fresh smoked whitefish. The wine list includes a separate booklet entirely dedicated to the wines located within the limits of the former duchy of Savoy. This poetic experience unfolds in an elegant contemporary dining space that opens out onto the terrace and takes in the silvery shores of Lake Annecy, the cleanest lake in Europe. An exceptional foil for this slick and bold gastronomy.

name: La Grand'Vigne - Les Sources de Caudalie
review: Only a few kilometres from Bordeaux, this place is a true corner of paradise nestled in the vineyards. It has been given a completely new look, in harmony with its natural surroundings. Nicolas Masse is the chef behind La Grand'Vigne, the hotel's fine dining restaurant. He is squarely focused on one goal: to showcase the Aquitaine terroir (and its vegetable cornucopia) and wines, especially those of Pessac Léognan. The white wine brings out the pearliness of the line-caught hake cooked with courgette flowers, drenched in a fish stock with white wine infused with nasturtium; the red wine beautifully accompanies the Pyrenean suckling lamb cooked rare and garnished with small Médoc chanterelles and a bugne (fritter) stuffed with confit shoulder.

name: Mère Brazier
review: Eugénie Brazier (1895-1977), an exceptional chef who inspired an entire branch of French cuisine, obtained three stars in two different establishments. It is in her Lyon restaurant, on rue Royale, that Mathieu Viannay gives his take on the Brazier "legend". In a magnificent hybrid decor, 1930s stained glass windows and mouldings are blended with Saarinen Tulip chairs (a bold design move!) and the chef pays a vibrant tribute to the iconic dishes once served on the premises (Bresse chicken with truffles, crispy pike bread, a stunning Grand Marnier soufflé), infusing them with his talent and novel ideas. Be sure to try the lunch menu, which represents the best value for money. When it comes to dessert, pastry chef Rodolphe Tronc, who has worked for Pierre Gagnaire among others, takes no prisoners with his remarkable technique and his eye for detail, especially when it comes to his delightfully old-fashioned Norwegian omelette.

name: Le Coquillage
review: Hugo Roellinger began his career as an officer in the Merchant Navy, before returning to dry land in France… and to cooking, a passion that he has nurtured since childhood. He trained with the crème de la crème of the chef world, patiently refining his art. Today his dishes are a testament to the forging of a true culinary personality. He is now at the helm of the family ship (a château magnificently perched over the Bay of Mont Saint Michel), where he demonstrates astounding conviction and a deep-rooted sense of modesty. In the dishes, home-grown aromatic herbs and vegetables as well as fish (and shellfish) caught in the Bay of Mont Saint Michel mingle with numerous spices from further afield, in the greatest Saint-Malo tradition. The emotion rises to a crescendo over the course of the meal, thanks to a bewitching interplay of flavours and masterful creativity.

name: Relais de la Poste
review: The Coussau family are champions of classicism. Chef, Jean, and his niece, Clémentine, conjure up heart-warming food that pays tribute to the splendid produce of les Landes: foie gras, poultry, Chalosse beef, salmon from the Adour River and fish from Capbreton. A closeknit network of local suppliers enable them to rustle up signature dishes that the regulars come here in droves to sample: scrambled eggs with black truffles, warm duck foie gras with raisins and sole with cèpes. In autumn, you may sample roast woodpigeon or hare à la royale, without forgetting a superbly airy and creamy Grand Marnier soufflé, filled with a refreshing sorbet of bloody orange. Fine French dining at its best in a knockout location between the Atlantic Ocean and pine forests.

name: La Grenouillère
review: Few chefs show such a strong culinary personality as Alexandre Gauthier in La Madelaine-sous-Montreuil (near the northern tip of France). The story unfolds in a space with two tiered metal rooftops (designed by architect Patrick Bouchain) and views onto the verdant surroundings and the kitchens. This is the laboratory in which the chef cooks up "contemporary cuisine with French roots, liberated from its certainties and preconceptions". Like an alchemist, he teases out flavours in on-point dishes, each a vignette of creativity in which the ingredients sing the praises of the seasons. Artistic and experimental cuisine, to be savoured in this old Picardy farmhouse imbued with a luxury that remains close to nature.

name: Le Chabichou by Stéphane Buron
review: Stéphane Buron, a well-established chef and Meilleur Ouvrier de France in 2004, faithfully perpetuates the heritage of this institution: premium ingredients prepared in time-honoured tradition, a repertoire full of finesse and welcome variations on the classics... fine work! Nowadays they serve a single set menu of five to nine courses that highlights the ingredients of the region, down to the trolley decked with fine mountain cheeses. As for the decor, the interior exudes a hushed elegance: carpeting, coffered ceiling, comfortable immaculate-white designer chairs, modern tables with smoked glass tops. On top of that, charming service and a great wine list.

name: Au 14 Février
review: It is obviously all about love at Au 14 Février: love for ingredients, love for technical artistry, the love of a good job well done. Japanese chef Masafumi Hamano crafts dishes like real works of art, always finding that extra ingredient that boosts the whole dish and makes the decisive difference. He is like a master of ceremonies at a lavish wedding between France and Japan (another love story!), hosting a wedding party at which we tuck into the banquet unabashedly. Marinated salmon steak with anchovy-garlic cream and celeriac purée; pan-fried duck liver with mango quarters and crunchy endive leaves; or monkfish piccata served on a lemon and chickpea carbonara... Will you, too, be enamoured?

name: La Palme d'Or
review: Some places you fall in love with at first sight and La Palme d'Or is one of them. In the fabulous Art Deco setting of the Hotel Martinez, diners look down on the famous promenade of La Croisette and the Bay of Cannes, while savouring the luxury and refinement so beautifully brought together here. Of course, all this would be worth nothing without high-calibre cuisine. No worries on that score: chef Christian Sinicropi, a local man, has matters entirely in hand. At each stage of the "Mouvements" set menu, he homes in on one ingredient, supporting it with elements from its own ecosystem. The result is coherent and sophisticated, right down to the remarkably precise desserts by Julien Ochando. Definitely worthy of a Golden Palm award.

name: Maison Jeunet
review: In this elegant and opulent château near the River Loue, Flemish chef Steven Naessens tirelessly perfects and revisits the classics that have made the reputation of Arbois's emblematic restaurant. His approach entails scouring the produce of the terroir for all the nuances of possible marriages of flavour with Jura grape varieties: snails in Savagnin broth, Bresse chicken with its famous vin jaune and morel sauce, hare à la royale etc. The wonderful wine list dedicates pride of place to Burgundy and Jura wines. As for the decor, the monumental paintings and tableware are the exclusive creations of prolific Besançon artist Charles Belle.

name: La Côte Saint-Jacques
review: This edifice on the banks of the Yonne is superlative! Founded by Marie Lorain in 1945, the establishment rose to fame in the hands of her son, Michel, and then her grandson, Jean-Michel. This modest, dedicated chef has now passed the baton on to his nephew, Alexandre Bondoux. Regulars can rest assured that the signature dishes are going nowhere (special Gillardeau oysters in an "ocean terrine", homemade black pudding); nor are the flashes of inspiration (caviar-flavoured île flottante; Crisenon char with peas and almonds). A symphony of flavours, high-flying craftsmanship and seasoning in an exquisite gourmet repertory, underscored by slick service.

name: Le Blue Bay
review: After moving from Martinique to Monaco and from Alsace to Belgium, Marcel Ravin, who exhibits a distinct culinary personality, signs off on creative cuisine that transports us to the West Indies. With flawless technical prowess (superb sauces), he recounts his personal history, including his happy youth spent in Martinique. He references the dishes cooked by his grandmother (calalou, blaff, "next day's bread"), which he reinterprets with panache, incorporating the fine ingredients of these parts: poultry and veal from Piedmont, fish from the Mediterranean, vegetables and aromatic herbs from the kitchen garden. An appealing cuisine bursting with West Indian flavours, nicely rounded off by the fruity and spicy creations of pastry chef Floriane Grand. Sit back and enjoy this culinary experience in the lavish setting of the Monte Carlo Bay Hotel and Resort, on the edge of the Larvotto Peninsula, with a superb terrace opening out onto the sea.

name: Sur Mesure par Thierry Marx
review: So much has been said about Thierry Marx: a great traveller, savvy alchemist, fan of tai chi, and head of the kitchens of the Mandarin Oriental – the luxury "haute couture" Parisian hotel that tailor-made this restaurant for his extravagant culinary creations. Step into this new world – immaculately white and distinctly cinematic, it is like something out of A Clockwork Orange or Gattaca. Everything bears the chef's signature style, not least his unique set menus, a succession of dishes with astonishing flavours. He brings his precise technical skill to bear on the ingredients, cleverly dabbling with transparency, flavours and textures. Soya "risotto" with oysters and chanterelles; trompe-l'oeil egg mimosa; line-caught pollack, plant-based oyster shell, pesto… What an experience.

name: La Voile - La Réserve Ramatuelle
review: This hotel, as exclusive as they come, is the work of architect Jean-Michel Wilmotte, who has integrated it perfectly into its natural surroundings. The restaurant housed in the hotel commands a sublime view of the sea. Born in Manosque, chef Éric Canino has been influenced by his long and fruitful collaboration with the inventor of the healthier "cuisine minceur", Michel Guérard. Inspired by the master, he composes his own Provençal cuisine, with fruit and vegetables, fish and seafood (plus some poultry), enhanced with aromatic herbs and olive oil – butter and cream are practically banished. From the tuna rubbed with exotic spices to Bresse chicken subtly combined with lobster, each recipe aspires to be healthy and light.

name: Le Pressoir d'Argent - Gordon Ramsay
review: British chef Gordon Ramsay (born in Scotland) is a true culinary talent who has already been awarded three Michelin stars in England. He signs off on Le Pressoir d'Argent's menu, which is brought to life by the talented Romain Lorenzon, who breathes a touch of modernity into the classic cuisine. It all comes together to enhance that French art de vivre – the opulent and refined decor and ultra competent service, the celebration of the finest ingredients from the abundant Bordeaux and Aquitaine region (foie gras, truffles, caviar, fish), the superb cheese trolley… and the solid silver Christofle lobster press that is moved from table to table. The competence of the three sommeliers is remarkable, as they advise you on the 1 000-bottle selection, two thirds of which are from Bordeaux, naturally!

name: L'Auberge des Glazicks
review: This former blacksmith's workshop was transformed into a farmhouse inn by the chef's grandmother. Back then it attracted workers and locals, who came for simple and invigorating fare – soup, vol-au-vents, leg of lamb. Under the impetus of Olivier Bellin, who returned in 1998, the transformation of this family-run Auberge was complete: inventive and versatile, the chef came into his own, brandishing an increasingly strong culinary personality. He works with an extraordinary network of carefully selected small-scale producers in Finistère, and there is a card on each table listing where each ingredient is from and who produced it. His dishes marry sea and land as if they were the most natural of partners: potato soufflé stuffed with oyster jus; langoustine and pig's trotter; cheese tortellini and trout eggs.

name: La Table Lionel Giraud
review: The place is named after Abbé St Crescent, who in the Middle Ages opened his doors to pilgrims on the Camino de Santiago. The arcades and bare stones may be a throwback to the distant past, but today the decor is ultra-modern, with finely crafted black and white polished concrete floors and sculptural one-piece seats. Lionel Giraud, son of a restaurant owner, is a strong advocate of locally sourced produce. An inventive chef, he honours ingredients from the most noble (Mediterranean red tuna) to the most modest (green beans) and everything in between, such as an authentic Corbières buffalo mozzarella. He is also a proponent of ikejime, the Japanese method of killing fish that maintains the quality of the meat and is argued to be more humane.

name: JY'S
review: Schillinger is a name that resonates particularly strongly in Alsace. First there was Jean, then his son Jean-Yves, who, after a period on the New York City restaurant scene (Destinée, Olica), returned home in 2002. Here in his restaurant on the edge of the Champ-de-Mars park, he is full of bright ideas. His cuisine embraces one tradition after another with disconcerting ease – Alsace, the United States, Brittany and Japan. Confident in his strengths, he has a no-holds-barred approach – as in, for example, his Breton lobster cooked in a Cona coffee maker and served with basil pasta and lobster nem, or lemon soufflé with tarragon and olive oil ice cream... not to mention the trolley decked with exquisite bite-sized desserts. A unique experience and exceptional flavours.

name: Auberge du Cheval Blanc
review: His mother was a seamstress, his father an ironmonger: not a restaurant owner in sight. And yet, here is the young Pascal Bastian, who became a commis at chef Fernand Mischler's Auberge du Cheval Blanc. Then he completed stints at some prestigious restaurants (including Les Crayères, in Reims, with Gérard Boyer), before returning to the Cheval Blanc. Now husband-and-wife team Carole and Pascal run this noble coaching inn (18C) that allies the charm of Alsace with contemporary refinement. Spaced-out tables mean guests enjoy a sense of privacy during this fine dining experience. The chef is a dab hand at cooking both classics and inventive dishes, and his comprehensive menu is full of finesse. He honours his region with high-quality ingredients – tuck into the big morels stuffed and glazed with a meat jus. If you want to stay longer in the region, guestrooms are available.

name: Auberge de l'Ill
review: The Auberge de l'Ill is much more than just a restaurant. It embodies the Alsace inn in all its glory – an inviting and friendly place, untouched by the passage of time, where every customer is welcomed like a member of the family… It is an institution in the region, but also renowned in France and beyond! Since it was established in 1882 (between Sélestat and Riquewihr), the restaurant has made a name for itself thanks to its matelote with Riesling and dishes based on game from the region. Marc Haeberlin, grandson of the founders, now serves traditional dishes (lobster timbale, frog mousseline, foie gras with spices) alongside more personal, more modern creations. The legend lives on.

name: Le Montgomerie
review: After a distinctly warm welcome, you are led to your table in the cosy little restaurant room – complete with exposed roof frame, tables covered in black leather, silver cutlery and fine glassware, and floral arrangements of white roses. It's hard to imagine a more intimate setting in which to let the creations of talented Dutch chef Pieter Riedijk work their magic… "Le Mont d'Or": creamy vacherin cheese, red cabbage and apple, melba bread tuile; cauliflower, creamy jus with sparkling Savoie wine and fermented garlic, seared scallops. And for dessert, the bold delights created by pastry chef Sébastien Vauxion (also chef at Le Sarkara) are fantastic – for example, "Le Siègle": roasted rye cream and velouté, pear in white wine, blueberry confit.

name: Le Puits Saint Jacques
review: Once a coaching stop on the Camino de Santiago, this typical old Gers house resounds with the lilting accents of the South-West of France. Bernard Bach, the long-time head chef here, has passed down his passion for cooking and his knowledge of regional ingredients to his nephew, chef William Candelon. Now running the show, he is rising to the challenge with style. While respecting the establishment's DNA (the culinary heritage of the South still takes centre stage), he does not shy away from unexpected and striking flavour combinations. Plus, thanks to his keen sense of proportion, he has no difficulty drawing us into his world. Beautiful presentations, fine ingredients, undeniable technical mastery: this institution is in safe hands.

name: Lalique
review: Château Lafaurie-Peyraguey is the quintessence of French art de vivre. The ceiling of the lavish dining room is adorned in 120 gilded Lalique crystal leaves and the conservatory commands a fine view of the vineyards. Chef Jérôme Schilling, who boasts an immaculate CV (including Guy Lassausaie, Joël Robuchon, Thierry Marx and Best Craftsman of France 2022), devises menus around the rich flavours of Sauternes produce and its world-famous wine. Scallops are paired with vine shoots, farm-raised pigeon with wine sediment and apples and caramel with the estate’s 2003 vintage… A subtle blend of classicism and regional specialties, the food is served in magnificent crystalware by Lalique and Bone China tableware, raising table arts to a whole new level. Intelligent, precise cuisine which aims to exalt the distinctive identity of Sauternes, which naturally enjoys a star position on the extensive wine list.

name: La Table de Franck Putelat
review: The fortified Cité Médiévale is part of the time-honoured heritage of Carcassonne and its region… and the same could almost be said of Franck Putelat. In his place at the foot of the ramparts of the medieval town, this native of the Jura, who has made the Aude département his home, cooks the produce from his large (one hectare) vegetable garden, in line with his culinary concept of "classic-fiction". This translates into a clever rendering of the old gourmet hits, which the chef revisits according to what inspires him on that day. Three examples that have become iconic are his parmentier with sea fig, cassoulet with pigeon supreme and pigeon leg sausage, and bouillabaisse with duck foie gras. Appetising visuals, flavour and finesse, to be savoured in a lively atmosphere, in the company of a very diverse clientele. Pastry chef Alexis Pocinho crafts a particularly balanced selection of sweets. There are four rooms available for overnight guests.

name: Christophe Hay - Fleur de Loire
review: Chef Christophe Hay is now installed in this new location, a converted 17C hospice right on the banks of the Loire. The centuries-old stone building looks out over the river, from which the chef draws all his inspiration. His interior designer, Caroline Tissier, was again on board to transpose his vision on the second floor of this fine hotel, which also includes a brasserie, a patisserie and a spa. In a modern space replete with premium materials, the chef can once again serve his creative fine dining repertoire and classic dishes, which are remarkable not only in their lightness, but also flavour and texture. He always takes pride in highlighting the best ingredients from the Loire Valley, fish (exclusively) from the Loire, caught by fisherman Sylvain Arnoult, vegetables from his own kitchen garden (which has also grown) as well as from local market gardeners, meat from his Wagyu farm; Ossetra caviar from Sologne; grilled eel; barbel; carp "à la Chambord"... A successful relocation!

name: Bras
review: "My family, friendship, Aubrac and cooking" are, in Sébastien Bras's own words, the four cornerstones of his life. Faithful to his father's heritage, but armed with a sensibility all of his own, the chef draws ingredients (flowers, herbs, vegetables) from his natural surroundings and his own gardens, before showcasing them on the plate. The flavours come thick and fast; the emotion often sneaks up on you, and you can almost hear the earth sing as you tuck into certain dishes. If you would like to stay over, lovely guestrooms with bay windows looking out onto the Aveyron countryside await you. From one generation to the next, Le Suquet continues on its exceptional and appealing path...

name: Paul Bocuse
review: No nickname can sum up the impact of the "pope of gastronomy", Paul Bocuse. An outstanding chef, as talented in the kitchen as he was in business, his passing in 2018 left chefs the world over speechless. He was the one who brought the kitchen teams and their chefs out of obscurity into the light: he was, in a way, the first of the modern class. Since the death of the great chef, the elite team of the establishment (two Meilleur Ouvrier de France chefs, a pastry chef who is a world champion in iced desserts) has been keeping his legacy alive, with crayfish tail gratin; VGE truffle soup, sea bass in a puff pastry crust, Bresse poultry en vessie…; and a magnificent dessert trolley. In Collonges-au-Mont-d'Or, the story is by no means over.

name: La Table d'Olivier Nasti
review: Ah, Kaysersberg! This small village on the Alsace wine route comes into view between two valleys – you can't miss the iconic red façade of Hotel Le Chambard, which houses La Table d'Olivier Nasti, Meilleur Ouvrier de France 2007. The chef's objective is to showcase the terroir and restore tradition in a series of creative, visually arresting, even playful dishes. To this end, no ingredients are off limits: game, morels from the Vosges, foie gras, eels from the Rhine, truffles and even Arctic char. He has created a personal menu that takes the seasons into account and pays particular attention to sauces and decoctions. As for the wine, talented and enthusiastic sommelier Jean-Baptiste Klein is a mine of information. The Chambard's guestrooms are decorated in a chic, refined style, and let's not forget the gorgeous spa.

name: Serge Vieira
review: A native of Clermont-Ferrand, Serge Vieira was destined for a career as an industrial designer before he changed direction and became a chef. It was a good call: after observing and learning in renowned establishments (Dominique Robert, Régis Marcon), he went on to win the Bocuse d'Or in 2005. In his contemporary location – all stone, iron and glass – in a medieval fortress with a 360° view of the surroundings, he is playing in the big league. His dishes are skilfully composed down to every last detail, and his culinary techniques never take precedence over flavour. One last thing: you can even book a guestroom complete with breathtaking views of the Cantal mountains.

name: Flaveur
review:
The Tourteaux brothers, Gaël and Mickaël, are inseparable. Not only did they attend the same hotel school in Nice (and sit exams in the same room) and both train at the Negresco during Alain Llorca's time there, but they also share the same motivation to run their own place, delivering good, honest, tasty fare. The result of this fraternal alliance is Flaveur, a project into which they ploughed all their energy to the point of receiving a Michelin star in 2011, and a second one in 2018.
How might the "Tourteaux touch" be summed up? A certain kind of confidence, boldness and measured risk-taking. For example, when it comes to local ingredients and spices from afar, it's not either/or, it's both! A scorpion fish from Nice comes up against a fish broth enhanced with vadouvan, a heavily aromatic blend of Indian spices... They often go out on a limb, but the risk always pays off. Fine and masterful cuisine with character from start to finish. Bravo!

name: Takao Takano
review: One cannot help but be impressed by the trajectory of Takao Takano's career. Originally from Yamanashi Prefecture, Japan, he didn't stick with his law studies for long, instead devoting himself to his true passion: cooking. Since 2013, he has been plying his trade in this elegant, pared-back restaurant located in the 6th arrondissement of Lyon. And if it has proved to be a hit with diners ever since opening, it is thanks to the original and refined dishes, which delight and surprise at the same time. They certainly fulfil the objective that the chef has set himself: "Keep it simple and delicious". Let's linger for a moment over the perfectly cooked fillet of Arctic char with crayfish tails, chanterelles and Chambéry vermouth, or the Poitou pigeon with Jerusalem artichokes, guanciale and Vaucluse truffle... Intelligently devised dishes replete with beautifully balanced flavours: that's Takao Takano down to a T.

name: Marsan par Hélène Darroze
review: Hélène Darroze reopened the doors of her restaurant on rue d'Assas in 2019 to reveal a completely new look in a cosy and elegant vein that suits this highly talented chef down to the ground. Needless to say, that special something that sets apart this descendant of a family of cooks from South-West France is still present in the dishes. Namely, the ability to scour these local regions (Aquitaine, Landes, Basque Country) for the raw materials she needs to nourish her culinary intentions, and the ability to highlight them in a given dish, for example, the splendid monkfish from small-scale fishing. Her rigour, insatiable curiosity and game-changing mixture of talent and intuition are also brought to bear on the dishes. An undeniable success.

name: Le Sarkara
review: Highly talented pastry chef Sébastien Vauxion takes you on a sweet journey, the likes of which you won't have experienced before. It feels unprecedented, or almost! His creations based on fruit and vegetables (but also chocolate) are quite simply astounding; take, for example, the celery-clementine, the grapefruit-beetroot, the chervil-tuber and the pear. And while the overall effect is undeniably sweet, rest assured: this is inventive and delicate cuisine, incorporating a brilliant interplay of textures and flavours, and even ultra-precise matches with high quality teas and coffees. One comes away feeling thrilled by the originality of it all. Imagine if desserts of this calibre were to be had in all the great restaurants of France.

name: L'Atelier d'Edmond
review: This place is reminiscent of a woodcut depicting an idyllic scene: a gorgeous chalet with a thackstone roof and a rustic-style, timber-panelled interior laid out around the majestic central fireplace. It rarely gets more quintessentially Alpine than this! Perpignan-born chef Benoît Vidal, who trained with Michel Guérard and Michel Trama, concocts a flavoursome cuisine that is firmly anchored in the present: for example, crayfish with pine zabaglione; flame-grilled Savoie trout and confit leeks; milk from the Ferme de l'Adroit, hay-infused ice cream… followed by a drink in the cosy little lounge on the mezzanine. Delicious. Two tasting menus (seven or 11 courses) at dinner and a 58€ lunch menu, which might just be the best deal in the Three Valleys.

name: Michel Sarran
review: Is it the spirit of the South? The poetry of the so-called Pink City? The personality of the chef, perhaps? Whatever the case may be, Sarran is a house more than it is a restaurant. The atmosphere, although all hushed tones, does not resemble those stuffy restaurants where you feel you have to tiptoe around. No, here, you eat of course, but first and foremost you live! Don't forget, Michel Sarran is a man of the South. Originally from the Gers département, he divided his time between the South-West and the Mediterranean. Then, in 1995, he settled in Toulouse, where he became one of the city's culinary ambassadors: "I like to delve into the drawers of my memory, play with lavender and violets, foie gras and parmesan, red mullet and pumpkin...". The restaurant is fully booked three months in advance on account of the chef's high profile.

name: Py-r
review: What a ball of energy this Pierre Lambinon is! Just a stone's throw from the Pont-Neuf, his cooking makes waves similar to the waters of the Garonne in heavy weather. Never short of ideas, he improvises with remarkable adroitness, from amuse-bouche (a real festival of flavours) to dessert, using to great effect the best produce from the market, in particular fish and shellfish available on any given day. The results are original, but he always pulls it off. Plus, the prices remain moderate in relation to the experience. As for the decor, you dine in a superb space where white predominates and the walls are hung with eye-catching paintings by contemporary artists. This place certainly has style.

name: Le Parc Les Crayères
review: In this mansion standing in superb grounds that used to belong to Louise Pommery, what would you expect but a memorable meal? In the manner of a true artisan, Meilleur Ouvrier de France chef Philippe Mille is constantly refining his style, which is based on elegantly reinterpreting the classics. Premium ingredients feature prominently on the menu (lobster, langoustine, foie gras, turbot) and are delicately prepared with a light touch, cleverly integrating materials associated with making Champagne: clay, vine shoots, vine leaves. Lastly, as expected, the Champagne list is astounding, with nearly 900 different types, carefully selected to pair up with the food. Dessert comes courtesy of the 2019 French champion Yoann Normand, whose series of sweet creations look as beautiful as they taste.

name: Ösch Noir
review: Ösch Noir is a cut above the local restaurant scene. First, on account of its chic, upscale interior (rather unusual in this rural area), but above all due to Manuel Ulrich's food. Having trained at the Öschberghof, this young native of Donaueschingen travelled further afield, working in kitchens in Lech am Arlberg and Baiersbronn, before returning to work in his home town when the hotel owners decided to open this elegant fine dining restaurant. Manuel Ulrich puts a skilful spin on classical cuisine, adding a perfectly judged dash of modern innovation to his balanced and yet robust dishes. The "Noir" and "Vert" (vegetarian) set menus propose real depth of flavour. You can count on first-rate service from sommelier Michael Häni's front-of-house team.

name: ES:SENZ
review: Formerly of restaurant Les Deux in Munich, Edip Sigl has now set up shop in the restaurant of Das Achental hotel. Known for his ambition and meticulous craftsmanship, there is no shortage of precision, harmony and finesse in the dishes sent out of the ES:SENZ kitchen. Guests choose from two set menus comprising six or eight courses: "Chiemgau pur" or "Chiemgau goes around the world". As the names of the menus suggest, the culinary focus is firmly on the region and the fine produce it yields, although a smattering of international influences is also occasionally in evidence. The restaurant's interior design sets the tone – modern Alpine chic may best describe the attractive decor. Enjoyably relaxed service and excellent wine recommendations.

name: Luce d'Oro
review: Everything the unique hideaway of Schloss Elmau offers in terms of luxury in the hotel and spa finds its culinary equivalent in Luce d'Oro. This is creative cuisine prepared using first-rate ingredients. Christoph Rainer, who made a name for himself at the helm of Frankfurt's two-star Tiger-Gourmetrestaurant, draws inspiration for his changing set menus from French and Japanese cookery. Interesting combinations and fine contrasts are par for the course here. The aromatic dishes have a sophistication that is reflected in the interior: untreated precious wood, pared-down design, warm colours, and the shimmering golden light that gives this place its name. A beautiful blend of comfort and elegance!

name: Tohru in der Schreiberei
review: The way this tasteful, top-notch restaurant in the heart of the city bridges the gap between history and modernity is absolutely harmonious. On the upper floor of this listed building, once the city's Schreiberei, you can savour a creative 10-course menu in Tohru Nakamura's fine dining restaurant, in which he incorporates his Japanese roots. In addition, the professional, well-coordinated service team will give you the best advice on wine and sake, plus they always have entertaining little surprises in store for you when presenting the dishes and drinks - for example, the "Sweet Victuals from the Market" is explained by referencing a "walk" through the Viktualienmarkt, one of Munich's markets. Each dish is presented in detail, with a particular focus on the origins of the ingredients, all of which are excellent quality!

name: OPUS V
review: Shopping and culinary delights under one roof? Head to the top of fashion retailer Modehaus Engelhorn Mode im Quadrat to investigate. A team headed up by Dominik Paul cooks modern and creative cuisine. The dishes making up the six-course set menu bowl over diners with flavours that range from bold and robust to low-key, subtle and highly elegant. It is all nicely pared down and wonderfully balanced, prepared using excellent produce. Opt for the savvy wine pairings, which occasion the odd revelation. At lunchtime (on Saturdays) the set menu is one course shorter. The sleek, contemporary surroundings have a Nordic feel, and there is the open kitchen. The highlight is of course the roof terrace with its view over the city! N.B. the restaurant also has its own entrance.

name: Lorenz Adlon Esszimmer
review: Dinner at the fine dining restaurant of the exclusive Adlon Kempinski at the Brandenburg Gate is an unforgettable experience! The sophisticated, classically opulent interior is matched by the wonderfully refined and creative cuisine. Consistently top-notch ingredients are used to create elaborate and exquisitely balanced compositions that showcase superb technical precision. The service is also outstanding: from the first moment, your needs are catered to in a courteous and professional manner; everything is perfectly coordinated. The set menu is accompanied by judicious wine suggestions plucked from a comprehensive wine list.

name: Falco
review: A Black Forest native in Saxony... Peter Maria Schnurr, born in Forbach in the Murg valley, learned his craft in Germany's top Michelin-starred restaurants. After starting out at Restaurant Fallert in Sasbachwalden, there followed stints at (among others) Hirschen in Sulzburg, Waldhotel Sonnora in Dreis, First Floor in Berlin and Im Schiffchen in Düsseldorf, where he worked under Jean-Claude Bourgueil. In the fine dining restaurant of The Westin hotel, he presents exceedingly imaginative, creative und technically accomplished dishes, in which highly diverse flavours sit happily side by side. Diners can opt for the set menu or order à la carte. Even the fabulous views of the city afforded from the 27th floor take second place to food as good as this! Then there is the friendly, efficient service and extensive selection of wines with a very good range of vintages.

name: Söl'ring Hof
review: You would be hard pressed to find a better location! When you ring the bell, the white gate opens and a paved driveway leads you to a gorgeous thatched country house enthroned on a dune at the edge of Rantum – sensational views of the North Sea guaranteed. The upscale interior is decked out in a Nordic style that combines elegance and cosiness, while the charming and professional service does the rest. The excellent wine recommendations come courtesy of restaurant manager and sommelier Bärbel Ring. Take a peek into the kitchen, where Jan-Philipp Berner's team puts together a creative set menu comprising finely balanced courses prepared using only the best – preferably regional – ingredients.

name: Obendorfers Eisvogel
review: Sebastian Obendorfer has now taken over the reins from his father Hubert. His unique tasting menu gives the classical repertoire a creative twist and draws inspiration from international cuisines. The fabulous cheese trolley is curated by famous Alsace affineur Antony! Decent wine pairings, with non-alcoholic alternatives available. The interior is modern, elegant and comfortable; the oval-shaped wine cabinet in the middle of the room is bound to catch your eye. The hilltop location and large windows mean diners can enjoy unobstructed views of the undulating landscape of the Upper Palatinate – magnificent sunsets included! Cordial and highly experienced waitstaff. Tip: Stay overnight at Der Birkenhof hotel.

name: etz
review: In a district in the northwest of the city, not far from the Pegnitz and its meadows, Felix Schneider is now cooking up a storm in this restaurant somewhat tucked away in a back courtyard (access via Kirschgartenstraße 6). The inventive dishes are born of the team's focus on sustainability, which means they grow their own fruit and vegetables and produce everything themselves, from ham to butter and miso to vinegar. Modern urban surroundings make for a pleasantly laid-back atmosphere. Bag a table near the open kitchen and you can chat to the chefs, who also deliver the food themselves. From 6.15pm you can tuck into a set menu (fish and meat or vegetarian) comprising 12 to 16 courses, to be enjoyed over four to five hours. Choose between wine and alcohol-free pairings.

name: Steinheuers Restaurant Zur Alten Post
review: The Steinheuer family is clearly on a mission to make diners feel at home! It is no wonder that guests (many of them regulars) have been flocking to these enthusiastic hosts for many years. One draw is the opulent and elegant dining space, the other is the cuisine prepared by Christian Binder (who, incidentally, is the son-in-law of owner Hans Stefan Steinheuer). This is classical fare that showcases regional ingredients while also giving a nod to international influences. Culinary finesse, harmony and depth of flavour are proposed in the form of two set menus dubbed "Blossoms" and "Roots". The ladies of the house, Gabriele Steinheuer and daughter Désirée – a trained sommelier – head up the charming and competent front-of-house team. It's good to know that the younger generation is continuing this restaurant's long tradition!

name: Restaurant Heinz Winkler
review: Iconic chef Heinz Winkler really put his Residenz hotel on the culinary map. After opening this place in 1991, he remained at the helm, steadily building it up to become a benchmark for classical fine dining at the highest level. Since his sudden death, the kitchen has stuck to its tried-and-tested formula: classic cuisine with modern touches made with excellent ingredients. Opt for one of the set menus or order from the à la carte selection, which includes Winkler's own legendary specialities – these are as much of a draw for diners as the elegant Venetian-style setting. The friendly and unflappable service extends to helpful guidance when it comes to the impressive wine list.

name: Haerlin
review: Visitors to Hamburg hoping for a combination of history, opulence and first-rate cuisine should look no further than this elegant fine dining restaurant housed in the legendary Fairmont Hotel Vier Jahreszeiten on the Neuer Jungfernstieg. For many years now, head chef Christoph Rüffer has been the guarantor of continuity and constant evolution with his seasonal set menus prepared using top-notch ingredients. His precise approach to cooking is plain to see in the sophisticated-looking dishes, but presentation always plays second fiddle to flavour. In keeping with the stylish and opulent setting, the highly attentive front-of-house team treats diners to outstanding service, and the wine list is excellent. We recommend opting for the wine pairings to accompany your meal – a Grand Cru version is also available.

name: Vendôme
review: Joachim Wissler has been running the kitchen at the elegant fine dining restaurant of the luxurious Althoff Grandhotel Schloss Bensberg since 2000. The classical French-based cuisine of this Swabian-born chef focuses on creative flavour combinations, which he serves up in the form of intricate and technically sophisticated dishes using ingredients that are consistently of the highest quality. There is a choice of two set menus (one vegetarian) composed of six or eight courses – you are also welcome to mix and match. First rate service comes courtesy of a competent front-of-house team that is always on hand and yet pleasantly unobtrusive. More delights are to be found on the wine list, with lovers of German Riesling particularly well catered for.

name: Speisemeisterei
review: Over the years, the Kavaliersbau (squire's lodge) of Schloss Hohenheim has become synonymous with sophisticated fine dining. This is largely down to Stefan Gschwendtner, who, having worked here at the Speisemeisterei since 2008, became head chef in 2016, developing and refining his own style along the way. The star of the show is undoubtedly the excellent produce, which is approached with an abundance of craftsmanship, technical skill and ideas, to conjure up highly intelligent and expressive dishes such as Danube salmon (supplied by Nikolai Birnbaum's fish farm) with yam, bacon and tosazu onion. You are looked after by an extremely competent and friendly front-of-house team, who also provide judicious recommendations when it comes to choosing your wine. In summer, diners may prefer to head out of the elegant dining area to soak up the atmosphere on the fabulous terrace!

name: Tim Raue
review: European cuisine that draws on Asia for inspiration – Tim Raue pulls off this modern and refreshing feat in truly original fashion. This Berlin-born chef has a style that is all his own and certainly unique in Germany. He works with a highly skilled team to turn out his flavourful creations. Diners have a choice of set menus dubbed "Kolibri" (hummingbird) and "Koi", with his signature dishes of "Wasabi Langoustine" and "Peking Duck" available in each. There is also the option of a vegan set menu. The appeal of this place lies in its daring to be different, with the lively urban ambience in no way detracting from the high standard of the cuisine. Marie-Anne Wild and her charming front-of-house team will make you feel at home in this sleek and elegant restaurant. Wine lovers will delight in the fantastic selection of open wines.

name: CODA Dessert Dining
review: Don't be fooled by the unassuming exterior of this Neukölln eatery, for it is home to a very special take on fine dining. The trendy, pared-down interior is dimly lit. Take a seat at the counter with its view into the kitchen or at the surrounding tables. The cuisine has its own style, which is certainly unique: René Frank and his team focus on patisserie techniques, using them to prepare innovative dishes, complete with umami flavours! The food is by no means limited to sweet treats. One really fun touch is the carefully considered mini cocktails that accompany each course of the set menu, available at two sittings: the first at 6pm with seven courses, and the second at 10pm with five courses. Relaxed and professional service. The fabulous wine list is principally devoted to sparkling wine from Champagne, Riesling and sake.

name: Rosin
review: TV chef Frank Rosin is a household name in Germany. The Dorsten-born chef opened this elegant restaurant back in 1991 and now forms a well-established team with head chef and long-time brother-in-arms Oliver Engelke. This is classic cuisine with a dash of creative flair. The service is absolutely second to none: headed by Jochen Bauer and sommelier Susanne Spies, the front-of-house team guide you through this culinary experience in a pleasantly relaxed yet professional manner. You may like to sample one of the wines from their own "Rosin & Spies" range. Good to know: the online shop sells vegetarian and vegan "Green Rosin" products such as burger patties, crackers, dips etc.

name: Jante
review: Tony Hohlfeld and his kitchen team conjure up elaborate, very complex and really well-thought-out dishes that are nevertheless pleasantly light and free of gimmicks – this absolutely remarkable cuisine is truly out of the ordinary! All of the components work together perfectly, creating a wonderful depth of flavour. They serve a set menu with an option to "upgrade". When making a reservation you can also order a vegetarian/vegan set menu. The unconstrained style of the food reflects the ambience in this semi-circular building with floor-to-ceiling windows. This is largely due to the refined Scandinavian interior and charming front-of-house team led by maître d' and sommelier Mona Schrader. Here the chefs are also on hand to explain the dishes to diners. We recommend opting for the non-alcoholic pairings!

name: AUGUST
review: Since this restaurant opened, the listed Haag Villa (1877) has been home to works of culinary art! You can soak up the distinctive atmosphere that lingers in these extraordinary buildings while sampling extremely personalised dishes that are born out of the chef's imagination, the like of which you will not find anywhere else. Christian Grünwald's cuisine is inspired by nature, by regions, by the sea, by the garden... The ingredients are exceptional, the dishes are finely balanced. They are served on illuminated "display window" tables, with decorative and edible items exhibited under their glass tops. All to be enjoyed in a stylish dining area with high ceilings, parquet floors and artworks. Then there is the enjoyably well-coordinated and unflappable service – Christian Grünwald himself is also on hand to shed light on his creations.

name: Le Pavillon
review: It is not only nature lovers who are drawn to the idyllic Black Forest landscape, thanks to the scenically located and family-run Dollenberg hotel. This marvellous resort is also home to a fantastic fine dining restaurant. Head chef Martin Herrmann celebrates the classics while remaining open to modern innovations. He cooks up an eight-course set menu, which you can also trim down to a shorter version. The appealingly pared-back dishes are prepared using high-quality ingredients, and the sauces are a real highlight! Then there is the cosy, elegant setting and magnificent views through the floor-to-ceiling windows, as well as the relaxed yet stylish service and knowledgeable wine recommendations. Sommelier Christophe Meyer proposes wines from his own "CM Edition" range.

name: Le Moissonnier
review: A real institution in Cologne. Since 1987 this enjoyably informal restaurant has been synonymous with savoir-vivre. Here, you are transported to bustling Paris with its delightful bistros. Charming Art Nouveau features lend a distinctive look to the pretty interior. Your friendly and obliging hosts, Liliane and Vincent Moissonnier, are consummate professionals when it comes to taking care of their guests. Fellow countryman Monsieur Eric Menchon has been on board as head chef since the beginning, wowing diners with an intensely flavoured cuisine that draws on his French origins. He puts an elegant spin on dishes that is unmistakably his own, while always keeping the spotlight firmly on the produce itself.

name: LOUIS restaurant
review: Tasteful boutique hotel LA MAISON happens to be home to one of Saarland's top restaurants. Its small dining area has high ceilings and a chic and modern decor that lends it a feeling of luxury, while the stylish and pleasantly relaxed front-of-house team led by sommelier Robert Jankowski creates a buzzing atmosphere. The creative menu combines modern French cuisine with international influences. The result is light, coherent dishes that do not feel contrived or overly fussy. On warm days you can enjoy the lovely terrace. Insider tip: Have a drink at the bar and mix with the locals!

name: 100/200 Kitchen
review: What an experience here on the third floor of an assuming factory building! In a loft-style space done out in an industrial-chic design, the open kitchen takes centre stage. Working at a fantastic Molteni stove, set to either 100°C or 200°C (hence the name) the chefs deliver a creative surprise menu that is aligned with the seasons. Get into the mood at the display bar with its range of raw ingredients. Respect for the produce is the motto here, with the emphasis on sustainability and small producers known to the house. With a passion and style that is all his own, Thomas Imbusch creates honest dishes that remain close to nature. To be enjoyed with organic wines or alcohol-free beverages. Opt for the three-course set menu at "Der Stundentisch", which lines the glass façade, or enjoy spontaneous offerings from the kitchen at "Die Empore". Ticket booking system.

name: bianc
review: Here, a native Italian brings the flavours of the South to Hamburg. Matteo Ferrantino, who, together with Dieter Koschina, previously ran the kitchen of the two-star Vila Joya restaurant in the Portuguese city of Albufeira, presents a modern and creative take on Mediterranean cuisine in the form of two set menus named "Emotion" and "Garten" (vegetarian). Each begins with an array of amuse-bouches and is rounded off with a series of equally delicate petits fours. In between you might opt for Iberico Secreto with shellfish, chorizo, pearl onion and Dijon mustard. With his great taste and considerable technical prowess he prepares premium ingredients, creating exceptionally interesting flavour combinations. Architect Julia Erdmann has designed a chic interior that has all the flair of an Italian piazza – plus a view of the kitchen.

name: Ox & Klee
review: Ranging from appetiser to chocolates, "Experience Taste" is a 14-course set menu in which head chef Daniel Gottschlich puts a creative spin on the six basic tastes of "sweet", "sour", "bitter", "salty", "fatty" and "umami", incorporating plenty of vegetables as he does so. There are two set menus: all year round "Ox & Klee" serves seafood, fish and meat, as well as vegetarian dishes, and, from March to late August, the 100% vegetarian "Klee" ("Clover") menu is also available. This is highly expressive and flavourful cuisine made from top-notch ingredients. The restaurant boasts a terrific location in the centrally situated Kranhaus 1, complete with industrial architecture and harbour view; the carefully considered decor enhances the pleasure of this culinary experience. If you're after something even more special, book the Chef's Table.

name: Ophelia
review: A place in which to simply sit back and drink in the experience, and not only out on the fabulous terrace with its views of Lake Constance. The Riva Hotel and its fine dining restaurant may bowl visitors over with its location directly on the lakeside promenade, but it is above all Dirk Hoberg's meticulous cuisine that captures hearts. This gorgeous Art Nouveau villa dating from 1909 provides a stylish, modern and elegant setting in which to sample a tasting menu composed of a series of refined dishes, complete with sauces inspired by the classics of French cuisine. The excellent wine list is international in its scope. Look out for the chef - from time to time he brings out dishes himself.

name: EssZimmer
review: It almost seems as if this glass restaurant is floating above the BMW Welt vehicle exhibition at the foot of the Olympic Tower. Upon exiting the lift on the third floor, you pass through a cosy lounge area before taking your seat in the restaurant, which is done out in a chic urban style. If you manage to bag a table at the floor-to-ceiling windows, you can enjoy impressive views of the exclusive cars on show. However, the equally remarkable modern and creative cuisine proposed by Bobby Bräuer's team is deserving of your full attention. The dishes are well thought-out, winning diners over with their depth of flavour and texture, with the odd playful element thrown in. You can put together your own set menu of five to eight courses. Check out the fabulous wine list with its great selection of labels from Germany and Austria. Elegant and professional service.

name: Horváth
review: This location has been home to different restaurants for 100 years. Made famous by legendary artists' café-bar Exil, which was founded by Oswald Wiener in 1973, this address retains a certain aura to this day. Keeping pace with the times, your two hosts, Austrian-born Sebastian Frank and his partner Jeannine Kessler, preside over a newly renovated interior that includes a striking mural by Jim Avignon and draws attention to the artistic history of this location. In the kitchen, Sebastian Frank gives free rein to his own unique style, which is perhaps all the more remarkable for its apparent lack of fanfare. This is clean and pared-down cooking that puts high-quality ingredients centre stage, often giving pride of place to vegetables. On top of all that, diners enjoy friendly, competent service and interesting wine recommendations.

name: Tantris
review: After undergoing a renovation that lasted several months, this Munich institution is now at the beginning of a new era. Although unchanged on the outside, the inside has been furnished with a few modern touches, including a striking walk-in glass wine cabinet. Fans of the legendary Tantris decor will be pleased to hear that the interior is as evocative as it ever was of the 1970s and has lost none of its charm and originality! What is completely new is the kitchen team, who take inspiration from French culinary tradition. The lunchtime set menu comprises four or six courses, while in the evening diners opt for either a six- or eight-course set menu. The recommended wine pairings are excellent – but be sure to peruse the impressive wine list in any case!

name: Gustav
review: Over the last few years, maître d' Milica Trajkovska Scheiber and head chef Jochim Busch have established a restaurant where diners can feel at home. In this outwardly rather unassuming building in Westend, you can expect food with plenty of character! This is modern cuisine that stands out for its individuality. Jochim Busch has the chutzpah to drastically pare down his dishes, which feature a beautiful interplay of contrasts and textures. A responsible approach to resources is really important to him, which is why selected regional and seasonal produce is the name of the game. The stylish, sleek and modern interior is of an equally high standard. Pleasantly unpretentious atmosphere; friendly, courteous and professional service. Insider tip: Some tables afford a good view of the kitchen pass!

name: Alexander Herrmann by Tobias Bätz
review: He is a Michelin-starred chef, a restaurateur, a cookbook author, and a famous face on account of his appearances on various TV cooking shows. We are of course talking about Alexander Herrmann. It is here at his traditional family-run Posthotel, located in Wirsberg, that he made a name for himself with this smart, modern and elegant fine dining restaurant. In the kitchen, he and head chef Tobias Bätz form a well-oiled machine, turning out creative, coherent and cleverly devised dishes brimming with their own ideas. The set menu (with meat or vegetarian) is served at 6pm and accompanied by Franconian wines. Friendly and confident service – even the chefs get in on the act. The small cards with interesting information about the ingredients are a lovely concept.

name: ammolite - The Lighthouse Restaurant
review: Just head for the eye-catching lighthouse if you want to find this exclusive restaurant in the Europa Park. The interior is timelessly chic and elegant, with its slightly transparent drapes bathing the round dining space in a warm golden hue and lending it a sense of intimacy and tranquillity. Seated on elegant velvet armchairs at tables decked with high-quality tablecloths, you are attentively and competently looked after by a well-coordinated front-of-house team. Head chef Peter Hagen-Wiest presents two fabulous set menus composed of seven courses: "Around the World" and vegetarian alternative "Green Forest". His cooking has classical roots but is open to modern influences, which he incorporates with a fine sense of balance. Then there are the outstanding wine recommendations, which are expertly explained.

name: GästeHaus Klaus Erfort
review: From the outside, this stylish white villa in the centre of Saarbrücken promises quality and elegance, and the interior certainly does not disappoint, thanks to its winning combination of historical features and modern clean lines. This harmonious blend of classic and contemporary also extends to Klaus Erfort's cuisine. In a set menu composed of four, five or seven courses, he presents nicely pared-down dishes that are full of finesse. It is also worth perusing the nicely put-together wine list. The front-of-house team takes a friendly and informal yet professional approach to its work.

name: Esplanade
review: This former schoolhouse in the centre of Saarbrücken is an exceptionally refined building that also houses a little boutique hotel with 16 spruce and beautifully decorated guestrooms. But it is the restaurant that garners the most attention: an elegant and modern, beautifully coordinated interior and an excellent front-of-house team headed up by Jérôme Pourchère, who is passionate about being a maître d' and sommelier. Then comes the cuisine, crafted by Silio Del Fabro, who can safely be described as a culinary talent. He combines classical fare with modern and Mediterranean influences. His dishes are clearly structured, rich in finesse and wonderfully balanced. Choose the "Signature" set menu or the à la carte dishes. At lunchtime you can opt for an interesting "plat du jour".

name: FACIL
review: A real oasis of calm in the middle of Berlin! Up here on the fifth floor of The Mandala Hotel, diners can sit on the pleasant little terrace amid the chestnut trees and fountain. It belongs to this elegant, light and airy rooftop garden restaurant, where even inside you almost feel like you're outdoors thanks to the all-round floor-to-ceiling windows. Beautiful bamboo plants give a nod to Asia. As well as the great location, Facil also boasts incredible food courtesy of Michael Kempf (culinary director) and Joachim Gerner (chef de cuisine). Rooted in classical cooking, it also skilfully integrates Asian and Mediterranean influences. Creative dishes brimming with flavours and aromas – the fabulous desserts are also worth a mention. All this is rounded off by the smart, professional service.

name: Hirschen
review: What is it that draws legions of visitors from near and far to this tranquil village in Markgräflerland? This is where Douce Steiner and Udo Weiler have their hotel-restaurant. Having met and fallen in love in 1995 while working for Harald Wohlfahrt, the couple took over Hirschen from her father, Hans-Paul Steiner, in 2008. Housed in a picture-perfect building that dates back over 500 years, the restaurant boasts charming, elegant dining rooms, a lively and cosy atmosphere, and fast-paced, friendly service. Try to sneak a peek through the glass windows into the kitchen: top-notch ingredients are used to prepare classic French cuisine enlivened by more modern innovations. Round off your meal with a digestif in the idyllic inner courtyard. A word to the wise: small shop with cookbooks, jams etc. Very tasteful guestrooms for an overnight stay.

name: Le Cerf
review: The culinary centrepiece of the Wald & Schlosshotel Friedrichsruhe has a classic, elegant style that is the very definition of opulence. Exquisite touches such as fine fabrics, fancy wallpaper and crystal chandeliers are perfectly in keeping with the historical castle. The cuisine is similarly classical but subject to modern interpretation by Boris Rommel and his team. The meticulous technical skill involved and the outstanding quality of the ingredients is plain to see, with individual components of dishes precisely worked out down to the last detail. There are two set menus (one vegetarian), from which you can also order à la carte. Friendly and professional front-of-house team; the head chef also likes to come out and chat to guests. Treat yourself to an aperitif at the hotel bar.

name: Meierei Dirk Luther
review: An elegant setting done out with gorgeous wooden tables and floor-to-ceiling windows – some seats afford a particularly good view of Flensburg Fjord. Beautiful vistas aside, here it is Dirk Luther's cuisine that will really impress. The Hamburg native does a fantastic job of bringing together classic and modern styles of cooking. The odd moment of sheer brilliance is in evidence here, as in, for example, the sautéed langostino served with curry foam, carrot and papaya chutney. It is also worth mentioning the exceptional quality of the ingredients – particularly when it comes to fish and shellfish. The charming service is agreeably relaxed and discreet, while remaining attentive and professional.

name: PURS
review: Housed in the Old Chancellery dating from 1677, this little gem is tucked away in an inconspicuous side street in Andernach. Axel Vervoordt's tasteful, modern design, which accounts for the stylish look of the hotel, carries over into the restaurant, where the eye is immediately drawn to the artworks on the walls and the glass-fronted open kitchen. This is where a dedicated team combines selected products in a technically excellent and expressive way. The wine list has been nicely curated and the efficient service is attentive and friendly. After your meal, staff will gladly lead you through the kitchen to the bar.

name: Courtier
review: This stately home estate dating back to 1896 makes for a wonderful setting with its romantic grounds dotted with old trees, its pond and its tantalising glimpses of the Baltic Sea. It goes without saying that in summer you will want to enjoy the fabulous views from the terrace. Head chef Christian Scharrer selects the best ingredients the market has to offer and transforms them into intensely flavoured, creative dishes, as in, for example, langostinos with autumn cabbage and truffle or scallop with fennel and bouillabaisse. And as you might expect from a stately home, diners are seated in sumptuous surroundings boasting stylish details such as chandeliers, wall paintings and stucco. Then there is the attentive and accomplished service provided by your cordial hostess, Nathalie Scharrer, and her professional front-of-house team.

name: Atelier
review: The fine dining restaurant of the Bayerischer Hof hotel serves modern cuisine that draws on classical as well as Asian influences. Using top-notch seasonal produce, Anton Gschwendtner and his team work meticulously to create dishes that are pleasingly pared down and extremely skilfully structured. The set menu has a variable number of courses, and there is also a vegetarian option. Your experience is enhanced by the professional, attentive and very friendly front-of-house team. As for the surroundings, in view of Axel Vervoordt's chic, high-quality interior, the name Atelier may not seem too far-fetched.

name: Essigbrätlein
review: You have to ring the bell to be admitted to this small restaurant in the middle of Nuremberg's old town. A lovely intimate setting for a meal, with its cosy and inviting atmosphere and charming and attentive front-of-house team. In the kitchen, the focus is on innovative cuisine that takes advantage of the seasons and selected producers. In line with their sustainable approach, the "leaf to root" philosophy is rigorously adhered to. Chef-patron Andree Köthe and co-head chef Yves Ollech – who have formed a well-oiled machine in the kitchen for years – have a penchant for using herbs, spices and vegetables, even fermenting and preserving them for later use. The creative natural cuisine is accompanied by astute wine pairings. Insider tip: request the vegetarian lunch menu when making your reservation.

name: Lafleur
review: Chef Andreas Krolik is synonymous with extraordinary dedication and continuous development. He brings together quality ingredients to create intense and absolutely coherent modern cuisine that is nonetheless rooted in the classics. Impressive precision, great depth of flavour. The vegan menu is also in great demand! This "contemporary classic fare" – as Andreas Krolik describes his cuisine – is complemented by a self-assured, very friendly and beautifully schooled front-of-house team led by restaurant manager Boris Häbel and sommeliers Miguel Martin and Alexandra Himmel. Premium-quality Coravin wine pairings. The glass annex of the Gesellschaftshaus Palmengarten makes for a stylish modern setting.

name: Liath
review:
Lockdown gave many people time to pause and reflect and, here at Liath, it prompted the team time to come up with something new. The room now sports a stylish, contemporary look – and when entering via the rustic market you’ll feel like Alice in Wonderland, as the place has a cosy, magical feel.
With just a handful of tables, it makes for a personal dining experience, with Damien Grey and his small team explaining the dishes personally to their guests. There’s an early evening sitting of 3 courses (the ‘Preview’) and a later sitting where they serve the full surprise tasting menu; both showcase Liath favourites from across the years, which have been continually reworked and perfected. Bold, original dishes are centred around the five tastes – salty, savoury, sweet, bitter and sour – which come together in perfect harmony, and excellent wine pairings further enhance the experience.

name: Aimsir
review:
Start with a cocktail in the lounge overlooking the garden, then head past hanging meats and jars of preserved produce to a wonderfully intimate dining room with just a handful of tables. Here, Jordan Bailey calmly leads the chefs in the open kitchen, while his wife heads the delightful service team – and their infectious pride radiates through all who work for them.
Having worked as Head Chef at Three-Starred Maaemo in Norway, Jordan brings together overwhelming passion, supreme craftsmanship and a great understanding of Nordic flavours, resulting in superbly balanced, original dishes which have real depth. The 18+ labour-intensive courses are all very different and make good use of preserved and fermented ingredients, with produce sourced from their raised beds and polytunnels, as well as from across Ireland.

name: Patrick Guilbaud
review:
This iconic Irish restaurant celebrated 40 years in 2021 and, while a large part of its success is down to the eponymous chef himself – who has certainly earned his place in Irish culinary history – it is also due to the team Patrick Guilbaud has built around him over the years, each of whom elegantly plays their part in creating an extra special experience for each and every guest. 
The restaurant is hidden within a Georgian townhouse, and oozes sumptuousness and sophistication thanks to features such as a gilt barrel ceiling and hand-crafted marquetry.
The accomplished cooking remains French at heart yet has evolved to show a restrained modernity and some bold yet superbly balanced flavours. Dishes showcase luxury Irish ingredients and the wine cellar and wine list are works of art.

name: Chapter One by Mickael Viljanen
review:
In the most exciting development in Dublin’s restaurant scene in years, Finnish chef Mickael Viljanen moved from the south of the Liffey to the north, to take over as Head Chef and co-owner of Chapter One. Set beneath the Writers Museum, the basement restaurant is elegant and stylish with some eye-catching art; ask for a seat at the chef’s table in the kitchen for the best view of the team at work.
Cooking focuses on prime luxury ingredients; Irish where possible, but sourced from further afield when needed to ensure the best quality. Classical French techniques combine with a subtle modernity, as well as plenty of creativity and personality, and the sophisticated, beautifully presented dishes are perfectly balanced, with striking natural flavours.  
The superb service team ensure everyone is well looked after and an Irish coffee makes for a memorable finish.

name: Ynyshir
review:
If you’re after a truly unique experience, then a journey to rural Wales and this part-Georgian house – painted matt black, with tipis in the garden – will tick lots of boxes. 
Lunch starts promptly at 12.30 and dinner at 5pm, which gives chef-owner Gareth Ward and his team the time to take their diners on an immersive culinary journey that starts with being shown all the fine Welsh produce that they’ll be experiencing in the 30 or so servings that follow. Originality comes in the form of assorted Asian influences that the kitchen use to produce an array of vibrant and contrasting flavours and textures. The chefs bring the dishes to your table themselves and talk through their composition, while a DJ plays in the dining room.   
Luxurious bedrooms complete the picture.

name: Raby Hunt
review:
This former drovers’ inn in a pretty rural village was originally part of the Raby Estate and its name refers to it being a favourite finishing point for the old hunt. It’s owned by the Close family, with son James heading up the open kitchen, which looks out over the sleek, clean-lined dining room.
Self-taught chef James is full of passion and in his pursuit of perfection, has never missed a service. His enticing, highly original menu is a showcase of precision, from a selection of snacks that reflect his global travels to signature dishes such as a seasonal salad of 48-52 top-notch ingredients, presented in a beguiling array of textures and temperatures. To conclude, you’ll find some of the country’s most sublime desserts.
Chic, restful bedrooms complete the picture.

name: Andrew Fairlie at Gleneagles
review:
Hidden away in the depths of the world-famous Gleneagles resort hotel is this intimate restaurant. It may be windowless but the room has an appealing classical elegance, courtesy of dark wood walls, clever lighting and colourful food-themed art. An oil painting of the late Andrew Fairlie takes pride of place on one wall and Head Chef Stephen McLaughlin and his team work to continue Andrew’s philosophy and keep his spirit alive.
Refined cooking has a French heart and a Scottish soul and, while techniques are rooted in the classics, there are also touches of modernity. Superb quality produce guides the menu, with 95% of the vegetables coming from their walled Victorian garden and each dish focusing on one main ingredient which is then skilfully enhanced by its accompaniments. Service is formal but comes with plenty of personality.

name: Le Manoir aux Quat' Saisons, a Belmond Hotel
review:
You cannot help but fall in love with this iconic country house restaurant. The setting is divine and a feeling of luxury envelops you, from the sumptuous lounge, via the magical interconnecting beamed dining rooms, to the conservatory overlooking manicured gardens.
Since 1984 it has helped elevate the standard of British cooking – and many who have gone on to become great chefs have trained here. As its name suggests, the seasons lead the way: wander the grounds and you’ll discover an amazing array of plants, as well as a 2,500 strong orchard boasting many rare varieties.
Legendary chef Raymond Blanc leads the team and, while the skilfully executed cooking has a classic French base, it also comes with a light, modern touch. Flavours are intense, combinations are sophisticated and the presentation shows an eye for detail. Desserts are a highlight.

name: Restaurant Sat Bains
review:
Its location – next to an industrial estate in the shadow of a flyover – might not be its best feature, but what keeps guests coming back time and again is the food. The kitchen’s skill lies in extracting maximum flavour from every ingredient, and this is evident in everything from the snacks on arrival to the unique cocktails themed around the five tastes: sweet, sour, salty, bitter, and umami. 
These five tastes also inform the 10 course menu, where refined, creative dishes feature plenty of playful elements. Produce from their urban garden and greenhouse – including honey from their beehives – is well-used, and one course (’a taste of the garden’), is served in the greenhouse itself.
Stylish bedrooms are also available, which provides the perfect excuse to go for one of their wine pairings.

name: Midsummer House
review:
A beautiful Victorian house with a lovely conservatory extension hosts this stylish restaurant. It’s set in an idyllic location overlooking Midsummer Common and the delightful first floor lounge and terrace make the perfect spot for drinks, looking out over the garden and the River Cam.
Experienced chef-owner Daniel Clifford has run this restaurant for over 20 years and his experience shines through. He, Head Chef Mark Abbott and their team are not the sort to rest on their laurels. Dishes continually evolve and, although they have a classic base, are packed full of personality and originality; this is a kitchen which is not afraid to push the boundaries. Luxury ingredients are generously used, flavours are measured, there’s an appealing range of different textures and many of the dishes are finished off at the table.

name: Moor Hall
review:
Charming grounds with a lake and a fountain lead up to this beautifully restored 16C country house, where you’ll be warmly welcomed by one of the slickest teams around. The Scandic-style restaurant is a truly striking space, with its blond wood tables, floor-to-ceiling windows and tempting cheese room – and the smoothness of the well-drilled chefs in the open kitchen is a sight to behold. 
Your meal commences with a tantalising array of snacks – the last served in the kitchen where you can chat with Head Chef Mark Birchall. His refined, highly original dishes feature some terrific English produce, including some lesser-known herbs and plants, and his versatility results in a range of cleverly blended flavours, textures and temperatures. The wine list will have oenophiles in raptures and contemporary bedrooms complete the package.

name: Hand and Flowers
review:
Tom Kerridge’s flagship restaurant sits within this characterful beamed pub; now a world-renowned institution. Find a spot in the comfortable bar or out on the terrace and choose from a dazzling array of drinks – including their own light beer – then head through to the quirky dining room divided by period beams and pillars.
Food is based around pub classics but those classics are elevated to new heights and are among the best in the UK. The sourcing of ingredients is given due reverence and execution is skilful and confident, while the dishes themselves are characterised by rich, powerful flavours – and the presentation is first-rate. Desserts are a real highlight and you’ll always find a soufflé on the list.
For those who want to make a night of it, luxurious bedrooms are dotted about the town.

name: Le Gavroche
review:
Le Gavroche’s longevity is legendary. Opened in 1967, this iconic restaurant has been a key player in the post-war culinary history of the UK and, as you descend the stairs into the intimate, clubby room, you’ll be transported back in time. It might have a formal air but it also has a comforting feel, and it’s a delight to see Michel Roux Jnr in his element, touring the tables and chatting to diners as he continues the family legacy.
The menu is a roll-call of refined, sophisticated French classics that delight and satisfy in equal measure – the soufflé Suissesse is renowned and luxury items lead the way, with the likes of coquilles St Jacques, turbot and lobster; if it all sounds so good that you simply can’t decide, go for the ‘Menu Exceptionnel’. The sommelier’s recommendations are spot-on and the cheese trolley is one of the best around.

name: La Dame de Pic London
review:
Anne-Sophie Pic’s London outpost is a charmingly run restaurant situated in the impressive Beaux-Arts style Four Seasons Hotel; an airy, high-ceilinged room with lots of white, plenty of light and some attractive modern art.

Cooking is rooted in classic French techniques yet delivered in a light, modern manner and dishes are elegant, refined and original, with tremendous attention given to their finer details. The kitchen source excellent quality produce and the delicate combinations of these ingredients are exciting and intuitive, with no superfluous elements on the plate. The well-structured wine list highlights wines from the Rhône Valley – home of restaurant Maison Pic, the Valence institution owned by the Pic family.

name: Da Terra
review:
Da Terra sits within an impressive Victorian hotel and, in contrast to the grandeur of the exterior, has quite an understated, modern look. Kick the night off with a cocktail in the bar while you look forward to the memorable, multi-course surprise menu to come. 
Chef Rafael Cagali hails from Brazil and his great grandfather was from Italy, and these influences, along with time spent working in Spain, come together in skilfully crafted, highly original dishes founded on Brazilian traditions. Colours burst through, presentation is striking, and the menu builds beautifully as you move from course to course, eagerly awaiting the next captivating combination of flavours. Dishes are delivered by the chefs with a detailed and passionate dialogue, and the wine matches are thoughtfully chosen, with admirable breadth and originality.

name: Ikoyi
review:
In a city of innovation, Ikoyi is a true original. Chef and founder Jeremy Chan has been steadily establishing close relationships with specialist growers and farmers in the UK to ensure delivery of the finest quality ingredients for his unique surprise menus – and that includes 100% organic meats, biodynamic vegetables and fish from British waters dispatched using the Ikejime method.
