This excellent restaurant focuses above all on choosing the best seasonal ingredients possible (including fish), as well as protecting the environment and showcasing the island’s traditions in its new, contemporary-style cuisine.

name: SanBrite
review: This restaurant has just a few tables amid a decor of elegantly recycled old wood, while a large window offers views of the stunning Ampezzo Dolomites outside. Your meal starts in a memorable way: waiters file into the dining room carrying mountains of creamy butter, which is served to every table accompanied by excellent bread with an incomparable texture. Owner-chef Riccardo Gaspari makes careful use of home-produced and regional ingredients, creating delicious cuisine in which mountain traditions are refreshed with modern touches, most noticeably visible in the desserts which are made without adding extra sugar. Sanbrite literally means “healthy pasture”, a name that definitely evokes the qualities of the cuisine served here.

name: Orto by Jorg Giubbani
review: With plenty of experience behind him, Jorg Giubbani is a young Ligurian chef who has developed a culinary philosophy that focuses first and foremost on his region. He pays particular attention to the quality of his ingredients, many of which, as the name of the restaurant suggests, are grown in the private garden surrounding the property (“orto” is the Italian for vegetable garden). The focus here is on traditional, seasonal flavours and produce, all enhanced by the chef’s creative skill. There are three tasting menus, with courses that can also be combined with his à la carte options. The wine list showcases wines from the region.

name: San Martino
review: One of the best restaurants in the area, San Martino focuses on fish dishes including classic favourites inherited from the chef’s father as well as more creative fare introduced by the new generation. The Colleoni family never fails to impress! Our inspectors particularly appreciated the constant search for perfection demonstrated by owner-chef Vittorio. This perfection is also evident in the private kitchen garden where flowers and vegetables are grown, emphasising the importance that this chef places on the provenance of his ingredients. The chef’s brother Paolo is responsible for the wine list, which is extensive and well structured, with a slight preference for French labels.

name: Il Falconiere
review: To get to this exclusive restaurant, you drive through an idyllic landscape of small lanes lined with dry-stone walls and fields belonging to the Baracchi farm estate, of which Il Falconiere and the magnificent hotel of the same name are a part. Many of the ingredients served here, such as wine and olive oil, are produced on the estate and the restaurant’s strong connection with its local landscapes is evident. Specialities such as Chianina beef, local garlic and pici pasta feature in dishes spiced with aromatic herbs and full of the strong flavours of Tuscany.

name: Pietramare Natural Food
review: In an elegant setting of dry-stone walls and Mediterranean vegetation, this intimate and elegant restaurant is now, following recent renovation, also home to an attractive cigar room with a lounge and fireplace. Although the menu is seasonal in feel and influenced by the region’s maritime and rural traditions (thereby offering guests an authentic culinary voyage around southern Italy), the focus here is resolutely modern and creative in tone. The restaurant now has an additional attraction – its “orto dei profumi”, an aromatic garden which is home to herbs and thirty different varieties of chilli pepper. Good wine list, including an interesting selection of sparkling wines.

name: La Caravella dal 1959
review: Housed in a 12C palazzo that was once the residence of the Piccolomini family, La Caravella occupies the wing converted during the Renaissance to store the ducal archives. An undisputed gastronomic icon on the Amalfi Coast with plenty of history behind it, this restaurant continues to attract a loyal following today. In the 1960s it was the first restaurant in southern Italy to be awarded a Michelin star and later also gained the title of restaurant-museum thanks to its vast, beautiful collection of ceramics by some of the greatest local masters from the 19C to the present day. There’s a nod to tradition in the cuisine here, with modern reinterpretations that are full of Mediterranean scents and flavours (the proverbial lemon makes an appearance in many dishes, from the creamy soup to the famous soufflé), as well as the vibrant character of the region and, above all, the sea (depending on the season and the catch). The outstanding wine list has few equals thanks to its extensive choice and excellent vintages.

name: Palazzo Petrucci
review: Just a stone’s throw from the historic Palazzo Donn’Anna, this restaurant housed in a new, modern building boasts views extending from the sea to Mt Vesuvius and from the Sorrentine peninsula to the famous islands facing the city. The cuisine here is of excellent quality, featuring modern, imaginative reinterpretations of local dishes created by chef Lino Scarallo. If you’re in the mood for a surprise and you’re willing to give the chef carte blanche, then go for the “Lino fai tu” menu. An aperitif in the piano lounge makes a pleasant start to your meal.

name: Atelier
review: The long-established Atelier is not only one of the leading restaurants in Domodossola, it is also the first ever in the Val d’Ossola to be awarded a Michelin star, adding to the tourist appeal of the town. Here, owner-chef Giorgio Bartolucci, flanked by his enterprising sister Elisabetta, has succeeded in skilfully and enthusiastically breathing new life into this restaurant which was founded by his parents, while his wife Katia oversees the impeccable service front of house with professionalism and a friendly smile. The bespoke open-view kitchen (made by local craftsmen and almost as big as the dining room) is definitely intended to be a distinctive feature which the energetic chef hopes will create a real connection between guests and his team. Flavour, variety and presentation are the keystones of the cuisine at Atelier, where the dishes are exciting, inspirational and occasionally feature intriguing reinterpretations of traditional local recipes.

name: Luigi Lepore
review: Although you hardly notice the door to this restaurant from outside, once inside you are immediately struck by the modern elegance of the decor with its vaguely Scandinavian feel. This mini gem occupying a 19C palazzo in Nicastro, the historic centre of Lamezia, is home to a young chef with impressive experience in France and Italy behind him. Here, he delights guests with contemporary dishes showcasing the produce of Calabria. Two tasting menus (Origini and A Mano Libera, from five to seven courses) allow guests to appreciate Luigi Lepore’s extraordinary cuisine to the full. Diners are warmly welcomed by the chef’s charming sister, Stefania, who oversees the front of house and describes dishes to guests.

name: Bistrot
review: Despite the name, this restaurant is not a simple bistro but rather a gourmet restaurant in which the excellent chef focuses on two key elements. The first is the restaurant’s own farm which supplies it with olive oil, herbs, vegetables and some meat; the second is the presence of two wood-fired ovens in which the chef bakes different breads, as well as cooking some of his dishes (lobster, in particular). The hospitality here is of the highest order, with exceptional service and a wine cellar (a visit is highly recommended) that is home to a selection of superb Italian and international wines.

name: Linfa
review: This restaurant is situated right in the historic centre of San Gimignano, yet slightly away from its main streets. Culture and a strong connection to the region are perfect companions to the fine flavours that chef Vincenzo Martella translates into delicious fish and meat dishes, often casually combining these different ingredients in the same dish. The beautiful presentation and attention to detail is echoed in the contemporary works of art that adorn the walls. Highly professional yet friendly service, with staff happy to offer recommendations, including assisting with your choice of wine.

name: Zash
review: The maze of lava walls emphasises this restaurant’s proximity to Etna, while guests will be enchanted by the 13ha of citrus trees with views of the sparkling blue sea in the background that greet them once through the entrance gate to this restaurant. The property, owned by the Maugeri family, stands on the “Riviera dei Limoni” in an area which is not part of the main tourist trail, despite its location halfway between Taormina and Catania. If you’re looking for somewhere to stop for a delicious gourmet meal, this is the place for you! Housed in a building once used for fermenting wine, the dining room at this restaurant is full of historic atmosphere, while the outdoor space immersed in Mediterranean vegetation and with its soft lighting is equally enticing. Chef Giuseppe Raciti has had experience working abroad and was already a chef de partie for master chef Santin at the age of 22. Here, he creates colourful and imaginative cuisine with a focus on local fruit and vegetables, many of which are grown in the hotel’s own kitchen garden. If you get here early, treat yourself to an aperitif at the beautiful poolside bar – a fitting start to a memorable experience!

name: La Preséf
review: Overlooking an internal garden, this welcoming Valtellina-style Stube restaurant decorated in sweet-scented cembra pinewood is the perfect setting in which to enjoy local specialities and vegetables grown in the restaurant’s own garden. Zero-mile ingredients (the restaurant takes its name from the word for “manger” in local dialect and also boasts its own dairy) and visual experimentation are the distinctive features of the regional cuisine served here, with fish from the lake, game, DOP Bitto cheese and even local truffles all appearing on the menu. There are two tasting menus: a creative 7-course menu and a more traditional 4-course option. Comfortable, welcoming guestrooms and a modern spa complete the picture.

name: Re Santi e Leoni
review: Housed in a 19C palazzo in central Nola, this restaurant has a bright, airy and elegant feel with high ceilings and an open-view kitchen to the rear. Attentive service accompanies your meal throughout, with a choice of options in which the clean, simple flavours of fish and seafood take pride of place (including raw options) with a focus on elegant and colourful presentation. Luigi Salomone, a well-known name for gourmet food-lovers, is at the helm here, having returned home to just a few kilometres from his native town, Saviano, having gained experience in prestigious restaurants elsewhere. Well-stocked wine cellar with over 550 different labels, plus three tasting menus (Re, Santi and Leoni).

name: Casa Buono
review: In this restaurant an experienced chef serves modern cuisine, with dishes offered on a set menu which changes daily depending on the season and market availability – fish from the Mediterranean takes pride of place. Quiet, simple and elegant in ambience, with a friendly and professional front-of-house welcome from the chef’s wife.

name: Rear Restaurant
review: The talented chef at this multifaceted restaurant serves a unique style of cuisine which ranges from raw seafood dishes to grilled meats. Rear’s modern, comfortable dining room allows guests to watch the chef at work in the beautiful open-view kitchen, in which maturing cuts of meat and a couple of tanks containing fresh shellfish can also be seen, all ready to feature in the chef’s delicious recipes. Professional service and a good selection of wines add to the appeal of this unmissable new restaurant on the road to Irpinia.

name: Gusto by Sadler
review: Situated within the exclusive Baglioni Resort to the north of San Teodoro, this restaurant carries the name of Claudio Sadler who, together with resident chef Park Kisung , creates light, Mediterranean-style cuisine with the occasional regionally inspired touch. This regional feel is especially evident in the use of typical ingredients from the island which are transformed into innovative contemporary dishes described as “edible works of art”. Our inspectors recommend the superb crudo di mare(raw fish and seafood), which offers an amazing variety of fish and shellfish. Last but not least, meals are served overlooking a beautiful garden and swimming pool to add a real holiday ambience.

name: Mec Restaurant
review: In the renovated high-tech setting of the Palazzo Castrone in the historic heart of Palermo, Carmelo Trentacosti serves up modern and elegant dishes with carefully selected flavours which are never overstated. Choose between two tasting menus (one of which is vegetarian) or à la carte options, including some dishes (such as the crêpes Suzette) prepared at your table

name: Il Palagio
review: Situated on the ground floor of the Palazzo della Gherardesca and surrounded by beautiful mature gardens, Il Palagio is a gourmet evening restaurant decorated in elegant, refined neo-Classic style. The cuisine focuses on reinterpretations of Italian culinary traditions in elaborate dishes that are full of flavour, while the menu changes with the seasons and is inspired by typical Tuscan ingredients. The overall generosity of the portions will leave a distinct impression, as will the preparation of some aspects of your meal in the dining room (such as the coffee, ground and brewed in an American-style glass cafetière at your table). The attentive service and excellent wine list add to its appeal.

name: Il Saraceno
review: This elegant, welcoming restaurant with a decor that shifts effortlessly from modern design to classic style provides the setting for serious Mediterranean cuisine with the occasional creative touch. The owner-chef here describes his cuisine as “simple”, although the ingredients are of excellent quality. Fish takes pride of place on the menu, alongside produce from Campania in tribute to Roberto Proto’s own memories and his parents’ native region. The extensive, well-chosen wine list offers a good selection of white and sparkling wines. At lunchtime a business menu provides an alternative to the à la carte options.

name: Storie d'Amore
review: Massimo Foffani and Davide Filippetto make a well-matched pair. Business partners in this intimate restaurant with the ambience of a private home since it first opened, the former oversees the front of house and the exhaustive wine selection (including a choice of over 200 different champagnes) with elegance and expertise, while the latter creates technical, creative and well-balanced dishes in the kitchen. The chef’s cuisine stands out for its high-quality ingredients (often sourced from small local producers) and its focus on the changing seasons.

name: Felix Lo Basso home & restaurant
review: Brilliant chef Felix Lo Basso’s menu is inspired by northern Europe: he offers one single menu that changes regularly depending on market availability and that requires all diners to book ahead and eat at the same time. Although the dishes are inventive and occasionally elaborate, the chef often creates original reinterpretations of recipes and ingredients from his native Puglia. Beyond the small rooms used for private dinners, the main dining room features an elegant counter along which guests can sit and watch the chefs at work, with Felice cooking and entertaining his diners with all the skills of a friendly presenter.

name: La Capanna di Eraclio
review: Whenever we visit Capanna di Eraclio, we have the strange yet wonderful feeling of coming home, despite not being from this region! Opened in 1922 and now in the hands of the fourth generation of the family, this restaurant has changed little – to our relief – since the time when a kitchen was first added to the inn that already stood here. The atmosphere is that of a simple, traditional family trattoria, yet with unexpected touches of elegance, while the cuisine focuses on the best ingredients that the Po delta has to offer. The owner, who works front of house, is an expert on the local area, so the traditional dishes on offer here showcase the region’s meat and fish with an authentic, natural and yet modern touch. An all-round harmonious experience!

name: La Zanzara
review: The Bison family’s iconic restaurant occupies a large 18C fisherman’s house in the stunning natural setting of Porticino in the Po delta regional park – a magical setting accessed via a walk through trees and across little bridges. An elegant dining room with an open fireplace and a romantic, nostalgic ambience provides the backdrop for predominantly fish and seafood cuisine (mainly from the Upper Adriatic). Eel is the house speciality (sometimes served grilled over the wood-fired barbecue), while the excellent wine list stands out for its extensive selection as well as the detailed descriptions that accompany every bottle.

name: Oseleta
review: Situated just a few kilometres from Garda on gently sloping hills planted with vineyards, Villa Cordevigo, home to the Oseleta restaurant, is approached via a superb avenue of cypress trees. There are just nine tables in this old hay barn converted into a veranda, where the elegant ambience and impeccable service make for a pleasant dining experience. Chef Marco Marras demonstrates his culinary skills on a menu that features fish, seafood, vegetarian dishes, specialities from the lake and meat options, all beautifully presented and prepared with surgical precision. Cheese-lovers will appreciate the small yet well-chosen selection of Italian cheeses.

name: Da Gorini
review: After working in several different establishments, Gianluca has now decided to put his talent to good use in his own restaurant. The warm dining rooms in this old house have a contemporary ambience – the blues music, use of wood and careful lighting all add to the impression of a private home – while the modern cuisine focuses on regional ingredients from the Savio valley, with a particular emphasis on grilled dishes. The list of aperitifs includes cocktails, sparkling wines and delicious juices made from fresh seasonal fruits.

name: Le Monzù
review: Between the 18C and 19C, the monzù (a local dialect adaptation of the French monsieur ) were the heads of the great aristocratic families of Campania and Sicily. Fine cuisine awaits you at this restaurant, where the views of the Faraglioni rocks, the sea and the island of Capri, especially from the outdoor terrace, go a long way to making this experience worthwhile. Your enjoyment is further enhanced by the blazing sunsets, the romantic twilight ambience and especially the cuisine of enthusiastic chef Luigi Lionetti from Campania, the child prodigy of Italian haute cuisine who conjures up classic regional dishes with modern flair and imagination.

name: La Buca
review: In fine weather, the outdoor space at this restaurant offers a romantic setting overlooking the canal port, while in winter the modern, elegant dining room provides a welcome refuge. Here, every detail – the furnishings, tables and lights – has been carefully designed to convey a sense of craftsmanship and create an ambience which is natural despite the painstaking design process. The minimalist approach is not restricted to the decor but is also a fundamental feature of Gregorio Grippo’s cuisine. Fish and seafood take pride of place on the menu, in a wide array of dishes from raw fish to classic Romagna seafood favourites, as well as more elaborate options, all of which showcase the quality of the fish, which is accompanied by vegetables and other seasonal ingredients. The wine list boasts an extensive selection of champagnes and sparkling wines.

name: Vecchio Ristoro
review: Despite its town-centre location and elegant ambience, this former 17C mill, which has retained its old wheel and millstone in the dining room, almost has the feel of the mountains. Here, the talented chef moves effortlessly between typical Aosta valley specialities, French dishes and international cuisine. The wine list offers well over 200 different labels, including carefully selected unusual wines alongside better-known options from leading producers. Excellent service.

name: Zur Rose
review: The long-established Zur Rose is a gourmet restaurant that has certainly made its mark along the romantic Tyrolean Wine Route. Here, chef Herbert Hintner serves his own version of creative contemporary cuisine which has a strong regional identity influenced by the Alto Adige, in an elegant building dating back to 1300 – the restaurant has been known as “La Rosa” since 1585. Ingredients and dishes change in line with the seasons, with two menus each season, one regional, the other vegetarian. Riding the crest of a wave for decades, Hintner’s cuisine never falters – especially now that his son has joined him in the kitchen. As a result, Zur Rose continues to offer an unmissable gourmet experience.

name: La Bottega del 30
review: You’d be forgiven for thinking that the name of this restaurant referred to its street number or the year it was founded, but in fact its origin has more of a fairytale feel: on the 30th day of every month a travelling salesman used to stop in this small, delightful village. In the meantime, a young French chef, Hélène, arrived here and fell in love with Chianti and its cuisine. She named her restaurant after the travelling salesman and so the fairytale continues! The cuisine here is simple yet attractive, with a focus on top-quality ingredients that are served in unfussy, traditional dishes. With its stone walls and souvenirs of a life dedicated to Tuscany, this restaurant not only offers an enjoyable gastronomic experience, it also provides a relaxing setting that appeals to all the senses and leaves guests feeling refreshed. In summer, choose between the inner courtyard and one of the few tables outdoors with views of the sunset (if opting for the latter, it’s best to book ahead).

name: Tivoli
review: This restaurant occupies an attractive Alpine house outside the town centre on the road to the Falzarego pass and at the foot of the Tofane mountains. Here, the chef shows himself to be completely at ease with both traditional cuisine and more creative fare. Using top-quality ingredients from this mountainous region, as well as fresh fish sourced daily from the markets at Venice and Chioggia, owner Graziano Prest creates delicious dishes full of generous flavours. Wine is another of his passions, hence the top-quality labels, historic vintages and renowned French bottles that can be found in the wine cellar here. The panoramic terrace boasts picture-postcard views of Cortina, as does the dining room – but only if you request one of the two tables by the window when you book!

name: La Parolina
review: Although La Parolina is situated in Lazio, chefs Iside and Romano bring together the influences of three neighbouring regions in their simply prepared dishes, namely Lazio, Tuscany (the beautiful rolling hills of which can be admired from the restaurant’s summer terrace) and Umbria. Ingredients include mushrooms from Monte Amiata, truffles from the Sienese hills, asparagus from Canino and hazelnuts from Monti Cimini, as well as vegetables from Umbria and fish from the nearby Lake Bolsena and the Tyrrhenian Sea. Partners in life as well as in the kitchen, these two chefs skilfully balance local traditions with more modern influences. A few guestrooms are available at the restaurant’s La Letterina.

name: Il Parco di Villa Grey
review: Situated in the elegant Villa Grey hotel, this restaurant occupies a classic yet modern dining room with floor-to-ceiling windows facing the hotel gardens, where meals are served in a delightful setting in the summer months. At the helm in the kitchen, Roberto Monopoli prepares creative dishes with influences from Italy and further afield, with a focus on fish and seafood. The service is elegant and professional.

name: Caracol
review: Once you arrive at the Cala Moresca hotel, a small shuttle bus takes you down to the rocks, where the sensation is one of being on the prow of a ship with the sea and the islands of Ischia, Procida and Capri standing proudly before you. This little gem of a restaurant boasts an outdoor space with a real southern Italian feel and owes its name to a snail-shaped feature on the ceiling (caracol is the Spanish for snail). Chef Angelo Carannante’s imaginative cuisine is full of Mediterranean flavours and successful combinations, while the wine list includes excellent wines from all over Italy, as well as international labels and sparkling wines, all of which can be enjoyed either in the restaurant itself or on the superb terrace jutting out over the sea.

name: Leon d'Oro
review: Situated in the historic centre of a small village between Brescia and Cremona in the Po Valley, this restaurant occupies a period palazzo with an interior full of history. From the exposed beams on the ceiling to the open fireplace, every detail here contributes to the traditional ambience in the dining room, which is enhanced by an outdoor space for alfresco dining in summer. The cuisine pays particular tribute to the region, with snails, delicious Brescia-style kid and game all featuring, although there’s also room for a few fish dishes and more creative options on the menu. The wine list clearly demonstrates how much care the owner has taken to quietly enhance his selection over the years, including only those vintages that he knows will delight his guests.

name: Poggio Rosso
review: You cross a magical landscape of hills dotted with cypress and olive trees, woodland and vineyards to get to Borgo San Felice, the luxury hotel that is home to Poggio Rosso. Here, multi-Michelin-starred Enrico Bartolini has chosen his child prodigy Juan Quintero, originally from Colombia, as chef at the helm. Despite the chef’s origins, the cuisine is fundamentally creative and regionally influenced, with just a few South American touches here and there. Juan has fallen in love with Tuscany and he interprets the region’s cuisine with real elegance and contemporary flair. All of this in a luxurious yet unstuffy setting, with service which is impeccable and always accompanied by a smile.

name: Piazzetta Milù
review: This restaurant is the result of an extraordinary family collaboration between Michele, Lucia and their three sons. It was the parents (their names form the restaurant’s acronym) who opened Milù as a pizzeria, and sons Emanuele, Valerio and Maicol who then helped to improve the quality of the cuisine. The Izzo family talk constantly about each other, demonstrating an obvious and moving affection for one another which spills into the hospitality that they offer here. Playing with textures, imagination and creativity, the chef focuses on flavours and ingredients from Campania in his dishes with only the occasional influence from elsewhere. Local produce and home-grown vegetables feature widely, with an obvious passion for tomatoes. The two tasting menus (Evoluzione and Milù) showcase the young chef’s skill and imagination to the full.

name: Il Refettorio
review: The cuisine served here is a far cry from the frugal meals that once provided sustenance to this former 17C monastery’s original inhabitants. Perched above the sea, Il Refettorio is now home to German chef Bob Christoph, who conjures up a selection of Mediterranean dishes reinterpreted with a light and balanced touch. The chef’s own definition of his cuisine seems to be a contradiction in terms, in that he describes his dishes as simple and yet complicated at the same time. Our inspectors would add that he pays careful attention to his ingredients and bases his modern cuisine on traditional recipes. Enjoy an aperitif sitting under the pergola of roses and Virginia creeper, surrounded by lush vegetation that creates a tranquil and meditative ambience.

name: Quadri
review: Situated on the second floor of the historic café of the same name, this elegant restaurant is run with consummate professionalism by the Alajmo family (also renowned for their three-Michelin-starred restaurant in Rubano), with chefs Silvio Giavedoni and Sergio Preziosa at the helm. With its ornate wallpaper bearing portraits of the owners, sumptuous chandeliers, view of St Mark’s Square and carefully restored 16C features, this is truly a restaurant for a special occasion. The opulence of the setting is deliberately lightened by the friendly service, which is occasionally playful and yet impeccable at all times. Skilful reinterpretations of Venetian and Italian classics feature on the tasting menus served here, although dishes can also be chosen à la carte. In addition to the historic Quadri café on the ground floor, the more informal Quadrino serves simpler, less expensive fare which is nonetheless interesting.

name: Bianca sul Lago by Emanuele Petrosino
review: The large windows at this restaurant allow guests to enjoy some of the most beautiful sunsets in the region, either from the dining room or perhaps while sipping an aperitif in the lounge bar – the chef has even dedicated a dish to this atmospheric occasion. Highly technical Mediterranean cuisine is to the fore here, with numerous dishes from Campania on the menu, accompanied by impeccable service and a good selection of wines that is still being expanded. Part of a smart hotel, the dining room is modern and minimalist in style. Definitely one of the best restaurants in the province!

name: Lunasia
review: One of the most original and imaginative chefs in the Versilia region is at the helm in the luxury Plaza e de Russie hotel’s showcase restaurant, where the bright, modern dining room overlooks Viareggio’s famous seafront promenade. Three tasting menus are available here: the first dedicated to fish, the second vegetarian, and the third focusing on meat, with guests able to choose courses freely from each menu à la carte style. Whatever you choose the dishes here are of a rare elegance, with occasionally striking presentations. Chef Luca Landi’s cuisine pays tribute to the region, using excellent ingredients such as local fish and produce from Tuscany’s inland areas.

name: Zia
review: Situated in a quiet residential part of charming Trastevere, this restaurant stands out among the district’s many typical restaurants for its fresh, elegant look, its professional approach and, last but certainly not least, its excellent cuisine. Guests are given a warm and enthusiastic welcome here, as they are introduced to the culinary world of chef Antonio Ziantoni. The chef’s recipes are accessible yet elaborate in their preparation, offering a real feast for the palate throughout the meal which will undoubtedly leave a lasting memory. The wine list boasts more than 350 labels and also includes an interesting selection of wines by the glass.

name: Impronte
review: A converted bus depot just outside the city has been transformed into this minimalist-style restaurant. Here, the chef works with carefully selected produce to create his own style of cuisine with a particular fondness for acidic and smoked ingredients, as well as the use of contrasting flavours. The options here include two tasting menus as well as the à la carte, plus a selection of raw fish dishes.

name: Kuppelrain
review: The cuisine, kitchen garden and wine cellar, along with the warm, attentive service provided by the whole family, are the key factors that have contributed to the success of this restaurant over the past thirty years. Hospitality is a value that its owners cultivate every day, in the same way as they tend their kitchen garden, take care preparing their food and keep an eye on their well-stocked wine cellar, which we highly recommend visiting. The castle overlooking the valley and the apple orchards that surround it provide the backdrop to a gastronomic and cultural experience that should not be missed by food-lovers visiting the Venosta valley. Welcome to Kuppelrain! Bistro service only at lunchtime.

name: Al Gambero
review: Antonio and Mariapaola, the current generation at the helm of this restaurant (ably assisted by the next generation), have had huge success here, having achieved and maintained a Michelin star for decades. The couple have embraced a culinary approach that focuses on traditional recipes, bringing them back to life and adding the chef’s own original twist. His dishes demonstrate a personal and delicate touch in the preparation of carefully selected ingredients, such as wild game and fish-based recipes, all of which require great skill on the part of the chef. The end result is delicious – reading the menu you’ll want to try almost everything! Both the service and the table settings are classic in style, as is the excellent, fairly priced wine list.

name: L'Asinello
review: Situated at the entrance to a romantic village in the Chianti region, this former stable has been converted into a quiet, elegant restaurant by a young couple, with a beautiful garden for summer dining. Here, guests can sit after dinner and enjoy the sound of neighbours calling to each other in the background, a pleasant reminder of life in Italy in days gone by. At the helm in the kitchen, the husband champions traditional cuisine which is minimalist in its choice of flavours and made from just a few well-balanced ingredients. The impeccably kept garden, which is as beautiful and well presented as his dishes, is also the chef’s work (he certainly has green fingers!). A real Italian culinary gem!

name: I Pupi
review: Although his name could easily be that of a theatre star, Tony Lo Coco is actually the owner-chef of the I Pupi restaurants, and the proud holder of a Michelin star. His wife Laura is at the helm in the small, elegant dining room with a modern and minimalist feel, which is dominated by a large gleaming cabinet-cum-sideboard. As for the cuisine, Tony demonstrates real care in his choice of local ingredients, working with the best local cheesemakers, fishermen, farmers and breeders – you can happily let him guide you through his imaginative and personalised Sicilian cuisine. We highly recommended the meat and fish tasting menus, the mixed menu to taste a bit of everything, and the chef’s stigghioladish (his own take on street food).

name: Materia
review: “I trained in traditional cuisine before moving to Noma in Copenhagen, which completely changed my ideas and perceptions and, in some ways, took me back to my origins in the valleys around Lake Como”, says Caranchini. “This is where my grandmother used to harvest wild produce in summer to preserve for the winter, when almost nothing grew at home”. The cuisine here is predominantly influenced by Italy and Asia, with a menu featuring plenty of vegetables, spices and aromatic herbs that the chef uses to create dishes full of concentrated flavours. If you enjoy innovative and original combinations, this is the restaurant for you as many of the dishes on the menu (including the desserts) offer something different, including recipes with more challenging and acidic and bitter flavours. The dining room is minimalist yet welcoming in style.

name: George Restaurant
review: This roof-garden restaurant in one of Naples’ most luxurious hotels (Grand Hotel Parker’s) boasts an open-view kitchen facing a breathtaking panorama that takes in Vesuvius, the Bay of Naples and the city itself, which extends below the hotel in an evocative display of sparkling lights. It’s a challenge for the cuisine to compete with so much beauty but young chef Domenico Candela is more than equal to the task. His cuisine showcases the culinary specialities of the city and further afield with extraordinary skill, combining superb produce and recipes from Campania with techniques learnt in France to produce truly remarkable reinterpretations of regional dishes.

name: Senso Alfio Ghezzi Mart
review: The talented Trentino chef at this restaurant has given his dishes a contemporary flavour – and how could it be otherwise given its location! Situated in the famous Mart (Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art), the restaurant offers just one tasting menu in the evening, which can also be reduced to four courses. The cuisine here has a real Italian flavour with its roots firmly in regional traditions, with dishes that are seemingly simple yet the result of sophisticated preparation and with a focus on elegant presentation. Although game and freshwater fish always feature on the menu, there’s also plenty of room for vegetables. At lunchtime, the bistro options are more streamlined.

name: Due Colombe
review: At this restaurant, the chef’s highly creative approach does not ignore his culinary roots, resulting in a successful reinterpretation of local peasant traditions and top-quality cuisine. Our inspectors highly recommended making your way to this thousand-year-old hamlet, where you dine in a deconsecrated church under a brick-vaulted ceiling. The fine cuisine celebrated here includes historic dishes that have become classic favourites, which can be chosen from the three tasting menus. A good example is the beef cooked with olive oil and served with polenta: “Nonna” Elvira made this dish in the post-war period and her grandson Stefano follows the same recipe today. The menu also includes a few fish dishes, while wine-enthusiasts shouldn’t hesitate to ask sommelier Federica for her recommendations – they won’t regret it!

name: Da Candida
review: This little gem of a restaurant in the centre of a small town boasts a charming ambience and a decidedly romantic feel. If you believe that food can take you on a journey, this quiet, elegant restaurant is the place for you, offering an exciting gastronomic experience where the flavour and elegance of French cuisine meet the scents and aromas of southern Italy. In the kitchen, owner-chef Bernard Fournier, assisted by young Sicilian Giovanni Croce, dedicates an entire menu to the glory of foie gras (don’t miss the peaty Scotch whisky variation), although he partly balances this out with his “La Tradizione” menu (which has more of a French focus), as well as his Mediterranean à la carte options, and his tasting menus. The wine list features a number of Italian labels.

name: Il Tino
review: Enjoying an attractive location in the Nautilus Marina, overlooking the Tiber and the boats moored along it, this restaurant decorated in a modern, minimalist style represents a childhood dream for its chef, who learned his craft from observing his grandparents, both of whom were excellent cooks. Following years spent gaining experience abroad and in Italy, including an informative period with Gualtiero Marchesi at L’Albereta, Usai now creates contemporary cuisine with a strong regional character, prepared from top-quality seasonal ingredients and enhanced with cutting-edge techniques. His cuisine is also open to more exotic influences, including from Asia, the aesthetic quality of which reflects the chef’s own love for elegant presentation. The restaurant’s kitchen garden, visible from the steps leading into the dining room, provides the many herbs that are used skilfully by the chef to add colour and even more flavour to his delicious fish and seafood dishes. Excellent wine list, plus the highly recommended option of starting your meal with an intriguing cocktail!

name: AALTO
review: Situated in the heart of Porta Nuova, the most modern district of Milan and an area that “is liked by people who are liked” (to use the words of an old advertising slogan), this restaurant occupies the first floor of the Torre Solaria. Take a seat at one of the elegant tables arranged in an orderly chessboard-like fashion and enjoy chef Takeshi Iwai’s delicious, top-quality cuisine which demonstrates both Asian and European influences. The various options are all highly personalised and prepared from exotic ingredients, the use of which is effective yet always subtle and understated. The IYO Omakase sushi bar (a “restaurant within a restaurant”) shares an entrance with AALTO, although the two spaces are kept separate, and the food served at the bar is prepared by sushi master Masashi Suzuki.

name: I Caffi
review: Housed on the first floor of a 16C palazzo in the historic centre, the frescoed gastronomic Stanza del Sindaco acts as a backdrop for elegant Piedmontese cuisine in this gourmet restaurant, with the occasional fish dish also featuring on the menu. The bread, pasta and small selection of pastries prepared daily, the different types of meat (from the Piedmont and elsewhere), various cheeses and fresh vegetables (many of which are organic), homegrown herbs and excellent fresh fish are all carefully chosen and of the highest quality. The menu is further enhanced by the addition of mushrooms and truffles from the local area in season.

name: Gambero Rosso
review: Gambero Rosso was founded in the 1970s, when Anna Maria and Giuseppe Sculli decided to pay tribute to the sea that they had previously left as emigrants. Since then, the restaurant has become a focus for the whole family and today, a new chapter is being written with the arrival of sons Riccardo and Francesco at the helm. Fish-lovers will be in their element at this restaurant, which is one of the most popular in the region. The dishes are made from the best fish caught daily along the Ionian coast, with raw fish dishes, including excellent antipasti, attracting customers from all over Calabria. The fresh pasta options are also excellent, while the main courses combine fish and seafood with vegetables. The restaurant also makes a commendable effort to work as much as possible with local producers and suppliers.

name: Qafiz
review: Although getting to this restaurant is not easy, the pleasant drive that takes you through Campania’s beautiful countryside dotted with countless olive trees makes it even more worthwhile. At the end of your journey, you arrive at an elegant late-18C villa with its adjoining old olive-oil that is now home to a refined and simply decorated restaurant with just four tables laid out under a typical cross-vaulted ceiling. This tiny gem of a restaurant is home to one of the most interesting and talented chefs in the region, ably assisted by an excellent front-of-house team. Many of the ingredients used in the dishes come from Calabria, including famous specialities such as sardella fish paste and ‘ndujasausage, as well as other lesser-known products. Fish and meat both feature, as both are readily available just a few kilometres from the restaurant. The beautiful lounge bar is the perfect setting in which to enjoy a cocktail overlooking the swimming pool and well-tended garden. If you would like to eat alfresco in summer, make sure you book ahead as there’s only one table outdoors!

name: Rossellinis
review: Although the dining rooms at this restaurant are elegant and sophisticated, it is the summer terrace that steals the show thanks to its views of one of the most stunning stretches of the Amalfi coast – a striking picture of cobalt-blue sea and verdant mountains. This delightful, romantic experience starts with an aperitif in the garden, where the regional aspect of the cuisine is immediately obvious in the delicacies served. One of the dominant features of the chef’s cooking here is its light touch, where technique and balance go hand in hand in dishes made from local ingredients with the occasional influence from further afield. The sommelier assists guests with their choice of wines from an extensive selection which finds place for local labels alongside wines from outside Italy.

name: Locanda del Pilone
review: Situated just a few kilometres from the town, this restaurant stands on a hill with 360° views of some of the most breathtaking vineyard scenery in the area, where vines stand in neat rows extending into the distance and take on extraordinary colours in autumn. Here, in a classic and elegant setting, the surprising and imaginative menu also includes a few regional specialities, all prepared by a chef who demonstrates remarkable skill and creativity. The excellent wine list offers a wide selection of champagnes in addition to the usual top-quality local labels. Delightful guestrooms make extending your stay in this charming setting a real temptation.

name: Pashà
review: This restaurant is housed in one of the most important historic buildings in the town – the Seminario Vescovile (Bishop’s Seminary). The austere, majestic exterior contrasts with the contemporary elegance of the dining room, while the cuisine continues to focus on dishes firmly rooted in the region, albeit with the occasional modern twist. Chef Antonio Zaccardi is at the helm here, creating various tasting menus on which he demonstrates skills and techniques acquired over the years, focusing on just a few ingredients so that every dish explodes with intense and generous flavours. His wife Angelica Giannuzzi is equally as talented, creating pastries and desserts that are out of the ordinary and full of personality. Antonio Magistà oversees the front of house with skill and elegance, fully confident in the restaurant’s excellent wine list which is dominated by champagnes and wines from Puglia and Bordeaux.

name: Sensi
review: All five senses will be satisfied by a visit to the gourmet restaurant of the Hotel Residence. Housed in a splendid 18C palazzo just a few metres from the famous cathedral, the restaurant boasts an interior design which combines modern and functional features with the building’s classic look, using a colour scheme which is typical of the Amalfi Coast. Although the cuisine focuses mainly on Mediterranean fish and seafood, the menu also features a few meat specialities.

name: Osteria del Viandante
review: The Viandante has been given a new lease of life thanks to careful renovation which has left it more beautiful and refined than ever. The dining rooms, embellished with either frescoes or wallpaper, are extremely elegant, while the splendid porcelain showcases regional dishes made from local ingredients to the full. There’s something for everyone on the wine list – fans of French wine especially will be in their element.

name: Nazionale
review: Situated in the hotel of the same name in a typical mountain-style property, this elegant restaurant offers two welcoming dining rooms with open fireplaces and a profusion of wood, where friendly service adds to the warm atmosphere. Specialities served here include char, snails, an excellent selection of game, Sambuca mutton and local butter, as well as herbs and vegetables from the restaurant’s own kitchen garden. A special mention should be made of the bread, in particular the delicious “pane sflogliato” (literally, layered bread). All in all, full marks for the remarkable cuisine, which succeeds in showcasing the valley’s gastronomic gems and which will appeal to even the most demanding of palates!

name: Don Alfonso 1890 San Barbato
review: A grand hotel requires a big name, so it’s only fitting that this elegant, stylish restaurant with floor-to-ceiling windows offering beautiful views of the garden and swimming pool is run by the Jaccarino family. The cuisine here is inspired by classic favourites, as well as reinterpretations of more regional recipes, all made from carefully selected and top-quality local ingredients such as “crusco” peppers. The modern, technical cuisine showcases small local producers and forgotten flavours. There’s also an excellent selection of wines from southern Italy (and elsewhere). Not to be missed!

name: San Giorgio
review: An elegant restaurant boasting careful attention to detail in its decor, San Giorgio serves top-quality local fish alongside a few meat specialities such as foie gras and suckling pig. The cuisine here is Mediterranean in style and full of colour and flavour, while the warm, professional welcome offered by the Scala brothers adds to the appeal. With a wine list of the same high standard as the food, this is a restaurant to come back to!

name: Dalla Gioconda
review: Between the blue sky and the Adriatic Sea, at the highest point of Gabicce Monte, Dalla Gioconda is the gourmet rebirth of a renowned dancing venue in the town. The design is warm, conceived and created with sustainability in mind. Thanks to a long experience at the Osteria Francescana of Massimo Bottura, the talented chef Davide Di Fabio creates precise and beautiful dishes, cooked with the best ingredients of the territory and of their own garden. The cellar hides real gems, and the summer terrace offers moments of sheer beauty.

name: Kitchen
review: Nestled amid the greenery of a private park, Kitchen is an elegant restaurant which serves creative Italian cuisine with a focus on seasonal ingredients and a perfect balance between produce, technique and flavour. The chef uses herbs and vegetables from the restaurant’s own biodynamic kitchen garden which can be seen in front of the entrance. This natural bounty provides the basis for the “Green” tasting menu; the other tasting menu is called “L’Italia secondo noi” (literally, “Italy according to us”); there’s also an excellent à la carte. . Service is attentive without being intrusive, plus there’s an excellent selection of wines.

name: La Terrazza
review: A luxurious setting and breathtaking views make La Terrazza at the Eden hotel one of the most scenic restaurants in Rome. Situated on the top floor of the exclusive Dorchester hotel, the restaurant boasts soft lighting that allows the beautiful views of this historic city through the large windows to be enjoyed to the full. At the helm in the kitchen, Fabio Ciervo from Campania creates elegant dishes in which top-quality ingredients are transformed by careful preparation and skilful techniques. The à la carte offers a fabulous selection of delicious fish and meat options, while the new X Years tasting menu celebrates the long relationship between Ciervo and the Eden by showcasing his signature dishes.

name: L’Alchimia
review: The parquet floor, wood-beamed ceiling and exposed brickwork lend a warm ambience to this restaurant, which is bright and airy during the day and romantic in the evening thanks to its soft lighting. The cuisine here will appeal not necessarily for its creativity but for its honest dishes in which top-quality Italian ingredients are prepared with imagination, and occasionally transformed with intense flavours. Additional features include a small, beautiful brick-vaulted wine cellar (open to visitors), plus an adjacent bar-bistro which serves quick lunches and excellent aperitifs.

name: Alpenroyal Gourmet
review: Originally from Molfetta in Puglia, Porcelli has closely studied the produce and characteristics of Alpine cuisine, learning to master its different techniques, flavours and combinations, while at the same time introducing influences from his native region. Housed in the luxury hotel of the same name, this restaurant takes guests on a culinary voyage from the north of Italy to the south, while seated comfortably in an elegant setting with soft lighting. Our inspectors describe Mario’s cuisine as “sophisticated and based on ingredients from the region and elsewhere, all beautifully and elegantly presented”.

name: I Castagni
review: In the countryside outside Vigevano, this rustic country house with a portico has the feel of a private villa, thanks to its antique furniture and paintings by local artists on the walls. For more than 30 years, Enrico Gerli, together with his wife front of house, has run this restaurant with dedication and professionalism, creating classic-modern cuisine which showcases the culinary traditions of Lombardy as well as a few fish-based dishes. A wine cellar home to around 600 labels from around the world adds to the appeal.

name: Zum Löwen
review: “The provenance of my ingredients is really important to me. My kitchen is a place in which I can give full rein to my imagination – for me, cooking is all about expressing my love of life.” And Anna certainly has plenty of enthusiasm and imagination! Her restaurant is situated in a skilfully restored old farm, where everything from the hay barn to the old stalls has been refurbished and enhanced to more modern standards. The front-of-house service is overseen by Luis, who is happy to help guests choose the best wine pairing for their meal. Although you may come here for the food, you soon realise that the setting also makes the journey worthwhile.

name: Vintage 1997
review: A hushed, stylish restaurant with a red velvet decor and tables covered with immaculate tablecloths, Vintage 1997 is one of the region’s finest addresses and has hosted some of Turin’s most famous personalities over the years. The cuisine focuses on classic-regional dishes reinterpreted using contemporary cooking and preparation methods, especially on the Luna Park menu (book in advance), while the Punt e Mes, menu showcases the specialities of Piedmont to the full. In this region renowned for its meat dishes, the excellent em>Gran Crudo di Pesce (raw fish specialities) comes as a pleasant surprise. Champagnes and other non-Italian wines are imported directly from producers.

name: Locanda Margon
review: Young chef Edoardo Fumagalli arrived in the small town of Ravina with plenty of international experience behind him. Now in his third year at the famous Locanda Margon, a restaurant with views of Trento and the Adige valley, he puts all his heart, energy and creativity into three tasting menus (one of which has been designed to combine perfectly with the Ferrari sparkling wine made by the winery that owns the restaurant). His menus showcase local ingredients, which he prepares with technical expertise, occasionally combining them with produce from other parts of Italy. Although the adjacent Bistrot is designed to be more informal in character, it offers the attraction of reliable Italian cuisine and the option of dining alfresco.

name: Spinechile
review: Situated in a magical location amid the wooded slops above Schio, this restaurant is not easy to find – even once you get to the village, you’ve still got a way to go! From here, you take a winding and occasionally narrow road, the last section of which is just a dirt track, continuing up to an altitude of 600m, where you eventually reach an elegant old mountain lodge. Corrado Fasolato, a talented and highly experienced chef, offers a menu that features classic dishes alongside more creative options. Guests flock here because of the restaurant’s reputation and leave delighted by new discoveries. The wine list is justly famous and is divided into three sections: one dedicated to white wines; another to red; and the third to sweet wines. Spinechile is run by life and business partners Corrado in the kitchen and wine expert Paola front of house.

name: Hyle
review: Located on the wooded Sila plateau famous since Greek times, this restaurant aims to take guests on a culinary voyage through the region, from the hills overlooking the sea to the high mountain peaks. Although spanning just a short distance, this covers a fertile area which boasts a rich diversity of ingredients. Enhanced by the experience of chef Antonio Biafora, the restaurant’s focus is on top-quality local produce (vegetables, aromatic herbs, walnuts etc) sourced from local farmers and growers, creating a chain which is both economic and socially responsible. In addition to its à la carte options, guests also have the choice of two tasting menus, the regional character of which is emphasised by their Calabrian names (Pùzaly and Chjùbica). The first, a seven-course menu, takes its name from the Greek word “pisseres” which means resinous, while the second refers to the ancient road that linked Paola to Cirò Marina and consists of eleven courses, all full of flavour. Excellent value for money!

name: Dattilo
review: In the world of haute cuisine still dominated by male chefs, Caterina Ceraudo stands out for her authoritative presence and large personality. Her restaurant is housed in a charming agriturismo which offers simple guestrooms decorated in attractive, rustic style, a beautiful swimming pool shaded by mature olive trees, and traditional produce such as wine, olive oil, orange and cedro marmalades and fruit juices. Add to this Caterina’s modern, creative and yet unfussy cuisine made from local ingredients and you have a winning formula.

name: La Speranzina Restaurant & Relais
review: A romantic, Mediterranean-style restaurant in the heart of Sirmione, La Speranzina has an elegant and minimalist-style decor in which light, discreet colours dominate in the comfortable dining room, while in summer the terrace boasts spectacular views of the lake and castle (a few of the tables stand right over the water). Whether you choose fish, meat or vegetables, Fabrizio Molteni creates dishes with excellent technique and precision, as you would expect from one of master-chef Gualtiero Marchesi’s last students (Marchesi himself is mentioned in some of the dishes). There is also an option to head into the kitchen, where you can watch the chefs prepare either your main course or dessert. A superbly stocked wine cellar, with an excellent choice of champagnes and renowned labels, and three stunning panoramic suites complete the picture.

name: Aroma
review: The open-view kitchen is the first thing guests see when they arrive at this delightful restaurant boasting views of Ancient Rome from the Colosseum to the dome of St Peter’s – a truly memorable sight! The name pays tribute to both the city and the aromas imbued in the Mediterranean cuisine served here. Local specialities also feature on the menu, often with a touch of creativity added by chef Giuseppe di Iorio. The Aroma Bistrò next door overlooks the Parco del Colle Oppio and serves simpler, quicker versions of the dishes offered at the main restaurant.

name: Imàgo
review: Imàgo, the panoramic restaurant at the beautiful Hassler hotel (which stands at the top of the famous Spanish Steps in Piazza di Spagna), provides the stunning setting for young chef Andrea Antonini, who creates beautifully presented and imaginative cuisine inspired by ingredients and traditions from Italy (and occasionally Lazio). Antonini recommends his “blind” tasting menu, which selects what he considers to be the best dishes from his à la carte. The extensive and well-chosen wine list includes a good selection of non-Italian wines, with a particular focus on France, while the superb views of Rome are the icing on the cake, contributing to what is an elegant and unforgettable dining experience. Excellent service completes the picture.

name: Romano
review: Opened in 1966, Romano is a real culinary institution in the Versilia region, serving cuisine made from top-quality ingredients, with a particular focus on local fish. Although its philosophy has not changed over the years, current chef Nicola Gronchi should be applauded for adding a hint of contemporary flavour and technical expertise to the cuisine, while still retaining everything that this restaurant does best, namely serving fish of the highest quality (there are also a few meat dishes), including the occasional typical Versilian recipe.

name: Dolce Stil Novo alla Reggia
review: Housed inside the Torrione del Garove, this restaurant boasts an attractive terrace overlooking the Reggia di Venaria gardens with their geometrically sculpted bushes and hedges, as well as the palace’s Court of Honour. Here, chef Alfredo Russo serves regional cuisine with a modern and appealing touch, surprising guests with the occasional fish and seafood speciality on a culinary journey that spans Piedmont to southern Italy. Don’t miss the imaginative and carefully prepared desserts, while the well-structured wine list (on an iPad) also includes a good selection by the glass.

name: RistoranTino & C.
review: An elegant Alpine-style ambience in a beautiful stone building on the road to Sestrière, where Martino and Chiara offer a warm welcome to guests and serve contemporary-style cuisine with a modern twist. In addition to the good selection of wines (around 300 different labels), there is also a choice of special beers and saké.

name: 'L Chimpl
review: The family-run Gran Mugon hotel offers guests a friendly welcome that extends to its gourmet restaurant (‘L Chimpl), where you’ll find an excellent and undeniably talented chef at the helm. Stefano Ghetta uses a multitude of ingredients in his dishes, which he skilfully brings together in coordinated combinations where flavours and textures sometimes blend together in harmony yet also sometimes offer striking contrasts. Many of the ingredients are sourced from the region or the valley itself, demonstrating the chef’s impressive knowledge of this mountainous region. By the end of your meal, you’ll be surprised by the unusual wealth and variety of ingredients that originate from this mountainous region, one that could be described as challenging for a chef, especially in winter. In a reflection of the menu, the wine list also focuses on regional labels, some of which are well worth discovering.

name: Due Camini
review: This is the most romantic restaurant in the Borgo Egnazia resort, where the soft candlelight creates a hushed, magical atmosphere that makes it perfect for a special occasion, dinner with a loved one, or simply a gourmet meal. Enjoy excellent service as you embark on a gastronomic journey that introduces you to specialities from chef Domingo Schingaro’s Puglia, dishes inspired by the region, and recipes influenced by the wider Mediterranean (depending on the menu). Many of the ingredients are sourced from the hotel’s own kitchen garden.

name: Re Maurì
review: Situated in the Lloyd’s Baia hotel between Salerno and Vietri, in an elevated location overlooking the port, this restaurant offers splendid views of the bay from the floor-to-ceiling windows in the dining room which become even more stunning from the terrace where meals are served in fine weather. Specialities from Campania feature on the menu alongside dishes with a more international influence and ingredients from outside the region. Make sure you leave space for dessert: the cook worked as a pastry chef before coming here and the care he takes with his desserts is truly remarkable.

name: Osteria Altran
review: Situated in a small village about 40km from Trieste, the Osteria Altran offers gourmet cuisine surrounded by the verdant landscapes of the Friuli countryside. In what was once a simple farm, owner Guido Lanzellotti has brought this seemingly rustic yet delightfully romantic restaurant to life, creating modern cuisine that focuses on top-quality ingredients and careful preparation. The new lounge-cum-library adorned with cookery books is available for small private events as well as pre-dinner or post-dinner drinks.

name: Osteria della Brughiera
review: Opened in the 1990s by Stefano Arrigoni together with his parents, the Osteria della Brughiera takes guests on a timeless culinary journey in a setting of rich brocade and linen tablecloths. Lulled by the melodic creaking of the parquet flooring and warmed by the crackling fire during the coldest months, guests enjoy surprisingly creative cuisine which includes traditional recipes and more elaborate dishes, from raw fish and seafood to offal. The wine cellar is as impressive as the cuisine, featuring a selection of labels from around the globe.

name: Pierino Penati
review: Surrounded by the greenery of the Brianza hills, this villa on the outskirts of the village offers a delightful garden and an elegant dining room with a veranda. Chef Theo continues the family tradition here, focusing on a culinary philosophy that has successfully adapted to modern trends around healthy eating while also remaining faithful to the traditional cuisine that has made the restaurant famous. Although in the past very few fish dishes featured on the menu, there is now an equal emphasis on varied meat and fish options, while the wine cellar boasts a selection of renowned labels alongside lesser-known – but often just as good – wines.

name: San Martino
review: A smart, elegant restaurant with a bright, minimalist decor in which large tables are well spaced out to create an exclusive feel. The chef’s wife brings a touch of friendly informality to the restaurant, along with an impressive knowledge of the excellent wine list, which offers a wide array of sparkling wines and champagnes. The cuisine here is modern and personalised, with a slight emphasis on fish, although meat dishes also feature. “Food doesn’t just relieve hunger”, says chef Ros, “but also reflects culture”.

name: Terrazza Bosquet
review: Housed in the splendid setting of the Excelsior Vittoria, this restaurant has an elegant dining room for the winter months, plus a charming terrace overlooking the Bay of Naples which adds to the appeal in summer. Originally from Sorrento, chef Antonino Montefusco is totally at home here, creating dishes that draw from the region’s culinary traditions thanks to his in-depth knowledge of local producers and ingredients, which also includes the use of organic produce grown in the hotel’s own gardens, such as oranges, lemons and olive oil. Four tasting menus are available, including a vegetarian option and a menu dedicated to the restaurant’s “Greatest Eats”.

name: Il Buco
review: Housed in the cellars of an old monastery in the heart of Sorrento, Il Buco has long been one of the town’s leading restaurants thanks to its gourmet dining and homely ambience. In this brightly coloured setting with exposed tufa stone and elegant decorative details, owner-chef Peppe Aversa (an inspiration for so many of his colleagues) creates simple, unfussy cuisine with a blend of traditional and modern influences. Tasting menus are offered alongside an à la carte featuring fish, seafood and locally sourced meat, all of which are skilfully and simply prepared to preserve the ingredients’ authentic flavours. The restaurant has recently added a new dining room with a more contemporary feel, where an open-view wine cellar (with more than 1 000 labels and a good selection of wines by the glass) takes pride of place.

name: La Locanda del Borgo
review: In this restaurant in the province of Benevento, young chef Luciano Villani creates menus that focus on simplicity, organic produce from the Sannio region and an uncompromising philosophy. The restaurant is situated within the Hotel Acquapetra Resort&Spa, once an old farmhouse that was transformed by a family of architects into the luxurious hamlet you see today, where antique furnishings and modern cutting-edge facilities combine to ensure a delightful stay in elegant surroundings. The gourmet restaurant adds to its appeal, featuring cuisine that is delicious and always recognisably regional (according to our inspectors), albeit with the occasional influence from elsewhere. There are two tasting menus: Aqua (fish dishes only) and Petra (dedicated to meat dishes). Aperitifs are served in the charming bar next to the restaurant.

name: La Ciau del Tornavento
review: Housed in a typical building dating from 1931 situated amid the Barbaresco hills, this spacious restaurant boasts spectacular views through its floor-to-ceiling windows and – even better – from its terrace. Take the time in between courses to head out on to the terrace, from where you can appreciate magical views which extend as far as the Alps on the clearest days. The cuisine more than equals the beautiful setting, offering an extensive à la carte of meat and fish dishes that range from classic favourites to new creations, in a celebration of the past that is open to modern influences. The wine cellar is legendary – it is of such a high quality that really nothing could be added to improve it – and can be visited on request.

name: Castello di Fighine
review: A dirt track leads to this magical setting – an 11C castle perched among the Tuscan hills which is now privately owned and has been restored and renovated over the past 15 years. Situated in the hamlet surrounding the castle, the restaurant boasts a beautiful terrace shaded by wisteria where meals are served in fine weather. In the kitchen, the successful partnership between new resident chef Francesco Nunziata and three-starred Michelin chef Heinz Beck is immediately obvious. Two apartments are available in Casa Parretti for anyone wishing to prolong their stay here.

name: Marco Martini Restaurant
review: Marco Martini defines cuisine in three words: eyes, stomach, head – it is memories of flavours from bygone days that provide the impetus for his own creations. He is certainly not lacking in curiosity or a willingness to try new things, as he shows in his modern, imaginative dishes, each of which have their own story to tell, inspired by memories and emotions. The wine list is also intriguing, with a selection of little-known yet interesting labels from small producers appearing alongside more famous names. The dining room recalls a winter garden with a mix of styles, plus there’s a terrace-cum-lounge for aperitifs, imaginative cocktails and snacks. The gourmet menu is also available at lunchtime if you book ahead.

name: Venissa
review: Far away from the tourist hordes, Venissa is situated in a small walled vineyard dating back to the Middle Ages – complete with 14C belltower – on the small island of Mazzorbo, a magical setting which is perfect for a short stroll before settling down to eat. In addition to the Dorona di Venezia vineyard, the restaurant also has a kitchen garden which provides most of its vegetables, including unusual varieties such as “castraure”, a type of local artichoke. Once out of the garden, you come to a small wooden bridge which links Mazzorbo to neighbouring Burano, where you can complete your visit to the lagoon by exploring the lacemakers’ shops and admiring the colourful local houses. The main focus here, however, is the cuisine – and excellent cuisine it is too! Chefs Chiara Pavan and Francesco Brutto describe their dishes as “ambientale” (environmental) because of the close connection between the lagoon and the Upper Adriatic: the menu features plenty of fish and vegetables and almost no meat. Guests choose their number of courses and the dishes come as a surprise, accompanied by organic wine pairings. At the Osteria Contemporanea next door the dishes are simpler but still full of flavour.

name: Spazio7
review: Situated on the first floor of the Spazio Espositivo della Fondazione Sandretto Re Rebaudengo, an organisation dedicated to contemporary art, Spazio7 is home to talented chef Antonio Romano, who creates innovative dishes influenced by the region and the seasons that will appeal to all the senses. Two tasting menus are available, as well as an internationally influenced à la carte. There’s also a bistro-café on the ground floor that serves simpler options at lunchtime.

name: Umberto De Martino
review: The bright and elegant Umberto De Martino restaurant, located in the hills overlooking San Paolo d’Argon, is the perfect choice for cuisine full of the sunshine of the chef’s native Sorrentine peninsula. Whatever you choose, the cuisine prepared by this humble, determined and practical chef is excellent in every way. There are three tasting menus available (one of which is vegetarian), from which guests can choose combinations of individual dishes if they wish.

name: Laite
review: “Plissn”, “Asou” and «Verpai” are the three tasting menus (the latter a surprise menu) served at this restaurant run by Fabrizia Meroi. Laite occupies a beautiful, typical mountain property situated in a quiet district and featuring two Stube-style rooms (one dating from the 17C, the other the 18C) decorated with a profusion of wood. Regional recipes and seasonal local ingredients take pride of place in the cuisine, accompanied by wines chosen with enthusiasm by Elena, Fabrizia’s daughter (there’s also a good selection of wines by the glass). Careful attention to flavour is the focus here rather than overly complex dishes, so that every guest can enjoy the delicious food and head home with wonderful memories of this fabulous gourmet experience.

name: 12 Apostoli
review: A historic restaurant in the heart of the city of Romeo and Juliet, 12 Apostoli tells the story of different architectural, cultural and culinary influences. The restaurant was opened in the 1920s and has evolved thanks to the hard work of the Gioco family, the fourth generation of which has renovated the colourful frescoes by Pino Casarini that adorn the dining room and brought fresh life to the cuisine with the appointment of talented chef Mauro Buffo. The culinary options here focus on just one tasting menu, which can be extended into an “experience” by booking an aperitif, as well as a visit to the restaurant’s historic underground galleries (wine cellar and Roman ruins). The meat and fish dishes served are rooted in the flavours of Verona yet created with technical, creative and conceptual flair.

name: Del Cambio
review: Founded in 1757, Del Cambio boasts a combination of romantic period furnishings and contemporary artworks that come together to create a highly elegant setting. Here, Matteo Baronetto, a chef who has made a major contribution to the development of avant-garde Italian cuisine in the early 21C, skilfully offers modern and creative dishes alongside more traditional fare on a menu that is concise yet meaningful without being excessive. For a more direct gastronomic experience, our inspectors recommend booking the chef’s table to savour a menu created on the spot for a maximum of four diners. There’s also an excellent café-cum-bistro and pastry shop,Farmacia Del Cambio , and “Il tavolo della cantina” – located in the wine cellar, this spiritual heart of the restaurant is home to 19 000 bottles and is perfect for informal dinners and wine tastings.

name: Al Sorriso
review: Fans of Piedmontese cuisine will be in their element in this restaurant situated in the attractive Novara hills. The owner here is constantly on the lookout for excellent local ingredients, while his wife (a literature graduate and self-taught chef who is passionate about cooking) creates dishes which have become classics, and which are influenced by traditions and prepared with seasonal ingredients such as aromatic herbs, game, mushrooms and truffles. The wine list is particularly extensive.

name: La Credenza
review: Chef Igor Macchia claims to have fallen into cooking by chance: he started inventing his own meals as a boy, when he had to make his own lunch after school because his parents were still at work. This experience lit the spark that has fired his overwhelming passion for cuisine ever since, an all-consuming interest that only increased during his years studying at hotel school followed by years gaining experience working abroad. With its welcoming dining room and touches of modern elegance, La Credenza is in fact a veranda with large windows letting in plenty of natural light and overlooking a charming garden where coffee and evening aperitifs are served. The cuisine here (meat and fish) is highly creative and clearly described by business partner Giovanni Grasso. Sommelier Franca will talk you through the impressive wine list: more than 1 500 labels are stored in two cellars, which are open to the public.

name: Oasis - Sapori Antichi
review: One of this region’s leading restaurants, Oasis-Sapori Antichi has a strong culinary character that focuses on the local region, its soil and its traditions, all of which form the basis for chef Michelina Fischetti’s cuisine. The chef’s intention here is to create recipes that are open to new food trends and influences, while remaining faithful to a simple style of cuisine that is clean, ethical and prepared using only the best ingredients possible. This welcoming family-run restaurant (hospitality is in the Fischetti’s DNA) offers guests elegant dishes that not only demonstrate seasonality and biodiversity but also showcase the best of the region. A highly versatile restaurant that is perfect for celebrating a special romantic anniversary, as well as introducing fine food to a younger clientele who may be experiencing the world of haute cuisine for the first time.

name: Balzi Rossi
review: This historic bulwark of Italian cuisine on the French border has had a facelift: there’s now a new, elegant and contemporary dining room, although the spectacular view of the Côte d’Azur from the small terrace remains unchanged. The cuisine has its roots in the past with dishes which have been served here for decades, now reinterpreted with a skilful touch of modernity.

name: Carignano
review: The gourmet gem in the Grand Hotel Sitea’s crown, Carignano serves highly creative cuisine rooted in Piedmontese culinary traditions and yet also open to influences from further afield. Situated in the aristocratic heart of Turin, the restaurant’s immaculate white dining room has just a few tables, so booking is highly recommended.

name: Magorabin
review: The owner-chef at this restaurant focuses on recipes firmly rooted in local traditions, using ingredients sourced only in Piedmont. These are showcased on a single tasting menu (“Im-ma-gi-nà-re”) from which guests can choose either five or nine courses. A keen globetrotter, Marcello Trentini prepares regional dishes with a symphony of flavours and a rare combination of boldness, sensitivity, gourmet touches and techniques influenced by his many travels. Situated next to the restaurant, the “Casa Mago Lounge Bar” provides the perfect setting in which to enjoy top-notch cocktails accompanied by tapas and other delicious snacks prepared by the chef.

name: Condividere
review: “The enjoyment of eating” is the mantra of this restaurant, whose name (the Italian word for “to share”) refers to an original idea dreamt up by Lavazza in partnership with talented Spanish chef Ferran Adrià. At the helm here is Federico Zanasi, also from Spain, who focuses on two key elements in his cuisine, namely produce and technique. His menus I Classici, Festival, Gran Festival are served in a modern, contemporary-style dining room with a New York feel, created by the famous stage-designer Dante Ferretti, while the friendly, young and attentive staff are on hand to ensure that guests enjoy the experience to the full, accompanied by music in the background. Dessert and coffee are served in their own dedicated room.

name: Moma
review: Situated between Via Veneto and Piazza Barberini, Moma is a modern, multi-faceted restaurant that serves informal dishes at lunchtime and more creative traditional fare in the gourmet restaurant on the first floor, which also includes a small outdoor dining space that allows guests to make the most of Rome’s mild climate. The balance between textures and combinations and the attention paid to presentation and top-quality ingredients are the key features here, resulting in regionally inspired cuisine that also includes creative dishes such as risotto with camomile, smoked eel, honey and oregano. This focus on the region and its fine local producers is also evident on the wine list, which leans towards labels produced by small artisanal wineries. The young staff are attentive and keen to ensure that your evening is a resounding success.

name: La Primula
