Pick and choose from the different categories to create a bespoke tasting menu that could include a thrilling tempura-fried soft-shell crab in a spiced tomato broth, or a roast chicken worth every moment of its 75-minute preparation. Don't miss dessert, like the passion fruit tart with ginger-lime sorbet or chocolate ganache tart with Madras curry ice cream.

name: Little Pearl
review:
The team behind Rose’s Luxury and Pineapple and Pearls is also behind this "little pearl." Its youthful vibe and carriage house mien make for a nice contrast. There is an enjoyable dichotomy in the dining room by way of historic elements from the original structure mixed in with updated design details. Seats are close together, but the space is very inviting even as the volume of chatter increases. Chef Aaron Silverman’s cooking focuses on modern, seasonal fare starring approachable ingredients that merely add to their signature affable, yet fanciful, style. Behold the pumpkin schnitzel with sauce grenobloise or the angel eggs. 
The multicourse tasting menu clocks in well under $100; and the eclectic wine list makes it absolutely worth adding a pairing.

name: Elcielo D.C.
review:
This concept from Chef Juan Manuel Barrientos can be found adjacent to Union Market's La Cosecha. Presentation is the cornerstone here, with an admirable level of showmanship and dishes embody a love letter to the chef's native Colombia.
À la carte is the rule in the front room, but make your way down to an intimate space for serious culinary sorcery. This is deeply personal cooking that utilizes the bounty of fish, grains, and tropical produce. Behold a carrot soup with guava jelly (inspired by the chef's grandmother) or hamachi atop a plantain chip (a nod to his Japanese chef mentor). Your meal's culmination may be as chimerical as its commencement, with an ice-cold plate bearing a swipe of lulu ice cream sprinkled with apple-basil powder.

name: Esmé
review:
Together with his co-owner and wife, Katrina Bravo, Chef Jenner Tomaska lays bare lofty ambitions at this airy atelier. The minimalist, well-lit space evokes an art gallery, complete with a high-concept tasting that's aimed at blurring the boundaries between art and dining.
The show begins with intriguing bites served at standing tables just inside. The multi-course meal that follows features a variety of dishes, each offered on custom pieces made by local artists. Flavorful compositions showcase unexpected combinations like a seared rouget fillet set atop a bean purée and shaved matsutake mushrooms. Accompanied by a bowl of beans in an Ibérico ham consommé studded with tender "pearls" of apple, the dish's sweetness works wonders against its savory essence.

name: Next
review:
Whether you come to experience the cuisine of ancient Rome or Hollywood, a meal here is pure dinner theater. These culinary themes are unique and exceptionally thoughtful, leaving happy crowds waiting to see what's "next."
While the earlier Italia menu showcased complex ingredients, flawless flavors, and extraordinary textures (think cacio e pepe, guanciale-wrapped branzino, and veal cheek agrodolce atop a savory bread pudding), the Tenth Anniversary menu celebrated the best moments in the restaurant's last decade. Highlights included fish and chips, complete with balsamic dressing and a malt vinegar "sea foam." The Basque cheesecake was delightfully decadent.
Servers are fully vested and display an encyclopedic knowledge of each prevailing topic.

name: Galit
review:
Its exterior is unassuming, but one step inside the rustic-chic hot spot and you'll be smitten by its lively vibe, warm hospitality and seductive aromas. Acclaimed chef Zach Engel brings his experience to bear on this personal brand of modern Middle Eastern cuisine. His prix-fixe allows diners to make their own selections from a range of options, but sharing is key to cover the most ground. Kick things off with salatim (spreads and pickles) accompanied by flame-kissed pita. Even familiar dishes offer surprising depth, like creamy hummus or crackling-crisp falafel with mango labneh.
Dessert manages to be just as tantalizing as the savory fare. Sample an updated spin on baklava with white chocolate and raspberry for a wonderfully elegant finale.

name: Elske
review:
A vivid neon sign signals the entry into this stylish spot. Elske, Danish for "love," is a hip and elegant offering brought to you by husband-and-wife team, David and Anna Posey, and what they do here is pure culinary magic. The spacious setting is equal parts minimal and intimate; while a lovely patio, complete with an open-air campfire, is perfect for a single sip or several.
The chefs' deeply creative ethos is reflected in this menu with seasonal, responsibly sourced dishes, each rendered with impeccable skill. A night in their hands might unveil salt-cured anchovies fortified with a Meyer lemon oil or cured hamachi with kohlrabi and kombu. A compilation of charred leeks and oats is topped with a clothbound cheddar "bèchamel."

name: Kasama
review:
Husband-and-wife chefs Tim Flores and Genie Kwon have branched out to launch this iteration of their culinary dreams. The dinner tasting, which is an evolution of their wildly popular café, reflects their training, experience and heritage. Naturally, the result is an ambitious, clever and distinct meal, where traditional Filipino food is given a creative spin in such items as maitake mushroom adobo with mussel emulsion; "pancit" reflecting Spanish influence with Serrano ham; and an elegant take on "halo-halo" combining Asian pear granita, pandan ice cream and freeze-dried mandarin.
The design is clear upon entry—an impressively equipped kitchen framed by a counter where diners watch the action unfold. Banquettes tucked under the windows make for plush seats.

name: Porto
review:
Striking, dedicated and delicious are an apt way to describe this passion project from Chef Marcos Campos and Owner Daniel Alejandro Alonso—both of whom are champions of La Brújula, the noted women-owned conserva company. A stone-carved chandelier, metallic accents and hand-painted ceramics are merely some of the flourishes of this dreamy room. 
Still not besotted? Think of the menu, dominated by ingredients cooked on an open flame. Find a perch at the horseshoe bar and let the team tease your taste buds with uni toast accompanied by cauliflower crema; or Galician octopus with judión bean purée. Using seaweed in place of spaghetti, pasta do mar is the epitome of invention. Close out with pan con chocolate, starring pork-fat brioche and brown butter foam.

name: Omakase Yume
review:
This small and clean dining enclave brought to you by Chef/owner Sangtae Park is lined with planks of blonde wood and offers two nightly seatings at its eight-seat bar.
Dishes tend to headline top ingredients that are smartly paired and well executed. Savor the chef's unfaltering focus on Japanese cuisine by way of deep-fried nasu hirame; Edo-style sushi featuring madai, akami, and chutoro; as well as slices of Wagyu beef atop sushi rice. Other delicacies like torigai (heart clam), correctly aged sayori, or grilled misoyaki flaunt a thorough study in product sourcing, fresh flavors, and delectable textures. Sweet and custardy tamago, followed by matcha panna cotta—deeply colorful, full-bodied and tart with creamy buttermilk—bring the meal to a close.

name: Topolobampo
review:
This jewel in Rick Bayless' crown welcomes a rush of diners for original Mexican food with an upscale twist. While you have to walk through cacophonous Frontera Grill to get here, the serenity that greets you is well worth it. The menu, boasting a panoply of flavors and textures, spins with the seasons all the while highlighting regional cuisines and holidays. Though each dish is rooted in tradition, there's no shortage of flair, as in kampachi sashimi decked with the flavors of street corn. There's also a canon of sauces treated with appropriate reverence. To wit, Oaxacan mole chichilo is a symphony of dried chiles, nuts and spices, and makes a sublime counterpoint to lamb loin.
Drinks are noteworthy, but teetotalers will relish those agua frescas.

name: Mako
review:
Veteran chef B.K. Park has spun out this inspiring shrine to omakase. With nothing but a lone plaque marking its entrance, this Japanese delight can be tough to spot. But once inside, the surrounding din of traffic fades and you’ll be transfixed by the team's dedication to sushi.
Mako is a hot ticket, with just 22 seats from which to savor the smartly considered omakase. Throughout the evening, the chef and itamae showcase their style through unique adornments, like sudachi juice and sesame-pepper soy. Equally enticing are cooked items, like braised abalone or black cod with burnt scallion ponzu. Not to be outdone, chawanmushi stocked with mushroom and crab is the essence of elegance. Dessert is not an afterthought, as in sweet potato with whiskey caramel.

name: Boka
review:
This is the kind of retreat where one can sink in and never leave. It exudes elegance with a bit of romance and quirk—thanks to walls covered with ornate escutcheons and whimsical paintings. Against these dark pebbled backgrounds, find plush oversized booths, banquettes, and mirrored light bulbs.
Chef Lee Wolen turns out a widely appealing modern menu that uses global accents. Appetizers, like delicate ricotta ravioli with summer corn and smoked buttermilk, or an intriguing plate of lightly cured kampachi crudo with green strawberry and kohlrabi, thrill. For entrées, the roasted dry aged Rohan duck matched with roasted shallot and plum jam is a standout.
Finally, hazelnut and chocolate mousse with caramelized condensed milk ice cream is delightful.

name: Schwa
review:
There comes a point when a pared-down style jumps from being easy-to-miss and becomes hard-to-forget. When a lack of any FOH staff means the service is playfully all-hands-on-deck. When the explicit rap music reflects the chefs’ ethos, going well beyond laissez-faire to the point of “we don’t give a damn.” You probably won’t either once you taste the food. 
The welcome cocktail and canape may be a summery concoction of watermelon and Pastis paired with a watermelon-poached oyster. Medallions of quail are dusted with jerk seasoning and plated with onion rings and candied guava for a stimulating combination of flavors, while tender beef loin is plated with a clever raspberry remoulade and accompanied by a powdered mustard-dusted milk bun, inviting diners to make a sandwich.

name: Goosefoot
review:
This plate-glass façade may seem understated, but Goosefoot is truly distinct. The 12-course menu showcases classical technique and contemporary artistry; a more approachable five-course menu is offered midweek.
Begin with a bowl of creamy pumpkin soup with fresh bits of crab and pheasant sausage, then tuck in to a bowl of tortellini served in a brodo of parmesan, pecorino, and Burgundy truffles. Finally, a single diver scallop proves that one is not the loneliest number with a delicate sweetness courtesy of the lobster, coconut, and lemongrass-scented sauce. Though BYOB, the next-door wine store stocks a limited selection.
The Goosefoot experience ends sweetly, with handcrafted chocolates and a warm send-off from Chef Chris Nugent and his wife, Nina.

name: North Pond
review:
This charming Arts and Crafts building may have started life as a warming shelter for park ice skaters, but today it is a special and intimate dining room. The space always sparkles, thanks largely to rustic exposed brick and windows overlooking the park and eponymous pond.
Chef Cesar Murillo's expertise lies in churning out a menu of hyper-seasonal food. Subtle global inflections are another enticing facet of his tasting menu, which might unveil the likes of tagliatelle tinted gold with saffron and tossed with mussels escabeche. Sweet corn gazpacho poured over poached octopus and heirloom cherry tomatoes is worthy of applause; and a flourless chocolate-hazelnut cake with ganache and goat milk sorbet follows close on the heels of the soigné, savory meal.

name: EL Ideas
review:
Dining here is like attending an underground dinner party prepared by a merry band of misfit cooks in Chef Phillip Foss’ home (he lives upstairs). There is one seating, everyone is served at the same time, and meals are prepaid so guests can linger. The BYOB policy merely reinforces the restaurant's resemblance to a test kitchen.
The cuisine works wonders by pushing—if not completely disregarding—traditional boundaries. For instance, a croquette filled with Caesar dressing and set on romaine is to be eaten by licking the plate; while oil-poached salmon with everything spice draped atop a "bagel purée" is served with dill and cream cheese meringue. The French fries and ice cream course, designed to look like a milkshake, is ingenious and unforgettable.

name: Sepia
review:
Housed within a 19th-century print shop, this urbane dining room mixes original details with modern touches. Muted tones in the exposed brick walls and custom tile floors complement newer elements like floor-to-ceiling wine storage and dramatic chandeliers.
Chef Andrew Zimmerman’s menu is a delicious amalgam of American cuisine with hints of Southeast Asian, Korean, and Mediterranean tastes. Gnocchi may seem commonplace, but this version is memorable thanks to the rich flavors of lamb sugo and ciabatta breadcrumbs. Chicken is downright exciting, served crisp-skinned with a buttery Albufera sauce, crumbly chestnuts, caramelized fennel, and sausage. Desserts keep the bar high, and may include a toffee-coconut cake with chocolate ganache and burnt caramel.

name: Temporis
review:
This jewel box is the epitome of subtlety, serenity, and sophistication. Year after delicious year, the kitchen team flaunts their supreme talent. Each dish is a personal expression of their passion and vision. Playful delicacies include butter-brushed corn, dotted with an Espelette pepper and corn purée and finished tableside with summer truffle; classic-gone-grown up creations include a vanilla pasta with lobster, tarragon, black truffle sauce, and Satsuma powder. Seared Wagyu topped with curls of green papaya, drops of tamarind, jackfruit, and coconut purées displays a harmony between sweet and savory.
A sphere of cherry blossom mousse arrives with a cake base, tonka bean gelée topping, and cherry sorbet for a stunning final bow.

name: Claudia
review:
After years of searching for a brick-and-mortar home, Chef Trevor Teich landed upon this welcoming Bucktown location. Named after his mother, Claudia is über cool and contemporary. Modern art adorns its walls and midnight-blue velvet covers the booths. Tables up front are tightly spaced but ideally situated to face the kitchen, where the synchronized team prepares an intensely creative prix-fixe.
The bento box—featuring the likes of a scallop cracker with preserved egg yolk, squid ink madeleine and a caviar-topped potato beignet—sets the stage for a memorable experience. Tempura-fried snails with black truffle and woodsy pine-flavored meringue is a legacy favorite, while pâté en croûte is flaky, buttery and oh so addictive.

name: Maison Nouvelle
review: On the lively Chartrons market square, this pretty stone building is the newest and latest establishment of chef Philippe Etchebest, also behind Bordeaux’ Quatrième Mur. Guests are greeted like old friends and immediately feel at home in this tasteful, welcoming interior. Philippe’s unwavering commitment to good food and to working only with top local produce shines through and is clearly shared by his talented team. The tasting menu, entirely seasonal, features a few of his signature dishes, such as ravioles of mushrooms and sautéed foie gras, as well as some exquisite vegetarian recipes. Welcome to "Etxe Beste" ("new house" in Basque)!

name: Le Kléber - La Maison Bonnet
review: Julie and Sébastien Bonnet have settled in a picturesque village a few kilometres from Crest, their previous headquarters. In an edifice dear to his heart (it was formerly the Demeure de Grane, a local institution where he carried out his apprenticeship), Sébastien enthusiastically demonstrates that he is as talented and that his seasonal fare, equally poised between surf and turf produce, is as enticing as ever. His dishes are precise, sophisticated, even playful at times. The bread and brioche baked in their own bakery are finger licking good. The splendid wine list, with Rhône wines in a prominent position, adds the final flourish to this gourmet masterpiece.

name: Jean Imbert au Plaza Athénée
review: Often a pioneer over the course of its glorious history, the legendary luxury hotel on Avenue Montaigne always seems to have something new up its sleeve. By entrusting the reins of its iconic restaurant to media darling Jean Imbert, Plaza Athénée unleashed a tornado on the Parisian restaurant scene. The "chef to the stars" with the mischievous smile takes us where we least expected: supported by a crack team, he sets about irresistibly reworking the French classics with generosity (lobster and spiny lobster "en Bellevue", veal Orloff, beef Richelieu, farandole of desserts enthusiastically presented by a duo of pastry chefs). The decor has also been revamped in a classic and chic vein that has restored the brilliance of the gold of the Regency Salon. Seated at the majestic central marble table d'hôte, how can you not fall under its spell?

name: La Table de l'Ours
review: High up in Val-d'Isère, a luxurious hotel that feels like a plush chalet hosts this fine dining restaurant, now redesigned with a preponderance of wood, stone and mirrors. Antoine Gras, a young chef from Auvergne who worked with Arnaud Donckele and René and Maxime Meilleur in Saint-Martin-de-Belleville, is a loyal member of the team and has shown his mettle in various roles. Conscientious and passionate about what he does, he maintains the strictest respect for ingredients, which he showcases in delicious and unfussy dishes. The flavour combinations are spot on, as in the whitefish, blood orange, walnut and Maltese sauce. The youthful front-of-house team is contagiously enthusiastic, especially the sommelier, an ambassador for Savoy wines.

name: Miraflores
review: Chef Carlos Camino, a native of Peru, takes you on a cheerful tour of French-Peruvian cuisine in a lovely contemporary-style dining area complete with open kitchen. This chic and refined space is the setting for the sincere and personal cuisine of a chef whose maturity and commitment elevate top-notch produce. Striking flavours and interplays of textures: intelligent, poetic cuisine, such as the hierba luisa ceviche, tiger's milk with black cocoa, or the palo santo braised pota (giant squid), seafoam and nikkei sauce. A tasty and adventurous place.

name: FIEF
review: FIEF is a play on words, meaning Fait Ici En France (Made Here In France) and HQ, because its chef, Victor Mercier, who rose to fame in the French Top Chef TV show in 2018, ONLY uses 100% French produce. Sichuan pepper from Gers, Soustons peanuts, Poitou pigeon, Brittany fish, Montpellier yuzu, French satay, Burgundy miso, even the ice cream is flavoured with sweet clover instead of vanilla. On the basis of this culinary ethos, the virtuoso chef flawlessly crafts flavoursome dishes flanked by gutsy sauces rich in character and personality. Take a seat at the counter to enjoy the experience close up and chat with the chef and his team who explain the ins and outs of each dish in real time for a truly fascinating insight into the culinary mindset of Victor and his talented troupe.

name: Au Gourmet
review: Ludovic Kientz (who previously worked at Au Crocodile, in the days of the great Émile Jung) and sommelier Sandie Ling (his partner, who was trained by Michel Bras, most notably) have turned this country inn set in a large garden into a taste sensation. The chef takes obvious pleasure in preparing seafood and sauces, plus vegetables from his own garden, in a classic style of cooking with a modern twist. For instance, scallop carpaccio, black truffle, leek vinaigrette, lime gel; supreme of plump "royal" quail, quail leg ravioli, fricassee of vegetables and a jus that brings it all together.

name: Les Foudres
review: The Chais Monnet restaurant leads into a theatrically staged room that is still home to the huge hundred-year-old vats in which cognac was stored! No detail has been neglected in the next-door dining room from the exquisite contemporary silverware to the crystal glasses. The cuisine is similarly meticulously crafted in order to enhance regional produce. The beautifully dressed plates showcase delicacies such as blue lobster cooked in shellfish oil, aïoli of roe and spring vegetables; whole roasted pigeon, hibiscus pickles and beetroot with shiso; chocolate biscuit with fleur de sel, crunchy peanut and creamy butterscotch.

name: Les Ducs de Lorraine
review: In the heart of the capital of the Vosges, this gorgeous Tudor-style manor has high ceilings, stained-glass windows, precious woods and moulding that combine to provide an exceptional backdrop for your meal. Stéphane Ringer and Rémi Gornet preside in the kitchen, while Karine Ringer and Antoine Lecomte are in charge front of house. Your two chefs deliver delicate and creative cuisine made with fine produce – lobster, langoustines, scallops, caviar, sweetbreads – that is perfectly cooked. A trolley of delicious desserts makes for quite a finale (including a superb and intense dark chocolate gâteau with a biscuit layer lightly steeped in whisky). There is nothing stiff about this renowned restaurant – just quality food, time after time.

name: Le Donjon - Domaine Saint-Clair
review: This stylish Normandy manor offers an enticing array of dishes that pays homage to seafood, brought to you by Gabin Bouguet, a chef whose commitment is beyond compare. The menu, which the chef devises while at Fécamp fish auction, might feature cockles, lobster, sea urchins or scallops. He draws on these ingredients to produce high-flying dishes that throb with flavour, incorporating intense jus and sauces, and even the odd touch of irreverence, much to our delight. Some dishes linger in the memory: a delectable piece of monkfish, cooked at a low temperature and accompanied by a subtly smoked labneh and a cockle vinaigrette – the kind of intense and addictive concoction one would like to see more often. Meals are served in a somewhat eclectic room decorated with a fresco by Jean-Charles de Castelbajac, with views of Étretat and its cliffs on the horizon. Individually decorated guestrooms for those wishing to prolong the experience as well as a bistro with a terrace next to the pool for more informal dining. Weekend brunch during the summer.

name: L'Odas
review: Ideally located in the heart of the historic city, two minutes from the cathedral, this restaurant is the work of Olivier Da Silva. He effortlessly regales diners, conjuring up seasonal, consummately balanced dishes, offset with the occasional citrus note to add zest and vivacity. Plants, vegetables and fish are showcased in a mystery menu and diners are entertained by watching him at work in the theatrically visible kitchen. Let’s not forget the pleasant patio screened from view and the slick, yet unstarched service. An experience that involves taking the time to savour food created by an instinctive chef.

name: Logis de la Cadène
review: Nestled inside a small pedestrianised courtyard in the centre of Saint-Émilion, the Logis de la Cadène wins over diners with charming service throughout that never falters and enhances the experience here. Once installed in a comfortable armchair in the classic, elegant dining room (exposed stonework, old parquet flooring), let the culinary show begin. The cuisine showcases the best of the local terroir in accomplished and inventive dishes such as the lamb served in different ways (the rack is served pink and comes with a reduced carcass jus, while the shoulder is stuffed with tiny girolle mushrooms from the Médoc). These culinary delights are accompanied by astutely selected wines, with over 900 labels on the wine list.

name: Holen
review: “Seasonality on the plate” is the mantra of this talented chef, who has worked at the prestigious Auberge de l’Ill, as well as with renowned names such as Michel Bras and Emile Jung. His Breton-inspired recipes demonstrate his dedication to top-quality ingredients, including vegetables grown by small local producers using permaculture principles, and fish sourced from small boats that avoid intensive fishing (as a result of which he has been awarded a “Green Food” label). Holen also has his own kitchen garden and makes his own compost. The final result is ethical cuisine that is full of flavour and elegantly presented in the form of surprise menus, all served in a bistro refurbished with natural materials. Delightful!

name: La Chaumière
review: In this elegant 21C century inn located on the outskirts of Dole, chef Joël Césari is continuing on his path as a nature lover, finding inspiration in local ingredients: vegetables, fruit, herbs, mushrooms and freshwater fish. His inventive cuisine varies depending on availability at the market of produce and fish: seared lake char, trap-caught lobster and a passionfruit and tarragon espuma, Bresse poularde in two courses, including a remarkable exotic take on this French classic. N.B. The fine dining restaurant is only open from Friday evening to Saturday evening; during the week, Bistro La Bagatelle takes over with a bistronomy menu offering good value for money.

name: Les Belles Perdrix de Troplong Mondot
review: Perched on a small hillock, the highest point of Saint Émilion, this prestigious winery has reopened its restaurant after a lengthy renovation and the result lives up to our expectations! The minimalist dining room embraces a view of the splendid vineyards of an estate, for which preserving biodiversity and nature is a number one priority. In line with this ethos, the chef, David Charrier, concocts healthy, spot-on food that calls upon recipes which highlight produce from the property and a handful of meticulously selected small producers in a bid to pursue the estate’s quest for excellence in a spirit of freedom and discovery. The polished service is emblematic of French joie de vivre. Don’t miss a tour of the splendid winery.

name: Le Brittany
review: This elegant Brittany sports a huge stone fireplace and vaulted windows which command a splendid view of the bay of Roscoff. Gourmet marine delicacies figure prominently on the menu thanks to the flawless quality and freshness of the local seafood. Loïc Le Bail’s menu also reveals a soft spot for the homeland of Mishima and Miyazaki, which is far from a coincidence as his wife and sous-chef are both Japanese. The magnificent seaside setting invites us to meditate and wind down.

name: Solstice
review: If there are "writers' writers", then there are chefs' chefs. Meilleur Ouvrier de France, pillar of the Ferrandi chool, promoter of culinary design, restaurateur in Seoul, Éric Trochon is that sort of chef – admired and yet relatively unknown. He has now set up shop in this modern and intimate restaurant alongside a Korean sommelier, who also happens to be his wife. The decor blends designer furniture with raw plastered walls; things are also kept simple on the menu, which offers just two boldly flavoured options, from starter to dessert. The textures and contrasts hit all the right notes, as in the Coco de Paimpol bean broth with pickled fennel and melon, and meadowsweet granita or the (really) crispy and melt-in-the-mouth sweetbread with ricotta and green and yellow courgettes.

name: Origine
review: Former sous-chef at Maison Lameloise in Chagny, Japanese chef Tomofumi Uchimura, like many of his compatriots living in France, impresses with his mastery of French cuisine. He is enthusiastic about Burgundy produce and elegantly enhances local ingredients – snails from Vernot (accompanied by an airy and delicious emulsion of mature Comté cheese and vin jaune), char from Veuxhaulles-sur-Aube (with an excellent sauce pôchouse), Charolais beef (with an elegant medley of carrots). For him, nothing is off limits as long as the quality is up to the mark. His wife Seiko provides professional service front of house, welcoming diners into the elegant and contemporary dining room. The sommelier helps you find your way around the wine list.

name: Le Pourquoi Pas
review: The restaurant of Hotel Castelbrac is named after the boat of Commander Charcot, famous seaman and polar explorer. Born in Dinan, chef Julien Hennote has also explored other culinary universes ranging from the French Riviera to Polynesia. He professes a fondness for produce he sources locally and from sustainable coastal fishing boats (hand-picked scallops and abalone, lobster and seaweed), to which he adds his own ambitious spin, resulting in crisp, flavoursome dishes as if art directed. The desserts are wickedly decadent. The cosy dining rooms leads onto a panoramic terrace overlooking the pirate town of St Malo.

name: Akrame
review: A stone’s throw from la Madeleine district, exuberant Akrame Benallal, a live wire if ever there was, nonetheless operates in a surprisingly secretive establishment, hidden by a huge coach gateway. A fan of Pierre Soulages’ work, the modish, cutting-edge interior is dominated by black, with a few photos and a striking sculpture of a man falling embedded in the ceiling… The menu features a healthy portion of the dishes responsible for Akrame’s success in his previous establishment on Rue Lauriston: inventiveness, high quality ingredients and exquisite plating. As is to be expected, the Akrame is proving to be a firm hit with Parisian city slickers.

name: Auberge du Pont d'Acigné
review: Close to Rennes, on the banks of the River Vilaine, this granite building is worthy of our full attention. Owners Sylvain and Marie-Pierre Guillemot met while working for Alain Passard. Sylvain prides himself on his "instinctive, up-to-the-minute cuisine", drawing on regional produce with a sense of invention and real technical skill. He particularly cherishes his relationships with his producer friends, from whom he sources seaweed, chilli, ginger, poultry and, of course, butter. The elegant and light-filled interior, the terrace overlooking the river, and the lovely service add to the pleasure of this gourmet interlude. Very fine wine list.

name: La Dame de Pic
review: A landmark on the map of great Parisian restaurants: Anne-Sophie Pic opened her Parisian location a stone's throw from the Louvre. It may be 550km from Valence, where her name has left such a mark on the history of cuisine (her father and grandfather also secured three Michelin stars there), but it embodies her signature style. Delicate, precise cuisine, coupled with a lively sense of inspiration: such is the hallmark of this grande dame of gastronomy. Her feel for the harmony of flavours, freshness and accuracy is ever present, always shored up by the cooking times and seasonings she has down to a T: berlingots with farmhouse Camembert, smoked corn and sweet vernal velouté; monkfish roasted in hazelnut butter, cruciferous leaves, green jus with Vietnamese coriander; Tarte tatin-style Williams pear, beer ice cream and sobacha.

name: Shang Palace
review: The Shangri-La, a luxury Parisian hotel, takes us on a voyage into deepest Asia to an opulent imaginary paradise. On the lower floor of the hotel, the Shang Palace restaurant transports diners to Hong Kong, amidst jade inlaid columns, finely carved screens and crystal chandeliers. Cantonese cuisine plays the leading role, served in an assortment of dishes that are placed in the centre of the table. Each dish is a masterclass in precision and subtlety. The dim sum are exquisitely soft and fluffy, while the gently seared aubergines, chicken and dried fish dish showcases the full range of skills and art of Cantonese cooking. The discovery menu is a treasure trove: fried langoustine wonton with sweet and sour yuzu sauce; assorted dumplings with shrimp, pork, crab roe, beetroot, vegetables and mushrooms, Shang Palace bao with pork belly and pickles…

name: Jin
review: Wedged in between the Louvre Museum and Place Vendôme, this appropriately swish establishment caters to ten diners at most, who are lucky (and rich) enough to book a seat at the handsome chestnut wood counter. Diners admire the dexterity of chef Taichi Sato as he prepares sushi and sashimi with textbook precision using only the highest calibre ingredients (the fish, from Brittany or Spain, the fish is matured to be served at the optimal moment). All the menus are "omakase", meaning the diner leaves the choice to the chef (with premium ingredients commanding higher prices). From starter to dessert, you are in for a consummate culinary performance. Discreet, slick service. Superb sake selection.

name: Pertinence
review: Ryunosuke Naito and Kwen Liew met at Restaurant Antoine in 2011. Ryunosuke is Japanese and has worked in some of the top houses of Paris (Taillevent, Meurice) and Kwen is Malaysian. Together they have created this elegant minimalist setting, depicted by light wood and Knoll chairs, whose understated, cosy vibe is perfectly in keeping with their characters and ethos. In the kitchen, they craft market-fresh dishes overflowing in powerful flavours, brushing the cobwebs off French culinary tradition along the way. Spot-on cooking as the name suggests…

name: La Table des Frères Ibarboure
review: The third generation of the Ibarboure family quietly presides over the fate of this lovely family property and grounds. The sons, chef Xabi and Patrice, Best Pastry Maker of France 2019, who honed his talents in establishments from Paris to New York, rule over the kitchen. Fine Basque produce is showcased in seasonal menus: Adour salmon, Kintoa black pig, red fruit from Mendionde, gingerbread from Ainhoa, Espelette pepper, Pyrenean lamb, Ossau-Iraty cheese. They delve freely into the estate’s vegetable garden, concocting dishes such as courgette flowers stuffed with langoustine or vegetables on a bed of herbs with an emulsion of rocket leaves and tomato water, that are emblematic of their flair for adding a creative spin to family favourites.

name: La Table de Xavier Mathieu
review: Born and raised in Marseille, Xavier Mathieu is a true-blue Provençal lad. He was introduced to the world of gourmet cuisine by a family friend, master chef, Roger Vergé and finished his apprenticeship with Joël Robuchon in Paris before returning to this splendid family home in the heart of the sweet-scented scrubland of Luberon. Xavier, who sports a distinctive white shock of hair, breathes new life into Provençal traditions and each dish offers a new twist on his roots. Pistou, beans, garlic and basil soup; leg of lamb baked in hot Garrigue sand: his recipes are surprising, highly personal, and influenced both by his region and travels to distant lands (jambalaya of crayfish tails, sweetcorn and potatoes). To be sampled in the swish exclusive setting of a refurbished drystone farmhouse whose foundations date back to the Order of the Knights Templar of Malta.

name: Don Juan II
review: Moored by Debilly footbridge, on the Right Bank overlooking the Eiffel Tower, the magnificent Art deco Don Juan II yacht, adorned with wainscoting and thick carpeting, awaits you. Set sail for a 2hr30min cruise with none other than Frédéric Anton, an outstanding captain, at the helm! The chef of the Pré Catelan has selected a few of his emblematic dishes (ravioli langoustines, roast venison with autumn truffles, hot chocolate soufflé) to regale passengers. Meals are served against an ever-changing backdrop as you glide down the Seine, viewing some of the most iconic monuments of the City of Light, commented by the crew, as you wallow in the lap of luxury…

name: Yam'Tcha
review: Adeline Grattard was given and continues to demonstrate a rare gift – a remarkable feel for the ingredients she uses in her cooking. In her restaurant on rue Saint-Honoré, this young chef chooses just two or three ingredients which she then focuses on to the full. Here, you won’t find showy demonstrations of her techniques or any form of ostentation, just subtle, rarely seen combinations which appear completely natural. Trained alongside Pascal Barbot (L’Astrance) and having spent several years working in Hong Kong, she brings together ingredients of extraordinary quality (mainly from France and Asia) – examples include her XO sauce, black rice vinegar, and shellfish jus. All these can be superbly paired with a rare selection of Asian teas (yam’tcha in Chinese translates as “to drink tea”). There’s no set or à la carte menu – just the element of surprise and inspiration that comes from the day’s market-sourced ingredients.

name: Automne
review: Japanese chef, Nobuyuki Akishige, who boasts a 5-star CV with spells at the Atelier du peintre in Colmar, the Vague d’Or in St Tropez with Arnaud Donckele, the K2 in Courchevel and the Pyramide in Vienne, signs seasonal, subtle and disciplined dishes with proper Gallic overtones using top-quality goods. A characteristic bistro interior provides the perfect foil to a legible repertory whose harmony of flavours results from spot on cooking, illustrated by roast duck breast and purée of parsley roots and kalamata olives. Unbeatable value for money. If only there were more neighbourhood hangouts like this!

name: Ochre
review: Welcome to the world of Baptiste Renouard, so young and already a seasoned veteran – he honed his skills for over 14 years, boasting stints at Lasserre, Robuchon, Alléno, Laurent and L'Escargot 1903, no less! Finally in his own kitchen, he treats us to creative amusingly entitled (in French) recipes, which are something of a nightmare to translate, as they often involve puns and oblique references to the main ingredient. The food is vibrant, joyful, technically flawless and plants play a major role: 70% of the herbs and flowers used by the chef are picked by the man himself on the nearby Impressionist’s Island.

name: NESO
review: The endearing and heavily tattooed Guillaume Sanchez crafts high-spirited, no-holds barred cuisine in a fashionably stark interior, depicted by an impossibly high ceiling and sporting a metal façade on the street front. Cold-steamed extractions and fermented vegetables: the chef works only with fish and vegetables, selecting stellar pure-bred French ingredients, to which he adds his inimitable and imaginative hallmark and high-flying technical expertise. Varied flavours and textures, art-directed, if unusual plating, the menu unfolds to reveal little bombshells of flavour and, while some were “disconcerting” to say the least, the food clearly bears witness to the establishment’s bold, distinctive culinary identity.

name: Les Climats
review: The location – in the former Maison des Dames des Postes, Télégraphes et Téléphones, which housed the postal and telecommunications operators from 1905 – is unusual! The sumptuous interior embraces Art Nouveau style: old mosaic floors, a ceiling whose arches are embellished with a floral pattern, original brass light fittings, stained glass windows etc. The refined and creative dishes take inspiration in French cuisine. And let's not forget the two large glass-walled cellars, home to one of the most extensive selections of Burgundy wines in France.

name: L'Arcane
review: Led by Laurent Magnin, the youthful team of L'Arcane has left 39 rue Lamarck to take up residence a little higher up, in the former premises of Chamarré Montmartre. With his dishes, the young chef continues to show all the qualities that we already know he possesses. Technical prowess and flavours are a given – a perfect example being the delightful light pea mousse enhanced with yellow lemon zest and black lemon powder. The time spent here over a meal, whether in the form of a surprise menu or à la carte, is always time well spent. Finally, let's not forget the great wine list, which doesn't hesitate to push the boundaries.

name: Lasserre
review: Close to the Champs-Élysées, this Directoire-style private mansion certainly makes an impression. René Lasserre (d 2006) came to Paris to learn the trade while still a teenager and by the end of his career his restaurant had attained iconic status. This emblem of Parisian gastronomy celebrates its 80th anniversary in 2022. The dining space, located on the first floor, is luxuriously decorated with columns, orchid planters and green plants, silver tableware and knick-knacks, crystal chandeliers, Chinese porcelain etc. Another element that adds to the magic of the place is the remarkable and now famous retractable roof, which can be opened in summer, bathing the tables in natural light. Chef Jean-Louis Nomicos, who knows the establishment well, refines tradition with a dash of personality: stuffed macaroni, black truffles, celery and duck foie gras in a light gratin; "André Malraux" squab, French peas, parmesan emulsion with sage.

name: Frédéric Simonin
review: Frédéric Simon had long frequented top restaurants and great chefs, from Ledoyen at the Meurice to Joël Robuchon, before he became a Best Craftsman of France in 2019. Out went the black and white geometric lines as Frédéric set about creating a venue of his own with parquet floors, white walls and bevelled mirrors. This “Parisian apartment” (his own words) is the perfect foil to his precise, delicate and poised cuisine – special mention for his stocks and sauces. Not afraid of the odd inventive, even Japanese note, he dares unconventional combinations, particularly in his evening tasting menu (5 or 8 courses). The lunchtime menu is a steal, as is the list of wines by the glass.

name: Neige d'Été
review: Summer Snow – the name is eminently poetic, thus befitting the work of Japanese chef, Hideki Nishi, who trained at Taillevent and the George V in Paris. The oxymoron also hints at the plays on contrast and minimalism that are the hallmark of this craftsman. Painstaking Japanese precision and a repertory as Gallic as the Marseillaise come together in exquisitely curated, subtle recipes with a strong focus on arrivals of fish and vegetables straight from Brittany and barbecued notes. Poised, perfectly judged and rich in counterpoints, the food is as stunning as the snow in summertime…

name: Le George
review:
A magnificent Baccarat chandelier, immaculate white colour scheme and delicate floral arrangements all contribute to the chic yet relaxed decor designed by Pierre-Yves Rochon at this restaurant, where guests are left in no doubt that this is part of the exclusive Four Seasons George V hotel! At the helm of Le George since September 2016, Simone Zanoni has definitely made his culinary mark here with his Italian-inspired dishes.
And although the menu also features delightful maritime-inspired touches, it is Italy that takes pride of place here. Zanoni’s dishes are light and served in small portions, with particular attention paid to the flavours and cooking methods of the Mediterranean. Meals are served in the dining room or in the high-ceilinged veranda enabling guests to enjoy the courtyard setting whatever the weather.

name: L'Orangerie
review: In an all-white, Lilliputian venue (18 seats only) within the mythical George V Hotel, the menu is the work of Alan Taudon. His cooking, which is unabashedly healthy with a focus on vegetables, dairy produce and seafood, has voluntarily eschewed meat. The dishes are flavoursome and marvellously flanked by some devilishly enticing desserts. The wine list features a selection of the knockout vintages from the cellar of its illustrious next-door neighbour, Le Cinq.

name: Nomicos
review: Having run the kitchens at Lasserre (one of the temples of classical French cuisine) for many years, Jean-Louis Nomicos is now well installed in this restaurant bearing his name. For this bard of gastronomic tradition, who was born near Marseille and grew up in a world where bouillabaisse is king, culinary arts and techniques are first and foremost about the senses and pleasures of the palate. It is within these parameters that he reveals the full potential of his successful recipes and top-notch ingredients – Mediterranean wherever possible, of course – including his signature macaroni with black truffles and duck foie gras. The contemporary decor provides the perfect foil to this chef’s culinary endeavours.

name: Yoshinori
review: The latest spin-off of chef Yoshinori Morié (formerly Petit Verdot, Encore, L’Auberge du 15) is already a hit! Within the walls of an entirely refurbished former Italian restaurant (bare stone, white rafters, Japanese woodwork, designer lighting, white table linen and chinaware), the chef treats us to refined, vegetable-based, graphic cuisine, presented as a seasonal menu. For instance, tartare of milk-fed Corrèze veal, clams and cauliflower, or monkfish with lotus blossom and mushrooms, or pigeon, cèpes, dates, carrots and combava: so many unabashed odes to elegance and taste. Excellent set lunch menu. Love at first bite.

name: Le Sergent Recruteur
review: Chef Alain Pégouret has inherited his love of precise, painstaking work from Joël Robuchon. To see for yourself, you only have to enter Le Sergent Recruteur, a historical tavern on the Île Saint-Louis that has been converted into a fine dining restaurant. The former chef at Laurent displays an impressive command of his craft. His subtle dishes abound with well-defined flavours – you can sense the solid classical foundations – and linger in the memory on account of their sense of harmony, the sophistication of the jus and sauces, and the perfect cooking of the different elements. This establishment exudes a hushed and elegant atmosphere that artfully brings contemporary design into these old walls. A successful revival.

name: Tomy & Co
review: Two minutes from Rue Saint Dominique, this establishment bears the hallmark of Cambodian-born chef, Tomy Gousset, who is forging ahead in a no-holds barred, gleeful approach. A relative latecomer to food (23 years old), he perfected his skills at the Meurice, Taillevent and Boulud in New York. Today he plays a gourmet-bistro score, firmly in tune with his era, placing his “karma” (his own words) at the service of taste and the ingredient in a genuine spirit of local sourcing. His motto: “Simplicity and sophistication”, or, in our words this time: “A slap up good meal”!

name: Apicius
review: Housed in a sumptuous 18C private mansion that calls to mind a small palace, Apicius is named after this Ancient Roman epicurean who is said to have written the first cookbook. Chef Mathieu Pacaud is keeping the flame alive at this legendary place with a magnificent terrace that amounts to a remarkably bucolic garden in the city. The dishes perpetuate fine bourgeois tradition and achieve a synthesis between classicism and creativity. Time passes, Apicius changes… but remains!

name: Jacques Faussat
review: Jacques Faussat, born in Gers and proud of it, clearly aspires to the simplicity of his childhood roots. A simplicity also passed down by Michel Guérard and above all, Alain Dutournier. Jacques’ meeting with the latter, also born in Gers, proved to be decisive in his career, starting with ten years spent in the kitchen of the Trou Gascon. Hand in hand with chef Geoffrey Rembert, they sign flavoursome cuisine made with intelligently crafted produce in a bid to nurture the flavours and aromas. Eater-friendly prices.

name: Le Pavillon - Hôtel Westminster
review: Le Pavillon of the Westminster Hotel, a 1930’s luxury hotel and a landmark of the Côte d’Opale, invites diners to take a seat in a hushed dining room, depicted by a black and ochre colour scheme and hung with huge animal-themed tapestries, to sample William Elliott’s creative culinary fare. His surf-turf combinations and his balanced dishes that go straight to the essentials are highly appreciated, such as wild turbot, cherries, almonds and a milk of ‘fishbones’. The terrace overlooks the iconic Canche lighthouse.

name: Le Baudelaire
review: Relax in this stylish, trendy restaurant, nestling in the heart of an arty, cosy luxury hotel that embodies the new Parisian chic. The dining area is laid out around an inner courtyard with a winter garden where it is heaven to snuggle up with a good book and a cup of tea. A haven of genteel tranquillity illustrated by black lacquered tables, comfy armchairs, loft-inspired windows and sleek white walls. Tuck into the vegetable-focused cuisine by chef Anthony Denon (from La Table du Connétable in Chantilly, another model of classicism), and the decadently enticing desserts by Pierre-Jean Quinonero.

name: L'Écrin
review: “A quest for the perfect blend” could be the motto of the luxurious Écrin located in the Hôtel de Crillon. Sommelier Xavier Thuizat and chef Boris Campanella have reversed their roles, overturning the traditional order of precedence in an unheard of, exciting approach: here the choice of wine determines that of the food! Each diner thus enjoys a personalised experience depending on the wines and number of courses selected. The range of combinations is staggering when you think of the 2,300-strong wine bin. This approach also demonstrates the unorthodoxy, technical agility and perfect harmony between the teams. The chef conjures up elegant dishes, overflowing in character which seek to mirror the wine’s bouquet as much as possible. A unique sensory experience in the finest traditions of French art de vivre.

name: Comice
review: A Canadian couple, Noam Gedalof from Montreal and Etheliya Hananova from Winnipeg, had the brainwave to open their first restaurant in Paris after honing their skills around the world. The chef, formerly of The French Laundry, California, draws his inspiration from Gallic traditions, to which he adds a modern spin. His mission is to highlight seasonal ingredients with the utmost care, tailoring the menu to the produce. This flavoursome score is sampled in a natty modern interior, whose deep blue walls are hung with landscapes by contemporary artists, and with an open kitchen to the rear. The front of house is in the hands of the chef’s warm welcoming wife and the couple certainly lives up to their compatriots’ reputation for good cheer.

name: L'Atelier de Joël Robuchon - Étoile
review: Beyond its two restaurants in the French capital, L'Atelier de Joël Robuchon is literally making its way around the world. This venture was born a stone's throw from the Arc de Triomphe, on the lower level of the Publicis Drugstore on the Champs Élysées. A red and black colour scheme; a long counter along which diners sit on high stools, with a view of the kitchen team as they work; a hushed and meditative atmosphere. The Robuchon brand represents a contemporary approach to fine dining. The menu allows the customer to choose between small tasting portions or regular portions. A final touch that will please wine lovers: all the wines by the glass are served from magnums.

name: Ze Kitchen Galerie
review: Under its hybrid name, Ze Kitchen Galerie toys with the boundary between art and cuisine. In this pared-back space, furniture and designer tableware coexist with colourful paintings around a glassed-in kitchen that enables you to enjoy the show of the team at work. At the stove, William Ledeuil gives free rein to his passion for the flavours of South-East Asia (Thailand, Vietnam), which provide him with plenty of inspiration. Galanga, ka chai, curcuma, wasabi, ginger… So many herbs, roots, spices and condiments from around the world that brilliantly enhance classic French recipes. His menu – based on fish, broths, pasta, a la plancha dishes – comprises a range of inventive, modern and nicely crafted dishes that will take you on a journey of flavours and colours.

name: Sushi B
review: On the edge of the delightful Louvois Square, this microscopic restaurant (eight seats only) is well worth a visit. The interior is the quintessence of pared down zenitude: upholstered armchairs, elegant counter, fine glassware, starched cotton napkins and exquisite chopsticks… Marble is omniscient, extending as far as the rest room and the Japanese toilets! However, it is the chef’s talent that draws foodies likes wasps to a hive! This master craftsman works only with the freshest ingredients, crafting them with surgical precision. It is a truly captivating to watch him crafting sushis and makis, all the more so as their flavour then explodes in the mouth, without ever being overpowered by soy or wasabi – his immaculate judgement is truly phenomenal. The complimentary textures and balance of his other dishes are equally awesome.

name: L'Arôme
review: Breathe in an aroma, a perfume, a bouquet… such is the enticing agenda that awaits diners at this elegant establishment near the Champs-Élysées, decorated by interior architect Emma Roux. True to its name, the restaurant has a terrific wine cellar, with 400 carefully selected labels. A devotee of seasonal produce, chef Thomas Boullault prepares refined contemporary cuisine. The set menus change every day according to the market stalls. You will fall under the spell of the delicate, balanced flavours: seared bluefin tuna smoked in hay, veal chop with morels… Aromas, scents and flavours: it's on point!

name: Alan Geaam
review: We’ve all heard of the American dream, but Alan Geaam prefers the French version! Having fled his native Lebanon at the age of 10 and settled with his family in the United States, he moved to Paris aged 24 with just one idea in mind: to make his way in the world of gastronomy – his true passion. He started out washing dishes, then became a chef’s apprentice before gaining a place at a cookery school and climbing the rungs of the gastronomic ladder. Now at the helm in his own restaurant, he has exploded on to the culinary scene as he brings together all that he has learned over the years. His original recipes skilfully combine France’s rich heritage with touches from the Lebanon in a true mixing of cultures, and his commitment and passion shine through in each and every dish. A fine dining experience.

name: Helen
review: Founded in 2012, Helen has already made a name for itself among the fish restaurants of well-heeled Paris. The menu features only wild fish sourced from fishermen who bring in the catch of the day on small boats, which is then lovingly and simply prepared. Rather than fussy frills, the goal is to enhance natural seafood flavours (the fish is served raw, grilled, seared on a plancha, steamed, etc.) – heaven for seafood lovers! The menu varies depending on availability, for example a carpaccio of seabream with lemon caviar, marinaded sardines, young turbot roasted in sage and pancetta, red mullet à la meunière… Everything is a masterclass in precision and know-how and some fish are even filleted and served tableside. The elegant dining room, perfectly at one with this understated ethos, sports a modern, minimalist vibe… Helen is the quintessence of elegant simplicity.

name: 114, Faubourg
review: Situated within Le Bristol, this brasserie is truly one of a kind! The interior will win you over at first glance: interspersed with imposing gilded columns, it has large luminescent dahlia motifs on its orange walls. At its heart, a grand staircase opens up, leading down to the lower level where tables rub shoulders with the open kitchens. Chic, shimmering, both bustling and intimate, this place hits all the right notes. As for the food, this is a discreetly original take on the French classics we know and love. Dishes are carefully presented and flavours are beautifully combined. This is a lesson in how things should be done.

name: La Grande Cascade
review: Transformed into a restaurant for the Universal Exhibition of 1900, it mingles Empire, Belle Époque and Art nouveau styles whose bewitching charm culminates in a rotunda dining room with a glazed roof that leads onto a superb terrace. Suits come here to savour the spirit of early 20C Paris and the ‘country’ air of the Bois de Boulogne. Georges Menut lovingly takes care of the establishment, pampering and nurturing its image of grand old lady. However, she has also kept up with the times as the presence of Frédéric Robert, a virtuoso chef, with stints at Le Grand Véfour, le Vivarois and Lucas-Carton (where he worked with Senderens for ten years) bears witness. He has carte blanche to dream up subtle dishes, which bear his hallmark of distinctive flavours, ensuring that this dame remains one the capital’s top gourmet establishments.

name: Auberge Nicolas Flamel
review: Was Nicolas Flamel also an alchemist, as well as a rich bourgeois and former owner of the oldest house in Paris (1407)? Historians may disagree, but we have no doubt about chef Grégory Garimbay. This chef with a star-studded CV (Sylvestre Wahid, Alain Ducasse at the Plaza Athénée) transforms his ingredients into culinary gold. Jelly of courgettes and blackberries; field-grown tomatoes, smoked ricotta and sorbet of green zebra tomatoes; blue lobster from Brittany, green peas, shellfish jus: the new master chef of this distinguished establishment signs balanced, modern recipes, whose aromas and flavours are intelligently assembled, resulting in no-frills, down-to-earth, occasionally original dishes, like his chocolate and girolle mushroom tart. Ah! a culinary alchemist indeed!

name: Le Jules Verne
review: Frédéric Anton presides over the fate of this emblematic restaurant on the second floor of the Eiffel Tower. Accessible by a private lift, the magic of this 125m-high dining room instantly bewitches the diner, who is further captivated by the high-flying cuisine. Blue-ribbon produce, delicate, perfectly judged cooking and a knockout wine list – every detail has been puzzled and pondered over. For example, naturally cooked cod, spicy jus, fried garlic and fresh coriander or lamb in an aniseed flavoured jus. When booking ask for one of the tables near the windows, as the view over Paris through the tower’s iron fretwork is nothing short of spectacular.

name: MoSuke
review: Former Top Chef contestant Mory Sacko is now showcasing his talent in the former Cobéa, where the dining room has a brighter feel thanks to its new white colour scheme and light wood furniture and flooring. The restaurant’s name is a fusion of the chef’s first name and that of Yasuke, the first and only African samurai in Japan. The chef successfully mixes his Malian and Senegalese roots, his fascination for Japan and, of course, his passion for French cuisine and techniques, nurtured during stints with Christophe Moret and Thierry Marx. The end result is inspired and original dishes, including successful combinations such as sticky rice with tama-miso and mushrooms, and beef picanha with a tamarind mate sauce.

name: Virtus
review: A few steps from Aligre Market, the stylish dark blue façade hides a vintage interior dotted with Art deco details. It is now the haunt of a talented couple, Frédéric Lorimier in the kitchen and Camille Gouyer in the dining room. Inspired by his background of excellence (in particular with Arnaud Donckele in Saint Tropez), the chef meticulously, almost surgically crafts dishes using seasonal produce, thanks to flawless technique and exquisitely aromatic sauces: roast langoustines, almost scorched baby broccoli and a gutsy jus or veal sweetbread with confit of shallots and lemon-flavoured jus.

name: L'Innocence
review: From their kitchen opening onto the dining room, two talented chefs, Anne Legrand (L'Atelier Rodier, Le Clarence, Itinéraires) and Clio Modaffari (The Kitchen Gallery, Itinéraires, Frenchie) celebrate the food market and the seasons by means of a six-course surprise menu. Take, for example, the fine Ikejime tuna steak, the fantastically tender supreme of squab, or the excellent Cour d'Armoise chicken with its crispy yet melt-in-the-mouth skin. Carefully selected ingredients, punchy flavours and elegant interplays of textures: the colourful dishes made by this duo, who like to work with vegetables, meat and fish, are a delight from start to finish. Remember to book.

name: Aspic
review: Having left the world of finance to join the Ferrandi school of culinary arts, the chef at this restaurant then gained experience elsewhere (including the Ministry for Foreign Affairs and L’Épi Dupin) before opening his own restaurant in rue de la Tour d’Auvergne. With its retro feel, open kitchen and attentive service, Aspic makes guests feel immediately at ease. The carefully presented dishes are as impressive as the setting: the seven-course surprise menu showcases top-quality ingredients (free-range meat and poultry, line-caught fish from small suppliers, herbs and spices etc, all sourced from as short a supply chain as possible) in subtle, delicate dishes with just the right amount of creativity. Exquisite! br>

name: En Marge
review: Frank Renimel and his wife decided to quit the bustling city centre of Toulouse and head for the Lauragais hillsides – a region famed for its abundance of fantastic produce. They transformed a former farmstead into a gourmet loft decked in wood and stone, whose floor to ceiling windows embrace the rolling countryside. Perfectly in step with the seasons, the chef changes his menu monthly, blending local, rustic fare with noble ingredients such as caviar, truffles or cèpes. We are often bowled over by his craftsmanship such are the emotions created with each bite, as is the case with his new spin on cassoulet, a classic on the menu. To pleasantly prolong your stay, five guestrooms, exquisitely appointed by Isabelle Renimel, and a small pool, add the final flourish to a gourmet getaway, where the accent is on taste first and foremost.

name: Restaurant H
review: "H" stands for Hubert Duchenne, a chef who hails from Normandy and has worked for Akrame Benallal and Jean-François Piège (Brasserie Thoumieux). Behind an elegant and discreet façade, there is barely room for 20 diners in this intimate space done out in a chic and cosy decor. You will be treated to a well-devised single set menu that makes all the decisions for you and whose beautifully prepared dishes hit all the right notes. How about a succulent slice of golden-skinned Landes poultry served with a seared leek and celeriac mousseline, or the cockles from Dieppe, doused in a beurre blanc and served with shredded samphire and sucrine lettuce? Inventive and masterful cuisine that is all the more delicious for its exclusive use of premium produce.

name: Le Georges
review: Le Grand Monarque, which is home to Le Georges, has stood the test of time – the hotel’s first mention in the Michelin Guide dates back to 1900. This elegantly decorated property is ideally located between Paris and the Loire at a crossroads between the regions of western France. Trained in Narbonne as well as at the restaurants of Joël Robuchon and Éric Frechon, young chef Thomas Parnaud brings a breath of fresh air to this renowned eatery. A devoted follower of chef Auguste Escoffier, he enjoys creating reinterpretations of “à la Chartres” dishes in which tarragon is a key ingredient, such as his recipe for soft-boiled free-range eggs glazed with veal jus. Neither will you want to miss his Grand Marnier soufflé, a perfectly prepared classic that still graces the menu. From appetiser to dessert, it’s always a pleasure to dine at Le George. Simpler, seasonal dishes are served on the attractive patio. The hotel’s charming guestrooms provide the icing on the cake!

name: Le Chiberta
review: Le Chiberta à la Guy Savoy sports a black colour scheme, has adopted wine as its symbol and inventiveness as its guiding precept. Softly lit, the swish, understated interior by Jean-Michel Wilmotte is refreshingly and fashionably minimalist. Its most eye-catching feature is undeniably an amazing “vertical wine cellar” which boasts a whopper selection of Burgundy and Bordeaux tipples that adorn the walls like rare books in a library. The cooking of chef Irwin Durand (Joël Robuchon, Bernard Loiseau), supervised by the “boss”, adds a modern twist to tradition (quenelle of pike, suckling pig, veal’s head, foie gras), whilst respecting the seasons. Tasting menus (on themes such as truffles and caviar) and wine pairings.

name: Les Explorateurs - Hôtel Pashmina
review: In the heart of a magnificent hotel at an altitude of 2,345m, this high-flying establishment is well worth the climb. Josselin Jeanblanc has swapped his native Jura mountains for the Alps, devising meals that crescendo over the course of simple and inspired creations using ingredients sourced from all over France. As soon as they arrive on stage, the immaculate presentation of each dish catches the eye and starts the tastebuds tingling. Porkpie, sweetbread and gratin dauphinois, lamb in a casserole of hay or poultry and morels spotlight the chef’s consummate technical mastery (as do the decadent desserts) and his determination to be not just ‘another’ luxury hotel restaurant... Vegetarian menu. The attentive, friendly service adds the final touch to this alpine masterpiece.

name: Le Pily
review: Pierre and Lydie now reign over the revolving bridge in a swish, modern edifice whose glazed walls command a matchless view of the harbour. What better venue to celebrate the fish from small boats, lobsters and shellfish from Cotentin, so beloved of the chef? The entirely meat-free menu focuses on surgically and delicately curated seafood, sprinkled with creativity and the odd distinctive Japanese or exotic touch: a Salsa Criolla of red mullet; pollock in yuzu and milk kefir; fillet of seabass with cockles and green veggies in ginger beer…

name: Racines
review: When a talented young chef from Rennes, Virginie Giboire, embraces her roots (or "Racines"), the result is pleasing, contemporary cuisine in the form of elegant dishes. Boasting an impressive wealth of experience (of which we will only mention her stints alongside Guy Martin and Thierry Marx who, she says, "taught her everything"), she delivers clever and well-defined cuisine that always hits the mark, proposed in a short menu. Interesting interplays of textures, subtle marriages of flavours, and always the finest ingredients, often from small-scale Breton producers. All served up in a lovely, bright and modern setting.

name: La Marande
review: In the local dialect, ‘marander’ means ‘go and eat’. On the Tournus road, this handsome house, built out of Burgundy stone and set in a landscaped garden, is definitely worth a gourmet halt before a good night’s sleep. The owners, Élisabeth and Philippe Michel, are clearly determined to bequeath the tradition of hospitality and the love of exceptional produce to their team in this elegantly contemporary house that feels like a home. In the kitchen, the chef consummately and delicately curates striking dishes rich in generosity. The stonking choice of Burgundy wines and the knock-out patio add the final flourish to this excellent establishment.

name: Armani Ristorante
review: This restaurant is in an original location on the first floor of the Armani store in St-Germain-des-Prés (not far from the church). The interior is pure and elegant, in the designer's style, of course: a palette of beiges, banquette seating, glossy walls, subdued lighting… Might this be just another shopfront in all but name? On the contrary, this ristorante is one of the best Italian eateries in Paris. Chef Massimo Tringali, former sous-chef at Casadelmar in Porto-Vecchio, works with high-quality ingredients in the spirit of contemporary Italian cuisine. It is fresh, tasty and skilfully done: a fine piece of work.

name: Le Chiquito
review: This stylish 17C house, characteristic of the Paris region, is the quintessence of gourmet and bourgeois hospitality, depicted by a string of elegant sitting rooms. Chef Anne-Sophie Godry, former right-hand woman of the previous chef, is now at the helm of this institution that continues to attract epicureans like bees to honey. Godry has remained true to the establishment’s pedigree, gourmet ethos, as the house’s emblematic dishes bear witness: veal sweetbread with a foamy butter or textbook Paris-Brest, filled with a chicory-flavoured custard. It is as if time has stood still in the land of good food. The 400-strong wine bin adds a final flourish to this appetising and highly recommended portrait that is further enhanced by polished service with a smile.

name: Trente-Trois
review: This plush, wainscoted Belle Époque dining room is located at number 33 in a discreet edifice, lining what is known as the Golden Triangle near the Champs Élysées. Michelin-starred chef Sébastien Sanjou (also of Le Relais des Moines in the Var) has a knack for selecting premium produce, with which he composes a voluntarily concise menu, signing subtle, up-to-date, seasonal dishes. His food hits the spot every time from the impeccable cooking and superlative jus and sauces to the delicately judged flavours. We tasted a marvellous risotto of spelt, violet artichokes served iced and as crunchy crisps with a hint of coriander in a delicious jus overflowing in gutsy aromas.

name: Hostellerie la Montagne
review: In this peaceful Haute-Marne village that was dear to Charles de Gaulle, this fine 17C stone house is surrounded by beautiful grounds that blend into the countryside. But once inside there is not a hint of nostalgia, either in the contemporary decor or in the dishes – not even in the set menu dubbed "Je vous ai compris!" ("I understood you!" – de Gaulle's famous declaration). Chef Jean-Baptiste Natali has travelled extensively, from Marrakesh to London to New York. He cooks up a contemporary take on French fine dining (with frequent nods to his travels) by working with fine produce such as langoustines, red mullet, lobster, Angus beef and sweetbreads. Tomatoes, caviar and oysters; roasted langoustines royales with an iced currant jus; seared fillet of red mullet and lime mousseline are indicative of his sound craftsmanship. Cosy and comfortable guestrooms.

name: L'Atelier de Joël Robuchon - St-Germain
review: Bathed in a studied semi-darkness, two bars face each other around the central kitchen where the dishes are prepared under the gaze of the guests, who sit at the counter on high stools. An interpretation of the idea of a "chic canteen", a Western version of Japanese teppanyaki and sushi bars, with a menu of "customisable" cuisine in the form of small portions and plates and choice ingredients. Caviar on a soft-boiled egg and smoked salmon in puff pastry; fried whiting "Colbert style" with herb butter: nearly 80 different dishes are served at lunch and dinner. Not forgetting the house staples, king crab ravioli, suckling lamb chops and Joël Robuchon's famous mashed potatoes.

name: Aux Pesked
review: You might be in town, but there’s a sense of already being in the countryside at this restaurant decorated in resolutely contemporary style and boasting sweeping views of the verdant banks of the River Gouët. And as you would expect, pesked (“fish” in Breton) takes pride of place here – ultra-fresh and cooked with the utmost care by chef Mathieu Aumont, such as the wild ormer harvested three days before to ensure that their texture is creamy and they are at their best. And when it comes to choosing your wine pairings, make sure you take the advice of Mathieu’s wife Sophie. Maritime-inspired cuisine at its best.

name: Thierry Schwartz - Le Restaurant
review: Thierry Schwartz, who describes himself as an Alsace native at heart and by birth, believes that nature's rightful place is at the centre when it comes to cooking. This ethos is borne out by his commitment to local producers and by his title of Knight of France's Order of Agricultural Merit. To set the scene: think lots of wood, nods to nature, seasonal vegetables on display, and a log burning fire. Thierry concocts three remarkable set menus in which the produce (from Alsace and permaculture) is sufficient in and of itself: pure spelt, arctic char, wild sorrel, organic farm eggs... to be washed down with a fine, natural wine. The choice is yours – from the 1,500-strong bin!

name: L'Escarbille
review: Abutting the railway lines, this spruce establishment (the former station café) has morphed into a gourmet restaurant, depicted by a chic, modern vibe and adorned in photos and artwork. The recipes are the work of a seasoned chef, backed up by a crack white-jacketed team. The flawlessly cooked and seasoned ingredient takes the limelight, flanked by delicious tipples from meticulously selected winegrowers, who are also presented on the menu. The establishment also serves meals on the leafy outdoor patio in fine weather and offers a valet parking service. A feelgood hit!

name: Aida
review: The whitewashed facade of this small bolthole tucked away in a lane blends in so perfectly with its surroundings that you may even miss it entirely! Behind its spruce façade lies a jealously kept secret, namely exquisite Japanese cuisine. The pristine white interior is both elegant and minimalist, in line with the visual charter commonly associated with restaurants in Japan. Take a seat either at the counter (nine seats only) for a close-up view of the teppanyaki griddles or in the small soberly appointed private dining room with its tatami. As you sample a single tasting menu, you will discover subtle, precise cuisine that carefully crafts culinary ties between Japan and France. The seasonings, cooking, carving, cutting, slicing and chopping are all at the service of the main ingredient, which is presented as simply and as artfully as possible. Sashimi, Brittany lobster, chateaubriand steak or sweetbread, cooked on the teppanyaki griddle, and served with fine Burgundy wines, painstakingly selected by the chef. Dutiful, professional service.

name: Relais Louis XIII
review: This edifice, steeped in history, stands on the cellars of the former Grands-Augustins convent and it was here on 14 May 1610, an hour after his father King Henry IV had been assassinated, that Louis XIII learned that he was the next king of France… The memory of this rich heritage lingers on in the ornate dining room which sports half-timbers, bare stone, wainscoting, stained-glass and wall hangings, although the profusion of heirlooms is set off by a few cutting-edge details (glazed cellar, modern sculptures). The setting with a sense of occasion is the perfect foil to the food of chef Manuel Martinez, an ardent champion of Gallic culinary classicism. After training at Ledoyen, the Crillon and the Tour d’Argent, the Meilleur Ouvrier de France (Best Craftsman of France) decided to settle in this prestigious establishment to pursue high-flying French culinary traditions. Enduringly popular with regulars, in particular for the excellent eater-friendly lunchtime prices!

name: Anne
review: The Pavillon de la Reine, a magnificent residence in Place des Vosges, is named after Anne of Austria, Queen of France and wife of Louis XIII, who once lived here. In the restaurant, overseen by Mathieu Pacaud, the chef reinterprets classic dishes with skill and real talent, using top-quality ingredients which are full of flavour. An excellent dining experience awaits, whether you choose the intimate and romantic setting of the library lounge or, in fine weather, the lovely verdant courtyard garden.

name: Ima
review: “Cooking has always been a means of travel for me”, explains chef Julien Lemarié, who has plied his trade in London, Tokyo and Singapore. At his restaurant, Ima, which means “now” in Japanese, this talented culinary technician conjures up instinctive cuisine showcased on tasting menus that combine subtlety with regional and Asian influences. Lemarié enhances his dishes with broths, infusions, spices, aromatic plants and algae. And for those keen to enjoy the full Japanese experience, make sure you take a seat at the bar. It's now your turn to travel!

name: Benoit
review: To immerse yourself in the vibe of a genuine Parisian bistro, venture over the threshold of N°20 Rue St Martin. The establishment first saw the light of day in 1912 and the cheerful banter of the old Paris market hall seems to echo still. Initially a Lyon-styled bistro, it was run by three generations of the Petit family, who nurtured its vintage charm and its woodwork, copper pots, mirrors, velvet banquettes and closely packed tables all reek of Belle Époque Paris. Everything down to the plates bears the B monogram, further adding to the authenticity of this bistro that is light years from the trendy boltholes of today. When the business changed hands and became part of the Ducasse Group in 2005, it lost none of its old-fashioned atmosphere. Proudly and heartily traditional, the recipes feature country produce that is expertly and generously cooked. The menu reads like a turn-of-the-20C cookbook, rich in perennial favourites that you practically never get to taste anymore… except here!

name: OKA
review: The Brazilian owner-chef, Raphaël Régo, who boasts an enviable CV (Ferrandi, Joël Robuchon, Taillevent) signs a creative repertory at Oka, underscored by his distinctive culinary identity. He successfully navigates between France (fish from the Vendée coast) and Brazil, always with a focus on outstanding produce. Meals are served in a cosy, smart interior, which sports an open kitchen, where you can admire the artist chef at work. His visually sophisticated and minimalist dishes cleverly play with contrasting flavours (sweet, spicy, acidic) and textures, without ever falling foul of the flaw of showing off! You can trust the insights of the gifted sommelier for his wine pairing suggestions. Exquisitely personal, artfully curated and divinely flavoursome – classy! Love at first bite!

name: La Scène Thélème
review: At number 18 Rue Troyon, art, particularly theatrical art, meets gastronomy. In fact, the restaurant is named after the Abbaye de Thélème, a utopia by Rabelais and on some evenings, between 7-8pm, you may be treated to a drama production (50 seats only) before you sit down to dinner. The novelty is such that is sure to prove a hit among the discerning gourmets of Paris. On the food side, Japanese chef, Yoshitaka Takayanagi, and his team sign subtle, delicate dishes, rich in personality and made from first-class produce. High precision work, all the finer thanks to the splendid eater-friendly prices! Hush – the curtain is rising!

name: Ekaitza
review: Guillaume Roget, former chef of Saint Jean de Luz’ star restaurant, Brouillarta, has crossed Socoa Bay to take over this kitchen in Ciboure on the Ravel docks above the port in a location that is perfectly suited to this restaurant, whose name means ‘storm’ in Basque. The interior sports a sober, airy vibe with lots of space between tables and a glimpse of the open kitchen to the rear of the dining room. Top of the range Basque ingredients are quietly crafted, jazzed up with the occasional bold association and flanked by a deluge of fine sauces. Wine lovers may like to know that the 5 courses of the Arnoa menu are prepared according to the wines chosen by the customer – the chef is a former sommelier.

name: Assa
review: On the outskirts of Blois, this 1930s building overlooks the River Loire, whose waters are reflected in the dining room. Anthony and Fumiko Maubert (he is French, she is Japanese) have chosen this location to ply their trade.
