For a long time, Anthony worked alongside Arnaud Donckele (La Vague d'Or), while Fumiko has a twin vocation of nutritionist and pastry chef – indeed, her creations are remarkable for their lightness and low added sugar content. Every morning (assa in Japanese), this couple devises the daily menu together, drawing on produce of impeccable quality and numerous Japanese condiments and ingredients. Sanshō berries, wild yuzu, nori seaweed broth, matcha tea and azuki red bean paste are harmoniously combined with the handiwork of small-scale producers based in the Loire area.

name: Au 14 Février
review: Japan boasts two of the world’s four museums devoted to the cartoonist Raymond Peynet, who created the famous lovers in 1942. Some of his Japanese admirers thus naturally chose the small village of Saint Valentin to celebrate February 14 in culinary style. You are invited to take a seat in a suave, contemporary interior whose white walls are sometimes upholstered in red leather, either opposite the bar or alongside the conservatory, adorned with the occasional poster or lithography by Peynet. The 100% Japanese white-jacketed brigade conjures up a subtle new take on modern French fare, offset with the occasional Japanese touch. The sommelier knowledgeably plays his role to perfection.

name: Le Carré d'Alethius
review: Between Drôme and Ardèche, this "Roman house" dedicated to senator Alethius has a distinct air of Provence. The villa is arranged around a square courtyard, a gorgeous verdant patio that you can sit out on in fine weather. Having worked for Jean-Michel Lorain at La Côte Saint-Jacques, Olivier Samin moved on to work for iconic chef Anne-Sophie Pic at the three-starred Maison Pic in Valence – where he was sous-chef for a long time. He delivers fresh and refined cuisine, in tune with the markets (regional fruits and vegetables, snails from the Eyrieux, local cheeses) and the seasons (one set menu is devoted to truffles in winter, another to lobster in summer), and with a tremendous sense of balance: precise cooking, light and airy veloutés and creams. Truly delicious.

name: La Rotonde
review: Enjoy a delightful gourmet experience in a lush green oasis on the outskirts of the city. Under the baton of chef Jean-François Malle, the seasonal menus are composed around ingredients of the highest calibre: carpaccio of scallops from Morlaix Bay; Bresse poultry with butternut gnocchis, onions in cream and black chanterelles or royal hare and fresh truffles, without forgetting, his “world champion” pâté en croûte. Searingly good food.

name: La Tête en l'air
review: An enthusiastic and friendly young couple, Clément Raby from Paris and Estelle Mercier from the Gard region, have succeeded in turning heads with what they call their “cuisine libre” (“free cooking”). Served in a relaxed setting, this creative, original cuisine is spot on, with recipes that really work and just the right combination of flavours. On their “blind” menus, dishes aren’t announced until after you’ve tasted them so that guests can really give their senses and tastebuds a workout!

name: Louis
review: Near the big department stores, but in a quiet street, this small restaurant nurtures its cosy, intimate vibe. Brittany born Stéphane Pitré is at the helm, after a stint at Senderens, and he pays tribute to his father, grand-father and great grandfather here, all called “Louis”. He crafts distinctive signature menus served in 7 or 9 (small) courses (or in 3 for a quick lunch): tartare of Black Angus beef with blackcurrants and tempura oyster; slow-baked monkfish with Thai spices; roast haunch of veal with smoked burrata cheese from Île-de-France. The food is inventive, spontaneous and in harmony with market availability and the seasons. Polished French fare with a twist; for simpler, more homely bistro fare head to Le Cellier, just two numbers down the street.

name: Skab
review: This gourmet bolthole located behind the Arènes, just opposite the Musée de la Romanité, is run by chef Damien Sanchez, a local boy who has worked at the Cabro d'Or, La Réserve de Beaulieu, at Christopher Coutanceau's restaurant in La Rochelle and, now, in his hometown alongside Jérôme Nutile. His cooking easily wins you over with fresh and lively dishes that highlight the Gard terroir: sea bass cooked two ways, steamed and served tartare-style; monkfish tournedos, stuffed artichoke with pepper. As soon as the sun starts to shine, make a beeline for the patio shaded by maple trees.

name: Alchémille
review: This old bar has been transformed into a “living space” by a chef born in the village who has accumulated an impressive number of food awards. The son and grandson of a butcher, Jérôme Jaegle is just as much a market gardener and permaculture enthusiast as he is a chef with an impressive CV, having worked with famous names such as Jean-Yves Schillinger and Christian Têtedoie. Almost Scandinavian in appearance, his restaurant is decorated in light wood and natural materials and is named after Alchemilla, the favourite plant of alchemists. His creative and individual cuisine focuses, unsurprisingly, on herbs and vegetables grown in his kitchen garden, as well as other locally sourced ingredients. The set menus have different themes, with a focus on vegetables and the sea.

name: La Promenade
review: It may take a little getting to, but this family-run inn located in the middle of the countryside is a real godsend! At the stove, Fabrice, the son of the legendary Jacky, now retired, orchestrates a modern culinary score of hearty, festive dishes that are deeply rooted in the local land. Racan chicken and pigeon, Géline de Touraine (heirloom poultry), game in season, organic vegetables from market gardens, pike and premium produce from the ocean. Searingly good food, including offal that regularly finds its way onto the menu! Meals are served in a handsome contemporary interior. One of the best restaurants in the region and one of the best wine lists in France, both in terms of choice and reasonable prices.

name: Auberge de Montfleury
review: From the outside, this roadside inn opposite the station might almost strike you as nondescript, but it is well worth venturing over the threshold. It is in the hands of a couple of enthusiastic and committed pros, Angèle Faure and Richard Rocle. She is in charge of the friendly, yet slick service in the trendy dining room in the zeitgeist, while he crafts up-to-date food, poised between homely rural fare and modernity with a distinct preference for small producers. Pigs raised on pasture, snails, saffron, goat’s cheese, wild herbs picked by hand: everything is local.

name: La Table d'Hôtes - Le Quatrième Mur
review: At the Grand Théâtre de Bordeaux, a magnificent example of neo-Classical architecture, even dining is theatrical. Chef Etchebest's 12 guests share the same large table in a vaulted cellar, where they are privy to the behind-the-scenes workings of a restaurant, amid introductions to the dishes and the to and fro of the waitstaff. Everything here is a surprise: from the menu to the wine and food pairings, down to the cutlery that you choose yourself. The same spirit is to be found in the chef's dishes, which are unabashedly original and resolved to strike that harmony of flavours. The technique is impeccable (the foie gras des Landes fried and smoked in duck jus with orange!), plus you can enjoy the food while getting to know your neighbours at the table. Even when Philippe Etchebest is absent, he is still there – via video conference with the guests before the meal starts! An experience, truly.

name: À Contre Sens
review: “A Contre sens” means against the flow, but this establishment is clearly heading in the right direction. Chef Anthony Caillot is pictured in the middle of a herd of cows on his website, a reminder that this farmer’s son continues to forge strong ties with breeders, vegetable and fruit growers and small-scale producers. After stints in star restaurants and luxury hotels, this chef fell head over heels with this traditional house in a discreet street of Caen, where he greets guests simply and generously. Healthy first and foremost, Anthony’s cuisine is perfectly balanced between legibility and audacity. Normandy produce is transcended by high-flying craftsmanship and tiny exotic touches (yuzu, kimchi, ginger): mushrooms in a smoked vegetable stock, shitake, squid and langoustine ravioles; grilled scallops, barbecued cauliflower, mango and pepper condiment; raw and baked pear, honey ganache and hay ice cream…

name: L'Ostal
review: A true-blue local lad, Emmanuel Hébrard was trained by the best (Anne-Sophie Pic and Stéphane Raimbault, among others) and has vowed to defend his homeland (‘ostal’ means ‘house’ in the local dialect). His single set menu is thus deeply ‘local’ and seeks to shine the spotlight on regional ingredients: meat from the local butcher, veg from neighbouring cottage gardeners and cheese and eggs from surrounding farms. Respect for nature and farmers is the backbone of this establishment. The snug dining room (seating for twenty or so) sports a smart, contemporary look and makes ample use of natural materials (wood and stone), in keeping with the establishment’s culinary identity.

name: La Mare aux Oiseaux
review: A globetrotter and keen ornithologist, Éric Guérin has invented a universe all of his own. On an islet ringed by circular canals in the heart of Brière nature park, Éric has immersed himself body and soul in his region, although he is far from averse to putting a new spin on regional classics. Using first-class ingredients, he crafts “natural” dishes overflowing in personality, class, delicacy, vibrancy even poetry at times… Everything inside and outside is appealing, particularly the “exotic” guestrooms, ideal to extend your stay, while the warm, efficient welcome of the youthful and enthusiastic team adds the finishing touch to this bucolic portrait.

name: Baieta
review: "Here, the bouillabaisse cosies up to the aioli, and the pissaladière (tart with onions, olives and anchovies) competes with the socca (chickpea flatbread), just out of the coal-fired oven." Julia Sedefdjian (formerly of Les Fables de la Fontaine, also in Paris) is now happily thriving in her own establishment. Her colourful and fragrant cuisine is an ode to the Mediterranean (her "Bouillabaieta", a superb take on bouillabaisse, is a must) and fine ingredients, which she selects painstakingly and blends creatively, without forgetting her roots in Nice. The chef now solely proposes a series of surprise set menus. Welcome to Baieta – which means "kiss" in the Nice dialect!

name: Auberge des Saints Pères
review: One of the undisputed merits of the chef of the Auberge des Saints Pères is consistency. His unrivalled experience, modern cuisine with top-notch produce and virtuoso culinary technique (cooking, seasoning) all explain the establishment’s excellent reputation with a faithful crowd of regulars. The chef’s wife extends welcoming and efficient front-of-house service in a setting that is both pared-down and elegant.

name: La Pomme d'Api
review: Jérémie Le Calvez's excellent restaurant is housed in the fine 17C stone-built Le Clos Saint Yves, which was an important religious cabinet-making workshop until the late 19C. The chef leans into the zeitgeist with his array of fresh contemporary dishes. This fine and inventive cuisine highlights the best ingredients of the Breton region, while keeping in step with the seasons. The beautiful dining room with its exposed stonework overlooks a small garden. On the restaurant floor, Jessica runs the show. Charming guestrooms are available, should you wish to extend your stay and explore the region. A high-calibre experience thanks to this young enthusiastic couple.

name: Le Chantecler
review: On the legendary Promenade des Anglais, the stunning Negresco sits pretty at its seafront location; Le Chantecler, its fine dining restaurant, has "Meilleur Ouvrier de France" 2015 Virginie Basselot at the helm. In this exceptional setting, the Normandy-born chef doesn't beat around the bush, training her laser-like focus on serving up creative contemporary cuisine in the form of three set menus without options, made from the finest ingredients. Here, as elsewhere, simplicity wins the day, cf. the bass and oyster tartare with caviar or the just-seared cod on a bed of tapioca, peppered artichokes barigoule, lemon balm juice and nasturtia.

name: Le Cénacle
review: The plush atmosphere, depicted by a superb fireplace and a Caravaggio print, invites you to take a seat at this cenacle. Your intuition is confirmed as you sample the chef’s undeniable know-how, finely balanced between regional produce and contemporary notes, all of which founded on flawlessly fresh ingredients. Indeed, the chef takes pride in forging long-lasting partnerships with local producers (organic vegetables from Gers and breeders). He has a particular knack for enhancing simple ingredients, such as a roast rack of Monts Lagast pork, paccheri stuffed with brown and black chanterelle mushrooms. The lunchtime menu is a steal.

name: Hervé Busset
review: On the road to Santiago de Compostela, not far from the Abbatiale Sainte-Foy (decorated by Pierre Soulages), this former mill with a thackstone roof is reflected in the waters of the River Dourdou. This gorgeous green setting is where Hervé Busset has put down roots. Having been trained not by great chefs, but by the ethnobotanist François Couplan, he heads out every morning to gather wild herbs and plants with which to conjure up his healthy dishes that stay close to nature. Elderberry, plantain, ground-ivy, wild fennel, bergamot, burnet and borage flower sit alongside the fine local produce. Comfortable guestrooms for those who wish to extend their stay.

name: G.a. au Manoir de Rétival
review: This manor house overlooking the Seine is the HQ of David Goerne, a German-born chef in love with French cuisine. He unfussily invites guests to take a seat at the ‘table d’hôte’ in his vintage kitchen, whose walls gleam with copper utensils. In fine weather, meals are served on the panoramic terrace gazing down on the River Seine and Brotonne bridge. David enjoys improvising in front of diners, subtly and creatively incorporating herbs, peppers and other seasonings to highlight the essence of each ingredient. Enhanced by a genuine bouquet of herbs and flowers and a lemon emulsion, his incredible medley of fresh garden veggies on an egg yolk marinated in soy sauce sings an ode to the miracle of nature. Although a fervent champion of vegetables, David is also at home with lobster, foie gras or squab, depending on his whim and the seasons.

name: Le Belvédère
review: Guillaume Viala, who had planned on a career in science, swapped his test tubes and beakers for a chopping board and a knife. This Aveyron lad switched to catering after spending three years at Michel Bras. Since then, he and his sommelière wife have thrown themselves body and soul into this chic rustic inn that commands a priceless view of the grandiose natural amphitheatre of the ‘Trou de Bozouls’. Both nurture a contagious enthusiasm for traditional farming methods and wines from small winegrowers. Their squid from the Golfe du Lion slowly braised in a spicy jus, with smoked charlotte potatoes and chickpeas, dandelions and rocket leaves is a model of deceptive, almost childlike simplicity in which everyday ingredients are underlined thanks to consummate skill.

name: L'Écrin de Yohann Chapuis
review: Occupying a former orphanage made famous by Jean Ducloux, this restaurant now offers a superb setting for the cuisine of Yohann Chapuis, a chef who did much of his training at the Maison Lameloise. The iconic staples of yesteryear (still served at the Bouchon Bourguignon next door) have made way for a cuisine of “taste and emotions” which has its own distinct identity and character. The focus here is on the best seasonal ingredients, including crayfish from the Saône, turbot caught from small fishing boats, and Charolais beef, all beautifully presented. An excellent wine list and astute recommendations from the sommelier complete the picture.

name: Lucas Carton
review: The name refers to the long history of this restaurant: Robert Lucas set up his "Taverne Anglaise" here in 1732; Francis Carton joined their two surnames together in 1925 to come up with the new identity of Lucas Carton, which went on to be awarded three Michelin stars in the 1930s; Alain Senderens, who in 2005 decided to give it his own name in order to fully relaunch it. Today, the establishment has discreetly adopted the new codes of contemporary fine dining. Young chef Hugo Bourny (who has worked at Marsan, Maison Pic and La Vague d'Or, to name but a few) knows how to bring out the essence of fine ingredients with his instinctive cuisine, which draws on the very best of France's terroir – a special mention for the vegetables grown by small-scale farmers. The story continues for this iconic restaurant.

name: Leclere
review: Chef Guillaume Leclere’s restaurant now boasts new premises and a new decor: a large dining room with a futuristic, almost spaceship-like feel where stainless steel blends harmoniously with Montpellier stone, tiles and granite. The chef’s “cuisine d’arrivage”, as he describes it, focuses on a single menu which changes daily in line with the ultra-fresh ingredients available (Mediterranean fish, lamb from the Cantal etc), all of which are sourced from short supply chains. From tomatoes to fish, each ingredient is delicately prepared and presented to bring out its full flavour and visual appeal.

name: Yoshi
review: Monte-Carlo is famous for its casino, its prince, its clay tennis courts and its gastronomy! The restaurant at the Hotel Métropole pays tribute to Japanese cuisine with premium ingredients and flawless technique. Aromatic soups, sushi and maki are created with a focus on “yoshi” (kindness) by chef Takeo Yamazaki, whose cuisine – more fusion in style than authentically Japanese – has adapted to suit his international guests. It nonetheless remains precise, refined and assertive, as evidenced by the excellent “ghindara no saiko yaki” (fillet of black cod marinated in boiled saki and wrapped in a Japanese magnolia leaf). A real enticement to visit the land of the Rising Sun!

name: Pavyllon
review: There’s no stopping Yannick Alléno! The latest venture of this chef from the Ile de France region is a real winner with guests and rightly so. Offering space for just thirty guests at the counter (similar to a Joël Robuchon Atelier but with a more hushed feel), the restaurant serves refined, delicate cuisine based around classic recipes. Dishes are blended with interesting flavours and the occasional international influence, such as the tempuras which accompany the main courses. A smart yet relaxed setting in which to enjoy a splendid meal.

name: Le 1825 - La Table gastronomique
review: Hidden deep in the countryside, this small 19C château opens its elegant doors in the evening under the auspices of a youthful chef whose career has taken him from Daniel Boulud in New York to Yannick Alléno in Courchevel. He regales us with a culinary line-up with premium produce topping the bill. The squab (cooked just so), green lentils from Puy and barbajuan, with its excellent smoked vinegar extraction, were divine. The décor features a huge dining room set in the old conservatory, which sports high ceilings, bare stone walls, trendy furnishings and floor to ceiling windows overlooking the courtyard.

name: Les Hauts de Loire
review: Dominique Pépin, who was Rémy Giraud’s faithful second for over thirty years, is now at the head of this 19C hunting lodge between Amboise and Blois. The setting is truly magnificent, in particular the classically appointed dining room and the gloriously peaceful alfresco dining area… The chef sources top-quality ingredients, Touraine truffles, Sologne caviar, Loire fish, which he painstakingly incorporates into recipes that pay tribute to his classical training and his mentor. Regional game and fruit and vegetables from the property’s own garden are frequent guest stars in his recipes.

name: Pierre Reboul
review: Pierre Reboul has travelled far and wide. He was Michel Chabran's apprentice in Pont-de-l'Isère, then a member of the team under the great Jacques Pic (Anne-Sophie Pic's father) in Valence, before cooking in Paris at Taillevent and Rostang, and ultimately opening his own restaurants in Saint-Rémy-de-Provence, Tain-l'Hermitage and Aix-en-Provence. His playful, creative, slightly molecular style of cuisine comes into its own in the elegant setting of this 16C château. Texture, inventiveness, respect for seasonality (permaculture vegetables and sustainable fishing): he ensures the fundamentals are observed.

name: Le Restaurant du Cerisier
review: On the first floor of a bold contemporary behemoth in the heart of Lille, the former chef of Le Meurin, Mathieu Boutroy, can be seen performing in a superb theatrically visible kitchen. In a single set menu in which the fresh ingredients shout their name, he crafts perfectly executed dishes, including subtle sauces and jus. A few examples: premium cèpes, super-fresh lobster, lamb, served rare, in a crust of ras-el-hanout. Colourful, vibrant and aromatic – the appetising fruit of this cherry tree is well worth picking…

name: L'Émulsion
review: Established since 2011, this chef has earned himself a fine reputation for high-quality food: classical training, meticulous plating and surprising but apt plays on textures… The cuisine owes much to the first-rate quality of its meticulously sourced ingredients, 99% of which are local and purchased direct; in fact, the menu pays a fitting and fully-deserved tribute to its partner producers and breeders. The smart modern interior is divinely suited to this heavenly culinary emulsion.

name: Le Prieuré
review: Opposite the Palais des Papes, the small town of Villeneuve-lès-Avignon, like its neighbour on the other side of the Rhône, has a host of monuments – and Le Prieuré is one of them. The charm of this old cloister was enough to win over Jean-André Charial, chef and owner of the legendary L'Oustau de Baumanière, who has added it to his collection of prestigious restaurants. It also attracted up-and-coming chef Marc Fontanne, who chose to make this place the next stop on a promising trajectory that began at Auberge des Templiers and La Réserve de Beaulieu. Using great produce, he brings us his wonderfully subtle and tasty take on the cuisine of the South of France, e.g. cuttlefish perfectly cooked a la plancha, accompanied by diced lemon confit, asparagus, lardo di Colonnata and fruity olive oil. Pure joy.

name: La Table d'Hôtes - La Rôtisserie du Chambertin
review: Thomas Collomb is at the head of an outstanding table d’hôtes in Gevrey-Chambertin, in which nothing is left to chance! Flawless ingredients, most of which from organic, meticulously selected suppliers, recognisable, artfully presented dishes which unfold during a tasting menu rich in surprises and a stylish smart rustic interior. But there is more to come! The wine list is out of this world (well, this is the region!) and the service is professional and attentive, without being oppressive. The pinnacle of fine dining.

name: Le 1131 - Abbaye de la Bussière
review: It would be hard to imagine a more inspiring place in which to conjure up such refined cuisine than a 12C Cistercian abbey. Beneath these impressive ribbed vaults, a wonderful tribute is paid to the terroir of Burgundy (snails, frog legs, lake and river fish, blackcurrants and honey from the flowers growing in the gardens), not to mention a wine list that harbours many treasures. Prolong the meditative experience in the 7ha grounds. Luxurious guestrooms are also available.

name: L'Or Q'idée
review: Chef Naoëlle d’Hainaut chose a small side- street at the foot of the pretty church in the centre of Pontoise to open her first restaurant. The result is an elegant Scandinavian-inspired interior featuring bright colours, a glass-fronted wine cellar and open-view kitchen serving flavoursome dishes in keeping with the times. The delicious offerings here include a meaty, slow-cooked fillet of cod served on a lentil caviar with a lightly creamy mushroom sauce. Every dish showcases the same technical skill, harmony of flavours and refreshing honesty, accompanied by well-honed, relaxed and professional service from a young and efficient team. A restaurant that comes highly recommended!

name: Jérémy Galvan
review: In the heart of Lyon's old town, Jérémy Galvan has set up shop in one of the streets in France with the most Michelin stars – rue du Bœuf. Born in Savoie, the chef's path took him to Quebec. As the grandson of market gardeners, he is a proponent of locally sourced food; he takes very seriously the need to protect the planet and the farmers who live off the land. Inspired by nature, he grows some ingredients in his own vegetable garden, and his creative cuisine (one surprise set menu) is now something of an artistic experience: calling upon the five senses – it includes music – and the four elements, it is daring as well as breathtaking! The interior decor is a continuation of the ethos of the place (e.g. evoking fire through the colour bronze). An experience you will want to linger over!

name: Auberge Saint-Walfrid
review: Situated on the road from Metz to Strasbourg, this pretty little inn – once a farm belonging to the church in Welferding – has been run by the same family since the late 19C. Having taken over from his father who built up the auberge’s gastronomic reputation in the region, Stephan Schneider (fifth generation) is now at the helm here. Guests dine in a large, plush and warmly decorated dining room with old parquet flooring and cabinets laden with gleaming Sarreguemines earthenware. The chef is a staunch champion of tradition who works with local market gardeners (he also has his own kitchen garden) and buys whole animals that he prepares himself, including cured meats. Spacious guestrooms are also available.

name: Château de Vault-de-Lugny
review: The terrace of this stately home overlooking sprawling grounds and a 17C plane tree features in a novel by French author Michel Houllebecq. The Mauritian chef Franco Bowanee crafts subtle, up-to-date recipes, strewn with discerning exotic notes. His bang-on, straightforward food not only shines the spotlight on noble produce, but also on vegetables from the estate’s own cottage garden. Meals are served in a majestic setting ideally suited to this culinary adventure.

name: Le Gourmet de Sèze
review: Bernard Mariller, one of the chefs behind the revival of Lyon’s food scene in the 1990s, has been plying his trade in this street, just a few steps from the restaurant’s original address, for some thirty years. This son and grandson of farmers from the Saône-et-Loire, who boasts stints with Joël Robuchon, Jacques Lameloise and Michel Troisgros, has lost none of his inimitable energy! He crafts delicious modern cuisine based on seasonal, often noble ingredients (scallops from Erquy and line-caught Brittany seabass). His attention to detail and superlative sauce-making talents are still very much to the fore.

name: Têtedoie
review: In the wake of his mentor Paul Bocuse, Christian Têtedoie has built a small gourmet empire. Perched on Fourvière hill overlooking the city, the Têtedoie is a gourmet showcase. A champion of Gallic culinary traditions, this fan of contemporary art is committed to finetuning and even modernising this heritage. Bites of snails, foie gras and pistachio; “portfolio” of red mullet, carrots and game sauce; mallard duck, grilled chestnuts and Jack Be Little pumpkins: his dishes sometimes read like an abstract art exhibition. It’s impossible not to mention his signature dish: lobster casserole with a calf's head cromesquis that he has renamed HTV (after Homard Tête de Veau in French). Generous, sensitive cuisine depicted by an intelligent array of textures and flavours.

name: La Balette
review: Laurent Lemal unveils the full gamut of his talents in this idyllic seaside spot opposite the picturesque bay and village of Collioure. His distinctive cuisine focused on local ingredients exalts the plentiful fare of Catalonia, with a fondness for finely crafted surf and turf dishes (samphire; oysters from Leucate pond with basil and Bellota ham; red mullet with smoked onion greens, black pudding of octopus and reduction of fish soup with chorizo spices…). His wife Julie whips up exquisitely delicate desserts. A made-to-measure dining experience which is designed with the maître d’hôtel, who takes the time to talk to each guest before the start of the meal.

name: La Rotonde des Trésoms
review: The huge conservatory of this Rotonde commands a splendid panoramic view over Annecy Lake, sweeping diners off their feet, even before their first bite! Originally from Arcachon, Eric Prowalski adds flavours from southwest France to recipes which highlight sustainably grown local produce. This skilled craftsman deftly unfolds a repertory in which creativity never hampers the flavour, developing a delicious "dialogue" between his adopted land and his homeland. The refurbished, understated interior showcases a subtle blend of warm materials such as leather and oak.

name: La Table de Nans
review: Nans Gaillard, a local man and ambitious young chef, had a childhood dream of opening his own restaurant in La Ciotat, where he was born. After spending his childhood in Brittany then taking his first steps as a chef with some impressive stints in Paris, at L'Atelier de Joël Robuchon, among others, he has found what he was looking for: an inn dating from the interwar period, built above the cliffs facing the sea, with a terrace and tall pine trees. A dream setting, in which he pays tribute to regional produce in the form of his own refined take on classic cuisine: "cooked and raw" Provençal vegetables, fresh Robiola and herbs from the garden; lobster, confit carrots with ginger and lime, claw meat in ravioli, creamy Madagascar vanilla sauce...

name: L'Amaryllis
review: Welcome to this tranquil 19C watermill, by a millstream. It is flanked by a cottage garden, whose sole purpose is to supply the restaurant’s kitchen. After growing up in the Charolais countryside, chef Cédric Burtin did stints in Lyons’ restaurants operated by world-class names of the ilk of Paul Bocuse and Pierre Orsi. Today, his own restaurant enjoys a fine reputation in the region amongst the locals and a clientele from further afield. This subtle chef’s inventive hallmark and his flair for allowing fresh ingredients to shout their name, thanks to virtuoso technique and dishes that are as visually mouth-watering as they are satisfying and flavoursome, are second to none.

name: Au Déjeuner de Sousceyrac
review: A seriously reliable establishment, whose success is undoubtedly due to the professionalism and distinctive personality of chef Patrick Lagnès. His carefully designed recipes, often founded on a patriotic line-up of French classics, make ample use of fine ingredients, with, depending on his inspiration, the occasional more modern creation. The decadent desserts are the work of his daughter. Meals are served in a dining room characteristic of provincial France, appointed with wainscoting and classical furnishings. Good value for money.

name: Alain Llorca
review: Alain Llorca is an iconic character of French Riviera cuisine with high-profile stints at the mythical luxury Negresco Hotel and the Moulin de Mougins, amongst other fine food affairs. In his farmhouse in La Colle-sur-Loup, whose terrace commands a jaw-dropping view of Saint Paul de Vence, he gives free rein to his affinity for all things Mediterranean. The result is often an ode to seafood, steeped in subtle, delicate notes: seabass in an aubergine crust with garden veggies; Poupeton of courgette flowers with black truffles, but Tarn pigeon, foie gras and tender juicy beef also make guest star appearances.

name: Le 7ème Continent
review: This restaurant's incredible decoration (inside and out) was created by painter and decorative artist François Zenner, an amateur naturalist with a passion for plants. Also passionate about his work, and very much influenced by his time spent working under Bernard Loiseau, chef Laurent Haller is never at a loss for ideas when it comes to sharing his love of good food. In particular, he gives cookery classes and puts together themed menus. He likes to revisit the great classics of French cuisine and creates surf and turf combinations. His menu, a veritable ode to the market and its produce, is revised every month.

name: La Table de la Bergerie
review: This restaurant near Angers, in the heart of the Coteaux-du-Layon vineyards, is well worth your attention. It is the haunt of talented David Guitton, who hails from Loire Atlantique and who has trained under top chefs all over the world from the United States and Britain to Monaco. There is no à la carte menu here, but a voluntarily concise offering that reverently respects the seasons. David sources his ingredients from small, local producers, rustling up dishes that err towards minimalist so that the flavour can take centre stage. Regional wines, including the estate’s organic production, take pride of place on the wine list.

name: L'Aspérule
review: Keigo Kimura, who has lived in France for some 20 years, mainly in Auxerre, orchestrates his own take on French cuisine with a Japanese twist in this Dijon restaurant. Like all genuine Japanese chefs, his flair for precision and balance (presentation, cooking and flavours) is second to none, and his dishes are also sprinkled with tributes to the region: pinot noir or vin jaune sauces and mustard shoots. Last but not least, the wine cellar is an Aladdin’s Cave for connoisseurs.

name: Baumanière 1850
review: Courchevel, the quintessence of alpine luxury since 1947, is an exclusive ski resort where nothing is too beautiful or too good! In this plush chalet with family guesthouse overtones, gifted chef Thomas Prod’Homme, who trained at the Oustaù de Baumanière in Les Baux-de-Provence, accurately and elegantly slaloms between local ingredients, winter flavours and Provençal inspirations: gently seared stems of wild mushrooms and filtered mushroom coffee; endives, pears and walnuts, butter of roots smoked in pear tree wood chippings, foie gras; seared scallops, assorted seaweed and foamy whey. The chef’s creativity, ambition and bold risk-taking personality set the scene for a memorable meal.

name: Les Voiles d'Or
review: Thanks to his wealth of experience, Tristan Arhan's restaurant perched atop the cliffs of Le Pollet (looking out over Dieppe) hits all the right notes. For this chef who is passionate about seafood, it is the catch of the day that sets the agenda. Diners can look forward to exceptionally fresh produce showcased with understated finesse. The sleek and pared-down decor is perfectly in sync with the chef's approach. Courteous service is provided by the chef's wife. This place has been popular with Brits since it was featured on TV across the Channel. There are a few original guestrooms, plus a small terrace for sunny days.

name: L'Oiseau Bleu
review: This attractive stone mansion is something of an institution on Bordeaux’ hip ‘alternative’ Right Bank, currently in the throes of eco-development. The chef crafts pared-down, legible dishes that voluntarily eschew fancy technique in favour of his healthy preoccupations: produce and taste. The 6-course surprise menu unveils the full gamut of his know-how, inspired by the seasons and the harvest of small producers. Meals are served in a fashionably colourful dining room or on the huge south-facing alfresco patio overlooking the garden – heaven in fine weather! The small bistro next-door is ideal for foodies with a train to catch!

name: Maximin Hellio
review: Located in the heart of the seaside resort of Deauville, this restaurant with a sleek, modern frontage had the great idea of leaving part of the façade glass-fronted to enable passers-by to watch the chefs at work here. Inside, head chef Maximin Hellio, who has worked with Frédéric Anton and who then received a Michelin star in the family-run Voile d’Or in Sables-D’or-les-Pins in Brittany, champions the full bounty of Normandy, including fish and seafood. He showcases these ingredients in refined and creative dishes with honest and precise flavours, accompanied by interesting wine pairings which add an extra dimension. Very popular with locals.

name: L'Auberge de Bagatelle
review: A youthful and hospitable Franco-Belgian couple has breathed a new lease of gourmet life into this picture postcard country inn. The immaculately prepared, hunger obliterating, impressively rendered food is the handiwork of a ten-strong white-jacketed team, using deluxe ingredients (fera from Éric Jacquier, poultry from Cour d’Armoirie, Saint Eustache fruit orchards and seafood delicacies such as wild spider crab or grilled John Dory, etc.). The pinnacle of fine dining!

name: La Bonne Étape
review: The table at this restored farmhouse is laid with bread, fougasse, olives and olive oil, plus a host of colourful sun-ripened tomatoes – just some of the typical Provençal fare served in this restaurant where thyme, savory and lavender add to the fragrant scents of southern France. Chef Jany Gleize has been serving classic, gourmet Provençal cuisine which is full of flavour for almost half a century. With dishes such as cep mushrooms in ravioli or a flan, duck foie gras and mallard pie, hare “à la royale” and lamb from Sisteron on the menu, Provençal writer Jean Giono would have appreciated the strong and distinctive flavours of this rich cuisine. Guests come from far and wide to taste this chef’s “pieds et paquets” (tripe and trotters), served in a spicy tomato sauce which brings out the full flavours of the ingredients. A few spacious guestrooms decorated with period furnishings are also available.

name: Château du Mont Joly
review: This 18C manor house with a pink façade and Italianate columns overlooking the Saône Valley, is fully the equal of its name! With his wife, sommelière and a winegrowers’ daughter, Romuald Fassenet has turned this classical edifice into a stripped back, designer establishment offering a few guestrooms for a charming overnight stay near Dole. His straightforward, appetising food reveals his genuine passion for the Jura region (in fact, he was second to chef Jean-Paul Jeunet) and is founded on impeccable textbook skill. Yellow Jura wine features prominently in his fantastic sauces and his signature dishes include Bresse chicken breast in vin jaune with morels cooked in a bladder and “MOF” (Best Craftsman of France) duck pie.

name: Michel Trama
review: Michel Trama and Puymirol have a long history. This former champion diver and student of the decorative arts in Montparnasse owes his true calling to love… for his wife Maryse. She is the one who introduced him to fine dining. After a string of odd jobs, he settled down and opened a bistro on rue Mouffetard in Paris, with a copy of Michel Guérard's "Cuisine Gourmande" to refer to. In 1979 he set up shop in this splendid 13C country house in Puymirol, in Lot-et-Garonne: you can sit under the medieval vaults or on the lovely terrace, in the old cloister... It is time to indulge in a cuisine that incorporates both tradition and invention in an unchanging menu that makes several references to this establishment's heyday.

name: Maison Tiegezh
review: Tiegezh means "family" in Breton, which does rather say it all! The chef’s grandparents founded Brittany’s first factory to manufacture fresh pancakes. Today, Baptiste Denieul, a gifted young chef who honed his skills at the Bristol with Éric Frechon, invites you to enter this stylish interior, which provides the perfect foil to his delicate, bang on cuisine: fish, vegetables from the garden and farm produce. His wife Marion puts the final touch to this family melody. Nowadays, Maison Tiegezh boasts a gourmet restaurant, a bistro crêperie and also a modern, sophisticated hotel with six rooms for overnight stays and longer… A delightful break in the heart of Brittany’s enchanted forest of Broceliande.

name: Les Fresques - Château des Vigiers
review: On the crossroads between Dordogne, Gironde and Lot-et-Garonne, the Vigiers Castle is a splendid 16C Périgord edifice, set in grounds that are home to a vineyard and a well-known golf course. This several hundred-year-old castle houses a restaurant whose walls are appointed with frescoes dating from the Renaissance period. Virtuoso chef Didier Casaguana paints from a palette rich in flavours and aromas, directly inspired by the region. This Toulouse boy, who admits to an overriding passion for nature and small producers, also works with noble produce from the land of abundance that is southwest France, which he crafts into surprise menus: tartare of oysters with Prunier caviar, pigeon with chicory and hazelnut and a dessert that revolves around strawberries and tarragon sorbet…

name: L'Orchidée
review: This orchid invites us on mouth-watering, gourmet voyage. The modern, scrupulously crafted Thai cuisine is elegant and perfumed, illustrated by a tom yam of blue lobster, coconut milk and galanga or Vosges squab, served with sweetcorn, girolles mushrooms, polenta and red curry. Delicious from start to finish and a phenomenal success story.

name: La Tour des Vents
review: At the top of a hill, surrounded by the Bergerac vineyards, next to the ruins of a windmill, this beautiful, opulent restaurant affords unforgettable views of the surroundings. Chef Damien Fagette promotes the local produce of the Périgord by working with Blonde d'Aquitaine beef, foie gras and free-range Périgord chicken. Prepared with great care and skill, his contemporary cuisine is a succulent alliance of fine ingredients, accurate cooking and well-defined flavours. Grilled squid, shallot with red wine and chorizo churros; variations on lamb (roasted saddle, confit shoulder rissole and leg marinated kebab-style); warm Grand Marnier soufflé. A wonderful experience.

name: L'Aquarelle
review: This rather stark contemporary cubic edifice offers a gourmet halt in the heart of the Royans countryside. Chef Xavier Taffart is the son of an oyster farmer, so it goes without saying that his familiarity with Charentes oysters is pretty extensive. His creative inspired approach to cooking is founded on working with flawless local produce. A fan of surf and turf dishes, he also enjoys adding the odd exotic touch: shredded crab, aromatic ponzu stock and smoked egg yolk; slow-baked pollock in almond milk… A fashionable designer vibe depicts the spacious panoramic room, spreading as far as the contemporary tableware by a Poitevin artisan and the knives by a La Rochelle cutler. This attention to detail is equally present in the exquisite plating that demonstrates the chef’s graphic inclinations.

name: Jean-Marc Pérochon
review: Seated behind the restaurant’s floor to ceiling windows, admire the sun’s rays glinting on the ocean. A talented skipper has dropped anchor here in the person of Jean-Marc Pérochon who went to sea at 17, crossing the channel to Scotland, before cruising around Europe and as far as the West Indies. In his hotel-restaurant, his cooking is both minimalist and sprinkled with exotic flavours, extractions, stocks and emulsions, leaving our tastebuds aching for more. He believes in working only with first-rate goods, namely fish and shellfish from the fish auction at Saint-Gilles-Croix-de-Vie (which dominate the menu), but also Challans poultry and vegetables from local growers.

name: L'Éveil des Sens
review: It is impossible to miss this restaurant and its striking, oxidised metal fretwork façade on the way out of town. It is the lair of chef Nicolas Nobis and his wife Isabelle, who met in Alençon and honed their skills under Bernard Loiseau and Georges Blanc. Wood prevails in the tasteful, understated interior and the same ethos, erring towards simplicity and nature, can be tasted in the food. The chef loves working with plants (hyssop, verbena, etc.) and vegetables from local growers. His precise timing and seasonings are guaranteed to awaken all five senses, which are in for an unforgettable experience.

name: Intuition
review: Make your way upstairs from the Brasserie les Capucines, which serves simpler fare, to this understated, plush restaurant overlooking the castle of Saint Lô. After acquiring a faithful following of regulars in Coutances, Mickaël Marion has returned to his birthplace and opened the floodgates of his creativity. A steadfast champion of local produce, he frequently goes walking in the countryside and marshes to pick plants and herbs. Back in his kitchen, he waves his magic wand/spoon and lo and behold - meadowsweet ice cream, pesto of wild herbs and lovage appear! He is a past master in the art of subtly assembling stellar Normandy produce – scallops, fish from small boats, with a dash of exoticism. A fine dining experience to remember.

name: Le Grand Cap
review: Erwan Houssin and his pastry chef wife, Pamela, decided to drop anchor in Leucate, which is not a surprise when you see the view that embraces the Sète coastline as far as the Albères mountains. In front lies the sea and its riches, while behind stretches out sweet-scented scrubland, vineyards and olive groves. Born in Brittany, Erwan grew up in the Hérault mountains and is perfectly at home with meat and fish from the Atlantic to the Mediterranean. Aubrac beef is served with Catalan anchovies and Corbières lentils, Brittany blue lobster rubs shoulders with Bigorre bacon and Guilvinec langoustine is paired with Pyrenean caviar. He picks his own wild fennel, thyme, rosemary and savory from the surrounding cliffs, using them in amazing herbal teas, jus and sauces…

name: Château de Sully
review: Grandiose is the term that springs to mind when describing this 18C château, set in landscaped grounds planted with Lebanese cedars and sequoias. Take a seat in one of the plush dining rooms or in the bright conservatory to savour the chef’s predominantly Normandy-focused cuisine: vegetables, cheeses, foie gras and, of course, line-caught fish.

name: Le Saint-James
review: An iconic establishment if ever there was, for many years the Saint James was the realm of Jean-Marie Amat, an avant-gardist who called upon Jean Nouvel to renovate his premises, making his establishment a benchmark in design. This magical venue, dubbed the balcony of Bordeaux, overlooking the vineyards, pays tribute to Aquitaine producers from Gironde caviar to Bazas beef. The chef, Mathieu Martin (formerly the second chef here) is now at the helm of this prestigious restaurant. The quality and brilliance of the food is as unwavering, fresh and flavoursome as ever and the youthful chef makes no bones of his love of plants, such as tomatoes served “from the skin to the seed”, also in keeping with his zero-waste ethos. Have no fear, the Saint James is in good hands!

name: La Licorne Royale
review: A continued presence in this half-timbered house in a small Normandy village since 2008, the chef here has proved himself to be an extraordinary culinary craftsman. Working with high-quality ingredients, elaborate and finely tuned techniques, and combinations of balanced and subtle flavours that accentuate the experience, he regales guests with a delicious tasting experience. The seasonal menu (featuring, for example, scallops, truffles and turbot, a selection of cheeses, and dessert) is the restaurant’s best-value option. The chic, classically inspired decor features numerous references to the battles of Napoleon.

name: L'Essentiel
review: This contemporary bistro is the HQ of Frenchman Charles Thuillant and Korean Mi-Ra Kim. The globetrotting couple, who met in Ze Kitchen Gallery, a temple of Franco-Asian cuisine, also has stints at Robuchon, Dupin and Chateaubriand under their apron strings. They however chose to open their restaurant in Deauville, where Charles spent his holidays as a child. Together, they conjure up vibrant, lively dishes in which Normandy country produce is mixed with perfectly judged Asian influences: cod and haddock fritters, piquillo pickles, velvety butternut, pan-fried foie gras and sesame, fried egg, mousse of white tarama and roe of flying fish, ravioli of marinated beef with mushroom stock…

name: L'Aupiho - Domaine de Manville
review: Set in a luxury hotel complete with a golf course, spa and pool, L’Aupiho pays a vibrant tribute to regional traditions, which is hardly surprising given its location at the foot of the Alpilles and the Baux… This passion for Provence is embodied by a youthful Belgian chef, Lieven Van Aken, who kicked off his career in Brussels before working under Michel Guérard. His recipes are meticulous, but they are also bold and powerful: vegetarian bouillabaisse, saffron rouille; smoked and grilled sweetbread, tartare of seaweed and Mediterranean langoustines. Century-old plane trees set the refreshing scene on the leafy patio.

name: La Passagère - Hôtel Belles Rives
review: The first thing to strike guests at this hotel, where Scott and Zelda Fitzgerald played out their tempestuous romance in the 1920s, is its magnificent setting. It’s not easy for a restaurant to hold its own in such a location and yet La Passagère does just that. The chef signs elegant cuisine that showcases many of the Mediterranean’s culinary gems, in dishes such as raviole of spider crab, caviar platine and a foamy verbena mousse or a marinière of shellfish with confit cauliflower, not forgetting the heroically wondrous desserts. The restaurant terrace commands a jaw-dropping view of the sea and the Esterel mountains.

name: Vincent Favre Félix
review: Vincent Favre-Félix has opened the doors of this stylish, modern villa abutting an historic edifice of Annecy-le-Vieux. The chef, who has the build of a rugby player and boasts a fine regional CV (Père Bise at Talloires, Auberge de l’Eridan and Auberge du Lac at Veyrier-du-Lac), never lacks in subtlety or delicacy. Always guided by regional produce, his culinary gifts are expressed boldly and creatively, through beautifully designed ‘carte blanche’ menus that also unveil his signature dishes, such as arctic char smoked in hay. In summertime, make a beeline for the exquisite patio in the flower-decked garden and savour this fine dining experience.

name: Ed.Em
review: Ed.Em is a contraction of Édouard and Émilie who met at Régis Marcon. He is a young chef with an enviable CV, who started at the Quai d’Orsay, before heading to Philippe Rochat and Lameloise, and she is a talented pastry chef who adds the final flourish to a fine meal. The chef’s tasty menus, rich in first-class ingredients, are full of personality, yet subtly delicate, such as pike with chanterelles, quail stuffed with foie gras… A pleasant halt on the wine road.

name: Le Vieux Logis
review: This reliably good traditional restaurant is housed in the utterly charming setting of a converted tobacco drying barn, all done out in stone and painted wood. Indeed, the whole site – the local stone buildings of an old agricultural property that was originally a priory – is delightful. Head chef Vincent Arnould, a Meilleur Ouvrier de France, is an enlightened custodian of tradition. A native of the Vosges who fell in love with the Périgord, he selects the finest produce for his modern and appealing cuisine with solid classical foundations. At lunchtime, the restaurant proposes a reasonably priced set menu featuring what might be described as Périgord-style tapas. A new take on fine dining.

name: Ô Flaveurs
review: What a gorgeous place! With its exposed stonework, beams, floorboards and fireplace for those cold winter evenings, this authentic little 15C castle will delight those of a romantic disposition. Out on the terrace, a principally Swiss clientele indulges in a wonderfully fresh and flavourful array of dishes prepared by Jérôme Mamet, who is meticulous when it comes to the aesthetics of his cuisine. This inventive and talented chef only works with carefully selected, often organic, ingredients of the highest quality, including whitefish, pike, perch and crayfish from Lake Geneva and line-caught wild sea fish.

name: Les Funambules
review: Chef Guillaume Besson has no equal when it comes to juggling dishes! This minimalist and contemporary space is the setting for a delightful dining experience with its white walls decorated with paintings and photos, its parquet flooring and wooden pieces including a magnificent gnarled teak table base. The set menu dubbed "sur le fil", made with impeccably cooked ingredients, is a masterclass in clear and simple presentation. Modern, clear and precise, occasionally bold, the dishes are always balanced, which is hardly surprising given the name (a funambule is a tight-rope walker!).

name: Auberge de la Mine
review: Formerly the canteen of the local iron ore mine (closed in April 1970), this inn has been the lair of the same chef for over 30 years. Trained classically, his watchword is simplicity and the food is an open book of straightforward authenticity, albeit with flawless technique and inspired creativity, illustrated by brill with green peas and lemon butter. This enticing seasonal score is served in two elegantly appointed dining rooms that manage to avoid the stuffy formality that can be characteristic of such places… What a treat to go down the mine!

name: Auberge À la Bonne Idée
review: Chef Sébastien Tantot (previously Gérald Passédat's executive chef at Le Petit Nice) is thriving in this attractive "inn" (with bare stone, beams, fireplace). Located on the road to Pierrefonds, it lies in the Compiègne Forest, in a medieval village. As the set menus (95% vegetarian) illustrate, the chef is particularly fond of vegetables, fruit and aromatic plants and herbs from his kitchen garden, showcasing them in refined and balanced cuisine that is also visually appealing, a case in point being the bold montage of strips of raw button mushrooms and foie gras with cubes of eel.

name: Le Colombier
review: When it comes to cooking, nothing beats simplicity. Chef Laurent Kleczewski has been making a case for this idea since 2002 in this peaceful Normandy building: drawing on beautifully fresh produce, he composes delicious and flavoursome dishes without ever resorting to showmanship. A few exotic notes – more precisely, Asian ones – are judiciously incorporated to elevate the dishes: a clever balance that never detracts from the basic ingredients. The bill is very reasonable, particularly at lunchtime and the cosy interior combines the feel of the original decor (old red-brick fireplace) with more contemporary touches.

name: Hostellerie de la Pointe St-Mathieu
review: There’s a real surprise awaiting you in Plougonvelin at the western tip of Brittany, where Nolwenn Corre has taken over the helm of this Hostellerie opened in 1954 by her grandparents and taken over in 1988 by her parents. This family affair has managed to evolve with the times while retaining its traditional appeal, thanks to its old stonework and a monumental fireplace which blends harmoniously with the decidedly contemporary furnishings. The young female chef is very much at ease and full of determination in the kitchen, where her dishes owe as much to her skill as to the 100% local ingredients that she uses, including langoustines from Guilvinec, scallops from Brest harbour, fish from Le Conquet, and vegetables from a neighbouring farm.

name: Le Cerf
review: In a group of pretty buildings accessed via a paved inner courtyard and a spruce garden, this former coaching inn has been transformed into an enticing restaurant and hotel. This institution was a bright culinary beacon for a long time thanks to the talent of chef Michel Husser, who passed the reins to Joël Philipps. Bringing to bear his expertise, the chef demonstrates his finesse and delicious eclecticism in the form of a short à la carte menu and two set menus: langoustine tartare; grilled octopus and Iberian chorizo; classic opera cake with wild blueberries and lavender.

name: Le Saint-Estève
review: Amidst vineyards and olive groves, this luxury property abuts Sainte Victoire mountain. It is now the home of chef Julien Le Goff, fresh from Porquerolles in 2019, who signs a repertory in tune with the zeitgeist and laced in Mediterranean accents. Fish and seafood enjoy a special place with langoustine, line-fished seabass and lobster, but turf produce is equally well represented with pigeon, beef and venison. The terrace overlooking the countryside is particularly enjoyable.

name: La Galinette
review: It is always a pleasure to see and taste such regularity. A star establishment since 2004, this fine house is the haunt of Christophe Comes, a talented and versatile chef. A champion of local produce right from the word go, most of what he cooks comes from his own 6-hectare (no less!) garden where he grows vegetables and fruit (mainly citrus and tomatoes). Fish from local boats also enjoys a prominent position on the menu. Add to that excellent value for money, €33 for the lunchtime “Crop of the Day” menu, and you will be making a beeline straight for this excellent eatery.

name: Le Jardin de Berne
review: A vineyard (1,000 hectares no less!), a five-star hotel with a spa, a Michelin-starred restaurant and a vegetable garden: this half Provençal, half Tuscan edifice is home to chef Louis Rameau, formerly second chef here. He sings an ode to the Upper Var thanks to garden vegetables, herbs and flowers and wine and olive oil from the estate. The cheeses and other ingredients are local and organic: ‘scatter-brained’ leek with a velvety lemon and saffron sabayon, confit of lamb in a bread crust or a mind-blowing chocolate delight by fiendishly talented pastry chef éric Raynal. Open evenings only, surprise menus with several courses.

name: Soléna
review: Behind the discreet façade close to the centre of Bordeaux lies a lovely, comfortable interior. The truly amiable young chef, Victor Ostronzec, with a neat blonde beard, has been honing his undeniable talent here since 2016. He stands out from the crowd with his technical, creative cuisine and inspired presentations, and always has something up his sleeve that elevates a dish. His clear desire to surprise diners is a pleasure to see. On top of that, the good news is that his work is nicely enhanced by attentive service.

name: Au Vieux Couvent
review: With its decorative half-timbering, emblematic of this part of Alsace, the inviting mushroom-coloured building that houses this restaurant catches the eye from afar. Close to the flower-decked banks of the Brunnwasser, it was once a dependency of Koenigsbruck's Cistercian abbey. In this setting, sample the dishes of Alexis Albrecht, who has worked at some top restaurants (Au Crocodile, with the Pourcel brothers and Jacques Maximin). His generous seasonal cuisine makes the most of the terroir and local produce, such as fish from the Rhine and game from the Ried… and he uses an abundance of vegetables and aromatic herbs from the family garden that he cultivates with his father.

name: Le Hittau
review: You may well miss this former sheepfold tucked away in verdant greenery with its exposed timberwork on the beach road. It is however well worth keeping your eyes open! Chef Yannick Duc treats diners to spontaneous, vibrant recipes that are tailored to modern tastebuds, displaying a strong predilection for first-class seasonal produce, in particular freshly caught fish. The chef also enjoys mixing seasonings, spices and peppers, jazzing up his pigeon with beetroot and pumpkin with a dash of long red Kampot pepper or his sweetbread and prawns with a dusting of green Malabar pepper. Served on the garden patio in fine weather.

name: Au 14 Février
review: Au 14 Février stands on rue du Bœuf, among the Renaissance mansions, cobbled streets and arcaded galleries in the heart of historical Lyon. A wonderful location in which to sample the surprise menu of chef Tsuyoshi Arai, whose talent and imagination are no longer up for discussion. Born in Kyoto, he belongs to the large family of Japanese chefs who have fallen for France's culinary heritage. He elevates exceptionally fresh ingredients (Miéral poultry, Wagyu beef) by playing on textures, bitterness and acidity: peas, broad beans and snow peas with tamarind, crab and caviar; beetroot tarte tatin with strawberries and foie gras; squab cooked over a cherry wood fire… At every meal, he enchants his clientele with his seasonal symphony. On top of that, the service is extremely obliging.

name: Les Genêts
review: This fashionably refurbished country house, which lies a few miles from Sables d’Olonne, is now the haunt of a talented couple, Nicolas and Amélie Coutand. The chef spent time at Troisgros in Roanne and L’Amphitryon in Lorient, among others. An advocate of fresh, seasonal produce, his approach is creative, joyful and flavoursome and regional ingredients, be they noble or less so, such as sardine, mackerel and hake, take pride of place in his menus. A huge 1400m² cottage garden adds a veggie flourish to his light, delicate dishes at prices that make sense.

name: LuluRouget
review: Trained under Michel Troisgros, Ludovic Pouzelgues is one of the faces of the city's fine dining revival. A stone's throw from the famous Machines de l'Île, he heads up this restaurant with a pleasing, comfortable and contemporary interior. Here, the finest produce reigns supreme (the fish markets of La Turballe and Le Croisic are nearby); it is prepared with precision and inventiveness to create surprise menus based on what the market has to offer. Modern cuisine that is full of personality: a real success.

name: Albert 1er
review: Pierre, Marcel, Joseph, Clothilde… since it was founded in 1903, this restaurant has been run by four different generations, with Perrine Carrier now in charge. Chef Damien Leveau's cuisine draws on the culinary traditions of Savoie and Piedmont, using produce from the region (Arctic char and whitefish from Lake Geneva, snails from around Mont Blanc, pork and lamb from the surrounding farms), enhanced by what is grown in the aromatic garden: oxalis, lovage, citrus thyme, savory, lemon balm or sage. To savour in an elegant and understated space.

name: L'Opidom
review: You only have to take a look at chef Jérôme Roy’s star-studded CV (Gagnaire and Troisgros, together with a star earned at the Couvent des Minimes at Mane-en-Provence) to know he has a purpose in life! Born in Loches, he has returned to his homeland in the company of his spouse, and they have created this smart, modish venue. It is a delight to sample his modern, creative fare that keeps pace with the seasons and which is meticulously sourced from top producers. The result is crunchy foie gras from Landes, confit of ginger, shellfish marinière with chlorella (algae); roast saddle of lamb in sweet spices, lime jus, melt-in-the-mouth red peppers, mango purée, gnocchi of Charlotte potatoes with fresh herbs and a drop-dead dessert of vanilla, Saint Domingue dark chocolate, pistachio praline, perfumed with gold rum.

name: La Magdeleine - Mathias Dandine
review: Mathias Dandine made his childhood dream come true when he became chef at this handsome 18C mansion with a terrace shaded by mature plane trees, situated far from the noise of the city. Here, his cuisine is in perfect harmony with the setting, where he celebrates Provence with breathtaking skill. His unfussy, pared-down Mediterranean cuisine shuns unnecessary frills, with no particular effort made to impress foodies. Yet behind the apparent simplicity, the chef’s recipes demonstrate real mastery in cooking methods, textures and balance of flavours. In fine weather, make sure you take a seat on the terrace shaded by Mediterranean trees.

name: La Table de Castigno
review: This establishment is idyllically located in a lovely Occitan village in the heart of St Chinian vineyards. The village has become something of a foodie wonderland, thanks to a plethora of upmarket guesthouses, art galleries and fine dining joints, such as the Castigno. Run by a duo of chefs, Stéphan Paroche and Justine Viano, their four-handed, often vegetarian repertory stars first-class Mediterranean ingredients, rich in colour and flavour, accompanied by carefully selected tipples from the region and further afield. The old stone walls oozing with charm add the final cherry to this mouth-watering cake.

name: Ursus
review: Housed within one of the resort’s fine hotels, this restaurant loves nature, with a name that pays tribute to the last species of bear in the Savoie. Its dining room resembles a forest with its slim tree trunks separating each of the tables into little copses, a ceiling covered with a canvas representing leaves, and magnificent tables carved from walnut wood. The chef here also loves gathering wild herbs and plants while out walking in the mountains. Once second in command to Jean-François Piège, he creates contemporary-style Alpine cuisine with real technical wizardry, resulting in generous dishes which are full of flavour while respecting the seasons and constantly searching out the best local ingredients. The cheese selection focuses exclusively on the Savoie and is accompanied by an impressive wine list.

name: La Grange de Belle-Église
review: Some restaurant and village names instantly conjure up a picture of ‘la vieille France’ and La Grange de Belle-Église is the quintessence of this gourmet bucolic image. We expect to taste traditional recipes, lovingly crafted from first-rate produce sourced from the surrounding countryside, and we are not disappointed. This former coal barn has been converted into a peaceful, cosy sanctuary that is a temple of good food. Chef Marc Duval is a champion of old school culinary tradition, although he does allow himself the odd more modern creation. Blue lobster, crunchy spring veggies in cream or veal in truffles. Meals are served in a plush dining room which leads into the manicured garden in fine weather.

name: Auberge de la Charme
review: In a small Burgundy village, close to the racetrack, this place is both rustic and pared down in terms of its style: exposed stone walls, exposed ceiling beams, a flagstone floor and an old bread oven set into a wall. The restaurant is run by a pair of chefs, Nicolas Isnard and David Le Comte, who met in Gilles Goujon's restaurant in Fontjoncouse. They share the same passion for fine dining and Asia, the reaches of which they regularly explore. They propose a carte blanche menu, the concept of which may be disconcerting, but it works a treat: just let yourself be transported by this creative, generous and multi-influenced cuisine, inspired by the travels of these two globetrotters.

name: La Maison Caillet
review: Chef Pierre Caillet, awarded the title of "Meilleur Ouvrier de France" in 2011, not only boasts faultless culinary technique, but also wins us over with his feeling for the ingredients and contagious energy. Original creations (his exuberant scallops in a passion fruit crust are a perfect example), interplay of textures and flavours, fine produce from the Normandy terroir… and let's not forget the judicious use of herbs and vegetables from the extensive kitchen garden: a winning formula. Last but not least, this 19C inn also has inviting, cosy guestrooms with private terraces overlooking the lake.

name: Reflet d'Obione
review: Is it possible to reconcile gastronomy with gluten-free, tasty and healthy cooking, particularly by cutting the levels of fat and sugar? Yes! After training in star restaurants in Switzerland and France, even in Australia, thirty-something Laurent Cherchi proves his commitment to the environment here. A few steps from the pretty Canourgue Square, he selects his often organic and always ultra-fresh produce locally from Cévennes to the Mediterranean (Aubrac beef, Camargue salt marsh lamb, Larzac Tomme cheese). Each dish has been pondered and puzzled over and technique and accuracy are de rigueur, illustrated by the pearlescent flesh of hake fish, carrots, parsnips and bergamot. The vegetables are the stars of the show. The interior sports a stripped back vibe by way of three dining rooms, the first of which overlooks the kitchen.

name: Château d'Adoménil
review: In the heart of the Lunéville countryside, this charming little Classical château is nestled in wooded grounds. You pass through a solemn series of rooms that have lost none of their historical character, with old wood panelling, parquet floors and open fireplaces. The dining room overlooks the grounds. A few subtle baroque and contemporary touches brighten up this fabulously austere backdrop, which is in keeping with the chef's cuisine – traditional cuisine enhanced by modern touches. Previously a pastry chef, the talented and discreet Cyril Leclerc (who hails from Lorraine) loves beautiful produce. He treats it with respect – you only have to look at the accuracy of his cooking and flavours. Curated by his expert wife, who manages the restaurant, the wine list is fittingly splendid.

name: Likoké
review: Likoké is the most Belgian of the restaurants in Ardèche! Cyriel Huysentruyt, in charge of the dining room and the wines, works side by side with Colombian chef Guido Niño Torres, who adheres to the establishment's globetrotting ethos: over the course of a single set menu, he presents playful and colourful dishes like so many invitations to head off on a journey, sometimes inspired by a memory, an encounter, a past event… There are some real moments of brilliance, such as an incredible caramelised and meat-like celeriac served with mushrooms and vin jaune. Everything is sourced from the surrounding area – organic and natural wines from the region, cheeses and vegetables from local producers, organic trout from Mt Lozère, Mézenc beef etc. Confident cooking that never fails to surprise.

name: L'Auberge Basque
review: Close to Saint-Jean-de-Luz and the coast, this old Basque farmhouse has a more modern wing overlooking the Rhune (Larrun) mountain and the countryside. It is here, in the heart of the Basque Country, that Cédric Béchade and his wife Marion decided to set up shop. He is hardly an unknown in the gourmet world: previously sous-chef to Jean-François Piège at the Plaza Athénée, he trained in Biarritz at the Hôtel du Palais under Jean-Marie Gauthier before joining the Hostellerie de Plaisance after the departure of one Philippe Etchebest. In the kitchen, this creative chef uses high-quality Basque ingredients, treating them with all the care they deserve.

name: L'Esquisse
review: The former second-in-command to Laurent Petit at Le Clos des Sens in Annecy-le-Vieux, Stéphane Dattrino has branched off on his own to create this attractive restaurant. Behind its discreet façade, tables for two predominate and despite its deliberately relaxed feel, the service here is very much on the mark. The chef’s strong imprint is clearly evident in cuisine that is rich in flavour and colour, with a seasonal palette that incorporates high-quality local ingredients including plants and vegetables (wild garlic, wild asparagus etc). Delicious dishes full of finesse include the duxelle de champignons tart with cep pastry, and crispy calf’s sweetbreads with a squash medley.

name: Le France
review: Situated between Morteau and La Chaux-de-Fonds not far from the French-Swiss border, this restaurant welcomes guests to the heart of the Haut-Doubs mountains. Here, chef Hugues Droz offers guests typical Franche-Comté hospitality, just as his father and grandfather did before him, paying careful attention to the seasons and with a judicious blend of regionality and inventiveness. He also enjoys creating themed meals, such as his mushroom-based menu where morel mushrooms feature in every course, including the banana morel and speculoos ice cream dessert. Other skilfully prepared recipes feature ingredients such as lobster, Morteau sausage, Bresse poultry, arctic char and foie gras. The German proverb “as happy as God in France” hits the nail on the head!

name: Auberge La Fenière
review: The mantra of Nadia Sammut, daughter of Reine Sammut and now at the helm of the Auberge, is “a commitment to creating a better-tasting world”. Here, gluten, refined white sugar and milk have all been banished from the kitchen, to be replaced by an impressive skill set focused on different types of flour (chickpeas, split peas and rice, in particular) and fruit sugars. These skills are showcased on a unique and bold tasting menu that draws on the history of the region and Nadia’s family. In the dining room, her partner Ernest, a highly enthusiastic sommelier, selects fish that abide by the ikejime method of preparation. The vegetable garden also has its part to play for this duo in creating healthy and natural Southern French cuisine, which looks to the future and the Grand Luberon for its inspiration.

name: La Table d'Olivier
review: At Olivier’s Table, Pierre is in the kitchen, while his partner Fanny, former pastry chef, oversees the dining room. Normandy-born Pierre has enthusiastically embraced Corrèze, his land of adoption, creating this stone house furnished in a modern vein with designer lighting in the town centre. The bargain basement prices are astounding and his cooking in tune with the zeitgeist ticks all the boxes: enticing, suave and colourful: foie gras, fillet of beef, soy and Nori seaweed; line-fished pollock, carrots-peppers and chorizo; strawberries, jasmine and lemon…

name: Le Prieuré
review: Located in the centre of this wine-producing village in the Côte Roannaise, this restaurant occupying a traditional granite building adjoins a magnificent 15C priory crowned with a multi-coloured varnished tile roof in typical Burgundian style. A contemporary wooden porch has brought a touch of modernity to the delightful setting. Chef Thierry Fernandes, who hails from the area (as does his wife who runs the front of house), creates classically inspired cuisine in which strong technique and flavours are evident in every dish.

name: La Signoria
review: This exclusive aristocratic estate, just a few minutes from Calvi, is surrounded by pine forest and vineyards, with snow-capped peaks on the distant horizon… Meals are served on the terrace overlooking a Mediterranean garden rich in scents from roses to eucalyptus. The perfect backdrop to food that showcases exquisitely presented Corsican produce: poached langoustine, tabouleh of herbs and an iced stock of Corsican fish; slow-roasted “fish from our coastline”, cabbage steaks, girolles and pattypan squash… Prolong the experience and book a night (or two) in one of the estate’s delightful villas or suites with spa. Seasonal lunchtime menu at the Bistrot.

name: Nicolas Carro - Hôtel de Carantec
review: After a successful spell at La Table d’Olivier Nasti in Kaysersberg, Nicolas Carro has returned to his homeland (he comes from Loudéac). He is at the helm of this iconic Brittany establishment, made famous by chef Patrick Jeffroy and which commands a jaw-dropping view over Morlaix Bay. Like his illustrious predecessor, he celebrates local produce, both turf (vegetables and meat such as guinea fowl and lamb from Monts d’Arée) and surf (shellfish and fish from small boats). Delicate, intelligent dishes with pleasant contrasting textures that are flawlessly prepared and seasoned… His cooking effortlessly hits the spot every time and the story continues in Carantec. Pleasant rooms for overnight stays.

name: Colette
review: French author and feminist before her time, in the 1920’s Colette fell in love with Saint-Tropez and bought a little house next to the Hôtel de Sezz and its restaurant, hence the establishment’s name. Experienced chef Philippe Colinet crafts stripped-back cuisine that pays tribute to Mediterranean flavours and vegetables: roast pigeon, gutsy jus, chickpeas and sesame oil; grilled oyster, cream of shallots, cress purée and charcoal bread. The gourmet menu is only available in the evenings. Airy, spacious dining room whose pared-down décor is ideally suited to the hotel that celebrated its 100th anniversary in 2020.

name: Château de Pray
review: Upstream from Amboise, on the south bank of the Loire, this medieval castle, remodelled during the Renaissance, catches the eye with its two massive towers. The building presides peacefully over vast formal grounds, where the art of living, Loire style, is alive and well. The orangery, part of which is built into the rock of the hillside, is oh-so elegant, and on sunny days it is a real treat to sit on the pleasant terrace looking out onto the gardens. Chef Arnaud Philippon's cuisine flirts with the zeitgeist: toasted white asparagus, nasturtiums and egg yolk sauce; pan-roasted blue lobster, chickpeas from the Loches area, buckwheat and blackcurrant shoots; hot soufflé with Touraine blackcurrants and fresh blackcurrant sorbet. Delicate execution, balanced flavours, ingredients sourced from local producers: this is château life at its best.

name: La Mère Germaine
review: En route for the French Riviera, the movie stars of Paris, from Mistinguett to Jean Gabin and Fernandel, used to stop off here. Keen to maintain this heritage, the restaurant has kept the name of its founder, Germaine Vion (1922), as well as a devotion to fine food. In a village beloved of wine connoisseurs, the establishment curates suave dishes (red mullet with potatoes in saffron or mallard duck roasted whole, beetroot and juniper). Huge murals depicting Belle Époque Paris set the scene indoors and the patio commands a panoramic view of the vineyards. Knock-out selection of Châteauneuf-du-Pape wines.

name: Le Foch
review: In this excellent restaurant situated along the famous tree-shaded Promenades, chef Jacky Louazé attracts a loyal and devoted clientele. His success is undoubtedly due to his distinctive and inventive cuisine, with fresh fish and shellfish taking pride of place on the menu. Blue lobster, cereals and spices, citrus fruit; maritime-inspired dishes; whole bass cooked in a Vallauris clay crust; turbot in semi-salted butter; and potatoes from Noirmoutier are just some of the top-quality delicacies showcased on the menu here.

name: La Dame de Pic - Le 1920
review: In the Four Seasons Hotel, Anne-Sophie Pic is adding a new Alpine twist to her classics, such as a “berlingot” filled with a runny sauce made with Beaufort and Abondance cheeses and a touch of absinthe or a white millefeuille that comes in a version of Leatherwood honey, eucalyptus in fine jelly and slightly acidic blackberry, while her lamb is marinated in lemon balm and Chartreuse liqueur - so deceptively simple and yet so complex. Consummate subtlety, as much by the striking contrasts in flavours as by the textures.

name: Le 1862 - Les Glycines
review: Le 1862, the main restaurant of the hotel Les Glycines, has an enticing agenda in store for you: the original, vibrant dishes are impeccably cooked and made with top-notch ingredients, including vegetables from the kitchen garden. At this former coaching inn, located between the train station and the River Vézère, they serve market cuisine with subtle harmonies of flavours, as well as very accomplished sauces.
