The chef elevates the finest of ingredients from the local area – pigeon, foie gras, Sarlat Tomme and vegetables – and diners get to sample it all in an elegant contemporary space that gives onto the terrace-loggia overlooking the park. Impeccable service and good wine advice.

name: Fleur de Pavé
review: If you liked Itinéraires, you will love Fleur de Pavé, an establishment firmly in the zeitgeist where Sylvain Sendra is pursuing his culinary research with the same enthusiasm and flair as in his previous HQ. He whips up modern dishes that draw inspiration from all over the world, featuring deceptively spontaneous plating and blue-ribbon ingredients, such as the highly exclusive vegetables of Asafumi Yamashita. Rather than bowl us over with flashy technique, the chef seeks to lay the emphasis squarely on flavours, whilst upholding the menu’s promise – for which he has our heartfelt thanks!

name: La Maison dans le Parc
review: Chef Charles Coulombeau and his wife Roxane (front of house) have brought a breath of fresh air to this renowned restaurant in Nancy, which occupies a fine residence next to the opera house, just behind one of France’s most beautiful squares. Having worked at Les Prés d’Eugénie, Lameloise and La Table des Frères Ibarboure, this young couple offer modern cuisine, masterfully prepared, enhanced by a touch of creativity and a nod to Japan (where the chef worked for several months). Citrus fruits (such as Buddha’s hand and calamondin orange) and Asian flavours go hand in hand with premium ingredients such as langoustine or Bresse chicken with nori. Don’t miss the delightful terrace overlooking the park. A real winner.

name: Le Favori - Les Sources de Cheverny
review: This new address is elegant, refined and in perfect harmony with the cuisine prepared by the chef (who previously worked at La Réserve in Paris), available via a fixed four- or six-course tasting menu based around the finest seasonal produce. The precise presentation, meticulous recipes, beautiful aesthetics and superb sauces bring out the true essence of the main ingredient, typified by the white radish steamed in its own vegetable water, lightly seared Dublin Bay prawns, citrus nectar and fresh turmeric. The meticulously prepared dishes and garnishes bring pleasure to the palate, enhanced by the restaurant dining room that blends seamlessly into the surrounding greenery. A precise, explosive and enchanting experience.

name: Maison Ronan Kervarrec
review: A vibrant, gourmet homage to Brittany! Ronan Kervarrec, whose CV boasts stints at the Hostellerie Plaisance in Saint-Émilion and La Chèvre d’Or in Eze, is thriving in his native Brittany as he tells his personal and professional story through food. The tale is well worth sampling and oozes with first-class ingredients all of which reek of Brittany: sarrazin wheat, buttermilk, fish, shellfish, seafood, butter, seaweed, crunchy gavotte wafers, heady chouchen and traditional salted butter biscuits… Floor to ceiling windows overlook the terrace opposite the garden. Overnight rooms and a small delicatessen to take a gourmet treat home also available.

name: La Table du 11
review: Following his first Michelin star in 2016, chef Jean-Baptiste Lavergne-Morazzani has redoubled his efforts, with the support of a solid and efficient team, to win over many more food-lovers in Versailles. His ethos – a natural approach to everything – is clearly apparent on his concise, no-frills menu with a sharp focus on the seasons and starring natural and sustainable ingredients (mainly organic) fish and meat, along with vegetables from his own kitchen garden. The impressive wine list comprises close to 700 labels, with many produced biodynamically. The exclusive location in the timeless Cour des Senteurs near the castle adds further weight to this unique dining experience.

name: Le Bon Accueil
review: This aptly named establishment (a warm welcome does await!) is an excellent option in the heart of the Haut-Doubs. For four generations, this inviting and comfortable chalet that is typical of the region has been practising the art of Jura-style hospitality. St Point Lake is across the road, Le Suchet mountain and Switzerland just beyond. Here, they put their heart and soul into providing good food that is an ode to the region. Chef Marc Faivre worked at Georges Blanc, Pierre Gagnaire and Maison Lameloise before returning to his homeland, where his fine and tasty cuisine delights diners: trout with blue cheese or absinthe, free-range chicken, morels and Jura vin jaune sauce (of course!) or roast pigeon, duck foie gras and artichoke.

name: La Table d'à Côté
review: Opposite Limère golf course, this is Christophe Hay’s second establishment. The contemporary interior is evocative of nature and the forest, the chef’s main inspirations, together with vegetables from his garden. Loïs Bée now runs the kitchen. The finely crafted, subtle food is of course seasonal and aims to work with local suppliers (game in season). The pike-perch steamed in woodland aromas will blow your mind!

name: Bruno
review: A restaurant owes so much to its owners… and in this traditional Provençal house, which in the 1920s was the home of the great-grandmother of the Bruno family, their generous spirit is very present! Under the watchful eye of Clément Bruno, a larger-than-life, benevolent father figure renowned for his veneration for truffles, and the two brothers – Samuel, front-of-house and Benjamin in the kitchen – uphold tradition with just the right measure of modernity thrown in. The truffle-based set menu is still on offer (the type of truffles changes in keeping with the seasons), but it now features more vegetables. Cheerful and attentive service completes the picture.

name: La Chassagnette
review: Bulls grazing, pink flamingos haloed by sunlight, canals, rice fields and the Rhône delta: welcome to Camargue and more specifically to la Chassagnette, a former sheepfold refurbished in the shape of a modern mas. Chef gardener Armand Arnal has firmly dug his fork into the soil of the organic vegetable garden and orchard around the property. In addition to plants, the chef has no taboos from meat from the wild bulls, lamb from the neighbouring shepherd and fish from Grau-du-Roi fish auction… Armand crafts creative, often surprising and sometimes even disconcerting recipes, mingling acidic notes and home-made vinegars. Three hectares of flower and vegetable gardens, greenhouses, hives and orchards, together with a magnificent leafy patio – heavenly!

name: Les Terrasses de Lyon
review: Perched up on the higher ground of Fourvière, this Renaissance convent now houses a charming hotel and restaurant with a panoramic glass-paned dining room that affords guests a splendid view over the rooftops of Vieux Lyon, whatever the season: it seems you can almost reach out and touch St Jean Cathedral. This place required a chef with plenty of vision! Enter David Delsart, who has mastered all aspects of French cuisine. He often puts a regional spin on his dishes, smoking his pigeon (or lobster) over Beaujolais vine shoots, cooking whitefish from Lake Geneva, salmon trout from Isère and snails from the Lyonnais mountains. The classic desserts are beautifully made: charlotte, profiteroles, warm soufflé…

name: Moulin d'Alotz
review: In this 17C Basque watermill nestling deep in a picturesque vale, a new conservatory extension commands a fantastic view of the countryside and lush green garden. In summertime, your nostrils will be titillated by freshly cut herbs served as appetisers. This mill is emblematic of the ecological, humanist and gastronomic ethos of chef Fabrice Idiart. The chef’s signature menu, “Ital”, features an exemplary harmony between plant and animal ingredients, in which ineluctable vegetables are underscored by plant and spicy sauces that characterise Fabrice’s distinctive, unorthodox approach. For example, the chef, also a reggae fan, crafts dishes ranging from a medley of sweet potato and cockles or delicately cooked hake à la plancha, jazzed up with a pil-pil sauce and scattered with aromatic herbs from the garden to wagyu beef reared in Navarre, a marvellous cut of marbled meat, enhanced by a Romanesco cabbage and broccoli.

name: Brikéténia
review: The tiny Basque village of Guétary is the HQ of one part of the Ibarboure family, the rest of whom can be found at the Frères Ibarboure restaurant in Bidart. In this characteristic 1930’s Basque house, formerly a hotel, Martin and his son David are in the kitchen, while Marie-Claude, David’s mum, warmly upholds Basque traditions of hospitality and his sister, Camille, dispenses insightful wine tips. The quintessence of a family business, although it must be said that David did skip the roost for a while, spending time with Pierre Gagnaire in Hong Kong. Father and son craft masterful dishes depicted by suave seasonings, a subtle play on transparency and contrast and perfectly ripe ingredients… The produce, most of which is Basque, is prepared as simply as possible. Delightful service.

name: La Table de la Mainaz
review: In Upper Jura at the Faucille Pass, a short drive from Geneva, this luxury hotel commands a drop-dead view of Mont Blanc and Lake Geneva from its contemporary dining room. The distinctive signature of gifted Julien Thomasson (former owner of the starred Ambassadeurs in Saint Chamond in the Loire) is immediately recognisable. He crafts appetising, up-to-the-minute food, flanked by masterful stocks and sauces, such as: Mijoux lamb (pink kidneys, roast fillet and slow-baked shoulder), gnocchis, artichokes and chickpea purée or red mullet, melting potatoes and vegetable stock…

name: La Nouvelle Auberge
review: On the doorstep of Munster valley, this “new inn” is a fully refurbished former posthouse. On the ground-floor, an Alsace bistro regales diners on weekday lunchtimes. Upstairs, the gourmet restaurant sports a suitably rustic, half-timbered dining room. Bernard Leray, who hails from Rennes in Brittany, has taken to Alsace like a stork to its nest. After honing his skills at Bernard Loiseau, Leray puts a delicate new spin on local produce. All his dishes demonstrate his painstaking work and consummate technique, such as Bresse poultry, a gutsy stock of black truffles and melt-in-the-mouth vegetable pie.

name: Auberge de la Brie
review: This local institution celebrated the 30th anniversary of its Michelin star in 2021. Ever popular with its loyal clientele, this charming restaurant has more than one string to its bow with its bright yet traditional setting (the dining room overlooks the garden), its personalised and impressively consistent modern cuisine, and friendly service from Céline, wife of chef Alain Pavard. The latter creates classically inspired cuisine which he has adapted to the times, thrilling guests with his top-quality ingredients and precise flavours in dishes such as roasted scallops with mango chutney, and veal fillet with celeriac and mushrooms.

name: Le Moulin de l'Abbaye
review: In this picturesque village where visitors can journey from prehistory to the Renaissance, this restaurant enjoys a truly stunning setting at the base of a cliff. This outbuilding of the Benedictine abbey of Brantôme also features a splendid terrace on the banks of the River Dronne, facing the town’s 16C angled bridge. Here, the chef’s fine, flavoursome cuisine is ably supported by a cast of superb ingredients, perfect cooking techniques and meticulous presentation. All in all, a venerable property with a contemporary and timeless charm.

name: Allium
review: Thanks to a crowd funding campaign, Frédérique and Lionel Hénaff have opened the restaurant of their dreams. The chef’s inventive streak is harnessed to a score that focuses on fresh produce and encompasses a multitude of ingredients (herbs, flowers) with a weakness for siphoned sauces. A tasteful, elegant vibe sets the scene in the dining room, which also boasts a handful of seats at the counter facing the open kitchen.

name: Les Trois Rochers
review: On the Odet estuary, opposite the pretty port of Bénodet, the view overlooks the sea on one side and a forest of pine and oaks on the other… You could do worse! The chef, who trained in Quimper and has worked in Brittany and Switzerland, aims above all to highlight the work of the craftspeople and producers of Brittany (essentially organic) in his menus. He combines regional delicacies with spices from further afield and fresh herbs on a constant quest to exalt the flavour. His langoustines ravioles and shellfish stock is out of this world!

name: Ambroisie
review: What initially draws the eye, right in front of us, is the lake hemmed in by wooded banks – the location alone is worth seeing. But above all there is the remarkable work of the chef – after all, that's what we came for… He excels at transforming fine ingredients (scallops hot-pâté style; Breton lobster with raspberries, dried caviar and mizuna; pigeon breast roasted and smoked on the barbecue). His trompe l'œil desserts are at once amusing and delicious (apricot, lemon, chestnut – depending on the season). For fans of truffles, the chef serves a truffle menu all year round: it wouldn't seem right not to indulge.

name: La Barbacane
review: Located at the heart of Carcassonne’s medieval citadel, the Hôtel de la Cité is a superb example of neo-Gothic architecture, built in 1909 on the site of the former episcopal palace, with magnificent gardens that adjoin the ramparts. Inside, the stained-glass windows, coats of arms and wood panelling endow it with an ambience worthy of 19C French architect Viollet-le-Duc. Originally from Bresse and former second in command here to Franck Putelat, Jérôme Ryon is a solid chef who enjoys a more classical style of cooking. He bases his recipes around ingredients of the finest quality, in particular fish and shellfish from the nearby Mediterranean, as well as game and mushrooms in the autumn. His delicious cuisine champions the region’s terroir in dishes such as fricassee of summer vegetables, braised sea bass, and fillet of Aubrac beef with foie gras... accompanied by an impressive cellar of Southern French wines.

name: La Vieille Tour
review: Visible from afar, the tower of this 15C house will guide you to this gourmet temple. Youthful chef Alexis Letellier regales his guests with well-crafted, modern food using top-notch produce. His recipes sometimes reveal an Asian influence and are regularly reinvented in tune with the seasons. We tasted melting foie gras, smoked eel, Granny Smith apple and coriander sorbet; turbot, spinach cannelloni, saffron and chorizo. The chef’s partner, Alice, greets guests professionally and cheerfully, offering excellent wine tips on the way. Delicate flavours, character and attractive plating: this place ticks all the boxes.

name: La Marine
review: Closed temporarily. With its panoramic view of the sea and the port, this local institution on the west coast of the Cotentin peninsula lies opposite the Channel Islands of Jersey and Guernsey (which can be glimpsed sometimes). The set tasting menus together with a few dishes showcasing locally caught fish offer an enjoyable culinary masterclass with modern French sensibility.

name: Villa de l'Étang Blanc
review: This White Pond is a small, protected expanse of water inhabited by birds that can be leisurely observed from the terrace or the dining room; in fact, bird watching sometimes seems to be one of the guests’ main occupations. A keen surfer, David Sulpice’s inspired, high-precision cuisine resembles a cruise through the best of Landes produce, which he consummately showcases: duck and asparagus from Darrigade farm, fish from small boats direct from Capbreton, authentic Pyrenean ewe’s milk cheese, citrus fruit from Thierry Dupouy in Eugénie-les-Bains. Meticulous cooking and flavoursome jus and zabagliones. All the ingredients are used in line with the villa’s zero-waste philosophy. The intelligent wine list cleverly surfs between prestigious vintages and small southwest France wine growers.

name: La Table de la Ferme
review: Murtoli defies classification in classical tourist terms. Poised betwixt the sea and the hills, this huge property, dotted with stone houses boasting private pools, is the quintessence of rural luxury and the most recent rooms combine modernity with vintage charm in a traditional Corsican architectural style. Supervised by Mathieu Pacaud, the Murtoli’s gourmet establishment shines the spotlight on fine Corsican produce, including from the estate, ranging from vegetables, cheese and honey to veal, lamb and olive oil… An alfresco meal on the patio shaded by a trellis and olive trees is an unforgettable experience.

name: Le P'tit Polyte
review: The Chalet Mounier is a family affair. It began with Marie and Hippolyte Mounier, who opened this hotel, the first in the resort, in 1933. Then came their son Robert, from 1971, and today it is Alban and his partner Angélique who are carrying on the tradition. The cosy little restaurant has an intimate atmosphere. Chef Tanguy Rattier proposes three tasting menus, one of which is 100% plant-based. The kitchen team does an excellent job of selecting fine ingredients and presenting them beautifully on the plate to create light and vibrant dishes. The same goes for the fabulous wine list, with its judicious suggestions. Le P'tit Polyte punches above its weight!

name: Le Quincangrogne
review: On the banks of the Marne, these premises have previously taken many forms (by turns a mill, a guinguette and even a retirement home!) and have now been transformed into a welcoming hotel-restaurant. In the kitchen is Franck Charpentier, a chef with quite a CV, including several Michelin-starred restaurants in luxury hotels. Being a fan of authentic taste experiences, he treats his diners to a simple menu that revolves around high-quality regional produce. Fine and precise combinations of flavours, meticulous and well-crafted visual effects: a delightful meal from start to finish. In season, you can even enjoy the beautiful terrace with its view of the nearby river. A choice stopover.

name: Le Village Tomohiro
review: The engaging façade of this picturesque inn on a pretty lane of historic Marly hides a modern restaurant in the zeitgeist run by a Japanese couple. The chef crafts surgically precise creations, rich in harmonious notes, textures and flavours, illustrated by his signature dish: goï cuôn of blue lobster and terrine of foie gras, confit of spring vegetables in olive oil and Aquitaine caviar.

name: Stéphane Tournié - Les Jardins de l'Opéra
review: In an entirely revamped room (parquet floor, wooden tables, wine cellar), flanked by a leafy interior courtyard covered by a glazed roof, this quiet, peaceful setting comes as something of a relief in the heart of Toulouse’s Capitole. The venue is the HQ of virtuoso Stéphane Tournié. A local lad, the chef boasts stints at Lucien Vanel in Toulouse, André Daguin in Auch, Taillevent under Philippe Legendre and the Crillon under Christian Constant. We love his knack of getting straight to the point thanks to fresh produce (preferable local and organic), tried and tested recipes and high-flying craftsmanship: soft-boiled hen’s egg in truffles, or pressed sweetbread and roast langoustine.

name: Jean-Claude Leclerc
review: This restaurant near the courthouse extends an invitation to all foodies rather than a summons to a hearing! For over twenty years, Jean-Claude Leclerc has been behind this very popular Clermont-Ferrand hideaway. The chef woos us with his new spin on time-honoured Gallic recipes, in keeping with the seasons, thanks to farm produce from Auvergne, Provence, and even Brittany, when it comes to turbot and sole. It is a masterclass in balance and skilful execution, overflowing with flavour, such as the seabream cooked in its skin, red wine risotto, seared onion and cuttlefish or lamb, violet artichokes and truffle potatoes.

name: Auberge Frankenbourg
review: In this small village perched in the foothills of the Vosges, this hotel-restaurant has been welcoming travellers since the start of the last century. The Buecher brothers, who took over the reins of this family-run business from their parents, preside with a cheerful enthusiasm. The delicious and refined ingredient-led cuisine conjured up by the eldest, Sébastien, succeeds in showcasing the best of the terroir in the form of a menu that is always changing. He puts a creative spin on traditional dishes, as in his roasted venison loin with a sweetcorn medley, or his flame-seared langoustines served with a potato and leek parmentier. Most of the fruit and vegetables come from their own garden. The younger brother Guillaume operates front of house, in a setting that combines wood panelling and minimalism. A few guestrooms are available.

name: Les Apothicaires
review: A hip establishment serving excellent food! Tabata, a Brazilian-born chef, met Ludovic in one of Paul Bocuse’s brasseries in Lyon – an auspicious start to their shared culinary voyage. In a cheerful, comfortable bistro vibe, with a library and banquettes, they treat guests to creative cuisine with a few Scandinavian and Latin American touches. An added bonus is making a reservation (from 11am on the same day) for one of the two last-minute bookings available that evening – a perfect solution if the restaurant is fully booked which, given its success, is generally par for the course these days.

name: L'Orée de la Forêt
review: Looking for a fine restaurant just outside Paris? This gracious, late-19C mansion is set in peaceful wooded grounds, ideal for a weekend in the country. The elegant bourgeois interior cannot fail but appeal thanks to the loving care and attention lavished by chef Nicolas Leclercq and his wife Yolaine. Nicolas’ grandmother first opened the restaurant back in 1956, at which time she made her butter from milk from her own cow! The large cottage garden (take the time to stroll around it after your meal) supplies the restaurant with fresh vegetables and herbs, which are picked by the chef’s father. Nowadays, the chef, who bakes his own sourdough bread, rustles up straightforward, colourful food that is in tune with the seasons.

name: Ithurria
review: With its location on the Place du Fronton in Ainhoa, facing the village’s pelota wall, you won’t find a more Basque setting! This attractive and traditional family property has retained its tiled flooring, wood beams, gleaming copper pots and pans, and vintage tableware. Assisted by his brother Stéphane in the dining room, chef Xavier Isabal is at the helm, now supported by his nephews Martin in the kitchen and Louis at the pastry station. A hint of modernity is evident on the enticing menu here, with Isabal sourcing his ingredients exclusively from local Basque producers, which he then supplements with his own fruit and vegetables. The local terroir is deliciously showcased via dishes such as Landes asparagus, sauce mousseline with pepper and crispy egg yolk; Koskera-style line-caught hake; and roasted rack of milk-fed lamb with confit shoulder.

name: Au Souper Fin
review: For over three decades, the owner chef, Éric Buisset, and his wife, Véronique, have been regaling us with unwavering commitment, as the numbers of regulars bear witness! Established in a delightful village in the Caux region, you will be served a fine medley of painstakingly selected flavours, based on top-notch fresh ingredients: duck foie gras from a local breeder, John Dory from the Dieppe coastline, apples from Normandy’s orchards and exceptional scallops… The chef, who was born in northern France but is Norman at heart, goes straight to the essence of fine flavour. Prettily appointed guestrooms should you wish to stay a little longer.

name: Restaurant Pierre Grein
review: Venture into the business zone to make your way to this handsome contemporary establishment – you won’t regret it! In a spacious, comfortable conservatory-cum-dining room, chef Pierre Grein curates cuisine according to Provençal traditions, adding a subtle, modern twist and meticulous, high-flying technique (illustrated by the trompe-l’œil desserts): velvety cauliflower soup, bouchot mussels, poulette sauce; seabass skin on roasted on one side, crumble of girolles and baby spinach leaves; a gold leaf hazelnut trompe l’œil of salted butterscotch, hazelnut praline mousse, chocolate crumble. Everything is made on the premises from top-notch produce. The knock-out titbits at the start of the meal and the friendly, efficient service, in particular of the sommelier, add the final flourish.

name: Buerehiesel
review: This lovely 17C half-timbered farmhouse was reconstructed stone by stone in the Orangerie Park, next-door to the Council of Europe. The conservatory dining room and patio command a bucolic view of this leafy haven. Éric, Antoine Westermann’s son, is following in his father’s footsteps. The regulars applaud his decision to keep some of his dad’s specials, such as frog’s legs sautéed in chervil, served with “schniederspaetle” (ravioles invented by the house), or the restaurant’s trademark brioche dessert served with beer ice cream and baked pear – to die for! Éric has nonetheless developed his own distinctive culinary signature, crafting modern dishes which acknowledge, but do not bow down to local culinary traditions.

name: Le Clair de la Plume
review: Nestling at the foot of Madame de Sévigné’s castle, Le Clair de la Plume embodies Provence’s traditions of hospitality and good food: olive oil from Nyons, guinea fowl and vegetables from Drôme, fish from the Grau du Roi fish auction and local strawberries and asparagus. This establishment sings an ode to first-class Mediterranean produce. Pastry chef, Cédric Perret, conjures up a sweet-toothed score in harmony with the seasons, frequently adding an unexpected vegetable note to his desserts.

name: Le Haut-Allier
review: In the heart of the Gorges de l'Allier, the windows of this family-run hotel-restaurant look out over the bridge and the river. Firmly rooted in this rural setting, the Brun family – Philippe and Michelle, ably assisted by their son and his partner – elevate and refine this rugged landscape. They give pride of place to the many ingredients to be found in this corner of the world: mushrooms, Auvergne meats and cheeses, farmed char, but also wild plants and flowers. Tuck into delights such as veal fillet mignon, port wine-glazed turnips, spinach gnocchi and a mustard condiment, or a surprising "alliance" of citrus fruits, carrots and almond milk served with a mojito sorbet.

name: Maison Medard
review: Wholesome flavours, jus, emulsions and sauces that melt in the mouth, illustrated by quenelle of sheatfish, white asparagus and langoustine cream or loin of pork and artichokes in a gutsy veal gravy. Their new take on the ubiquitous crottin de Chavignol featuring a light, unctuous, siphoned mousse surrounded by an acidic tomato juice is out of this world. The chef’s up-to-date, intelligent, delicate cuisine sings the praises of local produce, all of which orchestrated into subtle, colourful dishes. Chef Julien Medard and his wife Delphine (in charge of the dining room) warmly greet customers into their welcoming establishment which tastefully marries rustic and contemporary details.

name: La Chapelle - Château Saint-Jean
review: The restaurant of Château Saint Jean stands out firstly by its premium location in a former chapel, whose upper section is clad in copper panels almost like a dome, in a surprising and highly successful marriage of periods! The food is of the same ilk and chef Olivier Valade more than demonstrates that his star-studded background (Loiseau, Darroze) owes nothing to chance! His surgically crafted cuisine unveils excellent seasonal produce and overflows with character. If you then add the professional service and prices that make sense, you will not be able to resist this “invitation to culinary decadence” (their words).

name: L'Épuisette
review: An “épuisette” is a child’s fishing net, often forgotten on the rocks by the seashore and this establishment enjoys a matchless waterside location on the fishing port of the Vallon des Auffes. The house’s iconic “Fanny” menu is as dazzling as the July sunshine. The chef knows his business: the produce is flawlessly fresh, the recipes meticulous and the flavours distinctive – all of which with lashings of generosity. We sampled a bouillabaisse of capon, monkfish, galinette, weever and John Dory – to die for! A delicious port of call.

name: La Table du Boisniard
review: In the heart of Vendée amidst sprawling grounds facing a castle whose foundations date back to the 15C, this establishment is the work of chef Valentin Morice, who trained as a pastry chef. His creative flair, based on outstanding, often local ingredients, reveals a genuine passion for stocks and broths. The culinary score, which is unabashedly modern and fully respectful of the seasons, is served in a stylish dining room or on the patio in fine weather. Individually appointed guestrooms in the castle and exquisite chalets in the woods.

name: Loiseau des Ducs
review: Close to the Ducal Palace, this restaurant belonging to the Loiseau Group is housed in the 16C Hôtel de Talmay, a listed building. Chef Jean-Bruno Gosse, who has worked for Yannick Franques and at the Hostellerie de Levernois, continues to promote traditional Burgundy cuisine and Bernard Loiseau's classics, albeit in a more modern spirit. The enjoyment is enhanced by a splendid selection of fine wines by the glass!

name: Le Charlemagne
review: In the heart of this vineyard devoted to Corton-Charlemagne, Laurent Peugeot nurtures guests in a peaceful, contemporary interior, ideal to sample good food that wavers between France and Japan and which is dotted with surprising but inspired combinations. Out-of-the-ordinary creations, distinctively personal, based on the produce of the restaurant’s garden (and hives) and from local, stringently selected suppliers. The wine list is truly awesome, which is hardly a surprise when you learn that Laurent is both a wine connoisseur and a producer himself.

name: La Table du Connétable - Auberge du Jeu de Paume
review: The Royal Castle of Chantilly is the epitome of superlative with grounds by Le Nôtre, France’s second largest Fine Art Museum and stables of unrivalled opulence… First, treat yourself to a tour of this amazing estate, before taking a seat in this luxurious inn abutting the gardens. In a lavish setting, dripping with fine art, chandeliers and tapestries, sample a creative score with a strong veggie slant and the odd regional classic, albeit with a new spin. The next-door Jardin d’Hiver serves wholesome, seasonal dishes in the gallery or on the pretty patio terrace. Spacious, classically appointed guestrooms.

name: Frédéric Molina au Moulin de Léré
review: Deep in the Brevon valley, this former 17C mill is run by two passionate foodies: chef Frédéric Molina, a winegrower’s son who has worked all over Europe, and his partner Irene Gordejuela, who originally hails from a small village between the Rioja and the Basque Country. The latter welcomes guests in her charming accent and oversees the wine list which gives pride of place to local and Spanish wines. The couple have a shared philosophy of eco-responsibility: they promote sustainable local agriculture, using hand-picked producers, and even use biodegradable containers. The 4- and 8-course surprise menus are a real delight, as is the excellent local bread made with organic natural sourdough.

name: Les Clefs d'Argent
review: Over the years, this establishment, entirely renovated in a tasteful, low-key contemporary vein, has become a culinary benchmark in Mont de Marsan. It owes its success to Christophe Dupouy, who learned the trade in prestigious houses ranging from Ducasse to Michel Sarran. A committed champion of nature and local produce, his food is a patchwork of influences, mingling southwest France (particularly the Landes) and Benin – the place of birth of his wife Eugénie, who is in charge of the polished, yet casual service. The vibe is friendly and easy-going.

name: La Flibuste
review: This entirely glass-paned restaurant sits in the heart of the Baie des Anges marina, at the foot of an imposing white apartment block that undulates like a sail. The elegant, modern interior, appointed in soothing colours, boasts a splendid terrace commanding a view of the port. The chef rolls out delicious contemporary cuisine that makes the most of hand-picked, seasonal ingredients.

name: Le Prince Noir - Vivien Durand
review: With its castle stables, glass and concrete cube, views of the Pont d’Aquitaine suspension bridge and rock music as a backdrop, this restaurant has definitely caused a stir amid the gastronomic landscapes of the Bordelais. But not as much as the cuisine of Vivien Durand, a chef bursting with original ideas who reinterprets French culinary convention with a keen gastronomic eye. A daring gamble, given his seemingly complete dismantling of tradition, but we have to admit that he has succeeded! Through dishes such as oysters in a matelote sauce, grilled foie gras served with coffee-infused beetroot, and pigeon with carcass jus, his flavours are often dazzling and his ingredients (the vast majority local) showcased to their best. His cooking has a predominant and attractive “raw state” to it which is instinctive and speaks from the heart. Add to this a sincere eco-friendly approach and you have a winning formula.

name: Atmosphères
review: From Lamartine to Stendhal and Maupassant, many authors have waxed lyrical about the atmosphere of Bourget Lake and the view over the Bauges mountains. Chef Alain Perrillat-Mercerot has made this setting the backdrop of his lake-inspired, creative cuisine. Former second of Laurent Petit and also influenced by Ferran Adrià, he enthusiastically defends Savoie. Classically trained, his high-precision way with freshwater fish, local cheeses and wild blueberries is second to none. His signature dishes include duck foie gras, lime juice and gentian or his confit of aubergine with raspberry sorbet and sweet peppers. The enticing wine list celebrates Savoie, among others.

name: Aux Terrasses
review: After a tour of Saint Philibert Abbey, take a break on these enchanting terraces. Bare stone walls and large untreated solid oak tables set the scene inside, flooded in light thanks to floor to ceiling windows. The peaceful garden and the chef’s wife’s attentive service are also outstanding. The chef, Jean-Michel, is an enthusiast, capable of changing his gourmet offering from one table to another in the same evening. He operates entirely according to his whim. His food is thus rich in emotion and establishes a natural complicity with the region, particularly through the use of first-rate local fruit and vegetables and other top-quality ingredients, whilst yielding nothing in terms of high-precision cooking

name: L'Étang du Moulin
review: In summer, you may end up in this cosy yet contemporary inn at the foot of the mountains by a pond, after a daylong hike through the lovely Jura forests, having worked up a healthy appetite. In winter, kick off your snow rackets and admire the Christmas carol picture. The menu features deftly curated, traditional French staples and Jacques Barnachon frequently shines the spotlight on the region, with game in autumn and noble produce (turbot, langoustine, Simmental beef). Jacques is also a mushroom specialist, notably the morel, which is the star of his legendary signature stew. The gourmet restaurant, in which wood dominates, has reduced its seating capacity for the comfort of diners, who now have a view of the kitchen. Insightful wine list.

name: L'Arbre au Soleil
review: We first met Yorann Vandreissche at the Arbre crossroads by the cobblestones of the mythical Paris-Roubaix bicycle race, where he was successful for five years; he is now basking in the sunshine, opposite the marina of Lavandou harbour. With the help of his friend, Didier Anies (Best Craftsman of France 2020), he conjures up food that shines the spotlight on premium quality produce in a menu that displays a distinct fish and seafood slant. For example: a slab of super-fresh seabass with fennel cream, orange slivers and an orange-kumquat condiment… Refreshing, contrasted, skilful: each dish is an ode to fine craftsmanship!

name: Château de la Treyne
review: What a splendid spot! The River Dordogne meanders along the foot of this superb château surrounded by greenery, with its manicured driveway and pretty formal garden. The panoramic view from the terrace will take your breath away. The dining room is everything you'd expect: marble floors, wall hangings, coffered ceiling and carved wooden fireplace. Running the show in the kitchen is Stéphane Andrieux, who took up his first post as chef here. You can look forward to dishes such as Quercy lamb (fillet and chop) flavoured with za'atar, lamb shoulder parcels and Oriental-style vegetables, or an aromatic monkfish broth with curry and saffron.

name: Le Verbois
review: In the Guibet family, the reins of this former hunting lodge (1886) have been passed to Guillaume, who is following in his father's footsteps. His clever and creative cooking looks to the seasons, sometimes draws on Asian traditions (not surprising, since he worked at Kei, in Paris), and is always convincing. One fine ingredient prepared with skill and finesse comes after another, as in the perfectly seasoned fresh ceviche of gilthead sea bream, or the lovely medallion of sweetbread enhanced by a gourmet garnish and intense jus. The same dynamism is apparent in the decor, with its elegant wood, leather and metal fittings.

name: Guy Lassausaie
review: It was in 1984 that Guy Lassausaie first donned his chef's hat in this family-run establishment, founded four generations earlier, in 1906, in a suburb of Lyon that is now studded with Michelin stars (the late Paul Bocuse's Auberge du Pont de Collonges is not far away). Here, this "Meilleur Ouvrier de France" is forging ahead with his winning formula, which involves enthusiastically celebrating local (and, more generally, Gallic) culinary traditions, whilst giving a free rein to inspired recipes. For instance, crisp, line-caught hake, celery purée with pine tree oil, smoked bacon-flavoured meat jus, or a roast rack and confit shoulder of lamb... Comfort food meets consummate craftsmanship.

name: L'Arnsbourg
review: A young couple, Laure and Fabien Mengus, now conduct proceedings at this iconic restaurant. Previously, Fabien's talent had already shone through at Le Cygne, a neighbouring restaurant. Now he shows that he is perfectly at ease here in this culinary institution, building bridges between tradition and modernity – and that applies to the decor as much as to the food. Either ensconced in the lounge or near the bay windows overlooking the forest, you can look forward to varied cuisine that showcases great ingredients, as in the yellowtail confit with hazelnut butter, Daurenki caviar cream and beurre blanc. An exceptional experience.

name: La Table de Patrick Raingeard
review: In the luxurious setting of Hotel Cap Estel, you pass through a marble lobby before descending a few steps to arrive on a terrace with the sea as a backdrop. Head chef Patrick Raingeard's culinary artistry is given free rein here in a fine tribute to the Mediterranean… Trained by Alain Passard and Jacques Maximin, among others, this chef has a profound respect for the quality of his ingredients, and champions fishing that is mindful of preserving marine resources. A thread of inventiveness runs through the set menus (one of which is vegetarian), which are replete with international influences. An idyllic and discreet affair, as is clear from the large gates with an inconspicuous sign that beckons you down a hidden pathway…

name: Mon Plaisir
review: On the Lomont plateau overlooking the Doubs valley, this inviting country house extends a warm welcome at the entrance to the village. The snug interior with a comfortable sitting room and elegant dining room is entirely and generously devoted to fine dining. An admirer of Paul Bocuse and of the great Swiss chef, Freddy Girardet, Christian Pilloud is a classically trained craftsman who is open to new ideas. This meticulous artisan enhances exceptional regional produce (snails, free-range poultry, cheese from Burgundy and Franche-Comté). His seasonal menu features dishes such as pressed foie gras with truffle sweetbread, rock crab with combawa, white pudding of snails or rack of pork in a potato crust.

name: Pantagruel
review: Thirty-something Jason Gouzy, who hails from Rennes, is the epitome of generosity, like Rabelais’ well-known character and the restaurant’s namesake, but he is also subtle. He trained at the Ferrandi School before honing his skills at l’Assiette champenoise, the Bristol and the Baudelaire (Burgundy Hotel). Now alone at the helm, he worked with a fashion designer to create this understated gourmet cocoon, both bourgeois and romantic, in the heart of the lively Sentier district. The theatrically glazed kitchen shines the spotlight on his culinary talent from plays on textures to surf and turf recipes without forgetting smoked ingredients and spices, illustrated by smoked beetroot and sardines or the medley of blue lobster.

name: Maison Kieny
review: This welcoming posthouse (1850) near Mulhouse occupies a handsome Alsace abode in the heart of the village and has been transmitting Alsace’s outstanding culinary traditions for six generations! It is always a pleasure to take a seat in the plush, spacious dining room, strewn with period details, bare stones and beams, wainscoting and stained glass, just as it is always a delight to sample contemporary recipes that add an elegant new spin to Alsace classics, without forgetting the occasional nod to Japan, where one of the chefs spent many years.

name: Le Sérac
review: The discreet entrance opens into a large, bright and elegant room. The chef's cuisine is inspired by the seasons. The sharing menu allows you to indulge in fine cuts of meat or fish. In short, a fresh and colourful selection of carefully prepared dishes, such as calf's head and pan-fried foie gras or a tartlet filled with raw and cooked seasonal vegetables, and, for dessert, a delicious warm soufflé flavoured with passion fruit. Enjoy your meal in a pleasingly modern interior that offers views of the mountains. Attentive service. A lovely place.

name: Château de Courban
review: The stellar journey of Japanese chef Takashi Kinoshita has taken him from Tokyo to the north of Burgundy. In charge of the kitchens of Courban Castle, he unveils his unbridled love of Gallic gourmet traditions and Burgundy’s culinary heritage, in particular, all of which composed with characteristic Japanese precision and clarity. In the next-door garden, he grows Japanese herbs which he then intelligently inserts into his French repertory. All you have to do is take one bite of his melt-in-the-mouth Charolais beef, served with an incredible “sanchollandaise” sauce (hollandaise sauce with sansho) - sheer poetry!

name: Umami
review: Situated in the heart of Petite France with its attractive half-timbered houses, this restaurant combines flavours from near and far. Its name suggests as much: umami is the fifth flavour in Japanese cuisine, alongside sweet, sour, bitter and salty. Chef René Fieger’s travels have had a major influence on his cuisine, which is solidly rooted in classic traditions. This mouth-watering experience is all the more remarkable when you know that the chef is entirely alone in the kitchen, conjuring up dishes to delight his 16 guests. Highlights include slices of Black Angus beef accompanied by a potato pancake, shiitake mushrooms spiced with garlic, superb glazed sand carrots, and a creamy, powerful miso sauce with an almost coffee-like aroma. Unanimous approval for Umami!

name: Dan B.
review: This is certainly one of the most elegant restaurants of the region, in the heart of the charming picturesque village of Ventabren. The location, refurbished at great expense, is strikingly modern: Scandinavian furnishings, mirrors on the ceiling, not to mention the superb panoramic view over the Étang de Berre and the Vallée de l'Arc. With Toulon-born chef Dan Bessoudo in the kitchen, there is plenty to delight diners: the fresh and colourful cuisine is decidedly creative (the set menus are called "wood" and "concrete"), full of contrasts, and prepared using well-chosen local produce. A convivial atmosphere also prevails, making for a highly enjoyable experience.

name: Fontevraud Le Restaurant
review: Saint Lazare Priory is located in the heart of Fontevraud Abbey, one of Europe’s largest monastic complexes. The former’s cloisters have been morphed into a restaurant by designer Patrick Jouin and architect Sanjit Manku, who have staged a marriage between monastic minimalism and untreated materials to set the scene for Thibaut Ruggeri’s cooking. The latter, who hails from Megève and who won the Bocuse d’Or 2013, learnt the trade with iconic culinary names from Michel Guérard to Georges Blanc. A champion of good food and biodynamic farming, local produce takes pride of place (Racan poultry, Anjou pigeon) in a menu that keeps pace with his garden’s production and the moon.

name: La Table des Blot - Auberge du Château
review: This handsome, stylish 17C inn has not lost its opulent dining room, adorned in rustic rafters and a fireplace, and despite the occasional modern feature, one immediately feels at home in the plush, bourgeois setting that is often synonymous with good food. Eminently comfortable in this universe rich in heirlooms, the talented chef follows the seasons to craft creative recipes. His delicious rabbit terrine, a masterclass of textbook culinary technique, or the thick slab of ultra-fresh turbot leave us in no doubt as to the consummate skill and passion of this master chef. The extravagant chocolate medley dessert confirms our intuition beyond any doubt. The slick service further enhances this flawless score, orchestrated by a demanding, enthusiastic chef. Colourful, aromatic and flavoursome food. Treat yourself to an overnight stay by booking one of the pretty country house guestrooms.

name: La Robe
review: The word “robe” in French is used in oenology to describe the colour and appearance of a wine – an apt name for this restaurant in an attractive old house nestled in the centre of Montaigu, given the careful attention it pays to its wine pairings. Chef Xavier Giraudet, who has worked in many Michelin-starred restaurants, demonstrates his skills in the kitchen here, using local, seasonal ingredients (sometimes even from his family’s kitchen garden) and precise cooking methods to create dishes full of flavour and with a distinctly contemporary feel. The restaurant’s old beams and contemporary furnishings and paintings combine to give it a cosy atmosphere.

name: Le Jardin Secret
review: This secret garden is opposite the small railway station. The welcoming restaurant is the den of a youthful team, whose ambitious and seasoned chef, Gilles Leininger, finalist of the Bocuse d’Or selections, crafts market fresh dishes that are perfectly suited to today’s tastebuds: generous slice of porkpie with pickles; slightly rare, seared haunch of tender veal with creamy polenta and Kalamata olives; exquisite tart of wild blueberries from the Vosges. The other secret of this contemporary house is its splendid leafy patio in the back garden.

name: Jérôme Feck
review: This charming town is famous for Saint Étienne Cathedral, Notre-Dame-en-Vaux collegiate church and countless historic sites that bear witness to its illustrious past. In Hôtel d’Angleterre, chef Jérôme Feck aims to perpetuate Champagne’s gourmet traditions and the heritage of the town’s iconic restaurant. Also a pastry chef, he has knocked around from Langres to Reims via Épernay, so the Champagne region has no secret from him… A stellar chef, his flair for sauces and jus, which are gutsy and balanced, is particularly outstanding with special mention for his spicy sweet sauce that so deliciously enhances his pigeon dish. The ingredients are set off by carefully studied flavours that err towards acidic or smoky… More traditional fare in the somewhat incongruously named Les Temps Changent bistro next-door.

name: Radio
review: From the heights of the town, this fine hotel dating from the 1930s broadcasts a non-stop resounding tribute to the electro-magnetic waves and the triode vacuum tube that made possible the invention of the talkies and the wireless. Its trendy Art Deco decor has as much impact as it did on the day it opened, with its mosaic flooring, its decorative wrought iron and marriage of glass and mirrors. In the kitchen, chef Wilfrid Chaplain mixes the frequencies of his native Normandy and of his adopted region, Auvergne, a source of gentle, little-known harmonies. Technically proficient, he creates an ambitious, subtle and delicate cuisine that delights the taste buds: Charolais beef, raviolo of confit beef cheek, red wine aromatic jus; monkfish and watercress jus; mackerel marinated in lime, ash-baked celeriac. As for the platter of Auvergne cheeses, it creates a buzz all of its own.

name: L'Hysope
review: Nicolas Durif is nothing if not creative! He has taken up abode at the end of a pedestrian street in a quaint little village a short drive from La Rochelle. In an interior that smacks of 19C curiosity cabinets, Nicolas unveils his passion for collections, particularly tableware. Born in Alsace, he has named his restaurant after a plant, of which he uses up to 60 in summertime, sourced from France and the rest of the world. He adds discreet touches from his homeland via a spot of mustard, horseradish or cinnamon here and there. His surprise menus in 4-, 6- or 8-courses rich in citrus fruits, spices and Asian notes come highly recommended. Let’s not forget the sumptuous cheese trolley, laden high with a splendid range of perfectly matured cheeses.

name: Les Loges
review: Many Italians settled in Lyon during the Renaissance, attracted by its trade fairs, and these wealthy banking, printing and merchant families built themselves homes such as Les Loges. Beneath a modern glass canopy, you are invited to take a seat in a Florentine courtyard ringed by three floors of galleries to enjoy a candlelit dinner, during which time seems to stand still! The grandson of vegetable growers from the Lyon hillsides, Anthony Bonnet lavishes special attention on his ingredients, particularly the veggies. He works very closely with a network of growers and the seasons and taste are what guide his creativity. His dishes aim to trigger emotions in discerning gourmets thanks to a felicitous chaos of flavours and textures. Fully deserving of our praise…

name: La Table d'Antonio Salvatore au Rampoldi
review: Born in the southern Italian region of Basilicata, chef Antonio Salvatore has travelled incessantly, thanks to his profession: Spain, England and Russia – where he met the new owner of Rampoldi. In the former cigar lounge, he has created a tailor-made setting (only five tables), where he applies himself with unfailing rigour to serving top-notch contemporary Italian cuisine that is both tasty and precise. The sourcing – no surprise here – cannot be faulted: he draws on small-scale producers around Menton and San Remo, but certain produce is also imported from the south of Italy. A few examples of his dishes: bottoni di vitello tonnato; cabri dodici ore; texture di cioccolato… At the brasserie, meanwhile, the menu features a handful of modernised classics.

name: La Table de La Butte
review: Nicolas and Solenne Conraux are the third generation at the head of this hotel restaurant. Nicolas, in charge of the food, admits to a soft spot for the Goulven coast, visible on the horizon, and also for produce from the Brittany countryside. Oysters, lobster, pork, abalone, but also seaweed, vegetables and Brittany cheeses jostle for the leading roles in this star-studded cast of local delicacies. Almost every dish hovers between surf and turf, such as the Monts d’Arée pigeon, sautéed shallots, sage and poultry jus. The bread (baked in the chef’s own bakery) is wickedly good, as are the various Made in Brittany butters (seaweed, fleur de sel, etc). At the summum of fine food!

name: Ô Saveurs
review: In a picturesque hamlet a short drive from Toulouse, David Biasibetti elegantly exalts local produce, whilst boldly enriching his culinary palette with flavours from further afield: duck breast, beetroot and acidic cherries or pollock, coconut and vanilla stock and aubergine caviar with black curry… The know-how of this veteran craftsman can immediately be tasted, including in his decadent chocolate desserts – however, you should know that he did train as a pastry chef and makes no secret of his love of cocoa beans. One thing is certain – savour and flavour await you here.

name: L'Ekrin by Laurent Azoulay
review: L’Ekrin is the perfect fit for this elegant, luxury hotel, offering its guests an intimate setting in which to enjoy an aperitif by the open fire to the sound of quiet piano music in the background. Chef Laurent Azoulay, himself the son of restaurateurs, worked at the Oustau de Baumanière and for chef Pierre Gagnaire before taking the helm here. Skilfully playing with the flavours and traditions of different regions, Azoulay takes guests on a culinary journey through his native Provence and adopted Savoie. He includes the best Mediterranean fish on his menu, alongside ingredients such as pine honey, saffron and snails from the Savoie, as well as vegetables sourced from Éric Roy in Tours. The result is creative and colourful cuisine which is refined and delicate yet also offers some bold combinations.

name: Les Fresques - Hôtel Royal
review: Take a seat in the majestic dining room of this luxury hotel and admire the Art nouveau frescoes by Gustave Jaulmes. The show continues in your plate, as you tuck into dishes, subtly and precisely crafted with premium ingredients: fish from Lake Geneva (arctic char, perch, crayfish...), fillet of Abondance beef smoked in meadow hay, Bresse chicken with foie gras and yellow wine. The modest, enthusiastic chef, Patrice Vander, works only with noble produce, delving freely and frequently into the estate’s cottage garden. The exclusive, sophisticated ambience, like the breathtaking view and the attentive service add the final touch to this fine dining experience rich in gourmet memories.

name: Auberge du Cep
review: This emblematic Beaujolais restaurant, made famous thanks to the talent of chef Chantal Chagny who spent 44 years in the kitchen here, needs no introduction whatsoever! Her successor Aurélien Merot is cut from the same cloth with cuisine that is both generous and full of finesse. He champions the region's terroir beautifully (free-range chicken cooked in Fleurie wine, supreme of chicken stuffed with foie gras, and coq au vin in pastry), along with a particular focus on jus and sauces. Excellent value for money (the lunchtime menu is a bargain!) plus a fine selection of wines from the region.

name: Le Farçon
review: Tucked away in a spruce forest, the resort of La Tania is so close to, and yet so far from Courchevel! Julien Machet’s restaurant pampers and nurtures his guests and nothing leaves his kitchen that hasn’t been endlessly pondered and preened over. This “Savoyard peddler” (his own words) has devised a gourmet banquet that engulfs you in the history of the Duchy of Savoy by way of the best produce from Savoy, the Val d’Aosta, Valais and Piedmont, as far as the Mediterranean. Seasonal vegetables (a nostalgic nod to his grandmother Mado’s vegetable patch) are also invited to play a star role in the gourmet action at an altitude of 1400 metres. Fine dining with our head in the clouds.

name: Récif - Les Roches Rouges
review: A unique and magical place within a waterfront hotel and with a roof terrace looking out over the Mediterranean and the Île d'Or. Chef José Bailly draws inspiration from the book Provençal Cuisine of Popular Tradition by the poet René Jouveau, a major champion of the Occitan language and culture. Everyday ingredients, such as locally caught fish, olive oil produced nearby, ewe's milk cheese and vegetables from the surrounding gardens, go into this cook's modern and delicious, occasionally inventive dishes, which he plates meticulously. Plants and seafood take centre stage: dentex, celeriac and Tamaris mussels with burnt rosemary; pigeon, cucurbit and verbena-infused onions... Poetic and creative.

name: Le Moulin de la Gorce
review: In the 1970’s, Jean Bertranet, a renowned pastry chef from Limoges, transformed this splendid Renaissance watermill, complete with mill pond and romantic grounds, into a hotel-restaurant. The chef, who worked for Vincent Auriol back in the day, turned his business into a genuine institution in the area. Today, his son Pierre, equally enamoured of high-calibre gourmet traditions, adds a new spin to classical recipes with flair and delicacy that respect the produce. The handsome edifice also offers some delightful guestrooms to prolong your stay.

name: Le Refuge des Gourmets
review: In this small village of Upper Savoie that used to be the French capital of raspberries, foodies will find refuge in this low-profile inn. The plush, Belle Époque-inspired restaurant has been entirely refurbished in a contemporary vein. Following in his father’s footsteps, chef Hubert Chanove concocts dishes that cater to modern tastebuds, with creative notes inspired by local produce and wild herbs and flowers picked in the surrounding countryside. His dishes generally revolve around a season or an ingredient (crayfish and fish from Lake Geneva, game, morels, black truffles, etc). The Bistro is open for lunch (Wed-Sat and only by reservation).

name: Domaine du Colombier
review: Built on the ruins of a monastery hermitage in the heart of Provençale Drôme, this proud homestead first woos us with its bare stone walls, vaulted ceilings, vintage furnishings and patio. The cuisine celebrates regional and Mediterranean produce thanks to spot-on recipes: accurate, precise cooking, flavoursome, balanced recipes, all of which in keeping with the establishment’s sustainable development ethos.

name: Côté Cuisine
review: Between the town and the beach, this hotel-restaurant is run with a flair for fine dining by a team of professionals who are passionate about what they do. As for the decor, the large contemporary-style space keeps things simple with its waxed concrete floor, partially open kitchen and shelves filled with cookery books. Having trained at Le Bristol and at Taillevent, the pair at the helm deliver a subtle range of dishes that are replete with flavours, beautifully showcasing impeccable regional produce – at very attractive prices. Tuck in by the fireplace in winter, or on the pleasant terrace in fine weather.

name: Azimut
review: This small restaurant serves traditional fare that deliberately makes no attempt to introduce the latest culinary fads into its cuisine. Ingredients are chosen with the utmost care and showcased with simplicity to the fore, resulting in delicious sauces, dishes cooked to perfection, and a solid and assured gourmet experience. During one of our visits, the menu included escargots en persillade with a creamy Reblochon sauce, and braised fillet of guinea fowl with a meadowsweet sauce. The menu here is complemented by splendid wines from the Jura – the region (more specially the village of Bonlieu) where the restaurant sets up its summer quarters – as well as a good representation from Burgundy. Reasonable prices (for Courchevel) and friendly service add to its appeal.

name: Le Grill
review: On the rooftop of the iconic Hôtel de Paris, Le Grill and its sliding roof, has lost neither its mythical aura nor its breathtaking view! The establishment remains a staunch advocate of high-flying craftsmanship that calls upon excellent and bountiful local produce, adding a whole new dimension to barbecue cooking along the way. Examples include agnolotti piemontesi al plin, slabs of local turbot, rack of lamb with savory or young free-range chicken steeped in Provençal aromas. Other signature dishes include traditional soufflés, such as their mind-blowing hot raspberry and pistachio soufflé.

name: Pastis
review: Wend your way along the narrow Rue Terral to this comfortable and attractively decorated restaurant. It is one of Montpellier’s most popular eateries and you will quickly understand why! It is impossible to resist Daniel Lutrand’s cuisine, which is both inspired and inspiring, refined and delicate, in a bid to showcase the region’s top producers as well as more unusual ingredients (such as barracuda). An example: Candillargues chicken served with artichoke and hazelnuts and a reduced jus. As well as the sensibly priced lunchtime menu, you’re in for a treat with the “surprise” menu which varies depending on the chef’s inspiration. Cheerful, enthusiastic service by manager and business partner Jean-Philippe Vivant. Knockout wine list.

name: Le Manoir du Lys
review: The huge forest of Andaine surrounding this restaurant, depicted by light wooden wainscoting and a leafy terrace, is undoubtedly its ‘raison d’être’. Poised between Maine, Normandy and Brittany, these green lungs nurture and nourish the forest-inspired cooking of chef Franck Quinton. His way with mushrooms is out of this world: roast cèpes in thyme and laurel, girolles sautéed in rosemary, apricots and hazelnuts, chanterelles in cream of foie gras and parmesan or horn of plenty with ham and ciboule onion… If you stay the night, you can even go picking with him! This wholehearted chef is also a champion of local produce and his pigeons, veg and meat all come from within a few dozen kilometres. Delicate, appetising food served in an elegant, peaceful interior: heaven!

name: L'Observatoire du Gabriel
review: Exquisitely located in the central building of Bordeaux’ iconic Place de la Bourse, opposite the water mirror, the observatory is now part of the prestigious Château Angelus and Logis de la Cadène estates. The 18C sitting rooms have been revamped into a comfortable open space, depicted by oak floors, thick carpets, wainscoting and moulded ceilings. Also from Saint Émilion, chef Alexandre Baumard signs a contemporary score with a distinct seafaring slant, without forgoing classical delicacies, at least in spirit: sole in a crunchy mousseline; lightly smoked eel and a medley of onions… 6- or 10-course tasting menus and a stonking 600-bin wine list that errs between Bordeaux and Burgundy. Attention to detail and respect for tradition and creativity.

name: Le Gavrinis
review: The name of this country house is a nod to the nearby island of Gavrinis. The chef, who trained under Pierre Gagnaire, captures the spirit of Brittany as he proudly showcases the produce of this plentiful, vibrant region, with dishes such as his medley of locally grown mushrooms (pleurote, shitake), served roasted, in ravioles, in consommé or his steamed hake in butter served with a white wine, seaweed and Timut pepper sauce. A genuine gourmet halt, further enhanced by the ‘sustainable’ dining room adorned in driftwood and a soft colour scheme of ecru, oatmeal and grey. The exquisite patio, flower-decked in summertime, adds the final flourish.

name: Le Grand Contrôle
review: Alain Ducasse's establishment within the Airelles Hotel is finally open for business after a refurbishment lasting over five years! This luxurious establishment, steeped in history and inextricably linked to the Château de Versailles, mixes theatrical staging and tailored cuisine composed of dishes that seem to be art directed, all of which underscored by Alain Ducasse’s nature-loving DNA. Entrusted to chef Stéphane Duchiron, the food is a master class of technique, expertly cooked and seasoned, flanked by sauces and jus, to bring out the ingredients’ crisp, distinct flavours.

name: Hélène Darroze à Villa La Coste
review: Hélène Darroze fell in love with the Château La Coste, adding her own stamp to a genuine holistic work of art that showcases contemporary art and wine, on the doorstep of Lubéron. Deep in Provence, the chef has chosen to focus on fruit and vegetables: carrots and aubergines from Bruno Cayron, cherries from Florent Lazare and each dish is named after its producer. The result is delicate food, made with exceptional produce that is exquisitely yet simply presented. The menu also features a few of the recipes that have contributed to the success of this world-famous chef from southwest France, such as Gamberoni in tandoori spices or the Darroze Armagnac baba.

name: Jardin des Sens
review: It has been a long wait, but years after the project was first announced, Jacques and Laurent Pourcel have inaugurated their Garden of Senses within the superb 17C walls of the Richer de Belleval Hotel. Beneath imposing ceiling frescoes, we happily re-sampled the culinary skill of the Montpellier twins in which every detail is puzzled and preened over as they finetune Gallic recipes adding their hallmark creativity. Each dish is a culinary masterpiece, illustrated by a frosted tart of Costebelle tomatoes served with herbs, or the mouth-wateringly tender Occitania lamb, spring vegetables and tarragon condiment… Richer de Belleval, botanist and founder of Montpellier’s botanic gardens, would most certainly have appreciated this gourmet score that aims to keep Montpellier at the cutting-edge of France’s culinary scene.

name: La Chabotterie
review: With delicacies such as monkfish cooked in salted butter, radishes and a pearly curry-colza cream, or saddle of lamb rolled in herbs, minty aubergine and jus of roasted tomatoes, MOF chef Benjamin Patissier, who boasts stints with Patrick Henriroux, Pierre Gagnaire and Anne-Sophie Pic, ticks all the boxes: top produce, consummate skill, crisp flavours and artfully dressed plates. His wife, manager and sommelière, adds the final touch to this fine dining portrait, welcoming diners into a contemporary dining room, established in one of the outhouses of Chabotterie Castle.

name: Château de Beaulieu - Christophe Dufossé
review: A new era has begun in Busnes. Marc Meurin has handed over the reins of his establishment to another local lad who has returned home, Christophe Dufossé, former star chef in Metz. The new chapter in the story of Beaulieu Castle bears the hallmark of Christophe’s inimitable talent and enthusiasm. A self-avowed champion of organic, self-sufficient and sustainable cooking, vegetables loom large on the menu, without forgetting fresh fish from the North Sea. Delicious surprises galore!

name: Les Cèdres
review: Some establishments have chosen to shy away from media hype and les Cèdres is in that category. Betwixt Romans and Tain-l’Hermitage in Drôme, venture over the threshold of this restaurant, shaded by cedars and devoted to nature, and sample the work of the Bertrand brothers: Jacques in the kitchen and Jean-Paul in the dining room. Since 1988, they have lavished time, humility and talent on developing their enterprise. As Gallic as Gauloises and Jacques Tati, the menu focuses on flavour rather than fancy technique. The authentic warm welcome adds the final flourish to this hospitable establishment.

name: Prairial
review: The name means relating to prairies or meadows and it is definitely emblematic of the decorative and culinary approach of this Presqu’île restaurant, between Place Bellecour and les Terreaux. The Scandinavian-inspired interior sports light wood, bare stone and green walls. Gaëtan Gentil, ex-Agapé Substance (Paris), pays tribute to every form of meadow: fruit, herbs, vegetables and also cattle and fish from the region’s lakes and rivers. For example, suckling veal smoked in juniper and a purée of parsnip and lemon… Boldly creative cuisine in the zeitgeist, delicate and gutsy at the same time.

name: La Palmeraie - Château de Valmer
review: Poised between the sea, vineyards and orchards, this hotel-restaurant, a family-owned bastide dating from the early 20C, is tucked away in a lush garden dotted with hundred-year-old palm and magnolia trees. It is a superb resource, as is the Mediterranean vegetable garden where courgettes, aubergines, tomatoes, herbs and artichokes grow. Served in the garden or on the terrace shaded by a pergola, the cuisine proposed by Alexandre Fabris (formerly at La Signoria, in Calvi) skilfully combines an array of textures and flavours.

name: Au Crocodile
review: The stuffed crocodile in the window, a souvenir brought back from Egypt by a Napoleonic soldier, underlines the historic character of this iconic Strasbourg establishment, which boasted 3 stars under chef Émile Jung. Following a top to toe refurbishment that has preserved the spirit of the venue, it shines brightly on the culinary scene of Strasbourg. Chef Romain Brillat, former second of Gilles Goujon and a distant relative of Brillat-Savarin, a famous French gourmet, has achieved a balance between classicism and sophistication. Examples include his inventive take on scallops (including the roe and muscle) with black truffles or the more traditional slab of turbot in a crust of breadcrumbs, lemon and herbs. The polished tableside service is a pleasure to behold.

name: Le Vivier
review: This is a beautiful restaurant in every sense: in the capital of antique dealers, its terrace overlooking the green banks of the River Sorgue is a feast for the eyes. Diners are in safe hands with proprietor Patrick Fischnaller, who for a long time worked as a manager in top-class establishments in London. At his side, the young chef Romain Gandolphe, who has previously worked with Thierry Marx and Philippe Labbé, carefully blends flavours and textures to propose a selection of delicate, subtle dishes. Warm and cosy decor in the modern dining area as well as highly attentive service.

name: Les Agitateurs
review: These agitators, who have set up shop behind the port of Nice, are far from the hot air breed, indeed the threesome of partners overflows with talent! Chef Samuel Victori (former second chef at Passage 53) and his partner painstakingly and skilfully craft dishes rich in texture, flawlessly cooked and subtly seasoned. Local suppliers take the limelight: baker, independent fishermen, market gardener, breeder, potter and florist. Their mentor is Michel Troisgros, and their concept is original, enthusiastic, amusing, disruptive food, served in a lively, buzzy vibe. Attentive, efficient service. There is also a grocery store-cum-delicatessen to take goodies home and the lunchtime menu is a steal. We warrant that this is only the beginning of the story.

name: La Madeleine
review: Patrick Gauthier’s restaurant overlooks the River Yonne at the tip of an island shaped like the bow of a ship. In a setting where you’d be forgiven for thinking that you weren’t in the centre of a town, the interior design is inspired by his many trips to Scandinavia and Asia. Defining himself as a “cook first and foremost”, this chef, who is highly passionate about his work, continues to personally present guests with his everyday specials based on daily availability and deliveries. A great fan of markets and fish and seafood, he creates authentic, spirited cuisine full of flavour such as carpaccio of amberjack with seasonal vegetables; delicately cooked John Dory with a citrus beurre blanc; and black Bigorre pork with a full-flavoured jus and garlic confit. Plus, not just one but four cheese trolleys and an excellent wine list!

name: Frédéric Doucet
review: Frédéric Doucet's restaurant is a creative and exciting new take on established ideas of terroir and tradition. The son of bistro owners, he was born into the business, and cut his teeth in the kitchens of the greatest chefs, from Pierre Orsi to Paul Bocuse via the prestigious La Maison Troisgros. Nestled in the heart of a village with pointed towers and old weathered roofs, the chef breaks it down for diners: nothing but the finest ingredients from Saône-et-Loire, beef, goat's cheese or snails, prepared by means of rigorously applied classic techniques that do not exclude flashes of inspiration. Take, for example, the frogs' legs glazed in wild garlic served with colours of the local meadows or the exceptional fillet of Charolais beef, matured and infused with Burgundy whisky. Such delights are difficult to resist, as are the spa and very appealing guestrooms.

name: La Vieille Tour
review: The contemporary interior, which makes ample use of the light and materials such as glass and wenge wood, is admirably paired with the delicate, seafood menu of this country house opposite the estuary. An idyllic setting to sample deftly crafted, first-rate ingredients. Chef Nicolas Adam is not content with awakening your tastebuds, he is also the proud creator of a bakery and of the Rock’n Toques festival that takes place once a year, combining music and quality street food. The glazed wine cellar boasts some 350 references.

name: Le Figuier de Saint-Esprit
review: Straddling the ramparts of the old town, between the Musée Picasso and the Marché Provençal, this family-run country house is redolent of Provence. The fig tree adorning the patio is only the start. This is the family stronghold of Christian Morisset, whose curly moustache has almost become part of the heritage of Antibes. With his wife holding the fort in the restaurant, and assisted in the kitchen by his sons, the chef likes to cook with beautiful produce that he selects each week at the markets. The only concession to modernity is a screen that live broadcasts the action in the kitchen. His cuttlefish cannelloni with squid ink, shellfish jus, fresh basil leaves and his saddle of lamb cooked in Vallauris clay have become real signature dishes.

name: Les Plaisirs Gourmands
review: Do as the locals do and make a beeline for this discreet restaurant with its simple, freshly renovated decor to meet a remarkable couple – Guillaume Scheer in the kitchen and his partner, Charlotte Gate, the personification of smiling efficiency front of house. Guillaume, who has worked at the Pavillon Ledoyen in Paris and 1741 in Strasbourg, is fully versed in the pleasures of the palate, creating superb sauces and jus, cooking fish to perfection, and focusing on the freshest ingredients. His Provençal asparagus with truffle, an exquisite turmeric sabayon, and lime is a particular highlight.

Opposite the Palais Rohan, a classical masterpiece completed in 1741, this venerable restaurant sports a romantic look, both intimate and elegant, thanks to a chic baroque décor and soft lighting. The chef, Jérémy Page, whose CV includes 15 years in the Joël Robuchon group between Paris and London, signs delicate, precise recipes, strewn with passing nods to Alsace. His inspiration comes to the forefront in sauces and jus, such as rockfish bisque with lightly seared red mullet or breast of squab with a punchy jus deglazed with Nusswasser liqueur. Fine food paired with a splendid selection of Alsace wines (grands crus, organic, etc).

name: Apicius
review: Bang in the city centre, on the first floor of Saint Pierre Market, this swanky restaurant enjoys a lofty location. The stylish venue sports a series of beautifully appointed contemporary dining rooms and exquisite tableware. Chef Arkadiusz Zuchmanski, of Polish extraction, decided to move to France to fortify a vocation that took root in the kitchen of his forebears. He confesses an unbridled passion for noble ingredients and for Auvergne, which reminds him of the landscapes of his home city, Drzewica. The focus is on visually striking plating and honest, simply crafted ingredients, such as foie gras with hand-picked wild pepper or sautéed sweetbread with truffle parsnip.

name: Lamartine
review: Between Aix-les-Bains and Chambéry, facing the lake so dear to Lamartine, this restaurant, founded in 1964, is a local institution and a regional benchmark. A father and son team, Pierre and Valentin, are at the helm. Freshwater fish from the lake is treated with the respect that befits a Savoie restaurant, while aromatic herbs straight from the cottage garden and picked during forays into the countryside are naturally incorporated into traditional recipes that are firmly anchored in this mountain and lake environment, albeit with a new spin. Swish service and an elegant, romantic setting sign the final stanza of this enticing ode.

name: Les Rosiers
review: With such a surname, the Rosiers could well have specialised in roses rather than food. Instead of which, the first woman Best Craftsperson of France (in 2007), assisted by her spouse, conjures up enticingly unencumbered food. Even though their establishment has retained its characteristic Basque exterior, the interior sports a resolutely modern vibe, with stripped back walls, wooden floors and round designer-inspired tables. Our virtuoso never flaunts her technique, seeking rather to coax the taste and flavour out of first-class local produce, wild fish and shrimps and farm-reared poultry and squab, in particular. Andrée Rosier also enjoys jazzing up her dishes with the occasional dash of exoticism: from lemongrass and nori seaweed to ginger and lemon preserves. The Rosiers also manage two restaurants in Japan, which may well explain this predilection…

name: Le Restaurant des Rois - La Réserve de Beaulieu
review: One of the most opulent luxury hotels of the French Riviera, dating from 1880 and later extended in a Renaissance Florentine style, has been playing host to monarchs and Hollywood stars since 1900. Dining on the terrace facing the Mediterranean is a magical experience. The food is now conjured up by chef Julien Roucheteau, straight from Paris (Table du Lancaster, Scène Thélème). While remaining loyal to the establishment’s heritage, he is already adding his inimitable hallmark, depicted by graphic presentations and consummate craftsmanship with a specific theme for each dish: seafood, smoked, spicy, acidic, refreshing…

name: Pierre
review: In the southernmost town of Burgundy, this low-profile house in a pedestrian street is home to a benchmark of local gastronomy. The traditional architecture (bare beams and stonework and an old fireplace) is enhanced by contemporary touches. Since 1991, Christian Gaulin has been celebrating the classical union of regional produce and modern techniques. Whenever he can, this virtuoso technician sings a subtle ode to Bresse and Burgundy. Foodies can decadently indulge in tender Bresse poultry, melt-in-the-mouth foie gras, textbook-perfect quenelles of pike, a juicy Charolais tournedos steak and a Grand Marnier soufflé of head-spinning perfection. A believer in fine produce before all else, the chef cooks what he himself likes to eat – to our joy!

name: Castel Marie-Louise
review: This opulent early 20C manor house, on the Atlantic seaboard, offers the choice of dining in a revamped Belle Époque interior strewn with opulent bronze statues and silky curtains, the work of none other than Jacques Garcia, or on the alfresco patio shaded by pine trees.
