The modern menu of chef Éric Mignard, inspired by seasonal availability (fish and hand gathered shellfish from the islet of Batz, seaweed from Croisic), serenely navigates between classicism (illustrated by his crisp langoustine biscuit) and high-flying creativity (depicted by his knock-out association of cucumber and kiwi – refreshing and suave). Bang on food with a purpose.

name: Les Tables de Gaspard
review: An excellent time is to be had at this restaurant housed in a converted vaulted stable. Dating from the 16C, it is full of character, its iron and stone features blending harmoniously. After many years spent in Bora Bora, Virginie Blampoix and Sébastien Corniau returned to France to continue their culinary adventure. Chef Corniau stylishly fetes noble produce (scallops fished by divers, for example) in perfectly cooked dishes with well-balanced flavours. The food is generous, and the prices quite reasonable. Unsurprisingly, the formule is an attractive option and the restaurant is often fully booked (remember to reserve!). Three well-kept guestrooms available.

name: Le Relais des Moines
review: Nestling amid the greenery, this gorgeous 16C bastide looks out over the Massif des Maures and the picturesque village of Arc-sur-Argens. The son of restaurateurs from the South-West, Sébastien Sanjou has set up shop in the Var, where his early endeavours were supported by Jacques Maximin and Alain Ducasse. This native of Tarbes is savvily making the Mediterranean terroir his own, cultivating, for example, an exceptional partnership with market gardener Philippe Auda. Wonderfully ripe and juicy tomatoes, served with a basil sorbet and burrata and seasoned with olive oil and Baume de Bouteville vinegar, make for a fantastically sunny starter. This is typical of his cuisine: colourful and imaginative, with, at the heart of each dish, a wonderful ingredient that has been carefully prepared with respect for its original flavour.

name: Quai des Saveurs
review: Frédéric Sandrini invites us to hop on a train, get off at Hagondange station and make our way opposite to this “platform of flavour”. Your tastebuds will be delighted by the craftsmanship of this chef who believes in heritage and transmission and who gleefully disrupts local gourmet traditions. His imaginative, modern fare is constantly evolving, generously calling upon high-calibre ingredients, in particular abalone, hand-harvested by divers in the Bay of St Brieuc, fish from Guilvinec, poultry from Bresse and a cheese platter concocted by Hervé Mons. Meals are served in a pleasant, spacious, contemporary interior. Two surprise menus.

name: En Pleine Nature
review: Owner-chef Sylvain Joffre welcomes guests to this picturesque house by a roundabout. Sylvain is conscientious, serious and the antithesis of big headed. His goal is simple: serve first-rate food at prices that make sense. Bravo! Drawing from a list of local producers as long as his arm, he skilfully crafts generous recipes, frequently renewing his menu with dishes that reflect the seasons. In terms of the décor, the tasteful focus is low-key with the bonus of a leafy alfresco area shaded by parasols – ideal to enjoy the mild climate of Toulouse all year round without getting sunstroke! Highly committed to the environment, the chef has opened a shop next door that sells pastries, brioche and bread made with organic flour.

name: Le Corot
review: In the manner of the artist Corot, who painted the next-door ponds, the cooking of youthful Rémi Chambard is also inspired by nature. This high-flying technician, who boasts stints in exclusive establishments such as Biarritz’ Hôtel du Palais and the Sources de Caudalie near Bordeaux, is particularly enamoured of plants, but not just any plant: twice a week, he makes the most of what he calls his “urban harvest” in the cottage garden of the former king of France in Versailles! “Fresh, light and attractive” best define his work, presented during a single set menu. A fine dining experience in a fully refurbished, fashionably pared down and stylish interior, as befits the food.

name: Haut Bonheur de la Table
review: Situated between Steenvoorde and Saint-Omer in the heart of Flanders, Cassel is a beautifully kept little village built in brick and perched on the hill of the same name. with this small village comes a small restaurant: the tiny Haut Bonheur de la Table, housed in a beautiful 18C residence, has space for just twenty guests and is run by its owners who are passionate about fine cuisine. Here, Eugène Hobraiche carefully crafts contemporary cuisine that goes hand-in-hand with seasonal produce, using local fruit and vegetables in his dishes, as well as fish from the auction at Dunkirk. Grilled wild turbot with artichoke, samphire and coriander sauce, and grilled tuna with tomato water and green tomato sorbet are just two of the fish specialities on the menu.

name: L'Auberge de Saint-Rémy-de-Provence - Fanny Rey & Jonathan Wahid
review: Chef Fanny Rey is at the head of this grand old lady, rolling out flavoursome, market fresh fare with a soft spot for local Alpilles producers. By her side, Jonathan Wahid, her partner, a skilled pastry chef and former French dessert champion, cannot be rivalled for his knack with juicy southern ingredients drenched in sunshine, such as figs. The food is served in a designer interior, sporting a “wavy” white ceiling and bare stone walls.

name: L'Aparté
review: Situated in a modern district on the outskirts of Toulouse near the motorway to Albi, this old toulousaine-style house is the stomping ground of a talented chef whose skilfully prepared creations range from classic to modern. Don’t miss his vegetable casserole with truffles, or the game that he prepares in season – his hare “à la royale” is highly recommended! There’s a pleasant atmosphere here, whether you choose the dining room or the attractive patio-terrace shaded by a beautiful linden tree. Attentive service.

name: La Table de Philippe Girardon
review: The proud recipient of a Michelin star for more than 25 years, this restaurant shows no sign of becoming stale or routine in its dishes. Impeccable ingredients with a focus on the local region are the basis here for carefully prepared classic cuisine. This elegant 18C building nestling in 3ha of grounds was once a holiday residence for the bishops of Lyon. It now provides an inviting backdrop for dishes such as mi-cuit duck foie gras macerated in sake wine, and fillet of Limousin veal served with a savory-flavoured jus. A pleasant address offering good value for money.

name: La Closerie
review: This former post office in the Luberon is an ode to Provence where you can choose between the elegant and modern dining room or the small panoramic terrace. Having sourced his ingredients from local producers, Marseille-born chef Olivier Alemany (trained by Jacques Chibois, in particular) enchants guests with traditional cuisine enhanced by Provence’s superb sun-blessed natural bounty with its incomparable freshness. Meanwhile, in the dining room, his wife Delphine provides attentive and meticulous service. To ease their post-meal digestion, sated guests can explore the narrow streets up to the church and château of the charming village of Ansouis.

name: La Huchette
review: After 19 years spent at La Marelle, near Bourg-en-Bresse, Sandra and Didier Goiffon moved to this 1950s inn on the outskirts of Mâcon. It has been beautifully restored and retains its historical character; be sure to admire the hunting frescoes from the old Alsace Zuber manufactory. Here, the chef serves cuisine in his own image: fun and spontaneous, it is based on choice ingredients (market gardeners from the Saône valley, for example), with just the right amount of creativity. In other words, an enjoyable interlude, which you can even extend by reserving one of the comfortable guestrooms.

name: Moulin de la Tardoire
review: Teeming with history, this 16C forge was converted into a flour mill in 1854 and later into an olive oil mill. It now houses a charmingly bucolic restaurant situated by the river and surrounded by greenery. Here, chef Matthieu Brudo serves up seasonal cuisine with a focus on local ingredients, including snails from the Charente, trout from Magnac, squab and duck breast from Nontron, and other top-quality meats which he buys whole from small producers in the local area. Refined, well-crafted and carefully presented dishes that meet with our approval!

name: Le Pavé d'Auge
review: Situated between Caen and Lisieux in the heart of the Pays d’Auge, Beuvron-en-Auge is emblematic of Normandy with its 17C-18C half-timbered houses, manor houses, apple orchards and gardens decked in flowers come summertime. The restaurant, which occupies the village’s former covered market, sports an olde worlde feel inside and out. Chef Adrien Haye, former second here, reverently respects the seasons: oysters from Saint-Vaast, lobster from Carteret, John Dory, as well as foie gras, veal sweetbread, tripe and andouille sausage with baked apples. The quintessence of Normandy!

name: Moulin de Rosmadec
review: The first restaurant to be awarded a star in the Finistère (back in 1993!), the Moulin de Rosmadec is a gourmet benchmark of Brittany; it also enjoys a magical location with its alfresco terrace by the River Aven. Supervised by chef Christian Le Squer, the food sings the praises of Brittany’s country produce (sarrazin wheat, buttermilk, Plougastel strawberries) and local seafood (spider crab, langoustine, lobster). Enticingly presented, subtle sauces and reductions and delicate flavours. A high-flying culinary score, flanked by a splendid wine list.

name: Maison Decoret
review: This 19C building makes a bold visual statement with its large, transparent, cube-shaped conservatory. The decor was chosen by chef Jacques Decoret, who also brings his aesthetic sensibility and finesse to the plate. He has mastered his craft, selecting fine ingredients and steering clear of any ostentation (for instance, his duck foie gras from the Landes, pumpkin and orange). Bags of personality are to be found in the amuse-bouches and the meadowsweet sauce. If you wish to extend your stay, there are a few guesthouse-style rooms designed along the same contemporary lines as the rest of the property.

name: Les Oliviers
review: In Renécros Bay, it is a pleasure to enter this bright, contemporary restaurant which commands an unrivalled view of the Mediterranean. This stylishly elegant backdrop is the lair of energetic Jérémy Czaplicki, born in Toulouse and who worked for many years in Paris with Jean-François Rouquette and afterwards at the Château de Berne in Var. In the evenings (only!), he crafts colourful, flavoursome Mediterranean and Provençal cuisine. Seafood ingredients often top the bill of the three menus. In the daytime, the Bistro Lumière is open for lunch and tea. Inviting guestrooms.

name: Vieux Pont
review: Nestling in a leafy green site and dominated by its castle, the quaint village of Belcastel rises up on the right bank of the Aveyron River. Work up an appetite by strolling along its cobbled streets and up and down its steep paths! Quietly feeding hungry travellers is something of a tradition in this family-owned business opened by the grandparents of sisters Nicole and Michèle Fagegaltier, now at the helm. The enticing menu naturally highlights local delicacies such as lamb and veal from Aveyron and Ségala, Aubrac beef, Bigorre black pig and sweet onions from Cévennes, without forgetting fish and farmer cheeses. Stock of caramelised sweet onions, Laguiole braised cabbage, or Greffeuille lamb sweetbread, sorrel-flavoured mayonnaise and grilled leeks. This old bridge believes in food that satisfies the soul and the appetite!

name: Le Saint Placide
review: Located away from St-Malo’s tourist hordes in a district popular with locals, this attractive contemporary restaurant features a decor of organic curves, Fornasetti tableware, hanging lamps by Tom Dixon etc. Luc Mobihan, the chef at the helm, is a magician when working with fish, seafood and local vegetables, having spent time at the Château de la Chenevière in Port-en-Bessin and at the Amphitryon in Lorient, where he was the second in command to Jean-Paul Abadie. At Le St-Placide he conjures up enticing cuisine in keeping with the times, as showcased in dishes such as red mullet with crabmeat, Brussel sprouts and Breton saffron. Meanwhile, his wife Isabelle gives full rein to her love of the arts (and the table) and her passion for fine wine (Champagne, Loire, Burgundy etc). Attentive service.

name: Côté Jardin
review: On the Left Bank of the Loire on the road to Bourges, the fresh breeze comes as much from the river as from the stringently selected ingredients! Chef Arnaud Billard has a weak spot for seafood, which he sources twice a week from a fish wholesaler in Normandy: John Dory, hake, wild shrimps and many others. On the garden side, the ingredients come from a local grower who boasts over 300 varieties of vegetables. In the kitchen, this lad from Maubeuge signs flavoursome, market fresh cuisine brimming with subtle associations, such as wild turbot with spinach, einkorn and grassy jus. Suave, delicate dishes that satisfy both our eye and our appetite.

name: Toya
review: Tōya is a famous volcanic lake in northern Japan, in the heart of the Shikotsu-Tōya nature reserve. In the eyes of youthful globetrotting chef, Loïc Villemin, this region is something of a gastronomic Eden where wild fish, plants and herbs thrive and high-quality fruit and vegetables are grown. All of which has inspired this Zen-styled restaurant (overlooking a golf course) with a hip ‘natural’ slant! Our aspiring Buddhist monk chef has spent retreats in the top gourmet sanctuaries of France, notably with Jean-Georges Klein, Nicolas Le Bec, Bernard Loiseau and Arnaud Lallement. His love of fine produce is particularly visible in the mystery, sometimes vegetarian, menu. Cutting-edge skill and creativity depicted by his punchy multi-layered arctic char and celery with pike roe – a must-taste dish!

name: Kasbür
review: Founded in 1932, Kasbür has been linked to the Kieffer family for three generations. This restaurant on the outskirts of Saverne owes its name to the great-grandfather of the family, a farmer who made his cheeses here. His great-grandson, Yves Kieffer, has brought this beautiful building into the modern era with its semi-circular dining room opening onto the magnificent Alsace countryside. Having worked in the kitchen of La Tour d'Argent and Marc Meneau's restaurant in Vézelay, the chef has returned, driven by his strong sense of heritage and unwavering standards. He proposes high-quality, seasonal produce, a case in point being his scallops, medley of cauliflower and Aquitaine caviar.

name: Le Jardin des Plumes
review: A short walk from Claude Monet’s house, this half-timbered Anglo-Norman 1912 edifice extends an invitation to relax and enjoy the good things of life. The tasteful interior mixes Art deco features (worn blue and white floor tiles, peacock blue walls) with 1960’s white leather armchairs and glass and rosewood tables, while the lovely patio is flanked by a delightful, wooded garden. Normandy born chef, David Gallienne, who trained at the Manoir du Lys, continues to work with some of his former suppliers from Orne and Dieppe fishermen, whilst sourcing new ones. His inventive recipes feature unorthodox flavours and textures. The chef has opened a nearby guesthouse for overnight stays and a delicatessen in Vernon.

name: Le Passe Temps
review: Gallic cuisine does not appeal only to Japanese chefs: youthful Korean chef, Younghoon Lee, fell in love with the food of Molière in a French restaurant of Seoul. After honing his skills in the Paul Bocuse Institute and at Lasserre, he and his wife have opened their own establishment in the Brotteaux district of Lyon. Decorated in a minimalist vein, the dining area is boldly modern with a light wooden floor and a theatrically glazed wine cellar. Endowed with an acute sense of presentation and taste, he adds a new spin to French tradition, tossing in a few subtle Korean touches: tartare of melt-in-the-mouth red tuna with beetroot and fresh cream; slow-baked medallion of monkfish with white kimchi sauce. Lee’s vision of cooking is enthusiastic and wholehearted.

name: Le Grand Cerf
review: At the foot of the Montagne de Reims and on the road to Épernay, this imposing inn unabashedly brandishes its opulent style. Come evening, the elegant dining space done out in pale wood takes on a romantic air – the perfect setting for fine classic French cuisine delivered by head chef Dominique Giraudeau, who shone for many years in the kitchens of Gérard Boyer at Les Crayères. There he acquired a taste for noble produce, from wild John Dory to free-range milk-fed veal, as well as game, lobster, and truffles, to which a whole set menu is dedicated in season. Superb list of wines from the Champagne region.

name: La Sommelière
review: Both originally from Japan, owner and sommelier Shoko Hasegawa and chef Takafumi Kikuchi honed their skills at the renowned Au 14 Février in Saint-Valentin (Indre). Now, in this Lilliputian restaurant that seats only a handful of diners in the heart of historic Lyon, Ms Hasegawa is responsible for the attentive front of house, while the chef applies his almost surgical precision to distinctive and seasonal recipes: shellfish, tomato and cheese consommé; smoked duck foie gras and sweetcorn; “acqua pazza”-style line-caught croaker… The experience is enhanced by inspired wine-food pairings and prices that make sense. Be sure to book: tables here are snapped up fast!

name: Saisons
review: In the heart of Marseille, a stone’s throw from Place Castellane, this contemporary venue is the exuberant project of a duo of pros, both local lads. Chef Julien Diaz, who honed his talents in London and Corsica, works with sommelier Guillaume Bonneaud. Seating for thirty, a pared-down interior, depicted by wood, iron and untreated materials, spot on food-wine pairings and creative cuisine that bears witness to the establishment’s ethos, particularly in terms of seasonal and locally sourced ingredients from the Mediterranean and Corsica. The lunchtime menu is a bargain.

name: Le Cap
review: Make a beeline for the legendary Grand-Hôtel du Cap Ferrat, which dates from the early 20C. The hotel stands at the end of an enchanting peninsula facing the Mediterranean, hidden from view by lush gardens popular with guests from around the world. Here, you have a choice between the stunning dining room or the attractive terrace shaded by huge Aleppo pines. At the helm in the kitchen, chef Yoric Tièche (originally from Aix-en-Provence) takes his inspiration from Provence’s culinary history, creating superb dishes from his Mediterranean ingredients. Highlights include sardines, smoked haddock cream, potatoes and caviar; blue lobster with mint, aubergine and ras-el-hanout yoghurt; and marinated lisette (small mackerel) with fennel cream and rock fish soup.

name: Auberge au Bœuf
review: You can’t help but fall under the spell of this Alsace inn with its church pews, wood-panelled walls, regional furniture and small museum dedicated to Goethe (the village was once the setting for a love affair between this famous German writer and the daughter of the local pastor). The chef here – the fourth generation of the same family – serves delicate, refined seasonal cuisine which is skilfully crafted from carefully selected ingredients. He has created a small network of direct suppliers who provide him with outstanding fish from Plouguerneau, which he transforms into delicious dishes such as fresh brill with a variety of white asparagus. There’s also a Stammtisch, a “table d’hôtes” where regional specialities are served, plus four luxury guestroom-suites.

name: Le Pot d'Étain
review: A few minutes from Bartholdi's Lion de Belfort, Le Pot d'Étain is packed with gourmet delights, thanks to a talented chef, Philippe Zeiger, who has made his restaurant an absolute must for anyone who loves good food. Here, he showcases generous and tasty French cuisine that is prepared using superb seasonal ingredients (scallops, hare à la royale, truffles), such as the scallops with herring roe, lardo di Colonnata and vin jaune sauce, or back of venison, civet sauce, winter roots. These are dishes that really deliver what diners want! Also worth a mention: the wine by the glass is served from magnums (a rare treat).

name: Auberge Pom'Poire
review: Surrounded by apple and pear orchards, the aptly named Pom’Poire Inn was founded by a couple of former arborists in the Loire Valley. It is now in the competent hands of their son, Bastien Gillet, and his partner. Appetising, colourful, juicy fruit could well be what best symbolises Bastien’s cooking. Vibrant, finely judged, subtle (both the aromas and the textures): his dishes, laden high with fine fresh produce (fish, meat, fruit and vegetables) from local Loire farmers, overflow with flavour. There is much to recommend this scrumptious establishment, so why not take a bite?

name: La Renaissance
review: In the little town of Argentan, the modern lines of the contemporary parallelepiped extension of La Renaissance cannot be missed. Local boy, Arnaud Viel, is at home here, as is his neighbour, philosopher Michel Onfray, who prefaces the restaurant’s menu. Normandy takes pride of place with freshly sourced seafood from Carteret lobster to Veules-les-Roses oysters, without forgetting monkfish from Port-en-Bessin or Créances carrots and foie gras from Auge. Save room for the decadent dessert trolley laden high with miniature delights (not a common occurrence today!) and for the chef’s signature dessert: a sphere of multifaceted textures…

name: Pavyllon, un restaurant de Yannick Alléno, Monte-Carlo
review: Yannick Alleno’s gourmet counter food, after finding favour with Parisian city slickers, has set up shop in the Hermitage Hotel in Monte Carlo with the same sure-fire recipes. Namely, gourmet fare that boldly asserts a distinctive unorthodox culinary identity. The open kitchen faces the terrace and the impressive tasting counter in metallic wood, in an elegant blue colour scheme that echoes the nearby sea. In terms of food, the accent is on the seasons and wellbeing, anchored in plants, seafood and low-sugar desserts. In fine weather, meals are served on the Mediterranean garden patio commanding a view of the deep blue sea as a bonus.

name: Maison Claude Darroze
review: At this family-run hotel they are a dab hand at perpetuating traditions: you can enjoy classic cuisine, strewn with nods to Southwest France and washed down with a fine Bordeaux (600 appellations). The produce is treated with great care – for example, pigeon from Mr Duleau's, lamprey cooked with Sauternes, and line-caught John Dory confit with marrow) – and there is flavour and generosity in the dishes. Game lovers will appreciate the "hunting" menu (in season). To be savoured either in the modern interior or, in the summer months, on the pleasant terrace sheltered by plane trees. For those who would like to extend their stay beyond dinner, there are some pretty guestrooms available.

name: Auberge Saint-Laurent
review: This elegant and authentic 18C coaching inn with a long, flower-filled and welcoming façade is a local family-owned institution, appreciated as much by its regulars as it is by the many tourists on their way across Europe. They all sing the praises of the service and keen sense of hospitality, the snug and appealing guestrooms, and, of course, the excellent cuisine served here. Chef Laurent Arbeit presides over the kitchen, having learned his craft under Haeberlin and Ducasse. A proprietor who is very much in tune with the times, his delicate and harmonious cuisine is replete with well-balanced flavours. A resounding success.

name: L'O des Vignes
review: This stone building in the Mâconnais region is surrounded by a landscape of vineyards that extend as far as the Roche de Solutré. It is now the culinary fiefdom of a true Burgundian, Sébastien Chambru, who enjoyed an impressive spell at Le Moulin de Mougins, before heading off to Tokyo, where he was enthralled by the respect that Japanese chefs give to their ingredients. The author of several cookery books, he now conjures up his delicately creative cuisine here in Fuissé, applying his customary finesse and precision and an inspiration that changes in line with seasonal ingredients. Choose from a blackboard of more informal dishes and wines by the glass in the small adjoining wine bar. In fine weather, why not eat out on the pleasant patio-terrace?

name: L'Oustalet
review: In this wine-producing village, this pretty stone house, with a terrace that looks on to a small square dotted with old plane trees, provides the attractive backdrop for pleasing cuisine featuring supremely fresh ingredients, delicious and refined recipes, and astute combinations of flavours on a single menu served in several stages. Laurent Deconinck, the owner-chef, is a master at satisfying guests’ tastebuds, accompanied by efficient and flowing service, and a cellar full of wonderful surprises.

name: La Table de Chaintré
review: This quintessential country house, tucked away in a picturesque village in the heart of the Pouilly-Fuissé vineyards, is the brainchild of a friendly, industrious young couple. He scours the local markets for fine (organic whenever possible) produce, which he unveils in cleverly crafted dishes. For example, green asparagus with Brittany sardines, Normandy lobster with foaming butter, or a slice of farm-reared veal with multicoloured radishes and violet broccoli… The food is naturally enough washed down with a fine selection of Burgundy and Beaujolais tipples. The set menu changes weekly – all the more reason to return regularly!

name: Gordon Ramsay au Trianon
review:
Opened in 1910 on the edge of the palace grounds, the Trianon Palace hotel makes its authoritative presence felt by walkers who get close to it. A perfect place to host the work – and fiery character! – of Gordon Ramsay, already a three-starred chef in London.
The Scottish chef oversees the regular updating of the menu, which is implemented day to day by chef Frédéric Larquemin. It is a celebration of fantastic produce, taking a more simple and purposeful approach to the dishes. Well-managed creativity, appealing flavours… It all makes for a most enjoyable experience, not least thanks to a location that fits the bill: an elegant and luminous baroque dining space, with bay windows looking directly out onto the grounds.

name: L'Empreinte
review: A friendly young couple, who has worked in some of the region's finest restaurants, crafts dishes in keeping with the zeitgeist, which draw on their joint culinary heritage: respectively, Auvergne for Tiffany and Burgundy for Maxime. The set menus are at prices that make sense, while the cheese trolley boasts some 50 varieties. The hallmark of good food indeed!

name: Le Bénaton
review: In the heart of Burgundy, Beaune is famous for its annual wine auctions that take place in the prestigious Hospices, famous for their glazed tile roofs. A fervent champion of pedigree Gallic food and fine French wines, Japanese chef Keishi Sugimura, couldn’t have found a town that suits him better. Trained in Japan, the chef excels in the art of the porkpie, which earned him the title of vice world champion in 2013. He meticulously, almost surgically crafts fine seasonal ingredients into classical recipes rich in complimentary flavours, throwing in the odd dash of creativity from time to time: œuf parfait, dashi stock, Japanese wagyu; Corton pigeon served two ways. Also a cook, the chef’s wife pampers guests who are invited to take a seat on the patio in the garden come summertime.

name: Girardin - Gastronomique
review: This restaurant is housed in the Renaissance, stone-built Maison des Têtes, lavishly decorated with grimacing faces, which is an iconic listed edifice of the fine city of Colmar. With the help of two architects, Éric Girardin and his wife have gone all out with their minimalist, white and stripped-back interior. Even the tasting menu, which shines the spotlight on Alsace produce, cuts to the chase and each dish is the epitome of beauty, goodness and flavour. You will be won over by the exquisitely delicate Colmar mushroom duxelles with free-range egg yolk, or the delicious medley of venison and scorched pear. There is also a brasserie, plus guestrooms that sport a spirit of timeless elegance.

name: Mickaël Féval
review: Having previously worked with a number of great chefs (Antoine Westermann, Bernard Loiseau), Mickaël Feval has set up shop in the heart of Aix. His creative dishes showcase the seasons, local producers and classic produce (duckling from the Dombes, Challans poultry, foie gras, Dublin Bay prawn). The chef still likes to work with fish (a throwback to his stint working at Parisian seafood restaurant Antoine), as demonstrated by his tartare of sea bass with quinoa, grapefruit, avocado and a squid ink tuile, to be sampled in an unusual elongated dining space with small vaults and white walls. Be sure to order the rum baba! Professional and attentive service.

name: Auberge de la Tour
review: Located in the heart of a medieval village, this stone property with its corner tower and spiral staircase, is teeming with charm, and it is here that Renaud Darmanin has transformed this former café into a gastronomic outpost. Following his studies at the Chamalières hotel school, Darmanin went on to hone his skills at some of the world’s leading restaurants: at Paul Bocuse in Lyon; with Frédéric Anton at Le Pré Catelan in Paris; and at Le Parc des Eaux Vives in Geneva. He only works with the finest fresh and local ingredients (chestnuts, in particular), creating delicious, accomplished cuisine that skilfully combines the local terroir with spices from around the world.

name: Le Carmin
review: On Place Carnot, not far from the Hospices de Beaune, this restaurant with a modern façade occupies the ground floor of a charming old house. Having worked in the restaurants of Joël Robuchon and Alain Ducasse, chef Christophe Quéant draws from his experience to create modern, seasonal cuisine with a solid foundation in traditional cooking. His top-quality ingredients are transformed into unfussy, straightforward dishes with no unnecessary frills. The contemporary-style dining room, refurbished in tones of beige with exposed stonework, provides the setting for delicious dishes such as Burgundy snails with herb butter, and caramelised quail with mashed potatoes flavoured with summer truffles.

name: La Réserve Rimbaud
review: “Montpellier the Gifted”, as the city likes to bill itself, provides the backdrop to this well-hidden restaurant on the banks of the Lez. Slightly off the beaten track, it boasts a divine riverside terrace shaded by plane trees – a refreshing haven in hot summers. This modern and sophisticated Reserve is located in an old country house, an Ali Baba’s cavern of gourmet delights, unearthed from the little-known repertory of Languedoc-Roussillon. Former second of Alain Dutournier at the Carré des Feuillants, Charles Fontès signs intelligent compositions that revolves around the ingredient. Subtle plays of textures and flavours with an overriding goal of authentic simplicity. Seabream, squid and red mullet, Camargues eels and Lucques olives feature among the appetisers – Occitania on the table!

name: Le Sénéchal
review: A goldfish bowl on the table and works of art on the walls: the interior provides the perfect foil to chef Michel Truchon’s delicate, subtle cooking. A past master when it comes to plays on textures, he whips up artistically presented dishes that star fastidiously selected ingredients, such as mackerel from St Jean de Luz or market-fresh vegetables that he has a flair for enhancing. Crisp, simple flavours as forthright as they are complimentary – the chef has no time for fussy fripperies, to our delight! A few rooms for overnight stays.

name: Restaurant de Tourrel
review: It was within the walls of this splendid mansion that Charles Gounod played the first bars of his opera, Mireille, to the Provençal author Frédéric Mistral, who wrote the libretto. Today, in an attractive retro-style dining room with the occasional Art Deco touch, guests can sample a culinary score inspired by the region’s finest ingredients, including outdoor Provence tomatoes, Mediterranean squid and crayfish, and lamb from Crau.

name: Hostellerie de l'Abbaye de la Celle
review: Near Celle Abbey, this remote hostelry is housed in a stunning 18C edifice. Part of the Ducasse Group, the establishment boasts all the facilities one would expect in a luxury hotel. After training at the Louis XV in Monaco, chef Nicolas Pierantoni, born in Brignoles, is a true-blue local lad who grew up in the village. He subtly and intelligently celebrates Mediterranean produce, with a soft spot for vegetables, to which he adds lashings of gourmet generosity, depicted by his stuffed Provençal farcis with fresh herbs or his roast Dombes duck hen with rosemary. Down-to-earth, gutsy, rustic and flavoursome to the (culinary) core.

name: Le Champ des Lunes
review: This opulent 18C country house is steeped in charm from the extensive grounds, wellness centre, organic vineyards and permaculture vegetable garden to the contemporary art gallery established in the former wine-making cellars (the owners are art dealers). This picture postcard snapshot provides the perfect foil to food which showcases top-quality ingredients that pay an authentic homage to Luberon and Provencal produce. The stylish dining room sports a tasteful colour scheme and a summer patio overlooks the grounds.

name: Le Saint-Martin
review: The setting will take your breath away! Within the swish, elegant Saint Martin Hotel, whose rooms command sweeping views over the hillsides of Vence and the Mediterranean, your tastebuds are in for a treat. The chef, a keen sportsman and a born competitor, knocked around in establishments ranging from luxury hotels to more confidential houses to hone his skills. As a result, he curates delicate, subtle dishes underscored by intelligently inventive associations of ingredients. The wickedly decadent desserts are a high point of the meal.

name: Saisons
review: This 19C château, which houses the international hotel management school, (once under the aegis of Paul Bocuse), serves first-class cuisine. This is the work of Florian Pansin, who is supported by a superb team both in the kitchen and front of house. You will appreciate the finesse, the delicacy, the meticulous preparation, the colourful dishes: delicious roasted langoustines in a ginger and garlic crust; saddle of rabbit "intertwined" with smoked eel; a beautifully fresh rhubarb and mint dessert… Flawless technical skill and flashes of creativity. Put simply, this is tasty seasonal food at its best!

name: Le Panoramic
review: A star shines on the front of this high-altitude Alpine restaurant (elevation: 3 032m!) which is accessed by the funicular railway and promises a breath of fresh air as well as fine dining. In a snug interior that is all done out in wood, with sheepskins adorning the chairs and stags' heads mounted on the walls, staff in traditional costume serve up authentic, wood-fired dishes that are typical of the Savoie region. The focus is on cooking produce perfectly, whether it be prime rib of Black Baltic beef smoked over beech wood, or spatchcock pigeon royal; the accompaniments are certainly on a par, as demonstrated by the incredibly smooth and creamy potato mousseline served in a small cast iron pan. This place makes for such a wonderfully cosy change of scene that you will find it hard to leave.

name: Grand Hôtel du Lion d'Or
review: The Grand Hôtel du Lion d'Or is a gastronomic landmark of Sologne and owes its reputation to Marie-Christine and Didier Clément, a couple of professionals who are passionate about food. A true scholar when it comes to his region, the chef has spent his career resurrecting forgotten herbs and spices: grains of paradise, sand leek, angelica and lemon thyme, as well as vegetables such as parsnips or the vitelotte potato. He combines experience and curiosity, cooking in a classical vein, without affectation and his jus and sauces are particularly succulent. Take for example his Babylon-style pigeon, stuffed between the skin and flesh, now a signature dish of the house. Let’s not forget the knockout wine list which shines the spotlight on the Loire’s top wineries.

name: Le Manoir de la Régate
review: On the outskirts of Nantes in a beautiful residence near the Erdre, a chic and trendy decor (attractive pale wooden flooring, plant-covered wall at the back of the dining room, minimalist armchairs) and a menu of culinary delights awaits in this enticing restaurant. Chef Mathieu Pérou, who has worked in many Michelin-starred properties, skilfully combines fresh and elegant flavours in his beautifully presented dishes which he prepares using the region’s best ingredients. Front of house, his sister Anne-Charlotte oversees the highly professional service.

name: La Bastide
review: This iconic restaurant is in the capable hands of a talented team led by chef Noël Berard (former second-in-command here). Produce from the Luberon and the chef's modern Provençal cuisine is beautifully presented in the form of three tasting menus. High-quality ingredients (such as beef from the Luberon, trout from the River Sorgue, pork from Monteux), boldly flavoured jus and sauces, and a distinctive style that discreetly asserts itself. There is a magnificent terrace from which to admire the sunset... Good to know: this enchanting place in the Provençal countryside also proposes guestrooms (in the hotel) and a bistro.

name: L'Essentiel
review: Let’s get down to the basics (or the Essentials), rather than losing time in pointless conjectures. The ingredient rules in this family-run restaurant, next-door to the cathedral, and Éric Vidal is its virtuoso (yet humble) servant. For thirty or so diners, he organises a genuine banquet of flavour, thanks to delicately balanced preparations. Wild turbot baked in olive oil, pressed celery with black truffles; finely sliced mango and pineapple with passion fruit jelly and French almond tea cakes… The tasty culinary score is flanked by a selection of wines that is fully equal to the attractive menu. The slick, professional service adds a final flourish to the feast.

name: Auberge Le Prieuré
review: On the road between Bordeaux and Toulouse, in the heart of a tiny picturesque village near Agen, this country restaurant occupies a lovely, centuries-old stone house, whose terrace, shaded by ancient plane trees, faces a Clunisian priory founded in the 11C. A former stalwart of Michel Trama of Puymirol, chef Benjamin Toursel has forged his own distinctive modern style, scattered with bold, creative notes that frequently surprise the diner: tuna, cream of almonds, cherry coulis, green gazpacho; courgettes in salt, lemon paste, umeboshi plums, bottarga. A priory devoted to fine dining…

name: Julien Binz
review: On the Wine Road south of Colmar, the picturesque wine-growing village of Ammerschwihr nestles in Kaysersberg Valley, dubbed the valley of stars… - Michelin stars of course! Julien Binz, a veteran chef and former member of the Auberge de l’Ill team, for whom the world of cooking has no secrets, rustles up seasonal dishes with a thoroughbred, Gallic bias: tartare, roasted and warm cream of langoustines; roast fillet of venison, sweet potato cannelloni with foie gras and truffle. Julien treats us to a lesson in haute cuisine. The house sommelier, François Lhermitte, is never short of inspired tips.

name: La Ribaudière
review: This large villa has a garden that slopes down to the gently flowing Charente below, with the proud silhouette of Bourg-Charente castle, overlooking the vines, visible on the other side of the river. In the dining room with its slate-grey walls and large picture windows offering views of the charming terrace and the banks of the river, chefs Thierry and Julien Verrat (father and son) create fine cuisine where invention goes hand in hand with La Ribaudière’s natural surroundings. The owner of a vineyard and a truffle field, Verrat is passionate about the Charentais region, which is a real land of plenty. Here, he creates dishes that bring out the best of his excellent ingredients with delicacy and conviction, using the full panoply of local produce, ranging from Cognac and Pineau des Charentes to wild snails and fish from the nearby Atlantic.

name: L'Embrun
review: Now that the media frenzy has died down, Guillaume Pape is getting back to his roots. After competing on French TV's Top Chef and working with chef Olivier Bellin (Auberge des Glazicks), he has opened his own restaurant in modern premises in his native Brittany. Working in the open kitchen, he serves well-made seasonal cuisine de terroir dedicated to high-quality ingredients, such as sea bass, finely diced beetroot, fresh goat's cheese ravioli, beetroot juice with buttermilk or the chef's signature dessert, "douceur de lait": riz au lait mousse, dulce de leche, vanilla ice cream and milk opaline). His feeling for the visuals (perhaps honed by his time on TV) does the rest.

name: Sources
review: Two seasoned catering pros and brothers, Nicolas and Mathieu, who hail from Larmor-Plage, are at the helm of this venue in a prime location on Quai des Indes overlooking the docks and sailing boats. A muted soft grey colour scheme underscored by light wooden parquet floors and an open kitchen sets the contemporary scene. The food features a minimalist, highly effective slant, voluntarily low-key so that the ingredients, often maritime, can shout their name and flavour loud and clear: mackerel, langoustine and red mullet. A banquet of flavour, flawless craftsmanship and a genuine regional identity flow unheeded in this source.

name: Une Table, au Sud
review: Ludovic Turac, who boasts stints at Le Bristol and Guy Savoy, is happily at the helm of this restaurant, firmly anchored in the South of France. His inventive yet disciplined recipes overflow with regional flavours from Provençal vegetables to locally sourced fish and meat from the Southern Alps, further enhanced by panoramic views over the old port and the basilica of Marseille. His signature dishes “My version of aïoli” and “Local catch like a bouillabaisse” are always a delight, which is also the case of his passport menu in tribute to Marseille’s international maritime heritage.

name: Château Blanchard
review: Set in sprawling grounds, this handsome 1920’s edifice was inspired by the Italian Renaissance, hence the mythological frieze on the façade and the marble and mosaics… The elegant colonnaded dining room however sports a refreshing modern slant with embedded lighting, deep armchairs and exquisite tableware. Two brothers manage this family business. Chef Sylvain Roux conjures up dishes throbbing with flavour that aim to highlight top produce: artic char roasted in seaweed; locally reared veal with a crust of morel mushrooms; a wafer-thin strawberry, rhubarb and rose water tart. Sylvain’s brother, sommelier Frédéric Roux, who can be relied on for insightful wine-food pairings, has put together a wine cellar that will have many a connoisseur drooling.

name: L'Atlantide 1874 - Maison Guého
review: Just around the corner from the Musée Jules Verne, this fine mansion dating from 1874 overlooks the River Loire and the Île de Nantes. Through the restaurant's large panoramic windows, you can observe the boats as they come and go, Le Hangar à Bananes and the grey Titan crane – an emblem of the port city of Nantes. A Breton (from Vannes) who trained in Alsace at the Auberge de l'Ill before working as a chef in New Orleans and Hong Kong, Jean-Yves Guého conjures up a highly precise and refined array of dishes in which fish takes pride of place. The list of Loire wines is well worth perusing. Pretty, modern guestrooms with a view.

name: L'Atelier Alexandre Bousquet
review: In the hillsides outside Biarritz, this converted Basque farm is the HQ of Isabelle Caulier, a lass from Aveyron, and Alexandre Bousquet, a Tarn lad, who trained under Michel Guérard and Les Crayères. The latter creates dishes oozing in subtlety and delicacy, using premium ingredients with a distinct weakness for local produce. A felicitous harmony of flavours and textures in the form of set menus comprising four or six courses (plus a lunch menu). By way of example: turbot, spinach and caviar, or golden sautéed sweetbread with a medley of onion side dishes – an absolute treat! Confident, bang-on cuisine – a place to discover.

name: L'Évidence
review: Leaving the city of Tours to set up shop in this old house on a small square in the countryside was an easy step to take for Gaëtan Evrard, who is very fond of his native province of Touraine. Meat and vegetables from the region, fish sourced in Brittany: produce is celebrated here, elevated by a chef who has a talent for bold gestures – as in his beautiful Le Guilvinec cod fillet drizzled with a succulent sauce flavoured with saffron and Sainte-Maure de Touraine goat's cheese, or his brilliantly reimagined Nougat de Tours tart. To accompany your meal, choose from the excellent list of wines from the Loire, to be enjoyed in minimalist surroundings that provide the perfect foil to the chef's creative cooking.

name: Auberge Grand'Maison
review: The food here traverses the annals of French cookery: classical and tempting with immaculate plating. Christophe Le Fur, formerly the chef of the chancellor of the Paris academy, when he cooked both for the Dalai Lama and for Hillary Clinton, has returned to his roots (he comes from Cap Fréhel) to regale us with his generous, culinary score: crunchy-melting Ancenis poultry with foie gras stock; biscuit of pike, black wheat crackers and ricotta, red wine sauce.

name: Auberge de l'Abbaye
review: Located at the foot of Abbaye d’Ambronay, this bright auberge is depicted by a tasteful trendy interior. A native of nearby Nantua, Ivan Lavaux trained at the hotel school in Thonon-les-Bains before kicking off his career in the dining rooms of some of France’s finest restaurants, both in Paris and on the French Riviera. In his new life as a chef, he has proven to be an excellent artisan who, in his own words, respects the “logic of the ingredients”. These are painstakingly selected and invariably local, but without overlooking excellent fish, such as smoked Ain trout and macerated tomatoes, strawberries and raspberries. Two surprise menus at lunch and dinner.

name: Il Carpaccio
review: In the heart of the Royal Monceau, the corridor leading to your table is embedded with thousands of mother-of-pearl shells, in an elaborate and artistic tribute to the nymphs of Italian Baroque. The dining room, set in what looks like a conservatory painted in spring colours, resembles a genuine winter garden flanked by an alfresco area. In the kitchen, Oliver Piras and Alessandra Del Favero subtly conjure up Italian dishes that are deliciously free of fussy nonsense. Their cooking is meticulous, spot on and flavoursome and aims to highlight the natural tastes and flavours of painstakingly selected star ingredients. The same approach is true of the wine cellar which demonstrates a distinct soft spot for Piedmont and Tuscan wines. The decadent desserts by Quentin Lechat offer a new spin on classic Italian recipes.

name: Pure & V
review: (Planned to move to 7 Rue du Lycée in the first quarter). Pure & V is a play on words in French – pure dreaming! The owner, Vanessa Massé, a sommelière with a cast-iron CV, is unrivalled when it comes to unearthing first-rate natural wines. She works hand in hand with the kitchen team devising dishes of Scandinavian inspiration. The food is healthy, balanced and based on meticulously sourced ingredients with an unabashed focus on vegetables and fish. Friendly, buzzy vibe.

name: Frenchie
review: “Frenchy” chef, Grégory Marchand, learned the trade in top international restaurants (Gramercy Tavern in New York, Jamie Oliver's Fifteen in London, Mandarin Oriental in Hong Kong). He has now set up shop in Rue du Nil in a pocket handkerchief venue in the Sentier neighbourhood (bare bricks, beams, stones, view of the kitchen). It is invariably packed to the seams and has attracted a faithful cohort of celebrities. The chef's cooking, perfectly in tune with today’s international inclinations, with the bonus of unusual blends of flavours and savvy food and wine pairings, is fully deserving of its current media hype and success. A cheerful vibe flows between the kitchen and the dining room, embodied by the committed youthful staff, all of which proves that it is possible to offer a fine dining experience that is both fun and laid-back, yet highly professional.

name: L'Atelier du Peintre
review: Martin Schongauer, one of the greatest late-15C engravers and painters from the Rhine, was born just across from this establishment, whose walls date back to the Renaissance. Inside, there is a markedly different style! Chic and cosy, this is a decidedly contemporary setting. As for the food, Loïc Lefebvre's culinary personality shines through. This native of Lorraine, who learned his craft in Michelin-starred kitchens, delivers creative and colourful cuisine which clearly follows the seasons. Freshness and subtlety, precision and finesse go into his roasted Arctic char with beetroot carpaccio and rhubarb vinaigrette, or his monkfish medallion with bottarga and confit lemon.

name: Lait Thym Sel
review: Among the gorgeous half-timbered houses in the neighbourhood of La Doutre, we warmly recommend this gem run by a talented couple. The young chef, Gaëtan Morvan, who has experience at some of the great Michelin-starred restaurants, serves up an atypical culinary experience in 15 highly original sequences that make the most of ingredients from the region. Inventiveness, unexpected associations… we let ourselves be carried away into his culinary universe. In the dining room, Fanny Gardier provides efficient service and suggests excellent and environmentally friendly wines. N.B. It is crucial to book, as this small, cosy restaurant can only accommodate 16 diners.

name: Tour d'Argent
review: (Closed for renovation – reopening scheduled for spring 2023) Founded in 1582, this elegant auberge on the banks of the Seine became a restaurant in 1780. And it was at the turn of the 20C that André Terrail purchased it and had the brilliant idea of raising the building one floor to install a dining room, thus benefitting from one of the best (and unique) views of the Seine and Notre Dame cathedral. The soul of the Tour Argent has moved with the times, and its menu, a veritable palimpsest reinterpreted by MOF (Meilleur Ouvrier de France) chef Yannick Franques, has preserved the memory of several decades of French haute cuisine. Purists can rest assured, however, that the perfectly honed service is as spectacular as ever, crowned by the extraordinary wine cellar, home to around 300,000 bottles.

name: Les Trois Soleils de Montal
review: This property located on the Causse de Gramat, close to Saint-Céré, has a hotel with its restaurants, a peaceful garden, a pool, and a golf course not far away. This fine dining restaurant wins diners over with its elegant traditional interior looking out onto the summer terrace and the garden. The pre-Impressionist paintings on the walls point to one of the passions of the chef, who was an antique dealer in a previous life. Today, he devotes himself solely to cooking, delighting diners with quality produce and exceptionally fine craftsmanship. This lovely dining experience is also great value for money. Not to mention the attentive service courtesy of Madame Bizat.

name: Auberge des Templiers
review: Some things never go out of fashion… The stone walls of this former posthouse date back to the 17C and its half-timbered, pink brick façade is the quintessence of Sologne architecture. Take a seat in this timeless setting of wooden beams and crystalware, whose dining room overlooks magnificent grounds planted with hundred-year-old trees. Youthful Martin Simonart, of Belgian origins who honed his skills with Jean-Pierre Jacob in Courchevel and at Bourget-du-Lac, treats guests to modern, stripped back cuisine with a masterful layering of textures. Examples include Dany Ollivier's trout served warm, smoked yogurt, horseradish granita or Miéral pigeon, roasted and confit with a powerful jus – not to be missed!

name: Auberge du Vert Mont
review: Tucked away in the heart of the countryside, chef Florent Ladeyn, an ecological champion from the word go, is a standard-bearer of authentic Flemish fare steeped in gourmet flavours, albeit with a creative, instinctive spin. In a dining room, refurbished from top to toe with exposed rafters and overlooking the West Flanders hillsides, the chef unveils his passion for ember roasting, which he carries out in front of diners. Firmly committed to local produce, he strews his creations with flowers and plants from the region. And while his cone of Maroilles fries covered with a thin layer of caramelised onion has attained almost legendary status, we highly recommend his “blind” menu, which has to be for everyone at the table, rich in gourmet delights!

name: Le Pressoir
review: Originally from Saint-Brieuc, chef Vincent David used to visit this renowned Vannes restaurant with his grandparents when he was a boy – it was here that he developed a taste for Michelin-starred restaurants! Several decades later, having convinced chefs such as Dominique Bouchet and Marc Meneau of his talent, he took over this emblematic restaurant with its now pared-down decor. Passionate about meat and fish combinations, he creates a signature cuisine in which top-quality ingredients are perfectly balanced.

name: Le Kaïku
review: In the heart of this seaside resort where Louis XIV married the Infanta of Spain, Maria-Thérèse of Austria, it is a pleasure to step inside what is said to be the oldest building in town (16C). But there is nothing old about the menu served at the cosy, elegant restaurant that lies behind these high walls and mullioned windows. Basque chef Nicolas Borombo (from Bayonne), son and grandson of rugby players, set up shop here after clocking up experience in Paris, at the Hôtel Crillon with Dominique Bouchet and Jean-François Piège, and at the George V with Philippe Legendre. With a love for his region, he creates beautiful, original and refined cuisine that makes the most of regional ingredients.

name: Villa Salone
review: Back down in the valley after seven years at Le Roc Alto in Saint-Véran, Alexandre Lechêne has taken over this pretty mansion in the heart of Salon-de-Provence. Here he treats diners to creative cuisine that is pleasantly astounding and served in surprise menus with no choice: the ethos here is “Letting go”! His combinations of flavours are occasionally daring, but always fortuitous. For example, his carabinero prawns, stock of heads, Venere rice and cress is the epitome of balance and subtlety. Mouldings, ceiling frescoes and a lovely vintage tiled floor set the scene in terms of the décor.

name: Sushi Shunei
review: This establishment, entirely devoted to sushis, sports a pared down interior in line with the graphic charter of its Japanese forebears: light wooden furnishings and a counter that seats nine, all of which devoted to a rare gourmet experience. Sushi master, Shunei Kimura, has been unfolding his talents and skill in France for several decades now. All the fish is meticulously selected, aged and filleted with the utmost care, served at just the right temperature (with a rice from Nigata) and flanked by high-precision seasonings. Every mouthful embarks you on an authentic culinary voyage.

name: La Source
review: Originally from Cuzieu, which is a mere 2km away, Antoine Bergeron is very much a local boy. Ambitious and passionate about his work, he takes you on a surprise fine dining journey that subtly and creatively showcases ingredients from his hand-picked suppliers. Comfortably seated in the bright, contemporary dining room, you will enjoy a culinary tour of the region and the local markets. For example, pig's head served with sauce gribiche and onion pickles; Urfé pigeon and butternut squash; a hazelnut and lemon version of a Paris-Brest pastry. A genuine source of pleasure with special mention for the jus. Stellar craftsmanship.

name: Äponem - Auberge du Presbytère
review: Äponem means happiness in Pataxo and Amélie Darvas and Gaby Benicio definitely found their bliss in this inn of a 17C former presbytery. They stumbled across it by accident when on holiday in the region and it has become, in their own words, their “life project”. “Get back to the basics, to ourselves and to home-grown produce”, such is the goal of chef Darvas, originally from Paris, who is committed to working with ingredients sourced only from the local market and their own garden (seven permaculture gardens in all!). Amélie’s bold, transparent cuisine is perfectly paired with the insightful suggestions of fine regional wines by Gaby, a trained sommelière. Meals are served in the spruce interior overlooking the magnificent countryside or on the patio, shaded by a climbing wisteria. Every day is a new beginning for this committed duo and their team.

name: Pur' - Jean-François Rouquette
review: Two contemporary restaurants at the Park Hyatt: Café Jeanne at lunchtime and Pur', a more intimate space, for a really enjoyable dinner. The latter is obviously in keeping with the spirit of the hotel on the rue de la Paix, where luxury is synonymous with refinement, modernity and discretion. Ed Tuttle designed the interior, creating an atmosphere that is both comfortable and private, with just 35 covers. Every last detail has been thought out: the colour palette, the lighting and the space itself – a vast rotunda with a dome and a colonnade encircling it. Here, Jean-François Rouquette (Taillevent, Le Crillon, La Cantine des Gourmets, Les Muses) has found a place worthy of expressing his talent in all its brilliance. There is finesse in the way he marries excellent produce in his creative and inspired cuisine. Pure delight!

name: Alliance
review: Between the Left Bank and Boulevard Saint Germain, this restaurant celebrates the Alliance of two enthusiastic partners in a culinary adventure: Shawn and Toshi, respectively in charge of the dining room and the kitchen. Chef Toshitaka Omiya favours authenticity rather than fancy frills and his cooking is founded on fine seasonal ingredients which he aims to enhance, both for the eye and the tastebuds. His signature dish has become foie gras with pot-au-feu vegetables in ginger. Show-stopping simplicity, subtle blends and flawless craftsmanship depict his cooking, flanked by the decadent, almost wicked inspirations of pastry chef Morgane Raimbaud. One final word for the stripped back interior dotted with discreet nods to Japan that is welcoming and commands a fascinating view of the kitchen.

name: ERH
review: The initials E, R and H stand for water, rice and men in French (eau, riz, hommes): a mysterious and poetic name for this unusual place that shares its premises with a sake shop and a whisky bar. Japanese chef Keita Kitamura (previously of Pierre Gagnaire, among others) creates beautifully crafted market-fresh French cuisine that gives pride of place to vegetables and fish. At lunchtime he serves up some impressive culinary treats for a bargain price (three- or five-course set menus); in the evening, he composes tasting menus in line with the seasons. You might like to opt for food and sake pairings. Diners take their seats in an amazing contemporary space with a large glass roof and a long counter that stretches out in front of the open kitchen, where, as in Japan, the Japanese chef officiates. This is the place to try between the Halles and Montorgueil districts. Such talent, such character!

name: L'Archeste
review: An appealing façade and sleek, minimalist interior (dark brushed-effect painted walls, wooden fittings, large window letting in the light) for this restaurant created by a chef with a passion for produce who worked at Hiramatsu for 18 years, for ten of which he was head chef. He astounds diners with his modern, precise and coherent French cuisine, which casts a spotlight on premium-quality ingredients while doing a beautiful job of staying true to the seasons. No fixed menu here: the set menus change every day in line with the chef's inspiration. The name of this place is an homage to Alain Senderens and his restaurant L'Archestrate, but it is also a clever mix of "artisanal", "orchestra" and "art". In the end, what matters is that you enjoy yourself... and it just so happens that you will.

name: Le Faham by Kelly Rangama
review: The faham is an orchid native to the island of Réunion, famous for its subtle almond scent. Kelly Rangama (a Top Chef 2017 contestant) chose this flower to symbolise her civil and culinary union with pastry chef Jérôme Devreese and their joint creation: this sleek, elegant restaurant tucked away in the Batignolles district. Here the chef proposes a cuisine that abounds in vibrancy and delicacy, spicy but always subtle, with a touch of exoticism that makes all the difference. An example: her toothfish (fished in La Réunion) with sweet-sour carrots and ginger and a concentrate of tomatoes and crunchy rice. A genuine delight.

name: Oxte
review: This pleasant and cosy little restaurant in the Étoile neighbourhood, near the Arc de Triomphe, proposes delicious contemporary cuisine with Mexican influences. French ingredients are infused with condiments, herbs and spices by a talented and passionate Mexican chef who also gets involved with the service. Savvy and skilfully prepared dishes such as monkfish and roasted fennel, pastilla crumble and pastis broth or longfin tuna served ceviche-style with mussels and peppers, are turned out by a chef who cooks and seasons the produce beautifully. This colourful, punchy and well-seasoned food is so good you'll soon be back for more!

name: Pollen
review: As you wander through the narrow streets of Avignon, you will come upon this pretty restaurant with a large open kitchen. The chefs themselves deliver the food to your table while you take in the judicious wine recommendations of the enthusiastic sommelier (who is also a connoisseur of biodynamic wines). In the form of a surprise menu, chef Mathieu Desmarest proposes pared-down and balanced cuisine that evolves with the seasons by aligning with local producers. He takes advantage of ingredients of impeccable quality (octopus, bluefin tuna, pigeon). The subtle and creative dishes and marriages of bold flavours effortlessly win over diners.

name: Le Pavillon des Boulevards
review: A bona fide gastronomic institution in Bordeaux for several decades now, this traditional stone town house has a particularly inviting appearance. Here, chef Thomas Morel and his wife Célia give free rein to their imaginations, both in terms of the cuisine and the wine list. The couple serve creative cuisine which plays with different combinations of aromas and flavours and is accompanied by excellent wines from the region. A truly delightful dining experience!

name: La Liégeoise
review: The panoramic sea view from this first-floor restaurant on the seaboard is magical. This family-run hotel in the oldest seaside resort of the Opal Coast immediately bowls us over with its refurbished vintage vibe. Before dropping anchor in the Channel, Benjamin Delpierre worked for a while with Jean-Michel Lorain at the Côte Saint-Jacques and the Ritz with Michel Roth, before a spot of island hopping in the Caribbean in the company of his wife, today in the dining room. Fish and shellfish run the show here: red mullet, snails, oysters, razor clams and mussels – enhanced by the chef’s flair for seafood cooking.

name: L'Axel
review: In the heart of Fontainebleau, this smart and understated restaurant is run by a French-Japanese couple. Kunihisa Goto works closely with the seasons to offer a new take on French gastronomy and his partner works front of house. He is sincerely devoted to French cuisine, to its wines and iconic produce, from foie gras to snails. Having trained with the best, he reinvents the French classics with a certain aplomb, drawing on Japanese ingredients – daikon, lotus roots, nori, shiso leaves, Wagyu beef. His variation on the slow-cooked egg has become a classic, served with Comté cheese ravioli and sprinkled with truffles. Each dish delivers this same attention to presentation, this balance and this sense of indulgence. Responsive and courteous service.

name: Le Mas Bottero
review: Now near Aix en Provence, owner-chef Nicolas Bottero (formerly in Grenoble) signs enthusiastic, flavoursome, aromatic food. If we had to describe him, we would say he is discreet, modest and passionate. As a child, he spent time in the region at his grandmother’s house and he has remained attached to the colours of southern France and to the region in general, as his Mediterranean croaker with a shellfish minestrone, rouille stock or stuffed saddle of Provence lamb, asparagus and morel mushrooms bears witness. Local producers feature prominently among the suppliers, as does the small herb garden. The terrace behind the house overlooks a small garden.

name: AT
review: A stone's throw from the banks of the Seine, this small, quietly unobtrusive restaurant sports a minimalist interior in line with today’s quest for authenticity rather than hot air! Chef Tanaka, formerly of Pierre Gagnaire, is a fan of fresh ingredients and precision. Armed with boundless creativity and imagination, he conjures up enticing dishes that keep us drooling right up to the very end. The vaulted cellar in the basement is home to a wine bar and delivers take-away meals. It is also nice to know that you will always be surprised here, because the single set menu changes regularly.

name: La Petite Maison de Cucuron
review: Here, in this small yellow property imbued with a genteel Provençal charm, talented cordon bleu chef Éric Sapet pays full homage to market-sourced ingredients such as mushrooms (including truffles, to which he dedicates an entire menu throughout the winter), vegetables from local market gardens, Provençal cheeses, and game (hare à la royale). A devoted gourmet and wine-lover, Sapet already has a solid career behind him in the French capital, having worked at La Tour d’Argent and Jacques Cagna, in particular. Guest flock to his restaurant to savour dishes such as blanquette of scallops and quail stuffed with truffle rice and foie gras. Some even return on Saturdays for his cookery classes! A warning for those who have forgotten to book, as the restaurant is often full.

name: Bellefeuille - Saint James Paris
review: Built in 1892, this private mansion looks like a little château surrounded by greenery in the very heart of Paris. It became a hotel in the early 1990s, and it wasn't until 2013 that its restaurant opened to outside customers. This is one of the most exclusive establishments in the capital! Chef Julien Dumas (formerly of Lucas Carton) proposes high-quality cuisine replete with vegetables and seafood, as in the lobster from Les Îles Chausey with rhubarb and fennel flower. But meat lovers will be delighted by his mallard served with buckwheat variations and Andouille de Guéméné pork sausage, which is absolutely sublime. Astutely devised and masterfully prepared dishes to be sampled in a refurbished dining room done out in a natural decor that is perfectly in keeping with the chef's cuisine.

name: JAN
review: Young South African Jan Hendrik van der Westhuizen, who has worked as a chef on private yachts in Monaco and a reporter and photographer for a well-known magazine, has already lived several different lives… In his intimate and romantic little restaurant near the port, he cooks creative, personal cuisine in the form of a single set menu without options (five or seven courses), in which he plays on sweet and sour combinations, and dabbles in smoky, spicy and acidic flavours, serving up in this way an overview of South African cuisine. A favourite among customers visiting the French Riviera.

name: Maison Hache
review: Christopher Hache finally has a place to call his own. His cuisine eschews ostentation and that's no bad thing. Far from the Hôtel de Crillon and the grand Parisian restaurants where he learned his craft, the chef concocts a delicious tribute to Provence and the Alpilles. He does so by scrupulously selecting his fruit and vegetables, as well as opting for regional lamb and wines. Here, the focus is on local ingredients and producers. The dishes themselves are simple in form, straightforward, as natural and forthright as the flavours they exude (such as the superb lamb jus), with no unnecessary fuss or frills. Rounding off the picture: a chic setting, an inspired wine list and wonderfully comfortable guestrooms upstairs. All in all, an excellent establishment.

name: Tentazioni
review: She hails from Brittany, he is from Sardinia, they met in Corsica... and now they run a small restaurant in Bordeaux that punches above its weight. The chef's dishes are precise and always inspired, especially when they home in on first-rate ingredients: langoustines, spider crab, bluefin tuna and pigeon. Expect very contemporary cuisine, bursting with flavours and littered with references to Italy (put it down to the chef's origins), without ever lapsing into nostalgia or getting caught up in proclamations of identity. The tasting menus change every week depending on the chef's inspiration. It's a real pleasure from start to finish, right down to the lunch menu, which is excellent value for money.

name: Jérôme Nutile
review: Jérôme Nutile brings plenty to the table: "Meilleur Ouvrier de France" 2011, he notably presided over the heyday of Hostellerie Le Castellas, in Collias. In his Nîmes location, a converted farmhouse, he celebrates the seasons through delightful dishes: tender leeks cooked on Camargue fleur de sel, fondant of wild salmon confit; the traditional French classic of hare à la royale cooked two ways – in the style of Antonin Carême and Senator Couteaux's recipe, beautifully executed and tasty. Add to this the friendly and competent service, a fantastic list of regional wines, and you have everything you could ask for!

name: Numéro 3
review: This village was once home to the famous art dealer Ambroise Vollard, but also Picabia, Picasso and Cendrars, who is buried here. Julie and Laurent Trochain run their fine restaurant in a former hunting lodge that they have completely renovated. What a metamorphosis! Gone are the beams, the fireplace and even the traditional façade, replaced by an eminently contemporary, geometrical and designer setting. A native of Maubeuge who trained in some of the best establishments, most notably at Restaurant Pierre Gagnaire, Laurent champions local produce of the Île-de-France with his subtle and colourful cuisine. He covers all the bases: high-quality ingredients, a precise touch and innovative dishes. You can stay the night in the lovely guesthouse.

name: Maximilien
review: Jean-Michel Eblin, the chef-patron of this place in the pretty village of Zellenberg, is clear on one thing: he will never sell it! We can understand his almost visceral attachment to this establishment, which is built on a plot of (Pinot Noir) vineyards that belonged to his family. With impressive consistency, he creates cuisine based on solid classical foundations, with the occasional nod to modern innovation for good measure. Might you opt for his turbot, green asparagus and morels or, alternatively, the shredded scallop, truffle and baby lettuce? The produce is fresh and of excellent quality; it is all elevated by a fine wine list: they have ticked all the boxes here.

name: Qui Plume la Lune
review: Qui plume la Lune is a picturesque and romantic setting that has treated itself to a makeover for its 10th anniversary. One of the walls bears a quote from William Faulkner: “We ran out into the moonlight toward the kitchen.” Bare stone walls and natural materials (untreated wood, twigs and branches, etc) set the poetic scene. This temple of culinary delicacies is the dedicated work of a team determined to select only the very best produce – in line with a clear environmental ethic, hence the premium organic vegetables. Diners are invited to sample dishes that are a masterclass of expertise and precision, overflowing with vitality, fresh ingredients and flavours. A tasty culinary interlude awaits all who enter this temple of good food.

name: Agapé
review: In Ancient Greece, the word agape was used to describe the unconditional love of another. In this restaurant, it now stands as a byword for excellence, authenticity and talent. The menu here celebrates seasonal ingredients that the female Brazilian chef uses to create contemporary international dishes. Even when she lets her talent run wild, her controlled mastery of the cooking process shines through, with a total concentration on the concept of giving pleasure. The decor in the cosy, intimate dining room is defined by soft hues and walls adorned with works by contemporary artists. Agapé’s talent is further showcased by the successful fusion between kitchen and front of house and the astute wine pairing recommendations (the wine cellar features over 600 labels).

name: La Rotonde - La Table d'Aurélien Largeau
review: A gift from Napoleon III to his wife Eugénie in 1854, the Hôtel du Palais, the emblematic palace of the city of Biarritz, has just reopened after being beautifully refurbished. The restaurant is on a par with this splendid setting, thanks to chef Aurélien Largeau (who has worked for Christophe Hay), who rises to the challenge admirably. Eel from the South-West, John Dory from our shores, Baserri guinea fowl from the Basque country: local produce is elevated by his meticulous approach. Pastry chef, Aleksandre Oliver (previously of Gordon Ramsay's restaurant in Bordeaux), meanwhile, successfully combines seaweed and rhubarb!

name: Le Petit Hôtel du Grand Large
review: It would seem that the world of advertising can open every door! Hervé Bourdon, former Parisian art director, and his wife, Catherine, ditched their former lives to take over and transform this small hotel restaurant. It is idyllically located a pebble’s throw (literally) from the seashore, overlooking the pretty harbour of Portivy, with sea breezes and dazzling sunsets. A single set menu unfolds to reveal resolutely local produce including fish and shellfish, while the herbs, flowers and veggies are from one of the restaurant’s organic cottage gardens. The chef has a knack with fish that he sears on a teppanyaki, and if you are very lucky, you may be able to sample rare delicacies such as barnacles, which taste a bit like a cross between a lobster and a clam and are eaten with the fingers – out of this world!

name: Le Gindreau
review: In a small village overlooking the hillsides, the old village school has been transformed into a restaurant. Welcome to the Gindreau in Saint Médard. Chef Pascal Bardet, originally from Lot and who worked for Alain Ducasse for 18 years, particularly at the Louis XV, is flourishing in his own kitchen. “My cooking is entirely free of set rules,” confides this shy, but confident craftsman. His knack with regional produce, particularly truffles, is indeed second to none. Take a seat under the shade of the chestnut trees and watch the sun set in Quercy.

name: Le Violon d'Ingres
review: Continuity and change in the quest for quality: Christian Constant sold Le Violon d'Ingres to Bertrand Bluy, who also hails from southwest France (Lot et Garonne) and is the owner of Les Papilles (in Paris). Fans can rest assured, because the luxurious, neo-bistro styled establishment and the menu remain a loving tribute to la vieille France. The recipes are the combined work of two gifted and experienced chefs, Alain Solivérès and Jimmy Tsaramanana, who sing an ode to southwest France thanks to first-class produce. Remember to book, as tables get snapped up fast.

name: Alcyone
review: Chef Lionel Levy, a local lad who honed his skills with Alain Ducasse and Éric Frechon, is behind the helm of the Alcyone (named after the daughter of the god Aeolus), which opened in 2013 within the iconic Hôtel-Dieu. His creative recipes, liberally sprinkled with spices, always seek to shine the spotlight on Mediterranean delicacies, such as local fish (red mullet, scorpion fish, seabass) and Provençal fare from lamb to artichokes and sweet chestnuts. One dish sums up his distinctive approach: lamb ravioles, mushrooms, artichoke and lamb jus. The swish, understated interior is perfectly suited to the hotel.

name: Le Patio
review: This restaurant near the port has made it its mission to showcase the best produce from Aquitaine: asparagus from the Landes, lamb from Pauillac, oysters from the bay, pigeon, foie gras… Chef Thierry Renou also has a passion for Thailand, and travels there regularly. Buddha statues decorate his restaurant and there are hints of fusion food in his foie gras poached in coconut milk, his sole with a Thai broth, and his oysters and sushi flavoured with aloe vera. His cooking is distinctly contemporary and he pays particular attention to the aesthetics of the dishes, which also appear to have Asian influences. As for the famous patio, you are in for a treat: the glass-paned roof means you can have lunch in the open air or dinner beneath the starry sky.

name: Val d'Auge
review: Typical of northern France on the outside, with its red brick and grey awnings, small windowpanes and white brick frames, this restaurant conceals a smart contemporary interior. As a young chef, Christophe Hagnerelle was strongly influenced by his time spent alongside Joël Robuchon at Le Jamin, before moving to Beirut and later to Connecticut. Today, this master culinary craftsman creates precise, unfussy seasonal cuisine with a hint of inventiveness. The menu features excellent fish and seafood from the North Sea, including scallops, turbot, bass and John Dory depending on the catch of the day, as well as grouse and hare in season, veal sweetbreads and pigeon from Flanders. The lunchtime menu offers particularly good value for money.

name: L'Auberge de Montmin
review: Forclaz Pass (1147m) is not just paradise for paragliders, but also for fine food lovers. This inn has been refurbished and extended without losing its snug alpine appeal and is now home to chef Florian Favario who adds an increasingly creative spin to recipes founded on first-rate local produce (lamb and piglets, home-grown vegetables, seasonal fruit). He masterfully associates wildflowers, plants and herbs resulting in a feast of thyme, sage, oregano, agastache, hyssop, mint flower, etc., that brings extraordinary scents to dishes, which are already the apex of culinary technique and know-how. This approach to detail is visible even in the walnut tableware that the chef makes himself. The service is entrusted to a professional threesome of women, led by the ever-attentive Sandrine Deley. Sipping an aperitif before dinner on the terrace overlooking the alpine meadows is an unforgettable experience.

name: Auberge du Pont
