review: As spirited as the winds of Brittany (where he grew up), Rodolphe Regnauld harbours a great love for the produce of his adopted region. Here he showcases it in a series of meat and fish dishes: Guilvinec langoustine cooked two ways, raspberries, peas, Sturia caviar from Aquitaine; Rossini fillet of Salers beef served with foie gras from the Limagne plains and a rich gravy.

name: La Cachette
review: In the lower part of Valence, this hidden little gem is now even more tucked away since moving its premises into the cul-de-sac located behind the original restaurant. It is certainly still worth seeking out! You will get acquainted with a meticulous and inspired chef, Masashi Ijichi, who is originally from Japan. In this brand-new, modern setting, he delivers fine and delicate dishes that irresistibly combine flavours from the Drôme area with inspiration from Asia. Red mullet, courgettes, curry and white pepper; pigeon with black trumpet mushrooms; Japanese Wagyu beef, mustard and green beans. This excellent dining experience is made complete by the efficient service and outstanding wine list (superb selection of northern Côtes du Rhône wines).

name: La Bastide de Moustiers
review: In this fine bastide, savour Mediterranean cuisine that combines the flavours of ingredients direct from the market or the kitchen garden managed by two full-time staff (don’t miss the adjoining Jardin des Simples). The chef here conjures up meticulously executed dishes bursting with sun-blessed flavours such as rabbit with polenta and mustard-flavoured chips. The pleasant setting, including a plethora of olive trees and a plane tree-shaded terrace, adds to the attraction of this perfect resumé of Provence.

name: Divellec
review: The famous restaurant of Jacques Le Divellec (1983-2013) is now the lair of Mathieu Pacaud. The culinary theme continues to demonstrate a seafaring slant and the food keeps pace with the tides, paying a fine tribute to first-class seafood, such as sole meunière from small boats with hazelnut butter or wild young turbot from Brittany. Take a seat on the deck and savour the view over the Esplanades of the Invalides. The establishment has even extended its premises into a former bookshop, creating a winter garden-inspired room depicted by woven wicker panels.

name: Les Terraillers
review: Between Antibes and Cagnes-sur-Mer, this village owes its fame to its art glassware and its pottery, thanks to a soil rich in clay. In fact, Michaël Fulci’s parents opened their restaurant in a former potter’s studio, the kiln of which is now a delightfully snug lounge! In fine weather, the shaded trellis of the alfresco patio attracts diners like bees to honey… Michaël Fulci is a bona fide Mediterranean chef, who learned the ropes with legends such as Alain Ducasse and Roger Vergé, no less… The menu naturally enough overflows with fruit and veg from local markets, from courgette flowers and Menton lemons to figs. Truffles also enjoy the spotlight, be they black from Vaucluse or white from Alba. Sophisticated, flavourful food, drenched in sunshine, scents and flavours.

name: Le Clocher des Pères
review: Perched at an altitude of 600m, this restaurant occupying a former watchtower in the centre of the village looks out over the Belledonne mountains, including the Clocher des Pères. This setting teeming with character sets the scene for enticing cuisine created by Éloïse and Pierre Troccaz, the discreet yet dynamic couple at the helm. The latter, a chef who has patiently guided his career away from the beaten track, creates accomplished and creative cuisine which steers clear of routine and is partly improvised depending on market availability. His recipes are heavily influenced by the traditions and ingredients of the Savoie, as witnessed by dishes such as millefeuille of trout, lobster and diot sausage, and char with a Beaufort cream sauce, Savoie biscuit and blueberries. Charming service and pretty guestrooms.

name: La Table du Gourmet
review: In Riquewihr, Jean-Luc Brendel has built up an entire ecosystem: in addition to his fine dining restaurant, he has a modern winstub and also offers top-of-the-range guestrooms for overnight stays. At La Table du Gourmet, in the heart of the medieval city, the chef cooks beautiful seasonal ingredients with great care and a dash of creativity, making each dish his own. His set menu, "From Garden to Plate", showcases produce from his organic vegetable garden, such as the delicious kale served with game that is, of course, also from Alsace. Alsace also prevails on the wine list, with a few forays into Burgundy, and all this is enjoyed in surroundings that combine olde worlde charm (the building dates back to the 16C) and more contemporary touches in terms of furniture and lighting. You are in safe hands here.

name: Le Fanal
review: The lights of Le Fanal (“The Lantern”) will guide you to this idyllic setting looking out to sea in front of the port in Banyuls. Catalan-born chef Pascal Borrell has decided to drop anchor here having navigated the kitchens of several leading Parisian restaurants, including Ledoyen and Alain Passard. The main attraction here is of course fish, delivered still alive to Le Fanal every day. The creative, refined and sun-blessed dishes on offer include braised longline-caught hake with squid tagliatelle; baked wild turbot with saffron butter; blue lobster stew with Banyuls; fish tartare with herb-infused Argoudeil olive oil (an endemic and very rare variety); and local fish bouillabaisse.

name: Rustique
review: A wind of audacity has swept through Maxime Laurenson’s restaurant. Precise, legible dishes reveal each ingredient simply, with a firm focus on vegetables and a steadfast commitment to locally sourced produce. The single set menu (no choice) features a dozen or so courses, each of which stars the best of a region that spans Auvergne to the Alps. The interior is clearly inspired by nature (stone, wood, colour, plants) and the vibe is friendly. A down-to-earth establishment that is a favourite with Lyon’s foodies.

name: Louroc - Hôtel du Cap-Eden-Roc
review: The restaurant of this mythical luxury hotel plays its cards right. It combines attentive service (including the art of carving at a pedestal table), tableware produced for the most part by Provençal artisans, a breathtaking view of the Mediterranean, and the talents of chef Sébastien Broda. The pantry abounds with vegetables sourced exclusively in the hotel's own garden and from local market gardeners, as well as fish from small-scale fisheries and bespoke meats. This Mediterranean cuisine is exemplified by coherent dishes, such as trap-caught langoustines with a delicate celery jelly; red mullet roasted in a courgette flower; saddle of lamb from the Alpilles with Provençal herbs and pink garlic.

name: Hostellerie de Levernois
review: The tradition of hospitality is kept alive in this elegant house situated in the middle of extensive grounds dissected by a river. Here, chef Philippe Augé creates carefully prepared, seasonal cuisine based on classic principles, resulting in dishes such as green Acquerello risotto with frogs’ legs and Burgundy snails, and blue lobster with aubergine moussaka and a coriander and lemongrass shellfish jus. Make sure you save space for the cheese platter which includes over forty different varieties! A wine tasting cellar and shop complete the picture.

name: La Dune du Château de Sable
review: After a stint working with superstar chef, Gordon Ramsay, and another, more bistronomic experience in Lausanne, chef Anthony Hardy has been entrusted with the keys of Le Château de Sable. With a close-knit, devoted kitchen team, Hardy has confirmed his locavore tendencies with deceptively simple dishes: razor clams, garlic cream, samphire and Sturia caviar; lobster from the Breton coast, glazed turnip, Swiss chard, chorizo and lobster sauce. This is premium quality produce and the high standard is maintained from start to finish. Meals are served on the first floor beneath exposed wooden rafters… with a view of the coast to boot.

name: L'Aromate
review: An attractive restaurant situated near Place Masséna in the heart of Nice. The contemporary decor features a black, white and gold colour scheme; raw materials such as wood and granite; and a glass-fronted kitchen overlooking the dining room. All of this combines to provide the setting for a chef with an impressive career in top-notch restaurants behind him (Oustau de Baumanière, Plaza Athénée, Le Bristol, Louis XV etc). Here, the skilful and experienced chef prepares modern, creative and elegantly presented cuisine using top-quality ingredients from Nice and the Mediterranean region (San Remo prawns, red mullet, octopus etc).

name: La Table d'Asten
review: The first floor of this house overlooking the port is the backdrop of many a fine meal. After a remarkable career (Coquillage at Cancale, La Pyramide – Patrick Henriroux at Vienne and the K2 at Courchevel), chef Samuel Selosse now gives free rein to his creativity. Firmly rooted in the zeitgeist and always exquisitely presented, his cooking showcases first-rate ingredients, be they fish or vegetables, giving rise to delicacies such as his velvety soup of scallops, whiting from small boats or his fiendishly simple dark chocolate ganache. His sommelière wife runs the dining room with the same drive and sense of purpose.

name: Hedone
review: Don't be fooled by Balthazar Gonzalez's young age or his meek air: Hedone is proof that he is right on course and not about to waste time getting there! He has developed an effective concept: just five tables and a single set menu at lunchtime and at dinner, which allows him to give free rein to his creativity. You can expect to spend up to 3 or 4hr at the table, but the experience is more than worth the time! Excellent, even outstanding fresh produce, a preference for vegetables and seafood, explosive flavours with some real show-stopping moments. We can only salute his daring and applaud his skill.

name: Le Royal
review: Chef and Meilleur Ouvrier de France Jean-Denis Rieubland is in charge of this fine dining restaurant in the heart of the Champagne vineyards, where he creates delicate and meticulously presented dishes. You’ll acquaint yourself with his close attachment to the sea in several of his favourite dishes such as the roasted Dublin Bay prawns with Espelette chilli pepper and calf’s head cromesquis, and the combawa-flavoured crab, with caviar, mango and citrus fruit. À The contemporary dining room is devoted to champagne (note the gilded ceiling and the impressive, amber-coloured chandelier comprising 36 glass-blown shades) and to the women who played a role in the life of Napoleon Bonaparte, who once stopped off at this former post house. Superb contemporary guestrooms and a 1 500m² spa, not to mention the Bellevue brasserie offering simpler cuisine, complete the picture.

name: Le Fantin Latour - Stéphane Froidevaux
review: Year after year, Stéphane Froidevaux is enriching his culinary score and refining his style, armed with lashings of sincerity. Little by little, he has crafted a finely balanced cuisine, borne out by dishes, such as seared foie gras, sweetcorn and a stock perfumed with vin jaune; autumn ratatouille of crunchy and confit vegetables and a tonka bean/sea buckthorn vinaigrette. Meticulous, tasty and creative without being OTT, Stéphane’s handiwork bears the hallmark of his affinity with nature, depicted by the herbs and flowers he picks himself. The Brasserie du Fantin serves a bargain priced lunchtime menu, which is a hit with the regulars, as is the summer terrace.

name: Septime
review: Always on the lookout for new ideas, the team of Septime led by youthful Bertrand Grébaut stands out by its fresh, confident, always enthusiastic and occasionally even cheeky approach. Septime is the quintessence of the new breed of Parisian restaurants, resolutely hip and trendy, but also unwaveringly committed to good food. In the middle of Rue de Charonne, the venue is the summum of today’s modern codes and its spacious, workshop-cum-loft feel, untreated wooden tables and metal rafters offer a swish version of the current trend for industrial interiors. Slick, professional service. Of course, you may have to wait a while before you can get a foot in the door – in general bookings are made three weeks in advance…

name: Ceto
review: One of the most awaited hotel projects on the French Riviera of the last few years involved the top to toe renovation of the former Vista Palace on the heights of Roquebrune. Now called the Maybourne Riviera following a titanic overhaul lasting more than four years, virtuoso chef Mauro Colagreco (also of the Mirazur in Menton) has been entrusted with the culinary journey that takes our tastebuds on a whirlwind tour of Mediterranean delights. Precise dishes with crisp, straightforward, no-nonsense flavours are the name of the game, in a pared-down seafaring venue, perfectly suited to the menu, or on the terrace commanding an Instagram-worthy view of the sea, Monaco and Cap Martin. An unforgettable experience.

name: Avel Vor
review: An avel vor ("sea breeze" in Breton) blows through this high-calibre family-run establishment with a view of the Petite Mer de Gâvres. Chef Patrice Gahinet – experienced, passionate and generous (from amuse-bouche to dessert!) – pays tribute to Breton gastronomy, with the fresh sea air clearly suiting his refined cuisine. Having had the fishermen deliver his fish directly to his door, he elevates it, among other ingredients, to another level. Meanwhile, Catherine, the chef's sister, takes care of proceedings in the contemporary, refined dining space. The lunch menu served during the week is excellent value for money. Good wine list. Three pleasant guestrooms available.

name: Entre Vigne et Garrigue
review: Near Avignon, between cliffs and vineyards, this isolated Provençal farm does not compromise on authenticity. Sweet-scented gorse pervades the tastefully renovated interior, which sports a harmonious blend of period details and modern fixtures. In the kitchen, Serge Chenet, "Meilleur Ouvrier de France" and a Breton by birth, works with his son Maxime. Both share a love of all things natural and the seasonal ingredients gorged in flavour from this sun-drenched region. Together they concoct characterful Provençal-inspired market cuisine, such as Mediterranean red mullet in a fennel rouille, bouillabaisse jus or a duet of strawberries and confit of black olives, olive oil ice cream and a tapenade-flavoured madeleine...

name: Le Pont de l'Ouysse
review: On the banks of the Ouysse, an affluent of the Dordogne, this house is located at the foot of a cliff. In the Chambon family for five generations, it was originally built to feed the workers employed to rebuild the former bridge, swept away by a flood in 1966, one arch of which remains. Two brothers now run the family business, one in the dining room and one in the kitchen. Each expertly rendered classical recipe sings the praises of fantastic ingredients, such as pigeon cooked two ways, roast breasts and salmis of legs, or truffles harvested by the family. The patio shaded by linden trees adds the final irresistible flourish. Overnight stays possible in the hotel.

name: Sola
review: Just a stone's throw from the banks of the Seine, looking out onto Notre Dame, and yet here we are in Japan! This is Sola, with its tranquil interior done out in wood and, in the basement, the vaulted cellar with its tables arranged on tatami mats (be sure to remove your shoes). Japanese chef Kosuke Nabeta proposes a delicious fusion of the exacting standards of Japanese cuisine and the wealth of ingredients from rural France. He introduces us to traditional Japanese culinary techniques, which he wields with great skill (smoking, drying, marinating, fermenting, alternative cooking methods etc). Be sure to try his signature dish of foie gras and smoked eel! Harmonious, refined and personal food.

name: Quinsou
review: Opposite the legendary culinary school, Ferrandi, Quinsou (a chaffinch in Occitan) chirps a gourmet melody that has every chance of influencing the great chefs of tomorrow. In a modern, sharp-edged interior (cement tiles, bare lightbulbs), the chef, formerly of Sergent Recruteur, Antonin Bonnet, crafts distinctive dishes, which are unencumbered, delicate, sensitive and free of unnecessary frills, allowing the ingredient to shout its name. Line-fished seabass from Saint Jean de Luz, bouilla-thai sauce, Salers fillet of beef with roast cèpe mushrooms, garlic cream with sweet almonds… A single set menu that matches the chef’s enthusiasm.

name: Mavrommatis
review: Cypriot chef Andreas Mavrommatis and his teams orchestrate generous, well-crafted cuisine inspired by classic Gallic traditions using the best Greek ingredients: spanakopita-style morels, grilled squid and confit of onions in xinomavro, Lozère lamb with halloumi… A Greek culinary adventure that varies according to the season and the whims of the chef in a stylish, minimalist setting that provides the perfect foil to the inspired culinary journey.

name: A Casa di Ma
review: Lumio, a village in Upper Corsica, is the quintessence of light and flavour… The chef conjures up subtle, gourmet fare, enhanced by creative touches, and always respectful of the fine ingredients with which the island abounds. The “Di Mà” medley of garden vegetables or the roast seabass in mandarin oil with smoked carrots, stock of fish bones with citrus fruit, orange and calamansi caramel are amazing! The contemporary dining room leads onto an attractive terrace, setting the idyllic stage to savour minimalist recipes drenched in Mediterranean and Corsican flavours. Prolong this magical experience and spend the night at the hotel facing the Bay of Calvi.

name: Flaveurs
review: A colourful decor with a carpeted floor and chestnut-wood tables provides the setting for this fine gourmet restaurant situated in the heart of Valence’s old town. It was perhaps his grandfather’s job as a caterer that influenced the career choice of young chef Baptiste Poinot, who studied at the hotel school in Vienne, and took lessons with Michel Chabran in Pont-de-l’Isère, as well as with Anne-Sophie Pic and Joël Robuchon. Much thought has clearly gone into each of the dishes created by this sensitive chef, who seeks above all to convey an emotion through his cuisine using top-quality ingredients and highly skilled technique. The resulting flavours – sensations produced both by the taste and aroma of his ingredients – are particularly enticing.

name: Le Raisin
review: This plush and elegant place in the heart of Pont-de-Vaux can be relied upon for excellent traditional cuisine. Scallops with cauliflower; frogs' legs with parsley; Bresse chicken cooked two ways… The classics are subtly reworked by this seasoned chef, who cultivates finesse as much as originality; he revises his menu every month to reflect his current inspirations and the fresh produce on the market stalls. The wine list is also worth perusing, with a good choice of Burgundy labels. Attentive and smiling service.

name: Cyril Attrazic
review: To quote Cyril Attrazic: “I was in love with the Maison, even before I fell for cooking”. To explain, the Maison is the family hotel restaurant business founded by his grandmother in the heart of Aubrac, a high-altitude plateau that could be mistaken for the Mongolian Steppes. By virtue of farming traditions and the harsh climate, the restaurant doesn’t mess about with hospitality, albeit in a modern vein. The chef scrupulously applies the advice of his mentor, Michel Bras: only cook local ingredients (…) with an identity. He does just this, showcasing a giant cèpe picked in the next-door woods or the legendary Aubrac beef rich in the flavour of a thousand flowers, all of which is served in “his ecosystem”. It would be difficult to find anywhere better to taste and smell Lozère.

name: Accents Table Bourse
review: "An accent indicates where a person comes from; it tells us about their country, their region and their history. It is this idea of openness and discovery that I want to uphold, a cuisine made up of encounters and exchanges." These are the words of Ayumi Sugiyama, the Japanese proprietor of this contemporary restaurant with a Scandinavian vibe, as well as its pastry chef. The dishes are a combination of classic fare (succulent hare à la royale in season), more daring creations and subtle experiments with roasted and smoked flavours. From start to finish, balance and precision… as is the case with the owner's desserts and the sommelier's judicious advice. Warm and vibrant service.

name: Clos du Cèdre
review: An elegant master winegrower’s house, steeped in character and style, surrounded by a lush garden where a handful of tables are laid come summertime… The idyllic scene is set to sample the work of youthful chef Jordan Billan, who is brilliantly pursuing this house’s heritage. Pure-bred French classics deftly and delicately curated and tailored to today’s modern palates, using outstanding produce: crisp, crunchy langoustine, gribiche sauce and capers; poultry, cream of broccoli, quinoa and radishes, mustard and honey gravy… This recently revamped establishment also offers charming guestrooms that effortlessly blend tradition and modernity.

name: Sylvestre Wahid - Les Grandes Alpes
review: Sylvestre Wahid now plays host to diners in the heart of the resort. Assisted by his loyal team, the chef has gone with an intimate atmosphere for this new Alpine venture: from his open kitchen, he regales only around 15 guests per sitting in an exclusive setting. This tailor-made fine dining experience draws on his signature dishes, revisited at this mountain location according to his inspiration: Roscoff crab or lemon and seaweed dessert. It is safe to say that the chef has successfully acclimatised to Courchevel. Magnificent produce, luxury ingredients, comforting sauces, expert seasonings, impeccable technical skill and, above all, emotion shine through the generous tasting menu.

name: Le Mascaret
review: Very attached to his native Manche (the northern département with Cherbourg at its tip), the adventurous Philippe Hardy has worked in some prestigious Michelin-starred restaurants and in the kitchen of the French ambassador in Sofia. It was there that he met his wife, Nadia, a former principal dancer. Together they have transformed this former girls' boarding school into a chic and sweet little hotel-restaurant. All around, the garden and the vegetable garden thrive, providing vegetables and aromatic herbs grown from saved seeds. The other big thing at Le Mascaret is the sea: the chef never misses an opportunity to make a delicious dish with wild fish and shellfish, at a bargain price.

name: Nature
review: Nicholas Gautier is thriving in his new HQ in Armentières. His natural cuisine, underscored by solid classical foundations, is perfectly in tune with the zeitgeist and seeks to enhance splendid seasonal regional produce: fish from Boulogne and Dunkerque, among others. The food is served in surprise menus ranging from three to six courses. We adored the seabream with oxalis and black garlic as well as the line-fished croaker and white butter. A banquet of balanced and authentic flavours.

name: Origines
review: Is Adrien Descouls's inspiration for his exceptionally fresh cuisine his native Auvergne? Close to Issoire, in a modern building perched right next to the 14C castle, he demonstrates his talent without overplaying his hand: well-selected ingredients, showcasing of the local terroir, and all the ambition that comes with being a young chef. Lovely, comfortable guestrooms with pretty views of the surroundings.

name: Shabour
review: The man behind Shabour is Assaf Granit, the famous Israeli chef. Already at the helm of Balagan (also in Paris) and owner of a dozen restaurants in Jerusalem and London, he is also a TV chef, whose gigs include hosting the Israeli equivalent of Kitchen Nightmares. He set his sights on this 17C building in a lively neighbourhood between rue Saint-Denis and rue Montorgueil. Here we rediscover his trademarks: a lively atmosphere, rough and ready decoration with metal technical ducts visible on the ceiling, subdued lighting... and, of course, generous and surprising creative cuisine replete with Mediterranean influences, whose freshness gives it wings – for example, carrots with slow-cooked egg, tahimi foam, salmon eggs and tzimmes, or beef cheek and oxtail with mushrooms and polenta or, for dessert, chocolate mousse with olive oil and Maldon salt.

name: The Marcel
review: This historic eatery, a former working-class bolthole, is enjoying a second lease of life under the auspices of its owners. On one side is the Rio, a cultural venue which serves tapas to a backdrop of live music, while on the other is a gourmet restaurant graced by a spacious dining room, which commands a view of the kitchen and sports a vintage counter and bench seats, exposed timbers, bare stone walls and works of art. Chef Denis Martin expertly crafts recipes focused on Mediterranean delicacies, such as red mullet and a soft bread with squid ink, crunchy vegetables, shellfish and a stock of fishbones, or octopus in preserved tomatoes and olives. Heroically wondrous cooking…

name: Granite
review: Heading up this modern restaurant is Tom Meyer, a young chef who earned his stripes at the Hôtel de Ville in Crissier, La Chèvre d'Or in Èze, alongside Anne-Sophie Pic and who was awarded the title of MOF in 2022. He works with a dynamic, close-knit team with a clear vision: zero waste, zero plastic and well-being in the workplace. Through intelligently devised set menus, the chef celebrates well-sourced ingredients such as green asparagus from les Landes roasted on a Japanese BBQ or turbot in a subtle geranium-perfumed champagne sauce. It's fresh, delicate and meticulous: a real treat.

name: Restaurant De Lauzun
review: Pézenas has many claims to fame: Molière, for example, lived here for a while, it was the birthplace of a 1960’s French actor Boby Lapointe and it is now the HQ of Matthieu De Lauzun. Established in a winery, this new venue has enabled the youthful chef to unveil his manifold talents. A handsome contemporary interior, depicted by stone, wood and copper, sets the scene for flavoursome food rich in southern accents, such as the pastilla of poultry in a beetroot cannelloni (his signature dish), or melt-in-the-mouth lamb, cooked three times, in a tajine style. Splendid wine bin. Pop into the museum devoted to Boby, before or after your meal.

name: L'Or Bleu
review: Having gained experience in respected Michelin-starred restaurants in Switzerland and Chantilly, chef Alain Montigny (Meilleur Ouvrier de France 2004) is now at the helm at the exquisite Tiara Yaktsa hotel, which overlooks the sea from its vantage point facing the Esterel mountains. His delicious Mediterranean-inspired recipes change almost daily depending on availability and are balanced and delicately flavoured thanks to the use of top-quality ingredients and superb technique. Highlights include lobster, caviar and celeriac cream and a remarkable baked stone bass with pumpkin and cep gnocchi. The view of the sea and the red rocks of the Esterel from the terrace is truly spectacular. A treat for all the senses.

name: La Table - Hôtel Clarance
review: In the heart of historic Lille, this restaurant is housed in an 18C mansion that cannot fail but catch the eye. Making the most of meticulously sourced local produce and the hotel's own herb garden, the food dexterously weaves a culinary patchwork of different traditions, demonstrating a particular talent for fish, without forgetting some mouth-watering cuts of meat. You will be seated in one of two dining rooms appointed with period wainscoting, in the former library, which is home to a snug table at the foot of a spiral staircase embedded in the bookshelves, or, when the weather is fine, on the terrace overlooking the treelined grounds.

name: L'Atelier Yssoirien
review: This owner-chef, who was born in Auvergne of Dutch parents, deploys his culinary talent in this modern, designer-inspired workshop, depicted by an open kitchen, grey stone floor, rough wood planking and bare light bulbs. An inspired mechanic, he gets a kick out of fine-tuning dishes that are as delicate as they are inventive, made with ingredients from nearby (Boudes lamb, Mézenc beef, Billom black garlic) and further afield (brill from Brittany, Vendée eels). The memory of his beef tartare, wild white asparagus, strawberry pickles and a cream of egg yolk, beurre blanc and herb dashi lingers with us still. The greeting and the service are both professional and refreshingly unstarched.

name: L'Alter-Native
review: An Alter-Native, or another birth, even a rebirth, is how Gilles Goujon views this project in Béziers. In the town where he grew up and studied, the chef of the 3-star Auberge du Vieux Puits that needs no introduction, develops a seafaring, vegetable, sustainable concept that explores new culinary vistas. With vegetables from the aquaponics garden and delicacies drenched in southern sunshine, his executive chef, Quentin Pellestor-Veyrier rustles up generous, straightforward, appetising fare: stuffed tomatoes, goat’s cheese (Carrus farm) and basil pistou; estofinado (fish fritters), trout roe and Caesarean caviar (the fish isn’t killed to remove the eggs), with the backup of the emerging talents of the Goujon brothers, Enzo and Axel. Pleasant alfresco space in fine weather.

name: Marcore
review: After regaling the Pigalle neighbourhood in their Bouillon, Marc Favier and Aurélie Alary have elected to re-offend at the Marcore (a phonetic combination of their first names…), combining their manifold talents. They have created a multi-facetted establishment from the old Versance, on the corner of Rue des Panoramas with a bistro bar downstairs, gourmet nosh upstairs and a takeaway deli on the opposite side of the street. Chef Favier is a fervent believer in feel-good cooking that is technically understated with a spotlight on quality ingredients (John Dory, red tuna, wagyu beef). The result is legible, straightforward and finger-licking good!

name: Manoir de Lan-Kerellec
review: In this magical setting, the ceiling's splendid wooden rafters form the shape of an inverted boat hull, while the views extend out to the Channel and local islands. Young chef Anthony Avoine, originally from Normandy and formerly second in command here, is now at the helm of this gourmet restaurant occupying a beautiful manor house. The freshest locally sourced Breton ingredients are showcased on the menu which features a wonderfully creative array of dishes that often combine meat and fish together. Examples include John Dory, buckwheat pancake and pig’s trotter; and brill, tortellini with capers, baby spinach, coriander and a charcuterie sauce.

name: Substance
review: Matthias Marc – a chef who has honed his skills in a series of prestigious establishments (Le Saint-James in Bouliac, Le Meurice and Lasserre in Paris), and was a semi-finalist in French TV's Top Chef 2021 – serves a single set menu (five, seven or nine courses) that favours short supply chains and fine ingredients (turbot, bonito). The dishes stick close to the seasons and incorporate pleasing nods to his native Jura. Gnocchi cooked with plant charcoal, coulis of fermented watercress and Morteau sausage jus or lobster, cherry tomatoes coated in marrow bone and jus infused with geranium serve to illustrate his creative and readily plant-based signature style. A terrific list of 1 000 wines (including 200 champagnes), mostly organic or natural. Uninhibited, lively cooking: an excellent place.

name: Il Cortile
review: In a pedestrian street of historic Mulhouse, welcome to this 16C house, whose reputation is firmly established among the locals. Since 2001, chef Jean-Michel Feger has been devising Mediterranean inspired recipes, deploying modern techniques and consummate skill to curate enticing dishes that are rich in authentic Italian accents: vitello tonnato, pesto of dried tomatoes, deep-fried buffalo milk mozzarella. In fine weather, meals are leisurely served alfresco on the patio in a small courtyard. Pleasantly casual service.

name: Contraste
review: Why the name? This restaurant brings together one chef from Brittany, Erwan Ledru, and one from Perpignan, Kevin de Porre, who are childhood buddies; secondly, the premises combine a stylish vintage vibe set off by contemporary details; and finally, a reference to one of the greatest Selosse champagne vintages. The concise menu (flanked by a lunchtime menu and a tasting menu) unveils up-to-date, meticulous, flavoursome cuisine which calls upon top-drawer seasonal ingredients. The surf and turf combinations are particularly appetising (Brittany lobster and sarrazin wheat; monkfish, shellfish and Spanish chorizo or Spanish pork and Cancale oysters).

name: La Chapelle Saint-Martin
review: On the doorstep of Limoges, this small castel, once the home of a porcelain manufacturer, is strewn with knickknacks, antiques and old paintings. Chef Gilles Dudognon and his team meticulously scour the region for fine produce, which they blend into distinctive classical recipes, frequently sprinkled with inventive touches. After gazing at the grounds, dig into the “Timeless” Saint Martin porkpie (sweetbread, poultry, foie gras), line-caught seabass or stuffed pak-choi, resembling a ginger-sesame ceviche. Delightful guestrooms.

name: Gaya par Pierre Gagnaire
review: On the site of the former Ferme Saint Simon (an institution dating back to 1933), Gaya par Pierre Gagnaire has all the distinctive signs of a gourmet temple and its bright blue façade and pretty awnings catch the eye, as is often the case of select establishments. An exclusive clientele comes to wind down in the chic brasserie that is fashionably stark but has retained its gleaming copper and magnificent bar. The focus is on good food in a bid to cater to modern French sensibilities with a seafaring slant (carpaccio of seabream, pink radishes and grapefruit; giant langoustine, cream of Paimpol beans, scallion onions) and a fondness for veggies, although meat now also makes the occasional guest star appearance on the menu (“Venetian style” calf’s liver, for example).

name: Signature
review: The ebullient Coline Faulquier celebrates the Mediterranean virtues of sharing by means of a positively sun-drenched menu (also available in half portions so that you can try several dishes) and a tasting menu. The ingredients are carefully selected – from organic market gardeners and wild herb gatherers, fish from the Mediterranean – and you will enjoy tucking into her signature "Aïoli", comprising a mosaic of crunchy vegetables, monkfish and hake, aioli (both as a sauce and iced), ink tuile; or her fine catch of the day served au naturel with a light black-garlic glaze, blanquette-style bone jus, Buddha's hand, asparagus… Personality, enthusiasm, flavour: a true signature style.

name: Le Rigmarole
review: Chef Robert Compagnon and Californian pastry chef Jessica Yang have combined their talents to create this atypical restaurant, which is already hugely popular in Paris. Don't be fooled by the name – it could not be further from the truth! Nothing unnecessarily complicated in this tiny establishment, where conviviality and enjoyment are the order of the day: grilled meats, fresh pasta, nods to Italy, France and Japan, small plates to be shared among friends, chatting with a glass of wine in hand. Top-notch produce, as fresh as it gets.

name: Le Lièvre Gourmand
review: The chef of this establishment on the banks of the Loire trained with the Meilleur family at La Bouitte, and Au Rendez-vous des Pêcheurs, in Blois. Tristan Robreau chooses his suppliers carefully, and delivers fusion cuisine inspired by his travels in Asia. It has a well-formed culinary identity, for example, dried trout soba, Thai garlic; turbot cardamom, red endive. Terrific quality ingredients, confident technique and arresting flavours. This is balanced cuisine that continues to deliver on its promise: Le Lièvre Gourmand is still the best restaurant in town.

name: L'Ours
review: Jacky Ribault (Qui Plume la Lune, in the 11th arrondissement) makes no secret that he considers this Ours (bear), near the château de Vincennes, to be the pinnacle of his career. He designed it in his image, mixing volumes and shapes in a felicitous blend of wood, metal, stone and leather, creating a coherent setting for culinary creations of which he has the secret. Guaranteed to lift your spirits, the food is rich in everything we love in this seasoned chef, as talkative as he is enthusiastic: his instinctive hallmark, exquisite plating and raw inspirations that subtly underscore first-class ingredients. For example, the menu features understated Japanese notes, as well as more traditional fare, such as guinea fowl or brill with risotto of Venere rice in beetroot… A place of culinary pilgrimage if ever there was...

name: Les Sources de Fontbelle
review: Five minutes from downtown Angoulême, brace yourself for the shock of this architectural behemoth made entirely out of metal, glass and concrete, facing the forest. At the helm, chef Guillaume Veyssière signs creative cuisine that demonstrates his consummate skill. The bold striking setting suits him like a glove and his flair for theatrically presenting the appetisers is second to none. His endeavours to keep it local are both laudable, a case in point being the Gascon pork chop with roasted parsley roots, and efficacious. He also enjoys addressing flavoursome tongue-in-cheek references to rural traditions with his new spin on moules marinières and his Charentes casse-croûte (snack).

name: Le Duèze - Château de Mercuès
review: Clinging to the top of a hill overlooking the Lot valley, this superb medieval castle, altered countless times, has survived the centuries with grace. Having relinquished its position as a seat of episcopal power, it now has luxurious guestrooms and a fine dining restaurant in the capable hands of chef Julien Poisot, who at one point worked for Bernard Loiseau. A far cry from historical fare, contemporary cuisine is served within these centuries-old walls. Through his tasty dishes that offer a wonderful new take on tradition, the talented chef creates an ode to the terroir of the Lot. Choose from the list of very decent wines from the property to accompany your food, and when the weather is fine, opt for a table on the terrace in the main courtyard.

name: La Table d'Uzès
review: We have no doubt that this Table is THE gastronomic venue of the area. Two plush, stylish dining rooms with two equally swish patios, elegantly laid tables, and above all, an enthusiastic, exuberant chef, Christophe Ducros. His balanced, unequivocal dishes are pure-bred southern in inspiration and heritage. For example, his famous Costières pigeon, roasted whole; biscuit of Mediterranean seabass and bourride (fish, seafood and garlic); different textures of pears/hazelnuts, with bergamot as a guiding thread… The overriding coherence is crystal clear. Seated on a patio, shaded by a linden tree, you will be able to savour every instant of this gourmet escapade to the fill.

name: Le Art
review: In the kitchen of this magnificent 18C bastide, chef Matthieu Dupuis-Baumal serves boldly inventive dishes, in which Provençal notes meet subtle Japanese influences. The flavours are clear and always controlled, and each recipe brandishes a confident culinary personality. The setting is magical, complete with a magnificent terrace, and makes for a sumptuous backdrop for this firework display of flavours. The wonderful wine list includes a selection from the château.

name: Nakatani
review: After a decade working with Hélène Darroze, Shinsuke Nakatani is at the helm of this elegant, restful restaurant, decked in soothing colours and natural materials. Thanks to his acute flair for seasoning, cooking and presentation, this ultra-talented Japanese chef concocts a pedigree French score in tune with the seasons, in which the flavours and textures are seamlessly combined to create a consistent whole. Guests can savour a single set menu (4 dishes at lunchtime, 6 in the evening and which changes every two months), served by a crack team that is as low-profile as it is professional. Given the limited number of seats (just 16), it is advisable to book ahead.

name: Ivan Vautier
review: Proud Normandy chef Ivan Vautier, the former second-in-command to Michel Bruneau at La Bourride, and who also made his name at Les Crayères in Reims and at Le Divellec, the Parisian temple of fish and seafood, has now taken over this property away from the town centre and converted it into a space with a restrained contemporary feel. Proud of his terroir, this chef aims to showcase Normandy’s very best ingredients through each of his recipes: salmon from Cherbourg; Normandy asparagus; cereal-fed Normandy pork etc. Guests can extend their visit with a stay in the hotel, where they can also enjoy its spa facilities.

name: La Gourmandière - La Table d'Olivier
review: Like all self-respecting Bretons, Olivier Samson spread his wings to undertake a voyage that took him from Geneva’s La Réserve Beaulieu in the Parc des Eaux Vives to Anne-Sophie Pic’s establishment. The voyager and his wife have now sailed home, dropping anchor in this 19C stone farmhouse on the doorstep of Vannes. Seafood is one of Olivier’s signature themes as his seafaring dishes illustrate (langoustines, pak choi, green beans and Kari Gosse stock or blue lobster, courgette flowers, blackcurrant and fish stock). His talent for enhancing produce from sardines to pigeon, served with seasonal fruit and vegetables, is both commendable and impressive.

name: La Vieille Fontaine
review: Wood panelling, mouldings, tapestries and a fireplace are all part of the Provençal elegance of this historical establishment. Chef Pascal Auger is in his element here, cooking up delicious cuisine that is redolent of the South of France, as precise as it is well crafted, a veritable roll call of colours and flavours. For example, the monkfish tail with garden peas, raspberry and Mediterranean mussel or the tangy sweetness of finger lime with local strawberries and dill – a simply exquisite meal. On sunny days (and there are many in Avignon) you can enjoy these delicacies under the hundred-year-old plane tree on the pretty terrace facing the old fountain.

name: CIBO
review: Angelo Ferrigno, former chef of Maison des Cariatides, is committed to sourcing his ingredients solely within a 200km radius – so the menu features plenty of trout and catfish rather than turbot. He rustles up food in the zeitgeist rich in raw, natural and Scandinavian influences, in the shape of a single set menu in which acidic, bitter and umami flavours are more important than flashy technique or fancy presentation, without forgetting splendid vegetarian dishes. Excellent tips from the wine waiter. Be warned: tables are snapped up fast!

name: Ogata
review: Ogata could well be Japan’s other Embassy of Paris. This temple dedicated to Japanese art de vivre is located in a private mansion in the Marais, masterminded by Shinichiro Ogata, a world-famous designer and restaurateur, who seeks “beauty and balance in all things” (his own words). The essentially traditional Japanese food sports an omakase spirit, through a tasting menu comprised of immaculate seasonal produce that is perfectly suited to the restaurant’s suave sophistication. We tasted some remarkable starters (spinach, roast asparagus, fried squid, sashimi of horse mackerel), as was the tamago yaki, a subtly perfumed omelette roll. The best seats are at the counter. Pop into the shop or art gallery before leaving…

name: Auguste
review: In Gaël Orieux's small restaurant – barely 30 covers – the elegant contemporary interior with deceptively simplistic lines exudes an unexpected calm. A chic and "classy" space where you can enjoy a judiciously modern cuisine: "black pearl" cupped oysters, seawater jelly, horseradish mousse, Comice pear; sea bass with tomato compote, orange foam with cinnamon flowers. An enticingly varied menu made using high-quality produce. Gaël Orieux sources his supplies from the market and has made the choice to serve only fish species that are not endangered (black mullet, meagre, pout). As for the wine selection, it offers the opportunity to try something new at a reasonable price.

name: L'Impertinent
review: This place lives up to its name: insolent, cheeky and even irreverent! There is something rather rock'n'roll about German-born Fabian Feldmann, a creative chef who likes to break the rules. Which isn't to say he doesn't know the rules! This rebellious cook was classically trained in the finest establishments, like L'Oasis in La Napoule and Pierre Gagnaire in Paris. In his Biarritz restaurant, he gives free rein to his imagination – sometimes outlandish but always spot on. Beautiful raw ingredients, most notably fish from the Ciboure fish market, are cooked and seasoned with some originality. Semi-cooked and smoked mackerel with two servings of white asparagus (grilled and raw); roast lamb with celeriac, a herb and tangy mustard jus; Corsican pomelo, tarragon ice cream, almond cream and aniseed meringue.

name: La Condesa
review: La Condesa is a district of Mexico City as well as the restaurant of Indra Carrillo, who came to Paris from Mexico to study at the Paul Bocuse institute before working at leading restaurants such as the Bristol and Astrance. Trained by Meilleur Ouvrier de France chefs (notably fish and bread), Indra also spent time in Japan. Although his techniques are French, his culinary inspiration comes from many different cultures, including Mexico. A perfect example is his sweetcorn agnoletti pasta infused in broth with a spicy Mexican oil which is well on the way to becoming his signature dish. The chic, pared-down interior adds the final flourish.

name: Le Puits du Trésor
review: Jean-Marc Boyer is a true craftsman, and his passion is unmistakable: he finds inspiration for his cooking during solitary walks in the surrounding hills. Aromatic herbs, wild asparagus and wild garlic are used to dress up his colourful dishes that are rife with clean, well-handled flavours, such as mackerel marinated in cucumber or monkfish with carrots and ricotta ravioli. He arranges everything into a single set menu, over the course of which the surprises keep coming. The interior, designed by Régis Dho in a Japanese vein, provides the perfect foil to the chef's pared-down culinary vision. A note for those who are pushed for time: this is a restaurant with a leisurely pace.

name: Le Panoramique - Domaine de la Corniche
review: This charming hotel perched on a chalk cliff was commissioned in 1908 by King Leopold II of Belgium so that he could entertain his lover, Blanche de Vaughan, but it now caters to lovers of fine food. Sourcing local produce is central to the Domaine’s philosophy: scallops from the Bay of the Seine River, farm-reared lamb from nearby breeders and fresh fruit and vegetables from neighbours’ gardens and orchards. The resulting food overflows with fresh, crisp, wholesome flavours, while black truffles, foie gras from Landes (of course), langoustines and wild turbot nobly enhance creative cooking. When the weather is fine, alfresco dining on the terrace gazing down over the meanders of the Seine is an unforgettable experience in this aptly named establishment.

name: La Table Breizh Café
review: This Franco-Japanese gourmet establishment is on the first floor of a crêperie: welcome to the world of Bertrand Larcher. A champion of sarrazin wheat and Brittany’s culture, Bertrand started off by making pancakes in Japan, before returning to France with the same passion. Now in a dining room overlooking the bay of Mont Saint Michel, chef Fumio Kudaka mixes Brittany’s produce with Japanese techniques and seasonings. The lobster is served with seaweed, the chicken leg is marinated and fried karaage style and the brioche is filled with yuzu-miso cream and served with an ice cream of Japanese cherry petals. Top-notch ingredients, meticulous cooking, high-precision seasonings and lashings of delicacy. Simpler weekday lunchtime menu.

name: ES
review: This place is run by Takayuki Honjo, a Japanese chef who is a fan of French culture and cuisine. Having trained in prestigious establishments (Astrance in Paris, Quintessence in Tokyo, Mugaritz in the Basque country), he has designed his restaurant down to the smallest detail: a white and pared-down dining room, almost monastic, in which the modern furniture does not seek to attract attention. In this context, the meal resembles a kind of ceremony. Foie gras and sea urchins, or pigeon and cocoa: surprising pairings whose flavours mingle intimately. The harmony of his subtle creations recalls this talented young man's Japanese heritage.

name: L'Anthocyane
review: For chef Marc Briand, the experience is what matters before all else. Installed in the centre of Lannion, he rustles up modern Gallic fare, dotted with Japanese overtones, in tribute to his avowed passion for the Land of the Rising Sun. as a result, some of his high-precision recipes, based on super-fresh Brittany produce (langoustine, lobster, John Dory), are sprinkled with Japanese ingredients such as yuzu, shiitake, miso, etc. Lashings of imagination, art-directed plating, stylish elegance and high-flying technique complete this culinary score. Let’s not forget the warm, colourful interior.

name: Les Pêcheurs
review: Les Pêcheurs boasts a delightful, slightly elevated setting by the water's edge, hence the stunning view of the Lérins islands and the foothills of the Esterel mountains. Trained at this very restaurant, Nice-born chef Nicolas Rondelli went on to work in the kitchens of Alain Llorca, Michel Del Burgo, Jacques Chibois and the Negresco. His contemporary, seasonally inspired cuisine teems with the flavours of Southern France and showcases Mediterranean fish such as red mullet, John Dory, turbot and sea bass, alongside superb meat (suckling pig, venison and free-range veal). Whatever he cooks, he champions local producers and suppliers such as fisherman Tony from the port of Le Croûton, located just 50m from the restaurant!

name: Chez Michèle
review: Once a village café, then a family inn (revamped from top to toe), it is now a gourmet table with an enviable reputation in the Moselle Lake district. This illustrious restaurant is now in the capable hands of Bruno Poiré, Michèle’s son. After learning the ropes in the family business as a teenager, the chef honed his skills out on the road, in particular with Georges Blanc at Vonnas and Antoine Westermann at the Buerehiesel. He signs precise, generous dishes in tune with the zeitgeist that reveal a soft spot for Mediterranean recipes. A fine dining experience in a pleasantly stylish setting, further enhanced by polished, attentive service.

name: Les Hautes Roches
review: Overlooking the River Loire, this grand 18C manor house is at one with the tufa cliff, with its beautiful troglodytic guestrooms built into the rock. Here you will find chef Didier Edon, who is originally from Brittany but whose heart belongs to the Touraine region. He brings to the table a solid grounding and plenty of experience with which to create lovely traditional cuisine. The menu, dominated by fish and seafood, includes established favourites such as turbot in Béarnaise sauce, roasted langoustines, white asparagus and morels, or the soufflé with Grand Marnier orange liqueur. Another "must" is the terrace above the river.

name: René'Sens par Jean-François Bérard
review: Following on from his father René, Jean-Francois Bérard has taken over the family business – a fine restaurant in a fortified village on a hillside overlooking the picturesque Le Castellet. The splendid view embraces pine forest, palm trees and vineyards. The cook is also a keen gardener, and his green fingers are ever poking about in the next-door cottage garden, as the menus entitled “Vegetal” or “Walk in the garden” bear witness. Working solely with top-quality produce, enhanced by gutsy stocks, subtle emulsions and numerous home-grown herbs, the chef seeks to exalt the intrinsic flavour of each ingredient. Heritage and innovation are brought together in the quest for taste in a warm, unstarched ambience.

name: La Mirande
review: The warmth of the sun, the shimmer of colours, the sense of generosity: Florent Pietravalle's delicate, tasty dishes extol the South of France, the produce of its land, and its traditions (langoustine, John Dory etc). Here, everything is on point: from the bold and memorable flavours to the professional, distinguished and smiling service. Note the surprise menu based on remarkable, perfectly sourced seasonal produce from the region (at the end of the meal, you get a map with the names and locations of the suppliers). His dishes, at once technically sound and spontaneous, draw on his time with Jean-Luc Rabanel and especially Pierre Gagnaire. The setting is just as delightful: a superb 18C interior with a gorgeous garden, within the historical walls of La Mirande, a town house right next to the Palais des Papes. Delicious food in an elegant setting.

name: Roza
review: Shredded skate, pork fritos, lemon, espuma of brown butter; crunchy sweetbread, a variety of Jerusalem artichoke, pomelos, walnuts and citrus cream… Such are a few of the delicacies that await you at Roza, in the heart of downtown Nantes. The imagination of Jean-Françoise Pantaleon, who hails from the Loire region, knows no bounds. A fervent champion of his region, he does wonders with local ingredients, crafting dishes depicted by lashings of character, textbook precision and flavours to die for. The friendly, casual vibe is perfectly suited to the fashionable interior, further adding to this fine dining experience. A venue that stands out from the crowd.

name: Speiseberg
review: You will need to allow yourself a little time, but a meal here in the gourmet restaurant of the traditional Bergschenke – a Halle institution – is a real culinary experience! Chef Konstantin Kuntzsch shines a spotlight on excellent produce with his modern, pared-down and intensely flavoured cuisine. The single set menu on offer features dishes such as langoustine with melon, dashi and cucumber or young venison with celeriac and onion. The serving of the set menu begins at 7.15pm for all guests, with a maximum of 15 people taking part each evening. The lucky few take their seats in the modern, rather minimalist interior of this restaurant that enjoys a fabulous location on the upper bank of the Saale. Friendly and professional front-of-house team. A few lunch options on Sat and Sun, as well as coffee and cake.

name: Aska
review: Two restaurants with Swedish names under one roof. In contrast to the original restaurant Storstad, Aska is a compact sushi restaurant with a decidedly personal touch. The name translates as "ash", and the interior is accordingly dark in hue. Diners take their seats at the counter or one of the few booth tables to enjoy authentic sushi in the form of an eight- or 10-course set menu, served with two additional recommendations. Having learned his craft in his hometown of Osaka, sushi master Atsushi Sugimoto now transforms premium ingredients into the best classic sushi to be found far and wide! The attentive and charming front-of-house staff will be able to provide just the right sake to accompany your set menu, plus there is a "flat rate" for all-you-can-drink mineral water and green tea – a highly unusual offer in Germany.

name: PUR
review: The picturesque location on the Obersalzberg affords a fantastic mountain panorama for diners to enjoy! But the fine dining restaurant of the luxurious Kempinski Hotel Berchtesgaden has plenty more to offer than the view. First, the chic interior with its elegantly pared-down and modern design draws on a colour palette of soothing, harmonious tones. Then there is Ulrich Heimann's cuisine: he continues to impress with a tasting menu that is available in a varying number of courses. These are modern dishes prepared using select ingredients that follow the seasons. Not only is the food excellent, but the service is very friendly and obliging. On warm summer days, you can make the most of the wonderful terrace.

name: Mühle
review: As the new chef at the helm of Mühle, the fine dining restaurant of the small boutique hotel of the same name, Niclas Nussbaumer shows off his outstanding culinary credentials. He serves modern French cuisine replete with seasonal and creative influences, as well as the odd fascinating Japanese touch. The first-rate produce is often sourced from the region but also from further afield. The set menu is available in five to seven courses – opt for the cheese course to round off your meal. Harmonious wine pairings; there are also sake recommendations. The charming service team has a pleasingly personal touch, and the same goes for the chefs. Located a little off the beaten track, this pretty building dates back to 1603. There are also guestrooms – these are tastefully done out in a modern regional style that is in keeping with the restaurant.

name: Pietsch
review: An interesting modern concept that makes for a memorable dining experience. It all kicks off at 7.30pm when the guests for the evening arrive. At 7.45pm service begins with the first dish of the 17-course single set menu. In this trendy urban restaurant, diners sit on comfortable bar stools at the counter, from where they can watch the chefs at work in the open kitchen. This creates a sociable and entertaining atmosphere, with proceedings running almost like a theatre performance. There is a sense of invention in this pleasingly balanced and pared-down French-Japanese crossover cuisine that draws on regional influences. Not only are there fine wines, but also great home-made juices. A word to the wise: be sure to take a stroll through the tranquil village before dinner.

name: Traube
review: A beautiful historical house in a small wine-growing village. The couple who run the place have plenty of experience in high-end gastronomy (Maaemo in Oslo, La Vie in Osnabrück), and it's immediately obvious that professionals are at work here. Headed up by the charming Daniela Hasse, the front-of-house team is pleasantly informal, chatty and highly professional. Canadian-born head chef Brian Wawryk never fails to impress with his meticulous craftsmanship and well-balanced dishes. His modern cuisine has a clear Nordic character, but also focuses on regional tradition, including ingredients preserved the year before. Insider tip: in winter, try to bag yourself the small table in the "Kuschelecke" ("cosy corner") by the tiled stove! The leafy terrace beckons in summer. Bear in mind that Traube is also a great place to stay overnight.

name: Stadtpfeiffer
review: It isn't only concerts that attract visitors to the Neue Gewandhaus – the fine dining on offer at Stadtpfeiffer is also in demand. Detlef Schlegel took over the restaurant in October 2001 together with his later wife Petra. They are constantly investing in their business and also like to keep evolving in the kitchen. Come here to enjoy a contemporary take on classic French cuisine. His style is pleasantly simple and unfussy and the quality of the produce is second to none. The two set menus are brimming with market-fresh ingredients. Your hostess Petra Schlegel heads up the discreet, friendly and professional front-of-house team in this timelessly elegant restaurant. Incidentally, its name refers to the 18C Leipziger Stadtpfeifer, forerunners of the Gewandhaus Orchestra.

name: Schwingshackl ESSKULTUR Gourmet
review: In this former ferry house set on the banks of the Isar, your dedicated hosts Erich and Katharina Schwingshackl focus on classic cuisine made from first-class produce. This is cooking that needs no gimmicks; what counts here is bold, intense flavour sensations. The chef-patron effortlessly creates incredible harmony on the plate, skilfully imbuing each little detail with its own clear and concise aroma. Venison backstrap with apple and parsnip is just one of his memorable dishes! Meanwhile, Katharina Schwingshackl genially guides you through your evening, ably recommending bottles from the interesting wine list. Next to the fine dining restaurant is Schwingshackl HEIMATKÜCHE, where you can also have lunch. The terrace overlooking the river is wonderful. You might like to stay overnight too.

name: Roter Hahn
review: This townhouse in the heart of Regensburg has a long history behind it. It has been known as an inn for centuries, with the earliest written record of it dating back to 13C. Maximilian Schmidt now represents the third generation of the family at the helm. In a pleasingly informal atmosphere, they serve up modern cuisine that draws on the best of what the region has to offer, but also seeks inspiration in French, Scandinavian and Asian culinary traditions. The focus is squarely on the evening set menu, but you can also choose to dine à la carte. At midday, they also offer a shorter version of the evening set menu in addition to an attractively priced lunch option. Should you wish to stay overnight, individually decorated guestrooms are available in the hotel.

name: Coeur D'Artichaut
review: Slightly tucked away in an inner courtyard (pleasant terrace in summer) and only a few minutes' walk from the cathedral, this appealing "casual fine dining" restaurant awaits. In cosy surroundings, diners can gaze into the open kitchen – it is almost like being at the theatre. Here, French-born Frédéric Morel combines his Breton roots with influences from his adopted home in North Germany before adding the touch of modern creativity that is the hallmark of his cuisine. His stocks and sauces are outstanding! When selecting his high-quality ingredients, he is mindful of the seasons and the region in which they are sourced. The "Morel's Tasting" set menu, which changes every month, is composed of four, six or eight courses. Instead of wine, you can also opt for alcohol-free pairings.

name: Hummels Gourmetstube
review: An elegant affair: clean lines, lovely natural materials and pale, warm tones make for a modern yet cosy atmosphere in the fine dining restaurant of the 100-year-old "Gasthaus Hummel". On entering the restaurant you can sneak a peek into the kitchen, where a seasonal set menu is put together under the supervision of chef-patron Stefan Hummel, who makes a point of sourcing his selected produce from the region. Not only can you look forward to an abundance of flavour and finesse, but you can also expect great value for money. The dedication of the Hummel family is also plain to see in the friendly and competent front-of-house team, which is headed up by your cordial hostess. You might also like to extend your stay among the mountains and spend the night in the well-maintained family-run hotel.

name: VILLINO
review: This pretty property set amid the orchards seems almost Mediterranean, from the stylish, airy, high-ceilinged dining room, which is reminiscent of an orangery, to the charming inner courtyard with fountain. This is a real family affair comprising hostess Sonja Fischer, her daughter Alisa and her brother Rainer Hörmann, a trained sommelier. The front-of-house team provides professional and cordial service, including very good wine recommendations – and the lady of the house is always present too. Toni Neumann's cuisine is clearly influenced by Italian and Mediterranean cuisine, and also draws on inspiration from Asia. There are three set menus to choose from: one classical, one more creative and one vegetarian. Overnight stays are available at the hotel of the same name.

name: Kulmeck by Tom Wickboldt
review: Tom Wickboldt is no stranger to the island, having already made a reputation for himself here as a Michelin-starred chef. Now he has breathed new life into the previously somewhat traditional Kulmeck. By means of an ambitious set menu, he casts a spotlight on high-quality ingredients, adeptly combining and presenting them with a real sense of creativity. Great skill goes into balancing all the contrasting flavours. Guests are looked after by a charming, well-trained front-of-house team. The setting is modern and casual, with a kitchen that is partially visible to diners.

name: astrein
review: After working in Cologne's Himmel und Äd and Résidence in Essen, Eric Werner has been a great addition to the fine dining scene in this cathedral city since he opened his own small restaurant here in August 2019. Prepared in a semi-open kitchen, the cooking is modern and creative. The set menus "Schunkele" and "Bützchen" (vegetarian) harmoniously bring strong flavours and lovely spiciness to the plate. Those who do not wish to commit to a set menu can also go à la carte. The atmosphere is also just right: it is relaxed and easy-going here, and the service is competent, friendly and unpretentious. They are committed to advising you on wine – from their very well-stocked wine list. The pairings by the glass are spot on. A non-alcoholic alternative is also offered.

name: Weinschänke Schloss Groenesteyn
review: This historical half-timbered house is somewhat tucked away in tranquil Kiedrich. The estate's former tavern is rustic and cosy, with lots of warm wood fittings. Seated at bare old wooden tables decked with high-quality tableware, guests are looked after by friendly and attentive wait staff. Owner and head chef Dirk Schröer (previously of Caroussel in Dresden and the fine dining restaurant of Burg Schwarzenstein in Geisenheim) creates aromatic cuisine that combines classical elements with regional fare. Proprietor Amila Begic leads a front-of-house team that will be able to recommend many a fine wine from the region to accompany the delightfully balanced and well-structured dishes. The terrace commands a view of the vineyards and Scharfenstein Castle.

name: Werneckhof Sigi Schelling
review: Behind its smart yellow façade, the traditional Werneckhof, located close to the English Garden, has retained the stylish character of yesteryear and successfully combined it with chic retro armchairs and modern art. Chef-patron Sigi Schelling (who previously spent 14 years at Tantris) proposes refined dishes that draw on classical foundations and abound with harmonious textures and flavours. She steers clear of culinary trends, opting instead to focus on straightforward cuisine that keeps it seasonal. They serve a business lunch formula comprising three or four courses, and in the evening a more sophisticated five-course set menu. Then there is the pleasantly relaxed and professional front of house team, which includes a dedicated sommelier.

name: Bricole
review: The atmosphere here is really neighbourly, almost intimate – you immediately feel welcome! This is due both to the appealing bistro setting and to cordial and professional proprietor and sommelier Fabian Fischer. He has a pleasingly personal touch in his dealings with guests and a clear enthusiasm when it comes to recommending the most suitable wine. Steven Zeidler is in charge in the kitchen. His set menu creatively combines regional tradition with influences from across the globe. Take, for example, his belly and back of lamb with millet, aubergine and BBQ flavours, a perfectly balanced dish, or his kohlrabi with gazpacho, fennel and dill, which is light and fresh yet full of finesse. A 100% vegetarian set menu is also available. Good to know: there are also a few small tables to be had on the pavement in front of the restaurant.

name: Votum
review: Benjamin Gallein is no stranger to the region. His creative cuisine is one of the fine dining options available in the Leineschloss, which is the seat of Lower Saxony's state parliament. The restaurant is housed in the modern extension of this historic building situated on the Platz der Göttinger Sieben, close to the Leine River. The name Votum is a reference to the choices to be made within the set menu: diners decide on the order of the courses, on potential "upgrades", as well as the wine pairings (alcohol-free alternatives also available). The glass-walled dining area makes for an elegant setting, as does the beautiful terrace overlooking the river. Attentive and well-drilled service, with the chefs occasionally delivering the dishes themselves. Schorse and Casino Royale also belong to the hotel.

name: s'Äpfle
review: It isn't only hotel guests who are drawn to the charming and stylish Villa Linde on Lake Constance, and there is a good reason for that: this fine dining restaurant with its distinctly modern cuisine. The kitchen team's dedication to their craft is evident in their penchant for select ingredients as well as in their technical skill and winning flavour combinations, which are also beautifully presented on the plate. The feel-good factor here is also down to the space itself: a light and airy interior with comfortable furnishings and a down-to-earth atmosphere. And then there is the service team – cordial, attentive and highly competent. Make a beeline for the terrace in the summer!

name: Shiraz
review: It would be easy to drive straight past this small, slate-clad inn. Having set up shop here in 2017, Serkan Akgün is your welcoming host – with around 30 years of experience in the hospitality industry and world of wines behind him. Since October 2020, Alexander Hoppe has been responsible for the ambitious classic cuisine that draws on modern influences. He has a great passion for, among other things, patisserie. Order your dishes à la carte or opt for the set menu, which can always be supplemented with N25 caviar, for instance. The rustic style of the building has been tastefully and elegantly modernised. Then there is the gorgeous view over the Wupper Valley – also from the terrace.

name: Alte Liebe
review: Owner and head chef Benjamin Mitschele has long been known in Augsburg as a restaurateur. After starting out with a deli and café concept, he has now made fine dining his mission. The set menu that he proposes can be made pescetarian or vegetarian upon request. Close attention is paid to the quality and seasonality of the produce, much of which comes from the restaurant's own small market garden. The streamlined dishes win diners over with their originality, balance and precision. You can also enjoy ambitious wine pairings. In such a pleasingly laid-back atmosphere, amid the smart-casual surroundings, guests would probably be surprised to learn that this space used to house a bicycle shop. In summer, tables are set up on the terrace in front of the large windows of the corner building.

name: Irma la Douce
review: This classic contemporary restaurant is a real highlight of the fine dining scene around Potsdamer Platz. Chef Michael Schulz wins over diners here with a menu that incorporates elements of classic French cuisine as well as modern, creative ideas. The focus is laid squarely on flavour, with aromatic but distinctly unfussy dishes made from good-quality ingredients. A well-trained front-of-house team adds to the laid-back yet sophisticated atmosphere. You can also choose from a fantastic selection of fine wines from France. Incidentally, the restaurant is named after the US film Irma la Douce, which is based on the musical of the same name.

name: Troyka
review: Having moved from Heinsberg into this sleek and sustainable new building, the chef duo Alexander Wulf and Marcel Kokot present a set menu of very modern dishes replete with Russian influences. You are looked after by a competent, pleasantly relaxed and charming young team led by sommelier Ronny Schreiber – a real wine connoisseur, he surprises diners with interesting, not always conventional wine recommendations. In summer, the chic, pared-back restaurant is complemented by a beautiful terrace. By the way, the Russian name "Troyka" means "trio" and refers to the well-versed trio who run this establishment.

name: OX
review: In Darmstadt's city centre, the Rink brothers have established a pleasingly informal fine dining restaurant, which they run with total dedication. While David is at the helm in the kitchen, Norman is in charge of service. Both, however, are on hand to serve guests – with David never missing an opportunity to deliver his dishes to the table and talk diners through them personally. You can look forward to elaborate cuisine that showcases great technical skill and draws on high-quality ingredients. Two set menus are on offer: "Pure Taste" and "Vegetarian / Pescetarian". The interior is done out in a trendy, minimalist style; in summer you can dine out on the courtyard terrace.

name: Michael's Leitenberg
review: Who would expect to find a restaurant like this in the small district of Frasdorf? This establishment may be a little out of the way, but it is definitely worth a visit to sample the modern, creative, well-thought-out and thoroughly delicious cuisine. Select ingredients are showcased with consummate skill. There is a talented and ambitious young chef at the helm – but that doesn't mean classics like Wiener schnitzel are off the menu. Select a bottle of wine from the decent list or opt for the judicious wine pairings to accompany the set menu. Friendly and accomplished service; appealing modern interior.

name: L'étable
review: The only hint that you're dining in a former stable (French: l'étable) is in the name of this restaurant. This spruce historical house in the middle of the tranquil old town used to be a coaching inn. Where travellers and their horses once rested, dinners now settle in and enjoy friendly and attentive service in an ambience of understated elegance. Under the supervision of head chef Konstantin Kaiser, the kitchen team employs great craftsmanship and finesse to creatively transform excellent produce into dishes such as turbot served with La Ratte potato, artichoke and smoked eel velouté. The food is accompanied by a carefully considered selection of wines. For overnight stays, Hotel zum Stern proposes cosy rooms of various sizes. Parking space in the courtyard.

name: Gourmetrestaurant "fine dining RS"
review: The secluded, quiet location up here at Staufeneck Castle is wonderful, as is the view of the Fils valley. Head to Burghotel's fine dining restaurant to drink it all in via the large panoramic windows – in fine weather you can even see Stuttgart airport and the TV Tower! Guests take their seats in tasteful and elegantly minimalist surroundings to enjoy professional and charming service courtesy of the Swabian-speaking front-of-house team – yes, this is an authentic regional experience! Choose from two modern set menus, one of which is vegetarian. Rolf Straubinger and his long-time chef de cuisine Markus Waibel impress diners with really elaborate dishes that are agreeably light and subtle and full of interesting flavour contrasts. Alternatively, try out oifach andersch, which proposes traditional Swabian cuisine that also draws on international influences.

name: Gabelspiel
review: Located in the middle of Giesing, this small restaurant run by Sabrina and Florian Berger is a real hit! This is partly down to the completely unpretentious and pleasantly informal atmosphere – you can sense the owners' dedication here. Heading up the front-of-house team is the incredibly friendly and professional lady of the house, who ensures that everything runs smoothly. Another major draw is the modern cuisine made from regional produce. Served in the form of a set menu, the premium ingredients include such delights as char wrapped in nori. Florian Berger shows excellent technical skill and deftly applies his years of experience in Michelin-starred kitchens (including Hangar 7, Tantris, Restaurant No 15).

name: Acquarello
review: The Latin flair of this friendly, elegant restaurant is beautifully in keeping with the Italian/Mediterranean and French cuisine served here. Owner and head chef Mario Gamba, who originally trained to be a translator, is self-taught when it comes to cooking, although as the son of a restaurateur, you might say his passion for the profession is in his blood. The focus of his "cucina del sole" lies squarely on the quality of the produce, with the Italian-born chef really getting back to basics. There are, of course, fine wines from Italy to accompany your meal. Seated on stylish upholstered chairs at tables decked with high-quality tablecloths, you are attentively served by a well-trained team. The chef-patron's son, Massimo Gamba, is also part of the staff.

name: Clostermanns Le Gourmet
review: You reach Le Gourmet via the beautiful inner courtyard of the listed four-sided courtyard that has been extended to encompass a hotel. You can sit directly on the wonderful terrace or dine inside in a more private setting. On the way into the tasteful modern, elegant little restaurant, you pass the glass-paned kitchen, where a modern set menu with a classic basis is created. This is the domain of Thomas Gilles, who implements his own style here, complete with fine details and some unusual combinations. The pleasant service is remarkably friendly and natural, and the wine recommendations are excellent. Tip: consider staying overnight in one of the comfortable rooms of Clostermanns Hof hotel.

name: Camers Schlossrestaurant
review: Fine dining in stately surroundings! As befits an elegant castle, you first have to cross the moat and walk through the inner courtyard (home to what must be the finest terrace in Bavaria!), before entering the attractive minimalist-style restaurant room with a decorative white vault. Florian Vogel (previously of Kastell in Wernberg-Köblitz and Dallmayr in Munich) proposes modern cuisine that draws on classical, Mediterranean and Asian influences. The culinary concept could be described as a "round-the-world trip that starts and ends in Bavaria". Only top-notch ingredients are used, many of them sourced from the nearby Eichethof estate. You will be well looked after by the charming and professional service team, who are also on hand for interesting wine recommendations. The guestrooms in the adjoining hotel are done out in an appealingly clean design.

name: Sartory
review: The chic and intimate fine dining restaurant of the Hotel Maximilian's is housed in a building that is steeped in history. Under the supervision of Simon Lang (who has previously worked for Alfons Schuhbeck, Holger Bodendorf and Ali Güngörmüs, among others), classic cuisine is given a modern twist and served in the form of a set menu. The ingredients are selected according to their quality and seasonality – some of the herbs come from the chef's own garden. They also have their own honey. In case you were wondering, the restaurant is named after Johann Georg Sartory, Augsburg's legendary 19C chef.

name: Gasthof Krone
review: A delightful inn that is a perfect fit with its surroundings. Erik Metzger serves up appealingly pared-down classic dishes that are replete with harmonious flavour combinations and steer well clear of unnecessary frills. The quality of the produce is beyond question. To complete the picture, there is the cosy, old-fashioned interior.
