The charcuterie is Ikejiri’s forte and puts the focus on Tokushima pork. From this he derives his speciality, fromage de tête, prepared using cuts from the pig’s head. Also popular are the salted pork belly with stewed lentils and spareribs. There’s a reason why the shop’s logo is a pig.

name: SUSHI KOURIN
review: It makes perfect sense when you learn this is the sister establishment of Sotatsu in Hatsudai. The restaurant is named after Edo period painter Ogata Korin (1658-1716) of the Rinpa school – it was during his lifetime that nigiri first appeared at food stalls. Owner-chef Shinji Nitta is an admirer of Hanaya Yohei, said to have invented nigiri, and takes orders for single pieces as is tradition. Don’t miss the typical edomae toppings like tuna, gizzard shad and anago.

name: Pork Vindaloo Taberu Fukudaitoryo
review: Pork vindaloo from Goa on the west coast of India has its roots in the pork cuisine of Portugal. The sourness of vinegar blends with the spices, as the curry is made with vinegar rather than wine. The name of the shop means ‘vice president’ and is a pun on former US vice president Al Gore, whose name sounds like ‘Goa’. We’re looking forward to the day when this restaurant assumes the presidency of the curry world.

name: Yakitori Abe
review: The chef assembles the sequence of yakitori chicken cuts according to customer preferences. To their delight, he starts beer drinkers off with chicken breast and wine tipplers with chicken heart. Seasoning is simple: salt, sauce or soy sauce, depending on the item—whichever best brings out the flavour. The top recommendation is the chicken wings, which ticks all three boxes. The skin is fragrant, the meat and fat are sweet, and the umami unique to meat on the bone.

name: La Brianza
review: Chef Okuno plots Japanese ingredients onto local cuisines he studied in Italy. Meat raised in Japan – with production regions and brands written on the menu – is char-grilled. The key to the flavour of the Roman-style carbonara is the eggs, which are carefully selected down to the individual farm. Soft-boiled eggs are also vital to the Piedmont gratin-style truffles, shaved for the customer at the table. Authentically prepared seasonings interweave with the unique character of each ingredient.

name: anikò
review: The restaurant’s name derives from the word ‘anikò’ which, in the dialect of Italy’s Le Marche region, means ‘giving out plenty, a little at a time’. Guests who order the Maruke-no-Oka set menu can experience this approach to dining. Diners can have their fill of regional home cooking, including fried olives, fisherman’s soup and pasta in a boar sauce. The relaxing, comfortable atmosphere feels like Chef Iseki has welcomed you into his home.

name: L'AMITIE
review: Tucked away in a backstreet of the teeming student quarter of Takadanobaba is the red façade of l'Amitié. As French radio broadcasts play in the background, the proprietress leads the spirits of the diners with her bustling service. Lunch consists of set menus of appetizers and mains; dinners are à la carte. Country-style meat terrines, duck confit and hearty hometown cooking await the hungry diner. The restaurant recalls the ambience of Paris from Chef Miyashita’s training.

name: Washokuto Washu Ogata
review: The owner-chef at this counter-style kappo restaurant is from Akita and uses ingredients from there, including wild vegetables in spring, junsai in the summer and parsley in the autumn. One winter speciality is the Akita dish of kiritampo (pounded rice skewer), toasted, and used as dumplings in a stew. He also puts great effort into the dashi, which forms the core of Japanese cuisine. Prime examples include the vegetable ohitashi, kinmedai and saw-edged perch nitsuke.

name: Gracia GASTROBAR de Barcelona
review: The concept here is ‘a cutting-edge Barcelona gastro-bar’. Pairing modern ideas with local cuisine, it’s like a Spanish bar where you can enjoy à la carte dishes. Prime examples of this are the ‘Callos’ tripe stew and the ‘Caldoso’ fisherman-style rice dish. The experienced French-born chef creates original dishes, incorporating Japanese tastes like Kamakura vegetables and katsuo-dashi.

name: REI
review: The chef here aims to offer urban-style ‘main street Chinese’ food and, in support of this, he went for a modern decor and plays Western music. The à la carte menu includes everything from home-style dim sum such as gyoza dumplings and shumai steamed dumplings to orthodox dishes like steamed chicken with spicy sauce and stir-fried seafood with XO sauce. His principle is to make the most of the ingredients based on his experience in Cantonese cuisine.

name: Spice
review: The over 20 spices listed on the wall are the source of the restaurant’s flavours. These are used in Indian curries, made without flour. Onions stir-fried to an amber brown, miso and fish sauce are added for body. The aim here is to achieve a Japanese-cuisine-like harmony. Rice with added barley also plays a role. While chicken is the mainstay ingredient, a variety of curries are on offer, including spinach and oyster. Unique combinations keep the appetite whetted.

name: Tokihami
review: The menu tickles the fancy of gourmands. Wafers filled with foie gras and creamy crab croquettes are perennial favourites, while deep-fried tilefish with its scales on is also popular. Tsuyahime-brand rice from Yamagata Prefecture is cooked in an earthenware pot. Topping it with the shrimp-dashi curry is a good choice, as is the sirloin on rice topped with egg yolk. The Tsufuhan (‘Gout Rice’) comes extravagantly topped with salmon roe, karasumi, uni and caviar.

name: Tonkatsu Nanaido
review: This restaurant was opened by a yakitori chef who loves tonkatsu. The standard offering is brand name pork from Yamagata, but he uses pork from all over Japan. The selling point is the crispy texture of the batter. He fries it in lard because that’s what he was raised on, growing up in the working-class east end of Tokyo. Also, in the course of his main occupation he has acquired an eye for chicken, apparent in the free-range chicken cutlet.

name: yoyonam
review: Locals know the Yoyogi Fifth District (Go-chome) area as ‘Yoyogo’. Change the ‘go’ to the Vietnamese word for five, ‘nam’, and you get Yoyonam, expressing the owner’s desire to earn the love of its community. The fare consists of arrangements of Vietnamese home cooking, such as spring rolls and bánh xèo (crispy, rice-stuffed pancake). The use of Vietnamese tableware and Sông Bé pottery fosters an authentic atmosphere, while the sounds of the passing trains remind you you’re in Yoyogo.

name: bépocah
review: The yellow colonial-style façade and red-walled interior are emblematic of Peru. The chef, a third-generation Peruvian of Japanese descent, colours his cuisine with the traditional hues of red, yellow, green and purple. Aji limo chili peppers and quinoa are essential elements of his cuisine. Pisco sour, made from a distilled spirit called pisco, is the national cocktail of Peru. Exotic ambience and authentic cuisine will sweep you away on a Peruvian adventure.

name: Homemade Ramen Muginae
review: The owner-chef wants the natural flavours of the ingredients to come through in each bowl. The chicken-based soup using free-range chicken in the standard soy sauce flavoured ramen is rich in umami. A combination of dashi from beef, pork and seafood makes for a complex flavour. Numerous toppings are offered for customers to enjoy a variety of different tastes. The roasted wagyu and homemade wontons are popular.

name: Yoshoku Wine Fritts
review: ‘Fritts’ derives from the French word ‘frites’, meaning ‘fried food’, and sure enough, Fritts specialises in fried treats such as deep-fried shrimp and deep-fried minced meat cutlets. The ingredients are coated in coarse breadcrumbs, enhancing the fragrance of the batter. In addition to the fried items, Western-influenced dishes such as hamburger steak and gratin are also popular. The owner-chef’s experience with French gastronomy shines in the chicken-liver pâté and lamb stew.

name: SPiCE Cafe
review: Kazushiro Ito has travelled to 48 countries out of a desire to get to know the world. Of all the foods he tried, what drew him most strongly were the spices. He creates a fusion of seasonal ingredients and spices and opened this restaurant to convey that unfamiliar appeal to a Japanese audience. The biryani rice dish, cooked in an earthenware pot, is paired with corn in the summer and oysters in winter. He pursues little known tastes using Japanese ingredients.

name: Äta
review: ‘Port town bistro’ is the concept here. Various seafoods can be found on the blackboard. The bouillabaisse speciality features seafood, spices and herbs that all come together in the soup. You’ll find everything from familiar dishes like aioli and roasted shrimp to unique ones, like cold smoked mackerel. The ship cabin-like space also makes for the feel of a cruise.

name: Katchar Batchar
review: As you might expect from a restaurant whose name means ‘hodgepodge’, they mix various elements together with those of Indian tradition. Using Sichuan pepper, Thai fish sauce and adding soy sauce or miso as the secret ingredient is very much the approach of a Japanese chef. The chicken achari curry features two original elements in the form of chicken dashi and green chili pickles. We recommend pairing the Northern Indian butter chicken curry with cheese kulcha.

name: Katsuyoshi
review: Katsuyoshi was first founded in Shizuoka, then opened a branch in Ningyocho, carrying the same name. The interior of the shop, a refurbished traditional home, uses vintage wood to convey a retro feel. Copper and lacquer crockery reinforce the mood. Manning the fryers is a dedicated tonkatsu chef. Katsuyoshi batters the meat lightly, using an original oil blend. Specially made sauce, salt with ume powder and wasabi from the Amagi area of the Izu Peninsula create the Katsuyoshi style.

name: Tonkatsu Keita
review: The owner-chef says his dream is to make the pork that his family in Kagoshima fattens known around the world. Fine-marbled and well-textured, the black pork is a standard offering. He uses breadcrumbs of differing sweetness according to the quality of the meat. The use of lard for frying keeps the temperature from dropping, enhancing the flavour. He cooks it at low temperatures to preserve the moisture content and gives it fragrance by finishing it in a very hot pan.

name: MOELLEUSE
review: The chef brings seasonal ingredients in from all over Japan, and then brings their intrinsic tastes to the fore without affectation in his cooking. The sabayon sauce for the asparagus brought in from Saga is a spring speciality. In autumn, try the mackerel marinade flavoured with green mustard sauce. The wagyu rump, boned lamb, and other parts, slowly chargrilled uncut, make for a substantial, satisfying meal.

name: Sumatra Curry Kyoeido
review: This established curry restaurant has been around since 1924. The third-generation owner-chef carries on the tradition of Sumatra curry started by the founding chef. No flour is used, so the taste is determined by the stewed vegetables and the spices stir-fried in oil and fat. Main ingredients such as pork and chicken are cooked separately to draw out their flavour. The curry is served in a silver sauce pot, taking you way back in time.

name: Shuka Nomoto
review: The owner-chef creates unique dishes by incorporating Chinese tastes into Japanese cuisine, which he takes as his base. The sesame oil that adds flavour to seasonal ingredients in the aemono and the pork tongue shumai speciality are good examples. At the end come items like beef sinew curry and noodles with a savouriness imparted by shellfish. The dashi is made from ingredients used in the cuisine and has real depth of flavour, which he lets speak for itself.

name: LANBRoA
review: Amazement at the dishes served in bars in Spain, where she travelled to study Spanish, started this owner-chef on her journey of gastronomy. When Mikiko Isobe later joined a cooking school in San Sebastián, Spain’s capital of fine cuisine, she was charmed by the flavours of the Basque Country. The piquillo pepper stuffed with bacalao (dried and salted cod) is a dish she remembers fondly from those days. Both the fare and the interior ooze a Basque atmosphere.

name: Los Reyes Magos
review: The exotic mood of the interior and the gracious reception by the proprietress puts the diner in a sunny mood. The signature menu here is the Catalonian cuisine, a bequest from the previous chef . Pickled sardines impart the scent of olive oil and lemons. Hand-cut uncured ham and Catalonian tomato bread are made for each other. The marinera is a seafood paella made with mussels and shrimp. Each item is authentically Catalonian through and through.

name: Tomato
review: Chef Omino set out to create healthy curry. Focusing on the effects of spices and Chinese medicine, he came up with a curry seasoned with 36 spices. Sparing no time or effort, his old-fashioned preparations bring out the flavour. The curry and the other speciality, the stew, are equally good.

name: Meguro Sushi Taichi
review: Having hung out his shingle in his hometown, Taichi Tamura runs his sushi restaurant with his wife. This is a place to enjoy sushi prepared by a master in a family-oriented setting. Dishes alternate between snacks and nigiri, as he varies the presentation of items. The sushi rice is prepared with rice vinegar, to bring the sweetness of the seafood. Chub mackerel sushi paired with strips of seasoned and dried shio kombu kelp and rolled eggs matched with sea lettuce are distinctive touches.

name: ÉTAPE
review: Chef Kawamura trained in Paris before opening this restaurant. While based on traditional cuisine, he prizes the idea he learned from the French of bringing his own inimical style to the preparations. The uni pain perdu is uni with French toast. Wine goes well with the thick orange sauce of the shrimp and burrata dish. The name of the restaurant means ‘step’, the first of which he has already taken toward attaining greater heights as a chef.

name: roku
review: Chef Shimpei Sasagawa opened this ‘confectionery and cuisine shop’ with his pâtissier wife. The name, meaning ‘six’, comes from their birthday month and was chosen to be easy for the local residents to remember. Wild vegetables in spring and mushrooms in autumn are sent from his hometown of Kiso, Nagano; he also picks them himself. The speciality is wild game. A rice dish is served at the end for a more casual French dining experience. His wife’s handmade cakes are a source of pride.

name: Tonkatsu Hinata
review: Two very different types of pork are used here: Sangen pork, whose feed includes herbs used in Chinese medicine, is tender and refined, whereas Kagoshima black pork is lean and rich in flavour. We recommend the flavoursome rib roast if you go for the Sangen pork. The dinner set menu is interesting, with bite-sized pieces, fried one at a time, of everything from standard offerings such as sirloin and tenderloin to rare parts such as eye of round and jowl.

name: Shikinoshoku Saito
review: While following the traditions of Japanese cuisine, the owner-chef adds extra touches. The dinner à la carte features everything from first to last harvest ingredients and various cooking methods are employed. For example, anago is served as aemono, grilled and served with rice. He likes Chinese cuisine, so also serves spring rolls and spicy chicken. As there are many offices around, the focus at lunch is on teishoku such as ‘Tai and sesame with rice’ and ‘Whitebait with rice’.

name: jeeten
review: Based on yakuzen (medicinal food), the fare at Jeeten is wonderful for physical health. Owner-chef Katsuhiko Yoshida serves Chinese home cooking arranged in his own style. The steamed shrimp rolls use bean starch sheets instead of rice-flour wrappers. Steamed gyoza dumplings are accompanied by vinegar soy sauce into which whole grain mustard has been dissolved for a Western touch. Coconut milk is paired with warabimochi rather than tapioca. The flavour of each has a warmth that soothes the soul.

name: Onigiri Asakusa Yadoroku
review: Ingredients are displayed behind a glass case, as in a sushi shop. Yosuke Miura, the third-generation owner-chef, listens to his customer’s order and immediately begins moulding it by hand. Before taking over the reins here, he was a flautist. In classical music, you play what’s written on the music sheet. Onigiri is the same, says Miura; you don’t try to do something new. Yadoroku is a score handed down from his grandmother, one which he will reproduce faithfully.

name: Yakitori Shira
review: There’s just nothing like tucking into free-range chicken, says the owner-chef. He uses Shiga chicken for its savoury fattiness and Shizuoka chicken for its in-the-wild flavour. The basic offering is a five-skewer omakase set, which comes with thigh, meatballs and liver. You can add rare parts like shirako and glandular stomach, if you like. We recommend pairing the meal with wine or sake selected by the owner-chef, who is also a sommelier.

name: LA BETTOLA da Ochiai
review: Tsutomu Ochiai has been preaching the gospel of real Italian cuisine since the days when there was no basil, no rucola, and olive oil was almost impossible to obtain. The fully loaded menu of regional Italian cuisine makes you vow to return. Fish carpaccio and sea urchin spaghetti are Japanese-born Italian. Many dishes are seasonal, a treat for repeat visitors. Thanks to Ochiai, Ginza has become the 21st region of Italy!

name: La Trattoriaccia
review: Chef Teppei Kawai learned local cuisine in depth, having lived in Tuscany for fifteen years. He offers a traditional menu, as he wants to familiarise people with the tastes of Tuscany. In keeping with tradition, the Tuscan bread is made without salt, but the dishes are salted to go well with wine. The Italian ingredients, such as porcini mushrooms in the autumn and lacinato kale in winter, are also part of that tradition.

name: Neki
review: The name, meaning ‘close’ or ‘beside’, comes from the chef’s native Kansai dialect and was chosen as he wants his restaurant to be a true part of the Kabutocho district. He prizes the traditional ways of French cuisine but adds Japanese elements. For example, he uses firefly squid and wild vegetables and seasons them with sansho and black shichimi spices. He procures chicken and duck from Kyoto, which he uses in dishes that convey the appeal of his hometown.

name: Yakitori Kato
review: Skewers are assembled with small pieces and char-grilled to lock in their umami. Of special note is how different seasonings are used for each cut. Displaying his originality, the chef offers tsukune (chicken meatballs) flavoured with sansho and gizzards marinated in herb vinegar. He also adds beguiling twists to bring out seasonal flavours: in summer, high-sugar tomatoes are seasoned with garlic; in winter, yam is wrapped in nori and grilled.

name: Marugo
review: Working with his predecessor, the owner-chef has over a quarter of a century of experience. He chooses his pork not on brand but on quality, tenderness and the sweetness of the fat. The tonkatsu of pork loin and tenderloin is pale in hue. Deep-fried slowly at a low temperature, the aroma of the coating draws out the meat umami even more. Inheriting the teachings of his mentor, he carefully controls the heat as he cooks. It’s no wonder diners have been coming regularly since he opened.

name: Meishan
review: A chef who trained at a Sichuan restaurant runs this place with her sister. The Chinese character for ‘plum’, one of the ten famous flowers of China, is part of the name to evoke the fragrances of China. The sound and smoke from the Chinese frying pan makes its way to your table, along with the aroma. Try various Sichuan dishes, including soy-braised pig’s feet, spicy miso stir-fried eggplant, Sichuan boiled beef and hot and sour soup.

name: SUSHI SOTATSU
review: The restaurant is named after Tawaraya Sotatsu, the 15th–16th-century painter famed for his Wind God and Thunder God screen paintings. The basket clam ichiban-dashi is a thoughtful touch, meant to soothe the liver before drinking. The relaxed way of ordering sushi one item at a time underscores why having a ‘neighbourhood sushi bar’ is so enjoyable. Transparent billing (without any evasive ‘market prices’) is reassuring. Sushi the way it was meant to be is back.

name: Ponchiken
review: Ponchiken began when a yoshoku-trained chef hung out his shingle to pursue the world of tonkatsu. Two types of pork, with differing umami, are used for the tonkatsu. Fresh breadcrumbs and vegetable oil are used in accordance with the meat’s characteristics to draw out its natural flavour. Diners can use salt and a variety of sauces to adjust the flavour to taste. Beef cutlets and fried horse mackerel are deep-fried in lard to give them body, creating the unique flavours of this shop.

name: TRATTORIA BUCA'MASSIMO
review: The chef felt the appeal of Tuscany while he was in Italy, so decided to specialise in Tuscan cuisine when he opened his own restaurant. The speciality is meat dishes grilled over bincho charcoal and the top recommendation is the Florentine steak. The fragrance of the meat and smoke really stimulate the appetite. The portions are also generous. Enjoy all the meaty flavours with your group.

name: TEMPURA TSUJIMURA
review: Yokote took over the restaurant from original owner Tsujimura but shares the same desire to serve reasonably priced tempura in a casual atmosphere. Emphasising freshness above all else, he chooses the seafood himself. He also makes sure to serve ingredients like icefish, young ayu and oysters when they’re in season. Donburi (bowls of rice topped with different ingredients) and teishoku (set meals) are available at both lunch and dinner, a sign of the restaurant’s strong roots in the local community.

name: Hamacho Kaneko
review: The owner-chef is fond of the culture of enjoying sake and snacks before the soba comes, so serves various snacks and tempura. In addition to shrimp and anago, there are seasonal tempura items such as wild vegetables and young ayu. Lightly fried, they set the stage for the soba. The emphasis with the thin juwari soba noodles is on the kind of texture that makes them go down smoothly. ‘Meoto’ is a dish he learnt at the restaurant where he trained. You can enjoy both soba and udon here.

name: Araishoten
review: The chef trained in French cuisine in Japan, then worked in Peru where he learned about the local tastes. He communicates the appeal of Peruvian cuisine, which was nurtured by the Andes, the Amazon and the Pacific Ocean, and absorbed influences from various cultures. The standard items are ceviche, featuring white-fleshed fish marinated in salt and citrus juice. Lunch is a set menu, but at dinnertime you can choose according to your preferences.

name: Akebonobashi Kazu
review: Kazuya Matsuo focuses on à la carte dishes because he wants his guests to enjoy Japanese cuisine in a relaxed atmosphere. The approach is orthodox yet accented with ingenious touches: tilefish is salted and dried and the scales are scored to make it look like a pinecone before it’s grilled, while the karasumi-mochi usually prepared with dried mullet roe is substituted with marinated walleye pollack roe. Tender-simmered octopus and sea bream takikomi-gohan (seasoned mixed rice) are renowned.

name: Almayass
review: Almayass is where Lebanese and Armenian cuisine meet influences from around the Mediterranean. The original was founded in Beirut in 1996 and this large Abu Dhabi branch, where the circular booths are the prized seats, continues the tradition of offering an extensive and appealing menu of richly flavoured and carefully prepared dishes. Try the Kibbeh karaz, a wonderful marriage of lamb and cherries.

name: Otoro
review: Al Qana Marina witnessed many a restaurant opening in 2022 – and that included this contemporary Japanese spot, with a great terrace. The experienced chef, under the aegis of consultant-chef Akmal Anuar, has a diligent team supporting him. Signature dishes include yellowtail carpaccio, tuna tartare with yuzu dressing, Wagyu striploin with magnolia leaf and truffle jus and, of course, the titular otoro nigiri. The relaxed space has a funky feel and is dominated by a large open kitchen.

name: ťazal
review: It may be quite hard to pigeon-hole the style of cooking here as it’s an infusion of European influences and Arabic touches, but the results can be exhilarating. Dishes such as tanja short ribs and zaatar sea bream are as delicious as they are original; the crème brûlée kufana is another example. The modern room has an urban feel and the service is delightful. They do a very good weekend breakfast and coffee is also a passion of theirs.

name: Beirut Sur Mer
review: The name says it all – this is about enjoying Lebanese food by the sea. Managed by MBT and with an experienced team occupying the open kitchen, you can expect all the classics, from mezze to mashawi; and don’t skip the desserts as they’re good too. Portions are generous and prices are reasonable. The large, colourful and contemporary dining room also boasts a beautiful beachfront terrace. An ideal spot for post-cultural refuelling after visiting the nearby Louvre Abu Dhabi.

name: Futura Osteria
review: Situated along the Via Francigena near Monteriggioni the small medieval village of Abbadia Isola boasts a superb Romanesque church and a group of old buildings that once housed a monastery and its outbuildings. The Futura Osteria occupies the cellars where the monks once stored their wines, which now provides the setting for simple, delicious and resolutely seasonal Tuscan-inspired cuisine offering good value for money. The refined wine list, simple service and secluded terrace complete the picture.

name: Maso Palù
review: An annexe to the family farm with its organic apple orchards, this rustic, welcoming restaurant has been in business since 1984. The highly experienced family at the helm serve cuisine rooted in regional traditions with just a touch of imagination and modern influence. Open every day in summer, but only Friday to Sunday at other times of year.

name: Coquus
review: A welcoming contemporary-style restaurant in the town’s historical centre where the young owner-chef has plenty of experience behind him, including in his parents’ restaurant. At Coquus, he serves fresh cuisine which is seasonal, full of flavour and reasonably priced given the quality on offer. Efficient and enthusiastic service, with an outdoor space in the pedestrian area for summer dining.

name: Nole
review: Situated near the seafront in one of the iconic streets of this Adriatic resort town, Nole offers guests two different dining options: one section of the restaurant serves excellent dishes, light lunches and snacks, while the other specialises in gourmet dinners. Our inspectors particularly recommend the tomato, goats’ cheese and basil soup, the Abruzzi cheese and pepper tortello pasta with a ginger sauce, and the “pizzaiola”-style tuna.

name: 53 Untitled
review: Two enthusiastic young women, a welcoming bistro with a few small tables on the street, and a very contemporary approach to its cuisine, including its selection of wines and cocktails, all combine to make this informal restaurant a good choice. Despite the casual ambience, the cuisine here is excellent and includes various tapas dishes to share. Traditional Roman recipes feature on the menu alongside more classic and internationally influenced options.

name: Namo Ristobottega
review: This simple, tiny restaurant stands just outside the walls of Tarquinia, barely a kilometre from the splendid necropolis of Monterozzi (UNESCO World Heritage Site). The female owner-chef pays tribute to the Viterbo region with her imaginative use of seasonal ingredients in light dishes which are full of flavour, while the à la carte demonstrates a wide use of vegetables. The outdoor space offers views extending as far as the coast.

name: Nida
review: Located just outside the city walls close to a roundabout, this restaurant is home to a young Japanese chef who follows traditional recipes with impeccable tenacity. The raw fish dishes are highly recommended, although if you’re looking for a surprise menu then the omakase is a good choice. Two small, quiet and brightly decorated dining rooms provide the setting.

name: Vascello d'Oro
review: In business since 1887, this restaurant with warm traditional decor is situated in the town famous for bue grasso (“fat ox”), which you’ll find on the menu here from November to Easter. Enjoy typical, popular dishes from the Piedmont, such as meat and vegetable filled ravioli, finanziera stew, fried dishes, Russian salad and, of course, the famous boiled meats, all skilfully prepared in the traditional way. Desserts such as hazelnut cake and bonet provide a final flourish for the tastebuds.

name: Romanè
review: The decor is simple, almost spartan, and the service unpretentious in this new restaurant situated on the noisy Via Cipro (there is an outdoor space but we recommend eating indoors), where the main attraction is the seasonal, Roman-influenced cuisine. Full of flavour, the dishes are generously portioned and characterised by personal and imaginative touches.

name: Spoon
review: Located in the heart of the historic centre, just a stone’s throw from the beautiful 13C cathedral, this small but welcoming restaurant has a contemporary feel. The generous, modern cuisine, full of colour and flavour, focuses on meat dishes only and is prepared by two young owner-chefs who trained with Niko Romito.

name: FØRMA contemporary restaurant
review: Situated in a secluded, residential district that is part of L’Aquila’s historic centre, this delightful restaurant serves excellent bread, classic sauces and delicious creations prepared by a young chef who gained experience working abroad and now showcases the best of his region. An informal feel, excellent music and original cuisine in a modern setting.

name: Carnal
review: Carnal is the most informal and liveliest of famous chef Roy Caceres’s restaurants, with its music, colourful decor, smart service and even some dishes that are eaten with the hands! The restaurant has a young vibe, focusing on Latin-American cuisine such as tacos, ceviche and mango desserts made from seasonal ingredients (mostly from Italy) and accompanied by a choice of wine, beer and excellent cocktails (in the evening).

name: Dei Cantoni
review: Overlooked by the Malatesta castle, this restaurant offers two dining rooms decorated with exposed bricks that are reminiscent of the paving in the town centre. Sabina prepares delicious regional specialities for her guests – don’t miss the tortelli pasta stuffed with poppies and served with porcini mushrooms and courgette flowers, the pan - fried rabbit with thyme and preserved lemon, and the mascarpone cremoso dessert. Pleasant dining on the veranda in summer.

name: La Bucaccia
review: One of the best places to discover Tuscan cuisine, and that of Arezzo in particular, this restaurant serves exquisite dishes full of flavour. Just a few tables are laid out along the main street in the historic centre, while the two interior dining rooms are rustic and romantic in feel. Friendly and exuberant owner Romano merits a particular mention, providing guaranteed entertainment in between courses.

name: Caffè La Crepa
review: Overlooking a picturesque Renaissance square, the café here dates back to the early 19C and the trattoria shortly after. Today, the decor is a nostalgic mix of styles from the mid-19C to the mid-20c, including Art Nouveau. The restaurant not only appeals to the eyes but also to the tastebuds, thanks to its expertly prepared traditional dishes made from carefully chosen top-quality ingredients which are full of flavour. And if you’d like to take a souvenir home with you, there’s also a shop here selling food specialities and wine.

name: Il Ciabot
review: A discreet entrance leads into this rustic yet well-kept family-run restaurant near the town hall, where the dining room is heated by a fireplace in winter. The wife works front of house, welcoming guests and explaining the daily specials, while the husband is at the helm in the kitchen, preparing traditional, regional specialities, some of which are enhanced with the occasional modern twist.

name: Osteria del Gallo e della Volpe
review: A welcoming dining room with just a few tables and plenty of space in a family - run restaurant offering attentive and friendly service. The menu focuses on local traditional cuisine with the occasional personalised twist. Specialities include ravioli with a lamb ragù, lamb with mint and pecorino cheese, and nougat mousse.

name: Trattoria Ai Due Platani
review: If you’re looking for a traditional restaurant with the ambience of a typical country trattoria, then Ai Due Platani is the place for you. The menu features Emilian specialties such as tortelli pasta stuffed with pumpkin, pecorino pappardelle pasta with a duck and pine nut ragù, and veal fillet with a traditional tuna sauce. All highly memorable!

name: La Pineta
review: You will need a certain amount of patience to tackle the winding road through woods and hills to get to La Pineta, but the food makes the journey well worthwhile. There is a restricted choice – just one tasting menu, although the number of courses can be reduced – with the famous house speciality, fritto misto alla piemontese, taking pride of place. Spacious, welcoming guestrooms are also available.

name: Vecchia Lama
review: Enjoy a friendly welcome and excellent food in this restaurant that only serves meat dishes. The focus is on mountain specialities from Emilia, as well as truffles in season. Dine alfresco on the terrace overlooking the garden in summer. House specialities include ricotta and nettle tortelloni with porcini mushrooms and the slightly more expensive Fiorentina steak cooked on a hot stone.

name: Cile's
review: Situated near the sea, this bright little restaurant with an almost shabby feel uses plenty of wood in its decor, along with a blue and white colour scheme that makes it feel like a corner of Provence in the heart of Fano. The cuisine, however, remains firmly rooted in the local region with simple, very reasonably priced fish dishes and specialities from the Marche featuring on the menu. An amusing imaginative touch comes in the original names given to these dishes.

name: Osteria Mondo d'Oro
review: Described as an “osteria” (inn) by its famous, multi-Michelin-starred chef Giancarlo Perbellini, this restaurant provides a relaxed setting in which to enjoy delicious (and reasonably priced) Italian cuisine, including a few vegetarian options. Choose between the cosy dining room and an outdoor space (weather permitting) in a side street off the central Via Mazzini.

name: L'800
review: Period furniture, regional cuisine and a cheerful ambience are some of the characteristics of this old farmhouse which is named after the 1800s when it was built. Some of the ingredients used, such as snails and frogs’ legs, may come as a surprise: the restaurant specialises in these unusual delicacies, even offering a tasting menu totally dedicated to snails.

name: Al Convento
review: Although housed in the cloisters of a Franciscan monastery decorated with 17C frescoes, Al Convento has the typical feel of an informal restaurant thanks to its decor and open-view kitchen. Specialities from Cetara take pride of place on the menu, with a particular focus on anchovies. Dine alfresco on the small terrace in summer.

name: L'Acchiatura
review: Delicious cuisine from Puglia, including excellent orecchiette pasta with clams and chickpeas, served in a delightful ambience with a number of different rooms and internal patios. The same traditional atmosphere is evident in the attractive, well - equipped guestrooms, as well as in the picturesque swimming pool housed in a grotto.

name: CUCINA.eat
review: This gourmet bistro with a modern design and multifunctional dining space also boasts a well-stocked wine cellar, a shop selling kitchen utensils, and a delicatessen. The menu here showcases the scents and flavours of Sicily, featuring dishes made from ingredients purchased daily from the city market; at lunchtime, there’s a business lunch with a reduced choice of dishes. It’s worth noting that CUCINA.eat is, for the moment, one of the few restaurants in the city where you can bring your own wine to accompany your meal. You won’t even be charged corkage, although you may well be asked for a tasting!

name: Podere 39
review: Housing just a few tables (booking is recommended), this restaurant is attractively decorated with an original melting-pot of features which give it a rustic yet elegant feel despite its small size. Some of the ingredients come from the restaurant’s own farm (hence the name “podere”, the Italian for farm), with both meat and fish dishes featuring on the menu.

name: La Barca
review: Nestled between splendid beaches and bays, this restaurant focuses on the sea, not only in its views but also in its cuisine. The owner takes centre stage in the dining room, while the dishes prepared in the kitchen are varied, generous in size and reasonably priced, featuring classic recipes which allow the full flavours of the top-quality fish to shine through.

name: Il Latini
review: Perhaps not the best choice if you’re planning a romantic, intimate dinner, Il Latini has tables pushed close together, creating a lively atmosphere, and is often packed. But this is part of the charm of this historic trattoria where conviviality combines with simple, delicious traditional cuisine to provide an unforgettable dining experience.

name: Locanda Cacciatori
review: Opened in 1945 by the parents of the current owner in a charming setting surrounded by hills, this trattoria specialises in dishes from Piacenza, served in generous portions which are full of flavour and which introduce guests to the region’s simple yet excellent cuisine. To make sure you don’t get lost, set your satnav for Ponte dell'Olio, Viale San Bono and then drive for 2.5km.

name: L'Ortone
review: This Tuscan-style bistro next to Sant'Ambrogio market is simple both in its decor and cuisine, offering a menu which features a few regional dishes alongside imaginative Italian-themed options prepared from seasonal ingredients. Grilled specialities are also available, alongside an interesting wine list. Excellent value for money, although if you order the steak you’ll end up spending a little more.

name: Osteria del Miglio 2.10
review: Although the town may not be of major importance, the cuisine served at this modern restaurant (with a convenient car park) certainly is! Focusing on traditional local recipes and using seasonal ingredients, the carefully prepared dishes are both generous and full of flavour. Fair prices complete the picture and make this a restaurant a must.

name: Frammichè
review: Standing in open countryside at the end of a dirt road, this small farmhouse comes as a pleasant surprise. Enjoy generous portions of home - style cuisine under the outdoor pergola in summer or in the dining room with a huge fireplace in winter. House specialities include trofie pasta with courgette flowers and pine nuts, pork shank, and mille - feuille with chantilly cream.

name: Su Gologone
review: It is difficult to choose between the three delightful rooms in this restaurant. One has a huge fireplace used for roasting the famous porceddu (suckling pig), another, more intimate in style, is dedicated to a well - known ceramist, while the third is adorned with works by a Sardinian artist. Whichever you choose, you are sure to appreciate the traditional Sardinian cuisine served here.

name: Osteria Piazzetta Cattedrale
review: Run by a married couple with the wife in the kitchen and the husband front of house, this gem of a restaurant just a few metres from the cathedral stands out for its top - quality produce (mainly from Puglia), in dishes such as broad bean purée with seasonal vegetables. Other specialities include sformatino (a type of soufflé) with courgette flowers, spring onions and date purée; suckling pig with baked potato and wild greens; and warm sfogliatina pastry with vanilla cream.

name: Nerina
review: Simplicity, hospitality and informality are the keywords to describe this restaurant in the verdant Val di Non, which has been run by the Di Nuzzo family for more than 50 years. Guests come to Nerina time and time again to enjoy excellent Trentino produce, such as the casolèt cheese, Valsugana maize and mortandela salami, as well as its authentic house specialities, often made with ingredients from the restaurant’s own vegetable garden and occasionally with influences from elsewhere in Italy.

name: Boivin
review: Occupying an old house in the town centre, this restaurant is strongly influenced by the character and ideas of its owner-chef, Riccardo, who offers an original mix of traditional Trento cuisine and influences from around the world (including Korean kimchi and Japanese cooking methods such as tataki). Regional wines are to the fore on the reasonably priced wine list.

name: Podere San Faustino
review: In the heart of the Bassa Parmense region, this old farmhouse has retained romantic reminders of bygone days. The menu also has a traditional feel, featuring dishes such as egg tagliolini with a salami, sun - dried tomato and onion sauce, and braised pork cheeks with a fennel carpaccio in an orange marinade. There’s also a good choice of delicious desserts.

name: Trita Pepe
review: The cuisine served in this contemporary - style restaurant is authentic and genuinely local, with a few modern touches. There’s a tasting menu (mutton or cod by prior reservation), plus reasonably priced à la carte options. The house specialities include mutton tagliata and pineapple carpaccio flavoured with cinnamon and served with ice cream.

name: Borgo Spoltino
review: Borgo Spoltino occupies a 19C farmhouse amid hills and olive groves with views of the sea and mountains. Bright and with plenty of space inside and out, this restaurant is highly recommended for its local specialities and creative dishes, accompanied by vegetables grown in its own garden. The wine list offers a surprising snapshot of the region’s best wines – selected province by province – alongside a few labels from further afield. A good selection of extra virgin olive oil from the Abruzzi completes the picture.

name: La Locanda Gesù Vecchio
review: This restaurant right in the historic centre oozes authentic Neapolitan style thanks to its friendly atmosphere and the warm welcome from its young owner. Here, guests enjoy the best Neapolitan cuisine, including specialities such as the delicious Genovese ragù, a white sauce which, despite its name, is a speciality of Campania. The restaurant also boasts an interesting wine list.

name: Casa Gallo
review: Situated near the centre of Pompei, Casa Gallo is a quiet, informal restaurant with an open-view kitchen. The talented owner-chef creates traditional dishes from Campania, paying careful attention to the use of regional and, more specifically, local ingredients. Charming outdoor area, plus a good selection of wines from small local producers.

name: Vecchia Marina
review: Situated just a stone’s throw from the beach, this Abruzzi restaurant has developed legendary status among fish-lovers in the past 20 years thanks to a few key features – the flavour and freshness of its fish, the simplicity of its recipes and a value for money which is almost unequalled in Italy. Given its huge popularity, you would be advised to book well in advance!

name: Boccondivino
review: Situated on the first floor of a typical building in the historic town centre, this restaurant has two small dining rooms and one larger room lined with bottles. The cuisine is typical of the Langhe region, with braised veal in a Barolo sauce, tajarin pasta in a Bra sausage sauce and many other specialities.

name: Osteria la Fefa
review: Situated under the arcades, this restaurant has the relaxed, friendly ambience of an urban trattoria. Here, the female chef serves an extensive selection of dishes with fresh pasta and meat options taking pride of place on the menu (don’t miss the gnocco fritto with charcuterie), while her son skilfully oversees the front-of-house team. Make sure you leave room for one of the many delicious desserts!

name: Osteria dal Moro
review: A lively fish and seafood restaurant on the seafront, which is always busy thanks to its excellent value for money – booking ahead is highly recommended! Fish-based dishes only, all of which are announced at your table and which change regularly depending on market availability. The dishes are simple, rustic but full of flavour, which is why it’s easy to forgive the rather restricted choice of wine.

name: Dentella
review: Good food is guaranteed at this restaurant, which has been run by the Dentella family for almost a century. In a simple yet welcoming ambience enjoy homemade hams and salamis, casoncelli pasta, meat - based dishes, black Bracca truffles (in season) and game. Good selection of local cheeses. The best of Bergamo cuisine!

name: Hub
review: Created in 1983 among the pavilions of an old fair and now dedicated to helping the underprivileged, the Progetto H social cooperative is the ideal location for chef Leonardo Marongiu’s restaurant. Whether you choose the seven-course tasting menu, or the simpler daily set option, you’re guaranteed a feast full of delicious Sardinian flavours.

name: La Locanda del Falco
review: This restaurant may have changed management but its location in an old, carefully restored coach house with barrel vaults and brick walls remains the same. The regional cuisine has its roots in mountain traditions with specialities such as snails, lamb and local pastas on the menu. Young staff, plus a good selection of wines with a focus on bottles from Piedmont.

name: Trattoria Porteri
review: This long-established family restaurant has a history dating back 150 years, while the old town in which it is situated, although now surrounded by the modern city, has an even older history. Having run the delicatessen for a long time (some of its products are used in the restaurant), the family has also been in charge of the trattoria here for decades. Renowned for its traditional local cuisine, the restaurant serves specialities such as polenta, cheeses and meat dishes, including beef, lamb and horsemeat.

name: Osteria San Giulio
review: With its delightful location in an old rural abbey, warm welcome, friendly atmosphere and excellent “home-style” cuisine which focuses on the region’s classic dishes, this restaurant appeals to all the senses. Tastings of cured hams and cheeses from the surrounding area can be arranged in the beautiful garden by prior arrangement.

name: Castagneto
review: In operation for over 50 years, this restaurant has been run by several generations of the same family, always retaining its authentic feel and the same warm, relaxing atmosphere. The delicious Piedmontese cuisine includes specialities such as paniscia novarese (a rice and bean dish), Briona snails in their shell with garlic, butter and parsley, and bonèt pudding with hazelnut ice cream.

name: Kürbishof
review: Run by a married couple, this attractive, romantic inn in an old farm with a hay barn is home to two typical Stube-style rooms, one of which offers views of the Cembra valley. The menu focus on the best local ingredients prepared in traditional style with the occasional imaginative touch, including dishes such as pork grostl with potatoes, cabbage and smoked ham, and canederli di zucca (squash dumplings) with melted cheese and ground almonds. Charming guestrooms in the barn.

name: La Gioconda
cuisine: Cuisine from the Marches, Regional Cuisine
review: Situated in the heart of the historic centre, this restaurant pays tribute to the Cagli region and the Marche hinterland. Dishes feature the best local ingredients, such as truffles in season (both black and white), as well as a dessert in memory of local sculptor Eliseo Mattiacci (the “fabbrica del cosmo” made with yoghurt, wafers and strawberries). The wine list shows a strong preference for the Marche, but also features wines from further afield.

name: Osteria Bartolini
review: Although this restaurant now has a new name, its cuisine remains focused on fried fish, alongside other traditional Adriatic specialities such as cuttlefish, sardines, clams and squid. Dine either in the blue room with its maritime-themed decor or in a room adorned with evocative photos of fishermen. The tables laid out along the romantic canal port are popular in fine weather.

name: Il Gabbiano 1983
review: Overlooking the main square of this small village in the Lower Po valley, this restaurant prides itself on its love for local, traditional specialities such as cured meats, stuffed marubini pasta, goose and boiled meat dishes, with many recipes having been handed down over the years. If you’d like to take some food or wine home with you, there’s a well-stocked shop at the entrance.

name: Osteria Bartolini
review:
Situated near the canal port, shipyards and sailing centre,
this fully refurbished restaurant now offers a welcoming internal dining room in additional to its two outdoor terraces overlooking the sea, with views of the coast extending from Cattolica to the Ravenna promontory. The restaurant boasts a winning combination of top-quality fish, a friendly atmosphere and a final bill with no hidden surprises. Takeaway dishes are also available.

name: Osteria Ophis
review: Situated in the beautiful historic centre of Offida, this restaurant with a brick-vaulted ceiling is housed in the former stables of an old palazzo with a modern, inviting decor. Near the entrance, the display cabinet laden with excellent local cheeses is a fine sight, while on the left, a small window offers a glimpse of the kitchen. The regional cuisine is reinterpreted with individual flair by the chef, showcased on an à la carte that changes regularly (including truffles in season) and an excellent tasting menu.

name: Al Becco della Civetta
review: The owner - chef of this restaurant in a small village nestling in the Lucane Dolomites focuses on regional cuisine, serving dishes inspired by her two muses – her mother and grandmother. Dishes are often announced at your table and specialities include the delicious ficotto (fig wine). Stunning views of the grandiose mountain scenery from the guestrooms, which are quiet and welcoming.

name: Ca' d'Frara
review: Situated in the historic centre, this restaurant has a strikingly elegant and contemporary feel, with a menu divided between local specialities and more creative dishes. If you’re visiting fascinating Ferrara, we recommend the restaurant’s traditional cuisine, from the pasticcio in crosta di pasta frolla to the salama da sugo. Excellent cuisine and reasonable prices.

name: Casa del Vino della Vallagarina
review: A standard-bearer for local cuisine, this restaurant housed in the 17C Palazzo de Probizer in the town centre offers an outdoor area for alfresco dining in fine weather. Although the restaurant only offers a restricted set menu, this changes on a daily basis (single dishes can also be ordered from the menu) and there’s an extensive choice of desserts. All the bottles on the wine list, which showcases local wines, are also available by the glass. Attractive guestrooms on the top floors.

name: Bruxaboschi
review: You’ll need to allow plenty of time to get to the inland village of San Desiderio, where Bruxaboschi has been run by the same family and delighting guests since 1862, but the journey is certainly worth it. Justifiably famous, the cuisine pays tribute to local traditions (almost exclusively based on meat), starting with an excellent cima alla Genovese (a type of meat loaf), picagge and pansotti pasta dishes, and fried rabbit. Don’t miss the mushrooms in season.

name: Forma
review: Situated away from the sea at the foot of a medieval district, this intimate restaurant boasts a historic decor dotted with modern details such as black parquet flooring and industrial-style pipes. The cuisine created by the owner-chef demonstrates the same blend of traditional style and modern touches in imaginative meat and fish dishes with a personalised twist. The tasting menu offers excellent value for money.

name: L'Acquario
review: Located in the historic centre of an attractive village by the lake, this restaurant is a good option for anyone wanting to try Umbrian cuisine. Dishes made from freshwater fish (pike, carp, tench, eel and crayfish), as well as the famous beans from Lake Trasimeno and meat such as lamb and wild boar, take pride of place on the menu.

name: Angiolina
review: If you have chosen to dine at this small, quiet restaurant with a pleasant outdoor area, make sure you try the local anchovy specialities, alici di menaica (‘menaica’ refers to the type of narrow - mesh net used for fishing in this area). The menu also features other typical dishes from the Campania region.

name: Hosteria Grappolo d'Oro
review: Since the turn of the century, this long-established restaurant near Piazza Navona and Campo de' Fiori has been run by five local business partners, one of whom is the chef. Top-quality, classic and generous Roman cuisine (cacio e pepe pasta, roast lamb, salted cod etc) is to the fore here, served in an attractive, rustic-style dining room. The background music – a nostalgic 1970s mix of rock and blues – also deserves a mention.

name: Cibus
review: To describe the cuisine as regional would be an understatement – Cibus serves specialities from Ceglie, including family recipes, and has been using local ingredients for years, long before zero - mile produce became fashionable. The antipasti and delicious fresh pasta are truly memorable, making this restaurant a highlight of any trip to Puglia. Make sure you taste the suckling pig with a Primitivo wine reduction and Acquaviva onions, the Ceglia biscuits and the excellent cheeses.

name: Al Monastero
review: Enjoy excellent local hams and salami and other delicious regional specialities in this welcoming restaurant. The room with the typical fogolar stove is particularly charming, as is the one embellished with the fresco of Bacchus; the romantic terrace in the historic palazzo’s inner courtyard is also perfect in fine weather. Five delightful apartments with a mezzanine and cooking area are also available.

name: Antiche Sere
review: This renowned osteria situated in a district off the tourist trail is run by attentive and friendly female staff. Its dishes have a regional and traditional focus and are served in three small dining rooms, one of which shares space with the bar. Pleasant outdoor dining in the garden to the rear in summer.

name: La Canonica
review: You climb up to the charming village of Casteldimezzo to get to this restaurant, which is situated in courtyard-like setting featuring just a few houses which look inland rather than out to sea. The latter is just a stone’s throw away and provides the focus in most of the dishes served here. The choice of dishes is deliberately restricted to ensure that the ingredients are fresh and sourced daily, as in the delicious shelled clams with bread and potatoes, the passatelli pasta with shrimps, and the squacquerone cheesecake. The wine list is equally concise yet features some excellent labels.

name: Alla Pasina
review: In this beautiful, warm and welcoming country house, fresh pasta dishes take up much of the space on the menu – and deservedly so: whether you opt for more traditional or creative dishes, the pasta here is excellent. The region’s famous chicory also makes an appearance, alongside a selection of meat and fish dishes. Guestrooms are available for visitors looking to extend their stay.

name: Hostaria Viola
review: The Viola family has been running the Hostaria since 1909, skilfully bringing local gastronomic traditions back to life in the typical vaulted dining room, much to the delight of their guests. Traditional specialities showcased on the menu include delicious cured hams, fresh homemade pasta, guinea fowl, cotechino spiced pork sausage, and in season, the inevitable squash. Seasonal, regional cuisine which is full of flavour.

name: Me Cumpari Turiddu
review: With its old chandeliers, chairs and tables, this original and attractive restaurant offers its guests a feel of traditional Sicily. The cuisine focuses on typical Sicilian specialities, as well as offering a simpler, less expensive bistro menu. There’s also a shop selling food produce and a cocktail bar, which is open non-stop from 11. 30am until the early hours of the morning.

name: Osteria dai Coghi
review: Situated in Albarè, in a residential area where you would never expect to find a restaurant, Osteria dai Coghi is run by a young and enthusiastic team. Real care is taken both in choosing ingredients (often locally sourced, including fish from the lake) and in adding a few personal, more unusual touches to its dishes. Warm, friendly service.

name: Trattoria al Parco
review: This elegant house built in brick and stone boasts extensive tree-shaded grounds, a wine cellar next door, plus personalised, welcoming dining rooms. Here, the menu focuses on meat dishes, many of which are cooked over the grill, while the wine list features just a few labels produced by the restaurant’s own winery. A choice of excellent desserts completes the picture.

name: Il Tirabusciò
review: This restaurant in the heart of the old town is a must for anyone keen to try the cuisine of the Casentino region. The friendly chef is more than happy to provide information on his ingredients and to offer recommendations – the strong flavours in evidence and his delicious cuisine are sure to leave a lasting memory.

name: Agritur El Mas
review: Situated above the village, this authentic farm-restaurant raises cows, horses and pigs and produces its own meat, hams, salamis and cheeses (all on sale in the farm’s Cajelo Shop), which can be enjoyed on a menu which also features typical, often Ladin-inspired dishes from the valley. Attractive dining room decorated with old wood, plus pleasant guestrooms housed in the same building designed in line with environmental construction techniques.

name: Trattoria di Via Serra
review: It’s well worth heading off the traditional tourist trail to experience this trattoria, which is situated in Bolognina, the city’s historic working-class district which now has a very multicultural feel. Simple and informal and run by very friendly owners, this restaurant celebrates top-quality regional cuisine, with dishes ranging from piada to the delicious tortellini in a capon broth.

name: Antica Filanda
review: Although the view from this restaurant takes in the sea and the mountains alike, it’s the latter that inspires the menu. It features inland specialities cooked with the best local ingredients. Suckling pig is a particular favourite, appearing in a number of different guises, including cured ham and meat sauces. The restaurant also offers new, welcoming guestrooms.

name: Locanda Mariella
review: You need to book at least 24hrs in advance at this restaurant by sending an email and your choice of the three menus on offer (traditional, meat or fish). This long-established, legendary restaurant is one of the best trattorias in the province, if not the region. Still run by the same family, it has been delighting guests in this corner of the Apennines since the 1960s.

name: Palazzaccio
review: This traditionally rustic restaurant situated in the historic centre serves cuisine which is firmly anchored in the region, including numerous specialities made from typical ingredients from the Madonie, such as meat and mushrooms. The wine list gives just a hint of the delights awaiting wine-lovers – the new Quaranta wine bar just a stone’s throw away is home to countless bottles from Sicily and further afield, almost all of which are also available by the glass.

name: Trattoria Pomposa - Al Re gras
review: This trattoria is the more casual version of the nearby Michelin-starred L'Erba del Re. Although the cuisine is simpler than at the restaurant, the dishes are carefully prepared, the welcome is friendly and the female service attentive and professional. The restaurant is situated in the attractive historic centre, with parking (clearly marked with blue stripes) nearby. A taste of Emilian simplicity with a contemporary twist.

name: Magnagallo
review: This restaurant appeals on so many levels! It is easy to get to (just a few metres from the motorway exit) and offers a fine Emilian welcome and delicious local cuisine, including fresh pasta and its famous roast meats. Plus there is a tempting display of cakes laid out to greet you when you arrive.

name: Osteria Magona
review: You are certain to fall for the charm of this rural restaurant, whose excellent value for money attracts food - lovers from far and wide. Situated among olive groves and vineyards, the Osteria Magona serves a whole host of meat specialities with tartare, beef delicacies and roast dishes all featuring on the menu.

name: Violetta
review: This restaurant has a distinctly rural feel, from the old cart on display in the courtyard to the local flavours of the dishes. It is no surprise then, to find traditional agnolotti or tajarin pasta with cep mushrooms on the menu, alongside excellent steak tartare and finanziera (a local dish made with chicken liver and sweetbreads).

name: Osteria Bartolini
review: This young, attractive and friendly restaurant brings the maritime influences of Romagna to Bologna, upholding its traditions of fresh fish dishes which are simple yet full of flavour. “Fritto misto” (fried fish) is still the house speciality, although other classic fish and seafood dishes also feature on the menu. In fine weather, enjoy your meal in the shade of a huge century-old plane tree.

name: Armando al Pantheon
review: This small restaurant just a few metres from the Pantheon has been run by the Gargioli family since 1961, with the third generation now at the helm. Popular with locals and visitors alike for its traditional cuisine, which includes Roman and Lazian dishes, meat and fish options, and specialities such as offal, veal intestines, spring lamb, fresh anchovies, and sour-cherry tart.

name: Fonte alla Vena
review: Situated alongside the road that leads to the picturesque historic centre, this restaurant with simply furnished, informal dining rooms serves excellent cuisine full of intense, delicious flavours. The emphasis here is on Tuscan traditions, with a particular focus on rustic dishes and ingredients such as offal, Cinta Senese pork and fresh pastas. An address to return to time and time again.

name: Locanda Moscal
review: A simple, informal, friendly and colourful inn which also includes a restaurant popular with visitors to the lake as well as from Verona. Situated on the edge of the charming historic centre of Affi, the locanda serves generous cuisine which is full of flavour and made from top - quality ingredients.

name: Consorzio
review: This simple, informal restaurant with two dining rooms designed in a blend of old and modern styles acts as a backdrop for traditional cuisine which includes dishes such as pasta, offal, finanziera stew, Fassona beef and other Piedmontese specialities, all carefully prepared and cooked using top-quality ingredients. The nearby Banco Vini e Alimenti bistro is run by the same owners.

name: Laghetto
cuisine: Cuisine from the Aosta Valley, Italian

name: Il Cedro
review: A few kilometres from the monastery of Camaldoli, Il Cedro celebrates home-style Tuscan cooking, which is simple yet full of flavour. Two sisters are at the helm here: one in the kitchen, and the other offering friendly service front of house, where she announces the daily specials at your table. Fresh produce and specialities from the Casentino are to the fore.

name: Dalla Rosa Alda
review: The undoubted star of this restaurant is the Enbogonè tagliatelle – a pasta made entirely by hand and seasoned with a sauce made from borlotti beans, local extra - virgin olive oil and rosemary – although the menu features many other dishes. Simple, honest cuisine made mainly from carefully selected regional produce, accompanied by an excellent selection of local wines.

name: Fracia
review: Park the car and walk up a short track (about 50m) to this rustic stone farmhouse with panoramic views of the surrounding valley. A traditional oasis serving delicious local cuisine with a light touch and the occasional Mediterranean influence where, in summer, meals are served at stone tables in the delightful outdoor area with stunning views of the surrounding countryside.

name: L'Angolo del Gusto
review: Situated in the centrally located hotel of the same name, this restaurant is an excellent choice for anyone wanting to sample the mountain specialities of the Aspromonte region, with many ingredients sourced locally. The generous antipasti trolley (almost a meal in itself) and the bean and porcini mushroom soup are among the dishes that impressed us most. And for anyone wanting to stay here, the guestrooms are comfortable, especially the superior category rooms.

name: I Tri Siochètt
review: The sister and two brothers who once ran this trattoria, as well as the grocery next door, were considered a little mad – hence the name, which means ‘three madcaps’. The building has retained its attractive country feel and is now popular with gourmets for its fine local cuisine, such as tortelli (a type of ravioli) with herbs and parmesan.

name: Osteria Zanchetti
review: Situated at the top of a steep slope in Fossombrone’s beautiful historic centre, this osteria takes guests back to the 1920s thanks to its romantic decor. Here, having risen through the culinary ranks, the owner-chef makes full use of his expert techniques to create dishes that hover between tradition and a sense of fantasy using the best seasonal ingredients that the region has to offer. The concise wine list favours micro-producers and natural wines.

name: Osteria La Solita Zuppa
review: Situated in Chiusi’s historic centre, this restaurant has the feel of a typical Tuscan trattoria with its traditional vaulted ceiling. The chef’s love for regional cuisine is demonstrated by the revival of traditional recipes (including the use of a wood-fired oven), resulting in the full flavours that are so characteristic of this region.

name: Contesto Alimentare
review: A tiny modern trattoria with simple tables set close together, where the fine cuisine on offer is the real attraction. Using regional produce, the female chef prepares delicious specialities inspired by Piedmontese classics, such as tajarin pasta and plin ravioli which always feature on the menu. Other options such as salt cod with vegetables and lavender panna cotta with meliga biscuits (a typical shortbread from the Piedmont) occasionally make an appearance.

name: Impero
review: Now a culinary landmark in the province, this restaurant is run by two enthusiastic sisters who serve cuisine with its roots in local traditions and prepared using seasonal ingredients. Renovation work over the past few years has added to the style and character of the restaurant, which boasts a small garden for summer dining plus a good selection of wines.

name: Lokanda Devetak
review: Just two kilometres from the Slovenian border as the crow flies, this restaurant with its dual influences serves top-quality cuisine rooted in the gastronomic traditions of this border region. In business since 1870 and now run by the four children from the sixth generation of the same family, Devetak is an absolute must for anyone visiting the Friuli region.

name: Trippi
review: This long-established restaurant just outside Sondrio has been run for the past decade by Gianluca, whose experience injects new life into traditional dishes from the local region, as well as introducing the occasional Mediterranean twist. There’s a simpler menu at lunchtime, plus a good selection of local wines and cheeses on sale at takeaway prices near the restaurant entrance.

name: La Cucoma
review: Situated on the town’s main street, just 10min from Ravenna, this restaurant has been run by the Amadori family for over 40 years. Enjoy fish specialities in a classic-style restaurant with a friendly, family atmosphere, plus a few daily specials announced at your table, on a menu which is totally dedicated to fish and seafood. Apart from the raw fish dishes which are more expensive, the restaurant is renowned locally for its value for money.

name: Antica Trattoria la Grotta dal 1918
review: It takes a while to get here, along a road which wends its way through the hills, but the cuisine more than compensates for the journey. The food here is based on a careful choice of ingredients (including produce from the restaurant’s own farm) from as far away as the Apennines, with a few ingredients from elsewhere in Italy, with a focus on traditional recipes. Don’t miss the tortellini in brodo, or the game and truffles available in season.

name: Lo Stuzzichino
review: Situated near the church in the heart of the village, this restaurant, with its pleasantly informal setting, showcases products and recipes from Campania, including vegetables from its own kitchen garden. Meals are served either outdoors (in fine weather) or in the dining room (with an open-view kitchen) decorated with local ceramics.

name: Antica Trattoria da Miculan
review: A small bar busy with locals acts as a sort of “antechamber” to this typical trattoria with a summer terrace on Tricesimo’s main square. The restaurant, which boasts traditional regional features, such as the wood-burning stove known as a fogher, serves local specialities alongside a few fish dishes. In summer, there’s a tasting menu which focuses exclusively on fish.

name: Il Conte Matto
review: The castle’s 14C hunting lodge has been converted into a showcase for Tuscan produce with a panoramic terrace overlooking the hills and glimpses of the surrounding countryside from the guestrooms. Specialities include pici pasta in a Chianina beef ragù, veal tagliata seasoned with three salts and herbs from the garden, and cantucci biscuits served with dessert wine.

name: Villa Aurora
review: A typical restaurant in the province of Brescia not far from Lake Garda, Villa Aurora serves Italian cuisine with an equal focus on meat and fish dishes, as well as a few traditional specialities with a light modern twist. A bastion of local cuisine, the restaurant is run by a welcoming and experienced family. Don’t miss the desserts!

name: Alla Pace
review: Sauris is situated in a slightly secluded location which adds to its appeal. Occupying a beautiful 17C house near a charming little lake and picturesque mountain village, this restaurant has been run by the same family since 1804. This enchanting setting acts as the backdrop for a menu featuring delicious regional specialities.

name: Profumo di Mirto
review: This is a classic, simple neighbourhood restaurant where guests will immediately feel at home. Fish specialities take pride of place here, but it’s also worth taking your time over the copious buffet of appetisers which gets your meal off to a fine start. A few Sardinian dishes pay tribute to the owners’ native island.

name: Green T.
review: Not far from the Pantheon, this original restaurant arranged over four floors serves the type of fine Chinese cuisine which has graced official banquets in China ever since the time of Chairman Mao. The menu also features some surprisingly modern Asian dishes, making this restaurant a must for fans of Chinese cuisine!

name: La Chioccia d'Oro
review: A solid father - and - daughter team runs this restaurant in the heart of the Parco Nazionale del Cilento, where the traditional local dishes (meat and vegetables) can be enjoyed in the classic - style dining room or on the outdoor terrace in summer. Highlights include the stuffed rabbit with seasonal vegetables, cep mushrooms and potato bake, and the Cilento cannolini made with hand - rolled pastry and filled with confectioner’s cream.

name: Trattoria Ceriati
review: This attractive modern trattoria in a tranquil out - of - town location is run by two young partners with experience in the restaurant business. The cuisine is rooted in the traditions of Parma, with a choice of boiled meat specialities in winter and meat cooked over the barbecue grill and served on the outdoor veranda in spring and summer.

name: Antica Trattoria La Toppa
review: In the heart of a small, romantic medieval hamlet, this typical Tuscan trattoria opened in 1964 and continues to celebrate regional cuisine in all its glory. Highlights on the menu include soups and fresh pasta dishes. In summer, meals are served outdoors on the attractive street which is full of character.

name: Trippa
review: Simple, informal and with a slightly retro feel, this restaurant serves a range of dishes from all over Italy, including the tripe which gives the restaurant its name. Unfussy and uncomplicated, the cuisine prepared by the skilful young chef using top-quality ingredients makes this one of the best trattorias in Italy. House specialities include Milanese risotto with grilled marrow, vitello tonnato and, of course, the ever-present tripe!

name: La Cuccagna
review: There are many reasons to visit this excellent family - run restaurant in the village centre, the most important of which is the food – fresh vegetables, delicious first courses (the fresh troccoli pasta with wild chicory, cherry tomatoes and broad beans is excellent) and carefully selected meat dishes (the father was once a butcher! ). Close attention is also paid to the wine, with more than 500 labels just waiting to be opened in the beautiful wine cellar.

name: Mangiare Bere Uomo Donna
review: She’s from Hong Kong, while he’s from Suzzara – together this couple run this welcoming restaurant where their international focus extends from the dishes which feature on the menu to the wine selection and the couple’s love for applied arts. Once seated, you can either choose traditional fare, including a few delicious fish dishes, or you can be tempted by the decidedly Asian options. Whatever you decide, one thing’s for sure – authenticity and seasonal, locally sourced ingredients are guaranteed.

name: Al Bersagliere
review: A long - established restaurant overflowing with memorabilia, from the juke box to the old coffee machine dating from the 1960s, run by a family which has been here for generations. Guests can visit the wine cellar dating back to the 13C, there’s a good selection of spirits, and the cuisine showcases the best of the Veneto. Specialities include pasta and beans, bigoli pasta with duck and risotto all'Amarone.

name: Antica Locanda al Cervo - Landgasthof zum Hirschen
Le Antiche Sere
review: A small restaurant overlooking the lake in Lesina, where everything revolves around the professionalism and experience of the owner - chef, who selects the best produce from the lake region, including fish and aromatic herbs, and even produces his own mullet roe. Regional flavours are to the fore here, with the occasional modern twist.

name: Trattoria da Paeto
review: This small trattoria hidden among the canals in the countryside is run by a couple of partners who showcase the specialities of the region with professionalism and enthusiasm. The menu includes delicacies such as fish and vegetable couscous, and sfoglia pastry with cream and flakes of chocolate, as well as a few more modern dishes.

name: 13 Comuni
review: Situated in the village square, this restaurant is run by a couple – she’s front of house, while he’s in the kitchen – who use top - quality local produce to prepare a mix of traditional and modern dishes. House specialities include gnocchi with sheep’s ricotta cheese and hazel butter (the butter isn’t actually made with hazelnuts but is simply melted), and confit pork ribs in beer. The mountain - style decor continues in the simple guestrooms.

name: U.P.E.P.I.D.D.E.
review: Undeniably characteristic and refreshing! Dug out of the rock that once formed the old Aragonese walls, the four dining rooms in this restaurant run one into another under brick arches and then lead to the wine cellar, which is open to guests. The regional cuisine is as traditional as the decor, with specialities such as barbecued local meat and beef fillet in a plum sauce with wine and caramelised shallots on the menu.

name: Lerchner's In Runggen
review: If you’re looking for traditional cuisine from the Alto Adige, this is one of the best addresses for you! Here, you’ll find wood decor with an added romantic touch, staff in local costume and a menu which features the best produce from this delightful region of northern Italy. Specialities include potato ravioli stuffed with cheese on cabbage leaves, braised veal with Jerusalem artichoke puree and apricot dumplings with vanilla cream.

name: Osteria della Chiocciola
review: This restaurant has a wine bar on the ground floor and a dining room on the first floor, both simple yet attractive in style. The food is resolutely regional and traditional with an emphasis on local, seasonal ingredients. The tajarin pasta served with butter and sage is a perennial favourite on the menu.

name: Antica Trattoria Cattivelli
review: As its address indicates, this restaurant is situated on an island formed by a loop in the River Po. Since 1947, the Cattivelli family have been celebrating the best of the Lower Po valley’s cuisine here in a rural, river setting that is typical of the region. Highlights include the pisarei e fasò and fish from the river, although you can’t really go wrong here whatever you choose!

name: Andrea - Sapori Montani
review:
Situated in the centre of this small Baroque town with Greek origins (as its splendid theatre testifies), this attractive restaurant is run by a talented couple. Top-quality produce from inland Sicily, including fruit and vegetables grown on the family farm.
There’s also a good wine list offering a fine selection of Sicilian wines. In summer, dine alfresco on the terrace with views of the rooftops of the town.

name: Serendib
review: Serendib, the old name for Sri Lanka, means “to make happy” – an ambitious promise but one which this welcoming restaurant manages to keep! The cuisine here focuses on typical vegetarian options, as well as Indian and Sri Lankan dishes. The tasting menu introduces guests to different specialities and is highly recommended (especially if it’s your first time here).

name: Da Giocondo
review: An authentic restaurant, where the owners themselves are at the helm in the kitchen and front of house making sure that the rustic, regional cuisine served here is full of flavour. Daily specials, which vary depending on market availability (thus ensuring the freshest possible ingredients), are announced at your table, in addition to a small selection of dishes on the menu. House specialities include traditional hand-made pastas, each of which has its own name and which is typical of the Abruzzo.

name: Dell'Alba
review: In business since 1850, and now run by the sixth generation, this traditional and historic family trattoria is a mecca for fans of Bassa Padana cuisine.
