The simple yet authentic ambience is warm and welcoming, while the delicious cuisine – an extraordinary combination of specialities from Cremona and Mantova – is a real treat for the tastebuds.

name: Romani
review: This restaurant has a traditional feel, both in its richly decorated dining room and in its cuisine, the roots of which are firmly planted in the region. This is the place for guests who aren’t keen on reinterpreted dishes or exotic fare but prefer the classic flavours of Parma such as cured hams, fresh pasta, and roast and grilled meat, all served in a typical country farmhouse.

name: Osteria de Börg
review: Borgo San Giuliano is situated just a stroll from the sea in old Rimini, a district of narrow alleyways and brightly painted houses that once provided homes for local fishermen. It is also home to this excellent osteria-style restaurant with an outdoor space on the small square for summer meals and two smart dining rooms decorated with rustic vintage furnishings. This is the setting for typical Romagna cuisine which features top-quality cured hams, fresh home-made pasta (don’t miss the cappelletti in chicken broth) and meat including Mora Romagnola pork in various dishes.

name: Foresta
review: Situated in front of a dense fir wood, this restaurant comes as something of a surprise. The dishes are prepared with genuine local ingredients, resulting in food that is full of flavour. Don’t get up from the table without having tasted the pappardelle pasta with mushrooms and speck ham or the fillet of venison with a redcurrant sauce.

name: Cantina dei Cacciatori
review: The original sign painted on this restaurant’s façade hints at a history which dates back over a century. Situated outside the village and surrounded by sweet chestnut trees and tufa rock, what was once an old trattoria now serves typical Piedmontese specialities, such as meat and borage ravioli with butter and crispy pancetta, as well as dishes from further afield. Charming outdoor area for summer dining, plus an early - 20C wine cellar which can be visited by guests.

name: Locanda da Condo
review: Situated in the delightful Prosecco wine-growing region, Condo is a well-established trattoria which has been in the same family for generations, and which remains faithful to the gastronomic traditions of the Veneto. The dining rooms are welcoming and full of character, while the elegant veranda adorned with climbing plants is an attractive option in summer. The cuisine is both excellent and good value for money, making this restaurant an excellent all-round choice.

name: Raieü
review: Authentic fishing lamps hang above the tables in this typical trattoria, where one dining room boasts wooden furnishings and tables divided by benches, and the other is more traditional and brighter in feel. Regional cuisine takes pride of place, including highlights such as fish gnocchi with clams and cuttlefish stew. Freshly caught by the restaurant’s own boat, the fish is prepared following local recipes.

name: Dalla Libera
review: Although from outside this trattoria has retained its appearance of a historic family restaurant, inside you’ll be surprised by the smart, contemporary-style decor. The owner-chef selects seasonal and mainly regional ingredients, turning them into imaginative and yet unfussy dishes. Choose from simple, faster options at lunchtime during the week, all with the same high quality.

name: Da Flavio e Fabrizio "Al Teatro"
review: Choose the ground floor for a quick meal and the first floor for a special dinner in this restaurant near the cinema - theatre. In both cases, the menu focuses on traditional fish dishes from the Veneto, such as black and white tagliolini with squid, scampi and courgettes. The honey semifreddo with caramel is the perfect way to round off your meal.

name: Trattoria Cibrèo-Cibreino
review: This trattoria is named after the famous cibreo, a typical stew from Florence that Catherine of Medici was said to enjoy so much that she even attempted, unsuccessfully, to export it to France. It is often crowded, but there is no point in trying to book a table as they don’t take reservations. Roast rack of beef (gran pezzo) is one of the specialities.

name: Rosselli 77
review: An interesting and unusual restaurant - cum - antique shop, where the owner (who is also the chef) restores the furniture and other items that make up the decor and which are available for purchase. Piedmontese specialities take pride of place on the menu, which changes daily depending on market availability. Highlights include the potato salami ravioli on melted Taleggio cheese, the cappello del prete beef and the cremino al gianduiotto chocolate dessert.

name: Tipico Osteria & La Locanda del Capitano
review: The Locanda and the Tipico offer two menus showcasing traditional Umbrian cuisine (one gourmet, the other traditional); guests can then choose in which of the restaurants they would prefer to eat. The wine selection has recently been extended to over 400 labels, while the olive oils now have their own dedicated menu which includes the best oils from the region. With Giancarlo Polito at the helm, there’s no doubt that you’re in excellent hands!

name: Da Marchesi
review: Situated on a road that climbs through the Apennines between Romagna and the Marche, this small restaurant serves good, simple and traditional Romagna cuisine. The menu features home-made pasta and local meat dishes, as well as daily specials which focus on seasonal ingredients (don’t miss the “fossa” cheese from Perticara and the tortelloni with butter and truffles). Excellent value for money, making this one of the best trattorias in Italy!

name: QuarantunoDodici
review: Situated on the banks of the river, this seaside osteria run by chef Lele Usai (the Michelin-starred Tino is on the first floor of the building) is the perfect setting for a business lunch or an enjoyable dinner thanks to its excellent fish-based cuisine which is firmly rooted in traditional recipes. As well as the à la carte, the “Diario di Bordo” lists the daily specials, which showcase the freshest fish on offer here.

name: Trattoria Bibe
review: Immortalised by the Italian writer Montale in his poetry, this trattoria has been run by the same family for almost two centuries. The menu features traditional Tuscan dishes, such as pici pasta with wild boar sauce. Alfresco dining in summer. There are also apartments with kitchens for guests that wish to extend their stay.

name: La Brinca
review: The little village of Ne has become synonymous with La Brinca, a restaurant occupying an old farmhouse surrounded by greenery which in the past 30 years has become one of the best trattorias in Liguria and the whole of Italy. The restaurant tells the story of the Circella family – parents and offspring alike put all their heart, energy, passion and dedication into their work here… and it shows! The excellent local, seasonal cuisine is generous and tasty, accompanied by equally superb wines (over 1 000 labels are stored in the wine cellar) which are presented to guests with proper courtesy and attention.

name: La Campanara
review: The 16C rectory next to the Chiesa dei Miracoli has been transformed into a charming restaurant run by an enthusiastic couple. They serve delicious, home - cooked specialities from Tuscany and the Romagna. The house next door is home to an inn with six excellent guestrooms, a couple of which even include a Jacuzzi bath.

name: Il Sogno
review: An attractive country restaurant, where experienced maître d’ Silvano presides front of house, and the young and brilliant chef Marco is at the helm in the kitchen. Together they have created a delightful place to eat, where the focus is on excellent regionally inspired cuisine with the occasional individual and imaginative touch. House specialities include gnocchi with local chicken ragù.

name: La Baita
review: A family - run osteria in the town centre, where you walk through a well - stocked delicatessen selling the house specialities to get to the dining room. There’s an excellent choice of cheese and fresh, handmade pasta, as well as a selection of more than 1 000 different wines. Local, seasonal dishes such as cheek braised in wine feature on the menu.

name: Burro & Alici
review: With just a road separating it from the beach, this simple restaurant is similar to the many others dotted along the seafront in Marotta, the inspiration for the famous Italian song “Il mare d’inverno” (“the winter sea”) by Enrico Ruggeri. However, it’s the food that is the main attraction here – the colourful, generous cuisine of the Adriatic, with fish served in classic recipes occasionally finished with an imaginative and personal twist. Pizzas cooked in a wood-fired oven are available in the evening.

name: La Cucina dei Frigoriferi Milanesi
review: An interesting location in the artistic-cultural setting of the Frigoriferi Milanesi industrial complex for this restaurant with a modern feel both in its decor and its cuisine. The restaurant offers a "destructured" menu, which instead of dividing the courses into the traditional antipasti, starters and main courses, consists of different dishes which can be selected however guests prefer.

name: La Rosina
review: With over 100 years of history behind it, La Rosina is still looking good, thanks to renovation work carried out a few years ago which has given the restaurant a new look. Situated in an attractive location in the hills around Marostica, this excellent restaurant is a sound choice for good food in the province of Vicenza, serving modern regional and Italian dishes which are full of flavour. Enjoy beautiful views of the surrounding hills from the guestrooms.

name: Da Burde
review: Opened at the beginning of the 20C as a grocer’s shop and trattoria, this historic restaurant is a long way off the usual tourist trail. The two brothers who now run Da Burde have kept everything as it was, with cured hams on sale and a bar selling tobacco. The dining rooms to the rear are full of decorative detail, with wine bottles and a dessert trolley adding to the pleasantly convivial and informal atmosphere. Not surprisingly, the cuisine focuses on authentic local specialities.

name: Macok
review: This bright, colourful bistro is known by food-lovers across the country, and it certainly deserves its reputation. It’s family-owned and professionally run by a friendly team, and the menu is an appealing mix of colourful Hungarian and Mediterranean dishes. Classic flavours are in abundance but the presentation is decidedly modern; the beef cheek goulash is not to be missed.

name: Kistücsok
review: If you’re coming for dinner, make the most of it and stay over at this small hotel, which comes complete with its own swimming pool. Well-regarded locally, the restaurant is known for its consistently good interpretations of classic Hungarian dishes, which have been modernised both in their composition and their look. Flavours are fresh, with the occasional global influence, and prices are reasonable. The ‘Taste of the Region’ menu is always a great choice.

name: Mór24
review: Mór24 is the type of place we’d all like to have at the end of our street – only this one involves a walk up the hill. It’s run by an enthusiastic young couple, who travelled the world before returning home to open this trendy little spot, and the short à la carte of sharing plates reflects their travels. Everything is homemade and the cooking keeps things simple, letting the good quality ingredients speak for themselves.

name: Anyukám Mondta
review: Anyukám Mondta is everything a good neighbourhood restaurant should be. It offers something for everyone – from homemade pizzas to refined modern Italian dishes and tempting daily specials – and prices cover a wide range to suit all occasions, so you can easily eat at a reasonable price. Excellent produce is prepared with care, resulting in hearty, flavoursome dishes, while service is smooth, well-paced and comes with plenty of personality.

name: Sparhelt
review: Set away from the lakeside, in a busy residential neighbourhood, this all-day bistro is run with honesty and integrity. The menu has a Hungarian heart and perfectly reflects the seasons, with the likes of chilled fruit soups in summer and hearty, warming dishes in winter; if the native Magalitsa features, do order it. The smart terrace is always a popular place to sit.

name: Casa Christa
review: Roads fringed by almond trees and terraced vines lead to this stunning hillside spot with far-reaching views over Lake Balaton. It’s a restful place and comes with seven restored wine press houses which now play host to designer bedrooms with private saunas. Within the grounds is this beautiful, orangery-style restaurant with a lovely terrace and a concise menu of dishes bursting with Hungarian, French and Italian flavours.

name: Lunch Lady
review: Much like a grandmother who has prepared a feast for her family, Chef Nguyen Thi Thanh exudes a warm, loving presence as she looks over her bustling dining room. She is a long way from Saigon, where she ran a successful food stall, and with her she has brought her charismatic cooking to East Vancouver. The menu is endlessly enticing and inspires immediate decision paralysis. One could fill up fast on starters like fried black tiger prawns with fish sauce or beef carpaccio buried under a blanket of fresh herbs, pickled onions and lime vinaigrette. Garlic fried noodles are another big hit, but then will you still have room for the wagyu beef noodle soup? At the meal’s end, admirers are quick to approach and thank her like the local celebrity she is.

name: Vij's
review: When it opened back in 1994, this local staple was at the vanguard of Indian fine dining in North America, and it continues to make a compelling case for the gastronomic riches of the subcontinent. Namesake chef and owner Vikram Vij hasn’t slowed in spreading the good word, still maintaining a daily presence in the dining room, where he stops at tables to check that every guest is happy. He has little cause for worry, in light of the culinary treasure trove on offer: consider a signature dish of wine-marinated “lamb popsicles,” with a fragrant fenugreek sauce or opt for one of the vegetarian dishes, like a curry made with red bell pepper, portobello mushroom and paneer. A list of unique cocktails offers a perfect foil for the well-spiced cuisine.

name: Chupito
review:
Peek-a-boo...where are you, Chupito? You'll need to walk to the alley located behind La Taqueria to find this hidden gem. The beach may be missing at this fully covered outdoor taqueria where pebbles crunch underfoot and a shipping container subs in for a bar, but the flavors transport guests to Mexico just the same.
Come for a cocktail and the aguachile, but stay for the other winning dishes like a red pozole bobbing with carnitas and plump hominy. Carne en sugo, or flank steak with tomatillo and jalapeño pepper folded with braised beans and bacon, will have you scooping up every last bite. 
Order a postre even if you're full—you'll want to linger no matter the time of year.

name: Phnom Penh
review: In the heart of Chinatown, find one of the city’s most respected restaurants. Since 1985, this family-run institution has dazzled crowds with both Vietnamese and Cambodian dishes. The menu is massive, offering nearly 100 rice, noodle and soup preparations, but everyone knows to lean on the classics. You could almost make a meal out of #71, thin slivers of nearly-raw beef soaking in a tangy mix of pureed pineapple and fish sauce. It’s a deliciously original effort. Ordering a mound of golden-fried chicken wings coated in an addicting mix of salt, pepper and sugar is also a given. Beef luc lac with fried egg will round out a meal guaranteed to have leftovers. Be prepared to wait for a table; lines form almost as soon as the doors open.

name: Fable Kitchen
review:
This popular farm-to-table cafe has been drawing crowds to Kitsilano for over a decade. The setting is lively and comfortable, with exposed red brick walls, wood furnishings and two varnished wood counters seating a handful of diners facing the open kitchen. During daytime hours, the team turns out hollandaise-slicked eggs Benedict (and variations), Johnny cakes topped with pulled pork and tomato jam and thickly sliced challah French toast plated with caramelized apples and whipped mascarpone. A side order of rosti, two blocks of uniformly golden-brown finely shredded potato cakes accompanied by chive-flecked sour cream, is always a good idea. 
Dinnertime eats are equally hearty and satisfying, as in a short rib with polenta and grilled leeks.

name: Kin Kao Song
review: You're in for a real treat at Kin Kao Song, where diners come for a distinctive take on Thai dishes that aren't replicated anywhere else (well, except at their other outpost). Kin Kao Song's fare is driven by a creative spirit and the region's bounty. The lemongrass wings are a special surprise. These bite-sized beauties are deep fried and tossed in a fragrant lemongrass coating for a flavorful punch that delights. Pad Thai may seem like an obligatory order, but this savory version vies for best in class. Then, northern Thai laab with tender, rich pork is given a lift with tart fish sauce and lime broth along with crisp vegetables. Finally, mango sticky rice has that wonderful sticky-sweet appeal.

name: Anh and Chi
review:
The brother-and-sister team have crafted a clean, cool space outfitted with midcentury modern furnishings while nodding to the past—a blue neon sign by the bar is a relic from the former restaurant. For more than thirty years, their parents' restaurant occupied this spot, but Anh and Chi now welcomes a new generation of diners. 
The menu is a love letter to Vietnam. Gỏi bắp chuối cua lột, a salad of chopped softshell crab piled high atop a banana blossom, is cool and bursting with flavor. Chạo tôm bánh hỏi is prepared in a classic way, with grilled prawn mousse served with an array of fresh herbs, and there is pho, of course. The dessert menu changes daily, but if on offer, the house-made coffee mousse is a standout.

name: Oca Pastificio
review:
Although there may be a number of Italian-leaning restaurants and pizza spots scattered around Vancouver, this simple pastificio invites diners to pull up a chair and savor authentic, well-prepared pasta dishes.
They have bistro charm down pat, with black-and-white tiled flooring, a chalkboard emblazoned with the daily specials and a window onto an open kitchen. Consider the specials, then peek into the pasta rolling station and watch as your meal is made. A salad of romaine and chicory with oil-cured anchovy fillets and roasted red peppers is elegant in its simplicity. Tagliatelle with a wine-rosemary braised rabbit ragu is especially satisfying. There is just one dessert, but you'll be pleasantly full already.

name: Fiorino, Italian Street Food
review: Fiorino, Italian Street Food is a welcoming spot with just a hint of nostalgia (spy the framed photos and art). Giovanni "Gio" Mascagni presides over this serious Italian place where the bread-making skills he learned in Tuscany are on full display. At lunch, focaccia sandwiches and schiacciata, like the one stuffed with guanciale, drizzled with honey and spread with walnut crema, are the hot ticket. At dinner, it's all about pasta. Spaghettoni ai frutti di mare is a classic Italian seaside dish brimming with clams, mussels and prawns in a perfectly spicy arrabbiata sauce. Each strand is heady with flavor; the clams are tender; the mussels are meaty; and the tomato-based sauce is equal parts sweet, spicy and tart.

name: Say Mercy!
review: Intimate and welcoming, passersby stop in their tracks and do a double take, as it's clear that everyone is having a gloriously good time at Say Mercy! As for the food? It's a mash-up of Italian cooking with a BBQ nudge. Crudo kicks appetites into gear with sweet slices of amberjack in a caper-dill dressing, olive-serrano pepper relish and wafer-thin fingerling potato chips. Don't even think about passing over the BBQ Bolo—it's nonnegotiable. Short for "bolognese," it's a distinctive dish of house-made spaghetti tossed with pancetta, smoked pork butt and Grana Padana. Finally, the unique twist on the cannoli, inspired by banana pudding, is a great way to end the meal.

name: Nightshade
review: Nightshade is a plant-powered hipster cafe tucked within equally trendy Yaletown. Here, diners will discover a full list of well-crafted cocktails, local beers and a respectable wine list, along with a menu that roams the world. Executive Chef Chanthy Yen brings his unique spin to dishes such as a highly original, East-meets-West congee—creamy and fragrant, it is topped with tender braised fennel and puffed rice. Cauliflower coated in chickpea batter and nicely crisped is sided by a green chutney over a base of plant-based cheese for a modern take on the classic pakora. Sake-marinated yuba, yam tempura and hearts of palm sub in for a plant-based "sushi." Finally, crème brûlée, with lavender-infused vegan custard and a raspberry-hibiscus coulis, steals the show.

name: Little Bird Dim Sum + Craft Beer
review:
Longtime local restaurateur Jonathan Lee's vision of pairing classic dim sum with local B.C. craft beer was the impetus behind Little Bird, and trendy Kitsilano is the ideal home for this hip lair. Inside, it's contemporary cool—the floors, tables and walls are created in part from recycled chopsticks. 
It's a classic lineup of dim sum favorites. Sticky rice studded with savory pork and chicken and sweet goji berries is a must-order. Of course, there must be dumplings, and Little Bird's run the gamut from traditional (ha gow) to surprising, with sweet corn, cilantro and shrimp. Supremely fresh, savory and served steaming hot, these dumplings are the definition of comfort food.  
As promised, beer is king here.

name: Mo Xiao Guan
review: Noodles are either served in soup or tossed in a sauce and come in 3 portion sizes. Pork bone noodle soup with meat sauce is especially popular – the broth is simmered for 6 hours, giving it deep rich flavours. Wontons and dumplings are also their specialities; try wontons dressed in spicy bean sauce or dumplings in sour laver soup. It closes on random days so check ahead – and with just 8 seats it’s best to avoid peak hours.

name: Ming Ting Xiao Guan
review: A spin-off from the local household name Ming Ting Restaurant, this compact eatery is always jam-packed with diners hungry for its traditional Sichuanese fare. The room is bright and airy, while the semi-open kitchen lets diners watch the chefs flaunt their skills. Signature dishes include the silky smooth douhua, the unmissable Dad’s twice-cooked pork loaded with wok qi, and novel items like the durian spring roll. Reservations not accepted.

name: Lao Chengdu San Yang Mian
review: This ‘hole in the wall’ may lack bells and whistles, but it’s popular with locals. Soup and tossed noodles are divided into 3 trifectas, namely the ‘old’, ‘new’ and ‘more’. Blanched noodles tossed in spicy meat sauce with diced string beans in the ‘old’ category is the most popular item. Feel free to order wontons with chopped chillies on the side. And nothing cools your mouth better than a bowl of tofu dessert with red bean soup.

name: Chen Mapo Tofu (Qinghua Road)
review: Mapo tofu is a world-famous Sichuanese classic dating back to the Qing Dynasty. Word has it that this century-old shop is the true original source of this numbing, spicy dish, invented by Lady Chen. Silky tofu, ground beef and spices are cooked in a stone pot that stays hot for a long time, perfect with a bowl of steamed rice. Zhong dumplings and lotus leaf-wrapped steamed pork in spiced rice flour are also worth trying.

name: Yu Jiu Xiang
review: This simple neighbourhood shop has been serving traditional Chengdu cooking since 2014. Signature items come in big portions enough for a few to share. Blanched pork belly dressed in garlic sauce strikes a fine balance between meaty and garlicky flavours. Spicy fried chicken cubes with chillies pack the typically Sichuanese numbing, fiery oomph. With only about 10 tables and 3 private rooms, reserve your table ahead of time or arrive early.

name: Yangboying Za Jiang Mian
review: The owner-chef who used to work in a famous restaurant uses traditional techniques to make noodle soups and assorted toppings, each boasting a substantially different taste profile. Noodles dressed in meat sauce with sesame paste, red chilli oil and Sichuan pepper is a regional classic exuding intoxicating aromas. Those who prefer less heat may opt for dumplings in seafood soup that cooked with dried shrimp, cuttlefish and scallops.

name: Chanyue Vegetarian
review: Bamboo blinds, wooden furniture, elegant plants and sheer curtains impart serenity. The set menu changes every 15 days to reflect the 24 solar terms in the Chinese calendar; even the house-fermented vinaigrette used is different. Seasoned with ginger, garlic and chilli, the food is mostly Sichuan-style, with vegan items craftily disguised as meat and fish – bovine bolete as pork liver, bamboo fungus as beef tripe, konjac as squid.

name: Ting Yuan 399
review: The entrance sign shows ‘garden’ in Chinese, priming guests for a pleasing experience as they soak up the verdant setting. It’s also no stranger to food lovers in the know who flock here for the river fish dishes. Plump swamp eels from inland rivers are poached in a flavourful broth loaded with spices and herbs. When served at the table, the eels are drizzled with sizzling hot oil, their flesh being tender and juicy, but with a crispy chew.

name: Mind
review: Serving just 4 types of noodles, along with a few sides during the day and a menu of home-style dishes at dinner, this shop urges diners to slow down and mindfully savour their clean, simple flavour. Freshly wrapped wontons are dressed in red oil or served in seafood broth. Also look for the hawker carts where steamed rice cakes with red bean filling are made. The complementary ‘Laoying’ laurel tea is perfect to round out their sweetness.

name: Shudidanggui
review: Named after two Chinese herbs, the concept of a therapeutic diet is at the core of this establishment. Diners are greeted by an herbal tea sweetened with stevia, and the menu is built around Chinese medicines. The signature beef noodle soup is infused with dang gui, believed to improve blood circulation, making it a lunch time favourite for many. Yellow croaker with galangal and patchouli is also popular. Some dishes require pre-ordering.

name: Zhuan Zhuan Hui (Lianhua South Road)
review: Despite its hard-to-find entrance, this flagship of the chain has earned solid fandom among locals with its no-frills, home-style Sichuanese cooking that is frugally priced. Instead of severe piquancy that can pack a punch, expect a more tamed heat that caters to the palate of most. Braised crucian carp with Chinese patchouli is aromatic and tasty, while Chengdu-style twice-cooked pork renders rich meaty flavours. The homely atmosphere is also a plus.

name: Dumpling & Drinks
review: It doesn't take a rocket scientist to figure out the eponymous specialities of the house. Dumplings are freshly made daily in the open kitchen and six varieties are served each day, each to be ordered in units of 5. Those filled with pork and mushrooms, or beef and Chinese celery are the highlights. Nestled in a quiet neighbourhood, the cosy room features a clean and modern décor with a light wood and dark green colour scheme.

name: Organization South
review: Though it moved from Kuanzhai Alley to this spot in the south of town, diners still come in droves. The playful, retro décor with fake tree trunks and red lanterns is aptly matched by a menu disguised as a martial arts instruction book. Besides famous Sichuanese wok-fried dishes such as green chilli ‘ruthless’ chicken, and braised swamp eel, cold appetisers and seasonal offerings are also worth a try. The generous portions are great for sharing.

name: Rongrong Beida Pugaimian
review: Famous for flat noodle soup, this brand always attracts a long queue at the door. Diners can see the four chefs pulling a piece of dough to make the signature noodles – thin, soft, but with a lovely chew. There are two sizes and a few toppings to choose from, all boasting spot-on seasoning of the perfect amount of heat punctuated by a mild sweetness. Be prepared to share a table with strangers at peak hours.

name: Stiva Grischuna
review: In this 300 year-old chalet with charming wood-panelled rooms, the cooking is down-to-earth and regional. Whether traditional Grisons dishes such as Capuns and Maluns or classics such as "Norbert's Stroganoff" and cordon bleu - this is tasty fare and, furthermore, prices are very reasonable. It's best to book. Locals also dine here.

name: La Trattoria
review: In the charming Hotel Walther, one of Pontresina's most emblematic hotels, the lovely Trattoria has an authentic, lively atmosphere and a stylish rustic feel. The appetising menu embraces all regions of Italy, with delicious pasta as the centrepiece and the focus firmly on flavour and freshness. Friendly Italian service and a good selection of wines.

name: SALZANO
review: The restaurant of this family-run chalet hotel serves up an interesting concept in a friendly atmosphere: classics are available for lunch and dinner, with additional lunch menus on offer and a fine dining "nature-based" set menu in the evening, from Tuesday to Saturday. They use top-notch ingredients sourced almost exclusively from the immediate area, and pick much of the produce themselves.

name: La Pendule
review: From their “Club Sandwich” to seasonal dishes to the table d’hôte, diners here are treated to delicious meals in both the stylish restaurant and the more casual Stadtcafé. In summer, choose one of the tables outside under the archway. Magnificent vaulted cellar for special events. Traditional-style guestrooms are available at the Hotel Stadthaus.

name: Sonne - Bistro
review: Sonne's attractive bistro is another place to enjoy fresh and flavoursome food. The dining area is really inviting and the service comes courtesy of a friendly front-of-house team. Alternatively, grab a table on the delightful terrace. The classically based dishes can be ordered à la carte or you can opt for one of the set menus in the fine dining restaurant. The excellent wine list is the same in both areas.

name: Zum Wilde Maa
review: In the Matthäus quarter in Kleinbasel, this smart building on a corner has housed a restaurant since 1910. The owners, who have already made a name for themselves in the city with their previous restaurant, Bonvivant, serve tasteful, unpretentious cuisine based on good ingredients. Fair prices, very friendly service and good wine recommendations.

name: Alpenblick
review: The Anderhalden family have redesigned their rather secluded inn: there is now a restaurant-cum-living room – the lounge area with its fireplace is ideal for an aperitif – and the cosy "Stübli" with its beautiful wooden floor and elegant table settings. The chef-patron cooks up flavourful seasonal dishes, while the service comes courtesy of the attentive lady of the house, who is always on hand.

name: sunny bar by claudia canessa
review: This restaurant in the traditional Kulm Hotel is well loved. This is mainly down to the authentic Peruvian cuisine, which is based on very good, fresh ingredients and tastes great. The interior is also lovely, with its numerous decorative photographs contributing to the atmosphere, as does the lively, attentive and professional team working the restaurant floor.

name: Urnäscher Kreuz
review: Beautiful wood panelling, low ceilings, harmonious decor… It's really cosy in this pretty Appenzell building, and the service is friendly. Last but not least, the seasonal cuisine bowls diners over with its freshness and flavour. The wine list is respectable too. There is also an inviting terrace overlooking the Urnäsch River.

name: Les Ateliers Brasserie
review: If you’re a fan of delicious traditional dishes such as chicken fricassée and veal kidneys then the brasserie at Les Ateliers, run by talented duo Jean-Sébastien Ribette and Sahondra Verdan, is the place for you! Here, you can savour cuisine that fully embraces freshness and simplicity in a chic, industrial-style ambience.

name: Weid
review: At first glance, you wouldn't necessarily recognise this chalet above Weiden as a restaurant. But take a closer look, because the chef here is on a mission with his interesting concept: his crystal clear cuisine is full of flavour and based on top-quality produce from the surrounding area – the speciality is trout from his own farm. The garden terrace is wonderful!

name: Casa Casutt - Ustria
review: Linus and Therese Arpagaus propose a charming atmosphere in which to enjoy excellent cuisine made from fresh produce. The menu takes its cue from the region and includes local specialties such as capuns (Swiss chard rolls) and pizokel (buckwheat spätzle). Fans of veal liver, sweetbreads or tripe will also find what they're looking for. Fabulous garden terrace! Alternatively, there is the Sala too.

name: Gasthaus Zur Fernsicht - Swiss Alpine
review: A pleasant alternative to the gourmet restaurant, Gasthaus zur Fernsicht is friendly and modern with a great view of the lake through its glass frontage. “Swiss Alpine Food” takes pride of place here, with a focus on selected seasonal produce sourced from local farmers and producers. Reduced lunch menu, plus relaxed yet professional service.

name: Barranco
review: Eat, drink, make merry, meet friends… the Kreis 4 district is to Zurich what the Barranco district is to Lima. Nestled among a host of other restaurants and bars, the Peruvian district's namesake serves authentic modern Peruvian cuisine that is bursting with flavour, zing and spices. Equally appealing is the pleasantly unpretentious atmosphere complete with relaxed, nimble service. Great cocktail selection.

name: Muntanella
review: This is one restaurant offering two different types of dining: at lunchtime, a simple menu for skiers in a hurry (rösti, pasta dishes, burgers etc), and in the evening a more sophisticated menu with an emphasis on sustainability and regional produce, with dishes such as salmon trout from the Brüggli trout farm cooked in Arosa hay with Riesling-Sylvaner wine sauce, black salsify and Albula mountain potatoes. Don’t miss the glazed walk-in wine cupboard.

name: Netts Schützengarten
review: The front part of this restaurant is rustic in style (the food is often accompanied by a glass of beer from the in-house brewery), while the rear has a more elegant feel. The food includes Swiss classics such as Züricher Geschnetzeltes (sliced veal served in a cream and mushroom sauce), and international fare such as sesame seed-coated tuna served with wasabi mashed potatoes. Beer garden in the shade of the sweet chestnut trees.

name: Albrun
review: The journey up to this enchanting mountain village is something of an adventure, but the food is worth it! The rustic chalet-style interior belies an ambitious menu including roast black nose lamb with artichokes and chickpeas, as well as poached char with curly kale. There are even a couple of simple but well-kept rooms for overnight stays.

name: Nest- und Bietschhorn
review: This cosy, rustic restaurant is located in a hotel first opened in 1868, which makes it the oldest hotel in the Lötschental valley (the modern, Alpine-style rooms are particularly attractive). Excellent cuisine including Valais specialities such as duo of veal, braising jus with cooked wine, Hokkaido pumpkin and smoked potato gnocchi on the menu. Fine views from the terrace.

name: Bauernschänke
review: This historic restaurant offers a delightful dining experience, serving understated and intriguing regional cuisine, including vegetarian options and Asian-influenced dishes (many of which are designed for sharing). The menu also features house specialities such as pork belly gröstel served with pickles and butterhead lettuce. Friendly service and a lively, casual atmosphere.

name: Rössli
review: Whether you prefer the Rössli-Stube or the simpler dining room, this long-established restaurant built in 1772 offers friendly service and a mix of traditional and classic modern cuisine. The simpler daily specials are delicious, as are menu options such as pan-fried char and mashed parsnip. Outside you will find the Rosenterrasse and Rössligarten. Charming guestrooms are also available.

name: Osteria Fagetti
review: Standing on the main street, this small, carefully decorated restaurant with wooden floors and roughly hewn tables offers its guests friendly and attentive service. The simple cuisine is seasonal and full of flavour, with a focus on locally sourced produce. Recommended dishes on the menu include the homemade raviolini and the beef tagliata.

name: A la Vieille Auberge
review: This old inn definitely lives up to its name, as it is the oldest property in the area. Chef Éric Hamart offers guests delicious, seasonal cuisine such as millefeuille of crab, with a ginger-flavoured coconut milk emulsion, and Deux-Sèvres pigeon with a grape preserve glaze and a selection of side dishes. The efficient and attentive service comes courtesy of his charming wife, Myriam.

name: Zum Pflugstein
review: This distinguished vineyard farmhouse is the perfect place for food-lovers! Inside, attractively panelled rooms and a modern, elegant restaurant set the tone, while the outdoor terrace is truly idyllic. Excellent service overseen by the charming female manager. We recommend one of the dishes for two, such as the sea bass baked in a salt crust or the Chateaubriand.

name: Les Curiades
review: A truly historic restaurant which has been serving food since 1850. The present chef has experience in some of the finest restaurants, and it shows! His cuisine is elegant and refined, including dishes such as chuck beef braised in beer (paying tribute to the chef’s Belgian origins) and a delicious vegetarian menu which is always available. An unqualified success!

name: Anker
review: On the first floor, wood panelling and low ceilings provide a cosy setting in which to choose the appealing mix of traditional and international dishes on the menu. The calves’ liver with sage, onions and rösti, for example, is delicious. A significant amount of the restaurant’s meat comes from its own butchery.

name: Gasthof zur Sonne
review: A lovely restaurant practically right by the lake, with the small harbour opposite. Regional fare prepared by the second generation of restaurateurs. Chef Cäsar Meyer has inherited his passion for fish from Lake Zurich from his father who used to be a fisherman. Asian influences also feature on the menu. Delightful terrace and comfortable guestrooms also available.

name: Grotto Valmaggese
review: Situated in a slightly elevated location above the road, this traditional grotto-style restaurant with a large car park is quiet and cool in summer, with a dining room warmed by a fireplace in winter. Classic, well-prepared and generous cuisine with personal touches made using top-quality, seasonal ingredients. Sculptures by a local artist adorn the premises. Make sure you try the risotto with organic cheese, as well as the pancetta-wrapped Patanegra pork fillet with sweet peppers and patate sabbiate (roast potatoes coated with breadcrumbs).

name: Buech
review: Set in an idyllic location overlooking Herrliberg and Lake Zurich, this truly charming restaurant boasts stylish dining rooms that exude traditional charm. The views from the uniquely beautiful vine-covered terrace are stunning! Unsurprisingly, the few seats in the "wine huts" are coveted. In the kitchen, the emphasis is on choice produce from the region.

name: Alla Cantina
review: All the staff hail from Sicily at this beautiful historic restaurant on the village square but have been working in Switzerland for years. Authentic Sicilian cuisine is served in a rustic and welcoming setting that also hosts regular musical events: the only concession to Ticino are the polenta-based recipes. There’s a cool, tranquil outdoor space for summer dining, plus four attractive, inviting guestrooms on the top floor.

name: Victoria
review: In a chic, modern setting, a friendly front-of-house team serves high-quality, delicious cuisine. The menu proposes a pleasing mix of regional and international dishes. For a more casual alternative, there is the bistro bar – here you can order schnitzel or burgers, for example. Minimalist-style guestrooms are available for overnight stays.

name: Eintracht
review: There has been a restaurant here since 1870 and the current owners, the Meier family, have retained the restaurant's traditional feel while also introducing contemporary influences, both in the bistro and in the more elegant restaurant area. The same is true of the cuisine, with classics such as veal cordon bleu and gourmet set menus composed of three to five courses. Excellent wine selection. Simple daily specials are also available in the bistro.

name: Le Bologne
review: Next to the Fine Arts School, this vintage bistro cuts a fine figure with its cement tiles, globe lights and bare bulbs, as well as its bar, banquettes and bistro chairs. The dishes are carefully prepared with good seasonal ingredients: celeriac risotto and foie gras, lamb shoulder confit, cumin, asparagus and labne...

name: Pensiun Aldier
review: If you like your food straightforward and pared down to the essentials without compromising on taste, then you'll love the excellent Engadine cuisine at the pleasingly unpretentious restaurant of the charming little hotel of the same name. The dishes forgo any frills and instead focus on select, fresh local produce. Good wines at fair prices. Smaller menu at lunchtime.

name: Dal Mulin
review: This modern, rustic yet stylish restaurant in the heart of St Moritz has a friendly feel. The charming and attentive front-of-house team serves cuisine that has the same informal style as the setting but is far from simple, with a focus on carefully prepared, elegant and subtle dishes. The wine selection is outstanding – they even have their own wine shop!

name: Chesa
review: In this inviting restaurant, grab a table by the window to enjoy the magnificent view of Flims and the Tectonic Arena Sardona UNESCO World Heritage Site. Alternatively, there's alway the terrace. The menu is influenced by the chef's Alsatian roots, but there is also Mediterranean and regional fare. This place is very popular, so be sure to make a reservation! For overnight stays, there are pleasant, simple guestrooms.

name: Gül
review: This restaurant tucked away in an inner courtyard has a laid-back atmosphere and is pleasantly lively thanks to a vibrant soundtrack of Turkish music. And so the scene is set for the food, a modern take on traditional Turkish dishes – made in the open kitchen and, in keeping with the way in this part of the world, served in smaller portions or larger dishes for sharing.

name: Postigliun
review: Far above the valley lies the Sgier family restaurant, where Sandro (the son) and Guido (the father) serve up their tasty cooking. You should definitely try "Guido's capuns"! They also make game dishes with meat from animals they have hunted themselves. If you plan to accompany your meal with wine from their appealing selection, you can stay overnight in one of their guestrooms.

name: Josef
review: This trendy, urban restaurant and bar is in the middle of a residential area in Kreis 5 (fifth district). The atmosphere is lively and buzzy, and in light of their interesting concept it comes as no surprise that the place is well frequented: they serve tasty modern European cuisine with dishes in starter-size portions - and at a fair price. Good wine list and cocktail selection.

name: Aroleid Restaurant
review: If you’re looking for creative and “alternative” cuisine on the ski slope, you’ll enjoy this contemporary and rustic-style chalet restaurant where the array of interesting dishes feature Asian, Italian and French influences reflecting the chef’s international travels. Full of flavour with individual touches and options such as roast duck, consommé, leek and soba noodles on the menu.

name: Café du Levant
review: In a quiet little village in an attractive rural setting, you will find this friendly, down-to-earth restaurant. The property backs onto fields and the fresh air is a real tonic. They serve seasonal and richly flavoured regional French cuisine, which you can accompany with your choice from a good selection of wines from the Geneva region. Lovely terrace.

name: Rigiblick
review: In this restaurant overlooking the city, a rather soigné yet relaxed atmosphere awaits you. The kitchen team focuses on regional produce, which is used to create really delicious dishes. In summer, head for the leafy terrace. Tip: it is easy to get here by taking tram no 10 or the Funicular Rigiblick.

name: ZOLLHUUS
review: This friendly place is perfect for meat lovers. They specialise in steaks, some of which are matured in the restaurant's own dry-ageing cabinet. Vegetarian and vegan alternatives are also available. The first Saturday evening of every month is devoted to Wagyu beef dishes, and it's BBQ night every Thursday (Jun-Aug). There's a fabulous rooftop terrace with views of the Aare and the region. For overnight stays, the adjoining Hotel Kettenbrücke has elegant guestrooms with a minimalist design.

name: La Parenthèse
review: An opportunity to enjoy a gourmet meal in a simple and cosy small restaurant offering the warmest of welcomes on the outskirts of town. The cuisine follows the rhythm of the seasons, showcasing regional products in dishes such as citrus-marinated tuna with a lentil salad. To choose your cheese, you can head to La Cave!

name: Blaue Ente
review: Historic industrial architecture outside and a trendy and lively atmosphere (and some fine old machinery) within. The service is attentive and easy-going, while the menu includes dishes such as rack of lamb with garden cress risotto and Zurich egg on leaf spinach with potato foam and truffle. Make sure you try the flatbread specialities made from naturally fermented spelt sourdough.

name: Café Cher-Mignon
review: In this chic yet relaxed auberge, well-travelled Toulon-born chef Serge Coustrain-Jean creates bistro-style dishes at lunchtime and a gastronomic menu in the evening (make sure you try the scallops with a truffled parsnip purée and blood orange butter). Two chambres d’hôtes are available for guests wishing to stay the night. Take full advantage of the superb terrace in fine weather!

name: Restaurant du Quai
review: This inviting restaurant on the shore of Lake Geneva serves unfussy and tasty seasonal cuisine. Chef Jérôme Manifacier is a real pro. His motto is "take your time"; ours is to place our trust in him. Superb terrace shaded by the plane trees and with a splendid view of the lake and the Jura mountains.

name: Le Vallon
review: This lovely classical inn, elegant with its pink façade and green shutters, beckons to you to cross the threshold… The tastefully luxurious interior is adorned with bouquets of fresh flowers and floral wallpaper. French chef Christophe Raoux, "Meilleur Ouvrier de France", runs the show in the open kitchen, crafting fine classic cuisine – from pâté en croûte to fillet de boeuf Rossini and quenelles made with pike from the lake, one of the house's signature dishes. The friendly service doesn't put a foot wrong, and the wine list is excellent (including a selection of red wines, also in magnum format). In fine weather, enjoy the terrace and the verdant garden.

name: Grotto della Salute
review: A rustic grotto-style restaurant with a warm and welcoming ambience, where staff are happy to advise you on the seasonal dishes on offer. A whole page of the menu is dedicated to classic favourites, all of which are Mediterranean in style. The terrace shaded by huge plane trees provides a pleasant setting for summer dining, while an excellent wine list adds to the appeal.

name: Taverna Rosa
review: In the basement of Die Rose, you can enjoy typical Italian cuisine in a really pleasant rustic atmosphere. In summer, make a beeline for the delightful terrace. For groups of four or more, we recommend heading to Tavolata, where various dishes for sharing are served. Tip: the lunch menu in the form of the "Pranzo-Box" – as with the Japanese bento box, the dishes included in the set menu come in one box.

name: SALZHAUS
review: At this restaurant you will find an attractive mix of urban cool and historical setting, including some unusual exposed old masonry. The cuisine also combines international, regional and seasonal fare. There is a simple selection at lunchtimes and something more ambitious in the evenings. Try the Thai curry soup or the venison entrecôte with walnut malfatti.

name: Landgasthof Bären
review: The inviting exterior of this 17C half-timbered house gives a taste of the charming dining rooms inside. The house speciality is the Bären cordon bleu (an unbreaded version). Both the garden and the wall paintings in the cellar are well worth a look and the bright, functional rooms are ideal for an overnight stay.

name: Bacchus Bistro & Genussmanufaktur
review: This is a restaurant that really makes you feel at home. Due, no doubt, to the tasteful, upmarket decor, the friendly service and – last but not least – the good, fresh food. The lunch menu offers particularly good value for money. If you like to cook, Genussmanufaktur sells cheese, herbs, cakes, wines and more besides.

name: Moosegg
review: One draw of this elegant, modern restaurant is the phenomenal view of the Emmental and the Alps – best enjoyed from the terrace. Another is the excellent regional and seasonal cuisine. Diners can opt for a tasting menu in the gourmet area or indulge in tried-and-tested dishes in the "Beiz". There are also chic accommodation options here at an altitude of almost 1 000m.

name: Des Bains
review: Despite the many works of art on the walls here (all of which are for sale), this is indeed a restaurant and not an art gallery! Food-lovers will delight in the delicious traditional cuisine on offer, accompanied by a selection of local wines. The name of the restaurant is a reference to the old thermal baths of Roman Aventicum.

name: Chappeli
review: In this friendly, down-to-earth restaurant overlooking the village, the Hausmann/Köhli team propose a really fun dining experience! Your charming hostess takes care of the restaurant floor while the chef-patron showcases cuisine that is distinctly regional in terms of flavour and aroma. Excellent wine recommendations. Be sure to bag a table on the delightfully verdant garden terrace!

name: Schlüsselstube
review: Schlüsselstube is a bistro where they also serve outstanding food – and it represents really great value for money. Classics such as braised veal cheeks are delicious, and the desserts are extremely hard to resist! When it comes to wine, this cosy place also hits all the right notes. The service provided by waitresses in traditional dress could not be more charming!

name: Auberge de la Croix d'Or - Bistro
review: Claudia and Olivier Hiernard have combined bistro and restaurant at their charming inn. The delicious bistro fare on the blackboard is now complemented by a market-inspired "Menu du Marché", meaning flavoursome dishes are now served in both parts of the establishment. Just don't forget to leave room for dessert! On Friday and Saturday evenings, only a small selection is available.

name: Edo
review: You can be in the Swiss mountains and still enjoy authentic Japanese cuisine, including dishes such as Japanese fondue, grilled chicken with Teriyaki sauce, and delicious gyozas and sushi (takeaway dishes are also available). Here, legendary specialities from Japan are prepared in front of you with high-quality ingredients and meticulous care. Terrace with views of the surrounding peaks.

name: La Fleur de Sel by Carlo Crisci
Zum Alten Stephan
review: This restaurant in the middle of the historical old town is not only steeped in history, it is also a place to enjoy really good food. On the menu you will find "Stephan's Classics" as well as dishes that are somewhat more modern, but by no means contrived. The charming front-of-house team is managed by the proprietress. Delightful terrace in front of the building.

name: Landhaus
review: This former farmhouse dating from the 16C is now a really cosy restaurant with a fantastic view of Lake Constance – a delightful setting in which to enjoy the excellent food. The decor is a winning combination of sleek, modern design, warm wood panelling and nods to tradition. There is also a beautiful terrace and a hall that can be hired for events.

name: PINOT
review: The location may seem a little unusual but the food is really good! Set in the side wing of the modern Klinik Gut private hospital, PINOT boasts a fashionable, minimalist-style interior, an open kitchen and a great view. The chef, Roland Schmid, has made a name for himself in the region over the years. “Gourmet evening” with a set menu on Thursdays.

name: Adler
review: The name of the game here is "Gasthaus at its best" – this applies to the cosy dining rooms, the warm, attentive service, and chef Daniel Jann's cuisine. Whether you opt for Murmeltierpfeffer (marmot stew), Gitzi-Bratwurst (a goat meat and beef sausage) or asparagus dishes, meticulous craftsmanship and flavour are guaranteed. The focus lies squarely on the region. Eating here is fun! Stylish guestrooms are available for overnight stays.

name: La Grappe d'Or
review: A restaurant where superb flavours and a friendly, relaxed atmosphere go hand-in-hand. The cuisine here is strongly influenced by Northern Italy, from Venice across to Ventimiglia, thanks to chef Theotim Bioret who has quickly made his mark here. Meticulous presentation, precise cooking and delicious sauces combine to create a faultless dining experience. The only thing that you’ll want to do when you leave is to return as quickly as possible!

name: Kaiserstock
review: The Kaiserstock is no longer a well-kept secret – and the narrow, steep approach road is worth every effort. The chef clearly has a passion for cooking, creating delicious dishes such as homemade ravioli and Brischtner pears as a dessert. The ingredients are all locally sourced, while the rustic guestrooms are absolutely charming. Please note: cash payments only!

name: Chez Philippe
review: Philippe Chevrier from the Domaine de Châteauvieux is the brains behind this huge restaurant inspired by New York-style steakhouses. Relaxed atmosphere, meats sourced from the renowned Boucherie du Molard, fish caught by small-scale fishermen, dishes cooked over a wood fire, a truly authentic cheesecake and an expansive wine list. A real favourite!

name: Njørd café
review: Njørd Café is a spin-off of Njørden Restaurant, in a more casual culinary vein. It serves fresh and seasonal Scandinavian and Swiss cuisine in a modern, Nordic atmosphere. Breakfast and brunch are also served at the weekend. There is a charming terrace planted with herbs and flowers to the rear of the building. Hotel Hemma has a number of pleasant guestrooms.

name: Auberge Communale
review: This rather inconspicuous Auberge is located in a small set village slightly above Vevey. Run by the Konrad family, it not only offers guest rooms for overnight stays, but also serves really good food! Whether eating in the modern, understated restaurant or on the pretty terrace, you can choose from the delicious "Bistro" dishes or the "Gastro" menu. It is always tasty and prices remain very competitive.

name: Bären
review: Come here to enjoy seasonal cuisine that is straightforward, prepared with fresh produce and, above all, utterly delicious. You can dine à la carte or opt for a set menu. Here, the house specialty is spaghetti alla parmigiana. The lovingly decorated Gourmetstübli makes for a particularly appealing setting. At lunchtime, the choice is more limited but includes a rather sophisticated set menu.

name: Osteria della Bottega
review: This lively osteria is located on a steep little street in Geneva's old town. Against a chic industrial backdrop with an open kitchen, diners enjoy modern, seasonally inspired Italian cuisine and fine wines, as well as attentive and friendly service. It's best to book, as Osteria is very popular! Across the street there is a lovely terrace.

name: Collonge Café
review: This modern restaurant boasts a great location next to the historical town hall – the terrace laid out in the garden is charming. It successfully brings together modern Italian and French cuisine with seasonal influences, and also keeps an open mind when it comes to international ingredients. The service is friendly and competent. Tip: the great-value lunch menu.

name: Café de Peney
review: This lively and popular restaurant located on an arm of the Rhone calls to mind a vintage picture postcard: charmingly done out, with various antique objects and a wisteria-covered terrace. Fine ingredients are prepared to produce flavour and finesse. Specialities include, for example, pig's cheeks confit with Gamaret or the runny hot chocolate biscuit.

name: La Croix d'Or
review: This restaurant in the centre of the peaceful village of Ballaigues, not far from the French border is housed in a magnificent historical building. It is run by two French chefs, David Sauvignet and Damien Lanza, with professionalism and a passion for good food. They serve good seasonal French cuisine with just a hint of a Mediterranean influence. Interesting lunch menu, pretty terrace.

name: AuGust
review: This restaurant with its charming brasserie atmosphere is located in what was once the "butcher's quarter" – and the meat theme has been taken up here accordingly. Besides design features such as lamps and wall tiles, the open kitchen is what really draws the eye. They use meat from their own production or from Swiss producers. Vegetarian alternatives are also available.

name: Hirschen
review: This magnificent historical building ensemble has officially been labelled a "cultural asset of national importance". In the main building dating from 1684, you dine surrounded by stylish panelling and magnificent tiled stoves. The garden terrace under the old trees is fabulous! Delicious Swiss cuisine is what's on the menu. Some of the produce is sourced locally, such as the char and trout. Small lunchtime menu. Charming guestrooms.

name: DAR
review: This trendy, understated place is the charming sister restaurant of KLE. Here, the tasty plant-based dishes with Spanish and Moroccan roots, as well as other international influences, are ideal for sharing. There are two dinner services each evening, and drinks are served at the adjoining bar – before or after your meal. Sat and Sun brunch.

name: Auberge Communale Le Mont
review: Burgundy ham terrine, gherkin and fresh herb condiment; Jorat veal belly, pistachios and green asparagus: the Burgundian chef and Meilleur Ouvrier de France definitely knows his stuff. This is a fine dining version of modern French cuisine that highlights local and fresh ingredients and showcases small-scale producers. He successfully pulls it off, and keeps it affordable. Fine selection of wines by the glass.

name: Le 1424, La Fabrique Cornu
review: "La Fabrique" has many strings to its bow: it is a biscuit-maker, an interactive museum and, on the third floor, it houses this chic, contemporary restaurant with a panoramic view of the Vaud Alps. The ambitious and tasty dishes are made with a wide range of regional and national ingredients and given an international spin. Good value for money.

name: Boléro V Bistro
review: This chic bistro opposite the railway station is on the same premises as a gallery and a library, and has a bar where you can sit and enjoy tapas. The cuisine is modern, tasty and based on good ingredients. At lunchtime on weekdays, there is also a three-course lunch menu. You can sit out on the lovely terrace overlooking the public square. The bar organises regular evenings of live music.

name: Flamel
review: Housed in the historic, recently renovated LUGANODANTE hotel, this restaurant serves excellent contemporary cuisine, with a simple menu at lunchtime and more elaborate fare in the evenings (tasting menus and à la carte), including carefully selected Swiss meat, herbs and salads from their own organic kitchen garden. There’s also a mixology bar which, in addition to unique cocktails (made from their own home-grown or locally sourced ingredients), offers an array of beers, fruit juices and home-made chocolates.

name: La Bottega di Mario
review: With its mix of ristorante and salumeria in a historical building (1913), La Bottega is wonderfully inviting and lively. The tasty dishes, clearly influenced by Ticino, and the wonderful selection of salami and ham at the counter are equally tempting – here, the friendly mastri salumieri also take care of the cold cuts. Tip: try the house wine, a Ticino merlot from a six-litre bottle!

name: Le Café Valrose
review: Part of the same establishment as La Table de Valrose, this bistro offers a comfortable rustic-Alpine atmosphere, whether you are sitting on the terrace shaded by chestnut trees surrounded by mountains, or inside, by the fireplace in a wood-panelled interior. The lounge bar invites you to relax with a coffee, a cocktail or a drink in hand. You can opt for the good seasonal fare or one of the classics, such as the Valrose fondue (champagne version available...), malakoffs and the Valrose Burger (meat or veggie), which are permanent fixtures on the menu. The dessert trolley is in service for afternoon tea and there is also a short menu (served from 2pm to 7pm) in case you miss the lunch slot.

name: Gaijin Izakaya
review: This izakaya (literally "foreigner pub") is a really cool location. In the style of its Japanese namesake (pubs that serve small dishes), Daniel Shu, who was trained in Chicago and New York, and his business partner and team serve really good Asian soul food. The atmosphere is relaxed, with modern music played.

name: Bären
review: Choose between simple dishes served at the “GastStube” (to the front of the building) and more sophisticated fare at the “GnussStube”, both with a focus on largely regional and classic cuisine with a modern twist. There’s also the option of the “MundArt” gourmet menu, if booked in advance. Good selection of Swiss wines, including an impressive range of rare labels.

name: Zollhaus
review: This charming historical customs house dating from 1786 has been transformed into an appealing restaurant with a lovely atmosphere. The friendly and competent front-of-house team delivers the chef-patron's classical dishes, which bowl diners over with their excellent ingredients and flavour. Those who appreciate a good wine with their meal will also be catered for.

name: Höhwald
review: In this wonderful restaurant with its stunning view, Heribert and Silvia Dietrich serve up excellent regional cuisine in an atmosphere that could hardly be more welcoming. Try the maluns, a Graubünden potato speciality cooked over an open fire, or the tasty braised venison cheeks. The patio heaters make it possible to sit outside on the terrace even on cooler days.

name: L'Agape
review: A lovely, tastefully refurbished bistro featuring old tiled floors, wooden banquette seating, mirrors on the walls, a large chandelier fashioned out of old copper pans and a small counter. The place ticks all the boxes when it comes to friendly vibes. As for the food, chef Clément Thellier has created a short, savvy menu that makes your mouth water with its well-crafted and beautifully presented dishes: sweetbreads in barigoule, bacon chips, split peas with bacon; beef tenderloin, toast, pan-fried foie gras, baby vegetables and a potato emulsion; poached and glazed pineapple, toasted gingerbread and rum ice cream. In short, an enjoyable mealtime in Geneva at a reasonable price – not to be sniffed at!

name: Bistrot Dumas
review: This buzzy, often packed bistro, located in the Champel district, sports a striking decorative style with a patchwork ceiling of coloured glass and eye-catching columns. The traditional culinary repertory features deftly curated French classics, rich in flavour and aroma and entirely made in house. The slick service is both efficient and dutiful.

name: STÜVA in der Krone - Säumerei am Inn
review: These different Arvenstuben – one of which is the over 300-year-old Stüvetta – are a good alternative to LA CHAVALLERA. Here, all the cosiness of the Engadine region benefits from a modern touch. The tasty cuisine homes in on the essentials; they use mainly regional and seasonal ingredients. In fine weather, food is also served on the terrace.

name: Indian Rasoi
review: This restaurant not far from the Place du Rondeau is based on the interesting concept of serving authentic, hybrid Indian cuisine that is not tied to any single region. The droves of customers suggest this is a wining formula! The atmosphere is modern, the service friendly and attentive. In summer, the terrace is most pleasant.

name: Natürlich
review: The restaurant is located in a side street, not far from the River Rhône. It has a trendy, relaxed bistro atmosphere and serves modern, seasonal cuisine based on quality ingredients from the region. Dishes can be shared, or perhaps you prefer to opt for the five-course surprise menu. Shorter set menu at lunchtime. There is a good wine list with a number of organic wines. Tip: be sure to book!

name: One Degree North
review: As suggested by its name, which denotes Singapore’s geographical coordinate (one degree north in latitude), this establishment is dedicated to popular Singaporean dishes and Asian barbeque specialties. Singapore chicken rice and Cantonese crispy roast pork, are two traditional recipes enhanced by the young chef’s meticulous technical skills. These signature dishes bring popular Singaporean flavors alive in an authentic way, and exploring other cuisines in Seoul is always a fascinating gastronomic experience.

name: A Flower Blossom on the Rice
review: Located in a quiet alley away from the touristy bustle of Insa-dong, A Flower Blossom on the Rice is a restaurant that caters to the health-conscious diner, serving wholesome home-cooked fare using only certified organic ingredients sourced straight from the farm. The signature dish at this restaurant is the Bojagi Bibimbap — a log of cooked rice topped with five different sautéed vegetables in their multi-colored glory, encased in a crépe-thin egg omelet resembling a gift, tied with a seaweed ribbon and presented with a single flower on top.

name: FAGP
review: In a city where a plate of pasta is as ubiquitous as a bowl of kalguksu, it takes a good dose of creativity and knowledge of the genre to be recognized for one’s craft. Chef Lee Jong-hyuk is armed with both. FAGP is a casual restaurant that offers a simple yet inventive menu with a focus on the relatively humble pasta. There is a genuine sense of conviviality here, which comes as no surprise, as the chef says he revels in engaging with his customers while cooking in the open kitchen.

name: Bongpiyang
review: Famed for its authentic Pyeongyang cold buckwheat noodles and grilled spareribs, Bongpiyang is operated by the local Byeokje Galbi barbecue restaurant franchise. These legendary noodles, with a high buckwheat content, are served in a flavorful chilled beef broth, topped with slices of beef and fermented cabbage greens. Although cold buckwheat noodles are typically regarded as a seasonal dish enjoyed in the warmer months, this restaurant is busy all year round.

name: Pildong Myeonok
review: Located near Namsangol Hanok Village by Chungmuro subway station, this restaurant is a Pil-dong landmark that has been serving Pyeongyang cold buckwheat noodles for decades. The restaurant’s chilled broth has a delicate beef flavor, its subtlety both loved and disputed among cold buckwheat noodle aficionados. Another highlight of the restaurant is the buttery and tender boiled pork slices, served in thick slices with a dipping sauce. Homemade dumplings are also popular.

name: Yukjeon Hoekwan
review: Three generations spanning five decades have kept this restaurant in business since its opening in 1962. At the time, their iconic crispy thin-sliced bulgogi, grilled over open flames, was all that was offered on the menu. The dish became so popular that the name bassak bulgogi was patented. Today, the restaurant stands four stories high, still serving the same dish that has fed generations. Their coagulated beef blood soup with a clear broth is another stunner.

name: Mr. Ahn's Craft Makgeolli
review: Mr. Ahn's Craft Makgeolli is a most befitting venue for the Korean term banju, or alcohol accompanying a meal. What distinguishes this gastropub is its avoidance of the stereotypical Korean pubs and expression of the direction they should take—in this age of new Korean cuisine that is traditional yet imbued with a modern touch. At this charming spot, patrons can enjoy seasonally changing menus of savory Korean anju (snacks paired with alcohol), main dishes, as well as a wide selection of traditional liquors that simply get better with time. It’s a perfect place for both light meals and friendly social drinking—a versatile venue that appeals to distinct audiences.

name: Hadongkwan
review: This beloved family-owned culinary landmark, located on a busy side street in Myeong-dong, has been serving rustic bowls of beef bone soup since 1939. The version here is served in traditional brass bowls with rice already submerged in the hot soup. The broth is pure and rich with an unmistakable sweetness that can only result from boiling large amounts of beef for a long period of time. This old-fashioned, no-fuss eatery opens early in the morning and closes when its soup vats run dry.

name: Woo Lae Oak
review: Lauded as one of the best Pyeongyang cold buckwheat noodle restaurants in the city, Woo Lae Oak has been serving consistently stellar food since 1946. The family-operated establishment is tucked away in the back alleys of Euljiro 4-ga, a bustling business hub. The restaurant interior is spacious and spotlessly clean. Indulge in their legendary Pyeongyang cold buckwheat noodles, served in broth or in a spicy sauce, and their bulgogi, grilled tableside.

name: Filleter
review: “A space of seafood, by seafood, for seafood” captures the culinary ideology of Filleter run by Chef Jung Se-wook, the self-proclaimed and proven seafood aficionado. Naturally, the menu consists entirely of seafood. A cuttlefish dish, made with sweet-flavored butter, caviar, and katsuobushi, coupled with wood ear and cauliflower, is pure gastronomic joy when paired with wine and fish & chips made with cutlassfish deep-fried to crispy perfection. Filleter’s diverse seafood dishes, prepared from various recipes, are wonders that transcend the imagination.

name: Base is nice
review: Base is Nice is a vegetarian-friendly restaurant. Chef/owner Jang Jin-a had a fairly long career overseas as a restaurant consultant, food stylist, and food & beverage planner. The diner’s natural ambience and well-balanced, vegetable-centered dishes are proud manifestations of her lifelong culinary endeavors. Creations of rice and vegetables, accompanied by soup and side dishes, are refined and tasty. As Jang puts it, the restaurant’s menu is a way to experience everyday food through a natural, veggie-centered diet, and not thanks to a conscious approach to vegetarianism. Reservation required.

name: Jeongmyeon
review: A seven-seat stainless steel table and an open kitchen are all there is to Jeongmyeon, which means “noodles infused with meaning.” This one-chef operation serves noodle soups with meat. White noodle soup and red noodle soup are the only two dishes on the menu, but both offer deep flavor profiles. The broth, made with seafood, pork, and chicken, reveals a rich set of tastes. Garnishes topping the rice noodles, including thin slices of pleasantly chewy pork, onion, and red pepper, are truly a sight to behold. The red noodle soup, which can be made with varying levels of spiciness, is served with a bowl of rice for a filling meal.

name: Yurimmyeon
review: For over 50 years, this family-run eatery has been serving bowls of noodles to those seeking comforting nourishment. The fresh buckwheat noodles, one of its bestsellers, are made from scratch, daily, using premium salt from Bigeumdo Island in Sinan County, and buckwheat flour from Bongpyeong. Topped with seasoned vegetables, thin strips of egg garnish, and a dollop of sweet and spicy sauce, a bowl of these noodles makes for a satisfying meal. Garak-guksu, wheat noodles in piping hot broth, comes with a generous serving of fishcake.

name: Samcheongdong Sujebi
review: This local haunt has been an integral part of Samcheong-dong’s history since 1982. The signature dish here is sujebi — rustic hand-pulled dough soup served in a savory anchovy broth. The restaurant is also known for its potato pancakes, made with grated potatoes that are pan-fried until crispy on the outside and pleasantly chewy on the inside. Avoid the lunch rush if you don’t want to stand in line, but be warned — the restaurant is always busy.

name: Jungin Myeonok
review: When a restaurant continues to attract large crowds of hungry diners, then it is doing something right. The proprietor of Jungin Myeonok has had just one goal since day one — to continue the legacy of his parents for as long as he can, using only the best ingredients. The establishment’s legendary Pyeongyang cold buckwheat noodles are based on a tightly guarded family recipe handed down to him by his parents, who both hail from North Korea. The room gets packed quickly during lunch service, especially during the warmer months.

name: Myeongdong Kyoja
review: Myeongdong Kyoja is a family-owned place in operation since 1966. The restaurant, which offers only four items on the menu, specializes in dumplings and noodle soup. An impressive number of patrons flock here daily, largely because all the dishes, including its signature garlic-laden kimchi, are made in-house. Simple décor and service come with hefty portions at affordable prices. It has a sister operation in the same area of Myeong-dong.

name: Mandujip
review: Located in a trendsetting part of the city dominated by state-of-the-art fashion, this restaurant has stood its ground for 30 years with a humble dish that has wooed the palates of countless people — dumpling soup. Mandujip specializes in Pyeongando-style dumplings, filled with minced beef, bean curd, mung bean sprouts, green onions and sesame oil. Each order comes with six large dumplings in a clear, flavorful beef broth made with chunks of brisket.

name: Jinmi Pyeongyang Naengmyeon
review: According to owner and chef Yim Se-kwon, 20 years of experience in the kitchens of one of the most iconic Pyeongyang cold buckwheat noodle restaurants is the secret to the success of this place. The menu here is what you would expect to see in a typical cold buckwheat noodle restaurant. Other than the noodles, it offers staples such as boiled pork and beef slices, bulgogi, dumplings and Pyeongyang-style beef hot pot.

name: Geumdwaeji Sikdang
review: Located along a main road in Sindang-dong, Geumdwaeji Sikdang can be easily spotted by its gold-on-white-tile signage and the queue outside the door long after peak dining hours. The establishment serves up fine cuts of YBD pig, a cross breed between Yorkshire, Berkshire and Duroc. The texture of the pork is firm and meaty, with a good balance of flavorful fat that renders the meat supremely juicy. Items are is cooked on a cast-iron grill over coal briquettes that help keep the temperature constant. The restaurant does not accept reservations.

name: Yangyang Memil Makguksu
review: The not-so-secret secret to the longevity and success of Yangyang Memil Makguksu is that its noodles are made with 100% buckwheat and that they are made to order every time. The proprietor of the restaurant began his business many years ago for one reason only - buckwheat noodles were his favorite food. Although the restaurant specializes in the Gangwon-do Province-style cold buckwheat noodles, it also makes a fine bowl of spicy noodles composed with homemade kimchi. The basic spread is simple, but it’s rustic food at its best, made with love.

name: Tasty Cube
review: A combination of Chinese characters for heart, meat, noodles and restaurant make up the four-syllable name Jeongyukmyeonche. The cozy space, which only offers bar seating facing the open kitchen, is the brainchild of a group of friends who wanted to launch an eatery that focuses on a wide array of noodle dishes. Although Chinese and Southeast Asian flavors dominate the menu at present, the owners say the plan is to eventually introduce noodle dishes from other cultures as well. Signature dishes include beef noodle soup and noodles dressed with zhi ma jiang, a savory paste made with crushed sesame seeds.

name: Jaha Son Mandu
review: For over two decades, this restaurant has been attracting diners with a rustic dumpling recipe passed down from the owner’s mother and her grandmother. Although humble by nature, dumpling dishes are always elegantly presented. Their signature dish is mandutguk: plump pork, bean curd and vegetable dumplings nestled in a delicate beef broth, seasoned with homemade soy sauce. The main dining room offers a spectacular view of nearby Inwangsan Mountain.

name: Kyodaiya
review: When one can hear the dull tap of a blade against a wooden board every time a customer places an order, it’s a telltale sign that the chefs are serious about their craft. At Kyodaiya, that craft is Sanuki udon. The thick noodles are always cut to order to preserve their characteristic elasticity and smoothness until the very last minute. In addition to the classic kake udon, flavored with dried and smoked sardines and seasoned with light soy sauce, the chef brothers also offer classics like tempura udon and chilled bukkake udon.

name: Egg & Flour
review: As implied by its name, Egg & Flour is an Italian restaurant specializing in fresh, handmade pasta composed only with egg and flour. Even the entrance to the establishment greets us with sacks of flour and pasta rolling machines. The space is located along a winding alley in Haebangchon, yet the Itaewon skyline seen from the terrace and through the glass wall evokes majesty. The establishment’s signature offering is freshly made Italian pasta with a Korean twist – be it Jeju black pork ragù featuring red chili paste and fish sauce, burrata cheese, or roasted Ecklonia cava.

name: Limbyungjoo Sandong Kalguksu
review: Since 1988, this restaurant has been proving that a humble bowl of noodle soup can be truly memorable when done right. The pleasant texture of their hand-cut noodles, prepared daily from scratch, and immensely comforting broth, served piping hot and packed with flavor from the clams in all their naturally sweet glory, are stellar. Other favorites include Pyeongyang jumbo sized dumplings and noodles in cold soybean soup. Simple but warm service.

name: Tuk Tuk Noodle Thai
