After several years at Topolobampo, the husband-wife duo behind this gem have taken their knowledge and skills to craft this consistently delicious and inventive cuisine. And, the chefs’ deep understanding of Mexican ingredients has allowed them to create elegant and well-priced compositions. Chunks of slowly braised pork carnitas are hearty, tender and brought to an entirely new level with squash that pops with bright flavor—all balanced with a bracing tomatillo broth. For dessert, indulge in an excellent Mexican sugar pie topped with whipped cream and pecan toffee that is out of this world.
The space is comfortable and roomy, so that the steady stream of thirty-somethings never make it feel crowded. Curved booths and romantic lighting lend a warm vibe.

name: Chef’s Special Cocktail Bar
review:
Nostalgia is alive and well inside the colorful dining room, complete with oceanic hues, soft cushions, vibrant artwork and a U-shaped bar. A large dining area with proper tables is perfect for groups, while a semi-private nook serves family-style plates.
This throwback is a loud and happy place, thanks to an extensive menu of heartwarming Chinese-American classics. Crab rangoon and shrimp chips make an appearance, but don't miss those luscious dan dan noodles or "special combo" fried rice, studded with cubes of pork, shrimp and more. The bone-in pork shank with black bean sauce and charred cabbage is designated a "special" for good reason, and fried string beans in a rich, savory broad bean purée are a must. Finish with the sesame cake with jasmine and orange.

name: Proxi
review:
Here at Proxi, Chef Andrew Zimmerman seems intent on presenting his diners with a culinary whirlwind that blows from Thai beef salad to coal-roasted oysters with ssamjang butter and beyond. Otherworldly highlights reveal delicate duck dumplings floating in a pho broth with fried shallots and aromatic herbs. Regardless of the dish’s inspiration, it’s sure to be delicious in this kitchen’s capable hands. Desserts, like avocado mousse, are made with formidable talent.
The massive room is effortlessly cool and sleek, with blue-tiled columns set beneath the white-vaulted ceiling. It also features an open kitchen and myriad seating options for everyone—from solo diners to large groups. A front lounge is ideal for lingering and waiting for your party to arrive.

name: Mango Pickle
review: After traveling across India, Chef Marisa Paolillo was sufficiently inspired to return stateside and open a restaurant that celebrates its culinary diversity. Named for the country’s most popular condiment, everything here—from the colorful artwork to the rich curries—shows a deep appreciation for the sub-continent.The well-priced tasting offers an array of specialties. There is also a spring à la carte as well as a seven-course prix-fixe. Regardless of your pick, expect flavorful dishes that are a riff on the classics. Think of the onion-tomato sauce of butter chicken, ramped up with mushrooms and sundried tomatoes for a Mediterranean twist. Chana masala is spiked with ginger and garlic, while beef nihari spotlights a succulent black cardamom sauce.

name: Pleasant House Pub
review:
Classic English pies may be the specialty of this house, but don’t let that inspire visions of chintz and tea cozies—the interior here is decidedly modern, with marble-topped tables and hand-crafted pottery.
But the crowds come for the pies, and for good reason—they’re fabulous. The crust is flaky and buttery, and the inside, hearty and satisfying. Dig into the steak and ale, with its beef stew filling and side of minty peas, gravy and mashed potatoes, and you’ll be hunting for every last crumb. The comfort food hits also keep on coming, from rarebit mac and cheese with Trooper Ale cheese sauce, to fish and chips on Fridays. Of course, with much of the seasonal greens from local farms, rest assured that even a simple salad will be a revelation.

name: The Duck Inn
review:
Head to the Bridgeport warehouses, where this stylish, modern tavern—helmed by Executive Chef Kevin Hickey—feels like a diamond in the rough. Then make your way past the buzzy bar (pouring heady cocktails) to a semi-open kitchen, which is in full view of the decorous dining room, featuring wood tables and mid-century modern seats.
The cuisine may be coined as "working-class fine dining," but there is nothing lowbrow about this menu, which unveils a focused but diverse selection of small plates and mains. Japanese barbecue sauce and sesame seeds are the crowning touch to duck wings, while foie gras mousse with celery fronds and brioche is a study in fine flavors and textures. Of course, regulars know to save room for the Chicago-style duck fat dog.

name: Table, Donkey and Stick
review:
When American comfort food just won’t suffice, look to Table, Donkey and Stick for a helping of cozy Alpine fare. The rustic inn-inspired setting reflects its reputation as a gathering place where friends meet at the inviting bar or settle in at communal tables for whimsical, creative compositions.
To start things off, peruse the extensive charcuterie selection before tucking into boldly flavored and creatively plated dishes. Layered like a tower, the grilled lamb shoulder over a bed of creamy lentils surprises with every bite. Choucroute garni's rich beefy flavor is cut by the creaminess of the sauerkraut purée. Out-of-the box ideas keep coming through to dessert, where a scoop of pretzel ice cream atop a jalapeño caramel is equal parts spicy and sweet.

name: Frontera Grill
review:
This linchpin in Rick Bayless’ empire is decidedly unique in its homage to regional Mexican cuisine and displays a cult-like devotion to local product. From the table-shaken margaritas and the molés to the warm, uplifting music, you'll likely feel you're in Mexico. 
The ever-changing menu is cohesive, highlighting everything from the ceviches of Baja to the moles of Oaxaca. Begin with the sopa azteca—a nourishing pasilla chile broth poured atop tortilla strips, avocado, grilled chicken and jack cheese. A version of the classic from Morelia, enchiladas a la plaza are first flash-fried, then folded over seasoned cabbage, potatoes and carrots. Pair this with a side of spinach in green chile and you won’t be unhappy.

name: Gilt Bar
review:
Doughnuts, dry-aged steaks, and house-made pastas—Hogsalt Hospitality certainly has the lockdown on this corner of River North, but it all started in 2010 with this moody and imposing retreat. The bar up front mixes cocktails to a metronomic rhythm, while the back feels more intimate with studded leather banquettes and nostalgic lighting.
True to form, the restaurant excels at big plates and bold flavors. We're hooked on the fried chicken that arrives with a golden-brown crust and rich mashed potatoes. But, who then will order the beef cheek pot pie with bone marrow gravy? You won’t have room for dessert, but order it anyway. A towering slice of carrot cake with spiced cream cheese frosting and toasted coconut counts as a vegetable anyway, right?

name: Girl & The Goat
review:
The revolving door never stops turning as Girl & The Goat’s party keeps going. Even on a Monday night, guests linger for hours, shouting over the din at this sceney but always friendly stunner. Appropriately rustic wooden pillars and beams connect a warren of seating areas, from elevated platforms to banquettes to dim private corner nooks.
A pick-your-own-protein adventure, the menu is organized by ingredients with a dedicated section for goat. Start with freshly baked ham bread accompanied by smoked Swiss cheese-butter seasoned with coarse mustard and olive tapenade. End with an almost pudding-like “all leches” cake enriched with strawberry-rhubarb sorbet. The kitchen may even send out mini portions of menu items for solo diners—a truly thoughtful touch.

name: Mama Delia
review:
This hot mama greets diners with a marble bar along with an enticing cabinet display of premium conservas, oils, and spices. A series of top cocktails and sherries merely add to the allure. Set towards the back, the dining room is a visual masterpiece, thanks to plush red banquettes, vintage rugs, bright Moorish tiles, and wrought-iron chandeliers.
The kitchen is focused on cooking that is both ingenious and satisfying. To wit: foie gras, tucked into a "taco shell" composed of almonds and orange peel, is matched with membrillo; while pulpo canario is served with confit baby potatoes and chicharrón-infused olive oil. Albeit traditional, desserts like the tarta de Santiago (almond-flour cake with apple sorbet) deliver singular twists and turns.

name: mfk.
review: “First we eat, then we do everything else,” said M.F.K. Fisher, the food writer who serves as both the inspiration and namesake for this local darling. Thanks to large windows, whitewashed brick walls and silver-and-white tilework, the subterranean space manages to evoke a breezy oasis. Organized from small to large plates, the thoughtfully composed, Iberian-inspired menu follows suit.Daily specials are certainly worth ordering, including the clove-infused tender, shredded oxtail. Other simple, flavorful dishes, like warm boquerónes stuffed with marinated anchovies and Fresno chilies, or croquettes with Montamoré cheese and Sherry aïoli are equally tempting. A crumbly slice of Basque cake and an expertly pulled cortado end the meal on a high note.

name: Nella Pizza e Pasta
review: The name of this delicious Hyde Park offering belongs to chef and owner, Nella Grassano, a classically trained pizzaiola. Together with her restaurateur partner, Francesco, the couple’s warm hospitality is the icing on the cake to an experience built around solid cooking. Favorite items include house-made pasta, laced with pristine ingredients and cooked to al dente perfection; or blistered Neapolitan pies, so fresh and authentic they’ll transport you straight to the Italian countryside.Don’t sleep on the starters though, like calamari affogati braised to perfection in a spicy tomato sauce studded with salt-brined black olives. Sop up the incredible sauce with Grassano’s lip-smacking bread, baked in-house and served warm from the wood-burning oven.

name: Smoque BBQ
review: Shortly after doors open at 11:00 A.M., the room fills with patrons eager to dig into smoking plates of 'cue. Once inside, peruse the chalkboard menu; then order cafeteria-style before staking your claim among the communal seating.The half-and-half sandwich, piled with pulled pork and brisket, is the best of both worlds, with chunky shreds of tender pork and spice-rubbed slices of pink-rimmed beef spooned with vinegary barbecue sauce. The usual side dish suspects like zingy, crisp coleslaw and deeply smoky baked beans are anything but standard here, complementing main dishes as they should. For a sweet finish, look no further than pecan bread pudding drizzled with salted caramel-Bourbon sauce.

name: Birrieria Zaragoza
review: This Mexican institution specializes in a single item—birria—tender stewed goat accompanied by diced onions, cilantro, and house-made salsa. In fact, goat is all that’s on the menu, though you’ll get a few options as to how to enjoy it: on a plate or in a bowl, in a small or large portion, bone-in or bone-out. Opt for bone-in if possible, as it packs far more flavor.The bowl option drowns the goat in a generous dose of hearty goat consommé, while the plate is accompanied by handmade corn tortillas for build-your-own tacos, with a small side of consommé for dipping. You can’t go wrong either way, but if you’re feeling extra decadent, go for the goat quesadilla, a perfect trinity of pillowy tortillas, gooey cheese, and savory goat meat goodness.

name: etta
review:
This accomplished  team is at it again, bringing distinctive flair and flavors to their live-fire creations. Inside, the bi-level space is less about glitz and more about a natural and lush vibe. Lofty windows ensure ample light, but most of the action is over by the open-flame kitchen. Informed and pleasant servers steer diners through a panoply of inspired dishes, including complex salads, warming pastas, and wood-fired pizzas. Octopus panzanella with charred avocado, and farfalle pomodoro with creamy burrata are beloved, individually sized bites; while the mille crêpe with poached pear, oat streusel, and Earl Grey sorbet makes for an ingenious finale.
Happy hour (from Sunday to Wednesday) is perhaps the best time to sample well-priced wines and bites.

name: Mi Tocaya
review:
Boasting a lively, charming ambience; friendly, knowledgeable service; and a delicious menu courtesy of Chef/owner Diana Dávila, Mi Tocaya is a welcome addition to the burgeoning Logan Square food scene. Bring friends, order a clever seasonal cocktail, try something from the menu and you’ll no doubt leave with a renewed love for Mexican cuisine.
The short but intriguing listing of “small cravings” (antojitos) is influenced by the less-explored Aztec cuisine. Sample dishes like guisado de nopalitos, a fragrant, earthy stew with cactus, zucchini and charred chilies, served with delicious knobs of salt-dusted fried cheese curds and warm corn tortillas. But don’t overlook the warm tacos, sure to transport you to the streets of Mexico City.

name: Cabra
review:
Tucked into the 12th floor of the Hoxton hotel, this light-soaked and plant-draped beauty overlooks the Windy City's skyline. Its tropical vibe makes the perfect backdrop for Chef Stephanie Izard’s wonderfully inventive pan-Latin cooking, which she punches up with global touches pulled from her diverse culinary background.
The menu may lean Peruvian, but it also offers such favorites as ceviches, empanadas, botanas, and anticuchos. The kitchen takes liberties with traditional tastes, producing dishes that celebrate the area's vibrance and bounty. To wit: salmon ceviche with pistachio, avocado, and leche de tigre; as well as chicharrón del puerco with pickled vegetables and apple salad. Cool off with a swirl of coconut- and quinoa-topped vanilla soft-serve.

name: avec
review:
Fans have been clamoring for the dinner plates at this West Randolph mainstay for more than a decade—and now that lunch is on the menu, it’s official: Avec is a non-stop hangout. It’s a fun vibe, as diners are tightly packed at a long counter with communal seats in the chic wood plank-encased room; servers do a good job attending to the crowd.
Mediterranean flavors factor prominently in the kitchen’s stimulating creations, like a kale and carrot salad dressed with delightfully herbaceous and spicy green harissa as well as sunflower seeds for crunch. A thick slice of excellent whole grain bread spread with walnut-beet muhamarra is the foundation of an open-faced roasted salmon sandwich. Other delights—there are many—come and go with the seasons.

name: Sol de Mexico
review: Far more authentic than the average chips-and-salsa joint, Sol de Mexico brightens the scene and palate with a lively atmosphere (cue the mariachi music) and delectable house specialties. Walls painted in tropical pinks, blues and oranges are a cheerful canvas for Dia de los Muertos artifacts. To sample the kitchen’s skill, start with sopes surtidos “xilonen”—four molded masa cups with a variety of fillings like caramelized plantains doused in sour cream, or tender black beans topped with crumbly house-made chorizo. Then, move on to the pollo en mole manchamanteles, which translates to “tablecloth stainer.” Rich and slightly bitter with a comforting nuttiness, the aptly named mahogany sauce begs to be sopped up with freshly made tortillas.

name: La Josie
review: You don’t want to miss a morsel at this spiffy Mexican charmer. Tucked into a hip space that’s both stylish and comfortable, the dining room is flooded with light thanks to floor-to-ceiling windows, and the bar buzzes with energy as bartenders whip up colorful handcrafted cocktails.La Josie is modern enough where you might expect to find fusion, but this family-run kitchen leans traditional—imagine comforting dishes crafted with pristine ingredients and careful technique. Chef/owner Jose Luis Barajas (AKA Pepe) shows a particularly deft hand in his picture-perfect tacos stuffed with delicious pairings like shredded achiote pork, pickled red onions, and fiery salsa habanero; or tender Amish chicken with crumbled queso fresco and grilled corn kernel salad.

name: Gare aux Goûts
review: Chef Vincent Seviller has come up trumps in this establishment near the railway station. He invites diners on a bistronomic journey in a tasteful, modern setting. An experienced and talented craftsman, each dish is artfully presented, flavoursome and balanced. The lunchtime menu is chalked up on a slate, but more elaborate in the evening.

name: Le Jour du Poisson
review: Run by a trio who trained at Ferrandi, this spruce little bistro at the tip of the island is often fully booked, and so it should be. The menu, as short as it is tempting, is everything it's cracked up to be: fish features in many guises, short supply chains and natural wines are favoured, the bread is made in-house with flour sourced from Oléron. A friendly and charming place serving delicious food.

name: Le Cerisier
review: The menu of this small restaurant with a contemporary interior makes your mouth water in anticipation of the hearty, unpretentious dishes and the house speciality, the pâté en croûte, made with different ingredients from season to season. A duo is at work in the kitchen preparing delicious cuisine that highlights local produce such as Ardèche trout. The desserts are particularly meticulous – poached pear with mulled wine, vanilla and speculoos trifle, pear sorbet. The terrific wine list (600 labels) has a judicious choice of wines by the glass, and savvy sommelier Florent Chauvin's recommendations are on point.

name: Au Lion d'Or - Chez Théo
review: A pleasant and elegant inn, run by the same family since 1928. The chef brilliantly weaves flavours of today into the wealth of local specialities, without excluding the specialities of other parts of France! The selection of wines by the glass is short but well put together. Make the most of the beautiful terrace in summer.

name: Air Accueil
review: Near the Vitry - en - Artois airfield, this vast inn used to be an officers' mess. Today it is much more than a simple canteen! The food is delicious, and all the experience of chef Franck Gilabert shines through. There are numerous nods to local specialities, and the flavours really take off!

name: Le Nid
review: An establishment run by charming people: Emilie takes care of the customer's every need, while the chef rustles up seasonal cuisine, full of freshness and flavour, making the most of short food supply chains and local producers. A gourmet hideaway that fills up every day and offers excellent value and maximum dining pleasure.

name: Cheval d'Or
review: It is with great anticipation that you stop in front of this bright red façade high up in Belleville (in the east of Paris), having secured a table for one of the two evening services by booking well in advance. In this restaurant under the leadership of an authentic Japanese chef, ensconced with his team behind a long counter, you will get to enjoy fragrant dishes inspired by Japanese cuisine: Japanese binchotan charcoal grill, home-made soy ramen and onigri. Laid-back service from a friendly and dynamic team.

name: Le Malu
review: A military barracks under Napoleon III, the site has since been converted into a restaurant, where chef Ludovic Brethenoux brings in the big guns. Originally from Périgord, he trained, most notably, at La Villa Madie in Cassis. His affinity with the Vendômois area is evident in his precise and refined contemporary cuisine. A real treat.

name: Racines
review: A stone’s throw from the marina of Étaples and only 5km from Le Touquet, this new restaurant is focused on succulent wholesome fare made with carefully sourced local produce. The recipes of chef Pierre Chavatte hit the spot every time. The interior sports a contemporary vibe with semi-open kitchens and hanging light fixtures surrounded by roots, a passing nod to the restaurant’s name. Highly recommended!

name: La Loge Bertin
review: Behind this spruce green façade, you will find an enthusiastic team ready to take you on a gourmet adventure. The chef only works with fresh ingredients to create a market menu that is particularly appetising and enticingly presented. Take a seat in the contemporary bistro dining room (square, oak-coloured tables and wooden or upholstered chairs) and peep through the workshop-style window into the kitchen.

name: Le Rabelais
review: Housed in the pretty 17C vaulted room of an old wheat mill, this restaurant would have gone down well with Rabelais's insatiable Gargantua! Enjoy the tasty seasonal dishes that are meticulously prepared (the menu changes several times a week). This place is located in the immediate vicinity of Saint-Chamas's Poudrerie – the black powder mill founded in 1690. History, literature, good food: what more could you ask for?

name: Sellae
review: On the coattails of Mensae ("table" in Latin) in the 19th arrondissement, Sellae ("chair") is another restaurant in the Thibault Sombardier stable. The chef cooks up modern seasonal cuisine, with a penchant for the South of France and above all for indulgence! In this bistro-style interior, the produce is prepared with real know-how: snail ravioli with grass butter, crispy speck, sweet garlic broth; roast veal, casarecce with mushrooms, vin jaune emulsion...

name: Insens
review: "This attractive restaurant, whose name hints at the five senses and a taste for folly, is simple and convivial. ""Beef consommé and ravioli based on the idea of an onion soup""; tarte fine with persillade snails etc. Its chef creates dishes that are tasty, colourful and playful – and he clearly has a real knack for it. Probably the best value dining experience in Saint Étienne. Don't miss out! "

name: Etsi
review: Mikaela, a young chef of Greek origin, has turned her focus to the cuisine of her childhood, after cutting her teeth in some prestigious establishments. Here, she proposes strikingly fresh mezze with bold touches. The feta, olives, capers, charcuterie, cheeses and olive oil have all come straight from Greece. Enjoy in the exceedingly warm and friendly setting.

name: Lai'Tcha
review: In this annex of Yam'tcha, located at the foot of Église St-Eustache, you can enjoy simple but straight-to-the-point Chinese cuisine that is fragrant and made with fine ingredients. The short menu offers various dim sums, but also fresh home-made noodles, Imperial sautéed beef and an excellent salad of Galician beef, lamb's lettuce and oyster mushrooms.

name: Le Grand Bain
review: We love this trendy bistro in the bustling heart of Belleville, which has the feel of an old industrial workshop look, courtesy of its central island counter, glass partitions, untreated materials (brick and concrete) and numbered tables. Tuck into food served as small plates – chalked up on the blackboard – prepared by chef Emily Chia, who prefers to cook with vegetables and grains over meat and fish. The playlist reflects the clientèle of hipster night owls and discerning foodies who flock here.

name: Abri Soba
review: You may have heard of soba, Japanese pasta made with buckwheat, the reputation of which is currently snowballing around the planet. The chef of this restaurant has made soba his house speciality and serves it lunch and evening in an amazing variety of preparations: hot, cold, in stock or with finely sliced duck. Simply flavoursome – get out your chopsticks!

name: Kisin
review: When a Bib Gourmand chef from Tokyo arrives in Paris, the first thing he does is open a restaurant, tantalising and bewitching our senses. Diners will sample Japanese produce and genuine udon, made in front of the diner. Natural, additive - free ingredients, most of which are imported direct from the Land of the Rising Sun. Healthy, wholesome and succulent.

name: 20 Eiffel
review: In a quiet street a stone’s throw from the Eiffel Tower, this restaurant offers a understated interior full of light. On the menu, you can choose from a range of updated dishes, prepared by two chefs, all of which place the focus on flavour and taste. For example, a delicious fillet of wild Pollock with squash.

name: L'Antre Amis
review: The chef-patron at L'Antre Amis brings passion to his cooking. Using seasonal ingredients, he composes a short up-to-the-minute menu (Landes asparagus, Graubünden meat and devilled egg; cod loin fillet and creamy risotto with early peas), as well as tapas-style dishes for sharing. To be accompanied by your pick from some 200 wines. Pleasant contemporary setting and terrace on a quiet street.

name: Pottoka
review: Pottoka, a breed of pony native to the region, is the mascot of Bayonne's rugby club. Basque ingredients may be omnipresent in the dishes (Bayonne ham, chorizo, ossau-iraty), but the chef's approach tends more towards an unpretentious, creative "bistronomy" that is in tune with the times. A success on all fronts.

name: Mandoobar
review: Good authentic Korean restaurants are not two a penny in Paris, but this little restaurant, where the chef works behind his counter, is one of them: diners look on while Kim Kwang-Loc, as nimble-fingered as he is precise, creates the famous mandu (Korean dumplings) and tuna and beef tartares that make up the bulk of his minimalist menu. Passionate about Korean herbs, he seasons each of his delicate and tasty dishes with addictive flavours, perhaps in a quest to recreate his earliest culinary memories in Korea…

name: Brigade du Tigre
review: Both have trained with William Ledeuil, both are passionate about Asia, having traversed the continent, and now the duo who run the kitchen at Eels have joined forces to celebrate the joyful diversity of Asian cuisine in a bistro-style duplex. The result: small fragrant nuggets to nibble on your own or to share, concocted from quality products...

name: Les Tables d'Augustin
review: The Épinettes neighbourhood is home to this delightful little bistro, officiated by a pedigreed young chef (George V, L'Ambroisie...) with a genuine commitment to ecology. His tasty and flavoursome cuisine has plenty of character, and offers excellent value for money – especially at lunchtime. Regularly renewed menu depending on market availability.

name: Auberge Pyrénées Cévennes
review: Chef Pierre Négrevergne is really flourishing in this house that is over 100 years old. He delights diners with his tasty "grandmother's" cooking, which highlights French gastronomic heritage (home-made terrine, blanquette de veau à l'ancienne and grilled rice, millefeuille), served in generous portions. It is still a treat to eat here.

name: Cucina
review: The atmosphere is provided by a modern bistro decor and waiters in red and white striped t-shirts. The beautiful seasonal Italian menu is a treat from start to finish, from the antipasti to the dolci. Spaghetti aglio, olio e peperoncini; orecchia di elefante, patate novelle e salvia – it's authentic and tasty.

name: L'Oseille
review: This enticing bistro, complete with counter, glazed cellar, wooden chairs and benches, is smart and authentic down to its core. The chef’s concise menu takes you on a whirlwind of flavours, always in tune with the seasons. The starters are to share, followed by generous main courses and desserts. Simple and tasty!

name: Le Garriane
review: "Garriane" is the contraction of Garry and Ariane, and originality is the name of the game here! In the kitchens, Garry, an Australian, concocts seasonal, ingredient focused cuisine that is open to influences from around the world. At lunch and dinner, there is a single set menu. The restaurant is very small so it is best to book ahead.

name: L'Épicerie
review: Is the restaurant a grocer’s or is it the other way round? Whatever, this establishment is delightful, which is all that matters! Seasonal menu by Mathieu (in charge of savoury dishes) and Clémentine (desserts), all of which with 100% local produce. This unpretentious restaurant has been adopted locally, which is always a good sign. Beware, 20 seats only, so book before you come!

name: Les Résistants
review: These résistants believe that taste and traceability should be the backbone of all food. Indeed, the credo of owner, Florent Piard, is none other than "good food that respects natural cycles! " and he amply proves his case in this cheerful establishment. The concise menu changes daily in keeping with market availability and the prices are never outlandish. Natural wines bien sûr!

name: Le Petit Paris
review: In the heart of a picturesque Périgord village, this welcoming establishment is fronted by a large terrace overlooking the village square. Meals are served in two tastefully rustic dining rooms. The chef, a local lad, takes pride in showcasing regional produce. Carpaccio of foie gras and a port-based vichyssoise; melt-in-the-mouth beef chuck in a Pécharmant wine sauce and traditional Grand Marnier soufflé to finish.

name: L'Alicanta
review: L'Alicanta has been on the scene for a while, perched on the banks of the River Jonte, in the exceptional setting of the Gorges du Tarn. The chef puts in a solid performance, his cooking is replete with distinct flavours and his dishes are brilliantly assembled. Everything here is home-made and the menu changes with every season. Absolutely delicious!

name: Le Bac à Traille
review: The Japanese-born star chef of La Cachette has made his dream come true in this bistro, whose name pays homage to a former ferry that used to cross the Rhône. The market-fresh cuisine is impeccably crafted, always punchy and heroically flavoursome. A Franco-Japanese-inspired menu to share plus a selection of regional vintages. Unbeatable value for money.

name: Paris Méditerranée
review: The name pays homage to Brassens, who was born in Sète but also the chef, originally from Paris, and his wife, a native of Sète. The chef reinvents local recipes, in line with his mood and the catch of the day. The nearby tapas bar, Le Barbu, run by the same owner, is highly recommended.

name: Spoon
review: On the mezzanine floor of the Palais Brongniart, diners are drawn here by the promise of aromatic spices – tamarind, ginger, coriander, saffron. The chef's dishes are inspired by the Maghreb, India, the Middle East: Doha chickpeas with lemon caviar; amberjack, curry leaves and coconut milk; Fez pastilla with dried fruit, cinnamon and star anise.

name: Baca'v
review: Good wholesome food and a casual, down-to-earth vibe depict Émile Cotte’s approach. After a classical debut, he has decided to follow his own path and now adds a personal spin to bistro classics reworked to suit modern tastes. The regularly renewed slate menu is deliciously affordable and there is also a 5-course surprise menu.

name: Les Petits Parisiens
review: Now presiding over proceedings in the kitchen is Nathan Sindres, who has worked in some top restaurants (Anne-Sophie Pic, Gérald Passedat). This chef with the Midas touch is brilliantly ensuring the continuity of the establishment, cooking up bistro-style cuisine that is still in a delicious and hearty vein but more modern and lighter. Those with a sweet tooth will be tempted by the chocolate mousse, olive oil and fleur de sel.

name: Aux Plumes
review: Inspired, tasty and generously - served cuisine, whipped up by a youthful Japanese chef, ex - Astrance and Chamarré Montmartre, is what the lucky diner gets here. The produce is sourced from the best local merchants (next - door butcher Hugo Desnoyer) and the buzzing, friendly atmosphere features tightly packed tables. Don’t think twice!

name: Mets et Vins
review: This is the domain of chef Stéphane Prévalet, a major proponent of ingredients from the local terroir and home-made fare, who is adept at veering off the path of tradition. For example, tuck into the Dombes duckling cooked two ways: the fillet cooked rare and the leg prepared as a pastilla with dried fruit… in a refined space decorated with birch trunks. Our kind of place.

name: L'Hommage
review: In a neighbourhood that is best known for its plethora of Chinese eateries, this establishment stands out from the crowd with its French-style bistronomy and refined decor reminiscent of a Scandinavian-style loft. One can't fault the food, with its quality ingredients and on-point cooking and seasoning – eg the crispy tomato and watermelon tartlet, or the tender chicken flavoured with a tasty coconut milk and curry sauce.

name: Le Gantxo
review: Welcome to the Basque Country! Le Gantxo – named after a pass in pelota – gives directly onto the trinquet, the ground where the famous local sport is played. The chef revisits Basque cuisine in a very personal way, composing dishes that are up to the minute, often copious and always tasty. A firm favourite!

name: Maison Chabran - Le 45ème
review: Why not stop off in this verdant setting with its lovely garden while on the way to your holiday destination? This restaurant is a pleasant alternative to the main restaurant, which is a veritable institution of regional gastronomy. You can enjoy light and laid-back set menus: guinea fowl terrine with foie gras, olive chutney; vegetable risotto, parmesan emulsion; raspberry arlette for dessert…

name: Le Bistro Chapouton
review: Just 400m from its parent establishment, Le Clair de la Plume, the Bistro bears the same hallmark of quality: premium ingredients, textbook cooking, crisp, forthright flavours – trusty and dependable down to a tee. Organic poached egg, primavera vegetables, vinaigrette of fresh garden herbs or mashed whiting with an espuma of passion fruit and mango. Now add the delicious terrace in fine weather and the portrait will be complete.

name: Café A
review: The beating heart of Maison Aribert, Café A never sleeps – it is open throughout the week from breakfast to dinner. Remaining true to his "village café" theme, which reinterprets recipes handed down from mothers and grandmothers, the chef proposes fine bistronomy cuisine at affordable prices. The simple food is made from carefully selected ingredients. Memorable dishes include a simply addictive pain perdu made with brioche served with ice cream and caramel sauce. A safe bet every time. Brunch on Sundays.

name: Le Colvert
review: This delightful house surrounded by greenery was for many years a grocery - cum - bakery; now it is the meeting place of fine food lovers! The chef whips up market - fresh recipes in tune with the seasons – maillard duck, guinea fowl stuffed with goat’s cheese and mushrooms; fine selection of vintages to drink with your meal.

name: SaQuaNa
review: Is Alexandre Bourdas in the process of redefining the codes of gastronomy? He has made his SaQuaNa a social hub, open from morning to night, the idea being to make good food accessible to as many people as possible. The menu is varied, with influences from near and far, and always features signature dishes such as monkfish in coconut broth and combawa oil, or his emblematic pascade. A confident and inspiring culinary offering.

name: La Maison Carrier
review: Part of the luxurious Hameau Albert I hotel, this typical farmhouse is home to a friendly restaurant. They serve a beautifully devised seasonal menu – sample the charcuterie that they smoke and dry on site, and take your pick from the legendary and lavish buffet of desserts ("vré de toutes les tartes de la Grand-Mère"), including biscuit de Savoie and blueberry tart. Pleasant terrace.

name: Bistrot la Coulemelle
review: In the middle of the village, this is the delightful "bistro annexe" of Régis and Jacques Marcon's fine dining restaurant. The traditional pâté en croûte "Richelieu", skate wing terrine, roasted cauliflower and mushrooms, cheeses from Ardèche and Auvergne. What more can we say? This is hearty fare and devilishly good. The open kitchens lend the place an inviting feel.

name: Le Bistro des Glycines
review: One of the undeniable plus points of this hotel is its excellent bistro with a nicely decorated conservatory extension (untreated wooden tables, Shaker-style chairs). At lunchtime, diners tuck into good-value dishes in tune with the zeitgeist, eg semi-cooked tuna loin, sautéed vegetables with ginger, or cabbage from the garden stuffed with confit de canard. This creative and tempting menu is proving to be a well-deserved success!

name: Le Bastion
review: Take a seat in one of two pretty rustic dining spaces to sample "avant-garde country fare", inspired by Auguste Escoffier but with a modern twist. Great produce from the region is used – tomatoes from the Estarac Gardens, vinegar by Cyril Codigna, fish fresh from the market at Port la Nouvelle… Concise tapas menu and spacious terrace.

name: Le Pressoir de Bacchus
review: Such is the renown of Sylvie Grucker and her son that this pretty restaurant on the wine route is greatly in demand. Sylvie combines traditional recipes with an inventive streak in a bid to showcase regional fare: bacon-flavoured choucroute soup or duck shepherd’s pie, mushrooms and 12-spice sauce, side by side perennial favourites like granddad’s snails, ravioles of carp in a creamy, smoked sauce or Sylvie’s meringue and ice cream extravaganza! Local winegrowers and producers from the village (thirty or so) take pride of place on the enticing wine list.

name: Cozna
review: After a stint in several prestigious establishments in France and the US, Sandra and Léo have settled in a car-free street in historic Annecy. Tradition is their motto (“cozna” means cooking in the Savoie dialect), a credo with which their diners wholeheartedly agree. The food is delicious food and served with a smile. A genuine good deal.

name: Le Bistrot de Guillaume
review: Right in the centre of Moulins, the small dining area is light and intimate, already setting the tone, and we don't need to be asked twice to be shown to our table. But the best is yet to come: in his little kitchen, the chef/owner composes dishes that are at once fine and well thought - out, and a joy for the taste buds.

name: Clamato
review: Inspired by the oyster bars of the East Coast of the United States, this outpost of Septime owes its name to a cocktail that is very popular in Quebec, a Bloody Mary of sorts with the addition of clam juice – needless to say, you can try one here! The place has all the makings of a bistronomy hit, with its trendy decor and short menu that puts fish and seafood and vegetables centre stage, and draws on international influences. The ingredients are chosen with great care and prepared as simply as possible, then presented in plates for sharing. Please note that reservations are not possible: first come, first served!

name: Le Caillebotte
review: Chef Franck Baranger composes fresh and thoroughly modern dishes, the secret of which only he holds: marinated mackerel, sweet onion with cloves and pickles in honey; fish from the coast, chard stuffed with einkorn wheat and beurre blanc with dill… It's delicious, colourful, and goes perfectly with the friendly atmosphere of the place.

name: La Ferme de Victorine
review: An authentic farmhouse with a pretty rustic - style restaurant, from which you can even see the cows in the cowshed in winter. The chef is passionate about Savoyard produce, and always on the lookout for the best cheeses and cold cooked meats. An eminently pleasant restaurant and very tasty dishes!

name: Bistrot RG
review: Michelin-starred chef Nicolas Gautier (from Nature, just next door) and his brother Mathieu pay tribute to their father Roger Gautier's cooking (RG) with a short menu that offers delicious and hassle-free cuisine, with a bill that won't break the bank: foie gras terrine with port; calf's head in gribiche sauce and pan-fried mushrooms with garlic. A winning formula.

name: Les Maisons Du'O - Le Bistro Panoramique
review: Locally grown tomatoes and fruit, Ventoux spelt and pork: the chef hits the spot every time with modern recipes rich in Provençal accents, such as line-caught black hake, local beans with pistou and Barronnies chorizo. Excellent value for money menu and knock-out view of the Ouvèze from the spacious contemporary dining room.

name: Fidelis
review: At their location facing the ramparts, this professional couple are making a big splash with delicious and elegantly executed traditional cuisine: a fresh pea soup that is unctuous and bursting with flavour; an excellent poultry roast in its skin… crispy and melt-in-the-mouth, it is served with a delicious carrot purée with just a hint of ginger.

name: Richer
review: This place appeals as much for its arty "canteen" vibe as it does for its dishes, which showcase a fresh and tasty take on market-inspired cuisine, as in the long-braised beef chuck served on a fine broccoli purée. Bear in mind, though, that the only way to reserve is to show up at the restaurant.

name: La Capitelle
review: La Capitelle has plenty going for it. It offers a short menu that changes every two or three days and comprises of dishes made with quality ingredients (local, as far as possible). The traditional recipes are given a contemporary spin and are perfectly cooked. There is also an attractive vaulted dining area presided over by an imposing fireplace.

name: Ti-Coz
review: This picture postcard stone inn offers both country appeal and a modern elegant interior, reminiscent of an English club. The chef is a fan of flavoursome, traditional cuisine that shines the spotlight on the best of Brittany’s ingredients. A former sommelier, he pairs his recipes with a fantastic 500-strong wine bin.

name: Au Coin des Halles
review: A javelin throw from Langeais château, make a halt in this pretty tufa stone house. The period wainscoting and parquet floors are offset by contemporary furnishings, which add a bright, cheerful note. Chef Pascal Bouvier crafts inventive recipes, inspired by regional produce, illustrated by veal, baby carrots, sweet potatoes, tamarind and arabica jus or white asparagus, braised pork belly (kakuni) and roasted pomelos. The combinations are sometimes surprising but always spot-on for fine meals with the added bonus of charming service. The lovely terrace in summertime is the final cherry on the cake.

name: Le Bistro Urbain
review: At the helm of this bistro, which has just moved to a glamorous and more spacious location in the heart of Montpellier, is Cédric Sangenito, a chef with a seamless CV. His cooking is modern and a touch inventive, highlighting good fresh produce, especially vegetables; the menu is updated every week – although the rum baba, the emblematic dish of the house, is a mainstay, in various different guises. Furthermore, the bill won't break the bank and you receive a friendly welcome: full marks.

name: Côté Saveurs
review: A pretty, contemporary restaurant fitted out in the unlikely setting of a former fire station. At the helm, chef Stéphane Amalric is a familiar face for Villefranche folk. His cooking is a beautiful ode to local Aveyron produce and displays astute touches of creativity: cod ceviche and a fine sand carrot jelly, brownie with white chocolate drops and blueberries. Dishes like these are as pleasing to the eye as they are to the taste buds.

name: Le Médiéval
review: Burgundy chef, Pierre Creuzet, (former second chef under Jacques Lameloise) has set up shop in this small establishment in the historic town, concocting mouth - watering dishes that waver between traditional and more current recipes. His wife, Loren, a trained wine waiter, advises diners as to food - wine pairings. Unbeatable value for pleasure!

name: Au Bon Accueil
review: You will first be won over by the vintage charm of this 1960’s house, before you meet the talented team of the brother (in the kitchen) and his sister (in the dining room), who are both fast gaining in confidence. The food is on-point, the wine cellar savvy and the terrace very pleasant in season.

name: L'Océanide
review: Roasted scallops, tart carrot juice, filet of plaice roasted with thyme butter, shellfish jus... L'Océanid certainly maintains close ties to the sea. Chef David Garrec chooses his produce at the famous neighbouring Marché de Talensac, and the freshness of the fish, cooked to perfection, is unmistakeable! Authentic 1950s vintage setting, with an old-world charm.

name: Le Comptoir de La Butte
review: This extension of the gourmet flagship is also rich in culinary appeal. The modern layout sports an open kitchen and a shop to set your taste buds tingling… and they aren't disappointed when it comes to the generous traditional dishes with their roots in Finistère cuisine, nicely organised into a set menu.

name: La Pie qui Couette
review: This gloriously down-to-earth tapas bar run by a seasoned chef will knock the socks off your tastebuds. Market-fresh fare crafted with produce from the neighbouring market stalls. House specialties include matured meat, cod brandade, chopped beef tartare and île flottante (vanilla custard and meringue). Hearty helpings and an intelligent wine list. Tightly packed tables and the good-natured, jovial vibe characteristic of food courts set the buzzy scene. No bookings possible, open from 11.30am to 3pm and packed every day of the week. Thankfully there is also a table d’hôte option seating 12 people.

name: La Maison de Marie
review: This elegant pink granite house blends in beautifully with the surrounding coastal scenery. The chef shines the spotlight on the region’s star ingredients such as scallops from Cotes d'Armor and oysters from Lanmodez. His constantly changing menu, to the delight of the many regulars, adapts to market availability. Traditional culinary score.

name: Pica Pica
review: Former star chef of the Octopus and MOF (Best Craftsman of France) 2004, Fabien Lefebvre plays a gourmet score in this friendly eatery. No-nonsense Mediterranean fare, cleverly blended with other influences: selection of tapas (chickpea houmous with cumin and pita bread, croquetas de jamon), lamb kebabs (picas), zaatar and sumac, or grilled squid. More elaborate dishes with Gallic overtones are also on offer: salted cod, watercress and gnocchi with a foamy emulsion of lemon and caviar. A gourmet tip: save room for the decadent desserts! A down-to-earth, wholesome concept designed to be shared. The lunchtime menu is a steal. A resounding success.

name: Restaurant Anne & Matthieu Omont - Hôtel de France
review: This establishment, located on the main street of the village, proposes a culinary interlude. A young chef has taken over the reins of a restaurant that is well known to its following of regulars. He turns out masterful, determinedly creative cuisine, to be enjoyed in an immaculate modern setting. Comfortable rooms, ideal for an overnight stay.

name: Grain de Sel
review: (Move to new premises in the Pavilions de Saint-Ylie, Route Nationale, planned for spring 2023) In this welcoming restaurant, the chef concocts original, meticulous and tasty dishes, such as golden hake, different textures of salsify and Japanese mushrooms. The menu is regularly renewed, and in summer you can make the most of the pleasant terrace.

name: Lou Pinatou
review: He’s from the hills of Puy and she’s from Marseille. He likes forthright flavours and premium produce and she’s more of a pastry buff. Their gourmet culinary repertory is two-fold: in the old stone inn is a bistro that upholds traditions, while in a brand-new structure, you will taste gastronomic fare with a fine view of the valley to boot.

name: Le Bistrot
review: On the menu of this bistro near the theatre and the cathedral, you will find hearty Gallic seasonal recipes, starring fine ingredients that shout their name. The Savoie-born chef worked for a long time in Ducasse establishments. In fine weather, meals are served on a shaded terrace, which further increases the pleasure.

name: Au Plaisir Ambré
review: Inside Vauban's fortifications, this converted butcher's places a premium on fine ingredients. Freshness is the watchword of the skilful chef, who knows how to coax out the best flavours. Examples would be the slow-confit farmhouse pork belly, wasabi jus and parsnip purée, and the dark chocolate tart with coconut sorbet. Sheer pleasure.

name: L'Embellie
review: A youthful motivated couple is at the wheel of this restaurant set in former stables whose rustic cachet is enhanced by beams, ash wood tables and a fireplace. The up - to - the - minute cuisine takes a new look at regional favourites: meurette eggs, snail brioche and a frothy parsley sauce. Homemade ices and pleasant summer terrace.

name: Les Arpents
review: A stone’s throw from the castle, the burgundy-coloured façade of this contemporary bistro cannot fail but catch the eye. The tasteful interior sports walls covered in cream-coloured wainscoting and modern furniture. Two pals, who met at Tours Catering School, rustle up a flawless culinary score, delving freely into abundant first-rate local produce from asparagus and strawberries in season to Roi rose pork and goat’s cheese. Dishes may include crisp fillet of carp, Jerusalem artichokes and mushrooms, paired with a silky béarnaise sauce or lemon pie dusted with dried black lemon, a wickedly tempting detail that makes this dessert mouth-wateringly irresistible…

name: Au Bon Accueil
review: This restaurant, run by a young couple, is true to its name when it promises a warm welcome. In a bright, contemporary interior, the chef works with premium seasonal ingredients, most of which sourced locally, dexterously crafting creative recipes, such as roast langoustine with a shellfish emulsion or ballotines of free-range poultry stuffed with creamy parsley.

name: Les Petits Princes
review: This inviting street corner restaurant is not far from the tram line. The kitchen is visible through a glazed window. The menu features up-to-the-minute, appetising and never dull dishes such as tartare of meagre fish and citrus fruit, melon soup with fresh ginger and Espelette spices. Delicious terrace/courtyard to the rear at lunchtime.

name: L'Auberge
review: This Auberge not far from Hazebrouck was a tannery before it became an unpretentious eatery 100% true to the traditions of France's Nord. And now it is a restaurant with a friendly atmosphere, showcasing regional produce: brill, butter beans, sour cherries, chanterelles and veal juice. Good local classics and a chef who enjoys contact with his guests.

name: La Table d'Antoine
review: An inveterate traveller, the chef loves handling spices, and delivers tasty, full - flavoured cuisine. You can feel the generosity of somebody who is passionate about what he does. As for the decor, Volvic stone, a glass roof inlaid with plant motifs and Salers leather make for a contemporary evocation of Auvergne. Original!

name: B2K6
review: This pleasant bistro was born out of a meeting of minds between two culinary enthusiasts. Jerome Bru, former sous - chef to Anne - Sophie Pic, and Romain Billard, sommelier, also a graduate of some famous establishments. Enjoy the lovely cooking, which is in harmony with the seasons and uses local ingredients, accompanied by just the right wines. A great team.

name: L'Épicurien
review: Luck has nothing to do with the current reputation of this downtown venue, facing Jean Jaurès Fountain, as the darling of the town’s discerning epicureans. The stripped-back interior sports a distinctly Scandinavian feel, which given the chef’s Swedish origins is hardly a surprise. On the culinary front, he deploys his undisputed talent, adding a new twist to French classics and conjuring up enticing recipes in tune with the era: generous portions, well crafted and oozing with flavour. The intelligent wine list and crack table staff, as professional as they are friendly, add the final flourish.

name: Le Lisita
review: All your senses are awakened as you dine at this restaurant. Eat outside on the terrace facing the amphitheatres of Nîmes, and as night falls see the monument light up. On the menu enjoy sun - soaked regional cuisine that is generous and meticulously prepared. There is a nice selection of wines.

name: L'Aigle d'Or
review: Just a few hundred metres from the château you will come across this lovely spot. The restaurant is set in a country house where you can tuck into delicious food at a table near the fireplace or out on the shady terrace. The chef revisits tradition with his tasty fare.

name: M Restaurant
review: A cocktail of vitamins! Julien Gautier’s cheerful establishment adds a whiff of exuberance to Lyon’s well-heeled, tree-lined Avenue Foch. The smart interior sports a muted blue and flashy orange colour scheme, felt grey designer armchairs, linen tablecloths, a bar and a wine cellar encircled by a conservatory… The similarly charismatic service is as smooth as a silky béarnaise sauce. In the kitchen, the veteran and talented chef, formerly of Léon of Lyon, rustles up an appetising, market-sourced menu, combining flawless technique and know-how in a bid to pamper our tastebuds with delicate flavours tailored to modern appetites. The honey-flavoured madeleines served with a fromage blanc sorbet are awesome!

name: La Poutre
review: In the hub of a pretty village in the Jura lakes area, this family-run inn dating from 1740 plays on its rustic charm. Chef François Moureaux works with fine ingredients to create delicate and tasty contemporary cuisine, but doesn't neglect to revisit local specialities. As for the decor, the establishment is named after one notable feature: its 17m-long ceiling beam that comes from a 3m3 fir log!

name: Quai 17
review: Do not hesitate to try out this establishment set up within a charming hotel in a great location by the canal. Come inside and pull up a chair at your table in the plush dining room laid out beneath the glittering chandelier, and tuck into modern cuisine invested with plenty of Mediterranean flair, in which fish from Sète's market is king. For example, the pulled skate terrine, Sète-style bourride or roast monkfish, bottarga and artichokes. The magic of Sète on your plate.

name: Côté Saisons
review: This couple met at the Ritz. She was working front of house, while he was in the kitchens, which is the same formula they apply today in their own restaurant. Savour tasty and well put - together recipes in this 19C building with a garden and pretty terrace to cater to all seasons. In addition, the service is all smiles.

name: Auberge Saint Fiacre
review: The couple at the head of this pleasant inn in a small village near Valençay can be relied upon to whip up amazing food; everything is homemade and the chef favours regional ingredients to concoct his delicate, toothsome recipes. Served in a charming rustic interior or alfresco on the flower-decked terrace in fine weather. The establishment’s success and excellent value for money mean that bookings are essential.

name: Essentiel
review: On the picturesque Canal d'Ille-et-Rance, an original building with huge glass panes; inside, wood, brick and a metal structure lend the place an "urban loft" feel, making this a charming venue. Comfortable in her position at the helm, chef Blandine Lucas revisits the bistro classics, and is an adept of good produce – the many vegetables from their kitchen garden, in particular, come to mind. Examples of dishes include the bacon and mushroom ravioli, parmesan emulsion; saithe fillet, wheat risotto, leek cream.

name: La Closerie des Roses
review: Surrounded by rose bushes, this restaurant, which has stood on the banks of the Loire since 1938, affords a lovely view of the river and the abbey church – St-Florent-le-Vieil. In a lovely contemporary space, the chef serves up appealing traditional cuisine drawing on regional fare (pike-perch, pike, eel, young free-range pigeon, calf sweetbreads) accompanied by classic sauces (beurre blanc, shellfish jus, wine sauce).

name: Histoire Ancienne
review: Right in the city centre, this old-fashioned bistro is not ancient history, despite its name! It serves traditional fare and hearty canaille dishes that are as fresh as can be: Atlantic cod steak, vegetable waterzooi stew, cassoulet etc. It's tasty (meat and fish are cooked over hot coals), generous and not expensive.

name: Saku Restaurant
review: Saku is the nickname of the chef of this establishment tucked away behind a nondescript façade. He and his wife, both of whom are Japanese, prepare jubilant Gallic cuisine in keeping with today’s tastebuds, with the occasional Japanese tang. The produce is fresh, always in season, at common-sense prices, and the service is friendly and professional.

name: La Falène Bleue
review: Despite their youth, they have both clocked up several years of experience. Fabien and Hélène have combined their first names to create the Falène Bleue. Everything is simple and tasteful, from the food (sourced entirely from local producers) to the interior, dotted with pictures and objects picked up here and there.

name: Le Saint-Eutrope
review: You will love the vintage interior of this bistro (Formica counter, salvaged furniture and eclectic artwork), where British chef Harry celebrates French markets with dishes that hit the spot every time: fresh goat’s cheese, roast carrots and honey, followed by steak and chips with a pepper sauce and his superlative quince pie and double-cream quenelle to finish! Fine selection of natural wines. Uplifting!

name: Chez John
review: Welcome to Chez John: the lair of a talented English chef who is adding a new spin on regional produce. Take a seat indoors or on the secluded patio and dig into colourful dishes in tune with the seasons. After stints in top establishments, the chef is a past-master of technique and his delicate recipes mixed with unbeatable value for money have attracted a crowd of regulars. An antidote to Brexit!

name: Madame
review: This bistro somewhat defies description. Slightly outside the centre of Nancy, it is home to a passionate chef whose menus vary according to the seasons and her whims. The vibe is good natured, the food is savoury and you’re never bored. Let’s not forget the fine list of natural wines and the wine-food pairings. Merci, Madame!

name: Auberge de Combes
review: This quintessential inn – typical of the area – stands on the heights of the Orb Valley. The terroir expresses itself in no uncertain terms: the food and the landscape share a subtle yet rugged edge. Semi-cooked foie gras over grapevine embers, wood pigeon roasted in a wine sauce, sweet chestnut and pear tart… Meals are served within hundred-year-old stone walls or on the patio which commands a sweeping view over the valley. To be washed down with a glass of Faugères, of course!

name: L'Arôme
review: This small restaurant in a characteristic and colourful Marseille street looks like a classroom, with its old maps of France, blackboards, classroom chairs and menus presented in an exercise book. It serves flavoursome, carefully prepared Mediterranean dishes, such as cromesquis of veal. Laid-back atmosphere and a welcome as warm as the Marseille sun.

name: Le Bistro d'en Face
review: Chef-patron Hugo Brégeon and his wife Aurore, who is in charge of the restaurant floor, have set up shop in a small location, with a terrace that commands an uninterrupted panoramic view of the old town and the Dordogne River with its gabarres (traditional riverboats). The tasty, well-crafted food does the view justice: dynamic neo-bistro cuisine that brilliantly revisits some of the French classics – it is unbeatable value, and there is a nice choice of wines by the glass.

name: Côté Sud
review: This young couple with an impressive track record concocts simple cuisine, drawing on regional inspiration to deliver well-crafted dishes. You are sure to enjoy your visit to this stone house with a garden and pleasant terrace. Tuck into the slow-cooked egg with artichokes and black olives or saddle of rabbit stuffed with wood ear mushrooms, crushed potatoes and a red pepper coulis. The wine list focuses on organic and biodynamic wines. Charming service.

name: La Grange des Halles
review: Rungis is more than just the famous food market known to every chef, it is also an old town and home to a this somewhat idiosyncratic bistro. The venue provides the setting for the chef, whose CV mentions Le Taillevent and La Grande Cascade, to concoct market-fresh (what did you expect?) cuisine that combines visual appeal with crisp flavours. Very pleasant shaded terrace to the rear.

name: La Fleur de Sel
review: In the heart of the historic district, it is a pleasure to taste Vincent Guyon’s inspired craftsmanship. The menu might feature monkfish, fried artichokes barigoule, dried tomatoes, emulsion of artichokes, stock and Brittany curry or another house signature dish: beef tartare with oysters served with mizuna, caviar vinaigrette and grilled rice. Deftly crafted and consummately cooked.

name: Le Manoir de Kerbot
review: This 16C manor house (once an orphanage) has been converted into a retreat for food lovers. Guests are treated to fairly traditional cuisine – warm oysters, semi-cooked foie gras, catch of the day, farm-reared guinea fowl stuffed with Guémené andouille, gravy, organic vegetables: tasty and well-crafted recipes all the way! The service is very attentive, and the terrace overlooking a pond is delightful, as are the lovely guestrooms.

name: Spica
review: The former Café de la Préfecture was taken over in 2019 by a young Japanese chef, who spent time at the Maison des Cariatides among others, and his pastry chef partner. A fresh coat of paint, fashionably second-hand furniture, jazz music, tasty market-fresh fare and Burgundy wines without killer prices: voilà – the scene is set!

name: Le Clos Saint Martin - La Métairie
52 Faubourg St-Denis
review: Fans of neo - bistros are going to love this place with bare concrete and exposed stone, a concise, tempting menu, good wines and craft beers. Nothing is left to chance, down to the coffee, which is selected and roasted by the owner. Bear in mind the place doesn't take bookings and doesn't have a phone.

name: La Petite Ourse
review: Back in the city where they first met, Charlotte and Germain have set up a restaurant that expresses their warm and friendly disposition! It enjoyed instant success, and with good reason: ingredients selected with care (local and organic market produce and poultry; the same goes for the traditional bread), dishes that are full of flavour and good ideas. Simple and effective cuisine at highly competitive prices.

name: Bistrot d'Antoine
review: The lilting accent of the South of France can be detected in this bistro, where a really convivial atmosphere reigns. Things hot up in the kitchen, with dishes such as old-fashioned pork casserole or knife-cut beef tartare – only the best makes the cut here. Crowded? Well, yes: Antoine has a huge (and well-deserved) success on his hands.

name: Bistrot Saveurs
review: British chef Simon Scott knocked around in London and Provence, before setting up shop in Tarn. A vibrant red façade leads into the snug trendy interior. This eclectic chef and master craftsman works exclusively with first-class ingredients (preferably local) in a bid to serve crisp, legible food oozing with flavour and aroma: cannelloni of king prawns wrapped in local courgettes, asparagus, truffle-flavoured mimosa eggs and squid ink ice cream; plancha seared slab of veal, foamy mashed carrot and nigella blossom, carrots in cream of cumin and carrot tops… Searingly good food throbbing with flavour!

name: Italie là-bas
review: This enthusiastic couple is living proof that Italians do it better: while he pampers guests in the dining room, she rustles up mouth-watering Italian dishes using fresh ingredients, including a vegetarian menu. Venetian-style sardines in saor, vitello tonnato with hazelnuts, coffee and bottarga, crispy risotto – food throbbing with authentic, wholesome flavour. Buon appetito!

name: Ô Saveurs
review: This fully refurbished restaurant, depicted by a bright, contemporary dining room, has acquired a firm following of regulars with good reason. The owner-chef deftly devises delicate, vibrant dishes that allow the ingredient to shout its name, while making ample use of local herbs. Talent meets taste: asparagus, poached egg with morel mushrooms, crispy sarrazin wheat; truffle-flavoured poultry, mashed turnips and green peas…

name: Le Denti
review: This dinky restaurant off the busy tourist track is the haunt of a couple with a passion for ‘denti’ (a Mediterranean fish). Both are talented, versatile cooks and together they craft flavoursome market cuisine with a weakness for fish and a reverence for the seasons. With only a handful of tables, bookings are snapped up fast, so book ahead!

name: Le Bouche à Oreille
review: This blue-ribbon establishment lies behind a tasteful glazed façade. The chef crafts bold, generous dishes overflowing in big-boned, traditional flavours, but not without personality and accompanied by the occasional original twist, such as a tomato and mozza gyoza (dumpling) served with a delicious tomato and pepper gazpacho. His friendly and efficient wife takes care of the front of house, dispensing insightful wine tips on the way.

name: Le Cèpe
review: It all starts with fine produce from the local land, mountain porcini or fish from the neighbouring lakes, which the chef comes out and proudly present to diners. He then turns it into delightful, fresh dishes, all the tastier for the unbeatable prices. A place that is quite simply comfortable in its own skin.

name: Fleur de Sel
review: In the heart of a picturesque village in the Cher valley, close to the Château de Chenonceau, a contemporary and friendly bistro treats its guests to fresh seasonal cuisine crafted by a talented chef. Mickaël Renard honed his skills in some top establishments, from the Hostellerie de Levernois (in the days of Jean Crottet) and the Côte d'Or in Saulieu (alongside Bernard Loiseau) to the Auberge des Templiers. Today: "perfect" slow-cooked egg with herring and leeks; hake fillet from Brittany with cumin cream, new potatoes and mushrooms in a herby oil. Two menus-carte that change every two months, and a lunchtime menu du jour on weekdays – all at very reasonable prices!

name: Bird
review: In the heart of a small town, this former tea room on the pedestrian square near the town hall is where the son of the house, after working in top establishments, now deploys his talents preparing market - fresh food: tataki of beef, whiting, asparagus and baby new potatoes. Scandinavian - inspired dining room, terrace overlooking a fountain. Delicious prices.

name: La Table de Haute-Serre
review: In the wine storehouse of a château in the heart of the vineyards, this restaurant exudes the very particular charm of truly authentic places. Charcuterie rack, butcher's block, ham slicer and cases of wine herald a wonderful moment of gourmet delights, rounded off by wines from the estate. Rotisserie evening every Friday. Just delicious.

name: La Maison de Kerdiès
review: This restaurant on the tip of Trégor province was originally a signal station, before being converted into a summer camp, then a restaurant. From inside, you can enjoy a panoramic view of the Bay of Morlaix. But your attention will soon be drawn back to the food, which encompasses regional dishes (catch of the day with far noir) and more traditional cuisine (chicken ballotine with mushrooms).

name: Le Carré de l'Ange
review: After a break, chef Paul Fontvieille is back in the kitchen, having lost none of his enthusiasm or infectious sense of humour. Each inspired recipe has been endlessly puzzled and preened over to produce flavoursome dishes (the creative desserts are to die for). Served indoors or on the lovely terrace overlooking the village.

name: Julien
review: Local folklore is celebrated by waiters in traditional costume and a characteristic wooden Vosges decor. In a lively, yet sophisticated atmosphere, you will be treated to tasty, copious regional preparations: sauerkraut, veal kidneys, sweetbread and bouchées à la reine. The food is as heart-warming as the rooms, the grounds and the hotel’s magnificent spa facilities.

name: La Table du Pouyaud
review: In the upper reaches of Périgueux, chef Gilles Gourvat (a local lad) has set up shop in a tastefully restored farmhouse. His modern recipes pay tribute to Périgord traditions, in which local produce (truffles in season) is cast in the star role. Examples: whole duck breast roasted with cèpes; scrambled eggs and truffles; semi-cooked duck foie gras smoked in hay. Heavenly.

name: Le Balcon
review: Chef Jean-Philippe Gauthier is upholding the traditions of this former coaching inn, which has been in the family since 1951. House specialties include: terrine of quail with plums and armagnac and a knockout trolley of matured cheeses. Meals are served in an interior that blends character and authenticity. Charming welcome and service. Rooms for overnight stays.

name: C'la Vie
review: From a long line of bakers, chef Richard Durand has made C'la Vie a real mecca for food lovers. The food is good and life is good! The daily menu features terrific ingredients (most of them local), the flavours are distinctive, and the focus is firmly on dining pleasure. Enjoy your meal in the pared-back dining area inside, or on the terrace in the shade of a hundred-year-old plane tree. A fine selection of wines that celebrates the Rhône Valley and Languedoc, and rightfully so.

name: Épices et Tout
review: This small restaurant with an unobtrusive façade will wake up your taste buds. Beautifully prepared dishes, fresh produce, and judiciously deployed spices. For example, organic creamy slow-cooked egg with mushrooms, guinea fowl with seasonal vegetables and sweet and sour sauce or citrus macaron. An appetising menu to relish on the small terrace in summer.

name: L'Angle Saint-Laurent
review: This smart and appealing setting with exposed stone, painted beams and soft lighting is to be found at the corner of rue St Laurent and rue des Bouchers. Ingredients from the region take pride of place on the menu (Bayeux pork, Normandy oysters... ), and feature heavily in the delicious, original and beautifully made dishes.

name: La Vieille Forge
review: Beyond the rustic façade of this charming 16C house some lovely surprises lie in store: chef Laurine Gutleben's dishes give pride of place to fresh produce and free rein to creativity, for instance the beef shoulder confit with a meat jus and dauphine potatoes. Great wine list, with a selection from Alsace and beyond.

name: Bistrot du Pollet
review: Let us make no bones about it: in this bistro, it is the sea that decides, and the dishes depend directly on the local catch. Enjoy squid, foie gras du pêcheur, sole du bistro or scallops with lentils. Quality and freshness are the order of the day, and what generosity in the preparations!

name: So
review: After notching up experience in some fine establishments, Japanese chef So Takahashi works alone in the kitchen, and his partner, Rié, is front of house. He uses ingredients that are bought directly at the neighbouring market to concoct French cuisine interspersed with Japanese inspiration. The result is finely executed, light and flavoursome. So good!

name: La Beaugravière
review: It feels as if time has come to a standstill at this family-run inn – and that is meant in the best possible way! Now in his 70s, chef Guy Jullien cooks up a delightful culinary offering that is sure to win over confirmed traditionalists: foie gras flan and cream of truffle soup, fattened Bresse chicken with truffles, roast rack of lamb with thyme, vanilla-raspberry ice cream vacherin… not to mention the simply irresistible truffle set menus. This is food in a classical vein that is as tasty as it is hearty, to be savoured peacefully in the shade of the trees in fine weather. The wines also hit the spot: the impressive cellar contains many treasures from the region. A real gem!

name: Le Flaveur
review: This restaurant is tucked away in a side street set back from the marina and the walled city. Harmony reigns in the kitchen, where a duo of chefs composes dishes made with ultra-fresh ingredients. Locally sourced produce takes pride of place on the menu: buckwheat, the daily catch of small local boats, Brittany-reared pork, Bruyère Blanche poultry, farm-range eggs, without forgetting the excellent homemade bread.

name: Balsamique
review: The peaceful little terrace at Balsamique is a real draw, especially on summer evenings! The young chef has more than one trick up his sleeve: his creative, rather original cuisine is based on impeccable produce (fish from Boulogne-sur-Mer, for example) and scattered with lovely Asian influences. Efficient service and a fine selection of champagnes.

name: DZ'envies
review: You can trust David Zuddas to satisfy your culinary desires – or envies! In his restaurant, which has a trendy canteen feel, the chef gives free reign to his love for his vocation and fine ingredients. Diners choose between a three, four or five-course menu or pick from a list of traditional French and Burgundian dishes. It's a treat.

name: Le Terminus
review: Last stop! All food lovers please get off at Le Terminus, an old train station converted into a friendly little bistro. Some places you simply must call at, and this is one of them. Try the hearty traditional cuisine, such as leg of lamb with homemade mashed potato or rum baba. Good value – and plenty of flavour – for your money!

name: Le Bouchon Bourguignon
review: Within the contemporary setting of this annexe of Yohann Chapuis' fine dining restaurant, treat yourself to generous and meticulous Burgundian-inspired cuisine. The regional classics are present and correct: "Maison Greuze" pâté en croûte, eggs meurette (in a red wine sauce), fresh frog's legs in a parsley sauce, Bresse chicken with morels and vin jaune, Charolais beef. For dessert, the floating island with pink pralines or the Mâcon wafers will round off your meal perfectly.

name: Le Tiroir
review: This establishment in the working-class district of Vaise, appointed in a characteristic trendy bistro vibe, is irresistibly endearing! The work of a youthful team, the food slaloms between iced tomato soup served with a mousse of white balsamic vinegar and a more patriotic Gallic line-up (tartare of beef, foie gras) – the menus and carte are regularly renewed. Excellent value for money and pleasure, including in the evenings.

name: Chez Mon Jules
review: The dining room is adorned with assorted paraphernalia and wooden tables and chairs. You will be treated to scrumptious regional fare, such as homemade rennet with foie gras or lacquered pork belly from Dieulefit with regional veggies. In fine weather, take a seat on the shaded terrace and sample the splendid view.

name: Le Grapiot
review: Established in a famous wine-growing village, this welcoming restaurant is the stronghold of a fervent defender of flavour and fine produce. His cooking is ideally paired to the local wines, which is all the better as his list of Jura wines is one of the best in the area. Good value-for-money.

name: U Licettu
review: Could this pink-rendered villa, decked in flowers and overlooking the gulf, have found the secret of authentic Corsican food? Whatever the case, you can be certain that you will sample wholehearted, full-bodied dishes made with first-class ingredients in keeping with time-honoured culinary traditions: nothing goes to waste from pig’s trotters to tails, the meat is slowly spit-roasted on the open fire or the lady of the house hovering nearby to check you finish your plate. Beverages included in the menu. Highly recommended.

name: Arbequina
review: The chef's aromatic and tasty Mediterranean cuisine demonstrates his talent for letting the ingredients do the talking. Looking at the menu, you might settle on the marinated and charred mackerel, gaspacho with Vera pepper and pistou, or line-caught hake, young and creamy grilled courgettes. To savour in a contemporary bistro setting.

name: La Table d'Élise
review: Conveniently opposite the fishing harbour, this seafood restaurant, an offshoot of the gastronomic La Marine, shines the spotlight on exquisitely fresh fish and seafood. The high-flying technique and hallmark of chef Alexandre Couillon can be tasted here in a bistro version at prices that won’t break the bank. Love at first bite!

name: Comptoir Breizh Café
review: Breizh Café is the result of a stroke of genius: the idea of mixing Breton traditions with the Japanese flair for presentation. Inviting modern decor with a counter facing the open kitchen, as in Japan. Local ingredients (100% organic buckwheat, oysters from Cancale, butter from Bordier) and a few contemporary touches, such as buckwheat pancakes rolled up like maki. Good choice of ciders.

name: Le Pélican
review: Olivier Guenoun, chef of this family business since 2010, crafts recipes that appeal to modern tastebuds in a menu dotted with daily specials that vary with market availability. Just like the regulars to the Pelican, open your beak wide to sample a slice of Nantais cake, a ubiquitous regional classic, treated to a new twist with roast pineapple and a mojito sorbet!

name: Les Mets d'Adélaïde
review: Are you sure you don't want to go back to school? Les Mets d'Adelaïde may well make you change your mind! The restaurant has taken up abode in the old village school, whose playground doubles as a summer patio. Rather than a nostalgic interior, however, expect a minimalist décor and a masterclass in contemporary cuisine. The service deserves a gold star!

name: Les Arômes
review: In this 1930s house basking in the aromas of Provence, unflappable hostess Françoise Besset and her husband Yannick officiate. His innkeeper's soul has not changed and he continues to regale guests with fresh and inventive regional cuisine. Enjoy in one of the charming little dining spaces or, in fine weather, on the terrace on the veranda overlooking the garden planted with olive trees. An exemplary place.

name: La Table Bâgésienne
review: The spruce façade of this former coaching inn invites you to cross the threshold and admire the revamped interior, complete with a glazed wine cellar, from which you can select your own bottle. The food is depicted by generous country fare to which the chef enthusiastically adds his own inimitable hallmark.

name: Restaurant du Dauphin
review: This pretty 16C house at the foot of the Porte St Julien proposes homemade cuisine for the modern palate with a smattering of exotic touches. The tuna ceviche with coconut milk and ginger is a good example. The interior has grey and raspberry tones. Fine selection of wines by the glass.

name: Auberge La Gaillotière
review: Rows of vines hug the walls and patio of this converted wine storehouse, which now sports a fresh rustic vibe. The food juggles intelligently and appetisingly between classical roots and modern influences. The menu changes once a fortnight in a bid to keep pace with the seasons. Fine local wines (Muscadet, Val de Loire, Vendée Fief) at prices that make sense take centre stage. Service with a smile.

name: Les Flots
review: A picturesque blue and white house (1890) overlooking the beach. You have two choices: a vintage bistro full of charm or a contemporary bistro with a striking view of the waves (flots)! Whatever your choice, you will be treated to fish and seafood with a strong preference for seasonal and locally fished produce.

name: Le Cygne
