review: This picturesque half-timbered Alsace edifice has successfully kept pace with the times and its veteran chef conjures up modern, bistro dishes. Examples include a mouth-wateringly juicy pink duck breast with golden rendered crispy skin served with a delicately orange-perfumed and slightly spicy gravy jus. Choice between two menus in a pared-down refreshingly minimalist interior.

name: L'Assiette au Jardin
review: The setting comprises a small bistro-style dining area with shelves filled with delicatessen products, and a pretty extension. Sit back and tuck into tasty food, where tradition is nicely combined with influences from far and wide. The menu, which changes every two weeks, highlights local or regional produce. A charming place.

name: Maison Joanto
review: Joanto means ‘Little John’ in Basque, yet this house certainly doesn’t deserve a diminutive! For example, its fine traditional architecture and warm, vibrant character are more than worthy of applause, which is even truer of the enticing recipes of its chef, who boasts stints in top establishments. You can expect an explosion of Basque Country flavours: carbonara-style squid, braised chuck beef in red wine, choux pastry filled with cream, pistachio and citrus fruits. Fantastic value for money.

name: Le Rendez-vous des Gourmets
review: Since he opened this splendid country restaurant, Didier Doreau has turned it into a genuine gourmet stronghold. Terrine of pike à la Chambord, pâté of game served warm drizzled in jus, traditional calf’s head, Grand Marnier-flavoured baked citrus fruits… You can expect a pageant of traditional Gallic staples, made with fresh, crisp produce, crafted into dishes that exalt and respect the intrinsic flavour of each ingredient. The chef is renowned for his way with game in season (hare, venison, wild boar, etc.), which further adds to the well-deserved success of what has become a culinary benchmark in the region.

name: La Table d'Auzeville
review: In the heart of a village in the suburbs of Toulouse, this white house is now run by Grégory Truilhé, who was previously second in command here. Regulars should rest assured that the chef remains faithful to the establishment's reputation, composing cuisine that sings the praises of the great classics. Tasty and well made – a pleasure.

name: Cabane
review: In his first solo venture, youthful Jean-François Bury, whose CV boasts stints at the George V and the Shangri-La, without forgetting the Top Chef 2017 TV show, is masterfully regaling Nanterre with bistronomic cuisine. Modern recipes and generous helpings, such as pork belly, sweet garlic cream and fregola sarda. Food that combines familiarity with flawless execution.

name: Auberge de l'Île
review: Chef Pierre Koniecko has set up shop in this plush venue on Vienne Island, where he regales his guests with hearty, flavoursome creations, such as hake in bacon and croutons and braised, buttered cabbage. Delicately presented, premium ingredients served in a contemporary interior or, in summertime, on the exquisite riverside deck patio – heavenly on hot sunny days!

name: Le Bistrot de Villedieu
review: Laurent Azoulay has embarked on a new culinary adventure in this village in northern Vaucluse since June 2020. The veteran owner chef, currently of the star EKrin at Méribel, whisks up provençal fare in a locally sourced bistro register. The flavoursome, flawlessly executed repertory is rich in character and some of the dishes are cooked in the wood-burning oven of the open kitchen. Meals are served in a contemporary bistro setting, or, in fine weather, on the shaded terrace on the village square.

name: Le Clos aux Roses
review: We warrant you will leave soothed and reassured after spending a few hours in this handsome stone house. Firstly, because of chef Armelle Krause’s delicious cooking, using excellent local dairy and poultry produce, for example, but also the exceptional location of the restaurant in the heart of a flower - decked village, fully the equal of Giverny…

name: Au Petit Vatel
review: A genuine institution, “The” place to eat in Alençon is in the hands of seasoned chef Julien Perrodin and his wife, Barbara, in the dining room. They propose contemporary seasonal cuisine founded on top-notch regional produce (the chef is a local lad), without forgetting a wickedly tempting dessert trolley. The menu will make your mouth water, before your tastebuds sample the flavoursome fare, often with an exotic spike and as generous as the region. Prices that make sense.

name: Les Épices Curiens
review: When strolling around the area you could easily cross over into Belgium without realising it. But the former train station of this border village, since converted into a lovely restaurant, will encourage you to stay in France. Sample the inspired cuisine and nicely prepared dishes, all paired with good local wines. Lots of taste!

name: La Table de Léo
review: This stone - built house in the heart of the village has a pretty terrace overlooking the church square. Inside, you will discover a great little restaurant with a chef who dares to branch out from the usual regional fare. He pays special attention to his ingredients and how best to present and cook them.

name: Le Moulin Fouret
review: In an Instagram-perfect picture of the French countryside outside Bernay, we fell head over heels with this imposing country house smothered in Virginia Creeper and its waterside terrace shaded by birch trees, without forgetting the historic mill, whose cogwheels are still intact. This idyllic venue is even more so by the fireside in wintertime, providing the perfect foil to chef Cédric Auger’s culinary ethos: first-rate fresh ingredients, consummate craftsmanship and cooking and polished table arts. The regularly changing seasonal menus pay tribute to the chef’s homeland, Normandy. Cosy guestrooms to make the most of this rural paradise.

name: L'Aubépine
review: L’Aubépine is flourishing in the hands of a youthful researcher, now on a quest for flavour. Chef Manuel is a staunch advocate of locally sourced produce, whose ingredients he seeks to exalt, respecting both their texture and nutritional value. Everything is made in house and the menu changes weekly depending on the market.

name: Cartouches
review: It would be impossible to count all the cartridges in the game bag here, between the wine list with a natural slant, the cured meats to nibble, the cut of meat to be shared and, above all, the simple, flavoursome market cooking. There is never a dull moment in the company of Nicolas Brousse and his wife who treat their clients as if they were old friends.

name: La Maison de Celou
review: Clinging to the ramparts of the historic village, this lovely house embodies the art de vivre of Provence. The chef crafts spot-on dishes, steeped in originality, illustrated by scallops on toast with spinach and confit of tomatoes. The decadent desserts are fiendishly tempting, even addictive. Superlative sweeping view over Mont Ventoux and the Luberon range from the terrace.

name: Côté Bastide
review: At a slight distance from the town centre, this is the headquarters of Laurence and Cédric. She is the chef and produces tasty cuisine in step with the seasons. While he is a trained sommelier and chooses the best wines (notably Bordeaux) to accompany the dishes concocted by his partner. A duo that works wonders!

name: Minami
review: This tiny Japanese restaurant is crammed with regulars. The minimalist interior provides the perfect foil to well-crafted Japanese fare with the occasional foray into a traditional Gallic repertory. A few examples: sushi of foie gras, caramelised eel or jasmine-perfumed crème brûlée. A few tables are laid on the patio in fine weather.

name: Le Kitchen
review: In the student district of the Louis Lumière and Jean Moulin Universities, this Kitchen is thriving. The interior, a delightful blend of Art deco and Scandinavian (as is the owner), holds only eight small square tables. The pastry display case (to eat in or take away), the work of the owner’s pastry chef companion, sets our tastebuds drooling and the kitchen is open for breakfast and teatime, as well as lunch (but is closed in the evenings). Organic local produce, vegetables mainly, take pride of place on the table.

name: Le Bistrot du 11
review: You guessed it: La Table du 11's team is also behind this place that is located in a touristy pedestrian - only street not far from the palace. Fine produce makes up the menu - carte: egg, lentils and parsley; cod, pointed head cabbage and taramasalata; hot chocolate tart, vanilla...

name: Au Bon Pichet
review: It is a delight to eat at this restaurant that has been run by the same family for four generations! Like his forefathers before him, the chef concocts good traditional recipes: smoked pork shank with potato sauerkraut, pike perch quenelles and matelote sauce... The convivial service and winstub decor confirm that the rules of good living never go out of fashion!

name: Le Bon Temps
review: By the side of the legendary Nationale 7 road, this small eatery may not look like much but is a reminder not to judge a book by its cover! In the kitchens, it is a couple who cook up delicious and hearty market-fresh cuisine, in alignment with local producers. Potato blini with oyster mushrooms; grilled pluma pork with Madeira sauce, potato gratin… Fresh produce (especially the vegetables), the joy of a good job well done and unbeatable prices.

name: L'Atelier
review: Cyril Haberland is a chef whose credentials speak for themselves (he worked alongside Thierry Marx, during the Cordeillan-Bages period). He and his wife opened L'Atelier in the centre of Périgueux, creating a modern space with a friendly atmosphere where you feel at ease right off the bat. Through his cooking, the chef fetes the farmers of South-West France and his cherished regional ingredients, such as wild mushrooms sourced by local pickers, Périgord black truffles and local snails. He works with these ingredients, showcasing them in nicely presented modern dishes, for example: pain perdu with pullet and pink garlic, calf sweetbreads with a lemon glaze, butternut confit, pineapple, candied citron and coconut biscuit.

name: La Flèche d'Argent
review: The name "The Silver Arrow", as Mercedes Benz were known on the Formula 1 racetrack, is a reference to the Circuit de Charade. In a plush space, chef Clément Lorente cooks up contemporary cuisine with creative touches, served as four- to seven-course set menus. Market menu at lunchtime; brunch on Sundays.

name: Le Beaujolais
review: With such a name, this Beaujolais could not do otherwise than pay tribute to a region famous for its fine food and wines! The friendly couple that runs this house has hit the nail on the head with hearty wholesome fare. Examples include traditional andouillette, whole grain mustard sauce and sautéed potatoes.

name: Ô Saveurs
review: Chances are it won't be the charm of the location near the train station that draws you here, but the restaurant has more than enough of its own merits. Where shall we begin? Oyster and salmon tartar, crunchy courgettes, lemon jelly, creamy dill foam; cod in a crust, langoustine bisque and Coco de Paimpol beans; millefeuille, cream with Timut pepper and roasted pineapple.

name: Le Paris-Brest
review: The new Rennes train station chose an emblematic Breton chef to reinvent its station restaurant: Christian Le Squer, chef of the three-star restaurant Le Cinq at the Four Seasons Paris. He playfully revisits the traditional cuisine he grew up with, adding contemporary touches. A combination of design (by Jouin Manku studio), bistronomy and a wine list curated by Eric Beaumard (Breton sommelier). You're in for a treat if you stop off here.

name: 1er Mets
review: A stone’s throw from the town hall, this postage - stamp restaurant is in the hands of an enthusiastic young couple. The chef devises fresh, modern menus that keep pace with the seasons, such as maki - smoked fera fish in a tarragon, mustard and egg yolk sauce. Gracious, smiling service.

name: Les Plaisirs
review: This friendly family - run inn is tucked away in a village perched high up in the Nice hinterland. The young owner - chef, descended from a long line of restaurant owners, throws his heart and soul into preparing Provençal recipes using impeccably selected regional produce. Authentic flavours, enticing dishes and endearing prices! Well done!

name: L'Émotion
review: Two chefs, Michaël Ruat and Mickaël Méjean, childhood mates from Puy-en-Velay, have teamed up in this eatery. The interior sports a preference for natural materials and designer details (handsome glazed wine cellar). The food forges a culinary path between regional Haute Loire ingredients (green lentils, premium Mézenc beef) and a more contemporary score (tartare of red tuna, citrus fruits, fennel sorbet and crunchy pesto).

name: Le Café des Arts
review: Make a beeline for this peaceful town and meet Virginie and Antoine Préteux, a young yet experienced couple. Antoine conjures up flavoursome recipes, sprinkled with modern twists to suit today’s palates. His recipes are inspired by market availability and the seasons in a bid to celebrate regional, often organic produce. Spruce, colourful interior.

name: La Table d'Hôtes
review: Not far from the seaside resort, this family restaurant is the stomping ground of a couple who have experience working in some fine establishments. Yoann Lavalley has bought the stove which he used during his apprenticeship and uses it to create seasonal cuisine that is both flavourful and indulgent. The sommelier, his wife, has curated a nice wine list that represents excellent value for money. Fish of the day, local meat, Normandy cheeses… A pleasant place.

name: Café Brochier
review: This handsome building is an institution in this Vercors village. Dating from 1867 and recently taken over by a youthful enthusiastic couple, it is home to a historical cafe adorned with frescoes dating back to 1912. Locally sourced ingredients play the lead roles on the menu, which changes regularly. Respect for the seasons goes hand in hand with respect for the produce, culinary skill and flavour. Three unpretentious rooms upstairs.

name: Auberge de l'Abbaye
review: A few steps from the romantic ruins of Hambye Abbey, this classical hotel - restaurant is now in the hands of a young couple. The chef in fact learned the trade here, before moving on to other fine establishments; now he serves flavoursome traditional cuisine, free of unnecessary frills. A litany of gourmet pleasures in store.

name: La Récré
review: This restaurant is housed in a former village school for boys. You will notice evidence of its previous incarnation in the decor with blackboards and geographical maps hanging on the walls. On the menu, the dishes are creative and make good use of locally sourced ingredients. It is enough to make us sign up for evening classes!

name: Le Margote
review: In his restaurant facing the Bassin du Roi, chef Gauthier Teissere, assisted by his wife Marguerite in the dining room, plays a modern, unabashedly modern score, jazzed up with occasional Asian note. The stylish, snug interior is the perfect foil for dishes that reverently respect the seasons. Each plate is a masterpiece, illustrated by a tartare of red tuna, avocado, chimichurri sauce or risotto of haddock with croutons in lemon butter.

name: Le Saint-Georges
review: In his restaurant, just a roll of the dice from the casino, Paul Courtaux doesn’t gamble with our appetites. He crafts vibrant, flavoursome cuisine, which cleverly shines the spotlight on regional produce, illustrated by frothy cold fish soup with an aïoli of cuttlefish and mussels, or a slice of Ségala veal simmered in lemon, basil, aubergines, tomatoes and parmesan… The splendid regional wine list deserves special mention, as does the charismatic welcome.

name: Hostellerie du Prieuré
review: This 18C former convent is the haunt of a chef in love with regional produce (plums, Vasperviller perch, etc.). The portions are generous and the desserts by Maeva (the owners’ daughter) are wickedly delicious. The house signature dish is a ballotin of pig’s trotters stuffed with foie gras. A few practical rooms.

name: Vidal
review: In this restaurant opened in 1984, the Vidal family (father, son and daughter-in-law in the kitchen, Mrs Vidal front of house) serve a delicious repertoire that is an intelligent take on tradition: tasty dishes that highlight a series of small local producers (noire du Velay lamb, fin gras du Mézenc beef, market gardeners...). Aurélien's pâté en croûte is a fine technical feat and deserves a special mention.

name: PY
review: In this dinky brasserie in a classy neighbourhood, Pierre (in the kitchen) and Yuko (front of house) are a champion team. Take a seat in a trendy décor to sample hearty, well-crafted dishes that set the tastebuds tingling: Basque black pudding à la plancha, fried squid and creamy mushy peas – without forgetting the knockout desserts, such as creamy grapefruit, olive oil biscuits and mango sorbet. The evening menu features a wider range of top-notch ingredients (lobster, beef fillet, sweetbread).

name: La Croix Blanche
review: At this former coaching inn, you can enjoy the modern cuisine of chef Jean-François Beauduin, who learned his trade in Michelin-starred restaurants. His tempting menu abounds with wonderfully indulgent treats, which does not preclude finesse – the warm duck and foie gras pâté, shredded Brussels sprouts and langoustine sauce is a case in point. Seasonal and local ingredients are de rigueur. Note the selection of more traditional dishes, such as beuchelle tourangelle (creamed kidneys and sweetbreads). Charming service courtesy of the chef's wife, in a delightfully rustic setting. The pleasant terrace in the shade of mulberry trees is a real highlight.

name: Auberge du XIIème Siècle
review: In a village that Balzac particularly loved, this Auberge is something of an institution. The thirty-something chef, Kévin Gardien, now runs the inn, flanked by his partner Stéphanie Marques, who is in charge of the service. Regional produce takes pride of place in the modern, appetising dishes, all of which at reasonable prices. A quintessential French country inn!

name: L'Alcôve
review: Just behind the cathedral, this restaurant has been treated to a makeover and a new name, whilst retaining its culinary hallmark: expertly crafted, market-fresh recipes as full of flavour as they are flawlessly prepared. Examples include spider crab, crunchy veg and vinegar sorbet; whole grain risotto with asparagus, confit artichokes and an emulsion of wild garlic. Enduringly popular, all the more so because of the eater-friendly prices.

name: Briket' Bistrot
review: The Ibarboure family hotel also has this pleasant bistro, which is independent of the gourmet restaurant. The chef creates meticulous, delicate and flavoursome food in a refined setting. Basque ingredients dominate the menu, as you might expect, but not to the exclusion of exotic dishes. The team is young and friendly, the prices remain reasonable. A real treat.

name: Le Confidentiel
review: Among all the restaurants (which include some real juggernauts! ) surrounding the lake, this place proves that good things come in small packages. In a tiny, light - filled dining room you can enjoy dish after formidable dish, the bold flavours going hand in hand with the friendly and relaxed atmosphere. Now that you're in on the secret, you know what to do.

name: Le Jean Moulin
review: Guests are invited to take a seat in one side or another of a long dining room, divided by a glazed wine cellar, in a designer décor of industrial loft inspiration. The perfect foil to taste Grégoire Baratier’s cuisine in the zeitgeist. The menu changes very regularly, but here are two examples to give you an idea of the market-fresh cooking: thick ravioles of snails and fondant leeks, emulsion of garlic and parsley, scattered with wild herbs; confit of braised veal, mousseline of chervil root, caramelised winter vegetables and a gutsy gravy. Crisp, well-crafted and rich in tributes to Lyon’s culinary heritage.

name: Le Tilleul de Sully
review: This country inn stands in the shade of the old lime tree. The vegetable patch is full of courgette flowers, carrots, round cabbages and redcurrants, and the chef uses them to excellent effect in his dishes. Enjoy this tasty local cooking in front of the fireplace or outside, overlooking the fruit trees.

name: Au Colombier
review: By the River Saône, a fine 18C building that feels like a cross between a hip guinguette and a country house. The food is resolutely contemporary: carpaccio of gilt - head bream with lemongrass, saddle of rabbit stuffed with wild basil... without neglecting the classics, such as the wonderful pan - fried frogs' legs. Good taste and character.

name: La Table de Pablo
review: Delicate and decidedly creative cuisine based on good regional ingredients: this restaurant surrounded by vines and cherry trees is a real find. Try the surprise menu, inspired by the offerings of the markets and small-scale local producers. The chef-patron takes care of everything himself, both in the dining room and the kitchen. Special mention for the peaceful terrace, where you can hear the cicadas' call.

name: Manoir de la Pommeraie
review: Not far from Vire is this 18C building that may look rustic at first glance, but turns out to be fine... Running the kitchens is a pair of chefs (also a couple): Masako, a Japanese pastry chef, and Julien, like her, trained in several renowned establishments. A good place, for both savoury and sweets!

name: L'Envers du Décor
review: This old bakery has been transformed into a smart, contemporary restaurant with a totally minimalist feel. Chef Aurélien Jousseaume has previously earned his stripes working in Michelin-starred kitchens for Etchebest, Guy Savoy and Guy Martin. To-ing and fro-ing between his open kitchen and the restaurant floor, the chef, who seems to be living his best life, takes charge of orders and presents the dishes himself. His delicious seasonal cuisine has a laser-sharp focus on sauces and jus, all of which are sure to remain in the memory of diners (eg a creamy Amaretto jus served with mushrooms, a veal jus with prunes served with calf sweetbreads).

name: Villa Mirasol - Bistrot 1912
review: Villa Mirasol has entrusted the fate of its restaurant to Philippe Lagraula, a chef from Landes, who earned his stripes under Troisgros and Bras. His strong points are well known: presentation, originality, harmonious flavours, qualities that are illustrated by uncomplicated modern cuisine, such as black pudding with yellow pepper, runny egg and "cosa crocante".

name: L'Athome
review: In his new restaurant complete with wine shop, chef Lionel draws on his strong culinary background as well as good local produce – organic market garden vegetables, small-scale fishing – to create delicious set menus offering excellent value for money at lunchtime and an appetising tapas menu in the evening. Edwige provides friendly and efficient service.

name: La Table du Sommelier
review: A father and son duo work in this pleasant, contemporary bistro. The result is tasty food that skilfully revisits the terroir and an impressive choice of wines by the glass with almost 400 to choose from! In summer, there is a choice of two terraces – either beneath the pergola or in the open air. Highly recommended!

name: Au Cheval Blanc
review: "The soul of a winstub... and all the flavours of the region lovingly presented: blue trout, venison steak with sauce grand veneur, kirsch mousse etc. The same spirit is mirrored in the decor: lots of wood panelling and two ""stuben"": rustic rooms that are typical of the region. Finally, a special mention for the absolutely exemplary service. "

name: Le Biniou
review: The chef draws his inspiration from Brittany, as evidenced in dishes such as cream of Coco de Paimpol bean and mushroom soup. But he is also open to other influences: you may want to opt for his pan-fried foie gras, beetroot broth and smoked eel. Meticulous food, smiling service, a digestible bill and a location just a few blocks from the beach.

name: La Ferme de Cupelin
review: Not content with clocking up an impressive CV (Senderens, Flocons de Sel, Murtoli), chef Romain Desgranges is first and foremost a Saint Gervais man, and that makes all the difference. He celebrates the ingredients of his region in meticulous dishes, with game in season (deer, pheasant), old-style terrines and delicious home-made bread. A delight.

name: Le Central
review: The Troisgros family's other gourmet establishment. Michel and Marie-Pierre dreamed up this bistro-cum-grocery in a 1920s hotel. The warm, vintage decor is inspired by the grocery stores of yesteryear. You can sample a concise menu, possibly picking into à la carte suggestions, whose influences vary (traditional, Indian, Asian, etc). The place is always busy: a well-deserved success.

name: Auberge de La Mère Duval
review: Alexandre and Mélanie Baranzelli are thriving in a new venue oozing with country charm: picture a stream spanned by two bridges and a watermill! The chef, after honing his skills in top establishments, demonstrates his fondness for traditional recipes from his native Normandy, to which he is increasingly adding his own distinctive culinary hallmark.

name: Mensae
review: Cuisine of the moment, full of freshness and with spot-on flavours. Among the classics, on the menu all year round, the frogs' legs, garlic and parsley or the mousse au chocolat praliné are good enough to spark a riot. The decor has the good taste to make itself discreet. The small sidewalk terrace is welcome in summer and the lunch menu is a boon.

name: La Chaumière
review: This family-run place, a 19C coaching inn, has been in the hands of chef-patron Philippe Arnault since 1992. He is ably assisted by his wife, daughter and, in the kitchen, his son-in-law, Sébastien Provendier (who has previously worked for the Meilleur family and Passedat). Tuck into delights such as trout gravlax with beetroot, buckwheat pancake and horseradish cream, in a pleasant dining room with large bay windows giving onto the inner courtyard. There is a shaded terrace to be enjoyed in fine weather and six guestrooms done out in a modern style inspired by the Sologne region.

name: L'Équilibre
review: "Run by a couple of 30 - somethings, who believe in hearty, wholesome food, this restaurant fully deserves its resounding success. The chef concocts inspired and balanced recipes using top - quality, market - fresh produce: flawlessly poached egg with cream of leeks and ginger; haddock and carrot pickles. Outstanding value for money. "

name: L'Araignée Gourmande
review: Settle at your table in this bright, modern interior and experience the talent of Thierry Chouin. This Breton chef may have a particular penchant for fish - based fare, but that doesn't mean he snubs lamb and potatoes. He fetes the ingredients with nicely turned - out dishes, each a lovely homage to tradition.

name: Mamagoto
review: Mamagoto is Japanese for tea party. Seasoned chef Koji Tsuchiya serves an appealing selection of dishes you can share (or not!), combining Japanese and Basque influences – for example, sea urchin with parsley sayon or grilled squid with pesto. The wine list includes some unusual natural wines. A simpler set menu at lunchtime.

name: Le Muratore
review: When it was established in 1870, this place with a superbly preserved Belle Époque decor was named after Mr Muratore, a liquor - maker and confectioner. It is now run by the engaging Marc Serres, who proposes delightful cuisine, starring fish from the lake (Arctic char, perch etc). Finally, let's not forget the gorgeous terrace beneath the boughs of the lime trees.

name: La Chênaie
review: The focus here is on good old-fashioned nosh, served generously and unfussily. Traditional French family favourites with the occasional more contemporary note, served in stylish dining rooms and, in particular, in the conservatory overlooking the grounds, planted with century-old oak trees. Dishes you might taste include meat stew with foie gras, quails stuffed with foie gras, upside-down apple pie and saffron ice cream. Prices that make sense and friendly service.

name: Le 62
review: Top marks for this restaurant that masterfully titillates our tastebuds thanks to the perfectly judged seasonings and harmonious flavours of the gifted young Vietnamese-born chef, who trained at Chamalières and the Belle Meunière in Royat. Polished bistronomic cuisine rich in French overtones, illustrated by farm-reared pork chop, sauce Grand Veneur, risotto and spring vegetables. The desserts are equally high-flying, depicted by yellow peach and an unctuous vanilla custard and whipped cream. Excellent value for money and a small courtyard patio add the final flourish to this irresistible establishment.

name: Les Bouteilles
review: Next to the Marché de Talensac, an impressive wine bar/bistro: appealing wine - inspired decoration, excellent food based on quality products (Italian cold cuts, rough - and - ready canaille dishes, fresh fish) not forgetting – the clue is in the name – a memorable wine list (700 types), with a particular penchant for Burgundy.

name: La Table d'Inomoto
review: Having formerly worked at the Pavillon des Boulevards, Seiji Inomoto now runs this very beguiling bistro. You can expect beautifully prepared fusion cuisine drawing on France and Japan, in which "modest" ingredients are elevated by perfect cooking and an astute sense of seasoning. The cooking is good, often original, and you won't believe the value for money. Don't delay!

name: Voyages des sens
review: After learning the ropes in the company of legendary chefs, Nicolas Morelle has opened his own establishment in this pretty village. He works hand in hand with small local producers, devising intelligent, subtle dishes that hit the spot every time, such as trout, horseradish emulsion and organic seasonal veggies. A cheerful casual vibe sets the scene and curious connoisseurs can keep an eye on the kitchen and the chef through a window to the rear.

name: La Table du Fleuve
review: The brainchild of Thierry and Julien Verrat, this Charentes restaurant is distinctly bistronomic in style. The menu keeps pace with the seasons. For example, semi-preserved duck foie gras and truffles; tartare of trout with herbs and its caviar or raspberries with pineau des Charentes topping and steamed meringue. On fine days, meals are served on the terrace. An aristocratic yet welcoming setting devoted to good food.

name: La Pomme d'Or
review: A slice of The Golden Apple (La Pomme d'Or) is always delicious. A young couple from Brittany has taken over this restaurant, a former coaching inn with a slightly revamped dining area. The modern cuisine draws on the Sancerre terroir and Breton roots: vegetables from the garden, tomato water broth; pork tenderloin fillet, seasonal vegetables. You can see straight away that the chef is a pro (cf. the presentation of the dishes) who never forgets the sine qua non: how it tastes! The chocolate gianduja praline with a gavotte biscuit crisp is a wonderful dessert. The wine list, unsurprisingly, gives the floor to Sancerre wines, and that is fine by us!

name: Gribiche
review: We fell head over heels with this endearing bistro! Traditional dishes, jazzed up for modern tastebuds and served generously, are enticingly chalked up on slate menus: porkpie, calf’s head gribiche sauce, lamb shank and desserts to die for with lashings of salted butter and cream. Fine choice of reasonably priced tipples.

name: La Table de Catusseau
review: Kendji Wongsodikromo, owner - chef of New Caledonian extraction, fell in love with southwest France and his wife, Nadège, whom you will meet in the dining room. The enthusiastic, young couple does not lack experience as the first taste of their market - fresh, carefully crafted dishes made with tasty, regional ingredients will confirm.

name: Bistrot Saint-Sauveur
review: Black chairs, white curtains: welcome to Claude Sutter's world, which boasts an attractive, pared - down style that is never showy. The chef's bistro cuisine is a joy to relish, from the grilled andouillette to the tarte sablée à la banane. Pots simmer away, meats hang and our appetites stir. The hardest thing is to choose!

name: Brasserie d'Asten
review: On Binic port, this contemporary brasserie has large bay windows overlooking the sea. The chef with a glittering track record (Le Coquillage – Maison de Bricourt in Cancale, La Pyramide Patrick Henriroux in Vienne and K2 in Courchevel) likes to cook up his enticing brand of "bistronomy" cuisine, incorporated into set menus that represent good value for money.

name: L'Ô à la Bouche
review: At the head of this pleasant restaurant is a foodie couple who travelled to faraway lands and seas before dropping anchor in Cahors. Jean - François concocts gourmet dishes such as: salmon marinated in fennel or wild seabass, pan - fried chard and Lautrec pink garlic cromesquis. Enough to make your mouth water!

name: L'Auberge du Pas de Vent
review: L'Auberge du Pas de Vent… a splendid name, like something dreamed up by Tolkien. This authentic inn in the Landes serves bold and lively cuisine that remains aloof from fads and gimmicks. The menu fetes the terroir: farm-reared Chalosse beef, free-range fattened duck, veal from calves fed on their mother's milk, pure ewe's milk cheese from a village shepherd and home-made sourdough bread (without additives). Here, tradition is not a dirty word. Butternut soup and dried lomo sausage, cuttlefish broth with star anise, steamed leek and diced chorizo: the hearty dishes hark back to grandmother's home cooking. It's an enjoyable mealtime, while in the next room, people play a game of ninepins… Warm welcome, attentive, professional and efficient service. We couldn't ask for anything more.

name: La Fourchette à Droite
review: This place is run by a pair of experienced industry pros. A friendly welcome is extended by the hostess (who is left-handed, hence the fork being on the right in the restaurant's name), while her chef husband cooks up a storm. The dishes encompass much of Brittany's best, with lovely seasonal ingredients. Booking recommended, as places are limited at this small, inviting place.

name: Ishikawa
review: Chef Yugo Ishikawa has set up shop in this minimalist restaurant with a long dining room located in a busy pedestrian street in the heart of the city. He throws himself body and soul into painstakingly crafted, traditional Japanese dishes. Daily specials might include tonkatsu shoulder of pork in breadcrumbs, tuna tataki with ponzu oroshi, tsukemono pickled vegetables and a range of delicious dishes. Worthy of a genuine izakaya in downtown Tokyo.

name: La Dariole
review: In the heart of the old town and not far from the cathedral, this 15C half-timbered house showcases an easy alliance of old stonework and cosy touches. The chef, who even trained here when he was learning his trade, hits the mark with delicious cuisine that is in tune with the times. The seasonal menu changes regularly and features appealingly tasty dishes such as pork chop with potatoes and a caper jus.

name: Racine
review: "The name refers to not just one racine (""root""), but several: the chef's Burgundian roots, a great source of pride for him; the origins of the ingredients he uses (90% of which are produced within a 100km radius). His tasty and well - balanced dishes do the rest. Small delicatessen and wine bar on Thursdays and Fridays. "

name: L'Espérance - Stéphane Carbone
review: On the canal towpath connecting Caen to the sea, this rust - coloured building was taken over by Stéphane Carbone, head of L'Incognito, in Caen. The dishes turn out to be tasty and made with considerable care out of top - notch, fresh ingredients; those hungry for French classics can still get the calf's head with sauce gribiche.

name: Les Fuchsias
review: Normandy's finest produce – oysters first and foremost – is showcased in contemporary and tasty dishes. Three possible spots in which to tuck in are the rustic - style dining area, the glass - roofed conservatory overlooking a remarkable garden planted with palm, mimosa and eucalyptus trees, and, come summer, the pretty terrace.

name: Auberge du Pont de la Zorn
review: Marquetry art from Atelier Spindler, antiques, lightened beams and untreated wood tables: the dining area displays its Alsace heritage with pride! On the menu: tasty regional specialities, such as bœuf gros sel (boiled beef), and flammkuchen in the evening. Bucolic terrace on the bank of the River Zorn. Then there is the impeccable welcome and service – this place deserves its success.

name: La Chaumière
review: Put your skis away! You won't be able to resist this lovely thatched cottage at the entrance to the resort with an interior where wood predominates. On the menu find a fine selection of Catalan dishes, delicious tapas and good regional wines. The proprietor likes the finer things in life (choice meats, locally grown vegetables) and has even set up a ham cellar!

name: Au Relais des Ménétriers
review: The time is long gone when ménétriers or itinerant fiddlers went from inn to inn but hospitality is still the rule at this Relais, as is good food! The chef concocts true traditional French cuisine and buys his vegetables from local farmers. You can't argue with the results, which are generous and tasty.

name: L'Atelier L'Art des Mets
review: The youthful chef proposes up - to - the - minute, distinctive cuisine, whose mainstay is wild herbs, which he learned to know through a local herb picker. Lamb’s quarters, wild lemon balm, purslane, mugwort... The culinary score is poetic and rich in flavour, illustrated by the slow - cooked, farm - reared, maize - fed chicken in lamb’s quarters with slow - cooked artichokes. Fine art at the service of taste!

name: Chez Davia
review: This endearing establishment, run by the same family since 1953, was founded by grandma Davia and taken over in 1985 by mum, Alda, who still greets guests. Since 2016, Pierre Altobelli, whose impressive CV features star establishments in France and Asia, concocts tempting recipes rich in the flavours of Nice. Every detail is perfect, and the ingredients are meticulously sourced. Served in a welcoming vintage bistro décor steeped in authenticity. Heavenly!

name: Le Bistrot d'à Côté
review: In a pedestrian street lining Place de Jaude and St Pierre les Minimes Church, chef Ludovic Raymond proposes tasty food in the zeitgeist, made from first-class, seasonal ingredients. Examples include hen casserole in an aspic of lentils and Charroux mustard or Atlantic cod with mashed pumpkin and mango vinaigrette, followed by a mint-yuzu cheesecake to finish. Tempting selection of cocktail and spirits.

name: Fine Gueule
review: In Nice's old town, opposite the town hall, this restaurant's newly refurbished interior is organised around an open kitchen and a counter where customers can sit to eat. But the real pleasure is to be found in the food, with traditional dishes chalked up on the board each day, including for starters the home-made pissaladière, devilled eggs or calamari a la plancha.

name: Simple et Meilleur
review: Baked trout, Reblochon fondue, cold cuts and cheeses from the region, blueberry tart, or rabbit sautéed with mustard, tarragon and creamy polenta. Savoie produce takes pride of place at this attractive, cosy restaurant set up by René and Maxime Meilleur, who earned three Michelin stars at La Bouitte. The menu is an ode to the terroir, replete with dishes to be sampled in a rustic-style Savoyard bistro interior decked out in pale wood and with large bay windows looking out onto the mountains. In winter, you can ski right up to the door. Tapas served on the ground floor.

name: Aux Trois Pastoureaux
review: Jean - François Lucchese used to be a pastry chef, which goes some way to explaining his neat and precise dishes. He likes to define himself as a ‘craftsman of taste’, taking care over associations of ingredients, cooking times and seasoning. His dishes are packed with flavour! Among his specialities, the ‘medieval menu’ takes diners back in time.

name: Les Trois Bourgeons
review: This contemporary bistro, with its understated decoration, has blossomed in an old cellar of famous Chablis producer Domaine Laroche. An Asian team, who trained in some of the top French houses, invites its customers to partake in a fine dining experience inspired by regional recipes, revisited with taste and imagination. Unbeatable value for money.

name: O2C
review: A former helicopter pilot who now devotes himself body and soul to cooking, Christophe Bellegaud is at the controls of this restaurant, which sports a tasteful cream and chocolate colour scheme. He uses local ingredients to create 100% homemade up-to-the-minute market cuisine that is always spot on. Chantal, the second “c” of this o2c, gracefully caters to diner’s needs.

name: Hyacinthe & Robert
review: Chef Damien Le Quillec named his restaurant after his two grandfathers. In this unusual setting – previously a garage, cleverly converted into a contemporary loft – he channels his talent into crafting ambitious dishes that appeal to the modern palate. Meanwhile, he has opened a convivial little bistro next door – Numéro 100, where he serves bistronomy fare in a home-from-home atmosphere.

name: Les Coloquintes
review: This restaurant installed in a former silk - throwing factory is run by a young couple – he in the kitchen, she front of house. They propose contemporary cuisine, aiming to keep supply channels short and respecting local produce, trout, chestnuts, fruits etc. In summer, get a table in the shade of the lime trees.

name: L'Estacade
review: This pleasant eatery on the quayside, opposite the fish market, is managed by two young people with experience in some elite establishments. They propose hearty and meticulously made food that makes good use of regional produce (fish, shellfish and seaweed, of course, but also meat). The lady of the house is a radiant hostess. Smiling staff and attentive service.

name: Le Brélévenez
review: This pretty stone house in Brélévenez (a neighbourhood in Lannion) is run by Monsieur and Madame Le Marrec. Business is going strong, and this is not by chance: the well thought-out and tasty food is in tune with the land and the seasons. One last thing, the space is modern, refined and a pleasant place to be.

name: Pho Tai
review: In a quiet street in the Asian quarter, this small Vietnamese restaurant stands out from the crowd. All credit to the chef, Mr Te, who arrived in France in 1968 and is a magnificent ambassador for Vietnamese cuisine. Dumplings, crispy chicken with fresh ginger, bo bun and phô soups: everything is full of flavour.

name: La Table des Armaillis
review: Excellent value for money in this restaurant that specialises in tasty dishes inspired by the Savoie terroir (salted Arctic char, waffle and wild garlic cream; farm-reared chicken supreme, potatoes, prunes; Tatin-style apple, walnut biscuit, fromage frais-honey sorbet). The contemporary interior is tastefully dotted with Alpine details. Definitely one of the best establishments of the area.

name: La Chaumière de Pomper
review: Well - known in the region, this pancake house rustles up crêpes made from 90% organic buckwheat flour and 10% wheat flour, resulting in a mixture so light and airy the crêpes are even crispier than the norm. In fact, it even has a name in Breton kraz! If you can’t make your choice, we suggest sticking to the classics! Impressive list of ciders.

name: Le Bistrot 270
review: The Domaine du Colombier’s sibling restaurant offers well-structured, bistro fare, inspired by tip-top quality ingredients. French staples take pride of place in the wholesome, savoury recipes: semi-cooked duck foie gras; haunch of tender veal; shepherd’s pie. In fine weather, the terrace near the pool and the pool-house bar overlooking the meadows and the fortified town are heavenly.

name: Mokko
review: Arthur Hantz, a self-taught chef who started out washing the dishes, has adopted a no-holds barred, complex-free approach and his modern bistro at the foot of Montmartre gets right down to brass tacks. The menu (carte or slate only) features a devilishly effective strategy: creative, vivacious, market-fresh cuisine with the odd Asian influence. A few examples: lightly seared cockles and scallops, pho emulsion, pimangue spice; free-range chicken, vitelotte potato crème, violet cauliflower, roast parsley roots, jus of milk-fed veal and toasted sarrazin.

name: Le Patio by Lou Caléou
review: Having worked together in some renowned establishments, chef Guillaume Dercourt and pastry chef Amandine Sabot decided to open this restaurant in Sommières with a stonework interior and a charming patio for summer. What's not to love? The cooking is resolutely modern in its form and draws playfully on the traditional French repertoire: tielle sétoise ravioli, slow-confit shoulder of veal, blanquette garnish or, for dessert, the delicious Paris-Brest. A real treat.

name: Agastache
review: This brand-new bistro is the brainchild of two gifted young partners who honed their skills in Lyon. The unfussy, up-to-date interior sets the scene for instinctive, updated and well-crafted dishes. Fine seasonal produce and a distinct fondness for vegetables result in food that combines formal elegance with flavoursome coherence. Now add lashings of generosity and a friendly atmosphere and you will find yourself in one of the best newcomers on the left bank.

name: L'Aillet
review: This chef’s cuisine manages to balance a trendy bistro vibe thanks to a definitively contemporary look with a clear commitment to sustainable agriculture. He is also a past master in the art of tradition and roasted joints, a skill we can only applaud, as we ask for more! A welcome addition to the Arcachon Bay culinary scene.

name: Le 1825 - La Table bistronomique
review: Tucked away in the countryside, this bistro is housed in a small 19C château. It is presided over by an experienced chef, who regales guests at lunchtime (only) with a remarkable repertoire in which the techniques learned in top establishments do justice to impeccable produce – the food is simple, fresh and fragrant. In the huge dining room that occupies the former orangery, original materials are combined with modern furnishings.

name: Cécile
review: In the lively, bustling Carmes district, this culinary gem is the work of a youthful, close-knit team. The food hits the spot every time from the starter to the dessert and we are not about to forget their incredible veal porkpie with foie gras and morel mushrooms, which was divine! Thank you Cécile.

name: Le Radis Beurre
review: Chef Jérôme Bonnet found the perfect location for his restaurant on Boulevard Garibaldi in Paris. He prepares tasty, well-crafted cuisine that bears the hallmark of his early years in southern France. The pork loin with braised endives, Mimolette Vieille cheese and a pearlescent jus is just one dish that will certainly grab your full attention.

name: Une Table à Deux
review: After learning the ropes in Toulouse, Morgane and Nicolas made a beeline for Korea and Malaysia to research new flavours. Back in their hometown, they have chosen the Carmes district to regale diners with playful recipes that blend Mediterranean and tropical flavours, resulting in impressively curated and beautifully balanced dishes. Fantastic value for money lunchtime menu.

name: Manger & Dormir sur la Plage
review: It sounds like the title of a song from the 1980s. This young and relaxed restaurant facing the sea offers marine-inspired cuisine, with a mouthwatering choice of shellfish, fish, and of course oysters: the establishment belongs to the Gillardeau family, the famous oyster farmers. The large terrace offers a lovely view, with the Île d'Oléron on the horizon. As for accommodation, "Dormir sur la Plage" has four large very well-appointed junior suites.

name: Auberge de Port Vallières
review: The welcoming establishment of Marie-Hélène and Bruno Leroux offers sustenance to discerning foodies in a chic contemporary setting. Flavoursome cuisine, rich in regional delicacies, awaits you in this stylish, inviting restaurant, whose chef cannot resist prime ingredients: truffle-flavoured homemade white pudding, poultry sauce; seven-hour roasted shoulder of French lamb in thyme… Slick service. The wine cellar is a treasure trove of regional tipples! Good food comes first in this auberge where you are always welcomed with a smile.

name: Le Dauphin
review: This place is just the ticket for fans of Normandy's specialities: oysters from the bay of Isigny - sur - Mer, Swiss Normandy pigeon, and Vire andouille sausage. The onus is on ingredients from the region but the chef also knows how to compose more original recipes. Elegant and bright decor.

name: Le Canut et les Gones
review: A unique atmosphere, somewhere between bistro and secondhand shop – formica bar, wooden floorboards, vintage tapestry, collection of old clocks on the walls –, modern cuisine in tune with the seasons, a wine list boasting over 300 types... In a little - frequented area of La Croix - Rousse, this is definitely one to try out.

name: Le Toi du Monde
review: This renovated barn in the upper reaches of Flumet offers modern, tasty dishes whose presentation is flawless. The produce, some of which comes from the huge vegetable garden (practically an acre!) is seasonal and top-notch. On this particular day: delicious home-smoked salmon tartare and cod roasted in garlic butter. Comfortable guestrooms and concerts every other Saturday evening. Flavoursome, buzzy, friendly.

name: Bistrot Louise
review: The small terrace facing the church resembles a traditional walnut drier… Welcome to this walnut-growing village where Yann Tanneau (formerly of MadaM in Grenoble and who trained at Ducasse) has set up shop. A fan of fine produce, he whisks up gutsy cuisine in menus that change weekly. Guaranteed to please, excellent value for money at lunchtime and refreshingly informal ambience.

name: Le Rousseau
review: (Transfer planned to 16 bis cours Saint-André in Pont-de-Claix in early 2023) The face behind Le Rousseau is youthful Élie Michel-Villaz, who remains steadfastly true to his defining mantra: simplicity. The score is fresh, carefully crafted, paired with lovingly selected wines (300 references – many natural or biodynamic)… and served in a friendly vibe. A short supply chain business that is going strong.

name: Côté Mer
review: The picturesque little port of Cancale is depicted by quaint fishermen's houses and salty sea air. Unsurprisingly, this seaside restaurant overlooking the bay serves primarily local seafood (scallops, oysters, lobster and abalone), but not to the exclusion of other local produce, such as lamb from the salt marshes. All of which at eater-friendly prices.

name: La Ferme de la Haute Crémonville
review: To see verdant Normandy again, to admire the horses of the neighbouring stud farm, to dream of the pastoral life: this authentic half-timbered farmhouse is so pretty that it makes the most intractable city-dweller want to retire to the countryside. In these parts you will come across calves, cows, pigs and… traditional delicacies: cep ravioli with chanterelle cream, crunchy vanilla millefeuille; not forgetting the steaks cooked over a wood fire. You have barely put down your knife and fork before you are planning to return to these lovely dishes and bucolic setting.

name: Auberge le Nézil
review: With its white façade with small windows and thatched roof, this cottage is the epitome of a Brière inn! The chef concocts his meticulous cuisine, adding the odd bold twist here and there that he always pulls off with great skill, as can be seen in his grilled scallops, lentils, Granny Smith and smoked bacon; Vendée duckling, olive purée with black garlic, parsnip croquettes, passion fruit vinaigrette... Original dishes, good produce (eels and frogs), along with a real sense of generosity make this a highly recommendable place! Fireplace, beams and floor tiles. One for the inveterate gourmets.

name: Le 6 à Table
review: In a peaceful village, this small square whiling away the days in the shade of the church makes a picture - perfect scene. The chef uses seasonal ingredients as much as possible, mostly also local (figs, cheese, vegetables), and demonstrates care and finesse in the preparation of his dishes. To savour in the modern interior reminiscent of an atelier, or on the terrace.

name: Arkadia
review: A magnificent surprise awaits you along the Ardèche gorges: chef Marvin, born in Brittany, regales diners with uninhibited cuisine using locally sourced produce (vegetables and cheese in particular). The dishes are legible, appetising and the menu is renewed every fortnight; the infectious gaiety of Philippine in the dining room is quite irresistible.

name: Le Saint Marc
review: The scenic village of Aups, south of the Verdon Gorges, invites you to make a bistronomic halt. Chef Alexandre Dimitch and his small team play a local, bistronomic score, rich in generous flavours, with truffles in summertime and bouillabaisse and bourride by the fireside in winter. Wine lovers may like to know that the next-door wine cellar becomes a wine bar in the evenings.

name: EssBar
review: The outwardly unimposing restaurant run by Daniel Baur and Olga Jorich is situated only a few steps away from the Hofgarten public park. Pleasant atmosphere, plus flavoursome dishes prepared from good-quality ingredients and offering good value for money. Neither will you be disappointed by the wine list! Attractive protected terrace to the rear.

name: Treibgut
review: As a sophisticated alternative to Seestern, Treibgut adds to the gourmet credentials of the Lago hotel. Modern cuisine is served in a trendy and exceedingly stylish interior. There are also dishes for sharing, e.g. steak cuts, whole fish or snack platters. They offer a nice selection of goods from their own bakery, butcher's shop and ice cream factory.

name: Rotes Ross
review: If you are a fan of fresh and seasonal regional cuisine, the Bogner family's restaurant will be right up your street. This place is cosy and the service comes courtesy of friendly and well-drilled waitstaff managed by the lady of the house. As for the wine, the focus is also on the region. In summer, the leafy courtyard terrace is in great demand. You can also spend the night in one of the well-kept, comfortable guestrooms.

name: Gutsküche
review: This restaurant in a converted sawmill serves up delicious, unfussy regional fare with an emphasis on sustainability and great fresh (organic) ingredients. Try the sweet and savoury bites at the GutsDeli café and delicatessen shop, as well as organic produce from the Wulksfelde estate's on-site farm shop. The gardens are lovely in summer.

name: Schweizer Wirt
review: This place has been synonymous with tasty cuisine for years. The fresh, regional dishes are made with excellent ingredients. Stripped back to the essentials, they eschew any frills. The atmosphere in the restaurant is charming and the waitstaff are friendly. This beautifully situated traditional inn also has a fabulous terrace. You can park directly in front of the building.

name: Wirtshaus Mättle
review: Dating from 1848, this inn has been given a tastefully modern makeover. High-quality, market-fresh produce is used to conjure up cuisine that looks to the Mediterranean as well as the local region for inspiration. In addition to à la carte dishes (the whole roasted trout, for instance, is a house speciality), a surprise menu is also on offer. Gorgeous terrace. Located in the basement, bar-cum-restaurant THEODOR is ideal for events.

name: Jouliard
review: This French bistro has been set up in a well-maintained townhouse located a little outside the city centre. The kitchen proposes classic fare such as confit chicken with herbs and scalloped potatoes, as well as more modern dishes like fjord trout with potato foam, braised carrot and passion fruit. Lovely terrace out front.

name: Felsenbirne
review: This modern, chic and comfortable restaurant is located right in the pretty old town, not far from the Elbe. Owner and chef Felix Mikulla uses seasonal ingredients – his dishes are fresh and delicious, as well as good value. In summer, diners can make the most of the terrace in the inner courtyard.

name: Asam Schlössl
review: Shane McMahon is no stranger to Munich's gastronomy scene. In his charming restaurant just outside the city centre, the Irish-born chef serves tasty Bavarian cuisine into which he skilfully weaves his personal touch. Here you will find pub classics, but also modern dishes, as well as steaks barbecued in the Big Green Egg.

name: Zöllner's Weinstube
review: Surrounded by splendid gardens, this 18C half-timbered sandstone building is as charming on the outside as it is on the inside. Sitting beneath a striking vaulted ceiling, diners can enjoy regional as well as Mediterranean-inspired cuisine made from first-rate produce. There is also an excellent selection of Franconian wines. In summer, the terrace is a must!

name: Weinstube
review: These former stables have been converted into a delightful restaurant, in which terracotta tiles, warm colours and an old brick ceiling lend a real country feel. The international cuisine on offer follows the seasons closely. Diners are well looked after by a friendly and professional front of house team. Charming and elegant guestrooms are available in the Hotel Am Brühl.

name: Weingut
review: How about dining in a chic and trendy modern restaurant after a stroll through the city? Choose one of the daily specials from the blackboard or simply opt for some tapas or a glass of wine – you can also buy bottles here. The service is very friendly and attentive. Decorative wine racks and high tables contribute to the pleasant wine bar atmosphere of the place.

name: Lohmayr Stub'n
review: Chef Sebastian Oberholzner puts his heart and soul into his cooking, meaning his delicious dishes are much in demand. He uses seasonal and regional ingredients, making sure to know his suppliers and the origin of the produce. There is also a good selection of wines. Diners enjoy charming service in the setting of a fine historical building.

name: Bergfriedel
review: This has been a family-run business for years! The welcoming team serves delicious, fresh food that diners can enjoy as they take in the views over the Bühlertal. The wide-ranging menu includes traditional cuisine from Baden, vegetarian/vegan dishes and gourmet specialities. Add to that an extensive wine list. The chic restaurant extension is done out in a modern take on regional style. Pleasant overnight accommodation available.

name: Michaelis
review: Tasty and fresh food is served in this refined restaurant in a restored building from the Wilhelminian period, which also houses the comfortable hotel of the same name. The menu is classic – there are various set menus (one of which is vegetarian) and a sophisticated à la carte selection. Friendly and attentive service. In summer, the terrace behind the house is very appealing.

name: RÖHMS DELI
review: You’ll find a simple, modern concept on offer here with seasonal dishes such as codfish with two kinds of peas and rösti potatoes served in an uncomplicated modern bistro atmosphere. The dessert counter promises a choice of delicious desserts and there is also a three-course set evening menu. Expect excellent product and some great flavours.

name: SonneStuben
review: The regional and seasonal cuisine that leaves the kitchen wins diners over with its flavours and technical skill. The cosy dining rooms afford views of the old town's historical half-timbered façades and boast a lovely decor with various nods to the region. Take a seat on the pleasant terrace on the Marktplatz.

name: Staudenwirt
review: This restaurant with its small, well-kept hotel is a family business that has evolved over three generations. Each dining area feels quite different, from rustic to clean-lined contemporary style, and there is a beautiful terrace. The home-style cuisine is regional, but also modern and seasonal. Vegetarians are well catered for, too.

name: St. Urban
review: The comfortable dining rooms at St. Urban bring to mind the traditional charms of a Palatinate country inn. The good, regional food – including dishes such as medallions of beef in a pepper crust with bean cassoulet – is accompanied by local wines. The restaurant also serves an afternoon snack menu.

name: Allgäuer Stuben
review: The name may refer to the Allgau region in Swabia but the junior chef's passion for Mediterranean cuisine is plain to see. Try the house-made pasta, gnocchi or risotti – really delicious! But the mention of the southern German area is still pertinent, and you will be served in a friendly and courteous manner. The terrace is wonderful. Our tip: Monday is pasta day.

name: Gasthaus Schwanen
review: This inn dating back to 1912 gets everything right: friendly and dedicated owners, a charming atmosphere and good food made from regional and seasonal produce. They also serve schnapps made with fruit from their own orchards. Lunch is only served on request, except on Sundays. The Villa Pfarrhus, located a few metres away, proposes particularly comfortable guestrooms.

name: Die Alte Brauerei
review: Your friendly hosts Eric and Isabelle Dauphin have imbued their charming restaurant with a touch of French flair, which extends to the menu. High-quality produce is used to create delicious dishes that are also fairly priced. Their inexpensive lunchtime set menu is particularly popular. Access to the restaurant and the individually designed guestrooms is via the interior courtyard.

name: Behl s Restaurant
review: You really can taste the dedication of the Behr family in the excellent food on offer here as local produce is transformed into flavoursome dishes such as Blankenbach river trout with potatoes, orange carrots and saffron foam. Try for a table in the shady interior courtyard. The family also offers "spirit evenings" in its own distillery.

name: Kucher's Weinwirtschaft
review: Kucher’s offers a mix of charmingly mismatched antique tables and chairs, pretty decor and an almost family atmosphere. The sour kidneys with sautéed potatoes have been on the menu here forever – a classic that has plenty of faithful fans. Most of the meat used in the seasonal regional fare comes from the Eifel area.

name: Zur Linde
review: The Trautwein brothers run this 300 year-old former posting house with its charming mix of historical and modern decor with great dedication. The menu includes Swabian classics such as Gaisburger Marsch beef stew, maultaschen ravioli and veal tripe with braised oxtail, alongside seasonal offerings. The rustic vaulted cellar is available for events.

name: August
review: Long-standing tradition and really good food are what the Gehrke family stands for. The fresh, seasonal cuisine is imbued with international flair: roast leg of venison with a wild mushroom sauce; duck breast and cabbage with chorizo and raisins; hake filet on ribbon noodles and wok-fried vegetables. Wine cabinet with a great selection! Nice guestrooms at the Schmiedegasthaus Gehrke hotel.

name: Landgasthaus Gidibauer-Hof
review: You eat well here, and furthermore the regional cuisine comes at very fair prices. The home-reared beef, for example, is sure to whet the appetite. The ambience is friendly, cosy and rustic. The converted cowshed is a great venue for parties. In the hotel of the same name, the guestrooms are furnished with natural wood furniture.

name: Salt & Silver Levante
review: With this friendly urban restaurant, Salt & Silver in the St Pauli neighbourhood also has a Levantine version in addition to its Latin American eatery. Here you dine mezze-style, following the example of the cuisine of the southeastern corner of the Mediterranean: Levant-inspired dishes, both big and small, come together to the table and are made for sharing.

name: Landgasthof Schwanen
review: A Landgasthof – country inn – in the best sense! The Fräulin family is committed to its patrons; the whole establishment is very well looked after, from the restaurant to the comfortable guest rooms. The tasty food is fuss-free and influenced by regional culinary tradition – in the evening, the menu is somewhat more extensive. As for the interior, the dining rooms are done out in a traditional-rural style with the occasional modern touch.

name: Aldingers
review: Susanne and Volker Aldinger skilfully combine the traditional and contemporary here. The really tasty food can be enjoyed à la carte or as a set menu. Diners can choose from a range of regional and international dishes – from their "offal week" specialities to nasi goreng. The atmosphere is cosy and neighbourly, and there is a pleasant little terrace. Tip: the wines from their own winery!

name: Dorfstube
review: Dorfstube complements the hotel’s gourmet restaurant perfectly. The feel in the lovingly decorated, wood-panelled dining room is warm and homely as you sample the good, plain local fare by candlelight. Try the pumpkin and cheese ravioli with steamed rocket or the fishcakes with potato and cucumber salad. The local game is also very good.

name: Landgasthaus Hirsch
review: The Waldenmaier family (now in their fourth generation) cook excellent, seasonal, regional fare at their traditional country inn. The game is locally hunted, the bread comes from the little bakery next door, and even the schnapps is home distilled. There is also a pretty terrace on the first floor and a lovely rustic beer garden.

name: Nil
review: Diners are bound to enjoy their time here! This restaurant in the trendy Schanze district has a delightful ambience, the service is informal and friendly, and you can certainly expect to eat well. The delicious food follows the seasons and draws on international influences. Opt for the five-course set menu. Excellent and reasonably priced short wine list.

name: Zur Krone
review: In the centre of the village you will find this charming restaurant with its comfortable dining rooms. Ralf Restel serves simple, flavoursome regional fare with international influences. Try the boiled rump of beef with herb sauce and pan-fried potatoes or the breast of corn-fed chicken with stir-fried vegetables and curry sauce. In summer the best tables are those outside on the quiet leafy terrace.

name: Freihaus Brenner
review: Diners often come here for the freshly caught trout and char, but don’t miss out on the roast saddle of suckling pig with sage jus and romanesco or crispy fattened duck with red cabbage, which are also on offer. To enjoy the wonderful view, opt for a window table or the terrace in summer.

name: Erbgericht Tautewalde
review: Inside, the modern dining rooms are done out in a pretty, rural style; outside, there is a lovely courtyard with a view of the kitchen. The seasonal cuisine is regional and international, and they are keen to use local produce. You can choose between the "Landidyll" set menu and "A la carte menu". Overnight accommodation in the traditional Erbgericht.

name: Weedenhof
review: This pretty restaurant with its wood and dry-stone interior offers a warm and welcoming setting in which to enjoy flavoursome regional dishes including veal chop in a leek crust. Don’t forget to leave a little space for the excellent desserts – the apricot dumplings with zabaglione are excellent! There are also a number of pleasant guestrooms.

name: Mühlenhof
review: This family-run restaurant in the hotel of the same name is justly popular, for the food is well priced and the service fast and friendly. The seasonal, regional fare on offer includes dishes such as Baden pike dumplings in Riesling sauce. The good-value lunch menu is also a big draw. Don’t miss the delicious home-baked cakes.

name: Landgasthof Hirschen
review: The dedication of chef Verena Martin and her team is palpable. In a charming setting diners enjoy cordial service and good food that is made primarily with produce from the region and draws inspiration from the seasons. The kitchen staff put their heart and soul into their work – the motto here is ä weng eppis Feins, or "a little something fine" in the local dialect. Tip: "Unser badisches Menü" or "Unser großes Menü" (for two or more people).

name: Die Pfarrwirtschaft
review: Thomas Merkle’s second restaurant boasts a rustic modern interior and the same high standard of cuisine as his first. Here, guests can watch a varied range of dishes with regional and seasonal influences being prepared in the open kitchen. The serving staff are well trained and there is also a reasonably priced lunch menu.

name: HYGGE Brasserie & Bar
review: In Danish, 'hygge' describes a feeling of warmth, cosiness and well-being - just the atmosphere conjured up in this chic, stylish and relaxed timber-framed restaurant with an open hearth at its centre. The food is seasonal and regional, and includes dishes such as cod fillet with braised cucumbers, horseradish and mash. The bar-lounge is a trendy spot.

name: Fürstenfelder
review: This restaurant enjoys a beautiful location amid the Baroque buildings of a former monastery. Inside, guests sit under the beautiful Bohemian vaulted ceiling of the former cattle shed; outside, tables are laid in the courtyard of the Cistercian monastery. The cuisine focuses on regional organic produce, with an excellent buffet at lunchtime and equally tasty modern dishes served in the evening. Vegetarian and vegan options also available.

name: Landhaus Zum Rössle
review: Family tradition since 1780! Here the hospitality extended to diners is just as important as the tasty cuisine made from regional produce. Besides classic dishes, a surprise menu is also served. In summer the garden is a delight! There is a fantastic barn venue for parties. You can also stay overnight.

name: Gastwirtschaft Ferdinand Reuter
review: This traditional family-run establishment serves good-quality regional cuisine that takes its cue from the seasons. Classic fare and more sophisticated dishes both feature on the menu. The atmosphere is friendly and cosy – in the more modern section, diners take their seats at long wooden tables. Hotel Reuter, which houses this restaurant, has comfortable guestrooms.

name: Sülbecker Krug
review: If you fancy prime beef cooked in an oven heated to 800°C, then this restaurant renowned for its meat is a good choice. The menu includes classics such as rib-eye, rump or flank steak served on a wooden board with superb sauces. They also have a wine bar. Various promotions are also offered throughout the year – don't hesitate to enquire!

name: Zum Goldenen Anker
review: This 18C inn offers not only a comfortable stay (opt for one of the newer guestrooms), it is also a popular modern take on a rural restaurant. The fresh and tasty options include their "Oma Emelle" braised beef roulade with Burgundy sauce, red cabbage with apples and spaetzle. The main courses are also available as smaller portions.

name: Gasthof Alpenrose
review: This lovely, long-established restaurant is always busy and has a loyal following of regulars. Located close to the church, it has been run by the same family since 1868. Inside it has comfortable dining nooks, outside a secluded beer garden and terrace. The seasonal Bavarian cuisine often draws on ingredients sourced from the surrounding area. Charming guestrooms are also available.

name: Gasthaus Wolters - Zur Börse
review: Formerly a livestock exchange, this appealing inn is steeped in tradition. Behind the typical brick and half-timbered façade, tables are laid out in a pleasingly rural interior where diners enjoy a quality take on regional home-style cooking made using excellent produce. Friendly service completes the picture. Be sure to reserve your table – the Gasthaus Wolters tends to get booked up.

name: Landgasthof Zur Post
review: Since 1870, this house has been in the same family, already in its sixth generation. They serve down-to-earth regional and seasonal cuisine made from good produce. The ambience is cosy and rustic; in summer the terrace commands a lovely view of the countryside. There are also a few guestrooms and a holiday apartment. Excursions possible in the Naturpark Vogelsberg.

name: Weinhaus Stern
review: A popular address and deservedly so: an inviting, rustic-style interior, a pretty courtyard, friendly service and, last but not least, good seasonal cuisine. Chef Klaus Markert relies on honest craftsmanship and flavours, along with fine wines from the region. Be sure to try the house brandy production. Charming guestrooms are also available, and there are home-made fruit jams for breakfast.

name: Gasthaus Scherz
review: A native of Vorarlberg, Michael Scherz – no stranger to Cologne's gastronomy scene – focuses on Austrian cuisine, with classics such as Tafelspitz (boiled beef), Wiener schnitzel and Kaiserschmarrn (shredded pancake with raisins). Great Austrian wines. The service is speedy; the staff friendly and well-trained. Very nice terrace to the rear of the house.

name: Piccolo
review: Classical cuisine is given a modern spin here, to include regional and Mediterranean influences. Quality produce is transformed into dishes such as veal liver with sage butter, spinach and mashed potatoes, or Eifel beef entrecôte, red wine sauce and beans. You can choose à la carte or put together a three-course menu at a fixed price. Good wines from Austria.

name: Zum Rebstock
review: A fun place to eat! In this historic half-timbered house (in the family since 1750) you can sit back in the delightful wood-panelled interior and enjoy charming service and really good Baden cuisine. Tip: sample the array of starters and desserts as little "temptations" (Versucherle). Great wine list. Buy some home-made cherry or plum brandy to take home with you. You can also stay overnight comfortably.

name: Gasthaus Goldener Stern
review: This long-established restaurant in Rohrbach has been run by the Fuß family for three generations. The cosy, modern rooms are beautiful and the regional and seasonal cuisine is inspired by modern concepts. Attentive service provided by charming waitresses dressed in traditional costume. This is an exciting venue for a variety of events with a chic wine store in the basement. Smaller menu available in the attractive beer garden.

name: Zum Vaas
review: It is always a delight to visit a warm, lively and informal restaurant such as this one. The dedicated kitchen team prepares food for two menus (the "Klassiker" and the "Heuer") and the food is flavoursome and reasonably priced, with dishes such as beef bourguignon, root vegetables and cheese spätzle on the menu. A wine list featuring around 500 wines, mostly from the region, completes the picture. The hotel of the same name offers comfortable guestrooms.

name: Greifen-Post
review: The three dining rooms exude historical flair and cosiness. The cuisine is seasonal and uses many regional ingredients. Order à la carte or opt for the set menu and tuck into the tasty food – or you might like to try the surprise menu with wine pairings? Hotel guests can choose between lovely styles of guestroom: Renaissance, Romantic, Biedermeier or country house.

name: Kamin- und Bauernstube
review: Attentive service guaranteed, whichever space you are seated in: the rustic-style Bauernstube, the elegant fireside Kaminstube or out on the wonderful spacious terrace. Pair the tasty regional and international food with your choice from the select wine list of the resort's fine dining restaurant. On weekdays, be sure to try the set menu ("Menü der Woche").

name: die burg
review: In the centre of a small village, the Grom brothers run this restaurant with an inviting, chic interior design. The ambitious cuisine puts a modern spin on classical foundations. Opt for a set menu (vegetarian version available) or order from the classics à la carte. Weinbaar serves bar food and burgers in the evening. The hotel has convenient modern guestrooms.

name: Gasthof Brink
review: A place with charm! The traditional style that is cultivated here will evoke childhood memories for many diners. Family-run since 1880, the restaurant serves classic French cuisine that is down to earth and delicious. The pleasant setting has an elegant feel. The house-made pâtés and terrines are just as popular as the saddle of veal with Béarnaise sauce or the sole meunière.

name: Zum Kreuz
review: A father-and-son team look after the guests here. They serve modern fare, as well as traditional dishes such as veal escalope in cream sauce and cheese spätzle. You can opt for the ‘Genuss’ set menu or order à la carte. Try the Black Forest beef ribs and cheeks with black salsify, leeks, cabbage, spätzle and goat’s cheese.

name: LAMM
review: A really cosy place, where you will also eat very well: seasonal Swabian-Baden cuisine, with an emphasis on regional produce; some of the meat comes from the restaurant's own highland cattle. There are good wines to accompany your meal, as well as a special whisky offer. In summer, try and bag a spot on the terrace. Pleasant guestrooms also available.

name: Gasthaus Weißenbeck
review: You will find plenty of satisfied customers here, and no wonder! The mother and daughter Weissenbeck team cook up a storm using regional and seasonal produce – and the prices are fair. The lovely inn also makes for a cosy setting, and in summer the delightful garden terrace is most inviting.

name: Lamm
review: A modern ambience, a pleasantly informal atmosphere and the warmth of a traditional inn go hand in hand here. The menu whets your appetite with an interesting array of regional and international dishes. The set menus, which include a vegan one, are also excellent. A much sought-after place – for weekends you should book early!

name: Eggers
review: The motto may be "in plain German, with international influences" but Westphalian regional produce is clearly the focus in the kitchen. The dining space is inviting and there is also a lovely terrace. The "Hobby Room" is used for parties, cookery classes and the Sunday brunch "Müffet" (a mix of set menu and buffet). Quality, modern guestrooms are available.

name: Gasthof Blumenthal
review: A family business in its fifth generation and a Franconian inn just as we like them! The restaurant boasts a cosy interior and a glorious terrace. Enjoy the charming informal service in a relaxed atmosphere. Choose from a range of fuss-free and tasty regional dishes, including traditional favourites, all made with good ingredients.

name: GERHARDS GENUSSGESELLSCHAFT
review: Not far from the Deutsches Eck, a spit of land formed at the confluence of the Rhine and Moselle rivers, the historic Blumenhof lies behind ancient walls. Here too you will find the entrance to this modern, minimalist-style restaurant with its lovely vaulted ceiling. Sample the seasonal, regional cuisine inside or outside on the magnificent terrace. Try the braised beef cheeks with mashed potato.

name: Elefanten
review: In the heart of this charming town is this welcoming inn, which is run with great dedication by the Glässing family – now in its fourth generation at the helm.
