The classic, regional cuisine makes full use of what each season has to offer, often drawing on regional produce to conjure up flavoursome dishes. You might choose to pair your food with one of the locally produced wines on offer.

name: Zur Glocke
review: The Stoiber family have put their heart and soul into running this trendy, modern restaurant. This is particularly evident in the excellent cuisine, which evolves with the seasons and draws on quality ingredients. For overnight stays, opt for the classic rooms in the main building or designer rooms in the smart new building.

name: Melkhus
review: The former cowshed of this beautifully renovated historical Immenhof estate houses this charming alternative to the Rodesand restaurant. The food is fresh, seasonal and made using regional ingredients. A reduced classics menu is served from 3-6pm, as is coffee and cake. The terrace boasts a view of the lake, Kellersee. Pick up some home-made jam, souvenirs etc at the farm shop.

name: ROSE
review: The Tress family is all about organic and following the principle of nose to tail eating. The food is regional and seasonal, with vegetarian options too, and the wines are exclusively Demeter certified. The establishment includes a shop selling cookbooks, soups, stews, pasta etc. Should you wish to stay over, there is a guesthouse opposite.

name: Dorf-Chronik
review: This fine winegrower's house dating from 1747 stands in the centre of the town. Sandstone and half-timbering create a cosy atmosphere, while decorative pictures add a touch of modern flair. Charming courtyard terrace. Diners can expect delicious regional and seasonal cuisine, as well as friendly service from Marion Schwaab and her team. Head to the vinotheque to sample wines from the property.

name: Gaststube Zum Klosterbräu
review: This is how you imagine a historical Bavarian restaurant: wooden beams on the ceiling, floorboards, tiled stove – rustic, inviting and wonderfully cosy (or "zünftig" as they say in these parts). There is also a wonderful terrace. The cuisine is classic, regional and seasonal – served à la carte or in three set menus, one of which is vegetarian. There is a good selection of wines to choose from. Tip: Visit the Baroque Münster Heilig Kreuz in Bergen.

name: Chez Georges
review: Looking for a place where you will not only eat really well, but also enjoy friendly service in a smart setting? Here you can try regional classics and seasonal dishes from Baden and Alsace. The Kächele wine tavern has a more relaxed ambience. You can spend the night in the Schwarzwälder Hof hotel.

name: Gasthaus Ödenturm
review: As if straight out of a picture book, this beautiful inn stands on the edge of the forest. Diners can look forward to a friendly, family atmosphere and great food, which can also be enjoyed out on the delightful terrace. The dishes on the menu range from regional to Mediterranean. Whether you order steak, fish or local game, there is something for everyone. Modern yet cosy guestrooms for overnight stays.

name: Altdeutsches Restaurant
review: Florian Kellerbauer divides his menu into two sections "Unsere Heimat" and "Unsere Leidenschaft" (Our Homeland and Our Passion), in each the emphasis is on the quality of the ingredients. The service is friendly and charming. Thanks to its location in the historical centre, you can sit on the terrace in the heart of the action. The Deutsches Haus hotel, a patrician house from 1440, has comfortable guestrooms.

name: Speisemeisterei Burgthalschenke
review: The Großhammer family has been renowned for its good cooking for years! Diners can choose between the set menu or classic dishes. The cuisine follows the seasons, with ingredients being sourced in the local area. Laid out over three levels, the restaurant also has a lovely terrace. On a practical note: large car park.

name: Landhaus Tanner
review: The Tanner family wows its guests with a wonderfully warm and cosy atmosphere. This applies both to the chic and modern Alpine-style guestrooms and to the elegant restaurant, where you'll be served delicacies such as veal lights with bread dumplings, or roasted pike perch with Bavarian asparagus and a lovage-hollandaise sauce. Service runs continuously from 12. 30-9pm.

name: Gärtnerei
review: This chic restaurant located almost directly on a strip of restaurants in Berlin-Mitte serves up modern, tasty and fresh food. On the menu you will find plenty of vegetarian dishes. The wines are predominantly Austrian – the owner is from Styria. The interior is refined and, in keeping with the horticulture-inspired name, plants and floral motifs decorate the walls.

name: Schloss Niederweis
review: In the converted granary of this 18C castle, classic seasonal cuisine is served. You will be looked after in a friendly manner in an attractive modern ambience – the high historical roof timbering is eye-catching. In addition to a charming garden, there is a lovely ballroom and a registry office. On a practical note: easy parking.

name: Ponyhof
review: The sort of restaurant you would love to have in your own neighbourhood, thanks to its excellent cuisine. The next generation has now taken over the management of this long-standing family business. The kitchen serves modern dishes, but also classics such as cordon bleu and “dry aged” beef from the charcoal grill.

name: Freihardt
review: Eating here really is a pleasure! The cuisine is international and seasonal, the highlight being the Bavarian beef. A friendly atmosphere reigns in the restaurant and its conservatory, and the terrace on the busy street is a place "to see and be seen". Right next door is the restaurant's own butcher's shop, which has for many years employed so-called humane slaughtering methods.

name: Almer Schlossmühle
review: This carefully converted old mill next to the little Schloss Alme is a highly appealing restaurant that abounds with rustic charm. The delicious food features seasonal dishes from the regional repertoire as well as classic fare from the chef's native Austria. Head for the lovely terrace in fine weather. There are also guestrooms for an overnight stay.

name: Zum Falken
review: You can be sure of a warm welcome at Zum Falken with its old oak beams, lovely wooden floors and traditional rustic chairs and benches. Try the fresh Bratwurst sausage, which are served on Thursdays and Fridays, and the homemade fruit brandies. Function room in the old barn and wine tastings in the vaulted cellar.

name: Im Kittchen
review: This small restaurant is located in the middle of the old town, in a side street near the Eiermarkt. Both the charming interior and the appealing and varied selection of dishes make a good impression, as does the friendly owner, who is in charge of the service. Tip for overnight stays: the Michel Mort hotel right next door.

name: Villa Esche
review: Built in 1903 as an orangery in the grounds of a villa belonging to a textile manufacturer (which now houses the interesting Henry van de Velde Museum). Villa Esche is a friendly, modern restaurant serving tasty, seasonal dishes such as braised rump of beef with parmesan polenta and tomatoes. Try one of the tables outside in the lovely garden.

name: Renoir
review: "Classic" is the watchword here – when it comes to the food, as well as the tasteful, down-to-earth interior design. You can count on the wine pairings recommended to go with the tasty dishes made from good produce, as the chef is also a trained sommelier. Be sure to visit the small gallery in the building.

name: Anne-Sophie
review: We recommend getting a table in the light and airy winter garden: here you have beautiful views over the garden! The food is tasty and seasonal, with classics such as braised veal cheeks also proving popular. At lunchtime there is a reduced menu as well as inexpensive daily specials. The restaurant is located on the Schlossplatz, some 150m from the main hotel building.

name: Weinstube Brand
review: Weinstube Brand is everything you could wish for in a wine bar: comfortable and unpretentious with relaxed but efficient service. Eva-Maria Knefler looks after guests front of house while her husband Christian works in the kitchen. Try the delicious braised shoulder of beef and one of the sophisticated desserts that include mango mousse with mandarin and tarragon sorbet.

name: Vier Jahreszeiten Restaurant Imhof
review: You will certainly eat well at Andreas Imhof's restaurant. The cuisine is regional and uses ingredients selected with seasonality in mind. Dishes made with Allgäu heifer, for example, are popular. The interior of this friendly place is bright, refined and modern; outside, the beer garden is presided over by an impressive lime tree.

name: Anetseder
review: Traditional German public house culture is alive and well here, and at the same time they tap into the zeitgeist. The lovely dining space has a high ceiling and a trendy, modern feel and the waitstaff are friendly. They serve fresh and tasty food, with seasonal ingredients, preferably from the region, taking pride of place.

name: Joseph Naus Stub'n
review: This comfortable rustic-style restaurant (named after the first climber to reach the top of the Zugspitze) is not just an attractive place where you are looked after by very friendly staff; the food is also really good and fairly priced. For overnight stays the Hotel Zugspitze has well-kept guestrooms done out in a country-house style.

name: Seehaus
review: This is a gorgeous spot at any time of the day. In the summer, the terrace overlooking the lake is perfect for a relaxed lunch or afternoon cake, and in the evening, you'll be just as happy to sit inside – there's something romantic about this charming restaurant done out in warm rustic wood. They also serve fantastic modern and international cuisine. Tip: try the homemade pannacotta for dessert!

name: Brasserie Colette Tim Raue
review: A big name on the Berlin fine dining scene, Tim Raue has created a pleasantly down-to-earth brasserie of the sort you would normally expect to find in Paris. This place has a modern feel but exudes a slight touch of nostalgia too. The food here is excellent, and fans of classic cuisine will certainly find what they are looking for on the appealing menu. In the evening, you can also opt for the "Tim Raue Menü" or the seasonal set menu that changes every month. Lunch tip: "La table dressée".

name: Heinzler
review: Whether in the Jagdstube, in the Panorama Restaurant or on the great terrace (almost at the water's edge), here at the Heinzler brothers' you can look forward to good seasonal fare. For example: smoked fillet of Bodensee whitefish on a beetroot salad with horseradish mousse and potato pancake, or duo of veal in a peppercorn sauce with Brussels sprouts and fried potatoes.

name: Bistro
review: It's no wonder the lovely Bistro in this attractive old building draws the crowds: here the straightforward dishes are packed with flavour! The owner is in charge of the service, running the show with professionalism and genuine warmth. The small terrace with a view of the church and Marktplatz is also very attractive.

name: Tausendgüldenstube
review: The Hotel Blauer Engel offers not only lovely guestrooms, but also this restaurant. With its 340 years of tradition, it exudes historical charm! The tiled stove and wood panelling make for a cosy atmosphere. The service is personal and the food is very good, for instance the char in Riesling sauce. The terrace of the in-house brewery, Lotters Wirtschaft, is very popular.

name: Habbel's
review: Habbel’s offers a fine-dining experience beyond compare. International dishes such as tuna carpaccio coated in wasabi-sesame seeds and saddle of lamb in thyme foam with grilled vegetables feature on the menu, while the wine list offers around 1, 000 wines and spirits from the Habbel in-house distillery, including a 1977-vintage whisky!

name: Krietsch
review: This place used to be called Fuggerei – its name may have changed but it continues to be a great restaurant. At Krietsch, the cuisine is seasonal with a connection to the region, but it also draws on international influences. At lunchtime there are daily specials. Diners can sit inside, beneath the period vaulted ceiling, or out on the gorgeous terrace. Great location for a visit to the cathedral, which is just to the rear of the restaurant.

name: Geberts Weinstuben
review: Freshness, flavour, aroma – this is how you might sum up Frank Gebert's cuisine. He also likes to use produce from the region to create his classic dishes. The restaurant, located in a side street not far from the Rhine, is furnished with a touch of elegance; outside, meanwhile, it is pleasant to sit in the courtyard on the vine-clad terrace.

name: Wirtsstube im Hotel Burkhard
review: In the second restaurant of the hotel Landgasthof Burkhard, the cuisine is somewhat simpler, which does not detract from the quality. Dishes range from cordon bleu to sea bream with lemon. The dining areas are cosy and prettily done out – you can choose to enjoy your meal in the Wirtsstube or the Esszimmer. The inner courtyard terrace, which is shared with the Kaminstube, is also very appealing.

name: Seehof
review: Boasting a lovely lakeside location on the marina, this restaurant offers a popular terrace as well as its “Badische Weinstube” and panoramic “Alois” dining rooms. Flavourful and classic artisan dishes feature on the menu, including Salemer lamb’s liver with a quince and balsamic vinegar jus and European perch with chanterelle mushrooms. Accommodation is also available – the “boathouse” and rooms with views are particularly recommended.

name: Torschänke
review: Right next to the Obertor (the historical city gate), Torschänke is a really inviting restaurant. The atmosphere inside is cosy and pleasingly down to earth, and outside there is a lovely, leafy terrace. Dishes with French and Mediterranean influences are prepared using top-notch fresh produce and served by a friendly, attentive and proficient front-of-house team.

name: Talblick
review: Claus Weitbrecht is an expert in his field, having learned his trade in some of Germany's top establishments. His elaborate cuisine, including vegetarian dishes, is replete with flavour. No wonder this place is so popular! If you want to opt for the "Gourmet Menu", order in advance. There are pleasant guestrooms in the hotel, should you wish to stay overnight.

name: Schäck's Adler
review: Like something out of a picture book, Schäck’s Adler is warm and welcoming, its ambitious, flavoursome cuisine served in wood-panelled dining rooms. Menu options include zander dumplings in Riesling sauce and Elztal venison ragout with spätzle. You’ll also find the attractive Strumbel Bar and a number of beautifully kept overnight rooms.

name: Zum Dückerstieg
review: An attractive, cosy restaurant with rural flair which serves seasonal and regional cuisine. Here, you can look forward to flavoursome dishes that pack a punch. The delicious options on offer include salmon, North Sea prawns, sea bass, suckling pig and game. Steeped in tradition, this family-run business – now in its fourth generation – also has attractive, comfortable guestrooms for overnight stays.

name: Feilmeiers Landleben
review: This cosy and modern restaurant knows how to makes diners feel welcome. For Johann (who goes by Hans) Feilmeier, his "country life" cooking reflects both a love of his native region and a sense of duty. He cooks regionally and seasonally inspired food. Choose from one of the different set menus or order à la carte. Tip: the home-made jams!

name: Diergardts Kühler Grund
review: This excellent family business is now run by the fourth generation. Since taking over the reins, Philipp Diergardt has upped the ante – not least thanks to his first-class training –, at a restaurant which was already operating at a high level. He pours passion into his upscale bourgeois dishes, e.g. the pan-fried young piglet blood sausage. Then there is the tasteful country house ambience and attentive service.

name: Krone
review: Krone has been properly invested in: from the façade to the hotel rooms, everything is chic and high quality, the restaurant is modern and sleek. The food is very good, with select produce turned into aromatic dishes with plenty of flavour. At lunchtime, a smaller range of interesting options. If you are staying longer, Basel and Alsace are very close by.

name: Landhaus Lebert
review: In a small town about 10km from Rothenburg ob der Tauber, this cosy restaurant serves really flavoursome cuisine made from good-quality regional produce – importance is attached to sustainability. In summer, there is a lovely beer garden. Well-kept guestrooms for overnight stays, and a barn for private events. Tip: In the old shepherd's caravan, you can buy products made on site, such as lemon liqueur, spice mixtures, jellies and jams.

name: Landhotel Krone
review: Here, tradition rubs shoulders with current trends in cosy little spaces that feature an attractive blend of old brickwork, wood, steel and glass. The regional and seasonal cuisine is scattered with international influences. Daily 2-5pm snack menu. Medieval vaulted cellar for events. This family-run business also offers attractive, individually designed guestrooms and wellness facilities.

name: Rössle
review: This family-run restaurant serves fresh, flavoursome dishes made with choice produce. Their fantastic steaks and Black Forest trout from Oberprechtal go down a treat, as does the intriguing surprise set menu. To round off the experience, attentive service staff, a friendly atmosphere and a delightful terrace. The attractive guestrooms combine warm wood and sleek design.

name: Lucky Leek
review: Vegan, fresh, seasonal and with a personal touch – that's what this charming restaurant is all about. The tasty dishes are available as a three- to five-course set menu, with wine pairings, if desired. The pleasantly refined atmosphere is also a fitting backdrop for relishing the great food. (N.B. cash payment only up to €100.)

name: Gasthaus
review: Like the gourmet restaurant, Gasthaus also combines modernity and tradition, from the decor down to the menu. While things are a bit more casual here, the cooking is also really good – the quality of the sauces alone will convince you of that! You can put together your own menu – and even make it vegetarian. Friendly service.

name: Bar Mural
review: This hip bar is loud, lively and trendy – therein lies its charm! The short menu features various cold cut platters, as well as a selection of tasty and carefully thought-out dishes, which are also served as a set menu – a vegetarian version is available, too. For advice on what to drink, just ask the laid-back, well-drilled service team.

name: Lindenhof
review: Like their hotel, with its cosy individually designed guestrooms, the Hankhs' restaurant is also very popular. This is down to the excellent seasonal cuisine, which has regional and Mediterranean influences. You can order à la carte or opt for a set menu (vegetarian version available). Friendly and competent waitstaff. The small terraces in front of and to the rear of the building are delightful.

name: Weinhaus Anker
review: A restaurant that is steeped in tradition and run with great commitment. The lovely interior exudes a historical charm in which to enjoy French and regional dishes, and the service is friendly – hostess Elisabeth Deppisch is also a sommelière. In the winter, on Thu-Sat evenings, a short Franconian menu is served in the rustic vaulted Schöpple. You can also stay overnight in well-kept guestrooms.

name: Landhaus Hohenlohe
review: The interior at Hohenlohe comes in two styles: cosy and rustic or casually elegant. Matthias Mack’s cuisine is also a mix, offering Mediterranean dishes such as saddle of lamb in a Provençal garlic crust with pimento cream and baked saffron risotto alongside classics such as pan-fried beef steak and onions. The service is friendly and the restaurant also offers a few well-kept guestrooms.

name: Chicha
review: Bustling, loud, rustic, and just a touch “shabby”... Chicha has succeeded in creating an informal authentically South American atmosphere to complement its modern Peruvian cooking. Quality fresh products are ambitiously blended to mouthwatering effect, with dishes such as ceviche of meagre fish and Thüringer Duroc belly of pork with smoked banana featuring on the menu.

name: Beesten
review: Since 1906, over four generations, the Beesten family has put its heart and soul into running this traditional inn in the heart of Rheine. The owner himself is at the helm in the kitchen, preparing classic French and German cuisine peppered with seasonal influences. The interior is elegant and tasteful, while the service is charming. Take a seat on the terrace under the lovely old chestnut trees.

name: Die Halde
review: Situated at an altitude of 1 147m, this stylish restaurant successfully bridges the gap between history and modernity! The food is served in cosy traditional dining rooms, where guests are looked after by friendly, well-trained staff. Local produce is favoured, and the water comes from the house's mountain spring. There are also lovely guestrooms done out in a modern, regional style.

name: Gasthaus Sternen Post
review: This beautifully restored 1875 restaurant is a fine example of the dedication of its owner. Diners sit in comfortable rooms complete with tiled ovens to sample delicious dishes such as venison stew with spaetzle (a Swabian pasta speciality) and red cabbage or apple fritters with vanilla sauce. Overnight accommodation comes in the form of lovely country house-style rooms.

name: möbius
review: Leipzig-born Tommy R Möbius, a familiar face among the top chefs on the scene, runs this restaurant, which is also known as "lebensmittel.punkt". The concept here is rather novel: you can either choose fresh dishes from a very short menu to eat in, or treat yourself to delicacies to enjoy at home. Open Tue-Wed 11.30am-6pm, Thu-Fri 10am-6.30pm and Sat 10am-3pm.

name: bistronauten
review: A word to the wise: make sure you book, as this really appealing restaurant is always busy! Housed in an old railway station dating from 1903, the atmosphere is laid-back, the decor modern with industrial charm and the food excellent. On the blackboard there is a seasonal set menu – choose between meat, fish and vegetarian for the main course. They also have a selection of German wines. Dine at the counter to watch the chefs at work in the open kitchen.

name: Gasthaus Assenmacher
review: It's clear that Christian and Christa Storch put their heart and soul into running this place. The chef-patron wins over diners with his modern take on classic cuisine. Eschewing any gimmickry, he lays the focus squarely on quality produce and flavour. The lady of the house manages the friendly and attentive waitstaff. Pleasant little terrace to the rear of the building. Decent accommodation options at the hotel.

name: Schorse im Leineschloss
review: This pleasantly uncomplicated restaurant is the second in the cube-like extension of the Leineschloss, alongside Votum. The restaurant skilfully combines down-to-earth and modern, the cuisine has an international bent, but also regional influences. It's delightful to sit on the terrace by the Leinewehr or on the Platz der Göttinger Sieben. Coffee and cake in the afternoon.

name: Kuro Mori
review: "Kuro Mori" is Japanese and means "black forest", corresponding to the motto in the stylish restaurant of star chef Steffen Disch from Horben: “The Black Forest meets Asia”. The interesting and unusual cuisine ranges from sweet chilli pork to sweet curd cheese dumplings. The restaurant enjoys an attractive location in Freiburg’s Old Town.

name: Ostiner Stub'n
review: This typical regional inn sets great store by its regional ingredients. The menu is in constant rotation and devised in line with the seasons. There is also a set menu complete with wine pairings, which is popular with diners, and the service is attentive. In summer, the lovely terrace overlooking the garden is very popular.

name: Zur Krone
review: The dining rooms in this pretty 18C inn propose a pleasant setting in which to enjoy the good food, namely classic seasonal dishes such as game consommé with venison and porcini ravioli and vegetable "pearls" or Arctic char filet with aromatic garden herb sauce, kohlrabi and potatoes tossed in butter. You can also stay overnight here in well-kept guestrooms.

name: Schimmel's
review: This restaurant's striking red façade is sure to catch your eye, while inside you can expect a modern and stylish setting and a welcoming atmosphere. The open kitchen serves fresh and aromatic dishes prepared using plenty of regional ingredients to diners seated at beautiful wooden tables. The chef is friendly and attentive. They also offer pretty guestrooms and holiday flats.

name: Wirtshaus zur Sonne
review: This restaurant has been in the same family for over 300 years. Diners can sit inside in the wonderful, wood-panelled dining room or outside on the pretty garden terrace to enjoy the flavoursome fare. This includes tafelspitz (boiled topside of beef) galantine with radish carpaccio or pan-fried skrei cod with tomatoes and herbs.

name: Gasthof Schütte
review: This region, which is a popular destination for hiking and cycling enthusiasts, is home to this traditional family-run country hotel with its own spa facilities and lovely restaurant. There are regional, classic and international dishes on the menu, which is somewhat more limited at lunchtime. In winter, an open fireplace adds to the charming atmosphere.

name: Berggasthof Schlüssel
review: This mountain inn dating back over a hundred years is located at an altitude of 700m in the district of Pfaffenberg. Your dedicated hosts propose regional dishes that are in tune with the seasons and peppered with modern touches, to be savoured in cosy dining rooms with plenty of rustic charm. If you fancy a bottle of wine with your meal, why not stay over in the well-kept guestrooms?

name: Stumpenhof
review: Diners are in such good hands here that they can't help but enjoy themselves! The waitstaff are exceptionally friendly, while the owner herself, who radiates good humour, is always ready to cater to her guests' needs. On the menu: plenty of the classics of Swabian cuisine, such as tripe soup or creamy veal goulash (which is best enjoyed with the home-made spätzle).

name: Wirtschaft von Johann Gerner
review: The journey out here to the countryside is well worth it, because Detlef Gerner and his wife Tanja live and breathe hospitality par excellence in their cosy restaurant. The hand-written menu features flavoursome dishes based on seasonal and predominantly regional produce – incidentally, they bake their own bread. In summer, you can sit on the terrace out front. Overnight accommodation in the pretty "Häusla" (for two to seven people).

name: Kaltwassers Wohnzimmer
review: Wohnzimmer offers a cosy "living room" feel with some charming nostalgic touches inside and a designer atrium with view of the glazed kitchens in the interior courtyard. The modern regional cuisine uses fresh quality produce and includes dishes such as Wels catfish served with mashed potatoes and apples, kohlrabi and Ahle Worscht sausage.

name: Moarwirt
review: Here at the Bio-Landhotel Moarwirt, the excellent food is made out of primarily organic ingredients – indeed, the place has Naturland and Slow Food certification. The modern Alpine-style dining rooms are very pretty; in summer the terrace is a real hit. You can also stay overnight comfortably. N.B. weekly closures vary out of season.

name: Scheidels Restaurant zum Kranz
review: Conscious of their long family history (the restaurant is now run by the seventh generation), the owners here are committed to maintaining their traditions yet the food remains resolutely down-to-earth. Charming historic ambience, plus warm and welcoming staff. Simple, tasty dishes take pride of place, inspired by regional and seasonal produce. A vegetarian menu is also available.

name: Margaretenhof
review: This former farmhouse boasts a truly idyllic location. Inside, there are lovingly decorated rooms; outside, a wonderful garden terrace. Then there are your dedicated hosts and the excellent cuisine that ranges from regional to Asian, including sushi. Late Oct-Mar: "Wine & Dine" set menu on Friday evenings by reservation only. Try the afternoon tea (Sun and public holidays, 2-4.30pm).

name: Dutters Stube
review: The fourth generation of the Dutter family is now running this charming 16C inn. The seasonal and regional cuisine is a hit – the set menu being a popular choice with diners. The Dorfwirtschaft serves simpler fare, such as snacks, flammkuchen and rump steak. As an alternative to the terrace, there is the pretty summerhouse. Chef Arthur Dutter is a member of the charitable club known as "German Football Chefs".

name: Adler
review: Swabian tradition is at the fore here, but there are also forays into international cuisine. Classic dishes are ambitiously transformed and presented in a modern way; the ingredients are first rate. The restaurant is furnished to a high standard, remarkably well maintained and, with its regional charm, extremely cosy. You can also sit beneath the trees in the inner courtyard.

name: TISK
review: Situated in a quiet side street of Neukölln, TISK (old German for table) calls itself a Speisekneipe (food pub) – and the description works well. It offers a young, urban ambience and modern German cuisine with pepped-up flavours. Options include set menus (e. g. with meatballs or knuckle of lamb) and roast chicken for two people.

name: Oechsle
review: This friendly and contemporary corner restaurant serves up delicious food that is made using fresh, high-quality produce and also seeks inspiration in the south of Germany and Austria. The short wine list is reasonably priced. In summer you can take a seat at one of the tables out front on the street.

name: das asam
review: The hotel and restaurant have been integrated into a centuries-old monastery complex complete with a brewery. On the first floor you can dine under a lovely high ceiling with moulding and paintings – an attractive mix of clean lines and a historical setting. There are modern regional dishes such as Zachenberg lamb two ways with beluga lentils, pear compote and a spicy jus.

name: WEINreich
review: Situated right in the centre of a pretty little wine village, this is a wine bar with a difference. Purism and a modern spirit define the cuisine here which boasts influences from further afield than the local Palatine region. Dishes include Palatine pickled trout with sweet-sour pumpkin and rösti, and delicious curd-cheese dumplings for dessert. Charming, individual guestrooms also available.

name: Café Rapp
review: Originally a bakery and café, the family business is now also a restaurant, where quality, flavour and price are spot on. The emphasis is on regional and seasonal products – vegetables and meat are sourced from the village, herbs are grown in the kitchen garden. A must in the afternoon: the delicious fresh cakes! Pretty guestrooms.

name: Zum Goldenen Engel
review: The 500-year history of this restaurant is reflected in the pretty wooden façade and the country-style charm of the interior, which provides the perfect setting for its regional cuisine. Try the onion-crusted sirloin and in season, the goose is also excellent. Comfortable guest rooms are available for overnight stays – some are decorated in typical Black Forest-style, others are more contemporary.

name: Sennhütte
review: Whether you prefer good, home-style regional fare or something more modern, you’ll find it here at the Grether family’s restaurant. Menu options range from strips of calves’ liver in balsamic sauce with rösti to Arctic Ocean brown trout with marinated asparagus and miso mayonnaise. The unfussy food is fully flavoured and made using good, fresh produce.

name: Restaurant Corona im Hotel zur Post
review: It's a real treat to eat here! In this classic restaurant, Sergio and Kerstin Corona work as a well-coordinated team, providing charming service and Mediterranean-inspired cuisine. In addition to the "Méditerranée" and "Corona" set menus, from which you can also choose à la carte, there is also a bargain to be had in the three-course lunch menu.

name: Ramster
review: The chef at Ramster uses locally sourced products to create succulent dishes such as braised leg of Heidschnucken lamb or wild hare. These taste particularly good eaten on the lovely terrace overlooking the garden. If you fancy spending the night, the rooms, some of which have balconies, are comfortable and contemporary in style.

name: Feine Speiseschenke
review: This friendly restaurant is located in a small village in a quiet side valley surrounded by woods and meadows. It offers seasonal cuisine bearing regional and international influences. They even raise Scottish Highland cattle here. You can choose from various set menus (including a vegetarian one) or go à la carte and opt for one of the classic dishes.

name: Kleines Meer
review: Laid out over two levels, this convivial restaurant has exposed roof timbering that lends a pleasant airy atmosphere. Lake Müritz is just in front of the building, making the terrace with its small lounge area a popular spot with guests. Made from good-quality ingredients, the cuisine here is regional and seasonal; there are also vegetarian options. The hotel of the same name has well-kept guestrooms.

name: Bauernstuben
review: It's cosy and original here, lots of rustic wood and a lovely decoration! Diners sit at beautifully laid tables and enjoy friendly service. The seasonal regional cuisine is really tasty: game terrine, beef roulade, steaks matured on the premises... offal also features on the menu. In addition to the good food, you also have the option of staying in one of the lovely hotel rooms at Ochsen-Post.

name: DELI
review: Here you can enjoy a down-to-earth, relaxed atmosphere with interesting international and seasonal cuisine made from good-quality ingredients. If you’re just looking for light snacks, there is a small additional menu at lunchtime and in the evening (e.g. the “Deli-Box”). Attractive terrace with waterfall feature on Niagaraplatz, plus hooded beach chairs for relaxing.

name: Little John's
review: Little John’s is located in an attractive residential house dating back to 1905 and is decorated in Scandinavian style with a lively and almost intimate atmosphere. Your appetite is whetted as soon as you see the open kitchen in the entrance area – the food here is down-to-earth yet modern, using regional and seasonal produce. We recommend the mini set lunch at lunchtime. Please note: cash payments only!

name: Gasthof Berghof - Ursprung
review: Rustic wood matched with clean lines and fresh splashes of colour provide an ‘old meets new’ look at this restaurant. The decor is mirrored in Alexander Schütz’s excellent cooking, which comes both as an upmarket set menu or simply a hearty Bratwurst. The delicious food and reasonable prices make dining here a real pleasure.

name: Landgasthof Backers
review: The success of the Backers family restaurant (the fifth generation is now at the helm) is down to the snug ambience and, of course, the fresh and seasonal regional cuisine: the local venison and Diepholz geese are popular dishes. The restaurant is a long-standing Slow Food Alliance member. Try the "Backers zum Kennenlernen" four-course regional set menu with drinks and overnight stay.

name: Domschenke
review: This family-run restaurant is now in its third generation. Whether you sit in the rustic-style dining area with its regulars' table or in the pleasant conservatory, you are assured of friendly service. The menu features home-style, regional and more sophisticated dishes. Order à la carte or opt for one of the daily specials on the blackboard. In summer, make a beeline for the outdoor seating area, which is shaded by old trees.

name: Sommerau
review: The trip to the Hegar family's restaurant just outside Bonndorf is definitely worth it! Nestled in a quiet valley, surrounded by woods and meadows – the setting could not be more idyllic. There's an inviting terrace, but you can also enjoy the view from inside. The cuisine is regional and seasonal, made using top-notch ingredients. In the hotel of the same name, there are cosy, modern rooms and a beautiful sauna house, plus a natural swimming pond.

name: Gambero Rosso da Domenico
review: Domenico has been on his mission to showcase Italian cuisine in Franconia for well over 20 years, and has run this restaurant at the small marina with his wife, Teresa, since 2012. Here, they live and breathe hospitality, serving two set menus with dishes that can also be ordered à la carte. Astute wine recommendations come courtesy of the chef-patron himself. Gorgeous terrace overlooking the Main River.

name: Münstermanns Kontor
review: From the egg and butter trade to delicatessen and restaurant – this is the history of the Münstermann family business in a nutshell. In a pleasant setting, you can choose from bistro classics and international dishes, from steak frites to grilled salmon with curry cabbage and potato wasabi puree – uncomplicated, fresh and made with good ingredients.

name: Weinbistro
review: The second dining option in the Weinhaus Uhle is a wine shop and appealing restaurant in one. They are open all day long, from 12pm to 9pm, serving up tasty, uncomplicated dishes made with sustainably produced ingredients and organic produce. The nicely done out interior is also typical of the Weinhaus Uhle – sophisticated and exhibiting a certain flair. Excellent selection of wines.

name: Weinrestaurant Turmschänke
review: In this restaurant in the Nicolaiturm, the lovely historical details, such as paintings and original furniture dating from 1912, foster a rustic yet elegant feel. Enjoy seasonal dishes – served as a set menu or à la carte. Grilled dishes are also available. There are around 140 items on the wine list, which includes helpful hints. Special wine evenings are also organised here.

name: Gasthaus Widmann's Löwen
review: In the cosy interior here, they serve tasty regional and traditional dishes made from good, fresh ingredients. Try specialities such as the Ostalb lamb, for example, or classics like Maultaschen (German ravioli) or roast joint - the sauces are delicious, and luckily there are plenty of them! Don't miss the wonderful beer garden. There is also a nice playground.

name: Landgasthof Rebstock
review: In the heart of the wine village, the Keller family runs this cosy, rustic, centuries-old house, where the welcoming hosts offer fresh, seasonally inspired cuisine. They like to use ingredients from the region, but international influences can also be detected on the menu. The service is professional and very attentive. They also have guestrooms.

name: Weinhaus Zum Ritter
review: This converted 500-year-old farmhouse certainly has character. The many regulars come for the cosy atmosphere in the charming dining area (the old Swiss church window draws the eye), the cordial service and, of course, the fresh regional cuisine courtesy of chef-patron Thomas Hausin – his flavoursome dishes are clearly the work of a chef with experience at top-flight establishments! NB: different opening hours in summer.

name: schuberts
review: This town-centre restaurant right by the Lauter River offers a pleasant backdrop with a casual brasserie atmosphere for tasty regional and seasonal cuisine with Mediterranean influences. The cosy wine bar, Entennest, is also popular - the menu is the same here. If you would like to stay overnight, they also have lovely individually furnished guestrooms.

name: Gasthof zur Sonne
review: Set directly across from the Swiss border, Gasthof zur Sonne serves fresh, flavoursome cuisine with regional and Mediterranean influences in a country-style setting. Try the emmer risotto with Trollinger and grilled Calabrese salami or the duet of skrei and wild salmon in lemon sauce. The restaurant also offers three simple but beautifully kept guestrooms.

name: [maki:'dan] im Ritter
review: This exceedingly cosy and tastefully decorated restaurant is housed in the historical part of the Hotel Ritter. Here you can experience their special take on mezze dining in the evening. Rather than the standard order of courses, diners are treated to modern dishes served up in smaller portions – it's all about mixing and tasting!

name: Heim's Restaurant
review: In this approximately 300 year-old building, you can enjoy fresh seasonal cuisine in a tasteful setting. Each of the regional dishes can be paired with the perfect Moselle wine. Opt for the seats next to the windows with views over the vineyards and the Moselle. Kitchen opening hours: 12-9pm. Nice guestrooms in the Reiler Hof.

name: Mühle zu Gersbach
review: Guests lap up the charmingly informal service and tasty seasonal fare provided by the Buchleither familiy. The traditional classics you might expect sit alongside vegetarian dishes with a more international feel, which can be supplemented with meat or fish. You can also spend the night in this quiet village location.

name: Löwen
review: You’ll now find the fourth generation at the helm here, serving regional and international food with a seasonal bent based on good-quality, fresh produce. Try a plate of pan-fried whitefish fillet with herb mayonnaise, asparagus and carrots in the cosy restaurant or on the secluded terrace under the sweet chestnut trees.

name: Schneider
review: This restaurant has been run by the same family ever since it first opened in 1884. Stefan Püngeler now represents the youngest generation at the helm, putting the emphasis on good seasonal produce. Stick to the classics, or opt for the gourmet set menu. The wine list focuses on labels from the region. Accommodation is available in the small Sonnenhof hotel in the neighbouring village. For hikers, Dernbacher Haus on the edge of the forest is perfect for a pit stop.

name: Gasthaus Hofmann
review: The food on offer at Gasthaus Hofmann is seasonal and regional, the produce fresh, and in some cases homegrown. It is just this combination that attracts the many regulars to the friendly, rustic atmosphere of this country inn. Try the roast pork with crackling, potato dumplings and kohlrabi or the Kleinlangheim chicken. Guests from further afield may like to spend the night in one of the comfortable guestrooms.

name: Brasserie Colette Tim Raue
review: Tim Raue has his finger on the pulse with the concept behind this place: you could almost be in a French brasserie, what with the friendly and pleasantly informal atmosphere, and the really good, tasty food, such as chicken in puff pastry with truffle jus and Jerusalem artichoke. High-quality produce goes without saying.

name: Schwingshackl HEIMATKÜCHE
review: The second restaurant of Mr and Mrs Schwingshackl is also worth a visit. They use selected seasonal produce to cook dishes with a great deal of flavour, and diners get value for their money. The menu also includes dishes from the chef's homeland of South Tyrol. The terrace overlooking the Isar River is wonderful in summer!

name: Cervus
review: Centrally located, just a stone's throw from the train station, this lovely inn has also proved to be a hit with locals. A simple and fuss-free setting in which to enjoy the decidedly fresh and tasty food prepared in the open kitchen. In addition to more ambitious fare, classics such as schnitzel or roast beef also go down well with diners. Simpler and shorter lunchtime menu. Charming inner courtyard.

name: Adler
review: Ambitious, fresh and unfussy are the terms that best describe the mixture of regional and international cuisine offered by Uwe Zöller at this slightly out-of-town restaurant. Front of house, friendly Anne-Kathrin Zöller serves a range of dishes including scallops with Thai curry, and duo of lamb on a bed of wild garlic pesto with Barolo jus.

name: Carnozet
review: Tastefully done out in a modern take on Alpine style, this restaurant provides both excellent food and friendly service. The menu features an appealing selection of dishes, mostly made from locally sourced produce. There are also fantastic daily specials and, with any luck, you might get to try the "Beuscherl mit Serviettenknödel" – an offal dish with bread dumplings!

name: Terrone
review: Having started life a short 'pop up' down the road, Terrone is now settled in a waterfront residency within the walls of Fort St Angelo – and a spot on the terrace here is a must. Carefully prepared Maltese and Southern Italian influenced dishes burst with freshness; the Maltese lemon tart is a speciality.

name: Aldridge Lodge
review: This attractive house is set in a great rural location and run by cheery owners. The constantly evolving menu offers tasty homemade bread and veg from the kitchen garden. The focus is on good value fish and shellfish (the owner’s father is a local fisherman), with some Asian and fusion influences. Homely bedrooms come with hot water bottles and home-baked cookies.

name: Everett's
review: This proudly run, welcoming bistro is set in the heart of the city and dates from the 15C; sit on the ground floor with its barrel-fronted bar or in the intimate vaulted brick cellar. Modern menus showcase the best of the Irish larder and generously-sized dishes are assured, refined and full of flavour.

name: Land to Sea
review: The name sums it up perfectly, as the chef uses produce from the surrounding fields and nearby waters to full advantage. Local meats and wonderfully fresh fish and shellfish are prepared with care and a good understanding of flavours. If the crab salad is on the menu, be sure to choose it.

name: Cush
review: Family owned and run, Cush consists of a smart, modern restaurant, a traditional pub and comfy bedrooms; with views out over the rooftops to the fishing boats in the harbour. Local produce features in hearty dishes, with seafood naturally to the fore, and guests are well looked after by the friendly team.

name: Kai
review: A café by day and a laid-back restaurant in the evening, Kai (Maori for ‘food’), is run with real passion and has a gloriously cluttered, bohemian feel. Morning coffee and cakes morph into simple lunches and tasty dinners. Concise menus list vibrant dishes and produce is organic, free range and traceable.

name: Spitalfields
review: Set in a historic area of this city is this fittingly traditional-looking Irish pub, where the charming staff offer a warm and friendly welcome. It’s deservedly busy – drinkers are welcome but most are here for the food. Enticing dishes are fresh, flavoursome and great value, with the likes of oxtail and bone marrow Parker House rolls.

name: Pichet
review: You can’t miss the red signs and striped canopies of this buzzy brasserie – and its checkerboard flooring makes it equally striking inside. Enjoy snacks at the bar or classic French dishes in the main room; the parmesan agnolotti is a must-try. A good selection of wines are available by the glass or pichet.

name: Bell Inn
review: The Bell Inn’s rustic charm is hard to resist with its cosy bar, impressive inglenook fireplace and 16C origins. The large menu offers everything from a homemade burger to a muntjac, cep and bacon pie, and the wood-fired garlic, parsley and bone marrow flatbread is a must. Bedrooms are nicely furnished.

name: Kentish Hare
review: Behind the clapboard façade sits a spacious bar with bookshelf wallpaper and a modern extension where you can watch the chefs cooking steaks on two Big Green Eggs. Care is taken both in sourcing and cooking, and dishes are boldly flavoured and well-presented. Simpler dishes are available on the bar menu.

name: Leaping Hare
review: Sit on the lovely terrace and enjoy refined, boldly flavoured dishes at this beautiful 17C barn, which sits in a charming spot at the centre of a 7 acre vineyard. Carefully judged cooking relies on well-sourced seasonal ingredients – many from their own farm – and they have an impressive sustainability ethos.

name: Gunton Arms
review: This charming inn overlooks the 1,000 acre Gunton Estate deer park. Enjoy a tasty homemade snack over a game of pool or darts in the bar or make for a gnarled wood table by the fireplace in the flag-floored Elk Room. Dishes are fiercely seasonal; some – such as the Aberdeen Angus steaks – are cooked over the fire. Well-equipped bedrooms have a stylish country house feel.

name: Swan Wine Kitchen
review: This rustic modern restaurant sits above the shop in the Chapel Down vineyard and boasts a cosy lounge and a lovely rooftop terrace with views over the vines; naturally, wines from the vineyard feature. Refined cooking is full of flavour and relies on just a few ingredients to do the talking.

name: Dastaan
review: Dastaan means ‘story’ and this simple neighbourhood restaurant is the story of two friends, Sanjay and Nand. Northern India leads the great value menu; portions are generous, spicing is superb and there are many layers of flavour. Sauces are memorable, sides add to the experience and the homemade kulfi is a must.

name: Bryn Williams at Porth Eirias
review: If you’re after a relaxed, friendly environment, this striking beachside brasserie with faux industrial styling, blue leather banquettes and stunning sea views is the place to come. The owner is proud of his Welsh roots and it shows on the menu. Cooking is pleasingly unfussy and local seafood is to the fore.

name: Hitchen's Barn
review: When their lease came to an end, the owners of the Berkeley Arms in Wymondham upped and moved to this pretty little stone barn. It has a shabby chic bar and a rustic dining room and is run by a bubbly young team. The appealing menu of modern British dishes is fiercely seasonal and can change up to twice a day.

name: The Square at Porthleven
review: In summer, bag a table on the terrace of this small harbourside bistro; in winter, cosy up and watch the waves crash on the harbour wall. Coffee and cakes give way to snacks and sharing platters, then to modern classics which fly the flag for Cornish produce. They have a deli and ice cream shop next door.

name: Kota
review: Welcoming harbourside granary with thick stone walls, a tiled floor and an array of wood furnishings; its name means ‘shellfish’ in Maori. Menus mix unfussy and more elaborate dishes and display subtle Asian influences courtesy of the owner’s Chinese and Malaysian background. Many of the ingredients are foraged. Bedrooms are simply furnished – one overlooks the harbour.

name: Bonnie Badger
review: Tom and Michaela Kitchin have created their version of a pub in an old coaching inn dating from 1836. The bar serves pub classics, the dining room offers dishes with a 'nature to plate' philosophy and, in the garden, dishes are cooked on a Big Green Egg. Super comfy bedrooms showcase Scottish designers.

name: Cat Inn
review: Popular with the locals and very much a village pub, with beamed ceilings, pewter tankards, open fires and plenty of cosy corners. Good value cooking focuses on tasty pub classics like locally smoked ham, egg and chips or steak, mushroom and ale pie. Service is friendly and efficient – and four tastefully decorated bedrooms complete the picture.

name: Galvin Green Man
review: A friendly team offer a warm welcome at this lovely pub. The original 14C building offers all the rustic charm you’d expect but there’s also a modern barn extension and riverside garden. Classic British dishes are carefully constructed and full of flavour; those cooked in the wood oven are their speciality.

name: Burnt Orange
review: This smart, stylish restaurant is open from lunch until late, and is the kind of place where you can just pop in for a few small plates or while away the whole evening with dinner and cocktails. Colourful Middle Eastern dishes make good use of the wood-burning oven and are designed for sharing.

name: Cin Cin
review: Cin Cin’s loyal band of customers come for its great value Italian food – a mix of homemade pastas and small plates, where fresh ingredients are simply cooked and natural flavours are allowed to shine. You can create a different experience every time you come by sitting in a different place: in front of the open kitchen, at the horseshoe counter, gazing out the window onto the street, or in the calmer rear room. There's also another branch in London.

name: Chilli Pickle
review: A laid-back restaurant with a buzzy vibe and friendly service. The passionate chef uses good quality ingredients to create authentic Indian dishes with vibrant colours and flavours. Go for a thali at lunch and a kebab, grill or curry at dinner. Beside the terrace they also have a cart selling street food.

name: Longs Arms
review: It’s hard not to like this handsome Bath stone pub, set opposite a medieval church in a sleepy village. It’s a family run affair with the chef-owner proudly preparing a mix of pub classics and few more modern creations. Be sure to try the home-smoked meats and fish and the delicious homemade ice creams.

name: Beckford Bottle Shop
review: It’s now a wine shop and bistro but the building was formerly a tea merchant’s and a grocer’s, and many period features remain, including an old cast-iron range in the intimate basement lounge. The atmosphere is relaxed, the creative small plates offer great value for money and the wine selection is extensive.

name: Skosh
review: This bright restaurant is located close to the 12C Micklegate Bar; sit at the counter to watch the action. ‘Skosh’ comes from the Japanese word meaning ‘small amount’; a reference to the small plates for which the restaurant is known. Many dishes have Asian influences; choose around 6 or 7 between two.

name: Rick Stein's Café
review: A deceptively large café hidden behind a tiny shop front. The concise, seasonally changing menu offers unfussy dishes which display influences from Thailand, Morocco and the Med. The homemade bread is worth a try, as is the good value set dinner menu. Bedrooms are comfy and simply furnished; have breakfast in the café or small courtyard garden.

name: Broad Chare
review: Housed within a converted warehouse by the quay, Broad Chare is a ‘proper’ pub, with a cosy bar serving appetising bar snacks and over 50 beers, and a rustic first floor dining room offering a more substantial menu of hearty, punchily flavoured dishes. Fair prices and a friendly team add to its appeal.

name: Route
review: This simple bistro sits on a steep city centre street that once formed the route from the castle to the quayside. It has a concrete floor, a breeze block wall and an open kitchen to the rear. Regularly changing menus offer well-priced, gutsy small plates with punchy flavours and a British heart.

name: Deanes at Queens
review: This bustling modern brasserie offers great value, day and night. Those after coffee and cake or a cocktail should make for the bar, while the terrace is a great spot on a sunny day. Refined modern dishes are full of flavour and blackboard specials add to the choice; the Mibrasa charcoal grill is a feature.

name: Plaquemine Lock
review: A unique and very colourful pub named after a small city in Louisiana and with a menu centred around Creole and Cajun traditions. Dishes like gumbo with okra, blackened chicken, and crawfish with corn and potatoes are carefully cooked and packed with flavour. Big Easy style cocktails add to the fun.

name: Bancone
review: It’s all about freshly made pasta at great prices – and all in the centre of town; the highlight is ‘silk handkerchiefs’ with walnut butter. Start by sharing some focaccia or panelle with smoked duck. As the name means ‘counter’ this is where most want to sit, although there are tables available.

name: Popolo
review: Skimmed concrete floors and exposed brick walls give this restaurant a utilitarian feel; sit at the counter and chat to the chefs as they work. Italian, Spanish and North African influences feature on the menu of small plates. Pasta is a highlight and classic, simply cooked dishes allow the ingredients to shine.

name: The Barbary
review: The challenge is to stop ordering: they are so many appealing dishes on the menu that the urge to try everything is hard to resist. The former Barbary Coast provides the inspiration; there’s grilling over coals, baking in the clay oven and some raw dishes too. The zinc-topped counter seats just 24.

name: Peckham Cellars
review: A neighbourhood bistro and wine bar run by three friends, all from this part of South-East London. The well-priced, original small plates are rustic yet refined and full of flavour. They’re made for sharing, so choose three or four per person or, if there’s a few of you, order the whole menu.

name: Westerns Laundry
review: Primeur’s sister is set in a former laundry and has a similarly industrial feel. Arrive early for drinks in the courtyard then sit at one of the communal tables or the kitchen counter. Rustic British dishes – chalked on the board daily – are full of flavour  and designed for sharing.

name: Brawn
review: The kind of place everyone needs in their neighbourhood: passionately run with a relaxed, upbeat vibe and serving good value, reliably tasty food alongside some interesting wines. The menu evolves with the seasons and dishes are hearty and boldly flavoured. Sit in the back room to enjoy the buzz from the kitchen.

name: Imad's Syrian Kitchen
review: The affable Imad was a restaurateur in Damascus before fleeing and settling in London, and his desire to provide and nourish is evident at this sweet restaurant. The appealing, great value menu focuses on Middle Eastern flavours. Expect generous sharing dishes and plenty of lamb – and don’t miss the falafel.

name: Sagrario Tradición
review: Located close to Real Madrid’s Santiago Bernabéu stadium, this restaurant aims to revive old traditions with a special focus on the cooking of Madrid but with an updated take on the region’s dishes. Its impressive display cabinet is teeming with different cuts of aged beef as well as poultry and pork, much of which is cooked on the grill. The à la carte here features a choice of daily suggestions as well as the restaurant’s signature dishes (Torreznos (fried bacon), Callos (tripe), Ancas de rana (frog’s legs) etc). If is a sunny day book a table on the pleasant terrace in the square!

name: Magnolia Café
review: With just four large communal tables, Magnolia is a simple, cosy spot enlivened by bold colours, vintage décor, and chandeliers. Their à la carte menu offers tasty, well presented fare from across Thailand. Dishes are distinguished by vivid, gutsy flavours; fried sun-dried squid with peanut sauce and fresh watermelon with desiccated salmon are exemplars. In lieu of a dessert menu, they serve lovely complimentary pandan pudding. Do visit their wine shop next door.

name: Sri Trat
review: If you’ve been to the coastal province of Trat on the border of Cambodia, you’ll doubtless recall its fiery seafood and curries. At Sri Trat, the owners bring the province’s famed cuisine to Bangkok via their mother’s favourite recipes. They also honour her, not only with a funky mural, but also by expertly crafting eastern dishes like savoury stir-fried tiger prawn with garlic, chilli, and fish sauce and spicy sea bass soup with salacca and shrimp paste.

name: Baan Landai
review: Don’t let the slightly unkempt exterior keep you from visiting Chef Landai’s eponymous restaurant, where he practises the craft he learned from his mother. The interior exudes charm with its eclectic adornments and window to the kitchen where chefs whip up pan-Thai dishes like flavourful pork ribs with red wine sauce (plus several veggie offerings). Pair with flower tea, mocktails, or cocktails, and finish with mung bean marzipan and egg yolk in coconut milk.

name: Coscolo
review: This delightful village is famous for its “Cocido Maragato”, a dish that for centuries has, against convention, been served here in reverse order (first the meat, then the chickpeas, followed by the soup at the end). At Coscolo, the special feature of this legendary recipe is that it is prepared with products that are smoked, cured and prepared on the property using ingredients sourced from the local area. To this stew the Navarra-born chef here likes to add tiny details that add even more personality, hence the change of name of the dish on the menu to that of his restaurant (“Cocido Coscolo”). Leave your car in the car park at the entrance to the village as only local residents are allowed to drive in.

name: El Chaleco
review: A restaurant with a good reputation, now run by the daughter of the previous owners, who has managed to maintain its essence but with a fresher and more modern perspective. In the attractive dining room, divided into two separate spaces, guests can savour French-inspired cuisine which is unusual for this area. The cooking is mainly focused around a single set-price menu, although this is complemented by several chef’s suggestions and the occasional special dish at a supplement. Keep your eye out for El Chaleco’s frequent themed menus (lobster, seafood special, anniversary, Belgian etc).

name: Casa Pedro
review: Named after its owner, the Casa Pedro has been taking orders for over 30 years, during which time it has developed the secret to ensuring its customers always leave happy, based around consistent and professional family-style service. Choose between the tapas bar at the entrance, where you can select from a varied daily menu, the more classically inspired dining room, or a slightly more contemporary private dining space. Traditional, market-inspired cooking of a very high quality, featuring a choice of cured and red meats, fish, seafood and seasonal vegetables, many of which come with a “media-ración” option.

name: Zabala
review: Zabala is situated in the district of Los Arquillos, popular with tourists, just a few metres away from the Plaza Mayor. Behind its attractive stone façade, you’ll find two highly distinct spaces: one, at street level, with a meticulous contemporary look that includes a striking wave-like wood decor; the other, upstairs, home to carefully appointed dining rooms, a private section, plus one room crowned by a large vaulted ceiling. The dishes on the traditional à la carte, prepared using ingredients of the finest quality, is embellished with the occasional contemporary touch. The set menu is only available on weekdays.

name: S.B.L.
review: After 50 years, this Chinese restaurant was remodelled by the second-generation owner who is keen to make every aspect of the dining experience pleasurable. The menu features mostly traditional Chinese fare with a few creations that show novel twists. Stewed fish maw in gravy and X.O. scallops are among the recommended items. Quality ingredients handled with skill and experience is the formula that guarantees a good meal here.

name: Saiyud and Doctor Sai Kitchen
review: Since 2004, Doctor Sai has been serving pan-Thai dishes, including royal fare, following recipes from her mother, Saiyud, a former cooking instructor, in a setting reminiscent of dining at home. Start with an elegant appetiser like fried prawns and peanuts in an egg net, flower dumplings, or deep-fried pork wrapped in egg noodles. By dessert – try the sweet potato in syrup – you’ll guess this home, with its warm service, belongs to a royal from a bygone era.

name: Kha Mu Boran (Kathu)
review: Rice with pork legs, braised until falling off the bones, with Thai kale and pickled mustard greens, may be common, but the version found at this 3-decade-old shop is head and shoulders above the average. Sipping broth comes with meaty bones to be gnawed on. Fans of innards will rejoice over the options.

name: Meena Rice Based Cuisine
review: Don’t be alarmed when you pass through a rice field driving here, as this hidden gem is worth it. As its name suggests, this alfresco restaurant specialises in rice, alongside new spins on Thai classics. Most are garnished with fruits and edible flowers, giving them bursts of colour. Along with the five-colour rice balls, northern-style spicy minced fish salad is a delight. Vegans will enjoy their many options, including the spicy stir-fried eryngii mushrooms.

name: Baannai
review: Baan Nai, or ‘inner house’ in Thai, is thus named because the owner’s great grandfather built it on the innermost part of his land. The house, and recipes cooked by its occupants, have passed down through the family to the present day where, as a boutique hotel and restaurant, it serves delicious time-tested dishes like Taengmo Pla Haeng (watermelon with dried fish flakes), Nam Prik Long Rua and Khanom Pra Paii (sweet mung bean dumplings). Booking is required.

name: La Mundana
review: Located in a residential neighbourhood in the Sants district, La Mundana is a former “vermutería” (vermouth bar) converted into a gastro-bar… and one that is always full! Here, chefs Alain Guiard and Marc Martin enjoy toying with flavours from around the world to create dishes with plenty of culinary personality and creativity, most notably through the flavours of the Mediterranean, France and Japan. In this relaxed atmosphere, with tables set close together and an open-view kitchen, choose from a menu designed for sharing, on which two “absolute musts” stand out: the Mundana “patatas bravas” and the Asian calamares. The extensive choice of vermouths is equally impressive.

name: Brandstätter
review: A real Salzburg institution! The atmosphere in the various dining areas is perfect for a cosy dinner, but in the summer, you might prefer to sit out on the gorgeous terrace. Traditional Austrian fare dominates the menu, but you will also find dishes that take their cue from the seasons or from global culinary trends. The service comes courtesy of an attentive and well-drilled front-of-house team. Good to know: You can buy house-made jams to take home.

name: Gasthof Auerhahn
review: Run with great dedication, this friendly, family-owned restaurant is located at a slight remove from the city centre, close to the train station, but it's well worth making the detour for the excellent food – their appealing range of dishes includes the delicious Topfenknödel (curd dumplings). Dine in the inviting interior or out on the beautiful verdant terrace. For overnight stays, there are pleasant, well-kept guestrooms.

name: Reinhartshuber Im Gwandhaus
review: The Gwandhaus in the Morzg district is a draw for more than just folk costume enthusiasts; this stately residence set in beautiful grounds also houses an elegant restaurant, where you can eat very well. A must is the chef-patron's Topfenschmarren (shredded pancakes)! His wife oversees the service front of house with plenty of typical Salzburg charm. Wonderful terrace with mountain views.

name: DiningRuhm
review: Housed in a corner building in Vienna's fourth district, this impressive restaurant is popular with fans of modern Japanese cuisine. In an inviting minimalist-style modern dining area, you can enjoy fusion cuisine characterised by Peruvian Nikkei influences, incorporating a touch of the Far East and a dash of creativity. There is also a good selection of sushi. Opt for one of the set menus or order à la carte.

name: MAST Weinbistro
review: Set in a historical town house, this trendy place is a winning combination of modern wine bar and upscale bistro. It is very popular for its great food, is made with seasonal ingredients sourced from local producers – and at fantastic value for money. Organic and biodynamic wines are recommended to accompany your choice of dishes. There is an appealing outdoor dining area, too.

name: Vestibül
review: With a penchant for seasonal and regional produce, this restaurant serves flavoursome culinary delights such as freshwater fish dishes or classics like Wiener schnitzel. The imposing historical building, which also houses the famous Burgtheater, makes for a unique location with a stylish interior that has a typically Viennese feel with its striking columns and gorgeous stuccowork.

name: Woracziczky
review: Diners are given a warm welcome In this pleasingly informal inn (pronounced "Vorashitsky"). Both its laid-back atmosphere and Viennese cuisine are a hit, with house specialities such as beef tartare with avocado, or Tafelspitz (boiled veal) served with a creamy chanterelle sauce. The reasonably priced lunchtime set menu, which changes daily, is especially popular.

name: Mochi
review: A lively, informal restaurant serving authentic Japanese cuisine with some more modern twists, at very moderate prices. You can watch the chefs at work, preparing sushi rolls, yakitori or gyu don. At lunchtime, the food is served in bowls; in the evening the presentation is a bit more elaborate. Tables are much sought after, so book early! No reservation possible at lunchtime.

name: Lok Kei Noodles
review: This busy shop next to the pier still kneads the noodles with a bamboo pole just like old times and the flavourful broth is simmered with an array of seasonal fish. The owner’s wife insists on making wonton wrappers and cooking noodles by herself and she’s very specific about both the cooking time and the consistency of the noodles. Other popular dishes include crab congee, tossed noodles with dried prawn roe, and deep-fried wontons with crispy dace balls.

name: Din Tai Fung (COD)
review: The second floor of COD plays host to a plethora of casual eateries – and in the corner you’ll find this sizeable branch of the international chain. Din Tai Fung is rightly known for its exquisite xiao long bao but also special here is the steamed crab roe and pork dumpling. Other notables from the 70-odd Shanghainese dishes on offer include the excellent braised beef noodle soup. To finish, try the red bean glutinous rice cake.

name: IFTM Educational Restaurant
review: Being part of the Institute for Tourism Studies means that while the head chef is a professional, some of his brigade and front of house team are students – and the pride they have in their work is palpable. The menu is a mix of European and Macanese dishes – presented in a modern style using herbs from their own garden. There’s even the occasional Scandinavian touch (they cure their own salmon). 3-course set menu and tasting menu are offered at night.

name: Chan Seng Kei
review: This semi open-air restaurant has stood next to an ancient church for over 70 years and the 3rd generation of the family still focus on traditional Cantonese cooking. Seafood is the highlight as the owner works closely with local fishermen to secure the best catch – he prefers wild-caught fish about 500 to 600g for their tender flesh. Also try stewed duck with tangerine peel which takes more than 10 hours to make, with only a few available each day.

name: O Castiço
review: Ownership of this simple, unassuming little place with just five tables has now passed down to the late owner's son – though his spirit is still honoured in the atmosphere of the restaurant, which is as friendly and as intimate as it ever was. The food is also just as good – the home-style dishes are authentic and carefully prepared, with recommendations being the stewed pork with clams and the oven-roasted bacalhau with potatoes.

name: Lou Kei (Fai Chi Kei)
review: If you’re looking for a simple, good value supper, then Lou Kei may well fit the bill. Granted, it may not be in the centre of town, but every local and cab driver knows this lively place. For over 20 years, its sizeable selection of tasty noodles, congee and Cantonese dishes have won the hearts of countless diners. Sizzling Bombay duck with sand ginger delivers amazing 'wok hei'. Frogs' legs in claypot and crab congee are both highly recommended.

name: Cheong Kei
review: A family business since the '70s, this noodle shop sticks to its roots and its thin, fine noodles are pressed by bamboo pole in its own factory nearby. Their soup is cooked with dried prawns and dried plaice for 8 hours. The noodles with dried shrimp roe are great, but also try their wontons and dace balls that are served deep-fried or blanched; the fermented clam sauce is the perfect accompaniment to the dace balls.

name: Good Hope Noodle
review: Founded in 1971, this noodle shop once had several branches in Mong Kok, but this is the only one left. Regulars flock here for the duck-egg noodles – made fresh daily with dough kneaded with a bamboo pole for extra bouncy texture, to be topped with prawn-and-pork wontons, zhajiang sauce or braised pork trotter. Congee and snacks are also recommended. You can also witness how the noodles are made in the show kitchen by the entrance.

name: Tim Ho Wan (North Point)
review: Diners have been coming in droves since the day this branch opened. The soberly furnished dining room is always packed so expect to see a queue outside at peak times. The atmosphere is typical of a local tea house and hums with general contentment. There are over 20 dim sum choices on the menu that changes monthly. Don’t miss the shrimp dumplings with springy filling enrobed in translucent skin. The famous crispy baked BBQ pork buns never disappoint.

name: Tak Kee
review: It started out as a street-side hawker stall in the 1990s and still retains the casual, vibrant vibe. The second-generation hands-on owner shops for groceries every day and sometimes helps the experienced chefs with kitchen chores. Pork tripe and peppercorn soup is a culinary highlight, using peppers from Malaysia and Indonesia. Regulars also come for its spiced marinated goose liver, crispy chitterlings stuffed with glutinous rice and oyster omelette.

name: Hao Tang Hao Mian (Tai Wai)
review: An owner-chef with over 20 years of experience in French cooking opened this 20-seater specialising in just 12 noodle soup items, each with a specific soup base and toppings. The signature flat noodles in beef soup with Sichuan beef cheek and French braised oxtail takes two days to make, involving eclectic techniques. The flavourful seafood potage with crab, prawns and scallops works surprisingly well with thin Chinese noodles.

name: Brass Spoon (Wan Chai)
review: Diners have been queuing up for the tasty pho here since Day 1. The chef learnt to cook in France, where his family had a Vietnamese restaurant, and has recreated the vibe of a little ramen shop in Tokyo here. He uses U.S. Angus beef and Danish pork and, for the noodles’ soup base, slow-cooks beef shank bone for more than 16 hours. On top of the signature raw beef variety, do order Vietnamese sausage, beef balls, tendon, or tripe.

name: Tai Wing Wah
review: This bright, fresh and long-standing Cantonese restaurant serves dim sum and ‘Walled Village’ cuisine, alongside assorted Cantonese classics. Walled village-style five-flavour chicken boasts flavoursome, velvety meat. Other specialities include roast duck with bean paste and coriander; claypot rice with lard, premium soy sauce, steamed mullet with salted lemon; and, above all, the steamed sponge cake. Also check out the seasonal menu.

name: Shugetsu Ramen (Quarry Bay)
review: The second branch of Shugetsu in Hong Kong also prides itself on freshly made noodles and the broth prepared with sardines, mackerel, kelp and soy sauce from a longstanding factory in Ehime. Tsukemen, thick noodles to be dipped into a sauce before eaten, is particularly popular. Besides the portion size, diners can choose between rich and light sauce; cold and hot noodles. Don’t miss the shrimp abura ramen, exclusively available at this branch.

name: Megan's Kitchen
review: The menu offers many Cantonese dishes, but steamed minced beef patty with dried mandarin peel, and Yu Xiang eggplant in claypot stand out in particular. Better still, all mains come with complimentary rice, soup and dessert. Their famous hot pots spoil diners with an array of soup bases and good quality ingredients. Those who prefer a little privacy will appreciate the booth seating with sliding screens as dividers.

name: Trusty Congee King (Wan Chai)
review: As suggested by its name, you can really trust the quality of the food served in this long-standing congee shop. The menu has become more versatile in recent years with congee, noodles and snack sets available. All congee is cooked in fish broth that gives an extra dimension of flavour. Many rave about the pork liver and scallop congee, sticky rice dumpling with salted egg yolk and pork, and poached grass carp skin.

name: Eng Kee Noodle Shop
review: This family-run shop has been feeding hungry locals with Cantonese noodle soup since 1994. It prides itself on its signature beef brisket – braised one night ahead and steeped in a spiced marinade overnight for silky tenderness and deep flavours. Their oven-grilled char siu is made with pork shoulder and pork neck and has a juicy, springy texture thanks to the fine marbling. The deep-fried wontons also earn unanimous praise.

name: Tai Woo
review: One of the district’s most famous names, Tai Woo moved to these more comfortable surroundings in 2011 and, while the restaurant may be smaller than before, business is better than ever, with over 1,000 customers served every day. What hasn’t changed is the quality of the service or the cooking – along with a menu of Cantonese seafood dishes, such as fish fried rice with ginger, are favourites like sesame chicken baked in salt.

name: Sing Kee
review: The second branch of Sing Kee is a bright, tidy spot serving traditional, no-frills Cantonese food – something that’s increasingly hard to find in Central. Standouts include pan-seared salted chicken, and grilled tiger prawns in Malaysian curry sauce with crispy rice crackers. Specialities like double-boiled fish maw and pork lung in almond milk need pre-ordering. Come at lunch to take advantage of some reasonable prices.

name: Wing Lai Yuen
review: Originally a run-down shop in a squatter village, it moved to this location in 2000 and had a major facelift. But one thing never changed – the food is as delicious and affordably priced as always. The signature Dan Dan noodles come in two versions: a meat one with ground pork and a traditional one without, plus a spicy or mild broth to choose from. Shuizhu mandarin fish, a secret menu item that packs numbing heat, is great to share with others.

name: Din Tai Fung (Silvercord)
review: From Mr Yang’s first shop in Taiwan in 1958 grew a multinational chain with branches in all major Asian cities. It’s famous for good service, competitive prices and listening to its customer’s feedback, but mostly for its xiao long bao made on the spot. Taiwanese chefs visit regularly to ensure the quality is maintained. Even the vinegar, free of artificial colours and preservatives, is shipped from Taiwan. Expect long queues at peak hours.

name: Ah Chun Shandong Dumpling
review: The shop has a traditional feel to it. Green wooden window frames on the wall are reminiscent of old-time Hong Kong. Dumplings are handmade daily and only the freshest ingredients are used in the fillings. Try their most-ordered item lamb and Peking scallion dumplings. Or surprise yourself with the specialty, such as mackerel dumplings and cuttlefish dumplings. Shandong roast lamb and meat pie are also recommended.

name: Eight Treasures
review: This noodle shop moved here from Hung Hom in 2018 and has a loyal following. Beef lovers adore its signature beef brisket in a tonic broth simmered with eight herbs (hence the name) and beef bones for over 10 hours.
